articles.title: GhostAction Attackers Plant Credential Stealer Disguised as Font in 94 GitHub Repositories
articles.text:
The threat actor behind the GhostAction supply chain attack has expanded beyond injecting malicious GitHub Actions workflows into compromised projects to phish open-source developers and deliver a stealer malware disguised within a fake font file.
The latest evolution, detailed by OpenSourceMalware, signals that the attackers are actively refining their modus operandi in response to steps taken by GitHub to prevent the workflow from running.
According to the threat intelligence platform, the threat actor registered the domain "my-github[.]com" and pointed it at "193.32.204[.]199," the same IP address that's used as an exfiltration endpoint for data harvested from running the malicious workflow.
The domain was registered on October 9, 2026, 17 days after "my-gitlab[.]com" was registered. There is no evidence at this stage to suggest that the two code-hosting-themed domains are operated by the same threat actor.
"It follows the same my-<code-host>.com naming pattern, making it a useful pivot, but current infrastructure does not directly connect it to GhostAction," security researcher Paul McCarty said. "They use different registrars, registrant records, Cloudflare nameserver pairs, IP addresses, ASNs, and DNS designs, and no shared certificate or account artifact has been recovered."
Since then, the "my-github[.]com" domain has been used in a phishing email impersonating a GitHub security alert to target an open-source maintainer. The message, sent from "noreply@my-github[.]com" and on the same day the domain was registered, warned of a suspicious new login to their GitHub account from Moscow, Russia, and instructed them to click on a link to secure their account.
The deceptive page, per OpenSourceMalware, is said to have acted as a reverse proxy, harvesting the victim's password and two-factor authentication (2FA) code, and injected JavaScript that authorized an OAuth app with permissions to modify their workflows so as to facilitate a GhostAction-style attack.
The fake login page also includes JavaScript to silently authorize a GitHub OAuth device flow with repo, workflow, and read:org scopes, granting it broad permissions to read/write repositories, modify Actions workflow files, and gain visibility into organization membership and related organizational data.
The idea is the same as device code phishing, where the end goal is to obtain an access token from GitHub and exfiltrate it to "my-github[.]com" on TCP/8443.
"The script receives a device code and user code, loads /login/device, extracts GitHub's forms from the returned HTML, and submits them automatically," McCarty explained. "It inserts the user code, locates an authorization form, adds authorize=1, and posts the approval through the victim's authenticated proxied session."
"The victim does not need to type the device code or consciously approve the OAuth application. This kit goes further by automating the user-code and authorization steps through the reverse-proxied session."
By stealing a repository-scoped OAuth token, it gives the attacker a reusable API credential. Furthermore, the permissions granted through the stealthy OAuth authorization are consistent with GhostAction's ability to enumerate repositories and inject malicious workflow files under ".github/workflows/."
"The actor can now combine repository-scale automation with individual social engineering against people whose accounts provide access to projects, organizations, registries, and downstream users," OpenSourceMalware said.
To make matters worse, the campaign has also been observed incorporating a second-stage component that persists on developer machines even after the malicious workflow has been removed.
Specifically, the approach takes a leaf out of North Korea's playbook by committing three different files -
- A Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) tasks.json file with a "runOn: folderOpen" trigger that causes it to run automatically when the folder is opened in the application.
- A "public/fonts/fa-solid-400.woff2" file that contains a stealer payload designed to harvest AWS keys, PyPI tokens, npm tokens, Git logins, Kubernetes cluster credentials, SSH private keys, and AI provider credentials for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini. The font file name is the same as one used in North Korea's Fake Font/PolinRider campaign from January 2026.
- A second GitHub Actions workflow that's activated if the infostealer never runs.
The VS Code task is set up to auto-run the credential stealer, which, besides collecting data, installs a cron job that runs attacker-supplied code every five minutes. The collected data is sent to the same server over plain HTTP on port 8080. A total of 94 compromised repositories with the second-stage component have been identified.
As for the second CI workflow, it's the same as the original malicious workflow, but with added credential formats to look for and a fallback that uploads findings to a secret GitHub gist if the POST fails. The second workflow goes by the following names -
- lint.yml
- ci-check.yml
- build-check.yml
- repo-health.yml
- audit.yml
- code-review.yml
- test-suite.yml
- cache-cleanup.yml
OpenSourceMalware said the 94 repositories belong to 66 owners, out of which 15 have since been deleted, renamed, or made private. Of the still accessible repositories, most of them appear to have been largely abandoned, with one of them left untouched for more than nine years. Sixty-five of the 79 repositories went without a commit for more than a year.
"Stage 1 needs GitHub to run the workflow," OpenSourceMalware said. "On October 9, GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running, and the waves on October 10 and 12 extracted no secrets. Stage 2 adds a launcher that doesn't need a runner at all, and it arrived six days after the block. We can’t say the block caused it. We can say the operator moved to a place GitHub's controls don't reach."
To mitigate the threat, developers should revoke GitHub access and tokens from a clean device, change their passwords, audit their repositories, rotate every credential the workflows can reach, and alert users who have cloned the repositories.
"We don't know who the operator is, but their work suggests limited experience," Jenn Gile, co-founder of OpenSourceMalware, told The Hacker News. "The stealer's environment-variable filter misses most API keys, its home-directory search can time out and discard its own results, and a single IP handles exfiltration, phishing, and noisy internet scanning. That last mistake is why searching for the IP still finds infections."

articles.title: Marshall Heston 120 : la finition Cream s'invite sur la barre de son haut de gamme
articles.text:
Marshall Heston 120 : la finition Cream s'invite sur la barre de son haut de gamme
Plus claire et résolument désirable, la finition Cream arrive le 20 octobre sur la Heston 120, la barre de son Dolby Atmos la plus ambitieuse de Marshall. De quoi transformer le modèle en véritable objet de design pour le salon, et l'occasion de revenir sur un produit qui revendique son esthétique autant que ses performances home cinéma.
Marshall a toujours puisé dans l'esthétique de ses amplis pour dessiner ses enceintes. La Heston 120 ne fait pas exception. Chez Marshall, une barre de son n'est jamais un simple accessoire de téléviseur : c'est un objet que l'on expose, au même titre qu'une guitare accrochée au mur ou qu'un ampli posé dans un coin du salon. Jusqu'ici réservée à une livrée noire, la barre de son s'offre une déclinaison Cream. Plus lumineuse, cette nouvelle finition ouvre la Heston 120 à des univers déco plus clairs et contemporains. Le reste de l'appareil, lui, ne change pas d'un hertz.
Une couleur qui modifie le statut de l'objet
La finition Cream fait plus que rafraîchir une fiche produit. Associée aux commandes physiques crantées et aux cadrans inspirés des amplificateurs maison, elle déplace la Heston 120 du côté du meuble assumé plutôt que de l'électronique que l'on cherche à masquer. Les habitués de la marque y retrouveront la grammaire visuelle des Stanmore et autres Woburn, transposée cette fois sous le téléviseur. Un parti pris esthétique qui vaut autant que ses arguments techniques, et que Marshall place désormais au centre de sa promesse.
Home cinéma : Dolby Atmos et configuration 5.1.2
Sous le capot, la Heston 120 aligne onze amplificateurs de classe D pour 150 watts, répartis sur une configuration 5.1.2 compatible Dolby Atmos et DTS:X. L'enjeu est clair : restituer une scène sonore en hauteur sans multiplier les enceintes dans la pièce. Deux subwoofers orientés vers l'arrière et quatre radiateurs passifs se chargent des basses, ce qui permet à la barre de se passer d'un caisson dédié dans la plupart des salons. Les plus exigeants pourront tout de même brancher un subwoofer actif via la sortie prévue à cet effet. Quatre modes d'écoute, dont un mode nuit et un mode voix, ajustent le rendu selon le contenu.
De l'écran éteint à la playlist
Marshall n'oublie pas que sa clientèle est d’abord composée de mélomanes intransigeants. Une fois le téléviseur en veille, la Heston 120 redevient une enceinte musicale à part entière, connectée en Wi-Fi 6 comme en Bluetooth 5.3 avec prise en charge d'Auracast. Spotify, TIDAL et le service de radios « airable » sont intégrés directement, AirPlay 2 et Google Cast complétant l'éventail fonctionnel. L'application Marshall autorise par ailleurs un réglage fin de l'égaliseur et un calibrage acoustique de la pièce. De quoi justifier une présence au salon toute la journée, et pas seulement pour les séances cinéma…
La finition Cream s'inscrit dans une gamme home cinéma désormais étoffée, aux côtés de la Heston 60, du caisson Sub 200 et de la Heston 120 noire. Plus compacte, la Heston 60 reprend le même ADN (configuration 5.1 Dolby Atmos, design signature Marshall et finition Cream) pour les salons plus modestes. Pour la découvrir en détail, rendez-vous sur la page produit officielle de la Heston 120.

articles.title: Es posible ir preso por hacer música con IA: descubre si es mito o riesgo real
articles.text:
La condena de Michael Smith, un hombre de 54 años residente en Carolina del Norte, reavivó una duda entre quienes usan herramientas de inteligencia artificial (IA) para componer o producir canciones: ¿hacer música con IA puede derivar en una sanción legal o incluso en una pena de prisión?
La respuesta depende del uso. Crear una obra con asistencia tecnológica no es, por sí solo, un delito. Smith fue condenado el 6 de octubre de 2026 a 18 meses de prisión por un esquema de fraude de reproducciones musicales.
La Fiscalía del Distrito Sur de Nueva York sostuvo que obtuvo más de 8 millones de dolares en regalías mediante cuentas falsas, programas automatizados y cientos de miles de canciones generadas con IA. Recibió dos años de libertad supervisada y una orden de decomiso por 8 millones de dólares.
Qué riesgos hay al componer una canción con IA
Componer una melodía, escribir una letra con apoyo de un sistema generativo o producir una base instrumental mediante IA no configura, de forma automática, un delito.
El riesgo aparece si el resultado reproduce una obra protegida sin permiso, suplanta la voz de una persona, utiliza datos personales de forma ilegítima o se integra en una maniobra de fraude.
La diferencia central está entre la herramienta y la conducta. La inteligencia artificial puede intervenir en la creación musical, pero no elimina las obligaciones sobre derechos de autor, contratos de plataformas, identificación de contenidos sintéticos y protección de la identidad de artistas o terceros.
Por qué una persona sí terminó condenada por usar IA en canciones
El caso no castigó la generación de música mediante IA, sino la obtención de regalías a través de reproducciones ficticias. Entre 2017 y 2024, Smith creó miles de cuentas falsas en Spotify, Amazon Music, Apple Music y YouTube Music. Luego usó programas para que esas cuentas reprodujeran continuamente canciones de su catálogo.
La Fiscalía estadounidense indicó que la operación llegó a utilizar hasta 10.000 cuentas automatizadas de manera simultánea. Smith distribuía la actividad entre miles de pistas para evitar alertas de fraude. En abril de 2023, sus cuentas acumularon 80,9 millones de reproducciones fraudulentas en YouTube Music mediante planes familiares.
Qué sucede si la IA copia una canción protegida por derechos de autor
En Colombia, la Ley 23 de 1982 y las reformas posteriores protegen los derechos patrimoniales de autor. El artículo 271 del Código Penal prevé penas de cuatro a ocho años de prisión para ciertas formas de explotación no autorizada de obras protegidas, con ánimo de lucro y perjuicio para los titulares de los derechos.
En Argentina, la Ley 11.723 contempla sanciones de un mes a seis años de prisión para quien edite, venda o reproduzca una obra sin autorización. La creación asistida por IA puede generar un conflicto si el resultado copia una canción identificable o partes sustanciales de una composición ajena.
En qué países se debe informar que un audio fue creado con IA
En España y el resto de la Unión Europea, el Reglamento de Inteligencia Artificial establece obligaciones de transparencia para determinados contenidos sintéticos.
Los sistemas que producen audio generado o manipulado deben incorporar marcas técnicas que permitan detectar su origen artificial. Quienes difundan un audio que constituya una suplantación sintética deben informar de manera clara que fue generado o alterado por IA.
La norma contempla una excepción parcial para obras artísticas, creativas, satíricas o de ficción. Aun en esos casos, debe revelarse la existencia del contenido manipulado de un modo que no afecte la experiencia de la obra.
La música creada totalmente por IA tiene derecho de autor: una duda común
No existe una regla internacional única que otorgue protección automática a una canción creada sin intervención humana. En buena parte de los sistemas jurídicos, el derecho de autor parte de una creación atribuible a una persona.
La utilización de IA tampoco habilita a apropiarse de obras ajenas ni a simular actividad comercial. El caso de Smith mostró que la sanción penal apareció cuando la música sintética fue parte de una estructura para falsear reproducciones y cobrar regalías.

articles.title: ECOVACS DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone robot vacuum mop review - sets a new cleaning standard - Tech Guide
articles.text:
VERDICT
The Ecovacs DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone has established a new standard for robot vacuum mops. It's an investment in the cleanliness and hygiene of your home.
PROS
- Easy to set up and get started
- Excellent suction
- Next-level mopping
- Can be left alone for weeks
CONS
- Expensive for some
- Did leave dust behind after crossing threshold
- 
		
				
			VERDICT
Robot vacuum mops have come a long way with Ecovacs leading the way with its DEEBOT range and the X12S OmniCyclone has taken cleaning and convenience to another level.
Tech Guide has been testing the Ecovacs Robotics DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone since shortly after it was unveiled at the IFA Show in Berlin in September.
Ecovacs has packed in plenty of features and upgrades into the X12S which has a new level of power that makes it an effective cleaner so you can get on with other things.
At our place we placed the X12S OmniCyclone station in the corner of our main living area.
This action alone speaks volumes about the look and design of the OmniCyclone station which has a sleek look with silver brushed metal accents.
Ecovacs has even thought to tint the clear dustbin to disguise the collected dust but still make it easy see how much dust is inside when you get closer.
The unit is 38cm wide and 49cm long which is a relatively small footprint for a device as powerful as this.
Set-up is simple through the Ecovacs app and the first step is connecting the robot to your wireless network and running any firmware upgrades.
What the robot needed to do next is map your home. It went off and scanned our floor plan on its own which is then shown in the app.
The AIVI 3D 4.0 technology did a great job creating the map but also is always on the lookout for any obstacles and steers around them.
The OmniCyclone Station is where the robot charges and includes a clean water tank and a tank where the dirty water will be transferred.
It’s also where the dust is transferred from the robot into the dustbin which can be easily emptied cleanly and conveniently into your garbage.
Now at our place, our floor is mainly tiles with a couple of carpeted rooms and a rug.
There is also a laundry and a small powder room, which have slightly higher thresholds the robot easily got up and over.
We did notice a couple of times the force of getting up and over the threshold left some dust behind.
Usually it picks this up on its way out but there was one occasion where we had to clean it ourselves.
The X12S OmniCyclone robot has a side brush, an anti-tangle main brush, along with an antibacterial filter and a roller that extends to reach in closer to skirting boards and under cabinets.
The OZMO ROLLER 3.0 has improved downward pressure (4000 Pa) and higher-speed (260 RPM) scrubbing which means stains don’t stand a chance.
And the roller lifts by 1.5cm and a smart roller cover clicks into place when it moves from hard floors to stay clear of carpets to them dry and avoid cross-contamination.
The unit also has 27,000 Pa blast suction which offers 53AW of suction power.
Now we know how powerful this suction is.
At IFA in Berlin we saw the X12S suck a 25kg ball up a tube so it had no issue vacuuming dust and debris off the hard floors and carpet at our place.
X12S also has FocusJet Stain technology which can pre-treat messes with extra water through the front jets shift more stubborn stains.
This needs to be enabled in the settings and includes a way to control exactly where in your home you would prefer a no-spray zone to protect furniture and other surfaces.
We left this on and it was remarkable how it could identify these areas and soak them ahead of a thorough clean with the roller.
We normally move chairs and clear the floor when we deploy the robot but the X12S OmniCyclone can find its way in and around your furniture quite deftly.
Through a combination of its side brushes and true edge extreme edge cleaning, the X12S did a tremendous job in getting into those hard-to-reach places as well as under and around furniture.
The X12S did a great job controlling water flow so there was never any residual water. It just left dry clean floors in its wake.
In terms of cleaning quality, the X12S has set a new standard.
The robots of the past were good at maintaining a level of cleanliness but the X12S really gets to work to get through the dirt and dust and stains effectively and leave you with a spotless home.
Our tiles were clean and shiny and it was easy to see just where the robot had traversed our carpets with the suction leaving definitive tracks just like a powerful stick vac would.
The robot would regularly return to the station to clean the roller and to transfer dirty water and replace it with clean water.
At the same time it was also recharging its battery to reduce interruptions and create more efficiency.
X12S can restore 13 per cent of the battery in just 3 minutes.
The DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone is a complete cleaning solution that does a great job with your carpets and hard floors without you having to lift a finger.
It is really easy to maintain and can run on its own for weeks at a time.
The unit is priced at $2,999 which is an investment – it’s an investment in your time.
It means you get your time back instead of spending it vacuuming and mopping your floors.
VERDICT
The Ecovacs DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone has established a new standard for robot vacuum mops. It’s an investment in the cleanliness and hygiene of your home.

articles.title: Databuddy Analytics raises $500,000 from Y Combinator
articles.text: US-based AI-powered analytics startup Databuddy Analytics has raised more than $560,000 in total funding, including $500,000 in Seed funding from Y Combinator, alongside investments from Maza Ventures and through the a16z Scout programme. Founded in 2026 by Palestinian entrepreneur Issa Nassar, Databuddy Analytics develops an AI-powered product analytics platform that helps businesses identify conversion drops, customer friction and product issues through automated investigations and actionable insights. The funding will support the development of more advanced AI investigation capabilities, additional integrations, targeted hiring and improved customer onboarding, as the company seeks to expand its user base. Press release: Databuddy Analytics, the AI-driven analytics platform, has raised $500,000 in Seed funding from Y Combinator as it launches its AI intelligence platform. With investment from Maza Ventures and through the a16z Scout programme, Databuddy has raised more than $560,000 to date. The company's new AI analytics platform investigates conversion drops, customer friction and product issues on a team's behalf and brings the findings to them. Unlike the traditional web analytics approach, the platform proactively shows what changed and why, without the need to dig through reports and filters. Databuddy has grown to serve more than 3,000 businesses in the first few months since launch. "Teams don't want more charts; they want to know what's broken and what to do about it," says Issa Nassar, Founder of Databuddy. "We built Databuddy so that the answer is one question away. Y Combinator's backing lets us move faster on that and put it in front of far more teams." Issa Nassar grew up in Palestine, started coding at age 11 and dropped out of university. He was accepted into Y Combinator at 20, becoming the youngest founder in the Middle East to be accepted into Silicon Valley’s iconic accelerator. Tambi Jalouqa, Managing Partner at Maza Ventures, shared, "Most founders start by explaining the market. Issa started by showing us what he had built. Databuddy is one of those products that looks deceptively simple, which is usually a sign that someone has spent a lot of time thinking about the problem. Issa has the combination we look for at Maza: he's deeply technical, moves unusually fast, and seems more interested in making something people want than in looking like a startup founder. Those are often the founders worth betting on early." The funding will support deeper AI investigation capabilities, additional integrations and targeted hiring. Databuddy will also invest in onboarding and migration support, helping more teams connect their existing data and put the platform to work.

articles.title: Après les violents pillages, pourquoi l’état d’urgence ne permettrait pas de bloquer les réseaux sociaux
articles.text:
Après les pillages du 17 octobre, certains, comme Bruno Retailleau, réclame l’état d’urgence et le gouvernement le garde en réserve. Ce régime d’exception issu d’une loi de 1955 permettrait surtout des mesures individuelles, mais pas de couper librement les réseaux sociaux.
Depuis les pillages qui ont suivi les manifestations du 17 octobre, l'état d'urgence s'est invité dans de nombreuses conversations, des plateaux télé aux fils d'actualité, aussi bien c'est ceux qui réclament son instauration que ceux qui le vilipendent. Le gouvernement de Sébastien Lecornu a préféré miser lundi soir des couvre-feux localisés à Paris, Lyon ou Lille, tout en gardant le régime d'exception sous le coude « si c'est nécessaire ». Entre la loi de 1955, la jurisprudence du Conseil d’État sur TikTok et le règlement européen DSA sur le services numériques, les marges de manœuvre de l’exécutif sont pourtant plus étroites qu’il n’y paraît.
L'état d’urgence, un pouvoir d’exception, pas un chèque en blanc
Cette fameuse loi de 1955, justement, mérite qu'on s'y arrête. Votée le 3 avril 1955, en pleine guerre d'Algérie, elle a donné naissance à un régime d'exception que la Constitution ne mentionne même pas, et qui ne peut être déclenché qu'en cas de péril imminent lié à des atteintes graves à l'ordre public. Le président le décrète en conseil des ministres, pour douze jours maximum. Au-delà, seul le Parlement peut le prolonger par une loi, qui devient caduque quinze jours après une démission du gouvernement ou une dissolution de l'Assemblée. Dimanche soir, dans son allocution, Emmanuel Macron s'est bien gardé de franchir le pas, pour le moment.
Les couvre-feux instaurés lundi soir, eux, s'en passent très bien. À Paris, la place de la République et une partie des Halles étaient concernées de 23 heures à 6 heures. Un hélicoptère rodait d'ailleurs dans le ciel de la Capitale. À Lyon, c'était une partie de la Presqu'île dès 21 heures. Dans le Nord, l'arrêté préfectoral vise les mineurs non accompagnés, même si Denain a étendu la mesure aux adultes. Les préfets et maires disposent déjà de ce levier, à condition qu'il reste limité dans le temps et l'espace. Pour Antoine Fouret, avocat associé au cabinet Nausica Avocats, l'apport de l'état d'urgence se joue ailleurs, à savoir dans les mesures qui visent des personnes précises. Il s'agit de l'assignation à résidence, de l'interdiction de séjour dans un périmètre et, si le décret ou la loi le prévoit, des perquisitions administratives sans feu vert préalable d'un juge. Le changement est bien réel, car en temps normal, le droit commun ne prévoit même pas d'interdiction administrative de manifester visant un individu.
Les sanctions, elles aussi, changent d'échelle. Braver un couvre-feu décrété sous état d'urgence peut coûter jusqu'à six mois de prison et 7 500 euros d'amende, contre une simple contravention en temps normal. Il permet en outre de dissoudre des groupements impliqués dans les violences, et ces dissolutions survivent à la fin du dispositif. Chaque décision reste toutefois contestable devant le juge administratif, souvent en 48 heures. Elle doit reposer sur le comportement de la personne visée, pas sur ses convictions. La France a d'ailleurs été condamnée en 2024 par la Cour européenne des droits de l'homme pour une assignation à résidence prononcée en 2015. « Régime d'exception, l'état d'urgence n'en demeure pas moins un régime de droit », rappelle maître Antoine Fouret. Mais qu'en est-il des réseaux sociaux ?
Le précédent calédonien plane sur le blocage des réseaux sociaux
Couper ou brider les réseaux sociaux est presque un vieux serpent de mer de notre ère moderne, comme la remise en cause du chiffrement des communications d'ailleurs. Sur la radio RTL, Gabriel Attal, candidat Renaissance à la présidentielle, a plaidé pour un blocage « temporaire, ciblé » des réseaux sociaux, limité aux territoires touchés par les émeutes, comme nous le racontions ce matin. Il reproche à ces plateformes de rassembler les casseurs et d'entretenir un effet de meute. L'ancien Premier ministre connaît le sujet, puisque c'est lui qui avait fait couper TikTok en Nouvelle-Calédonie en 2024. Mais l'état d'urgence ne lui offrirait pas ce pouvoir, souligne Antoine Fouret. La loi de 1955 autorise bien le ministre de l'Intérieur à suspendre un site ou un réseau social, mais dans un seul cas : lorsqu'il pousse à commettre des actes terroristes ou en fait l'apologie. Un appel au pillage, aussi choquant soit-il, ne relève pas du terrorisme et n'entre donc a priori pas dans cette case.
Il y a toutefois le cas des circonstances exceptionnelles. Le Conseil d'État l'a balisée en avril 2025, en jugeant le blocage de TikTok décidé en Nouvelle-Calédonie en mai 2024. Une coupure n'est admise que si elle est indispensable face à des événements d'une particulière gravité, sans alternative technique moins intrusive, et pour une durée limitée. Décidée sans échéance, celle de l'archipel a été jugée illégale. La plupart des géants visés relèvent en outre du règlement européen DSA, dont l'application revient à la Commission européenne. Le gouvernement prévoit, lui, une visioconférence avec les plateformes, invitées à modérer les contenus.
Juridiquement, rien n'interdit de dégainer l'état d'urgence face à des violences urbaines. La France l'a fait en 2005, puis en Nouvelle-Calédonie en 2024, mais pas pendant les Gilets jaunes. Encore faut-il démontrer un risque sérieux que les violences se répètent, insiste l'avocat. Bruno Retailleau, lui, réclame « l'état d'urgence maintenant, sans attendre le couvre-feu ».
En attendant, la traque des pilleurs se poursuit surtout devant des écrans. Les enquêteurs épluchent les images de vidéosurveillance, mais aussi les vidéos publiées sur les réseaux sociaux, où certains se sont eux-mêmes filmés en plein pillage, comme nous l'expliquions. L'autre dossier, c'est celui des objets volés ont été remis en vente sur Vinted ou Leboncoin dans les heures qui ont suivi. Le gouvernement a réuni ces plateformes, qui viennent de s'engager à « transmettre régulièrement aux autorités un bilan chiffré des actions de retrait des annonces problématiques, des mesures mises en œuvre, ainsi que des signalements transmis aux autorités, avec un premier retour attendu sous 48 heures », comme l'a déclaré le gouvernement ce mardi 20 octobre.

articles.title: When the model takes away the moat
articles.text:
When the model takes away the moat
The need to democratize AI model ownership
There has been an explosion of AI-powered products released over the past four years, with most built on top of leading foundation models. Startups, enterprise software vendors, and even large incumbents route their core intelligence through APIs from the leading AI labs, and a growing but still narrow set of open-weight alternatives.
CEO and co-founder of Boltzbit.
This arrangement has most certainly enabled a genuine burst of AI products, but it has also created a structural fragility which can be remedied through the democratization of model creation and training.
Defining a wrapper
In its simplest form, an AI wrapper is a product whose core function is an interface sitting on top of a third-party foundation model's API, with little to no proprietary technology beneath that layer.
That approach can have a short lifespan and Jasper can illustrate that. Once the standout of the AI writing boom with a $1.5 billion peak valuation, Jasper saw its core market vaporized when ChatGPT introduced free, native writing features. Its revenue fell from approximately $120 million in 2023 to approximately $55 million in 2024. Jasper did survive, by redirecting its efforts toward enterprise workflows and brand-specific training.
Generally speaking, analysis shows that, among AI startups that have wound down in the US in 2025, 81% were "wrappers and apps". Copilots and assistants layered on foundation models, AI productivity tools, content generators, and vertical SaaS products whose core differentiation was an LLM front-end rather than proprietary data or infrastructure.
In Jasper’s case, and in many others, what pressured the company wasn't a competitor out-executing them. It was the platform they built on top of simply absorbing the feature they'd built their company around.
Not all wrappers are equal
It would be a gross generalization to say that all AI wrappers are the same. A thin prompt-and-display wrapper is different from a product that does heavy retrieval, tool orchestration, agentic workflows, or domain-specific fine-tuning. The latter can have real defensibility even while sitting on top of a third-party base model. The model call is one component, but certainly not the whole product.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Some companies also use multiple foundation models or fine-tune/distill their own smaller models for specific tasks after prototyping on a frontier API. Open-weight models add variety too as not all wrappers call a closed-source frontier model.
The wrapper problem
Regardless of where an AI product sits on the wrapper complexity scale, they all share the same problem. When a company's core value proposition depends entirely on an API call to a third party, that company does not fully control its own product.
It cannot control pricing changes, rate limits, deprecations, shifts in model behavior, or the possibility that the platform provider decides to compete directly in the same vertical.
This is not a theoretical risk, though how much it affects any given company likely depends on how much of its value sits above the model layer.
The economics of the wrapper
So what is the defensibility of an AI wrapper in practice?
The short answer is that it comes down to intellectual property.
Where a company benefits from an existing distribution advantage, established customer relationships, regulatory licensing, network effects, or years of accumulated brand trust, model-layer differentiation may not matter as much. But if what makes a wrapper distinctive is observable from outside the organization and replicable by a competent competitor within a limited period, it seems reasonable to expect it will eventually be replicated.
That is the unfortunate economic truth beneath the wrapper model. The cost of replication is near zero for the platform that controls the underlying model, and near total for the startup that doesn't. A wrapper's moat, if it has one, has to come from something other than the model call itself. Absent those, a wrapper is unlikely to have a lasting competitive advantage.
The barrier to the solution
At this point, you might be inclined to agree that model ownership is one solution to this problem. But that's easier said than done.
The reason so few companies own their models is not a lack of desire. It’s, more plausibly, financial. Training a frontier-competitive model requires enormous compute budgets, specialized talent, proprietary or expensively licensed data pipelines, and the infrastructure to run reinforcement learning at scale. These costs put model creation out of reach for all but the best-funded companies.
For companies to build on their own models as a norm, this barrier has to fall meaningfully. Several forces are already pushing in this direction, open-weight models being one of them. But even then, hosting and fine-tuning an open-weight model is no small task. It still demands technical talent and compute infrastructure most startups don't have access to.
True democratization of model ownership
Democratization, in this context, doesn't mean every company training a frontier-scale model from scratch. That goal is neither realistic nor necessary. It means democratization reaching the training layer the same way access to AI has been democratized for end users.
Democratizing model training and ownership could be what gives founders a lasting chance at turning an idea into a business that doesn't eventually get absorbed by a model provider as a simple feature. And if that happens, the stakes may go beyond individual business durability.
As things stand, access to models is cheap. Access to training is not. This needs to change. The ability to train an AI model should be fully democratized so that the value, the control, and the responsibility can be distributed rather than centralized.

articles.title: Microsoft's Bing Wallpaper App Hijacks Desktop Clicks to Promote Bing.com
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 20th 2026
Microsoft's Bing Wallpaper App Hijacks Desktop Clicks to Promote Bing.com
Microsoft's popular wallpaper application, Bing Wallpaper, has now been transformed into adware, according to a new report by Windows Latest. When a user clicks on an empty area of the desktop—not on any icon or menu—the application redirects them to Bing.com, Microsoft's search engine. Normally, this behavior would not be acceptable and would likely trigger a strong reaction from the community. However, Microsoft has limited this issue to occur only once every 24 hours. Repeated clicks after the initial activation do not open another browser window. Testing has confirmed that this behavior persists after the waiting period, even when Google Chrome is set as the default browser.
Interestingly, Microsoft tested a similar feature in 2025, which included a clearly labeled setting in Bing Wallpaper that allowed a desktop click to open Bing. At that time, the feature could be turned off, but this option is not available in the latest version of the application. Microsoft has removed the ability to disable this feature, meaning that every 24 hours, a desktop click will redirect to Bing.com. This change leaves users with less control over an action that is unrelated to managing wallpaper. The application has also reportedly displayed prompts encouraging users to make Bing their default search engine across installed browsers, even when the default browser is Google Chrome or another non-Microsoft browser.The only way to avoid this random redirect behavior is by choosing a different application to manage desktop wallpapers. For those who still want rotating Bing imagery due to its wide selection of images from around the world, Windows Spotlight is an option to consider. However, a third-party application might be the best choice, as it may only be a matter of time before Microsoft implements something similar in Windows Spotlight as well.
Source:

articles.title: Francis Ford Coppola y Carl Lewis estarán en el World Business Forum Bogotá 2026
articles.text:
El World Business Forum Bogotá 2026 reunirá a Francis Ford Coppola, Carl Lewis y otros seis conferencistas el 28 y 29 de octubre de 2026. El director de cine hablará sobre las similitudes de la dirección de una película con una empresa y el rol de la IA, mientras el exatleta hablará de la fortaleza mental.
La programación prevé la participación de referentes del cine, el deporte, la academia y la consultoría empresarial. Sumado a Coppola y Lewis, estarán Renée Mauborgne, Rita McGrath, Tricia Wang, Scott Anthony, Pilar Jericó y Efrén Martínez.
De qué hablará Francis Ford Coppola en Bogotá
Francis Ford Coppola, director, productor y guionista de películas como El Padrino y Apocalypse Now, participará en una sesión moderada. Según Martha Lucía Maldonado, country manager de WOBI Colombia, “el cineasta abordará la creatividad y establecerá la relación entre la dirección de una película y la conducción de una empresa”.
La conversación incluirá asuntos como la gestión de la incertidumbre, el desarrollo de talento y el uso de las narrativas para movilizar grupos de trabajo dentro de una organización.
Por qué la inteligencia artificial puede ser clave en la charla con Coppola
La relación entre inteligencia artificial y cine aparecerá como uno de los asuntos posibles de la conversación con Coppola. Maldonado indicó que el formato de entrevista permitirá abordar la discusión sobre el uso de estas herramientas en la producción audiovisual y su impacto sobre la creatividad.
La intervención del realizador ocurrirá en un momento de debate en la industria audiovisual sobre la utilización de sistemas generativos para tareas de escritura, efectos visuales y producción. “Todo el mundo habla de que se debe mantener ese valor humano del director director de cine guiando la película”, afirmó Maldonado.
Sin embargo, Coppola no ofrecerá una conferencia técnica sobre IA. Su participación se concentrará en creatividad, aunque el diálogo podrá incorporar preguntas sobre los límites, posibilidades y decisiones humanas detrás de las herramientas tecnológicas.
Qué mensaje compartirá Carl Lewis sobre motivación
El exatleta estadounidense Carl Lewis, ganador de 10 medallas olímpicas, nueve de ellas de oro, hablará de fortaleza mental, presión competitiva y rendimiento sostenido. Su presentación trasladará al ámbito empresarial algunas experiencias de su carrera deportiva, marcada por ocho títulos mundiales.
Maldonado señaló que Lewis se enfocará en “cómo mantener esa mentalidad de ‘yo sí puedo’” incluso en momentos adversos. El deportista expondrá su visión sobre la disciplina necesaria para sostener objetivos a largo plazo y la capacidad de buscar nuevos resultados después de haber alcanzado metas relevantes.
La participación de Lewis se integrará al eje de desarrollo personal. En este apartado, se propone tratar la resiliencia, el propósito, la autogestión y el bienestar como factores vinculados con la capacidad de las organizaciones para afrontar cambios y escenarios de presión.
Cuáles invitados abordarán la IA aplicada a las empresas
La especialista Tricia Wang, directora ejecutiva de Advanced AI Society y asesora de compañías incluidas en la lista Fortune 500, expondrá sobre inteligencia artificial, datos y conocimiento humano. Su intervención se centrará en la implementación de estas tecnologías dentro de las empresas y en su incidencia sobre la toma de decisiones.
Maldonado indicó que Wang hablará del “liderazgo humano en la era de la inteligencia artificial”. Planteará cómo preparar sistemas y agentes de IA para que operen dentro de parámetros definidos por las organizaciones, con énfasis en el criterio humano que debe orientar su uso.
Asimismo, el tema estará presente en las intervenciones de Rita McGrath, profesora de Columbia Business School, y Renée Mauborgne, coautora de Blue Ocean Strategy.
McGrath tratará los cambios en la competencia y el crecimiento en ambientes de aceleración tecnológica, mientras que Mauborgne analizará estrategias para identificar mercados y oportunidades fuera de la competencia convencional.
En el mismo evento habrán intervenciones de Scott Anthony, profesor de estrategia de Tuck School of Business, sobre disrupción y tecnologías emergentes; Pilar Jericó, especialista en liderazgo y gestión del talento; y el psicólogo Efrén Martínez, quien se referirá a propósito, resiliencia y autogestión.

articles.title: Why AI is upending traditional technology pricing
articles.text:
Why AI is upending traditional technology pricing
AI is breaking the link between effort, cost and value
You don't need to understand the mechanics of AI tools to understand what's happening to traditional technology pricing. AI is breaking the link between effort, cost and value that technology services have relied on for decades.
Imagine two managed service providers responding to the same production incident. One assigns an engineer who spends five hours tracing logs, checking dependencies and isolating the root cause.
The other uses AI-enabled observability to identify the issue in minutes, trigger the appropriate remediation and restore service before users notice. The second provider used fewer hours but delivered more value. Should they be paid less?
Senior Vice-President, Global Business Engineering, CGI.
Enterprise technology services are running into the same pricing challenge, but on a larger scale. The old pricing model equated more hours with higher cost and, in theory, greater value. But today, AI is enabling organizations to move from reactive support to self-healing operations. In our own client engagements, we're seeing auto-generated tickets fall by as much as 70%, roughly one in five operational events resolved autonomously, and up to 45% fewer major outages where predictive models are in place.
That should translate into straightforward cost savings, but the reality that CIOs and CFOs are grappling with is more complicated. AI can deliver the same or greater value, with significantly less effort, which undercuts the assumptions behind what they are paying for. Managed services providers are facing the inverse of this same problem: How do you price services when the traditional relationship between effort, cost and value no longer holds?
Increasingly, predictability is replacing capability as the bigger challenge to address.
What senior leaders are saying about AI
The challenges of identifying the right AI use cases are coming up in conversation after conversation with CXOs and increasingly with business leaders beyond IT. Leaders of all kinds are recognizing that a successful AI program begins with an operational problem, and the sophistication of the AI needs to be matched to the scale of that problem.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
That also means organizations must be willing to redesign their operations around what AI makes possible. Only then can clients and providers have a meaningful conversation about value and how to price it. For example, one enterprise client's finance team was struggling to get a single, accurate view of its cash position across dozens of markets and currencies.
Each region had recorded the same transactions differently for years, and leadership had spent more than five years trying to standardize the process without success. Before this, there was no credible baseline for measuring improvement, making it nearly impossible to agree on the value AI was expected to create.
A client’s business operations are often just as unsettled as the technology helping run them. The contracts holding the two together were built for a past world with more predictable staffing, fixed scope and stable demand.
There is no one right pricing model
The natural response to this uncertainty is to look for a new pricing model to replace the old one. But no single model solves the problem. Outcome-based, consumption-based, and AI-enabled pricing approaches each have advantages in the right circumstances and introduce new trade-offs. The challenge lies in creating enough flexibility to operate when effort, cost and demand no longer move predictably.
Outcome-based pricing works well when a result can be clearly defined and attributed. That gets much harder once AI-driven workflows start feeding into one another, making it difficult to trace which system or step contributed to a business result several automated stages downstream.
Consumption-based pricing ties cost to usage, which sounds fair until you run into the token paradox. While the price of a single AI query keeps falling, total spend keeps climbing anyway, because usage is no longer limited to one person typing one prompt. It's chains of AI agents running continuously in the background, each step triggering the next and including its own line item.
Take a lesson from a banking client running a 20-developer modernization program. Token costs per developer had climbed to roughly $1,000 a month. The team reduced that to $200 by routing simple work to lower-cost models, identifying usage patterns where token consumption was four times higher than the team average, and using deterministic automation for repetitive tasks where AI wasn't needed.
Gain-sharing models sound intriguing because the provider takes on more risk in exchange for a share of the outcome. However, they can become difficult to manage when both parties disagree about which improvements resulted from the provider’s work and how much credit each side deserves.
Why pricing flexibility is vital
These pricing models each assume either effort, cost or demand will remain predictable enough to price against. Increasingly, that is not the case.
While the market has not settled on a single approach, we believe hybrid structures have the greatest potential to become the preferred commercial model for AI-enabled managed services. A hybrid model combines a predictable base fee for core services, a variable component tied to AI consumption and outcome-based incentives where results can be accurately measured.
For CIOs, this approach provides greater budget predictability while offering some protection against consumption spikes. For providers, it helps manage AI consumption volatility while creating incentives for efficiency, continuous improvement and value creation.
Designing partnerships for uncertainty
The goal was never to find the perfect pricing model for AI, but rather to build commercial structures that can flex when conditions change again. That starts with determining clear baselines before any gain-share or outcome-based conversation begins.
It continues by intentionally building in scheduled points to recalibrate scope and pricing instead of being locked into the traditional three-year contract. Transparency around performance, costs, governance and AI outcomes also needs to be prioritized so that both sides trust the numbers.
We are still in the early innings of figuring this out. But it’s clear that AI is changing the role of the technology partner, from delivering capacity to helping enterprises manage uncertainty and accelerate business outcomes. Enterprises must build enough flexibility into their pricing models to adapt as the technology, demand and value equation changes.
While no one can perfectly price the future, we can design commercial models that evolve alongside the technology and the value it creates.

articles.title: From Email-to-Case to the Boardroom: How Inherited Agents Break Governance Built for Software
articles.text:
In Salesforce Agentforce, the recommended way to make an agent respond to events is a Flow: a record is created or a case is updated, and the Flow passes data into the agent's prompt. Separately, Email-to-Case and Web-to-Case turn inbound customer messages into case records; it is how airlines and hotels run support intake. Both are standard, documented, as-designed features. Chained together, they produce this path:
public internet → email → case record → agent prompt → agent action → case comment → outbound reply
An unauthenticated outsider now has a route into an internal agent's instructions, and the agent's reply leaves through the same door. Nothing was misconfigured. The finding, documented by researchers in August 2026, is a clean example of how agents that arrive inside existing platforms fail: through the application around them, not the model inside them.
The risk is in the application, and the application is the thing nobody re-reviewed
Which intake features are enabled, which triggers fire, which objects are exposed to guest users, which automation passes untrusted data where, and which model version the agent is quietly calling underneath: these are the variables that decide whether the Agentforce chain is a support-queue nuisance or a data exposure. A vendor risk review performed once at procurement sees none of them, because the agent did not exist at procurement. A prompt filter watching the agent's inputs does not know that a particular input originated from a stranger, because prompt filters do not understand Email-to-Case.
Securing an inherited agent therefore means understanding its host application at the depth its own admins do. That depth is the one thing a questionnaire and a scanner both lack. The City-Forum campaign, an active worldwide data-theft operation against Salesforce and ServiceNow instances running since March 2025, was found in exactly this territory: the gap between platform features and the configurations enterprises actually run.
Builders are multiplying, and some of them are agents
The platforms have made agent creation as accessible as making a slide deck. Marketing operations builds an agent to pull pipeline reports. Finance builds one to reconcile invoices. Each rides its creator's permissions, because that is what makes it useful. Shadow AI was an employee pasting data into a chatbot. Shadow agents are that employee's access, running unattended, multiplied across everything they were ever granted.
Increasingly, agents also build agents. A coding agent tagged into a chat channel can scaffold and deploy another agent as easily as it opens a pull request; an orchestration platform spins up sub-agents to divide a task, each with its own connections and none with its own review. Any governance model that assumes a human requested each agent is quietly obsolete.
Why governance keeps producing a document
Ask a large enterprise about agent governance and the answer is usually a document: an acceptable-use policy, a monthly committee, a set of principles nobody disputes and nothing enforces. Ask the operational question, how many agents are running right now, what can they reach, and who owns each one, and the document does not know.
The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 now describes the sharpest version of this gap under its "No Governance" category: a skill deployed and managed inside a third-party platform is unreachable by external scanners (OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 whitepaper, ast10-top10-whitepaper-2, published at owasp.github.io). The tools an enterprise points at the problem from outside cannot see inside the venues where most agents live. Governance fails most often because the rules get written before the security team can see the things the rules apply to.
The stack, bottom-up, with a test for each layer
The working order is bottom-up, and each layer is the precondition for the one above it. A practical way to check whether a program is real is to apply an operational test at each level.
| Layer | What it has to produce | The operational test | 
| Discovery | A continuously refreshed population across app configs, OAuth grants, network, endpoint, email metadata, and browser | Is the discovered count several multiples of the list IT keeps? If not, discovery isn't reaching where agents live. | 
| Posture | Every platform's agent-relevant settings, measured against how they should be configured | Can the team list the intake features and guest-user exposures wired to agent triggers on its top three platforms? | 
| Identity and ownership | An identity and a named owner per agent, with a lifecycle | Pick an agent at random. Does a human raise a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?" | 
| Usage | Who is building what, through which surface, with what data | Is there a sanctioned path that ships a business team's agent with secure defaults, or only a block? | 
| Agent controls | Least privilege against observed need, approval and quarantine for new agents, risk tiering that reflects each agent's full context | Does the same finding on a sandboxed dev agent and a customer-facing one show different severities? | 
| Runtime | Live inspection and intervention | Is it fed by the five layers above, or deployed first and enforcing blind? | 
The cost of paper compliance
The EU AI Act's penalties carry GDPR-level weight: up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited practices, up to €15 million or 3% for other violations. Every framework converging on it assumes the stack above exists. GDPR already showed what happens when it does not. British Airways (£20 million) and Marriott (£18.4 million) were not fined for having imperfect policies. Everyone has imperfect policies. They were fined because compliance existed on paper and could not be evidenced operationally when regulators asked. A governance practice built bottom-up generates that evidence as a byproduct: the inventory, the owners, the configurations, the review history.
Some platforms are designed to produce exactly that record. One leading example is Reco, which discovers agents across multiple vantage points, including the ones that never touch SSO, and assigns each a risk profile before any policy can be applied to it.
The Agentforce chain at the top of this article is not an exploit. It is a configuration, and configurations are governable, provided someone can see them. Chapters 1 to 3 of Into the Expanse cover the shift, the three launch vectors, and the governance practice in full: https://www.reco.ai/agent-ecosystem-security

articles.title: Dans les coulisses des tournages de Top Gun: Maverick et F1, l’épisode 3 de Color Matters est arrivé
articles.text:
Dans les coulisses des tournages de Top Gun: Maverick et F1, l’épisode 3 de Color Matters est arrivé
Comment conserver des couleurs fidèles lorsque les images d’un film proviennent de dizaines de caméras différentes ? Le troisième épisode de Color Matters nous plonge dans les coulisses de Top Gun: Maverick, The Phoenician Scheme et F1, avec un spécialiste de l’image hollywoodienne.
La troisième saison de Color Matters – Masters of Color se poursuit avec un nouvel épisode consacré à John Quartel, responsable de l'Imaging Science chez Company 3. Après avoir découvert le travail des coloristes et leurs choix artistiques dans les épisodes 1 et 2, cette nouvelle vidéo s'intéresse à la science qui se cache derrière les images des plus grandes productions hollywoodiennes.
De Top Gun: Maverick à F1
John Quartel explique notamment comment la science de l'image repose sur trois dimensions essentielles : la couleur, l'espace et le temps. Autant de paramètres qu'il faut maîtriser pour préserver les intentions du réalisateur, depuis le tournage jusqu'à la diffusion du film.
Il revient sur les défis techniques rencontrés sur Top Gun: Maverick, où les équipes ont dû intégrer plusieurs caméras dans les cockpits des avions de chasse. Chaque caméra possédant ses propres caractéristiques colorimétriques, il a fallu harmoniser les images pour obtenir un rendu cohérent.
Même problématique sur F1, avec des volumes considérables de séquences filmées par les caméras embarquées. John Quartel évoque également sa collaboration avec Wes Anderson et l'importance de certains cadrages pour distinguer les époques d'un récit.

articles.title: Une mission révolutionnaire : mais que va faire le rover français IDEFIX sur la lune de Mars, au juste ?
articles.text:
Le Japon vient de lancer MMX, une mission inédite pour ramener sur Terre des morceaux de Phobos, l’une des deux lunes de Mars. À son bord, le petit rover franco-allemand, IDEFIX, jouera un rôle crucial.
Mars n’est pas seule : notre voisine est accompagnée de deux petites lunes, Phobos et Deimos. Découvertes en 1877 par l’astronome américain Asaph Hall, elles ressemblent à deux gros cailloux difformes, souvent comparés à des pommes de terre.
Phobos, la plus grande, mesure environ 22 kilomètres de large. Et elle se rapproche inexorablement de Mars et finira, dans 50 millions d’années, par s’écraser sur la planète ou se disloquer en anneau. Deimos, elle, atteint 15 kilomètres seulement. Leur origine reste, à ce jour, un mystère : sont-elles les débris d’un impact géant sur Mars, ou des astéroïdes capturés par sa gravité ?
IDEFIX, un éclaireur sur Phobos
C’est justement la question à laquelle va tenter de répondre la mission MMX de la JAXA, l’agence spatiale japonaise. Elle a décollé ce 19 octobre à bord d’une fusée H3, depuis le centre spatial de Tanegashima, dans le sud-ouest de l’archipel.
La sonde va voyager environ dix mois dans l’espace pour rejoindre la planète rouge, où elle doit arriver en août 2027. Elle se placera ensuite autour de Phobos et y restera près de trois ans. C’est à ce moment-là qu’IDEFIX entrera en scène. Ce petit rover a été conçu par l’agence spatiale allemande (DLR) et le CNES. De la taille d’une caisse de boissons, il pèse 25 kilos sur Terre. Mais sur Phobos, où la gravité est infime, il ne fera plus que 15 grammes.
Largué fin 2028 ou début 2029, il tombera de 40 à 100 mètres, rebondira tout doucement, puis se redressera tout seul. Pendant 100 jours, il parcourra le sol pour repérer les deux sites où la sonde pourra se poser. Un éclaireur, en somme.
Comprendre l’origine de Phobos
Une fois que les sites seront choisis par IDEFIX, MMX viendra se poser à deux reprises sur Phobos, sur la face tournée vers Mars, puis sur celle qui y est opposée. Deux outils lui permettront de prélever de la matière : un carottier pour creuser sous la surface, puis un échantillonneur pneumatique, qui va soulever la poussière grâce à un jet de gaz. L’objectif est de récupérer plus de 10 grammes de roche.
La sonde embarque également l’instrument MEGANE de la NASA, un spectromètre à rayons gamma et neutrons qui doit repérer la présence d’éléments légers comme l’hydrogène. Ce point est crucial, et doit nous éclairer sur les origines de Phobos. En effet, ces éléments s’évaporent facilement quand la température monte.
Si la lune est née d’un impact géant, les débris projetés dans l’espace auraient été portés à très haute température, ils auraient donc presque tous disparu. À l’inverse, un astéroïde venu des confins du Système solaire en contiendrait beaucoup plus. Cette mesure devrait donc nous éclairer sur les origines de la lune
Une première mondiale
Le retour de MMX vers la Terre est prévu en novembre 2030, et la capsule doit atterrir en Australie en 2031. Ce sera une première : jamais un échantillon d’une lune martienne n’aura été ramené. Il pourrait même contenir des fragments de Mars, projetés dans l’espace puis tombés sur Phobos. De quoi mieux comprendre l’histoire de la planète rouge et, peut-être, l’origine de son eau.
Une course effrénée : la mission Tianwen-3 de la Chine, prévue pour 2028, doit rapporter des roches directement depuis la surface de Mars en 2031.

articles.title: CapQuest closes $1 million pre-Seed funding to expand globally
articles.text: UAE-based fintech startup CapQuest has raised $1 million in a pre-Seed funding round, led by Oraseya Capital and AMKM Family Office, to accelerate product development and international expansion. Founded in 2023 by Antoine Bruna, Marco Banfi and Anvita Varshney, CapQuest operates an equity management platform that enables startups and established businesses to manage ownership structures, capitalisation tables, employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs), vesting schedules, fundraising transactions and shareholder communications. The funding will support product development, increased automation, enhanced equity management tools and commercial expansion, as the company seeks to grow its international customer base. Press release: CapQuest, a Dubai-based equity management platform, has announced the successful closing of its $1 million Pre-Seed funding round, led by Oraseya Capital and AMKM Family Office. Founded by Antoine Bruna, Marco Banfi, and Anvita Varshney, CapQuest is transforming how companies manage equity, ownership, and investor relations. The platform enables startups, scaleups, and established businesses to manage their cap tables, employee equity plans (ESOPs), vesting schedules, fundraising transactions, and shareholder communications through a single, centralised solution. Designed to replace fragmented spreadsheets and manual processes, CapQuest helps companies simplify complex equity operations, improve transparency, and maintain accurate ownership records throughout their growth. Growing International Traction Since its launch, CapQuest has established a growing international presence, serving companies across 11 countries, with a strong focus on the Middle East, Europe and emerging markets. Its client portfolio includes notable companies such as Holo, Erad, Avenia, and Teylor, reflecting increasing demand for modern equity management infrastructure among high-growth businesses. CapQuest's continued expansion highlights the growing importance of effective equity governance as companies navigate fundraising, employee ownership, and increasingly complex shareholder structures. Accelerating Growth and Product Innovation The funding will accelerate product development, expand CapQuest's commercial presence, and enhance its equity management capabilities through greater automation and more advanced tools. “This funding represents an important milestone for CapQuest and a strong validation of our vision,” said Antoine Bruna, CEO & Co-Founder of CapQuest. “Equity management remains unnecessarily complex for many companies, particularly as they scale and expand internationally. We’re building the infrastructure to make equity management more accessible, transparent, and efficient. With a growing international customer base and an expanding suite of products, CapQuest aims to become a leading platform for equity and investment management, connecting companies, shareholders, and investors within a unified ecosystem.

articles.title: Modder Builds "Slurptop" Cyberdeck with Full Height Keyboard, Swappable Tool Batteries, and Trackball
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 20th 2026
Modder Builds "Slurptop" Cyberdeck with Full Height Keyboard, Swappable Tool Batteries, and Trackball
The concept of a cyberdeck is to customize hardware to better suit your specific needs and use cases, and a modder who goes by "Slurp Burgers" online has taken the concept to something of an extreme, with their take on a laptop, the Slurptop. Unlike many DIY cyberdeck builds, which are based on Raspberry Pi computers, the Slurptop uses a full-fat AMD Ryzen 7 7730U in the motherboard from a GMKtec M5 Ultra mini PC. As a result, it has somewhat better I/O than a traditional laptop, although the mini PC's three front USB Type-C ports were all used to connect the display and peripherals internally. 
The modder took the GMKtec innards and built a custom 3D printed shell around them, replete with a columnar-stagger ergonomic keyboard using MX-style switches and SA profile keycaps, a central num pad, and a trackball mounted at the bottom of the cyberdeck. Perhaps more interesting, the modder designed custom circuitry to be able to run the device off a 24 V Kobalt power tool battery, which is swappable in the event that you need an emergency charge. The modder says that, with light productivity use, like word processing, the battery lasts around five hours, but that could be increased with a bigger 8 Ah battery.There are a few nice touches that bring the whole cyberpunk/utilitarian aesthetic together, like the rugged handle with a built-in OLED display and the bright green dual-pole single throw toggle switch used to turn on the Slurpdeck. In addition to the trackball—whose PixArt PMW3360 sensor was harvested from a mouse and unique, hand-wired keyboard, the Slurpdeck also features a built-in hinged panel that contains an XP Pen drawing tablet in the lid. The full write-up is available on the Slurp Burgers blog.The charging mechanism is rather interesting. In an attempt to avoid the headache and potential hazards of designing custom charging circuitry, Slurp Burgers opted instead to use the stock charging hardware from the power tool battery. That means charging happens externally from the device, but it has a built-in, off-the-shelf, high-speed UPS switch that automatically switches the mini PC from the wall charger to battery power when wall power is removed. When you plug it back in, the cyberdeck automatically switches back to wall power, allowing you to remove the battery and charge it on the tool battery charger.
