articles.title: O Walkman está de volta: R$ 30 mil e acabamento em ouro • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
O Walkman está de volta: R$ 30 mil e acabamento em ouro
Nova versão promete reproduzir músicas com alta qualidade e é voltada para público mais exigente.
Resumo
- O novo Sony Walkman foi anunciado em duas versões, NW-WM1ZM3 e NW-WM1AM3, com preços de cerca de R$ 30 mil e R$ 15 mil, respectivamente.
- O dispositivo oferece reprodução de música em alta qualidade, com suporte a arquivos DSD, som de alta fidelidade e armazenamento de até 256 GB.
- O Walkman tem bateria com até 35 horas de autonomia e sistema operacional Android 16, permitindo a reprodução de músicas via streaming e download de aplicativos.
O Sony Walkman está de volta ao mercado, agora como um dispositivo premium voltado para audiófilos e profissionais da música. Com promessa de reprodução em alta qualidade e acabamento em ouro, o modelo foi anunciado por US$ 5,9 mil, cerca de R$ 30 mil em conversão direta. Há ainda uma versão intermediária à venda por US$ 2.999,99, aproximadamente R$ 15 mil.
O aparelho traz suporte a arquivos DSD (Direct Stream Digital), som de alta fidelidade e armazenamento de 256 GB, além de leitor de cartões microSD. Já em termos de conectividade, estão disponíveis Wi-Fi e Bluetooth, além de duas entradas P2, de 3,5 mm, permitindo escutar músicas tanto em um único canal balanceado quanto em formato estéreo, com sons independentes nos dois lados do fone.
Outro fator que contribui para a alta resolução de som é o uso de cobre “puro” no hardware, processado sem oxigênio. O produto conta ainda com tela de 5,5 polegadas e sistema operacional Android 16. Vale lembrar que a Sony saiu do Brasil em 2020, e o Walkman é um dos produtos que não deve chegar oficialmente por aqui.
Produto premium para audiófilos
O novo Walkman chega em duas versões na linha SIgnature Series: NW-WM1ZM3 e NW-WM1AM3. O diferencial fica por conta do design, com acabamento em ouro da opção mais robusta, a ZM3, além de maior espaço de armazenamento, com 256 GB contra 128 GB no modelo mais simples.
As especificações são praticamente as mesmas: o uso de OFC (cobre livre de oxigênio, em português) na composição promete maior qualidade de som, enquanto os fios internos trazem assinatura Kimber Kable para redução de ruídos e alta fidelidade na reprodução. Segundo a Sony, usuários poderão aproveitar as músicas exatamente como produzidas pelos artistas, nos mínimos detalhes.
Além do hardware, há soluções de software que reforçam a proposta premium do modelo. A fabricante garante tecnologia S-Master HX, suporte a arquivos DSD e otimização dos áudios reproduzidos, sejam eles processados localmente ou via Wi-Fi.
Vale reforçar que músicas tocadas pelo Spotify ou outros aplicativos de streaming terão uma perda natural de qualidade. Para ter maior qualidade, alguns apps oferecem recursos lossless nas configurações que vão garantir detalhes que ficariam de fora no processamento em MP3. De qualquer forma, a melhor maneira de escutar música em um acessório como o novo Walkman é por meio de arquivos baixados.
Bateria, conectividade e mais
Por ser focado em reprodução de músicas, o Walkman promete uma boa autonomia de bateria. São até 35 horas de áudio a depender do tipo de arquivo. Formatos mais pesados, como FLAC ou DSD, devem significar menos tempo, mas sempre numa média de 30 horas de música. Além das variações entre as duas entradas físicas (balanceado ou estéreo), a autonomia também muda de acordo com o tipo de conexão (até 41 horas no Bluetooth) e o aplicativo utilizado, com maior tempo garantido pelo uso do W.Music App nativo da Sony.
O sistema operacional do dispositivo é o Android 16, permitindo baixar apps, acessar internet e reproduzir músicas via streaming. Ainda assim, pela proposta de som mais robusto, o armazenamento máximo de 256 GB mal deve dar para os arquivos de áudio baixados localmente. É possível expandir a memória com cartão microSD.
Considerando a proposta, o Walkman também pode fazer sentido para músicos e produtores que quiserem avaliar seus trabalhos com maior qualidade mesmo quando não estiverem em estúdio. A opção de mobilidade é interessante, já que outros dispositivos vão ter uma reprodução com compressão e perder detalhes importantes no processo de gravação, por exemplo.

articles.title: Cómo vaciar la papelera de reciclaje de WhatsApp sin eliminar chats
articles.text:
Al momento en que el teléfono se queda sin espacio disponible, las aplicaciones pueden presentar fallos, el rendimiento baja y se complican tareas como instalar herramientas nuevas o actualizar el sistema.
En ese escenario, la administración de almacenamiento de WhatsApp permite eliminar archivos acumulados sin borrar los chats, una alternativa que muchos identifican como la “papelera de reciclaje” de la aplicación.
La función no aparece con ese nombre dentro de la plataforma. Está integrada en el apartado de Administración de almacenamiento, desde donde es posible detectar fotos, videos, notas de voz y documentos que ocupan memoria.
La herramienta permite seleccionar contenidos concretos y conservar las conversaciones, incluidos los mensajes de texto que pueden resultar necesarios.
En qué parte está la papelera de reciclaje de WhatsApp
La denominada papelera de reciclaje de WhatsApp se encuentra dentro de los ajustes de la aplicación. Para acceder, hay que abrir el menú de Ajustes, ingresar en Almacenamiento y datos y elegir Administración de almacenamiento. Allí aparece un resumen de los archivos que consumen más memoria en el dispositivo.
El sistema organiza el contenido por tamaño y por conversación. De esa forma, permite localizar con rapidez los videos extensos, las imágenes repetidas, los documentos recibidos hace tiempo o los audios que ya no tienen utilidad. El proceso elimina archivos multimedia, pero no borra el historial de mensajes del chat.
Cómo borrar archivos sin eliminar conversaciones en WhatsApp
Dentro de Administración de almacenamiento, WhatsApp muestra categorías como “Reenviados muchas veces” y “De más de 5 MB”, sumado a una lista de chats ordenados según el espacio que utilizan. El usuario puede entrar en cada apartado para revisar el material antes de tomar una decisión.
Tras seleccionar fotos, videos, audios o documentos, la aplicación habilita la opción de eliminar. Conviene revisar cada archivo antes de confirmar la acción, sobre todo si se trata de contenido laboral, comprobantes, imágenes familiares o documentos que no están guardados en otro sitio.
En qué cambia la ruta para encontrar la papelera de WhatsApp en Android y iPhone
El acceso a esta herramienta es parecido en ambos sistemas operativos. En los teléfonos con Android, el usuario debe abrir WhatsApp, tocar los tres puntos de la esquina superior, entrar en Ajustes y buscar Almacenamiento y datos. Desde allí encontrará Administración de almacenamiento.
En un iPhone, la ruta comienza en Configuración dentro de WhatsApp. Luego hay que elegir Almacenamiento y datos y, después, Administración de almacenamiento. Aunque pueden existir diferencias menores en el diseño de los menús, la función permite revisar y borrar contenido de forma selectiva tanto en Android como en iPhone.
Por qué liberar espacio en WhatsApp mejora el funcionamiento del teléfono
Los archivos recibidos por WhatsApp pueden acumularse durante meses en segundo plano. Grupos familiares, conversaciones laborales, canales y chats personales suelen concentrar imágenes, videos y documentos que pasan inadvertidos hasta que aparece una advertencia de memoria insuficiente.
Cuando el almacenamiento disponible desciende mucho, el teléfono puede responder con lentitud o impedir la descarga de actualizaciones. Pueden surgir errores al abrir la cámara, guardar fotos nuevas o instalar aplicaciones.
Cómo saber si todavía falta memoria después de la limpieza
Luego de borrar contenido de WhatsApp, es posible verificar el resultado desde la aplicación Configuración del teléfono. En el apartado Almacenamiento, está cuánta memoria está ocupada y cuál es el espacio disponible. Esa revisión permite saber si la limpieza tuvo efecto o si es necesario actuar sobre otros archivos.
Si el problema persiste, conviene analizar las aplicaciones que más espacio consumen, sumado a revisar la galería, la carpeta de descargas y los archivos duplicados.
Asimismo, un reinicio puede ayudar a que el sistema actualice el cálculo de memoria. En muchos modelos, se realiza al mantener presionado el botón de encendido durante 30 segundos, aunque el procedimiento puede variar según el fabricante.

articles.title: It sure is looking like the PS6 will cost over US$1,000
articles.text:
PlayStation’s next console is likely going to be even more expensive than you might think.
According to credible AMD leaker KeplerL2, Sony’s unannounced successor to the PS5, which will presumably be called the PS6, will have RAM + NAND components that cost “over [US]$680,” or roughly C$940.
It’s important to stress that this only pertains to memory and storage, not any other parts that would be necessary to build a PS6. As a result, it’s estimated PlayStation would be spending about US$1,000 (roughly C$1382) just to make each of these next-gen consoles. In other words, even if PlayStation decided to eat the costs and sell at a loss, this would still be extremely expensive for consumers.
The main reason for these astronomical costs, naturally, is the AI-driven global component shortage affecting the tech industry as a whole. This has led analysts to speculate that the PS6 will cost well over US$1000. For context, the PS5 Pro is currently priced at US$899.99/C$1,099.99, so the jump from that to the rumoured minimum PS6 cost isn’t actually that much, making it even likelier to be true.
Originally, people had once been expecting the PS6 would release in 2027, seven years after the PS5 and the same gap between it and the PS4. But given component shortages and associated price increases, it’s speculated that Sony might wait until 2028 or later now.
It’s worth noting that AMD had teased in February that Xbox was planning to debut its next console, codenamed Helix, in 2027. But given that it’s been the better part of a year since, it’s unclear whether those plans may have changed.
What we do know, though, is that physical games won’t be a part of PlayStation’s future. Starting in 2028, the company will only produce digital media, a decision it attributed to diminishing physical game sales. This is despite the fact that there are many reasons why the killing of physical media is damaging to the future of the gaming industry, from preservation and ownership standpoints to removing more affordable options for consumers.
Xbox, for its part, hasn’t committed to ending physical games production, although it’s currently running a program that lets users get digital versions of discs they own. Nintendo, meanwhile, has explicitly said it still plans to produce physical games while offering discounts for those who buy digital versions.
Source: KeplerL2 — NeoGAF Via: VGC

articles.title: Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes. Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The streaming service first previewed the idea at its Investor Day in May, where it also introduced AI capabilities that let listeners ask questions about what they’re listening to or watching and debuted new tools for managing creator sponsorships.
As the company explained at the time, memberships would help to “create a natural path to go deeper, unlocking new and exclusive experiences for fans and new revenue opportunities for creators.”
The feature is now rolling out to 34 markets globally, including the U.S.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube. Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment. To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.
Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
A handful of shows will offer memberships at launch, including “The Adam Friedland Show,” “Making Sense with Sam Harris,” “Shawn Ryan Show,” “The Sculpt Society,” “Two Hot Takes,” as well as YMH Studios, which is bringing memberships to 12 shows across its network.
Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics. Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

articles.title: Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots — chipmaker’s automated guided vehicles could run afoul of agency’s sweeping robot ban
articles.text:
Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots — chipmaker’s automated guided vehicles could run afoul of agency’s sweeping robot ban
These robots move chips between tools and sections of the fab.
Intel has asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to make an exception for the automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that the company uses to transport the sensitive silicon wafers and other materials, containers, and supplies needed to make the most advanced chips in its fabs. According to Bloomberg, the American chipmaker fears that its AGVs would fall under the blanket prohibition against foreign-made robots after they were added to the FCC’s Covered List.
AGVs are niche machines that chip fabs use to transport materials and supplies between tools and sections of the fab, helping ensure that the cleanroom conditions required for each manufacturing process are maintained. This makes them critical equipment for U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, but, apparently, there are no suitable domestic alternatives for these devices at the moment. Intel’s current fleet of AGVs requires continuous maintenance, including software and firmware updates, and if it’s forced to find a local supplier for its AGVs, the company says that it would take years, crippling the United States’ chipmaking efforts.
The biggest AGV suppliers are Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., while a few smaller businesses from South Korea and Taiwan are also trying to break into the market. It’s unclear why these companies haven’t applied for a conditional approval yet, which would allow them to continue selling these products in the U.S. while also promising Washington that they’ll set up a manufacturing base in the country. This is something that Netgear has already done, allowing it to continue selling its foreign-made routers despite being an American company.
Intel says that it remains unclear if updates to its AGVs would break compliance with the FCC, and that it’s asking the agency to issue a conditional waiver “out of an abundance of caution to ensure the ongoing operation of these specific AGV units.” While Team Blue is the only company concerned about AGVs at the moment, other chip manufacturers would likely need a similar waiver in the near future, especially as they build more fabs in the U.S. This includes TSMC, which is planning to build 12 more fabs and four packaging facilities in Arizona, Samsung, with its new Taylor, Texas, fab, and even Elon Musk’s Terafab, which has already begun construction.
Washington has been using the FCC to force companies to invest in American manufacturing. Its blanket bans on foreign-made products like drones and routers have affected some of the biggest brands in the U.S., including DJI and TP-Link. While these bans do not outright ban the sale of all products made by these companies, especially those that have already been approved before, they make it impossible for them to introduce new products and even release software updates to their existing product line. The FCC eventually walked back on the software update ban, but they still would not be able to register new products unless they build them in the U.S.

articles.title: GALAX Prepares GeForce RTX 5090 HOF with Swarovski Crystals
articles.text:
Monday, October 19th 2026
GALAX Prepares GeForce RTX 5090 HOF with Swarovski Crystals
GALAX has officially teased its GeForce RTX 5090 Hall of Fame Edition GPU, featuring unique details with Swarovski crystals. What the company originally showcased at Computex 2026 now appears to be a product scheduled for launch on October 22. The GeForce RTX 5090 HOF maintains the distinctive white aesthetic that GALAX GPUs are known for. However, this time, the design is enhanced with Swarovski crystals embedded across the GPU shroud, adding a nuanced touch. This should help the GPU stand out in all-white builds, especially when RGB lighting hits the crystals, reflecting and bursting in multiple directions.
Another interesting aspect is that the card is expected to feature dual 12V-2×6 power connectors, providing significant power headroom. GALAX has already offered its flagship GeForce RTX 5090D HOF Edition GPUs with dual 12V-2x6 power connectors, but this will be the first time an overclocking-focused graphics card receives such a luxurious finish with crystals. Initially, the GPU's appearance at Computex 2026 was thought to be a preview for the GeForce RTX 6090. However, it is now clear that the item will be more of a collectible, as GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs have become extremely expensive on their own.As a reminder, NVIDIA has denied reports that the GeForce RTX 5090 is being discontinued, confirming that shipments will continue despite industry-wide supply constraints that have led to severe shortages and prices far above its $1,999 MSRP. Some SKUs are retailing for the price of a small used car, with prices of $8,000 not unheard of. Therefore, we can only imagine that this GeForce RTX 5090 HOF Edition from GALAX will be an even more expensive option, as the Swarovski collaboration will likely add additional costs.

articles.title: Chris Lattner: AI Code Generation Doesn't Solve Software Engineering - EE Times
articles.text:
For AI chip companies, the promise of AI-based coding agents is compelling: generate the low-level kernels needed to get a model running on new hardware, optimize them for performance, and do it without the software engineering resources traditionally required.
But according to Chris Lattner, CEO of AI software startup Modular (recently acquired by Qualcomm, where he now serves as executive VP of software engineering), chip companies should be wary of the limits of AI code generation. Making a kernel run fast is a very different problem from building software infrastructure we can depend on, he told EE Times in an exclusive interview.
“Agents are good, but they’re like anything else; it’s a tool, and you have to use it the right way,” Lattner said. “What I’ve seen with agents is they make tons of throwaway code. So, if you’re building a product, you don’t want to agent-generate everything.”
Agentic code generation makes sense for projects that are well-defined and limited in scope (e.g., “make this kernel go fast”), which can be quantified, measured, and validated, Lattner said, but bigger projects require product design and software engineering and can’t be delegated to agents.
“If you’re a startup and you only care about getting one model working, or getting it to go fast, [then go ahead,] use AI tools to prove it’s possible,” he said. “But that’s not going to be great for when you want to sell your chip to someone else, and they want to run a model you don’t have access to.”
Lattner said that despite some high-profile companies’ performance claims for their AI-generated low-level software, there are still many unanswered questions, including the dollar cost to generate large amounts of code and its applicability to large, open-ended problems.
“I have heard of hardware companies that say they don’t believe in software anymore; they just want to use agents to generate everything,” Lattner said. “I think that’s interesting because they’re definitely using LLVM and still investing in compilers, but saying they’re not. So there’s a divergence between the party line and what’s actually happening.”
Writing performant low-level code for new and novel hardware has long been a difficult task for chip companies, and some are now relying on agents for this.
“Various people use [agentic code generation] as a talking point, particularly when their software is known to be problematic,” Lattner said. “So, I don’t really know what to believe in all these cases… great claims need great proof.”
Porting code
While AI is useful in some use cases, it can’t be used for everything, Lattner said. AI might help get a demo up and running, but this isn’t the same as writing a usable software stack with determinism and adaptability.
“The hard part about building a company or building a product or building something meaningful in the world is understanding the product requirements,” he said. “What is the marketing story? What is the product-market fit that you have to get for your product? I think that remains quite hard.”
At Modular, teams use agentic code generation for tasks such as porting PyTorch code into the company’s Max AI framework and for porting CUDA code to its programming language Mojo. Lattner said that porting code is a great use case for AI, along with specializing existing software (for example, specializing a matmul kernel for a specific size of matrix), since the agent can do this quickly and efficiently.
People will always need to know how to code, he said, since prompting in English isn’t precise enough to get a good result.
“It’s true things are changing very rapidly—I use AI to write code, and I wouldn’t go back, personally—but that doesn’t mean that writing code was the job,” he said. “If you go back five years, more code was read than written.”
Open source under pressure
The downsides to AI code generation are still making themselves apparent in the world of software. Lattner identified open-source projects, the backbone of much of modern software, as being particularly under threat.
“Open-source projects like LLVM are under assault,” he said.
Before generative AI, people who wanted to contribute to open-source projects were motivated by the satisfaction of identifying and fixing problems, most often because they were using the software themselves and wanted to contribute. Making changes meant they had to invest a certain amount of time. Maintainers, people who had been working on the project for a long time, reviewed contributions for quality and worked with the community to teach them the nuances of the codebase. Lattner said the investment in teaching contributors improved the code.
“Today, that model is broken, because people are just vibe coding tons of patches and sending them to tons of projects, and the maintainers are getting completely overwhelmed with AI crap,” he said.
The deluge of AI-generated code is increasing the workload for maintainers, who have to review and iterate code before accepting it, Lattner said.
“And then the submitter doesn’t actually care, so the investment back into the human doesn’t lead to a future maintainer; it leads to someone who walks away, or just sets up their agents to spam a bunch of different projects to try to get GitHub badges,” he said. “This is a huge issue, so a lot of projects have stopped accepting contributions.”
The response from open-source projects such as LLVM has been to consider working only with established contributors, a move Lattner described as “terrifying.”
“The value of open-source projects is the humans, it’s the relationships, it’s the tribal knowledge,” he said. “If you destroy that, there’s going to be a huge problem… Running an open-source project and making it successful has always been super hard, so this is another pretty big threat.”
This is a huge challenge for all open-source projects today.
Modular’s programming language, Mojo, was recently open-sourced, but contributions aren’t yet being accepted. Lattner said the company intends to open to submissions gradually.
“It’s not just about the lines of code; it’s about the social side of things—if you have an employee that’s investing their effort into someone else, traditionally the thought would be, we’re investing in you, and if you’re good we’ll hire you, or [something might come out of it],” he said.
Things will stabilize, Lattner said. AI code review tools will improve, easing some of the burden, but ultimately, code review is difficult to automate completely because it requires judgement.
“What you’re building doesn’t just need to pass a test; it needs to be able to support the architecture we need for tomorrow and the future,” he said. “Models tomorrow will be better and faster, but I think these are inherent structural problems.”
Max alliance
For startups without the resources to build a state-of-the-art software stack, Lattner is planning on opening up Max, Modular’s AI framework, by starting an alliance for hardware makers. The alliance is planned to kick off around the end of the year, he said.
“This will be a big deal,” Lattner said. “We’re saying to everyone who has chips: You now have software. A lot of startups have been asking for help, but we always had to say no; we couldn’t scale to support them. Now we’ll be able to say yes, you can do it for yourself.”
Coding agents can solve for a specific kernel for a specific chip, but today’s complex, disaggregated, heterogeneous data center needs orchestration, scaling, and management, all of which must be handled by software, Lattner said.
“We’ve been building this for four and a half years—now you’ll be able to use it and scale it for yourself,” he said.
This is part of Qualcomm’s plan for Modular, Lattner said.
“[Qualcomm] wants it to be an open ecosystem so [its data center chip] can compete on its own merits,” he said. “Qualcomm is modest enough to understand it can’t [overtake Nvidia]. There will be a lot of different players with great contributions in different parts of the value chain, but it needs to be an open ecosystem.”
The Max alliance will enable edge chip companies and markets such as China, which Lattner is looking forward to.
“This is going to be very, very fun and exciting,” he said.

articles.title: OYO-parent PRISM to nearly halve IPO fresh issue size to up to Rs 3,350 cr: Sources
articles.text:
OYO-parent PRISM to nearly halve IPO fresh issue size to up to Rs 3,350 cr: Sources
People familiar with the matter said the reduction in the issue size follows continued strong cash generation and an improving balance-sheet position, which has lowered the amount of capital the company needs to raise compared with what was originally envisaged.
OYO parent PRISM is planning to nearly halve the size of the fresh issue in its proposed initial public offering (IPO) to up to Rs 3,350 crore from almost Rs 6,650 crore, sources said.
People familiar with the matter told PTI the reduction in the issue size follows continued strong cash generation and an improving balance-sheet position, which has lowered the amount of capital the company needs to raise compared with what was originally envisaged.
"The original issue was sized before the company's more recent financial performance came through. With cash generation remaining strong and the balance sheet improving, the funding requirement has come down, allowing the company to reduce the amount of primary capital it raises.
"The objective is to raise what the business needs while keeping the capital structure efficient. The plan is to repay the residual debt over the next two to three years through cash flows generated by the business," a person familiar with the matter said.
Earlier, OYO had planned to raise up to Rs 6,650 crore through an IPO, of which around Rs 5,000 crore was intended for debt repayment.
The revised issue size comes with PRISM continuing to focus on reducing its outstanding debt.
Under the revised structure, most of the issue proceeds are proposed to be used towards repayment or prepayment, in part or full, of certain borrowings.
The revised issue comes as PRISM moves towards the next stage of its proposed IPO following its earlier filing of the uUpdated draft herring prospectus.
Moody's Ratings has revised the outlook on PRISM to 'positive' from 'stable', while reaffirming the travel tech unicorn's B2 corporate family rating.
Explaining the rationale behind ratings, Moody's said, "We expect OYO's EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation) to grow to around Rs 3,000 crore ($315 million) over the next 12-18 months as the company continues to scale and add new storefronts to its platform.
For FY26, OYO's EBITDA more than doubled to Rs 2,630 crore from Rs 1,080 crore in FY25.
OYO was founded in 2013 by Ritesh Agarwal, who currently holds a 30.52 per cent stake in the company. SVF India Holdings (Cayman) Ltd, a subsidiary of SoftBank Group Corp is the largest shareholder in the company, with a 40.04% stake.

articles.title: Entre expandir sus modelos de IA por todo el mundo o protegerlos, China tiene muy clara su decisión
articles.text:
El Gobierno chino se está preparando para dar un volantazo. Durante los últimos dos años su estrategia para competir con EEUU en el ámbito de la inteligencia artificial (IA) se ha sostenido sobre la distribución a gran escala de modelos con pesos abiertos que pueden ser ejecutados localmente. Su apuesta pasa por tener los modelos más baratos, personalizables y accesibles con el propósito de ser los más desplegados, y, así, debilitar a sus competidores estadounidenses desde un punto de vista económico.
Por el momento no hay ningún indicio que nos invite a prever que la estrategia de China va a cambiar en lo que se refiere a su apuesta por los modelos de IA con pesos abiertos, pero el Gobierno liderado por Xi Jinping planea introducir un cambio muy importante en su itinerario. Y es que, según SCMP, ha presentado un borrador que contempla prohibiciones y restricciones a la exportación de 23 tecnologías vinculadas estrechamente al desarrollo de la IA.
Esta iniciativa está siendo dirigida por los ministerios de Comercio y Ciencia y Tecnología, e involucra a los modelos de IA, los agentes y las tecnologías de diseño de semiconductores. Lo que persigue China es proteger sus tecnologías más avanzadas en un contexto en el que la IA y los chips son cada vez más importantes desde un punto de vista estratégico. Si esta iniciativa sale adelante, y es muy probable que lo haga en ausencia de una oposición real a la postura del Gobierno, podemos esperar que algunas de sus tecnologías más avanzadas no salgan de China.
UN VISTAZO A...
Este plan puede perjudicar a las empresas chinas que quieren crecer en el extranjero
Para algunas compañías chinas que compiten en el mercado de los modelos de IA, como DeepSeek, Moonshot AI o Z.ai, crecer más allá de las fronteras de China es importante. Los mercados extranjeros y los acuerdos con proveedores de computación en la nube representan una fuente de ingresos muy jugosa a la que no les interesa renunciar. Según Zhang Yi, fundador y analista jefe de la consultora iiMedia, las restricciones que prepara el Gobierno chino tendrán unos costes de adaptación que deberán asumir las empresas chinas.
El borrador del Gobierno justifica esta decisión amparándose en su obligación de proteger la seguridad nacional
Además, el borrador que han presentado los ministerios de Comercio y Ciencia y Tecnología establece criterios que condicionan sobre todo la distribución de los modelos de IA más potentes. Todos aquellos que han sido entrenados con datos considerados importantes para China, los que han alcanzado determinados niveles de capacidad computacional y los que superan los dos billones de parámetros podrán verse limitados por el Gobierno.
En la práctica esto implica que los laboratorios chinos podrían verse obligados a no distribuir algunos de sus modelos de frontera fuera de China. Es un cambio de paradigma importante en la estrategia de este país asiático que podría comprometer la competitividad de algunas de sus empresas de IA. No obstante, el borrador del Gobierno justifica esta decisión amparándose en su obligación de proteger la seguridad nacional, por lo que es poco probable que finalmente este plan no se lleve a efecto.
Lo que todavía no está claro es en qué medida afectará este plan del Gobierno chino a sus modelos con pesos abiertos más avanzados. Moonshot AI y Z.ai han firmado acuerdos de reparto de ingresos con grandes proveedores estadounidenses de servicios en la nube, como Amazon Web Services, para desplegar sus modelos. Estos acuerdos pueden implicar que los pesos de los modelos se transfieran fuera de China, lo que podría entrar en conflicto con las premisas del borrador que ha preparado el Gobierno chino. De ser así, algunos laboratorios chinos perderán oportunidades de negocio.

articles.title: Jeep pourrait faire renaître la Willys, mais pas forcément comme un vrai 4x4
articles.text:
Alors que les marques du groupe Stellantis semblent toutes se tourner vers leur passé pour trouver des inspirations pour les modèles futurs, Jeep n’avait pas encore relancé un design historique. La marque américaine, intégrée au groupe franco-italien et spécialisée dans les tout-terrains, pourrait faire renaître sa mythique Willys. Voici à quoi on peut s’attendre.
Un modèle urbain et électrique
Même si Jeep reste avare en informations concernant cet éventuel retour de la Willys, on peut raisonnablement attendre l’arrivée d’un véhicule électrique et urbain dans la gamme Jeep pour compléter le succès de l’Avenger. Au Mondial de l’Auto, Jeep a donné sa feuille de route pour 2030 et a ajouté qu’une piste intéressante serait d’imaginer des modèles compacts et électriques s’inspirant des produits mythiques de la marque. On pense évidemment à la Willys.
La Jeep Willys n’a pas de véritable descendante dans la gamme Jeep. Il y a bien le tout-terrain Wrangler, qui en reprend certains traits de design, mais le véhicule a tellement grossi qu’il est difficile de le voir comme une réinterprétation. Pour l’instant, Jeep ne confirme pas la production en série du modèle, mais la marque ne semble pas fermée à l’idée.
Un modèle urbain, mais pas tout-terrain ?
Jeep pourrait se servir de la nouvelle plateforme e-Car de Stellantis, qui servira déjà à la future 2CV, puis à la Panda, pour développer sa Jeep Willys électrique. L’idée serait alors de faire davantage un modèle urbain électrique et abordable qu’un véritable tout-terrain, comme l’était la Jeep Willys arrivée lors du débarquement de Normandie en juin 1944.
Conserver les qualités de tout-terrain chères à la marque Jeep paraît difficile avec cette plateforme, pensée uniquement pour les deux roues motrices pour l’instant. Toutefois, ce ne serait pas la première fois qu’un modèle Jeep serait proposé uniquement en deux roues motrices. L’Avenger a souffert quelque temps de l’absence d’une déclinaison à quatre roues motrices, importante pour l’image de marque de Jeep.
Jeep pourrait participer aux travaux sur la plateforme e-Car de Stellantis pour en proposer une version à quatre roues motrices. Cela permettrait aussi à Fiat de relancer la Panda 4×4, très importante dans l’histoire du modèle italien. Citroën pourrait également rêver du retour d’une Méhari, même si les versions les plus diffusées de cette dernière étaient à deux roues motrices, comme la 2CV. Tous ces modèles citadins à quatre roues motrices pourraient contrer la future Renault 4 E-Tech 4×4, qui semble en préparation du côté de la marque au losange.

articles.title: Elon Musk, Anthropic pledge to give away billions of dollars in shares - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Elon Musk, Anthropic pledge to give away billions of dollars in shares
SpaceX Corp. Chief Executive Elon Musk today pledged to gift a single share of the spaceflight company to every child in America.
“This will be the first of many,” Musk wrote in the brief X post that revealed the move today. The announcement came a few hours after Anthropic PBC pledged to donate at least 5% of its equity to a public benefit fund.
There were 72 million children in the U.S. as of last July, which suggests that Musk intends to give away 72 million SpaceX shares. That’s the equivalent of $10.5 billion at the company’s last closing price.
Musk didn’t specify how he plans to disburse the shares. However, he disclosed in an X post responding to Anthropic’s donation that he plans to give “shares directly to the public.” In another post, Musk wrote “thanks for helping enable this” to tech investor Brad Gerstner, who played a central role in the creation of Trump Accounts. Those are investment accounts that the White House opened for U.S. children earlier this year.
In July, SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell pledged more than $320 million of her shares in the company to the Trump Accounts program.
Musk’s charitable activities have drawn scrutiny in recent months. He maintains a charity that had more than $14 billion in assets as of December, but reportedly failed to meet minimum donation requirements over the past four years. The funds that it did disburse reportedly went to nonprofits aligned with Musk and his companies.
Musk pledged $1 billion to OpenAI Group PBC shortly after its 2015 launch. He only donated $38 million and later proposed to take majority control of the artificial intelligence provider, which at the time operated as a traditional nonprofit. OpenAI changed its organizational structure a few years later to accommodate its commercialization efforts.
The ChatGPT developer’s top competitor, Anthropic, announced a major charitable initiative of its own shortly before Musk’s announcement. The company plans to donate 5% of its equity to a new public benefit fund. Anthropic intends to add another 2% every time its valuation increases by 50% “above a set baseline.”
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will operate as a subsidiary of the AI provider rather than as a standalone nonprofit. The company indicated that one of the unit’s priorities will be addressing the impact of AI on the labor market. Earlier this year, Anthropic committed $200 million to external research initiatives focused on that topic.
The shares earmarked for the fund will come on top of the significant amount of equity the company’s employees have pledged to give away. Put together, the two initiatives will commit about 20% of Anthropic’s stock to charitable causes. That stock could be worth $400 billion if the company achieves the $2 billion valuation it reportedly hopes to reach in its upcoming public offering.

articles.title: Oura adds new fitness metrics to show how workouts impact your body | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As competition in the smart ring market escalates, Oura is introducing two new features to give people more insight into their workouts and how they impact their bodies. The company announced on Tuesday it’s rolling out Cardio Effort and VO₂ max metrics to expand workout tracking beyond exercise duration and heart rate zones.
While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By launching more advanced workout metrics, Oura is looking to differentiate itself from competitors.
With Cardio Effort, users will be able to see how much a workout taxes their cardiovascular system. This measurement is aggregated over the week relative to each user’s individual baseline to provide more insights. Oura explained that this metric shifts users’ focus from “How many minutes did I move?” to “Am I maintaining my fitness, building it, or overdoing it?”
Since Cardio Effort accounts for both intensity and duration, a shorter, more intense workout can yield a similar score to a longer, less intense one, the company says.
Oura notes that the metric has two components: Workout Cardio Effort and Weekly Cardio Effort. The first metric evaluates the impact of an individual workout, while the latter aggregates effort into a weekly total, categorized as “Light,” “Fair,” “Maintaining,” “Building,” or “Reaching.”
Oura measures elevated heart rate relative to each member’s long-term resting heart rate, avoiding the variability associated with maximum-heart-rate estimates. Weekly effort levels are then determined using personalized ranges based on recent activity patterns.
Cardio Effort is rolling out to Oura Ring Gen3 and later models.
As for VO₂ max, the metric shows how workouts contribute to long-term fitness. It measures how effectively the heart, lungs, and muscles work together to deliver and use oxygen during exercise. Previously, measuring VO₂ max typically required a lab test or a six-minute walking test. Oura can now estimate it passively using GPS-enabled workouts.
After completing five qualifying activities, users receive an initial VO2 Max estimate. Within the My Health Heart Hub, they can view their current VO2 Max estimate in ml/kg/min, their fitness category (Low, Fair, High, or Peak), how their estimate has changed over time, and when it was last updated. Users also receive insights highlighting meaningful changes in their VO2 Max or indicating when their estimate remains consistent.
VO₂ Max is launching in Oura Labs, the company’s hub for experimental features, for members with Gen3 and newer Oura Ring devices.
Oura says these two new features are designed to work together to show users how hard they’re working and how that effort is adding up over time.

articles.title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
articles.text:
As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips.
Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even pre-order a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit.
Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is a bare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950. It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Ars got to go for a ride in a Slate Truck over the summer, but we haven’t had a chance to shop for one. So I stopped by the Slate Experience Center so I could, er, experience the Slate.
Upon walking into the showroom on a Monday morning, the first thing I noticed was a marquee-style sign on the wall boldly and brightly serving as a price tag for the black truck parked in the middle of the showroom. The vibe was industrial-barn-chic-meets-SoHo-loft. Three other people were there, and another shopper entered as I left. One man alternated between sitting in the cab, peering at the truck as he walked around it, and peppering Manager of Customer Experience Steve Purdy with questions.
The showroom has been open since October 15, launching with a three-day event that offered ridealongs. Interest has been strong, Purdy told me, and while he couldn’t provide sales numbers, he said the response has been “incredible.”
“We’re really happy with the number of [$300] deposits we’ve gotten since we opened,” Purdy said.

articles.title: Toronto Game Expo returns next month with special Zelda guest
articles.text:
Toronto Game Expo returns for its second 2026 show next month.
Following an event in March, the video game convention will be held once again from Nov. 7-8 at Exhibition Place, this time at the Better Living Centre. The show will feature all kinds of gaming programming, including guests, hundreds of vendors, playable demos, tournaments and more.
Notably, the con will feature a special guest: American-Canadian actress Patricia Summersett, the voice of Princess Zelda from The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, Tears of the Kingdom and their Hyrule Warriors spin-offs.
View this post on Instagram
More information on Toronto Game Expo can be found on the con’s website. Tickets start at $30 for single-day admission and $50 for a weekend pass.
Notably, this is the second up-and-coming gaming convention happening in Ontario this fall. On Oct. 25 and 26, the second-annual Video Game Live Expo (VGLX) will be held at the International Centre in Mississauga. And in December, the inaugural Vancouver Game Garden will run at the Vancouver Convention Centre.
Given that we don’t have many consumer video game events in Canada, it’s great to see groups putting in efforts like these.

articles.title: Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance — vibe-coded xHCI98 driver works in Microsoft OSes up to Windows 7
articles.text:
Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance — vibe-coded xHCI98 driver works in Microsoft OSes up to Windows 7
If you've ever wanted to run Windows 98 SE on your mid-2010s or newer PC with fast USB hub support, here's your chance.
Windows 98 SE devotees can now enjoy (experimental) support for USB4 and Thunderbolt 3/4. Developer and maker Yeo Kheng Meng, who also enjoys retrocomputing, recently released the vibe-coded xHCI98 v3.0.0.0, enabling the practical use of generic USB 3.x, USB4, and Thunderbolt 3/4 host controllers on systems running Windows 98 SE, ME, 2000, XP, Vista, and 7. An extensive blog post by the dev provides further reading about the driver, compatibility, its creation, and usage.
Demo video “shows many different USB devices being hotplugged to a modern 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 with only xHCI controller.”
Some of you will be wondering why a project to bring USB4 (Thunderbolt 3 and 4) to PCs running Windows 98 SE exists. Retro computing fan Meng explains on his GitHub that this project should appeal directly to users of PCs from the mid-2010s that have xHCI-only (USB 3.x) chipsets and no legacy EHCI controller. However, older OSes don’t have xHCI drivers, and that’s where xHCI98 steps in. “Without xHCI support, even keyboards, mice, and flash drives need the BIOS's legacy support, cannot be hotplugged, and devices such as Ethernet and audio do not work at all,” explains Meng, revealing his motivation. “This project fills that gap.”
Impressively, xHCI98 drives a lot more than USB storage. It replaces Windows’ own USB port and hub drivers to facilitate the connection and use of USB 1.1 and 2.0 and SuperSpeed (USB 3.x) devices and hubs, UAS (USB Attached SCSI) storage through a second driver (xhciuas.sys), and Thunderbolt 3 and USB4 docks and NVMe enclosures through a third driver (xhcicm.sys).
Meng has developed and tested xHCI98 mostly on Intel hardware, as that is what he owns. Candidly, he admits “this is a solo human's project with AI assistance, so bugs are not unexpected,” even if you do have the same hardware as the dev - a 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 (Comet Lake xHCI, no EHCI). It stands up pretty well during the plug/unplug video demo above, though the test rig used is not quite the USB cart of death.
As a solo developer, Meng isn't shy to admit he leaned heavily on AI assistance to prepare the xHCI98 release. His vibe coding adventure was supported by Claude Fable 5.1 for planning, Claude Opus 5.5 for coding, and Codex GPT 6 Astra as an adversarial reviewer.
In addition to a few bug warnings, there are some other things to know about using this driver with the various older versions of Windows it supports, standby and hibernation, and more. The dev helpfully sketches out a process for checking your hardware, outlines various install methods, discusses updating, and talks about tuning the driver for those who will be jumping in at the deep end with this project.

articles.title: Yelp can now call on your behalf to check wait times at a restaurant | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Over the last few weeks, personal assistants like Instinct, Fo, and Muse have enabled users to call businesses for customer support and appointment booking. Following this trend, Yelp is adding the ability for its app users to get a voice agent to call a restaurant to check wait times.
The new feature, Check for Me, will show up on restaurant pages in the app, where users can enter their party size and phone number. The AI agent then calls on behalf of the user to check wait times and texts them the results to decide if they want to go to that particular restaurant.
Last year, Yelp debuted its voice solution for restaurants and service providers. With this new feature, the discovery platform is fulfilling the consumer side of the equation, though there is a possibility that a user’s agent will talk to the restaurant’s agent, and agent-to-agent communication might break down the conversation.
The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services. With the new OpenTable integration, users can easily book a restaurant without leaving the app.
Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats. Plus, you can access your chat history from the past 30 days in the app, with full history available soon.
Users can ask the chatbot to set custom reminders, such as sending suggestions for weekend activities every Friday. The company is also letting users build their own lists, starting with two “Been Here” and “Want to
Go” lists. You can filter your lists by location, category, and cuisine, reorder, add notes to items, and share them with others. 
Next month, the company will start showing weekly personalized recommendations based on your saved items and rankings. Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view.
To cap off all these changes, Yelp has been thinking about enhancing customer support and business processes through AI. In the new update, the company is releasing a new paid product called Smart Lead Reply, which can reply to customers and engage with them to qualify a lead. Business owners, who will be charged $30 per month for these services, can specify how an agent should handle a conversation with a customer. Other companies like Meta have also been courting small businesses with AI offerings to handle inbound customer inquiries.

articles.title: 'Turn any tank into your next UGV': France's Foreign Legion may get thousands of XXL robot mules built from retired tanks — though the demo inconveniently sits on one of only two AMX-32s ever made
articles.text:
'Turn any tank into your next UGV': France's Foreign Legion may get thousands of XXL robot mules built from retired tanks — though the demo inconveniently sits on one of only two AMX-32s ever made
KNDS and S2M's REFURBOT conversion kit resurfaces
- KNDS and S2M's REFURBOT show up at France's National Infantry Days as an "XXL robotic mule" for the Foreign Legion's 2nd REI, according to FOB
- REFURBOT uses the TOXO kit to turn retired armored vehicles into Unmanned Ground Vehicles, and was first shown in June 2026 as a 25mm-armed combat robot
- No payload, price, autonomy level, or contract has been published, and the vehicle remains a prototype for now
France's Foreign Legion may soon be moving supplies with a tank that no longer needs a crew.
At the recent Journées nationales de l'infanterie (JNI), the French Army infantry school's showcase held at Draguignan, defense outlet Forces Operations Blog (FOB) posted a video of what it called an "XXL robotic mule for the legionnaires of the 2nd REI."
The 2nd REI is the 2nd Foreign Infantry Regiment, a French Foreign Legion unit based in Nîmes.
From gun platform to pack animal in the making
The machine comes from REFURBOT, a project by French SME S2M Equipment and KNDS France. FOB described it less as a single robot and more as "a robotization kit to 'recycle' decommissioned vehicle fleets and rapidly scale up if needed," adding that it remains in the prototype stage, with other wheeled and tracked platforms under study.
When REFURBOT debuted at Eurosatory in June 2026, it was pitched as a fighter, not a porter. The demonstrator replaced a tank's 105mm turret with KNDS's ARX25 remote weapon station, which carries a dual-feed 25M811 25mm cannon with 280 ready rounds and a coaxial 7.62mm machine gun.
MILMAG reported the company's claim that it can engage light armor, drones, hovering helicopters, and infantry beyond 2,500 meters.
TOXO is the driving package, a bolt-on robotization package whose coverage credits variously to S2M, KNDS, or both. It pairs radar, lidar, GNSS, and a ring of cameras with drive-by-wire control, and its listed modes include leader-follower driving, route following, return-to-route, and waypoint patrol. That toolset suits a supply carrier at least as well as a gun truck, and the company's marketing slogan, "Turn any tank into your next UGV," makes the ambition plain.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The raw material exists. France built 3,571 AMX-30 family vehicles between 1966 and 1994, per Defence Blog, and Zone Militaire reports that the army's 12th Matériel Support Base has been dismantling about 50 AMX-30s a year since 2015. Zone Militaire also notes that it could apply the same approach to the Leopard 1A5.
The recycling story has a wrinkle; most coverage describes the demonstrator as a converted AMX-30. KNDS's own press release from the JNI, however, says REFURBOT modernizes and robotizes "an AMX-32 tank," and Army Recognition reported in June that the vehicle on display used a rebuilt AMX-32 prototype hull.
That distinction matters because the AMX-32 never had a fleet to decommission. It was an export derivative of the AMX-30 that failed to attract a buyer, and only two prototypes were ever built.
The demonstrator for a pitch surrounding recycling existing tank fleets therefore appears to sit on one of the rarest French tanks in existence. To be fair, it is a close sibling to the AMX-30, but the conversion has yet to be publicly shown on a vehicle pulled from an actual stockpile.
A mass, mobility and reliability question rolled into one?
The shift toward hauling is the clearest lesson that most modern militaries' tank divisions are learning from Ukraine. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense logged more than 100,000 UGV logistics and evacuation missions in 2026 up to August 20.
The robots doing that work are mostly small: the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade's UGVs carry 200 to 600kg to frontline positions, and Temerland's Gnom L2 tops out at 210kg. A turretless tank hull plays in an entirely different weight class, though neither KNDS nor S2M has published a payload figure.
Mass could also solve a problem small robots keep running into. General Vincent Breton, head of France's joint doctrine center (CICDE), said in 2025 that Ukrainians report their UGVs "overturn fairly regularly" on ground churned up by artillery. A main battle tank's hull would be much more resilient in such situations.
The appeal is obvious: armor, mobility, and internal volume that already exist, are already paid for, and, in some cases, are battle-tested. The open questions are less glamorous but equally concerning: a converted tank inherits a decades-old powertrain and the parts supply that comes with it, which could limit utility, reliability, and efficiency alike.
A tank-sized mule is also a large, hot, noisy target on a battlefield where FPV drones hunt anything that moves. Losing one costs no lives, which is the entire point, but each loss consumes a hull from a pool France has spent a decade shrinking.
Nothing published about REFURBOT answers most of these questions yet, and there is still no price, payload figure, or contract. This is despite tank recycling becoming a global idea; India's army, for example, is seeking industry partners under its iDEX ADITI 4.0 challenge to convert T-72s into remotely operated vehicles, with two validated prototype kits required in the first phase and operational unmanned T-72s targeted by 2030.
KNDS plans to prove REFURBOT through French Army tactical evaluations and the CoHoMa human-machine teaming challenge, according to Zone Militaire. Until those trials produce numbers, the Legion's XXL mule remains a promising prototype whose recycling story still needs a recycled tank.

articles.title: Samsung Taps TSMC for NVHBM Base Die Production
articles.text:
Monday, October 19th 2026
Samsung Taps TSMC for NVHBM Base Die Production
Samsung is reportedly collaborating with the world's largest chip maker, TSMC, to secure a base die supply for NVIDIA's newly announced NVHBM memory standard. NVHBM integrates the controller into the 3D HBM stack, significantly enhancing performance and efficiency. Compared to standard HBM4E, NVIDIA claims up to 30% more memory bandwidth, 15% lower HBM power consumption, and up to 25% more usable compute die area on the processing unit. In simple terms, NVHBM builds on the standard HBM architecture with base die customization, but there are a few strict requirements that must be fulfilled before mass production.
Interestingly, one of the requirements is that NVIDIA's base die in the NVHBM must be manufactured on TSMC's 3 nm node. Even though Samsung has its own 3 nm production lines, NVIDIA's IP is optimized for TSMC's nodes. This forces Samsung to collaborate with TSMC and become a customer, despite having its own production capabilities. However, this arrangement is only for the base die, which integrates directly next to the compute tiles. For memory, Samsung will continue using its sixth-generation 10 nm processes, which are typical for HBM manufacturing. This means that only part of the production will be handled by TSMC.Samsung has already developed advanced technologies like HBM4E, featuring memory speeds of 16 Gbps per pin. This development significantly boosts confidence in Samsung's Semiconductor division, which has been shipping HBM4E with speeds of 14 Gbps per pin since late May of this year. However, Samsung's active participation in the NVHBM rollout signals that customers are seeking more powerful alternatives. Considering the 30% NVHBM bandwidth improvement claimed by NVIDIA, a single NVHBM could theoretically achieve around 5.2 TB/s. On the power side, the 15% reduction in HBM power draw not only improves efficiency but also provides additional thermal headroom for the compute die.

articles.title: Building Physical AI Systems That Can Work in the Real World - EE Times
articles.text:
Physical AI brings AI into machines that must sense their surroundings, make decisions, and act in the physical world. The market opportunity is substantial: McKinsey estimates that AI-powered agents and robots could unlock about $2.9 trillion in annual economic value in the U.S. by 2030. However, realizing this opportunity depends on moving from working prototypes to products that can operate reliably, safely, and economically at scale.
That exposes a different engineering problem. In a prototype, teams can often add more compute, sensors, cooling, or power to prove that a capability works. In deployment, every added capability must fit within the size, weight, power, and cost budget, often abbreviated to SWaP-C, of the system.
Those constraints shape how a robot performs: How long it can operate between charges, how much productive payload it can carry, and how reliably it operates over time. The challenge is not simply adding more intelligence but integrating it effectively into deployable products.
A robot must continuously interpret its surroundings, decide how to respond, and translate those decisions into physical action. Doing that requires capabilities from perception and AI inference to planning and motion control to work together, while meeting different compute and timing requirements.
System constraints shape intelligence
Every physical AI system has a finite design envelope. Processors, batteries, cooling, sensors, actuators, and mechanical components all compete for space, power, thermal headroom, and cost.
In a deployable robot, every gram matters. A larger battery may extend operating time but adds weight and takes up space. More compute can enable more advanced AI models, but places greater demands on cooling and energy.
Consider a quadruped robot navigating challenging terrain. Much of its onboard energy and weight budget must support the basic demands of locomotion, while the same system needs sensing, perception, navigation, and control to operate autonomously. More sophisticated reasoning cannot be added in isolation. It has to fit alongside motors, batteries, sensors, and other components within the same finite system envelope.
This makes physical AI a capability integration exercise. As Arm’s Federico Pecora explains in a recent paper titled The Missing Science of Robotic Systems: Capability Integration in the Model-Centric Era, robot intelligence depends on how perception, planning, control, safety, and orchestration work together across different timing, compute, and memory requirements. The “robot brain” is not only the largest model that runs on an accelerator, but the system architecture that enables these capabilities to work together at the right rates and with the right level of assurance.
The tradeoffs also vary significantly by machine. A quadruped navigating rough terrain, a humanoid manipulating objects, and a stationary industrial robot may all be described as robots, but they require different combinations of capabilities—and different levels of compute performance, energy efficiency, responsiveness, and safety.
As robotic systems become more capable, the industry needs more consistent ways to describe those capabilities and connect them to the underlying system requirements. That is why we are working with the ecosystem to establish a Robotics Capability Framework, which seeks to establish a common language to define and compare intelligent robotic systems.
AI changes the design equation
AI is changing how robotic and autonomous systems are designed. These machines increasingly need to interpret changing environments, respond to live data, and operate predictably as conditions change.
Doing that efficiently requires compute, software, memory, sensors, and safety functions to be planned together. Multiple workloads operate simultaneously with different timing requirements and priorities.
Heterogeneous compute gives engineering teams flexibility to match each workload to the right processing resource. Demanding AI workloads may run on dedicated accelerators, for example, while CPUs coordinate the wider system and microcontrollers handle low-latency control close to the hardware.
The value comes from designing these components as one coordinated system, with workloads running in the right place at the right time, with the right level of priority and isolation.
Deployment makes compute architecture a competitive advantage
Scaling physical AI is about more than raw performance. Every new model, sensor, reasoning layer, or safety function must fit within the available size, weight, power, thermal, memory, and cost envelope.
The systems that scale will extract more intelligence from every watt, coordinate diverse workloads efficiently, and keep safety-critical behavior predictable as AI demands increase. Managing these constraints can extend operating time, preserve productive payload, and make fleets more practical and economical to deploy.
Physical AI will be defined by products that are capable enough to be useful, efficient enough to scale, and predictable enough to trust.

Physical AI Isn’t Just Bigger AI; It’s a Systems Architecture Challenge
