articles.title: Florida DMV hacked after police dept insecurely stored login info
articles.text:
The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) has begun notifying victims impacted by a recent data breach of driver’s license and motor vehicle data, but not everyone whose information was stolen will receive an alert.
In a notice posted Friday, FLHSMV confirmed that it took “immediate steps” after discovering that “a malicious actor accessed certain department records on September 4, 2026, using compromised credentials.” There’s “no evidence” that data has yet been misused, the department said, but law enforcement “determined the information potentially affected includes driver license and motor vehicle data, to include document images, and other personal information.”
FLHSMV is sending out letters to everyone affected, offering victims one year of credit monitoring from Sontiq, Inc. However, the state acknowledged that it may not have current contact information for many former Florida residents whose data was still being stored. Those potential victims can confirm if their data was stolen by emailing FLHSMV at customerinquiry@flhsmv.gov, officials said.
For all current and former Florida residents, FLHSMV recommended taking precautions, including monitoring financial accounts and reviewing credit reports for any suspicious activity. In a thread on the Florida subreddit, several Floridians confirmed that they had already taken officials’ third recommendation and placed “a fraud alert or security freeze with major credit bureaus.”
Some residents complained that they received notice only this week, even though the breach occurred more than a month ago. The breach was previously reported by news outlets.
ShinyHunters linked to hack
On a webpage describing the security incident, FLHSMV confirmed that an “international cybercriminal organization” was behind the breach but did not specify which group or how long they had access. Instead, officials claimed to have “promptly mitigated the breach, launched an investigation, and issued required notification to state authorities.”

articles.title: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool | TechCrunch
articles.text:
On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.
TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.
Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.
TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.
However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.
“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”
AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.
“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.
But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.
Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:
Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.
While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.
Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

articles.title: Video Interview: Applied Materials CEO on the Economics Behind Its $5B EPIC Bet - EE Times
articles.text:
Last week, Applied Materials held a grand unveiling ceremony for its $5 billion EPIC Center, which aims to bring chipmakers, equipment suppliers, and researchers together to accelerate semiconductor R&D and commercialization. The next day, at its investor breakfast session ahead of SEMICON West 2026, the financial strategy behind this center made more sense.
The figures presented speak loud and clear: By 2030, Applied Materials expects to gain more than two percentage points of wafer fab equipment (WFE) market share compared to calendar 2025, while maintaining gross margins of 54% and operating margins of 40% on a non-GAAP basis. The company also projects $2 billion in revenue from its eBeam equipment portfolio in calendar year 2026 and service revenue growth of more than 20% this calendar year, with service revenue exceeding $12 billion by calendar year 2030.
EPIC would be a strong catalyst for this growth. While AI demand is already expected to drive significant growth, a co-innovation lab like EPIC can help Applied Materials align with emerging architectures and get designed in early, ensuring that when those technologies scale, Applied Materials’ equipment is already built into the production line.
Just before the unveiling ceremony on Oct. 12, 2026, EE Times sat down with Applied Materials’ CEO Gary Dickerson to talk about the EPIC Center, the thinking behind it, and how it would operate. He told us, “AI is the most important race in the global economy.” He added, “We will bring companies through the technology stack—all the leading companies, from system companies, design companies, chip companies, material companies, and universities—to accelerate innovation, and it really is accelerating tokens per second per watt from concept to commercialization.”
The key focus of EPIC, he said, is to change the way we innovate. “EPIC is going to bring all of these innovators together, co-locating them together to accelerate innovation.”
The interview is available in full here:
In the interview, he also addressed how Applied Materials would work with partners and customers at EPIC, saying, “We work with all of these companies that are competing with each other, but they’re all in a race. They are all in a race to have better AI compute performance and power; also, a race to be able to ramp the number of good chips per wafer and yield, to close the demand supply gap that exists in the industry today. And so, for us, there’s a focus on innovation velocity but also trusted innovation. We firewall the teams that are connecting with each one of these different companies, and at the foundation of Applied Materials’ strategy is trusted innovation.”
Supporting the co-innovation theme, Applied Materials’ president of its semiconductor products group Prabu Raja said in a press statement, “Materials innovation has outgrown serial development—at today’s atomic-scale dimensions, many materials and materials interfaces behave in entirely new ways, and making them work at industry scale demands coordinated development and integrated solutions.” He said EPIC provides a place where materials, process technology, and equipment can be innovated in parallel, increasing the success rate of new materials and technologies. “Because our customers’ own engineers help optimize the technology before it ever reaches their factory, what leaves EPIC arrives at the fab ready to ramp to high performance and high yield sooner.”
Applied Materials said it expects the EPIC operating model to deliver returns for both sides of the partnerships. Chipmakers gain early access to next-generation materials and equipment, while Applied Materials gains visibility into emerging technology challenges across several generations, informing where the company directs its R&D investments to create value for customers and have its systems and services designed in.
Based on its expectations for semiconductor industry growth, Applied Materials said it is investing to more than double its R&D lab and manufacturing capacity from current levels by 2030. To date, the company has announced 15 EPIC Center partnerships with leading chipmakers, systems companies, equipment partners, and universities. It has also recently expanded its manufacturing infrastructure in Austin, Texas, Singapore, and Treviso, Italy.

articles.title: Finalement, la très belle XPeng P7 va être vendue en Europe
articles.text:
Les amateurs de lignes futuristes vont être ravis. XPeng s’apprête à commercialiser sa berline coupé P7 en Europe. Yu Tao, vice-président du constructeur chinois chargé du marketing, l’a écrit sur le réseau social Weibo, en marge d’une discussion sur le design de la voiture. Le site spécialisé EV a relayé l’information ce lundi 19 octobre.
« Elle est sur le point d’être commercialisée en Europe, et nos collègues européens sont très enthousiastes », a écrit Yu Tao. XPeng n’a donné ni date de lancement, ni marchés, ni prix pour l’Europe. En Chine, la berline est vendue depuis août 2025 et démarre aujourd’hui à 203 800 yuans (environ 27 100 €), contre 219 800 yuans à son lancement.
Présentée à Munich en 2025, déjà avec l’Europe en ligne de mire
Lancée en Chine le 27 août 2025, la deuxième génération de la XPeng P7 n’a plus rien à voir avec l’ancienne. La berline s’est offert une ligne à couper le souffle, futuriste à souhait, dessinée par le designer franco-algérien Rafik Ferrag. Elle a attiré une foule de curieux lors de sa première présentation européenne, au salon IAA de Munich, quelques semaines plus tard, en septembre 2025.
Numerama était présent et nous avons pu nous aussi admirer de près cette P7. Le plaisir avait pourtant un goût amer, car XPeng n’avait rien officialisé pour l’Europe. Sur le salon, son CEO He Xiaopeng expliquait seulement que la marque réfléchissait à accélérer l’arrivée de la P7 sur le continent. La berline jouait plutôt le rôle de vitrine. Les Européens, eux, ont dû se contenter de la plus familiale P7+, lancée en janvier 2026.
Jusqu’à 820 km d’autonomie et une recharge en 11 minutes pour la XPeng P7
On ignore également les motorisations qui pourraient être proposées. En Chine, la P7 est déclinée en propulsion de 367 ch avec une autonomie de 702 km ou 820 km selon la batterie, mesurée en cycle chinois CLTC, nettement plus optimiste que la norme européenne WLTP. La berline existe également en transmission intégrale, forte de 594 ch. Suffisant pour expédier le 0 à 100 km/h en 3,7 secondes. L’autonomie n’est pas en reste, avec 750 km CLTC. Enfin, XPeng annonce une recharge de 10 à 80 % en 11 à 12 minutes.
En Chine, ces performances s’affichent au prix d’une citadine électrique européenne. La P7 démarre à 203 800 yuans (environ 27 100 €) dans sa version d’entrée de gamme et culmine à 301 800 yuans (environ 40 200 €) pour le modèle le plus performant.
Évidemment, quand la berline débarquera en Europe, ces tarifs seront bien différents. Par exemple, la P7+ est vendue l’équivalent d’à peine 25 000 € en Chine, alors qu’elle coûte près de 46 000 € en France.

articles.title: ReactOS, le Windows open source, s'invite sur les partitions NTFS
articles.text:
ReactOS n'est plus limité au FAT32 : le clone open source de Windows peut désormais s'installer sur une partition NTFS. Son nouveau pilote peut d'ailleurs également formater un disque dans ce format.
ReactOS a récemment annoncé que son pilote NTFS était assez abouti pour installer et faire tourner le système. Le projet, toujours en alpha, s'approche peu à peu d'une première bêta.
Un pilote qui installe et formate, mais sans cache ni journal
Le système de fichiers NTFS date de Windows NT 3.1 en 1993, et sa version arrivée avec XP en 2001 est toujours utilisée par la plupart des systèmes Windows. Jusqu'ici, ReactOS devait être installé sur une partition FAT32. Or les développeurs ont pour but de rendre le projet compatible avec les binaires de Windows Server 2003. ReactOS doit donc être capable de faire tourner tels quels les programmes et pilotes de ce système. La tâche était beaucoup trop complexe en restant sur du FAT32.
Et le moins qu'on puisse dire, c'est que le chantier est long. La lecture seule du NTFS est arrivée en 2016, puis le chargeur de démarrage FreeLoader (le programme qui lance ReactOS) a su lire ces partitions en 2022. Il restait à pouvoir installer et utiliser le système dessus, et dix ans plus tard, c'est désormais possible. L'équipe ajoute que le formatage en NTFS est maintenant possible et compatible avec Windows.
Mais les développeurs ne s'avancent pas trop et il reste encore pas mal de travail. Le pilote n'a pas de cache et cela affecte donc les performances puisque le disque sera sollicité plus fréquemment. Notons également l'absence de journalisation. Il manque également la gestion de la sécurité, autrement dit des droits d'accès aux fichiers. Enfin, à ce stade il est évidemment possible de rencontrer des bugs pas encore connus à ce jour.
Fin janvier, pour les 30 ans du projet, l'équipe de ReactOS annonçait travailler sur ce pilote aux côtés d'un nouveau pilote ATA et la prise en charge du multiprocesseur.

articles.title: Data, not chips, will decide India’s AI and biotech future, say deeptech founders
articles.text:
Data, not chips, will decide India’s AI and biotech future, say deeptech founders
Founders of CoreMantle and Loopworm say compute and applications can be replaced, but trusted, context-rich data cannot, and India must take charge of it to scale AI and biotech.
When people talk about technology infrastructure, they usually mean semiconductors, data centres, and AI models. But the layer that decides how well these technologies work is the data underneath them, and India still has to build it.
At a panel discussion on 'The invisible infrastructure of the new tech order' at TechSparks 2026, moderated by Chhavi Mahajan, Chief Content Officer, YourStory, the panellists said India’s advantage will come from owning trusted, context-rich data in fields ranging from language AI to biotech.
Arvind Pani, Founder, CoreMantle, an AI data intelligence startup, said data is the one part of the technology stack that cannot be swapped out. “You can continue to replace compute. You can continue to replace the application, but you cannot replace the data,” he said.
Ankit Bagaria, Co-founder and CEO, Loopworm, an insect biotechnology company, said the gap is especially wide in biopharma, where too much work still happens through trial and error. Better data, he said, could cut the time it takes to bring a product to market.
Bagaria said biotech deserves the same attention as AI, quantum and chips, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic. He noted that India still imports about 73% of its key materials, including active pharmaceutical ingredients and reagents, from China. And although the country supplies a large share of the world’s vaccines by volume, that accounts for only about 5% of the market by value.
“We have operated in the biosimilar space for a very, very long time, where somebody else is discovering the molecules for us,” he said. He argued that India now needs to move into drug discovery.
Pani said the same need for local context applies to language. India’s internet was built for English users, which put up two barriers at once for most citizens, who had to learn the technology and a new language. Only about 4 to 5% of India’s population is comfortable using English alone, he noted.
He added that even English is not a solved problem for AI. Models trained mostly on American English often struggle with Australian or regional accents, and English as spoken across Indian states varies widely. “These are the nuances that nobody else will understand, that India will understand,” he said.
Both panellists agreed that a bigger dataset is not necessarily a better one. Pani said AI models built on smaller amounts of enriched, contextual data outperform those trained on large volumes of raw data. Many Indian language datasets are recorded in studios from scripts, he noted, so models trained on them perform well in controlled settings but fail in real-world conversations.
Bagaria said that across biological data, “it’s garbage in, garbage out.”
Loopworm spent about 12 to 13 months cleaning existing data while building a digital tool that maps the inner workings of the silkworm. The work had to be tailored to Indian silkworm strains and the pathogens that affect them.
Loopworm uses silkworms to produce sustainable animal feed and high-value recombinant proteins.
Bagaria said Loopworm chose silkworm because silk is over 98% protein, which makes the insect one of nature’s most efficient converters of plant leaves into protein. The silkworm has been domesticated for about 4,000 years, its genome was sequenced in 2007, and around 175 institutes in India teach sericulture and related biotech.
He added that this data-led approach has already cut a set of experiments from 10 months and Rs 25 lakh to two and a half months and about Rs 4.5 lakh. “I am sure that in 10 years’ time, all of us would be saying that the largest impact of AI has come on biotech,” he said.
Pani said proprietary data is already becoming a competitive moat. He cited legal AI company Harvey, which has changed both its models and its compute while keeping its domain-specific data as its core advantage.
On what needs to change, Pani said India must design technology for its own needs. He recalled that his previous company brought Indian language support to Android in 2011 through a partnership with Qualcomm, before Google did. “If we continue to think that somebody else is going to solve our problem, then we will always be behind the curve,” he said.
Bagaria welcomed government initiatives such as the BioE3 policy and the Research, Development and Innovation Fund. But he called for more public and foundational funding for basic data generation, such as the in-depth sequencing and characterisation of Indian organisms, because traditional investors are unlikely to fund fundamental science.

articles.title: Renault prépare du lourd pour les Scénic et Rafale électriques : 750 km d’autonomie et charge ultra-rapide à la clé
articles.text:
Renault prépare du lourd pour les Scénic et Rafale électriques : 750 km d’autonomie et charge ultra-rapide à la clé
Renault accélère sur la voiture électrique en développant une nouvelle plateforme bien plus performante pour ses SUV : le Scénic et le Rafale. Une évolution marquante qui promet de transformer la gamme dans les années à venir.
L’endurance des voitures électriques de Renault n’a pas fini de s’améliorer. Pour continuer sa conquête de ce marché, le patron de la marque vient de confirmer que les efforts se concentrent massivement sur le renouvellement des populaires gammes Scénic et Rafale à l’horizon 2028-2030. L’objectif serait d’atteindre les 750 km d’autonomie tout en offrant une recharge rapide digne de ce nom.
Un bond technologique majeur pour les prochains Scénic et Rafale, l’E-Space attendra
Au détour du Salon de l’Auto de Paris 2026, Autocar a eu droit à quelques confidences de Fabrice Cambolive, patron de Renault. Interrogé sur le potentiel lancement de l’E-Space, conceptualisé pour l’occasion, le dirigeant avoue que la marque n’est “pas capable de tout embrasser en même temps” et que ce monospace rétro “n’est pas un projet concret pour le moment”.
Alors que la priorité de 2027 sera le lancement du Trafic E-Tech, il précise la suite du programme : “la prochaine étape après cela sera le renouvellement des Scénic et Rafale, et ensuite nous devrons décider quel sera le prochain Espace”.
Pour ces deux modèles phares, la révolution passera par la nouvelle plateforme RGEV Medium 2.0. Dotée d’une architecture 800 volts, fraîchement inaugurée sur son dernier utilitaire électrique, cette base technique balayera enfin la limite actuelle des 150 kW en courant continu. Concrètement, passer de 10 à 80 % de batterie ne demandera plus que 20 minutes, contre une demi-heure aujourd’hui.
Le rayon d’action grimperait quant à lui jusqu’à 750 km sur le cycle WLTP en version 100 % électrique, voire près de 1 400 km avec un prolongateur d’autonomie. Un bond en avant conséquent alors que les modèles actuels de la gamme atteignent les 625 km pour le Scénic E-Tech Grande Autonomie et 1 000 km pour le Rafale hybride rechargeable.
Fabrice Cambolive assure ensuite que les lignes de son SUV actuel seront conservées, précisant que “le travail que nous avons accompli en termes de design est de qualité, donc le Scénic de nouvelle génération devrait vraiment rester fidèle à ce design”. Il adoptera toutefois un habitacle typé monospace ultra modulable ainsi que le nouvel écran panoramique OpenR sur toute la largeur du tableau de bord, qui équipera lui aussi le futur Rafale aux alentours de 2030.

articles.title: Nikkei discloses third data breach in a month, 1.8M records exposed
articles.text:
Nikkei Inc. disclosed a new data breach, the third in about a month, that exposed 1.83 million personal information records.
The Japanese giant says subsets of the data contained personally identifiable information and other sensitive details, but most records contained no identifying info.
The company said that 150,000 records contained at least one of the following data types: full names, email addresses, physical addresses, telephone numbers, and dates of birth. Email addresses appeared in 120,000 records.
The remaining 1.68 million records contain no identifiers, the company said, and no credit card information was exposed.
Nikkei Inc. is a major Japanese business news and financial information group, owner of Financial Times, the country’s largest business-focused media company.
The company employs over 10,100 people and has an annual revenue of $2.5 billion (¥393.8 billion).
According to a notice Nikkei published late last week, hackers used stolen credentials to access a development system within its network during the early morning hours of October 7.
The unauthorized access exposed personal information the company stored in the cloud.
Nikkei revoked the abused credentials and notified the Personal Information Protection Commission on October 11.
The company is currently examining the scope of the breach and noted that as of October 16, it had no evidence that the accessed information was misused or leaked online.
The company has also found no signs of system compromise or data tampering resulting from this incident, and has experienced no service outages.
The firm said those affected will receive individual notifications.
“We are working urgently to establish the extent of the damage and determine the cause, and will implement the necessary measures to strengthen security,” Nikkei stated.
This is the third cybersecurity incident that Nikkei disclosed recently. Earlier this month, the company disclosed a breach that occurred in late July, when hackers compromised an employee's Google Workspace account and accessed personal information belonging to employees and business partners.
In September, Nikkei announced that threat actors hijacked another employee’s Microsoft 365 account and used it to send spear-phishing emails to the firm’s staff.
BleepingComputer has contacted Nikkei for more information about the latest breach, and we will update this post once we receive a response.

articles.title: « C'est de l'argent public qui a été investi » : 3 bus à hydrogène à 1,7 million d’euros vont finir à la casse en France
articles.text:
En 2016, la communauté d’agglomération Castres-Mazamet (Tarn) a acheté trois bus à hydrogène fabriqués par l’entreprise locale Safra. Coût total pour ces trois bus : 1,7 million d’euros, dont plus de 500 000 euros de subventions de l’État. Après avoir été mis en circulation en 2018 et roulé moins de 5 000 km dans le réseau Libellus, ils finiront à la casse.
Trois bus achetés pour 1,7 millions d’euros, une destination : la casse
Autant dire que les trois bus à hydrogène fournis par l’entreprise Safra semblent ne pas avoir été à la hauteur des attentes. Comme le rapporte Franceinfo, Olivier Fabre, maire de Mazamet et président de la communauté d’agglomération Castres-Mazamet, explique : « Les bus n’ont jamais fonctionné. Ils ont très peu roulé. À chaque sortie, ils plantaient et tombaient en panne au bord de la route ». Son constat est sans appel : « C’est de l’argent public qui a été investi. On est victime de la défaillance de cette entreprise qui nous a fait de belles promesses. On s’est fait avoir ! ».
En septembre dernier, lors d’un conseil communautaire, la collectivité à donc voté la mise à la casse de ces trois bus à hydrogène. Une entreprise spécialisée va maintenant se charger de désosser les véhicules et de recycler leurs différents composants. Coût de cette nouvelle opération : 7.500 €, à la charge de la communauté d’agglomération.
Un remboursement impossible et un nouvel investissement dans des bus thermiques
L’agglomération a déposé un recours devant le tribunal administratif de Toulouse pour obtenir le remboursement des 1,7 million d’euros investis pour acquérir les trois bus à hydrogène, sans succès. Pour cause, en février 2025, l’entreprise Safra a été placée en redressement judiciaire. Elle est aujourd’hui officiellement tombée en faillite, mais a été reprise par le groupe chinois Wanrun, fin mai 2026.
Quoi qu’il en soit, la demande de remboursement ne semble pas aboutir, comme l’explique Olivier Fabre : « C’est impossible d’obtenir le remboursement. Personne ne répond ». Il regrette d’ailleurs que « cette histoire ternit l’image des véhicules électriques ». En fin de compte, les trois bus à hydrogène vont être remplacés par des bus thermiques, facturés 1,1 million d’euros, et « beaucoup plus fiables », selon le maire. Au total, il est donc question d’un investissement de près de trois millions d’euros pour trois bus, aux frais du contribuable.

Para solucionar este problema sin gastar demasiado ni hacer obras, en Ikea puedes comprar el organizador de cables FÖRSÄSONG, disponible por tan solo 7,99 euros.

articles.title: La pareja de Elizabeth Holmes recaudó USD 20 millones para una startup que evoca a Theranos
articles.text:
Billy Evans, pareja de la fundadora de Theranos Elizabeth Holmes, recaudó hasta USD 20 millones para una startup de diagnóstico médico llamada Haemanthus, según documentos revisados por The New York Times y citados por Wired. La empresa busca testear sangre, orina y saliva con un aparato de mesa.
El propio Evans se resiste al apodo que la prensa y hasta él mismo mencionan: “Theranos 2.0”. En un comunicado público, Haemanthus afirmó que “no es Theranos 2.0” y que su enfoque es “un paradigma diferente”, no una mejora de la tecnología que llevó a Holmes a prisión.
Sin embargo, en el documental You Can See Everything, dirigido por Nathan Fielder y Lance Oppenheim, Evans acepta esa comparación frente a cámara mientras discute con Holmes ideas de producto para la compañía, según reconstruyó Wired. “Podría pensar que esto fue lo más estúpido que hice”, dijo el heredero hotelero sobre su participación en el filme, en declaraciones al podcast All-In conducido por David Friedberg.
Una tecnología distinta a la de Theranos
Si bien Haemanthus fue fundada formalmente en 2024, Evans comenzó a trabajarla de manera oculta a finales de 2022. Apenas tiene presencia pública: no publicó productos y su perfil en LinkedIn es mínimo, indicó Wired. La compañía obtuvo una patente el 21 de enero de 2025 para un sistema basado en espectroscopía Raman, una técnica que analiza cómo la luz rebota en una muestra biológica para detectar patrones moleculares.
A diferencia de Theranos, que intentó miniaturizar análisis de laboratorio existentes a partir de una gota de sangre, la nueva startup plantea usar luz láser para leer información molecular que las pruebas actuales no detectan, de acuerdo con el comunicado de la empresa citado por Wired.
Eric Potma, profesor de química de la Universidad de California en Irvine y consultor de la compañía, explicó a la recista que “los ingenieros de Haemanthus son legítimos y están llevando la detección por Raman hacia direcciones interesantes”. Aclaró que su vínculo como asesor le impide profundizar más en los detalles técnicos.
El dinero y la falta de supervisión
Según The New York Times, Haemanthus había recibido el año pasado una inversión de USD 3,5 millones de “amigos y familia”. Wired reporta que esa cifra creció hasta unos USD 20 millones. La empresa les dijo a sus inversores que perfeccionar el sistema láser y llevarlo a un dispositivo portátil del tamaño de una estampilla demandaría tres años y USD 70 millones adicionales.
Materiales de presentación revisados por The New York Times sugirieron a inversores que la compañía no enfrentaría “ninguna supervisión regulatoria”, en parte porque el aparato se probaría primero en enfermedades veterinarias. El diario confirmó con el Departamento de Agricultura de Estados Unidos que esa agencia sí regula los diagnósticos veterinarios.
Evans manifestó a Times que la empresa está “en modo sigiloso” y que seguirá así: “No van a encontrar nada asociado con el nombre Haemanthus”. Las direcciones vinculadas a la empresa corresponden en su mayoría a viviendas particulares en un barrio de Austin, Texas, y empleados contactados por Wired se negaron a confirmar su rol.
Quién es el hombre detrás de la empresa
Evans se graduó en economía en el MIT y trabajó en LinkedIn y en Luminar Technologies, una empresa de sensores para autos autónomos, antes de fundar Haemanthus. Conoció a Holmes en 2017, durante un evento benéfico en la bahía de San Francisco, y la describió en una carta al juez como alguien que lo “cautivó” con su “asombro infantil”.
Esa carta fue una de varias que familiares y amigos enviaron antes de la sentencia de Holmes en 2022, cuando un tribunal la condenó a 11 años y tres meses de prisión por fraude contra inversores de Theranos. Una corte de apelaciones confirmó esa condena.
Según una persona cercana al negocio citada por The Wall Street Journal, Holmes no tiene ningún rol formal en Haemanthus. Wired también consignó que, en la documentación de constitución de la empresa, el nombre de Holmes no figura en ningún lado. Pese a eso, NPR había informado en 2025 que Holmes asesoraba a Evans sobre la startup desde la prisión federal donde cumple condena en Bryan, Texas, aunque la naturaleza exacta de ese asesoramiento nunca quedó clara.
Wired señaló que, de acuerdo con reportes periodísticos, Holmes podría trasladarse a una casa de transición el año próximo. Mientras tanto, Haemanthus sigue sin mostrar un producto terminado ni abrir su sitio web al público. El contraste entre el hermetismo de la empresa y la decisión de Evans de participar en un documental de varios años de filmación llamó la atención de Wired, que describió esa combinación como poco habitual para una compañía que se define a sí misma como secreta.

articles.title: Anciens HomePod : Apple leur offre deux nouveautés du HomePod mini 2 avec la mise à jour 27.2, sauf au tout premier modèle — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les propriétaires d’un HomePod 2 ou d’un premier HomePod mini vont récupérer deux fonctions présentées il y a à peine une semaine comme des nouveautés du HomePod mini 2.
Tout apparaît dans la dernière mise à jour 27.2 des enceintes. On apprend donc que les lumières synchronisées avec la musique et le verrouillage des commandes tactiles arrivent aussi sur ces anciens modèles. La version est en bêta pour les développeurs et les testeurs publics, et sa sortie est attendue la semaine du 26 octobre. Vous n’aurez pas à racheter d’enceinte, mais il faudra aussi mettre votre iPhone à jour.
    Pour aller plus loin
Test de l’Apple HomePod 2 : caisson de basses et son à 360°
            
Apple a dévoilé ces deux fonctions le 13 octobre, en même temps que le HomePod mini 2, avec sa puce S10 et Siri AI. L’annonce faisait partie d’une salve de nouveaux produits pour la maison connectée. Le nouveau modèle sort le 30 octobre. Les anciens devraient donc recevoir ses fonctions presque en même temps.
Des lumières aux couleurs de la pochette et un verrou tactile
La première fonction s’appelle Sound Glow en anglais. Apple la décrit dans son communiqué du 13 octobre : le dessus de l’enceinte s’allume et pulse au rythme de la musique. Il réagit en temps réel aux basses et aux aigus. Les couleurs reprennent celles de la pochette de l’album en cours de lecture. C’est une fonction qu’on aurait pu imaginer depuis très longtemps, et même dès la commercialisation de l’enceinte.
Les lumières suivent aussi les podcasts et les bruits d’ambiance, comme la pluie. On les active dans les réglages de l’enceinte, dans l’application Maison. On peut aussi passer par le centre de contrôle de l’Apple TV si les HomePod y sont associés. Apple précise en note que seule la commande vocale de l’effet exige un iPhone compatible Apple Intelligence.
La seconde fonction, Lock Controls, désactive complètement la surface tactile en haut de l’enceinte. Le but est d’éviter les commandes involontaires des enfants, des animaux ou d’un passant qui frôle l’enceinte (les propriétaires de chats comprendront).
Une fois le verrou activé dans l’application Maison, l’enceinte ignore les appuis courts, les appuis longs et les touches de volume. Vous pouvez quand même lancer et régler la musique avec Siri, avec l’application Maison ou en AirPlay depuis un autre appareil Apple. Les deux réglages sont indépendants : on peut verrouiller l’enceinte sans allumer les lumières. Cette option fait partie des nouveautés repérées dans la bêta d’iOS 27.2 pour le HomePod.
    Pour aller plus loin
iOS 27.2 : cette nouveauté repérée dans la bêta va corriger le défaut le plus agaçant du HomePod
            
Le HomePod de 2018 reste sur le carreau
Parmi les anciens modèles, seuls le HomePod (2e génération), sorti début 2023, et le premier HomePod mini, lancé fin 2020, reçoivent ces deux fonctions. Le HomePod original de 2018 n’y a pas droit, alors qu’il a lui aussi une surface tactile. Pour voir les nouveaux réglages dans l’application Maison, votre iPhone doit tourner sous iOS 27.2.
Par contre, le premier HomePod mini n’aura pas les deux autres nouveautés de la version 27.2. La première permet de choisir un HomePod comme sortie audio par défaut du Mac. Elle demande un HomePod mini 2 ou un HomePod 2, et un Mac équipé du Wi-Fi 6E (la version du Wi-Fi qui ajoute la bande des 6 GHz).
La seconde crée un son surround à quatre enceintes avec le nouvel Apple TV 4K, vendu 349 euros et livré à partir du 13 novembre. Il faut quatre HomePod mini 2, quatre HomePod 2, ou une paire de chaque : une paire à l’avant, l’autre à l’arrière.

articles.title: Data centre vs Cloud platform: Is there a difference?
articles.text:
You have probably seen the words “data centre” and “cloud” used interchangeably. They don’t mean the same thing, and the difference matters. It shapes how businesses buy technology, how regulators write rules and where investors see opportunity.
A data centre is a building. It is a secure, purpose-built facility with reliable power, cooling, security and internet connections, so that computers can run around the clock. A cloud platform is a service. It is software that lets customers rent computing power, storage, and networking on demand, switch them on or off themselves, and pay only for what they use.
Think of an airport and an airline. The airport provides the runway, fuel, and terminal; the airline provides the service you actually book. Every cloud platform runs inside a data centre, but most data centres do not offer a cloud platform. Owning an airport does not make you an airline.
Data centre grading and cloud computing standards
Companies that rent space for their own servers in someone else’s facility are buying what the industry calls “colocation”. A facility’s reliability is rated on a four-level scale from the Uptime Institute.
Tier I has no backup equipment, so any fault results in downtime. Tier II adds spares but has a single path for power and cooling.
Tier III has more than one path, so any part can be serviced without switching anything off; it is the level most serious operators aim for. Tier IV survives any single failure.
Be careful, though: “built to Tier III standards” is not the same as certified, so ask which certificate a provider actually holds.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology defines cloud computing by five features: customers can provision resources themselves, access them over the internet, share the provider’s pool of equipment, scale capacity up or down quickly, and pay only for what they use.
A bank that runs virtualised software in a rented cage has a more efficient setup, but it only becomes a cloud when self-service, automation, and metering are added.
Why this matters for Nigeria
Customers spent US$143.4 billion on cloud infrastructure in the second quarter of 2026 alone, with Amazon, Microsoft, and Google capturing about 63 per cent of that spending. None of them runs a full cloud region in Nigeria.
Amazon has a smaller facility called a Local Zone in Lagos, but for Microsoft, Google, and Oracle, the nearest full regions are in South Africa. So when a Nigerian bank says its data is “in the cloud”, that data is often outside the country.
That is why the Central Bank of Nigeria’s order to keep payment data on local infrastructure by 1 January 2027 puts this distinction at the centre of the debate. Moving data home requires local data centres and local cloud platforms that offer the ease, scale, and reliability banks expect. Operators such as MTN, which launched cloud services alongside a new Tier III data centre in Lagos in 2025, are starting to fill that gap.
Power and progress in Nigerian infrastructure
A Tier III data centre is built on the assumption that the public grid will fail. Rack Centre in Lagos runs entirely off-grid on its own 13.5 MW gas-powered system and reports 100 per cent uptime since 2013. Where electricity does matter is cost: generating your own power is expensive, and that shows up in prices. That is a real competitiveness issue, but a different story from “Nigerian data centres keep going down because of NEPA.”
When I chose a data centre for a bank’s workloads in 2012, there was only one commercial option worth serious consideration. Rack Centre in Ikeja opened in 2013 and later became the first facility in Nigeria and West Africa to win Uptime Institute Tier III design certification.
Today, industry counts put Nigeria at around 26 operational data centres, about 28 including those being built, with 210 to 300 MW of capacity expected by 2030. In my experience, the leading operators have not lost a minute of service to a power failure.
A data centre is the foundation; a cloud platform is what you build on it. Nigeria now has a strong, professionally run foundation. The next challenge, made urgent by data localisation and demand for AI, is building cloud platforms on top of it.
Policymakers, journalists, and business leaders should ask not only “Do we have enough data centres?” but “Do we have cloud platforms to make them useful?”
Remi Adejumo is a Cloud and Infrastructure Architect with over 20 years’ experience in cloud computing, data centres, virtualisation, and enterprise IT transformation across the UK, the US, and Africa.

articles.title: JEP 543 Finalizes Structured Concurrency in JDK 28, Ending Seven Preview Rounds
This mod lets Nvidia GeForce owners run a custom VBIOS without flashing the card
articles.text:
Enthusiast zone: Nvidia's signed firmware has kept BIOS modding off the table for GeForce owners for the most part. A new set of tools sidesteps that lock rather than breaking it, loading a custom VBIOS through the driver itself. It reopens a door enthusiasts thought was closed, but it arrives on a platform where power connectors are already at risk of melting on high-end GPUs and a single driver update could shut it down. Proceed carefully.
A developer has released three tools that let GeForce RTX 30, 40 and 50 series owners run a modified VBIOS without writing to the card's flash chip: a VBIOS editor for Windows and Linux, plus separate loaders for each operating system.
The cool trick is that nothing gets flashed. On Windows, the loader stores the edited image in the GPU's driver registry key, a spot where Nvidia's driver already checks for a VBIOS override every time the device starts. The tool then restarts the GPU, and the driver's GSP firmware boots from the custom image instead of the one on the card.
The Linux version takes a different route, patching Nvidia's open kernel modules so the GSP firmware starts with the custom image. Both projects build on earlier override research, which the developer credits directly.
The editor exposes settings overclockers have wanted back for years: board power limits, voltage ceilings, clock offset ranges, 12V input current and output overcurrent protections, fan PWM frequency and fan channels. Blackwell cards get the full set, while Ada and Ampere images are limited to fields the developer has validated.
The numbers shared so far are aggressive. On what appears to be an RTX 5090 FE, the board power ceiling rose from 600 W to 700 W and the NVVDD and MSVDD voltage ceilings from 1,110 mV to 1,150 mV. An RTX 4090 had its power limit raised to 671 W, confirmed by nvidia-smi, up from 550 W. In the developer's own testing, an RTX 5090 reached 800 W, an RTX 5080 went from 360 W to 500 W, and an RTX 5060 Ti from 185 W to 300 W.
It works in both directions, too. On an RTX A2000, the loader dropped the card's power floor to just 5 W, and the developer says voltages can be lowered to a hard floor of roughly 0.4 to 0.45V depending on the GPU generation. That makes the tools just as interesting for anyone who wants a cooler, quieter card with an undervolt baked in rather than applied by Afterburner at every boot.
No flashing means no bricked card from a failed write, but of course, it doesn't make the hardware any tougher. The 12V-2x6 connector on these cards is rated for 600 W, and there have been plenty of reports of RTX 5090 connectors melting at stock settings. Pushing 800 W through one is a big gamble, and with RTX 5090 and 5080 supply tight and warranty claims unlikely to cover a modded card, a dead GPU won't be easy to replace. The developer advises keeping a copy of the original ROM and testing on a GPU that isn't driving the display, and documents a Safe Mode recovery path, since Nvidia's driver doesn't load there.
As for how long this will last, the developer isn't optimistic, saying that Nvidia will very likely patch the method he's using in upcoming drivers and urging users to enjoy it while they can. Meanwhile, some enthusiasts are thrilled to see BIOS editing return, others want it purely for undervolting, and plenty are already joking about how many cards will die before Nvidia closes the gap.

articles.title: Chefe do Instagram admite que ainda não sabe como combater deep fakes • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Chefe do Instagram admite que ainda não sabe como combater deep fakes
Perfis usam avatares gerados por inteligência artificial para reproduzir conteúdo original.
O chefe do Instagram, Adam Mosseri, reconheceu que a rede social ainda não tem uma solução para perfis que reproduzem conteúdo usando deep fakes criados por IA. A prática tem sido relatada ao executivo por criadores no próprio Instagram, segundo o jornal britânico The Independent.
Um dos casos foi apontado pelo comediante norte-americano George Brett Olson, que encontrou uma conta que publicou uma de suas apresentações usando, no lugar dele, um avatar feminino gerado por IA. O vídeo mantinha o áudio e o texto da apresentação, mas a imagem foi substituída pelo deep fake.
O executivo da rede social afirmou estar “muito preocupado” com a prática, mas descartou uma proibição geral de conteúdos produzidos com a tecnologia e disse que discutiria medidas com a equipe da plataforma.
Segundo Olson, o mesmo tipo de conteúdo vem aparecendo em outros segmentos. Há perfis que usam vídeos de dançarinos como base para gerar gravações nas quais personagens criados por IA reproduzem as coreografias, por exemplo.
O perfil que reproduziu a apresentação do comediante tinha mais de 300 mil seguidores e direcionava usuários para uma página no OnlyFans. Outro perfil, citado pela também comediante Julia Jasunas, reunia cerca de 250 mil seguidores.
Mosseri respondeu diretamente à publicação de Olson no Instagram. Segundo o executivo, a Meta está preocupada com esses perfis, mas uma proibição ampla de conteúdo de IA não seria prática. “Vai ficar cada vez mais difícil de identificar, e nem todo conteúdo é ruim, embora haja muito lixo”, escreveu Mosseri.
Ele afirmou ainda que o Instagram pretende direcionar mais tráfego aos autores originais e reconheceu que a plataforma precisa avaliar como agir quando conteúdos são cópias integrais de produções desses autores. Há exemplos em redes vizinhas: o X, de Elon Musk, mudou recentemente seu algoritmo de recomendação para limitar o alcance de conteúdo copiado e promoveu mudanças no sistema de monetização para privilegiar criações originais.
Em outro comentário, Mosseri abordou as ferramentas disponíveis para solicitar a remoção de conteúdos. A plataforma permite denúncias por violação de direitos autorais, mas, segundo o executivo, o mecanismo nem sempre resolve as situações citadas pelos criadores.
Segundo ele, muitos criadores podem não ter tomado medidas formais relacionadas à proteção dos próprios trabalhos e que a rede precisa encontrar uma maneira “de ajudar esses criadores sem permitir que agentes mal-intencionados façam mais denúncias falsas”. Isso, de acordo com o executivo, “acontece o tempo todo”.
Mosseri abordou anteriormente essa encruzilhada no tratamento à IA na plataforma. Ele já disse que conteúdos gerados por inteligência artificial não deveriam aparecer para quem não demonstra interesse por eles, mas negou que os usuários devessem ter controle para bloqueá-los — isso continua a cargo do algoritmo.

articles.title: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent that has been gaining ground among developers as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight, affecting 1.4% of users of its online platform, OpenCode Console, where some users store the API keys, or digital passwords, they use to access AI services.
As the OpenCode team struggled to keep pace with the attack, the scramble to respond highlighted a growing problem: Companies without vetted access to AI models with fewer safety restrictions have a hard time defending against large-scale, AI-driven cyberattacks.
“We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the company wrote on X. “We have notified them all this morning via email.” Users who did not receive an email were not impacted, the company said.
While the company didn’t specify how the distillation attack occurred, leaked API keys can help users in countries with restricted access to American models generate the high volume of outputs needed for that process. Some skeptics called the framing an overstretch, arguing that the incident was a straightforward breach whose use for distillation remains unproven.
Overnight, developers began posting spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X: “I saw my Open AI, Anthropic, and Google AI spend alerts all fire off before going to bed wondering what was going on,” a developer wrote.
Other users reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on individual accounts; a few described totals above $1,000.
Anthropic and Google both blocked the API keys they believed were exposed, while OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode said refunds for unauthorized charges are underway.
The exposed keys were confined to Console, where some users had them in workspaces. The open source app and command-line tool were not affected, according to co-founder Dax Raad. “Note this is the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself, those keys never come to us,” he wrote on X.
Even as users and AI companies moved to disable the exposed keys, the OpenCode team was still under pressure. Raad said attackers had been trying to break into its systems nonstop for 48 hours, requiring the team to keep AI defensive agents running around the clock. AI models that the OpenCode team turned to for analysis helped for a while, but started refusing to work when the malicious code they were asked to examine activated safety filters.
“[T]hat was a bit frustrating,” he wrote on X.
OpenCode later received access to OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users AI models that are less likely to refuse requests for defensive security work. Raad said the access improved the team’s ability to investigate the attack.
OpenCode isn’t the first company to hit this wall. In July, AI platform Hugging Face said commercial AI models blocked its attempts to analyze activity logs from an intrusion by autonomous AI agents, which OpenAI later revealed were its own models running with safeguards lowered during a test. In a section of its blog post titled “The asymmetry problem,” Hugging Face wrote that guardrails “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.”
Security researchers have raised similar complaints, saying the restrictions are inconsistent and have pushed some toward foreign open-weight models, which anyone can download and run.
The weekend episode drew a response from David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
“OpenCode (and earlier Hugging Face) hit the same wall mid-attack: frontier models refused to analyze the very exploits needed for defense because the payloads tripped safety filters. The guardrails backfired,” he wrote on X.
The breach occurred the same night OpenCode made GLM-5.3-Flash free for users. The broader GLM-5.3 family has drawn attention from researchers who study open-weight models and note that its cybersecurity capabilities approached levels previously associated with restricted-access models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview.
OpenCode has not detailed how attackers gained access to the older system, how keys were stored, or the full extent of any misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. The company said the incident remains ongoing.
The breach lands amid a run of AI-enabled cyber incidents. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said a China-based hacker likely used an AI penetration-testing agent, which probes computer systems for weaknesses, and Claude in attacks on South Korean banks. Last week, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that AI agents, including some being tested by AI companies, had reached Indian organizations’ systems without authorization.

articles.title: ORICO Enters Laptop Market With Obook 15 AI Laptop
articles.text:
Monday, October 19th 2026
ORICO Enters Laptop Market With Obook 15 AI Laptop
ORICO, usually known for its storage and connectivity solutions, is officially entering the PC market with its first laptop design, the Obook 15 AI Laptop. For this initial design, the company has chosen AMD's Ryzen 7 6800H SoC, an eight-core, 16-thread mobile processor that can boost up to 4.7 GHz. The integrated Radeon 680M graphics handle visuals, and memory configurations include options of 12 GB or 24 GB running at 6,400 MT/s. Buyers can select up to a 1 TB NVMe SSD, and a second M.2 slot allows for storage expansion up to 4 TB. While not running the latest SoCs from AMD, the system wants to be a competitive solution price-wise. Obook 15 runs on Windows 11 out of the box and features a cooling system with selectable Eco, Normal, and Performance modes for fan profiles.
The Obook 15 boasts a 15.6-inch IPS display with a 1,920 x 1,080 resolution, an anti-glare finish, 170-degree viewing angles, and wide-frequency dimming. It includes Wi-Fi 6, a 54.29 Wh battery, and a bundled 100 W charger. Additional features include a 180-degree hinge, a physical webcam shutter, a full-size keyboard with a number pad, and a wide selection of ports. ORICO lists US prices starting at $689.99 for the version with 12 GB of RAM and a 256 GB SSD. A 12 GB/512 GB version is priced at $749.99, while the top configuration with 24 GB of memory and 1 TB of storage costs $899.99. The Obook 15 is now available in the United States and the Philippines, targeting students, office users, and content creators with its attractive price points, especially for this day and age, amid memory and storage shortages.ORICO is also focusing on software as a key feature of the product. The included XiaoAo AI Super Agent combines 11 specialized AI assistants, which the company claims can help automate workflows, manage a knowledge base, and control devices remotely. The usefulness of these capabilities in everyday work will depend on their implementation, but ORICO aims to make the Obook 15 stand out from conventional productivity notebooks.

articles.title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
articles.text:
This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand—potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology, and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations.
In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.
The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.
The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “reverse acquihire,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.
Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.
In the case of Character.AI, a motion filed by Character.AI’s legal counsel says that Disney required that the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy proceedings because of the startup’s “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.”
A spokesperson for Character.AI referred WIRED to Disney for comment on whether the deal was contingent on the startup declaring bankruptcy. Disney declined to comment on this story.
According to court filings, the deal involves “two interrelated and integrated” transactions—one before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, and one after.
As part of the first transaction, which occurred in September, Disney paid the startup $5.5 million, along with a refundable “good faith deposit” of $2 million. Disney also hired the “majority” of Character.AI’s employees, including the CEO, and agreed that it would let some of the now-Disney employees help keep Character.AI operational for five months.
Character.AI filed a petition for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12. Through the bankruptcy proceedings, court filings show that Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license for a huge range of Character.AI’s code, documentation, frameworks, tools, and “other artifacts,” including those produced for its trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure, and age-prediction technology. The list of IP included in the filings does not include users’ data (which can get additional protections in bankruptcy proceedings) or Character.AI’s website.
That license will be auctioned off in the coming months. If Disney is chosen as the winning bidder by Character.AI and a committee of unsecured creditors—and courts approve the deal—it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment. If Disney is not selected, the company will be refunded the $2 million deposit and receive a breakup fee.
In order to “preserve a competitive process,” Disney also agreed to permit the winning bidder to interview and potentially extend offers to up to 80 percent of “certain newly hired employees” that Disney already hired from Character.AI. Disney has the right to select which employees.
However, experts worry that bouncing Character.AI employees from one company to another in the span of months is unrealistic, and that the deal Disney and Character.AI have struck cannot be easily unwound.
In addition, Disney prepared a draft of a court order referred to as the “363 Free and Clear Order” in the filings, a version of which would be approved by the court at or before closing, that would clarify that this process should not be viewed as a merger of the two companies and that Character.AI would remain responsible for “any liability or other obligation” it might have, including any legal claims against it.
A spokesperson for Character.AI said they were unable to speculate on the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings and referred WIRED to the docket.
“There’s decades of corporate law that developed to deal with the problem of a buyer who always wants to take on all the assets and never wants to take on any of the liability,” says John Newman, a law professor at the University of Memphis School of Law and a former deputy director of the Federal Trade Commission’s Bureau of Competition. But the Disney-Character.AI deal is extremely unusual and structured in a way, he says, that “all those corporate law safeguards really weren’t built to guard against.”
Not its first rodeo
This isn’t even Character.AI’s first reverse acquihire.
In August 2024, Google reportedly paid the startup $2.7 billion to license its technology. A spokesperson tells WIRED that that license was for the existing AI technology at the time of the deal, and that Google also hired Character.AI’s founders and other members of its ML pre-training research team, but that the “vast majority” of the startup’s employees remained at the company.
In the following years, Google was named alongside Character.AI as a defendant in multiple lawsuits, including one that alleged a 14-year-old boy committed suicide after Character.AI’s chatbot “cultivated an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship.”
Google argued that because it was still a separate company from Character.AI, it was not responsible for the teen’s death, which it said occurred prior to Google’s licensing deal. The judge was not persuaded, determining that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged that Google was liable for aiding and abetting.
Google declined to comment for this story.
In January of this year, Google and Character.AI agreed in principle to settle that and a slew of similar lawsuits. “Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards,” Character.AI said in a statement at the time.
According to an order of dismissal in one of the cases, the overall settlement was approved by a California probate court in July, and the court tasked a referee to hear out all the issues pertaining to each individual settlement. On October 11, a day before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, the referee approved each settlement.
The Tech Justice Law Project and Social Media Victims Law Center, which represented plaintiffs in many of the lawsuits, declined to comment.
Despite losing key staff after the Google transaction and, according to the current CEO, struggling with profitability “at all times,” Character.AI continued to develop AI tools, including “real-time audio-driven FaceTime-style video generation with fictional characters,” according to the current CEO’s declaration.
In August 2025, Character.AI worked with an investment banker to try to find either a strategic buyer or investor. According to the bankruptcy filings, Character.AI and the banker received “consistent feedback” that its product and user base were “impressive,” but that the surrounding litigation and “regulatory overhang” made it unbuyable.
That November, Character.AI learned that a coalition of state attorneys general had started investigating the company. When the company filed for bankruptcy, the number of states and territories involved in the multistate investigation had climbed to 46.
According to a notice of interest filed in the bankruptcy proceedings by the National Association of Attorneys General on behalf of 40 states, those states’ investigations uncovered “serious issues” with Character.AI, including screenshots of Character.AI chatbots encouraging minors to hide their self-harm injuries and kill their parents.
A spokesperson for Character.AI says that the filing “is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform.”
The filings say that Character.AI was in the process of negotiating with the states over how to address the issues they identified, but did not reach any agreements before declaring bankruptcy.
If the deal is completed and approved by the courts, Disney will have both Character.AI’s staff and much of its technology stack, but will be able to sidestep the ongoing legal issues that contributed to Character.AI’s downfall, including the multistate investigation.
The states who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy have made it clear that they reserve their rights to challenge any bankruptcy plan, potentially setting up a fight over the ultimate outcome of the bankruptcy.
“It’s bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility,” says Newman. “And that’s what it looks like.”

articles.title: French rioters ransack eSports team premises and are seen looting RAM sticks from PCs — Team Vitality’s ‘V.Hive’ Paris HQ was wrecked during unrest
articles.text:
French rioters ransack eSports team premises and are seen looting RAM sticks from PCs — Team Vitality’s ‘V.Hive’ Paris HQ was wrecked during unrest
Reports also highlight eSports trophies being stolen, with gaming chairs being piled up in street fires.
Leading French eSports club Team Vitality has confirmed that its Paris HQ has been smashed up, with trophies, computer equipment, and more looted over the weekend. Thankfully, no team members or staff have been hurt. The team’s V.Hive premises were attacked by criminal opportunistic looters under cover of the widespread protests in France over issues related to school funding, living costs, and government spending cuts. Other shops, public buildings, and property have been smashed, looted, and sometimes burned.
Above, you can see the confirmation of the serious, unfortunate events seen over the weekend. “Our display windows were destroyed, and our trophies and computer equipment were stolen,” lamented the post [machine translation], while being thankful that no members, staff, or fans of Team Vitality were hurt. The bulletin ends with the news that the V.Hive will remain closed for now, until after damage has been assessed. More information is promised in due course.
There are a multitude of social media posts sharing images, videos, and pointing fingers at what they see as the cause of the protests, riots, and looting. Of course, fingers point in all directions, and unfortunately there are also reports of AI-generated rage-farming media, so keep a critical eye open should you dare to doom scroll.
Of course we’ve focused on the damage and looting of Team Vitality’s HQ due to the tech angle. The compendium of video clips shared by the news organization NEXTA provides evidence of the extent of the V.Hive attack. This 30-second clip appears to show rioters hammering at and kicking in the eSports HQ’s windows, taking items from the premises, and throwing gaming chairs onto bonfires in the street.
We also see accounts like ElBuni share clips of looters brandishing what appear to be eSports trophies from Team Vitality’s HQ (embedded above). The second clip shows looters with their hands inside gaming PCs opened up on the sidewalk. It looks like the hooded and gloved looter in the video is removing RAM sticks, an easily pocketable yet highly valuable PC component, as you will all know.
This morning, the French Prime Minister has called for local and partial curfews to contain the post-demonstration rioting. Meanwhile, there are concerns that there could be copycat behavior across Europe.

articles.title: Hacker übernehmen CDU-Mailkonto und verschicken 6.500 Phishing-Nachrichten – auch an Kanzler Merz
articles.text:
Hacker übernehmen CDU-Mailkonto und verschicken 6.500 Phishing-Nachrichten – auch an Kanzler Merz
In den vergangenen Tagen haben zahlreiche Politiker:innen der CDU eine oder sogar mehrere E-Mails erhalten, auf die sie lieber nicht klicken sollten. Denn statt echter interner Kommunikation handelte es sich dabei um getarnte Phishing-Mails von Hacker:innen. Sie hatten es geschafft, sich Zugang zu echten E-Mail-Adressen von CDU-Politiker:innen zu verschaffen und darüber betrügerische Nachrichten zu verschicken.
Phishing-Mail an Merz: Was in den Nachrichten stand
Wie Heise berichtet, hatten sich die Hacker:innen Zugriff auf das Konto des Geschäftsführers des CDU-Kreisverbands in Heilbronn verschafft. Wie es dazu kam, ist bislang nicht final geklärt. Möglich wäre, dass auch der Geschäftsführer zunächst Opfer einer Phishing-Mail geworden ist. Sicher ist, dass sie Angreifer:innen das Konto im Anschluss genutzt haben, um mehr als 6.500 Mails an CDU-Politiker:innen in ganz Deutschland zu verschicken, darunter auch Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz.
Nachdem der Vorfall entdeckt wurde, hat der CDU-Kreisverband das Landeskriminalamt eingeschaltet. Noch ermittelt die Polizei, ob es unter den Empfänger:innen jemanden gab, der betrügerische Mails geöffnet hat. Die Mails lockten unter anderem mit vermeintlichen echten Betreffzeilen wie „Einladung zur 19. Böckinger Prominentenpredigt“ oder „Ummeldung / … / CDU SBK zu CDU Neckarsulm“.
In den Phishing-Mails wurden die Empfänger:innen dazu aufgefordert, auf einen Link zu klicken. Dieser sollte angeblich zu einem Dokument führen, das sie ausfüllen müssten, um an den Veranstaltungen teilzunehmen. Was stattdessen passiert, wenn der Link angeklickt wird, ist nicht bekannt. Die zuständige IT‑Sicherheitsfirma empfiehlt allerdings Betroffenen, die auf den Link geklickt haben, umgehend die eigene IT-Administration zu kontaktieren und Passwörter zu ändern. Zudem sollten Anmeldesitzungen terminiert werden, um schon im System befindliche Hacker:innen wieder auszusperren.

articles.title: The Download: the claim shaking up AI and the internet’s agent problem
articles.text:
The Download: the claim shaking up AI and the internet’s agent problem
Plus: The US Army is trying to get AI agents to hack its enemies.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
“We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.
I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. We discussed what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.
Read the exclusive interview to find out what Cammarata’s claims could mean for AI.
—Will Douglas Heaven
Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
Until recently, you could split internet users into just two categories: bots and people. But personal AI agents are slowly but surely disrupting that divide by taking on online tasks, from booking flights to reserving hotel rooms. Meta’s Muse alone was downloaded 5 million times in its first month.
The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents.
If that demand keeps rising, the internet could be redesigned for agents rather than people. Find out what that could mean for the rest of us.
—James O'Donnell
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Moment Energy and its work to repurpose used EV batteries
Moment Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
Demand for energy storage is surging, with capacity expected to grow eightfold in the next decade. To meet that demand, Moment Energy wants to shortcut a supply chain that now flows largely through China by domestically repurposing EV batteries into new grid-connected storage systems.
Ongoing trade battles between the US and China have been a shot in the arm for the company. And soon, it will be able to categorize its repurposed batteries as domestic products in both Canada and the US, where it’s building its next plant.
Learn more about how Moment stands to gain from the current climate.

Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from carbon dioxide batteries to helium-cooled nuclear reactors.
