articles.title: From Microservices to Agents: the Next Evolution of Distributed Systems
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Agentic AI systems shift distributed systems design from orchestrating services to orchestrating decisions made at runtime.
- Unlike microservices, agentic systems introduce non-deterministic execution paths driven by context, reasoning, and tool selection.
- Decision quality becomes a first-class reliability concern alongside latency, availability, and throughput.
- Production failure modes often manifest as silent degradation in reasoning quality rather than explicit system errors.
- Effective agentic architectures require bounded autonomy, evaluation loops, and hybrid deterministic fallback systems.
| This article is part of the "Agentic AI Architecture" article series. In this series, we try to establish agentic AI architecture as a new type of software architecture that will likely dominate the industry for years to come. The articles, written by industry experts, cover various elements and aspects of agentic AI architecture. We aim to present the latest trends and developments shaping the new type of architecture as it enters the mainstream. | 
Distributed Systems Are Entering a New Phase
Over the past decade, microservices have reshaped how large-scale software systems are designed and operated. They enabled teams to decompose monoliths into independently deployable services, scale ownership boundaries, and evolve systems incrementally. For many organizations, microservices became the dominant model for building distributed systems at scale.
At their core, microservices solved a fundamental problem: how to decompose functionality across services and teams in a way that supports independent evolution while maintaining system reliability. They introduced explicit service boundaries, well-defined APIs, and predictable execution flows.
A new architectural shift is now emerging, driven by advances in large language models (LLMs) and reasoning systems. Rather than focusing on decomposing functionality, this new paradigm focuses on decomposing decisions. Systems are beginning to move from static orchestration models toward adaptive, runtime decision-making systems. This is the foundation of what is increasingly referred to as agentic AI.
Agentic systems differ from traditional services in a fundamental way. Instead of executing predefined logic, they dynamically determine which actions to take, which tools to use, and how to sequence multi-step reasoning processes. Execution is no longer fully specified at design time; it emerges at runtime based on context, goals, and intermediate outcomes.
This shift introduces new capabilities. Systems can become more adaptive, more context-aware, and better able to handle ambiguous or evolving inputs. At the same time, it introduces new forms of complexity that are not well addressed by traditional distributed systems thinking.
The goal of this article is to explore this transition in depth: how agentic AI architectures differ from microservices, what architectural patterns are emerging, what failure modes we are beginning to observe in production systems, and how observability and reliability practices must evolve. The discussion is grounded in experience operating large-scale distributed systems in domains such as search, recommendation, and serving infrastructure.
Microservices Solved Service Decomposition — Agents Solve Decision Decomposition
Figure 1: Execution Model: Microservices vs Agentic Systems
(Source: created by the author with OpenAI ChatGPT)
[Click here to expand image above to full-size]
Microservices architecture introduced a clear model for structuring distributed systems. Instead of a single monolithic application, systems were decomposed into services aligned with business capabilities. Each service owned a bounded context — a clearly defined domain of responsibility and data ownership — communicated via APIs, and could evolve independently.
This decomposition enabled faster deployment cycles, clearer ownership boundaries, and improved scaling characteristics. However, despite their flexibility, microservices still rely on deterministic execution. The control flow of a request is explicitly defined through service-to-service interactions.
In a typical microservices-based system, a request follows a well-understood path: it enters a service, is processed, calls downstream services in a defined sequence, and returns a response. Even in highly complex systems, the execution path is known in advance and encoded in the system's logic.
Agentic AI systems introduce a different model of execution. Instead of defining the full sequence of operations upfront, systems determine execution paths dynamically. Decisions about which tools to invoke, which data sources to query, and which strategies to apply are made at runtime.
This represents a shift from service decomposition to decision decomposition. Rather than distributing functionality across services, systems distribute reasoning across components that participate in a dynamic decision loop.
In practice, this means that execution is no longer a fixed pipeline but an adaptive process. A system may choose different candidate sources depending on context, dynamically adjust ranking strategies, or re-evaluate outputs based on intermediate results. The structure of execution becomes contingent on both input and evolving system state.
This change has profound implications for how we reason about distributed systems. It introduces flexibility but also reduces predictability. It replaces static workflows with dynamic reasoning paths, which are inherently more difficult to trace and debug.
What Makes Agentic Systems Fundamentally Different
Figure 2: Agentic System Architecture
(Source: created by the author with OpenAI ChatGPT)
[Click here to expand image above to full-size]
Agentic systems differ from traditional distributed systems in three key dimensions: control flow, state management, and failure semantics.
Control flow is no longer fixed. In microservices architectures, execution paths are designed and encoded ahead of time. In agentic AI systems, execution paths are determined at runtime based on context and intermediate reasoning. This introduces flexibility but also variability in system behavior, since different requests may trigger entirely different execution paths depending on user intent, retrieved information, or prior decisions made during execution.
The state also becomes more fluid and less strictly defined. Traditional systems rely on explicit state transitions and well-defined persistence models. Agentic systems, by contrast, often operate over an evolving execution context that is continuously updated as reasoning progresses. This context may include conversation history, intermediate plans, retrieved documents, ranking signals, tool outputs, or prior evaluation results.
Managing this evolving context becomes a core systems concern. Context often must propagate across multiple agents, tools, and services while remaining sufficiently consistent to support coherent downstream reasoning. In practice, many systems introduce shared context stores, execution-scoped memory, or structured reasoning artifacts to avoid context fragmentation and contradictory decisions across execution steps. As execution chains become longer, context management begins to resemble distributed state coordination problems seen in earlier generations of distributed systems.
Failure semantics also change. In traditional systems, failures are typically binary: a request succeeds or fails, a service responds or times out. In agentic systems, failures often manifest as degraded decision quality. The system may continue to operate but produce suboptimal outcomes due to incorrect reasoning, poor tool selection, stale context, or incomplete interpretation of intermediate results.
These differences fundamentally change how distributed systems behave in production environments. They also require new architectural patterns to manage complexity, reliably propagate context, and maintain predictable system behavior at scale.
Architectural Patterns in Agentic AI Systems
As agentic systems begin to appear in production environments, several architectural patterns are emerging. These patterns are not formal standards but rather recurring structures that help manage complexity and control variability in decision-making systems.
One common pattern is the separation of planning and execution responsibilities. In this model, a planning component is responsible for interpreting intent and determining a high-level strategy, while execution components perform deterministic operations such as data retrieval, transformation, or ranking. This separation allows systems to isolate non-deterministic reasoning from deterministic execution, improving reliability and traceability.
A second pattern involves the specialization of agents. Instead of relying on a single general-purpose agent, systems are increasingly composed of multiple specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct capability such as retrieval, ranking, evaluation, or orchestration. These agents collaborate to produce final outcomes.
This structure resembles service decomposition in microservices architectures, but applied to decision-making rather than data processing logic. While specialization improves reasoning quality and modularity, it also introduces coordination overhead and increases system complexity. Latency becomes more variable, and failure modes can propagate across agent interactions.
A third pattern is the integration of evaluation directly into execution loops. Instead of treating evaluation as an offline process, systems increasingly evaluate outputs during runtime. Based on evaluation results, systems may dynamically refine, retry, or adjust strategies.
This introduces feedback loops into execution, enabling more adaptive behavior. However, it also requires careful control to avoid excessive retries or runaway execution cycles. Constraints such as latency budgets, iteration limits, and confidence thresholds become essential for maintaining system stability.
A further emerging pattern is the introduction of tool abstraction layers. As agents interact with a growing number of services and APIs, teams are creating standardized interfaces for tool use. These abstraction layers decouple agent reasoning from underlying service implementations and provide a consistent mechanism for capability discovery and invocation.
Over time, this abstraction layer begins to resemble a platform for capabilities rather than a collection of individual services. It becomes a critical enabler for scaling agentic systems across teams and domains.
Across these patterns, a consistent theme emerges: complexity is shifting from service orchestration to decision orchestration. Systems are no longer primarily concerned with how services interact, but with how decisions are made, evaluated, and adapted over time.
Failure Modes in Agentic Distributed Systems
Figure 3: Silent Failure Modes in Agentic Systems
(Source: created by the author with OpenAI ChatGPT)
[Click here to expand image above to full-size]
Agentic systems introduce new failure modes that differ significantly from those observed in traditional distributed architectures. While microservices typically fail due to latency, availability issues, or data inconsistencies, agentic systems often fail due to degraded decision quality.
One important failure mode is cascading decision degradation. In traditional pipelines, failures propagate through explicit dependencies. In agentic systems, early incorrect decisions can subtly influence downstream reasoning, compounding degradation in output quality. For example, if a system selects suboptimal candidate sources early in execution, subsequent ranking and evaluation steps operate over reduced-quality inputs, amplifying the initial error.
This pattern is particularly relevant in large-scale search and recommendation systems, where early-stage candidate generation significantly influences downstream ranking quality. Even when infrastructure remains healthy, small shifts in early decisions can lead to noticeable changes in system outcomes.
Another failure mode is retry amplification driven by evaluation loops. Agentic systems often include mechanisms for evaluating output quality and retrying when results are insufficient. While this improves adaptability, it can also lead to excessive iteration cycles. Unlike traditional retry mechanisms tied to explicit errors, these retries are driven by subjective quality judgments, making them harder to bound and control.
Without proper constraints, evaluation-driven retries can increase latency, amplify backend load, and create unpredictable execution patterns.
A third failure mode is silent quality degradation. In many cases, system performance may degrade without triggering traditional operational alerts. Infrastructure metrics such as latency and error rate may remain stable, while user-facing quality deteriorates due to changes in decision-making behavior.
This is especially common in systems that rely on ranking, personalization, or recommendation logic. Small shifts in tool selection, reasoning strategies, or context interpretation can accumulate over time, leading to gradual but significant changes in system behavior. Detecting these issues requires evaluation-aware monitoring rather than infrastructure-centric observability.
Coordination overhead and latency accumulation also emerge as important concerns. As systems distribute reasoning across multiple agents, execution paths become more complex and less predictable. Each additional coordination step introduces variability in latency and increases the risk of partial failures.
Finally, state drift and context inconsistency can lead to reasoning errors across multi-step execution flows. When context is updated incrementally across agents or steps, inconsistencies in state propagation can result in contradictory or incomplete decisions. This is analogous to consistency challenges in distributed systems but manifests as reasoning drift rather than data inconsistency.
Observability and Reliability for Agentic Systems
Traditional observability models based on metrics such as latency, throughput, and error rate remain necessary but are insufficient for agentic systems. A new dimension of observability is required: decision quality.
Instead of only observing system health, teams must observe how decisions are made. This includes tracing tool selections, reasoning steps, intermediate outputs, and evaluation outcomes. Decision-level tracing provides visibility into how system behavior evolves over time and where degradation originates.
Monitoring changes in system behavior also becomes important. Over time, shifts in tool usage patterns, strategy selection frequencies, fallback rates, or retry behavior can indicate that the system’s decision-making process is drifting. For example, a sudden increase in retries or a strong preference toward a single strategy may signal degraded reasoning quality, stale context, or poor evaluation signals.
These behavioral shifts often surface problems earlier than traditional user-facing metrics such as engagement or latency. Observing how decisions are distributed across the system can therefore serve as an early warning mechanism to detect quality degradation before it becomes operationally visible.
Evaluation infrastructure plays a central role in reliability. Rather than being treated as an offline validation mechanism, evaluation becomes part of the runtime system. It provides feedback loops that guide execution and help maintain quality. However, these loops must be carefully constrained to avoid excessive iteration or instability.
Reliability in agentic AI architectures also depends on bounded autonomy. Systems must operate within clearly defined constraints such as latency budgets, retry limits, and reasoning depth boundaries. These constraints ensure that flexibility does not come at the cost of predictability.
Fallback mechanisms remain essential. Deterministic execution paths provide stability when agentic reasoning becomes uncertain or when system confidence is low. In many production systems, hybrid architectures that combine agentic decision-making with deterministic fallback pipelines offer a pragmatic balance between flexibility and reliability.
Progressive rollout strategies are also critical. AI-based capabilities should be introduced gradually through experimentation, shadow execution, and controlled deployment. This allows teams to build confidence in the system's behavior while limiting exposure to risk.
Ultimately, reliability in agentic systems requires a shift in mindset. Instead of treating failures as binary events, systems must be designed to degrade gracefully in decision quality while maintaining a predictable user experience.
The Road Ahead
Agentic AI architectures represent a natural evolution of distributed systems. Microservices enabled the decomposition of functionality; agentic systems enable the decomposition of decision-making.
This shift introduces new capabilities in adaptability, personalization, and dynamic execution. It also introduces new challenges in observability, reliability, and system design.
The most important implication is that distributed systems are no longer only about orchestrating services. They are increasingly about orchestrating decisions. This requires extending established principles of distributed systems engineering to a new layer of abstraction.
As organizations adopt agentic architectures, success will depend on combining flexibility with discipline. The same principles that enabled microservices to scale—clear boundaries, observability, reliability engineering, and platform thinking—will be essential in this new paradigm.
We are still early in this transition. However, the direction is becoming clear. Distributed systems are evolving from systems that execute workflows to systems that make decisions. Understanding and shaping this shift will define the next generation of large-scale software architecture.
| This article is part of the "Agentic AI Architecture" article series. In this series, we try to establish agentic AI architecture as a new type of software architecture that will likely dominate the industry for years to come. The articles, written by industry experts, cover various elements and aspects of agentic AI architecture. We aim to present the latest trends and developments shaping the new type of architecture as it enters the mainstream. |

articles.title: NCC device verification questions Nigeria's phone imports
articles.text:
Nigeria’s telecom regulator launched a device verification tool that lets buyers check whether a phone is approved for use on local mobile networks. But enforcing compliance across an import-dependent market could test the agency’s technical reach.
With 99% of smartphones imported into Nigeria and an estimated 63 million mobile devices sold annually, the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) faces a market structured around multi-layered supply chains, informal distribution networks, and varied entry routes.
Launched on October 7, 2026, the NCC’s Device Checker requires consumers to dial *315# to verify whether a phone meets Type Approval requirements—the NCC’s mandatory regulation that all communication equipment must meet before connecting to local networks.
The regulator says the tool is part of a broader effort to enforce its Device Management System (DMS) under Section 132(2) of the Nigerian Communications Act 2003.
The checker uses a phone’s International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI), a unique 15-digit identifier, to verify its status against the NCC’s approved equipment records. By linking device records to import declarations, the regulator says it can investigate whether a phone was properly declared to the Nigeria Customs Service and trace the business responsible for importing it.
However, the stakes are substantial in a market that imports an estimated ₦50 billion ($30 million) worth of mobile devices every month. Its near-total reliance on imports creates a complex supply chain that could hamper enforcement.
As a result, a consumer whose phone gets flagged risks navigating an informal multi-tier supply chain with no clear recourse, no standard refund procedure, and no guarantee of compensation.
How device verification works across categories
Consumers can check a mobile device’s status by dialling *315#. Selecting “Check this device” on the menu displays whether the handset is NCC Type Approved and verified for use. Alternatively, buyers can retrieve the 15-digit IMEI code by dialling *#06# and entering it on the NCC’s online portal.
These verification methods enable buyers to detect non-compliant devices before completing a transaction rather than discovering issues after payment.
For personally imported devices, the workflow differs. Individuals bringing phones into the country for use with local SIM cards must contact the NCC via its 315 helpline for guidance on individual verification.
Foreign visitors roaming on international SIM cards do not need to register their devices. Devices connected to a local network before October 7 are automatically allowed. However, new, unverified handsets imported by visitors are subject to a cumulative 30-day grace period per year before registration becomes mandatory.
Commercial entities importing SIM-enabled hardware—including smartphones, tablets, connected laptops, smart meters, and point-of-sale (POS) terminals—must verify compliance with type approval before distribution.
Regulatory responsibility lies upstream: original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), commercial importers, and primary distributors are legally required to obtain Type Approval before offering hardware for sale.
The distinction between consumer verification and enterprise registration is critical: consumers verify network eligibility, whereas supply-chain entities bear the burden of regulatory compliance.
Through the DMS portal, the regulator states it can track SIM-enabled devices back to primary importers, log total import volume, and initiate sanctions against non-compliant entities.
However, backend traceability does not guarantee immediate redress for consumers when an unapproved device is flagged post-purchase.
Enforcement challenges in a fragmented market
Sellers in Abuja’s GSM Village support the regulator’s initiative, yet there are concerns that structural complexities within Nigeria’s device distribution networks could impede implementation. Elsewhere at Banex Plaza in Abuja, TechCabal‘s findings from sellers were not different.
Nigeria records an estimated 63 million mobile device sales annually. Trade data from Volza shows mobile phone imports totalled 4,886 shipments between July 2024 and June 2025, involving 11 international exporters and 12 registered major buyers in Nigeria.
While import metrics do not quantify grey-market volume, the NCC’s enforcement partnership with the Nigeria Customs Service highlights lingering vulnerabilities around grey-market imports and border smuggling.
In 2024, the Nigeria Customs Service reported 3,555 contraband seizures. Although specific device counts were omitted, persistent illicit inflows indicate that unapproved hardware continues to enter retail channels, creating post-purchase compliance risks for consumers.
Regularising upstream accountability
The NCC states that approximately 231 million active devices registered before October 7, 2026, have been automatically onboarded into the DMS database without requiring subscriber intervention. However, the commission did not disclose the number of devices flagged or pending clearance.
Merchants holding inventory imported before that date can regularise their stock by registering their business documentation and uploading batch IMEI records to the NCC enterprise portal. Support is available via the 315 desk.
This transition window aims to protect compliant trade vendors from regulatory penalties on legacy stock.
Traders contend that regulatory enforcement must target primary importers rather than downstream micro-retailers who lack the technical means to evaluate upstream Type Approval status.
Secondary retailers rarely receive customs documentation or Type Approval certificates from distributors. While this does not absolve vendors knowingly trading in illicit goods, it creates operational friction when stock is acquired in good faith.
The NCC’s digital ledger could help trace undeclared devices to sellers and suppliers. But as Ogoh suggests, having “empirical data” is only the first step; turning that evidence into accountability and consumer refunds remains the bigger test.
The commission indicates that these audit trails help regulators distinguish between deliberate contraband trading and inadvertent distribution by secondary vendors.
However, audit trails alone do not determine financial liability or resolve refund disputes once non-compliant hardware has passed through multiple intermediaries to reach end users.
Enforcement and consumer protection
Consumer protection underpins the rationale for the Device Checker. Yet the tool’s impact will depend on whether enforcement mechanisms can penetrate multi-tiered supply chains to guarantee consumer indemnification.
Although the regulator maintains that automated verification prevents erroneous network blocking, dispute resolution remains complex. Nigeria’s Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 grants rights to repair, replacement, or refund for non-compliant goods, but practical enforcement across informal markets remains difficult.
The Device Checker’s ultimate success hinges on converting technical detection into actionable consumer safeguards. Identifying unverified IMEIs offers little relief to buyers left holding deactivated hardware without a clear, enforced refund path in informal trade hubs.
To scale sustainably, the NCC must strengthen inter-agency coordination with the Nigeria Customs Service to stop unapproved hardware at entry ports rather than at retail points of sale. Without stringent primary-importer enforcement and structured consumer indemnities, digital verification risks transferring systemic supply-chain failures onto consumers.

articles.title: Modern Warfare 4 has the best Steam rating for a Call of Duty game in 16 years
articles.text:
The big picture: Ahead of its official launch later this week, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is offering early access to its campaign for players who pre-order the game. As expected, thousands of players are taking advantage of the opportunity, and the vast majority apparently seem impressed with the gameplay, graphics, and storyline.
The game currently has 4,068 total reviews on Steam, including 3,438 from verified buyers. Of those reviews, 94% are positive, earning it a "Very Positive" rating overall and making it the best-reviewed Call of Duty release on Steam since 2010's Black Ops. The SteamDB ratings were first reported by Insider Gaming last week, when the game had around 900 reviews and an 81.5% positive rating.
In stark contrast to the overwhelmingly positive response to Modern Warfare 4, recent releases in the Call of Duty franchise have struggled to even reach the 50% mark. 2025's Black Ops 7 has a 38.7% rating on SteamDB, while 2024's Black Ops 6 and 2023's Modern Warfare III have ratings of 45.7% and 48.1%, respectively. The only other recent CoD title with a similarly high rating is Black Ops III, which currently has 84.3% positive reviews.
The positive initial reception for Modern Warfare 4 must come as a relief to Activision, which has struggled in recent years. Not only have the last few mainline CoD releases received lukewarm responses from players and reviewers alike, but the company has also faced significant financial and creative challenges, resulting in several rounds of layoffs since Microsoft's $68.7 billion acquisition of Activision in 2023.
However, Modern Warfare 4's unusually high rating could change considerably once the game becomes more widely available later this week and players get a chance to try its multiplayer offerings. These include 12 core 6v6 maps and the extraction-shooter mode "DMZ," in which multiple squads of up to three players deploy into an area known as the "exclusion zone."
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launches Friday, October 23, on Windows, Xbox Series X|S, PlayStation 5, and Nintendo Switch 2. It is the last big AAA release this year before the much-anticipated GTA 6 launch in November, with most publishers pushing their upcoming releases to 2027 to avoid clashing with Rockstar's open-world juggernaut.

articles.title: Google vuelve a cambiar los nombres de Gemini: qué hace ahora cada función
articles.text:
Google modificará la forma en que se identifican varias funciones de Gemini, con cambios que afectan a Gems, Skills, Spark, Tarea y Acciones programadas. La transición comenzará el 17 de noviembre para las cuentas personales, mientras que las cuentas de trabajo y centros educativos seguirán el mismo camino en 2027.
La reorganización importa porque algunas de estas herramientas cumplen tareas similares, aunque funcionan de manera distinta. Google trasladará los Gems a un formato llamado Skills, integrará Spark en el chat con el nombre de Tarea y mantendrá Acciones programadas como la opción destinada a ejecutar solicitudes en horarios definidos.
Gems pasará a llamarse Skills en las cuentas personales
Los Gems eran bots personalizados independientes. Cada uno se elegía desde una barra lateral y abría una ventana de conversación separada. A partir del 17 de noviembre, Google empezará a convertir de forma automática los Gems personales en Skills.
Después de esa conversión, los Gems desaparecerán de las cuentas personales. La nueva modalidad incorpora las instrucciones personalizadas al chat principal de Gemini, por lo que ya no será necesario entrar en una ventana exclusiva para usar cada configuración.
Para activar una Skill, el usuario debe escribir una barra diagonal dentro del cuadro de solicitud y seleccionar la opción que necesite. Gemini también podrá aplicar una Skill por su cuenta cuando detecte que sus instrucciones encajan con la petición realizada.
La principal diferencia es que varias Skills pueden utilizarse dentro de una misma conversación. Una de ellas puede establecer la imagen de marca de una empresa y otra puede fijar el tono de escritura. El cambio evita trasladar resultados de un bot a otro para combinar diferentes instrucciones.
Algunas funciones de Gems no estarán disponibles al principio
La migración tiene límites. Varias herramientas integradas que podían activarse dentro de un Gem todavía no funcionan con Skills. Entre ellas están Canvas, Investigación profunda, Aprendizaje guiado y la generación de vídeo y música.
Tampoco es posible compartir una Skill ni adjuntar archivos de Drive por ahora. Google ha indicado que ambas opciones llegarán próximamente. Por ese motivo, quienes tengan Gems que dependan de esas herramientas deben probarlos antes del 17 de noviembre.
La recomendación es hacer una copia de seguridad de las solicitudes guardadas. Para ello, se pueden copiar las instrucciones de cada Gem en un archivo Markdown y descargar cualquier archivo de conocimiento asociado. Así, el material seguirá disponible incluso después de que desaparezca la interfaz anterior.
Acciones programadas prepara respuestas según un horario
Las Acciones programadas permiten escribir una solicitud, definir cuándo debe ejecutarse y establecer la frecuencia. Gemini prepara el resultado en segundo plano y puede mantener hasta 10 acciones activas al mismo tiempo.
En la versión web, el chat correspondiente aparece marcado como no leído. En móviles, Gemini envía una notificación que puede mostrarse en la pantalla de bloqueo, de acuerdo con la configuración del dispositivo.
Esta función ya no requiere una suscripción a Google AI, aunque el despliegue para cuentas gratuitas continúa. También exige tener activada la opción Keep Activity. Gemini prepara el resultado durante la hora previa a la entrega, una característica que limita su utilidad para datos que cambian de un minuto a otro.
Google propone usos como un resumen matutino del calendario, la lista de tareas, los correos electrónicos o un pronóstico diario con ideas de vestimenta. Si la acción depende de la ubicación, Gemini usa el lugar donde se configuró. Un usuario que viaje seguirá recibiendo el pronóstico de su ciudad de origen hasta que modifique la acción.
Spark aparece como Tarea dentro del chat principal
Spark es el agente de Gemini que continúa trabajando después de cerrar el ordenador o bloquear el teléfono. Google está dejando de destacar ese nombre: en un rediseño en marcha, aparece como Tarea en un selector junto al cuadro de solicitud, mientras que su página se denomina Configuración de tareas.
Las páginas de ayuda todavía utilizan el nombre Spark. La función opera en máquinas virtuales de Google Cloud y puede desarrollar tareas de varios pasos en aplicaciones y sitios web. Por ejemplo, puede investigar competidores o vigilar precios de vuelos.
Google incorporó puntos de control. La herramienta pide aprobación antes de enviar mensajes, modificar datos, realizar compras o completar formularios web. También devuelve el control cuando un sitio solicita contraseñas o datos de pago. Estas medidas no son infalibles, por lo que las tareas importantes requieren supervisión.
Spark, o Tarea, admite hasta 15 procesos simultáneos y exige una suscripción a Google AI Pro o Ultra, además de Keep Activity activada.
La diferencia entre Tarea y Acciones programadas
Ambas funciones pueden activarse según un calendario, pero no son equivalentes. Las Acciones programadas generan resultados a partir de una hora definida. Spark puede reaccionar a eventos y completar procesos mientras el usuario no está presente.
Esa diferencia permite, por ejemplo, vigilar tarifas aéreas hasta que aparezca una dentro de un presupuesto o revisar la bandeja de entrada para cancelar suscripciones a boletines. Skills sirve para repetir instrucciones; Acciones programadas, para recibir resúmenes; y Tarea, para automatizaciones de varios pasos.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI Worker Accused of Bugging Conference Room Planned to Fly to Saudi Arabia, Prosecutors Say
articles.text:
A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been “mere days” away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings.
Abdulrahman Alfozan’s wife and young son also left the country the day after the 35-year-old Saudi national’s arrest, traveling on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in a memo Sunday seeking his continued detention.
“Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through,” federal prosecutors wrote. “He has ample resources —including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government.”
A federal judge in San Francisco sided with prosecutors Monday, denying a request by Alfozan’s lawyers to release him to home confinement. His next court date is Nov.
Alfozan’s lawyer William Pernik argued in court that his client had strong ties to the U.S. and was “weeks away from achieving every immigrant’s dream” — U.S. citizenship.
Alfozan had a naturalization interview with federal officials scheduled next month and has been a lawful permanent resident since 2020, his lawyers said in their legal filings. He has also lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley, they said.
Pernik said Alfozan is willing to put up “almost the entirety” of his assets — about $1 million currently in a U.S. investment account — to cover his bond.
“Everything this man has he’s willing to surrender,” he said, adding that Alfozan’s wife is also willing to return to the U.S. as she still holds a visitor visa that expires in 2033.
Judge Alex Tse appeared doubtful, questioning whether Saudi Arabia’s government would simply reimburse Alfozan if he fled and forfeited his bond.
After the hearing, Pernik said he was disappointed with the ruling but declined further comment.
Pernik had argued in court filings that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. They said the couple planned to spend Alfozan’s roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son.
But prosecutors said Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for Alfozan’s wife and son after his arrest, allowing them to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan had originally booked.
Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia.
Alfozan had told the unnamed person he wouldn’t leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. He had worked at the ChatGPT maker since July 2025 but was fired after his arrest.
Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn’t authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30.
Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information.”
OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office.
Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence.

articles.title: Usuários recorrem à IA para remover anúncios e mudar interfaces de TVs • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Usuários recorrem à IA para remover anúncios e mudar interfaces de TVs
Projetos usam ferramentas como Claude Code para criar launchers personalizados.
Modificações em sistemas de smart TV ganharam as redes sociais nos últimos dias. Os consumidores estão adotando novos launchers porque os nativos podem conter poluição visual, em especial devido aos muitos espaços de publicidade. O tema está em alta principalmente no X/Twitter.
Os projetos são compartilhados nas redes sociais e mostram agentes como o Claude Code sendo usado para executar alterações no Android TV. Os usuários mostram telas iniciais próprias com integração a widgets de tempo e calendário, alguns até com controles de automação de dispositivos de casa inteligente.
O vibe coding, ou “programação intuitiva”, é um modelo de desenvolvimento com inteligência artificial em que a pessoa descreve a um chatbot o que deseja criar, e a tecnologia gera o código a partir dessas instruções. O termo se popularizou em 2025 e tem sido um grande foco da indústria de IA nos últimos meses.
Ao mesmo tempo, desenvolvedores profissionais se preocupam com aplicativos criados sem preocupações com barreiras de segurança.
Um dos relatos foi publicado pelo desenvolvedor Ryan Doyle, que utilizou o Claude Code para modificar a TV e desativar anúncios e serviços de rastreamento. Ele também criou um protetor de tela personalizado que reúne previsão do tempo, calendário, dados de faturamento do próprio negócio entre outras funções.
Outro projeto, chamado cleanyourtv, surgiu após o desenvolvedor encontrar um anúncio na tela inicial da Xiaomi Mi TV usada por seus pais antes da abertura da Netflix. O projeto foi publicado no GitHub.
Após receber informações sobre o modelo da TV, o Claude Code acessou o aparelho pela rede local e desativou 25 pacotes instalados pela Xiaomi. O projeto também substituiu a tela inicial por um laucher personalizado com uma interface mais simples. Outros usuários vêm explorando as ferramentas para criar funções adicionais, como representações 3D da própria casa com controles de sistema de iluminação.
As alterações aproveitam ferramentas já existentes no Android. Os projetos usam principalmente o Android Debug Bridge (ADB), recurso de desenvolvimento que permite enviar comandos a dispositivos Android. O usuário precisa habilitar as opções de desenvolvedor e a depuração da TV.
Após isso, ferramentas de IA podem executar comandos pelo terminal para alterar configurações e gerenciar os app instalados. Por depender do ADB, o método é usado principalmente em aparelhos com Android TV ou Google TV, utilizados por fabricantes como Sony, TCL, Xiaomi, Hisense e Philips. Vale lembrar que a Play Store já possui launchers para quem quer apenas mudar a interface sem passar por todo esse processo.
Sistemas proprietários, como Tizen da Samsung e webOS da LG, não oferecem o mesmo método de acesso. Mas alguns usuários já começaram a divulgar soluções próprias para esses sistemas.
A disseminação desses apps criados com ajuda da IA ocorre enquanto o Google também começa a facilitar a execução de programas desenvolvidos para uso pessoal. Uma nova função da Google Play permite executar apps criados pelo próprio usuário com o Google AI Studio em dispositivos Android sem publicá-los na loja.
Segundo o TechCrunch, esses apps ficam disponíveis em uma área chamada Sua biblioteca pessoal, associada à conta Google do desenvolvedor. Eles não aparecem nas buscas ou nas páginas públicas da loja.

articles.title: EIF commits €20 million to Swedish VC BackingMinds to support underrepresented entrepreneurs | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Swedish VC firm BackingMinds has received around €20 million from the European Investment Fund (EIF) for BackingMinds Invest III in order to seek out promising entrepreneurs and businesses often overlooked by traditional investors.
The EIF, which is part of the Luxembourg-based European Investment Bank (EIB) Group, will be the first institutional investor in the fund – backed by the EU’s InvestEU programme. This follows their €50 million fund close in 2022 and its investment in Swedish entrepreneurship platform Techarena in 2025.
“The future is never where you expect it, and neither are the founders building it,” says BackingMinds Founding Partner Sara Wimmercranz. “Some of the most innovative companies in the Nordics are being built where venture capital rarely reaches. A network is a filter. It lets through what already looks like the network and repeats the patterns of the past. As investors, we need to be more open and seek founders out. The EIF’s commitment lets us do that on a larger scale.”
BackingMinds’ EIF commitment comes amid further institutional backing for specialised European venture funds in 2026.
In Sweden, Norrsken Evolve closed a €62 million pre-Seed fund, while Turbine Capital reached a €54 million final close for Nordic DeepTech investments, both with EIF backing.
Elsewhere, Berlin-based Auxxo closed its €33.3 million Female Catalyst Fund II, Copenhagen’s Climentum Capital secured a €60 million first close for climate HardTech, including €40 million from the EIF, and Munich-based Ananda Impact Ventures raised €73 million at first close for impact investments.
Together, these fund closings represent approximately €282.3 million, excluding BackingMinds’ separate €20 million EIF commitment.
“Europe cannot afford to leave talented entrepreneurs undiscovered simply because they are outside the traditional venture capital networks,” adds EIF Deputy Chief Executive Merete Clausen. “BackingMinds has shown that promising businesses can be found in places and among founders that investors too often miss. By supporting this fund, we are helping to unlock that potential and bring more capital to companies tackling some of Europe’s most pressing challenges.”
Founded in 2016, BackingMinds is a Stockholm-based VC firm, founded by Sara Wimmercranz and Susanne Najafi to address the gaps in capital distribution. Through its two earlier funds, BackingMinds has invested in 23 companies.
Of these, 46% have had at least one female founder, 43% have had founders with immigrant backgrounds and 71% were established outside a capital city.
The new fund will finance early-stage companies primarily in Sweden and across the Nordic region, aiming to find entrepreneurial talent beyond established venture capital networks. It will seek out businesses founded by women as well as by people with immigrant backgrounds and based outside capital cities.
The focus will also be on commercially promising companies that address environmental or social challenges ranging from reducing carbon emissions and upgrading energy efficiency to improving healthcare and bolstering education.
According to the EIF, their support is aimed at helping BackingMinds Invest III attract other institutional investors.

articles.title: Norwegian undersea cable builder pitches 2,800-mile transatlantic data link between Canada and Europe to bypass the US — Canadian majority partner sought to help fund and build new $620 million fiber connection to reduce reliance on American routes
articles.text:
Norwegian undersea cable builder pitches 2,800-mile transatlantic data link between Canada and Europe to bypass the US — Canadian majority partner sought to help fund and build new $620 million fiber connection to reduce reliance on American routes
Further attempts to reduce reliance on US infrastructure
A Norwegian company building fiber networks and data centers across Europe is looking for a majority partner to help fund and build a transatlantic undersea cable that would connect Canada with Europe directly, bypassing the United States. The project follows worsening relations between Washington and Ottawa, with the Canadian government looking to reduce direct reliance on its immediate neighbor, Bloomberg reports.
Project Leif Erikson, if it goes ahead, would stretch more than 2,800 miles, starting at the southern tip of Norway and ending up at Happy Valley-Goose Bay in Canada's eastern province of Newfoundland and Labrador. From there, it would continue underground over Canadian territory, passing through Quebec before reaching Montreal.
According to Bulk's co-founder, Peder Nærbø, the link would be part of a "sovereign cable system" for Canada. The project was touted to investors at a global investors summit, arranged by the Canadian government, in September, where the project claimed to provide "direct, secure, high-capacity data transmission for AI, telecom and hyperscale markets."
Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joy, meanwhile, met with Nærbø earlier this year, and although the department declined to comment on Leif Erikson itself, it told Bloomberg that security and resilience for Canada's infrastructure are "key priorities" for PM Mark Carney's government. Only a few undersea cables currently connect Canada without passing through the United States first, and none by a company owned by Canada. The biggest, called Topez, is owned by Google owner Alphabet and connects Canada with Japan.
As for Bulk, it has, up until now, laid more than 6,200 miles of cabling locally and at sea. Bulk's goal is to "unlock the Nordics' potential for... renewable energy to be utilized for digital infrastructure." Nærbø believes that "Canada lacks resilience" but "the game-changer was when the current situation with the U.S. escalated."
Leif Erikson has backers, according to the report, but the EU and Canada still need to plan and sign off on the project and its route. Additional financing will be needed to get started, too, with it expected to cost more than $620 million to build. Bulk itself has significant Canadian investment, with 65% of the company owned by a real estate subsidiary of Canada's Sun Life Financial Inc., with several Canadian pension funds also invested.
Leif Erikson is a project that Nærbø has sought to kickstart for the last five years without success. With geopolitical pressures and old alliances fraying, however, new opportunities for its development have given it steam. To that end, Canada and Europe intend to endorse a statement in Montreal on October 29 that the two will look for "the best way to enhance digital links between Europe, Canada and Asia through new subsea cable infrastructure."

It won't be without challenges, however, including a 1,180-mile underground route through Canada that'll require the backing of Indigenous communities. Meanwhile, other European efforts include an undersea cable project at the North Pole to link Europe with Asia to bypass Russia and the Middle East.

articles.title: Conduite autonome de niveau 4 : Volvo et Mercedes signent avec Nvidia, rendez-vous « la prochaine décennie » — Frandroid
articles.text:
Nvidia arrive à sa conférence GTC Berlin, qui ouvre ce mercredi 21 octobre, avec deux constructeurs « européens » de plus dans sa poche.
Volvo (groupe chinois Geely) le 15 octobre, puis Mercedes-Benz le 16, ont annoncé qu’ils élargissent leur collaboration avec le géant américain des puces pour viser la conduite autonome de niveau 4. Sauf qu’aucun des deux ne donne de date. Et Mercedes a justement renoncé en janvier au niveau 3, le niveau juste en dessous, sur sa nouvelle Classe S.
Les deux accords reposent sur les mêmes briques. Hyperion désigne l’architecture de référence de Nvidia : le calculateur et l’ensemble de capteurs que le constructeur installe dans la voiture. Alpamayo Stack fournit le logiciel de conduite à base d’IA. Halos ajoute un système de sécurité qui surveille le tout en parallèle.
Volvo travaille avec Nvidia depuis 2017. Son communiqué annonce une première dans une voiture de nouvelle génération, sans la nommer ni la dater.
Le constructeur sino-suédois promet une arrivée « progressive » de la conduite eyes-off (on peut quitter la route des yeux), puis mind-off (on peut décrocher complètement). Le texte ne contient même pas les mots « niveau 4 ». Nvidia, de son côté, présente Hyperion comme une plateforme prête pour ce niveau.
Mercedes va plus loin dans son annonce. Le constructeur allemand part de la CLA électrique, qui a inauguré chez lui une aide à la conduite de point à point en ville, développée avec Nvidia. Il précise que l’ensemble doit servir à de « futures applications de niveau 4 », dont des « robolimousines », autrement dit des taxis haut de gamme sans chauffeur. Sur le calendrier, on n’a rien d’autre que le titre du communiqué, qui parle de « la prochaine décennie ».
Magna et GM étaient déjà dans la boucle
Nvidia ne compte pas que des clients européens. En Chine, BYD et Geely (Zeekr, Polestar, Lynk&co, Lotus, Volvo) misent aussi sur la technologie américaine pour le niveau 4. Et dès mars 2025, lors de la GTC de San José, le site allemand Computerbase détaillait trois autres accords.
L’équipementier canadien Magna prévoyait de tester tous les niveaux, du 2+ au 4, sur la plateforme Drive AGX Thor, avec une démonstration promise pour la fin 2025. Nvidia présentait alors Thor comme sa puce embarquée la plus rapide : 1 000 TOPS, soit un million de milliards d’opérations d’IA par seconde.
General Motors, premier constructeur américain, comptait installer du Drive AGX dans ses futurs modèles, sans dire quelle version. Volvo, de son côté, passait par sa filiale logicielle Zenseact pour acheter des serveurs DGX. Ces machines restent dans un centre de données et analysent les données des capteurs, alors que les puces AGX sont installées dans la voiture.
Sur la route, le Volvo EX90 a été lancé avec une puce Orin épaulée par une ancienne Xavier. Depuis le millésime 2026, il embarque deux Orin, pour environ 500 TOPS, et Volvo a proposé aux premiers clients de changer gratuitement leur calculateur.
Pour Nvidia, l’automobile pèse encore peu. Sa division auto a rapporté 2,3 milliards de dollars sur l’exercice clos fin janvier 2026, un record, mais à peine plus de 1 % des 215,9 milliards encaissés par le groupe. Sur ce marché, Nvidia affronte Qualcomm, qui fournit sa plateforme Snapdragon Ride à BMW, et Mobileye, dont le système SuperVision équipe des Zeekr.
Le niveau 4, une promesse sans date
Tout le monde se réfère à la norme SAE J3016, publiée par l’association américaine des ingénieurs de l’automobile. Au niveau 3, la voiture conduit seule dans certaines conditions, mais le conducteur doit reprendre le volant dès qu’elle le demande. Au niveau 4, personne n’a besoin de reprendre la main : dans les conditions prévues par le constructeur, la voiture gère seule les imprévus et s’arrête d’elle-même sur le côté si besoin.
    Pour aller plus loin
Voitures autonomes : quelles sont les différences entre les niveaux d’autonomie ?
            
Mercedes connaît bien le niveau 3. Son Drive Pilot, homologué en Allemagne et vendu depuis 2022 sur la Classe S et l’EQS, ne dépassait pas 60 km/h dans les bouchons au départ. Depuis début 2025, il monte à 95 km/h sur autoroute, à condition de suivre un autre véhicule et par beau temps. Pourtant, Mercedes l’a retiré de la Classe S restylée en janvier 2026. À la place, la voiture reçoit MB.Drive Assist Pro, un système de niveau 2++ qui oblige à garder les yeux sur la route. C’est exactement ce que préparent également Tesla et Xpeng en Europe.
    Pour aller plus loin
Seuls Tesla et Xpeng font essayer leur conduite autonome au Mondial, aucun constructeur européen ne suit
            
Côté réglementation, l’Union européenne autorise le niveau 4 depuis 2022, mais seulement dans des cas très précis. Le règlement 2022/1426 limite l’homologation à des véhicules produits en petites séries, pour trois usages : rouler dans une zone délimitée, suivre un trajet fixe entre deux points ou se garer dans un parking prévu pour. Une voiture qui emmène son propriétaire n’importe où n’entre dans aucun de ces cas.
Bref, rien n’arrivera avant 2030, sauf retournement de situation.

articles.title: Russian bot activity plunged 84% after Ukraine hit Yandex data centers, but the bots were back at full strength within two days
articles.text:
Russian bot activity plunged 84% after Ukraine hit Yandex data centers, but the bots were back at full strength within two days
Day-long bot collapse saw major drop in traffic
- Ukraine's CCD says suspected Russian bot posts in its sample fell 83.6% on October 8 after a strike shut Yandex's Sasovo data center
- The same data shows volume back above pre-strike levels by October 10, with a smaller 42.6% dip after the Vladimir shutdown
- Cloudflare and Graphika found no comparable drop in Western political communities, though Russian-language Telegram output fell 5% to 15%
Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD) says suspected Russian bot accounts went almost silent after drones knocked out Yandex data centers earlier this month, with message volume across a monitored network falling 83.6% in a single day.
The findings come from an analytical report the CCD dated October 15 2026. Using Osavul monitoring software, analysts tracked 22,664 messages from 5,201 accounts showing signs of inauthentic behavior across 26 topics in Ukraine's Facebook and Telegram space between October 6 and 12.
The 83.6% figure is real, but the same report shows those accounts posting more than before within 48 hours, and independent data from Cloudflare shows that at least some of the malicious automation running on Yandex's cloud did not die so much as move house.
A collapse in automated traffic after the Yandex Cloud took a beating
The first collapse came on October 8, hours after a drone strike and fire shut down Yandex's Sasovo data center in Ryazan region, home to two of the company's three supercomputers.
Daily messages fell from 4,032 to 660, and active accounts dropped from 1,526 to 258. Telegram took the harder hit, down 90%, while Facebook fell 79.5%. A second, shallower dip followed the October 11 strike that Yandex said had completely halted its Vladimir site, with messages falling 42.6% on October 12, from 4,711 to 2,704. A subgroup of 98 accounts the CCD flagged for justifying the invasion or inciting hatred followed the same curve, down 77.8% on October 8 and 49.2% on October 12.
The most telling detail sits in the middle. The October 9 strike at Yandex's Kaluga campus, which the company describes as its largest, only partially took the site offline, and the CCD recorded no fall in activity that day. The two dips line up with the two complete shutdowns, as one would expect if these accounts depended on that infrastructure, though that's not proof on its own.
A surprisingly fast turnaround time?
What the 84% figure that the CCD touts leaves out is how briefly the silence held. Message volume recovered to 2,231 on October 9, then reached 4,585 on October 10 and 4,711 on October 11, both above the pre-strike level. The monitoring window in the report closes on October 12, so it cannot show whether the second dip recovered the same way.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The agency has also been downplaying the event on other forums; two days before the report, the CCD said posting in some clusters of the Pravda, InfoDefense and Nod of Time networks roughly halved for about 12 hours, and stressed that it had not recorded a significant overall decline across Russian bot farms.
On October 16, the CCD's summary of remarks by media literacy head Ivan Slychko described the effect as "a disruption of automation, not the complete disappearance of bots."
It also makes no mention of a similar comparison for ordinary accounts. On the afternoon of October 8, banks, retailers, mobile operators and news sites across Russia suffered outages. Without said information, it is hard to separate bot farms losing their servers from operators inside Russia simply losing connectivity.
The CCD is hardly an impartial player here; it is a body attached to Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, and it has an incentive to exaggerate victories even when the data doesn't always support them.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had already jumped the gun, telling the Warsaw Security Forum that after the strikes "it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms" and that might have been a deciding factor for how the CCD built its narrative.
Beyond Ukraine, the "bots went silent" story mostly rested on a Cloudflare Radar chart showing automated traffic from Yandex's AS13238 network falling to well under 1% of its recent peak on October 11. As we noted at the time, that traffic was far more likely to be crawlers than fake social media accounts, and "bot" is a loose word when automated requests make up around half of all web traffic.
Cloudflare's own post-mortem confirms it. Marina Elmore and Lai Yi Ohlsen found 99.5% of requests from AS13238 were automated, mostly verified Yandex search crawlers, and that the network supplied only about 7% of Russia-origin bot requests. Bot traffic from Russian IP addresses hitting the post, reply, and like endpoints of one social platform dipped just 5.7% across the event period.
Graphika reached a similar verdict from the other direction. Founder John Kelly's analysis of the AfD, MAGA and Reform UK communities that viral posts claimed had gone quiet found none lost their active accounts or heaviest posters.
AfD-linked accounts posted 40,365 times on October 11, 4% below the week before and well within normal swings, while MAGA mentions on X rose 25% in the eight hours after the Vladimir strike. Georgetown's Renée DiResta, writing in Lawfare, was blunt about the viral version: "It's a great story. But it looks like fiction rather than fact."
For now, the most defensible reading of the CCD's numbers is narrower than its headline. Knocking out the right data center can briefly cut the output of Russia-based accounts aimed at Ukraine. Keeping them quiet would mean hitting the servers they move to next, and on the evidence so far, that move takes a day or two.
As one analysis of battlefield computing puts it particularly well, resilience comes from designing for disconnection, and the bot operators appear to have learned that lesson faster than Yandex did.

articles.title: Uma falha expôs acesso a mais de 58 mil câmeras do Smart Sampa
articles.text:
Uma falha no Smart Sampa, sistema de vigilância da Prefeitura de São Paulo, permitiu o acesso indevido a mais de 58 mil câmeras após dados sigilosos ficarem expostos na internet por cerca de 11 meses. A brecha atingiu locais sensíveis, como creches, escolas e hospitais.
Segundo o UOL, o material incluía credenciais de acesso e informações sobre agentes de segurança. A prefeitura atribuiu o vazamento a um servidor e negou falhas nos mecanismos de proteção do programa.
Dados expostos permitiram acessar imagens
O repositório público continha 181 logins e senhas de usuários autorizados, dados de mais de 6 mil agentes de segurança e instruções para reproduzir o sistema em computadores e celulares.
Com essas informações, a reportagem conseguiu visualizar imagens de pessoas e veículos nas ruas da capital paulista, além de câmeras instaladas em creches, hospitais e centros de atendimento a dependentes químicos. A reportagem também acessou a plataforma da Sentinelx, empresa responsável pela tecnologia, sem precisar passar pela autenticação em duas etapas.
Após ser questionada, a prefeitura reforçou essa proteção. A investigação identificou ainda interfaces que, segundo um especialista em tecnologia ouvido pelo UOL, poderiam permitir a inserção de dados sem verificar adequadamente a identidade de quem os enviava.
Os riscos vão além da exposição de imagens. As credenciais também permitiam consultar informações pessoais e registros da base de dados. Entre os pontos mais preocupantes estão:
- Acesso a nomes, CPFs e placas de veículos.
- Consulta a boletins de ocorrência.
- Possibilidade de acompanhar a movimentação de agentes e viaturas.
Depois do alerta, os dados foram retirados do repositório público.
Especialistas questionam segurança e privacidade
Rafael Alcadipani, professor da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV) e especialista em segurança pública, alertou que o acesso às imagens pode revelar a movimentação de autoridades e equipamentos de segurança.
“Você pega uma estrutura que o Estado tem para enfrentar o crime, e que possivelmente pode ser utilizada pelo crime para enfrentar o Estado”, afirmou.
Pedro Saliba, pesquisador da Data Privacy Brasil, também criticou a exposição. “É uma falha gravíssima em termos de privacidade e vigilância”, disse.
Para Saliba, sistemas de monitoramento precisam respeitar princípios da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD), como segurança, transparência, necessidade e finalidade no tratamento das informações.
As dúvidas sobre a proteção dos dados se somam à falta de transparência em relação ao reconhecimento facial. Segundo a Prefeitura, o município não tem acesso ao código-fonte, aos modelos de inteligência artificial nem às bases utilizadas para treinar os algoritmos. A administração também informou que não são realizadas auditorias independentes desses modelos.
Os registros de abordagens mostram outro ponto de atenção. Entre novembro de 2024 e maio de 2026, 268 pessoas foram conduzidas a delegacias após alertas do reconhecimento facial e acabaram liberadas. Em 75 casos, houve inconsistências na identificação; em 181, os mandados estavam desatualizados; e, em 12, foram constatados problemas cadastrais.
Prefeitura atribui vazamento a servidor
Em nota, a Prefeitura de São Paulo afirmou que o vazamento foi provocado ilegalmente por um servidor, identificado, afastado e investigado pela Corregedoria da Guarda Civil Metropolitana. A administração negou fragilidades nos mecanismos de segurança e contestou a caracterização do episódio como falha na plataforma.
A prefeitura declarou ainda ter reforçado a proteção com senhas exclusivas, autenticação em duas etapas e validação por SMS para a criação de novas senhas. Também citou a fiscalização do Tribunal de Contas do Município e a existência de consultoria especializada em governança e privacidade.
O Smart Sampa utiliza reconhecimento facial para localizar pessoas procuradas ou desaparecidas e identificar veículos roubados ou furtados. A exposição dos dados, porém, coloca em questão os controles de acesso e a proteção das informações reunidas por uma rede de vigilância que abrange milhares de pontos da cidade.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Tolan, the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital.
The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by Upstarts Media. (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”)
Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos.
Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is now in the “double-digit millions.”
The startup is one of the few AI companions that have found some traction, as it claims to have more than 250,000 active users who have had more than 70 million conversations over the past year. Around 70% of its users are women, and 40% are parents, Tolan’s team told the news outlet. (Anecdotally, the app is said to appeal in particular to neurodivergent people, who may benefit from additional support, whether that’s emotional support or help with organizing tasks.)
Compared with other companions, Tolan seems to have found a balance between being helpful without being perceived as too weird. Compare that with the public shaming that Friend’s pendant-based AI companion faced; users dubbed Friend “very cringe,” The New York Times called it “hated,” and Wired said it “has no soul.”
Meanwhile, another former top contender in the space, Character.AI, recently filed for bankruptcy after its founder’s return to Google. (Its remaining staff is transitioning to Disney, which bought some of its assets.)
However, Tolan could end up facing increased competition from the more recent crop of AI agents, which help users plan, organize, and accomplish their tasks and goals, not just talk their way through them. For instance, Meta gave its AI agent Muse a cute avatar for its users to talk to, which it also plans to release as a hardware product in the future.
The startup also has to navigate the risks of offering AI-powered emotional support, given that multiple lawsuits have been filed against general-purpose AI app makers alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to users’ suicides.

articles.title: Trotz Milliardenschulden und Aktienabsturz: Warum Coreweave noch nicht vor dem Aus steht
articles.text:
Coreweave hat Milliardenschulden: Wie sich das auf die KI-Branche auswirken könnte
Coreweave stellt eine KI-Cloud-Plattform sowie Computing-Leistung in Rechenzentren für seine Kund:innen bereit. Dazu zählen unter anderem Microsoft und OpenAI. Seit März 2025 ist das Unternehmen auch am Aktienmarkt gelistet und konnte dort innerhalb von wenigen Monaten den Einstiegspreis von 40 US-Dollar pro Aktie auf mehr als 180 Dollar hochtreiben. Doch seither geht es für Coreweave stetig bergab.
Coreweave: Warum Investor:innen Bedenken haben
Zuletzt hatte die Coreweave-Aktie am 2. Oktober 2026 einen Stand von knapp 91 Dollar. Innerhalb von wenigen Wochen ist der Preis pro Aktie auf 65 Dollar abgestürzt. In den vergangenen sechs Monaten ist die Aktie um knapp 50 Prozent ihres Wertes gefallen. Und das hat einen einfachen Grund. Die Investor:innen von Coreweave haben Bedenken, ob sie ihr Geld überhaupt noch wiedersehen werden.
Das liegt an den enormen Schulden, die Coreweave in den vergangenen Monaten und Jahren auf sich genommen hat, um Rechenzentren weiter auszubauen und KI-Cloud-Computing voranzutreiben. Mittlerweile soll das Unternehmen auf einem Schuldenberg von mehr als 46 Milliarden US-Dollar sitzen, wie Wallstreet Online berichtet. In den vergangenen zwölf Monaten konnte Coreweave zudem keinen Gewinn einfahren. Der Verlust des Unternehmens beläuft sich auf knapp zwei Milliarden Dollar.
Sollte sich dieser Trend fortsetzen und Coreweave eines Tages vor dem Aus stehen, würden auch zahlreiche Kunden, darunter große KI-Riesen der Branche, die Auswirkungen fehlender Computing-Power zu spüren bekommen. Dennoch gibt es selbst unter denjenigen, die das Platzen der KI-Blase genau so vorausgesagt haben, Zweifel, ob das Ende schon vor der Tür steht.
Denn wie The Verge berichtet, kann sich Coreweave noch an einer Hoffnung festhalten. Es gibt immer noch ausstehende, vertragliche Verpflichtungen von diversen Partnerunternehmen, darunter wie erwähnt Microsoft und OpenAI. Insgesamt beläuft sich dieser Betrag auf 103 Milliarden Dollar, wobei 40 Prozent des Betrags bis 2028 an Coreweave gezahlt werden müssen. Das Computing-Unternehmen kann sich also noch zeitweise über Wasser halten und wäre sogar in der Lage, die Schulden mittelfristig zurückzuzahlen. Das ist allerdings auch nur möglich, wenn in der Zwischenzeit nicht noch beträchtlich mehr Schulden dazukommen.

articles.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
articles.text:
Sponsored
AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
Tech and finance are setting the pace on AI adoption. TripleTen research shows which skills will reach healthcare, education, and retail next.
Provided byTripleTen
The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line.
As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn't a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.
The AI adoption spectrum by industry
Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1).
Figure 1: The AI adoption curve remains steep across industries, but non-tech industry adoption rates are increasing.
Source: TripleTen, 2026
While tech leads the way, finance emerges as a clear second: 48% of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots, and 32% have been asked to automate parts of their workflow. This demonstrates how rapidly knowledge work integrates AI once clear use cases emerge.
By contrast, sectors like healthcare (18% asked to use chatbots) and education (25%) reflect lower initial exposure. Because these broad industry categories encompass a mix of specialized hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional personnel, and back-office administrative staff, universal adoption was never going to happen overnight. Integrating automated tools into compliance-heavy or human-facing operations requires a more deliberate pace, which is reflected by the lower numbers.
The AI skills workers are being asked to learn
Across all surveyed industries, 79% of workers report being asked to learn at least one skill they didn't previously have. Looking at the specific competencies demanded in tech today offers a preview of the skill sets likely to shift into other sectors (see Figure 2).
Figure 2: Workforces across industries are learning new skills.
Source: TripleTen, 2026
Although some of these sound like niche skills confined to tech, many of them will translate to frontline work across sectors—from hospital systems managing patient logistics to school districts processing administrative reporting.
One skill gets less attention than it should. Only 30% of managers and owners call judging whether AI output is right or wrong an absolute must, which puts it sixth on a list of seven. As AI tools reach more industries, this is the skill that catches mistakes before they cause problems. It is also where work experience helps most: To spot a wrong answer, you need to know what the right one looks like.
How early AI adoption helps your career
Early AI adoption offers clear professional leverage: TripleTen’s survey data shows that when managers learned a new skill or automation process from an employee, 88% of those employee-led AI innovations became standard company practice.
In early-adopting industries, employees who identify repetitive administrative tasks and use AI tools to streamline them have a voice in shaping organizational policy. As healthcare networks, educational institutions, and retail operations begin broader rollouts of AI-enabled software, workers who understand how to validate outputs, prompt models, and automate routine tasks will hold a strong advantage. Being the person who can streamline administrative overhead promises better chances for retention, promotions, and wage growth.
Ana Riabova, the AI strategy and enablement lead at TripleTen, says, “Everyone talks about saving time, but the real win with early adoption is expanding what you can actually do. People who get ahead are using it to handle things they used to have to hand off. It doesn't matter how senior or junior you are. You keep your core skills, but suddenly you aren't boxed in by them anymore.”
The AI resource gap: Who pays for training and how workers learn
If non-tech industries absorb these tools more gradually, the challenge for workers lies in getting access to quality learning resources. Workers’ out-of-pocket investment in training varies significantly by industry:
- Tech: $1,758 average (13% spent $0)
- Finance: $1,664 average (24% spent $0)
- Healthcare: $990 average (45% spent $0)
- Education: $883 average (42% spent $0)
Nearly half of healthcare and education workers spent nothing out of pocket on professional development last year. Furthermore, tech workers actively leverage a larger variety of learning channels (see Figure 3).
Figure 3: Professional development efforts mirror the AI adoption curve.
Source: TripleTen, 2026
Tech workers are nearly twice as likely as all workers to use AI chatbots as learning tools (48% vs. 27%), and more than twice as likely as workers outside tech (21%), effectively using AI to accelerate their acquisition of other skills.
However, ask workers whom they trust most to teach them a new job skill, and they choose someone currently doing that job (31%). Fewer pick an official certification program (19%), an AI tool (16%), or a university professor (6%).
Conclusion
The difference in AI adoption rates across industries is not a story of who is succeeding and who is failing. Rather, it’s a timeline of how technology diffuses through an economy. Tech and finance are testing the mechanics of AI integration today. For workers in healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing, the current phase provides a valuable window to observe which skills generate real productivity gains—allowing them to build those competencies before they become standard industry expectations.
This content was produced by TripleTen. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

articles.title: Revolut sufre una caída masiva y no se puede ni usar la app ni pagar... o acceder a tu dinero
articles.text:
Revolut ha confirmado una caída masiva de sus sistemas que está impidiendo a los usuarios poder acceder a la app (y por tanto a sus cuentas) o poder pagar. Desde esta mañana, múltiples usuarios han reportado que no podían pagar con las tarjetas de Revolut, ni tampoco a través de sistemas de pago de terceros.
Ahora la compañía ha confirmado que ha sufrido una caída generalizada de sus sistemas que afecta a varios de sus servicios, aunque están trabajando en ello. Se desconoce cuándo volverán a estar operativos o qué nivel de disrupción está experimentando la compañía, así como las causas de la misma:
Actualmente estamos experimentando una interrupción en el servicio que afecta a varias funcionalidades, lo que podría hacer que algunos servicios no estén disponibles. Nuestro equipo de ingeniería está trabajando activamente para restablecer el servicio por completo a la mayor brevedad posible. Agradecemos su paciencia y pedimos disculpas por cualquier inconveniente que esto haya podido causar.
Actualmente, la web de servicio de la compañía confirma que 31 de sus instancias están afectadas o no disponibles, incluyendo los sistemas de registro, inicio de sesión, transferencias o pagos con tarjeta, sin que haya trascendido cuándo volverán a estar disponibles.
Si eres usuario de Revolut, te recomendamos estar atento al estado del sistema de la compañía y, mientras tanto, usar otros servicios bancarios alternativos.
