articles.title: Reaction Dynamics plans rapid expansion to launch new medium-lift rocket by 2031
articles.text:
Reaction Dynamics is looking to raise hundreds of millions in funding and add nearly 300 employees over the next five years to send a new, more powerful rocket toward the stars.
At the SpaceBound Conference in Ottawa on Tuesday morning, the Longueuil, Que.-based rocket maker revealed its plans to develop and send a new medium-lift rocket to space by 2031. Dubbed Borealis, the medium-lift rocket is the larger sibling of Reaction Dynamics’ light-lift Aurora rocket. While Aurora is meant for payloads below half a tonne, Borealis is designed to haul a six-tonne payload to low Earth orbit for larger spacecraft deployments, satellite constellation launches, and other large space missions, similar to SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket.
“We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms.”
SpaceX’s rocket is so popular for shipping satellites to space that it’s started turning away customers past 2028. This has opened the door for Canada’s burgeoning space industry, including Reaction Dynamics. The company said it’s already signed 10 agreements and letters of intent with undisclosed prospective launch customers across Canada, the United States, and Europe.
“We see an opportunity to serve Canadian demand while providing additional dedicated launch capacity for customers in the United States, Europe, and allied countries,” Jesse Mikelberg, Reaction Dynamics’ director of business, tech, and strategy, said in an email to BetaKit. “As a result, customers would have greater control over their launch schedule and destination orbit.”
To give those prospective customers a ride to space, Reaction Dynamics has set some big-time goals. First, the company wants to launch Aurora into orbit from Canadian soil by 2028. The company will then build on that base of manufacturing investments, equipment, processes, and expertise to get Borealis into space by 2031, Mikelberg explained.
“Aurora will give us flight experience and practical knowledge of manufacturing, transporting, integrating, and launching an orbital vehicle,” Mikelberg said. “It will also help us establish customer relationships, spaceport operations, and credibility through execution.”
While Mikelberg makes it sound simple, it is literally rocket science. This requires a lot of manpower and capital. Reaction Dynamics is planning for a large influx of both.
Over the next five years, the company aims to increase its headcount from 68 employees to 350. To accommodate all the new staff, Reaction Dynamics is also looking to increase its manufacturing and testing footprint from 60,000 square feet to 375,000 square feet. The company sees a “strong foundation” for this expansion in Québec, Mikelberg said, but it’s also eyeing land in Ontario or Nova Scotia.
RELATED: First Canada, then the world: nation’s rocket builders see a bigger opening in space
Expanding a business like this, let alone one that builds rockets, isn’t cheap. Reaction Dynamics is planning to raise around $350 million CAD in new private investment across two rounds over the next five years: a Series B targeting between $70 million and 100 million CAD to support Aurora’s first orbital launch in 2028, and then a Series C, or a similar funding instrument, targeting between $200 million and 250 million CAD to aid development for Borealis’ first launch in 2031.
This funding would come in addition to the $50 million Reaction Dynamics has already raised to date from private investors and non-dilutive government funding sources.
“Our approach is to broaden the investor base as we demonstrate propulsion performance, establish manufacturing capacity, secure customers, and gain flight experience,” Mikelberg said.
Founded in 2017, Reaction Dynamics has been building rocket propulsion systems since long before space became one of the “key sovereign capabilities” in the federal government’s Defence Industrial Strategy. Under the DIS, the 2025 federal budget committed $182.6 million over three years to the Department of National Defence (DND) to establish a sovereign space launch capability.
Reaction Dynamics benefitted from Canada’s renewed focus on space earlier this year when the company was awarded an $8.3 million grant under the first round of the DND’s Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security (IDEaS) Launch the North contest to build out its rocket launch capabilities. Reaction’s younger Canadian rocket-building peers, Canada Rocket Company and NordSpace, also received that funding.
The IDEaS funding was announced alongside the federal government signing a $200 million lease with Maritime Launch Services to establish a government spaceport in Nova Scotia. Reaction Dynamics has also invested in MLS, and its spaceport just outside Canso, NS, is the planned location for Aurora’s first orbital launch.
“We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,” Reaction Dynamics founder and CEO Bachar Elzein said in a statement. “Aurora is how we get there in 2028. Borealis is how we build on that foundation to deliver medium lift by 2031. Nearly a decade of propulsion development and engineering, right here in Quebec, has brought us to this point.”
Feature image courtesy Reaction Dynamics.

articles.title: How a blockchain marketplace is unlocking clean gas production in Kenya - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme, supported by the Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation, UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Kenya-based Autonomous Systems Research (ASR) began by exploring how drones could support disaster response, wildlife and environmental conservation. Working in remote areas led founder Moses Gichanga to investigate another challenge: generating electricity without transporting fuel into the field. ASR is developing ways to turn waste plant material into gas and electricity, and using blockchain to track traceability of biomass, payments to suppliers as well as applications in mobile money and disaster response.
How did a hobby building drones turn into Autonomous Systems Research?
Back in 2011, my daughter was two and a half and needed amusing, so I made her a kite. When the kite got boring, I built a small aeroplane out of paper bags. One early version had an eight-foot wingspan, with a laptop strapped to it and car wiper motors working the controls. Then I asked myself what would happen if I strapped a camera to one and flew it in a national reserve. That was when I started flying drones in Tsavo National Park.
I began asking how we could use this technology to help elephants and other wildlife, and to conserve ecological areas. That grew into Autonomous Systems Research. Later, ASR received its first grant from UNICEF Office of Innovation. We used it to explore whether drones could be useful for disaster response planning, ecological conservation, wildlife and agriculture, and what data would come out of that work. Since then, we have flown missions with government agencies, including Kenya Wildlife Service.
How did conservation work lead you from drones to producing energy from plant material?
Some of the places where we work are very remote and have no electricity. Our drones need charging, so we used a generator. But it became unsustainable to keep carrying fuel into the wilderness. We looked at solar panels, but they took up space and time. So we thought about modifying a generator to run on gas made from biomass. Later, people in communities saw that we had electricity in places without a supply and asked where we got it. We began thinking about making gas and electricity available to them too.
Where would the biomass come from, and what could the gas and electricity be used for?
We still use drones to look for potential sources of biomass. Once we identify some, we send someone to find out whether we can purchase it or otherwise acquire it. We want waste biomass. We do not want to cut down trees, and we do not want people planting biomass to sell to us instead of growing food. Coffee bushes, for example, produce material when they are pruned. We can turn that into gas.
We have developed equipment that converts biomass into gas, which we can use to run an engine. Gas is the primary thing we produce, but we can generate electricity as well. We have a site near our rural office where we are working with people who provide biomass and receive gas. We are also in the process of bringing local primary schools into the project. We are also in the process of brining local primary schools into the project. We want to see whether – with the right safety checks, ventilation and supervision – the gas could be used to cook meals and heat water, as an alternative to open fires.
You began using blockchain to track biomass. What does it record, and where else might you use it?
We wanted an audit trail that someone else could inspect. For the biomass, we record where it comes from, what type it is, the quantity, who gave permission to clear it, what they were paid, if anything, and how much gas we produced from it. We also have a payment mechanism for people who provide biomass, connected to mobile money platforms, M-Pesa and Airtel Money. We are interested in carbon credits in the future, and for that we would need a record people can trace.
We are looking at other applications too. Through our work on payments, we have engaged a local bank and are building a platform intended to offer mobile money services using blockchain. We also do volunteer work in emergencies, and we have developed a ledger system that can record where survivors are and what help they need after a disaster, though we have not applied that in a real-world setting yet.
What is holding the gas project back from operating at a larger scale?
We can produce the gas, but we have not reached the point of liquefying it efficiently. At the moment, we store it without liquefying it, which takes up more space. If we could liquefy it, we could fit more into a cylinder and look at selling it on a larger scale. We have tried some basic methods, but they use too much energy to work commercially. Finding a better way to do it would require substantial investment.
ASR began with drones, but you are now developing energy and other technologies. Is the idea to test solutions at ASR, then build separate businesses around the ones that work?
Yes. ASR does research into systems that can run themselves. That includes the drones and, eventually, the gas plant. When we develop a project, we intend to incorporate it as its own company, with its own governance structure, while ASR continues doing research.
We do not plan for ASR itself to become the gas supplier. The gas business could sell the product and make money as its own company, although we would still expect to have a role in its governance. We want to take an idea through the research and testing stage and then allow it to become something that can stand on its own.
ASR is a for-profit company, but you describe social good as central to its work. How do those aims fit together?
Social good is front and centre in what we do. Our tagline is “tools for transformative change”. We are structured as a limited liability company and we intend to make a profit, but we engage in projects that have a social good component.
We hope to make a lot of money. We want to do it in a way that helps our neighbours make money too. The more money they make, the less they need from us or from donors. There is a limit to how long someone can keep holding your hand. At some point, you need to become self-sustaining.
Take the gas project. We intend to sell the gas, but I also think about children collecting twigs for firewood. If we can make gas affordable to their households, they would not have to do that. I do not see a conflict between the social purpose and the business: we want to produce the gas cheaply enough that we can sell it at a price people can afford. As we see it, it is easier to get a shilling each from a million people than a million shillings from one person.
UNICEF was ASR’s first backer. Beyond the grant, what did its support make possible?
The first grant let us explore whether drones could be used for disaster response planning, conservation, wildlife and agriculture. Later, when we approached other organizations, we could show them what we had done and what we had learned. We have since received grants from other organizations, including Kenya’s National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation, and done business with local government organizations.
We have also remained part of UNICEF’s alumni community since its investment. UNICEF organized a session for us with Google for Startups, and we later graduated from that programme. They organized seminars and workshops and supported our attendance at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting of the New Champions. Those opportunities helped us think differently about what we could do.

articles.title: Qualcomm Wins Key Claims Against Arm, but Damages Total Just $2 - EE Times
articles.text:
On Oct. 13, a federal jury in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware delivered a verdict in favor of Qualcomm. The jury found that Arm breached its Architectural License Agreement and intentionally interfered with the commercialization of Qualcomm’s custom Oryon CPUs. While the jury awarded Qualcomm just $1 on each claim, U.S. District Court Judge Maryellen Noreika must still decide Qualcomm’s requested remedy that could allow it to suspend royalty payments to Arm for up to five years.
“We are gratified that the jury found Arm breached its long-standing Architectural License Agreement (ALA) with Qualcomm, failed to honor its commitments, and intentionally acted to disrupt Qualcomm’s businesses,” said Qualcomm in an official statement. “This outcome is a victory for innovation and competition, and we remain focused on developing and delivering industry-leading semiconductor products including our Oryon CPUs to customers and consumers worldwide.”
The decision is the latest chapter in a four-year legal dispute between two semiconductor companies, ensuring that Qualcomm can proceed with marketing its custom silicon across smartphones, AI personal computers, and automotive platforms without the threat of legal injunctions or compulsory design destruction.
By finding Arm liable for contractual interference, leaking the 2024 license-termination warning letter, and failure to meet support commitments by withholding software patches and chip testing tools, the ruling stabilizes chip availability for major device manufacturers while shifting legal and financial pressure back onto Arm.
“We are pleased with the jury’s decision today finding for Arm on four claims and awarding only one dollar in damages on each of Qualcomm’s other two claims,” Arm said in its official statement. “Despite Qualcomm’s pursuit of this case in an attempt to deprive Arm of billions of dollars under our license agreements, the jury’s verdict confirms that Arm operated in good faith under its technology license agreement and its award of only $2 confirms the merit of Arm’s arguments in the case.”
Technical distinction driving the conflict
At the center of the conflict between Arm and Qualcomm is a fundamental distinction in how intellectual property is commercialized within the semiconductor industry. Arm operates as an architectural IP licensor rather than a silicon manufacturer. The firm defines the instruction set architecture (ISA), establishing rules governing how software instructions interact with computing hardware.
To monetize this technology, Arm offers two primary licensing structures: technology license agreements (TLA) and architecture license agreements (ALA). Under a TLA, a customer purchases off-the-shelf core designs, such as Arm’s standard Cortex series, and integrates them into a system-on-chip in exchange for licensing fees and per-unit royalties.
Under an ALA, the licensee pays for access to the underlying instruction set architecture, granting the right to engineer custom CPU cores, provided those cores maintain software compatibility.
Historically, Qualcomm relied on its TLA with Arm. However, as computational demands increased, Qualcomm sought to develop custom cores to improve energy efficiency and performance.
In early 2021, Qualcomm acquired Nuvia, a silicon startup founded by veteran chip architects holding an ALA with Arm tailored to data center processors. Qualcomm integrated Nuvia’s engineering team and designs into its roadmap, leading to the development of the custom Oryon CPU architecture.
Four years of cross-litigation
The transfer of Nuvia’s design work into Qualcomm’s product portfolio sparked strong resistance from Arm. In March 2022, Arm terminated Nuvia’s license and demanded that Qualcomm destroy all design files derived from Nuvia’s work. Arm asserted that its licensing frameworks prohibited transferring custom designs between distinct corporate entities without explicit consent and renegotiated terms.
When Qualcomm declined to destroy the technology, maintaining that its overarching license covered the development and commercialization of the Oryon cores, Arm filed a lawsuit in Delaware District Court in August 2022. Arm alleged breach of contract and trademark infringement, seeking an injunction to force Qualcomm to halt production of chips containing Nuvia-derived technology.
That initial phase of litigation concluded in legal victories for Qualcomm. In December 2024, a Delaware jury determined that Qualcomm’s custom CPU technology was properly licensed under Qualcomm’s existing ALA and that Qualcomm had not breached the Nuvia contract. On Sept. 30, 2025, the presiding judge issued a final judgment, affirming those jury findings and dismissing Arm’s remaining claims as a matter of law. Arm subsequently filed an appeal with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where the matter remains pending.
While defending against Arm’s claims, Qualcomm launched its own offensive in April 2024, alleging that Arm breached both licensing agreements by failing to deliver technical support, failing to provide reasonable licensing terms, and improperly interfering with Qualcomm’s customer relationships.
The conflict escalated in October 2024 when Arm issued a formal notice threatening to terminate Qualcomm’s overarching ALA entirely—a move that threatened to halt global production of Qualcomm’s Snapdragon processors. Arm withdrew the notice in January 2025, but Qualcomm incorporated the incident into its allegations of bad-faith conduct, leading to the October 2026 trial in Wilmington, Delaware.
The jury’s decision followed a five-day trial in which jurors evaluated licensing terms and corporate communications between the two companies. After receiving the case on Oct. 9, 2026, the jury returned its verdict on Oct. 13, finding Arm liable for breaching the “Architectural License Agreement” governing how Qualcomm uses Arm’s architecture to build custom processor designs.
However, the jury sided with Arm on five of the six breach-of-contract allegations, rejecting Qualcomm’s claims that Arm had violated those specific terms of its technology license agreement.
Financial pressure and win for open standards such as RISC-V
Beyond confirming Qualcomm’s right to commercialize its custom silicon, the October 2026 verdict introduces financial uncertainty for Arm. During the trial, proceedings highlighted a contractual provision that could permit a licensee to suspend royalty payments for five years if Arm commits a material breach.
As of today (Oct. 19), the judge has yet to rule on whether a specific contractual clause—which could allow Qualcomm to entirely cease paying royalties to Arm for a period of five years due to Arm’s material breach of the agreement—is legally enforceable.
If enforced, the financial consequences for Arm could be substantial. Qualcomm represents one of Arm’s largest revenue sources, accounting for approximately 10% of Arm’s total global revenue for fiscal year 2024. A five-year hiatus on royalty collections from Qualcomm would reduce Arm’s cash flows, impacting research funding and market valuation expectations following Arm’s initial public offering in September 2023.
For original equipment manufacturers, the verdict provides operational certainty. Handset makers such as Samsung Electronics, alongside personal computer manufacturers deploying Snapdragon 8 Elite processors and Oryon CPUs, can continue hardware production without risk of supply chain disruptions.
At the same time, the legal battle has altered industry perceptions regarding proprietary architecture licensing. Arm’s willingness to engage in litigation against its premier customer has encouraged semiconductor designers and cloud operators to accelerate investments in open instruction set architectures, such as RISC-V, to mitigate long-term risks.
For now, the Delaware verdict establishes Qualcomm’s legal authority to deploy its custom silicon, reshaping commercial boundaries across the technology sector.

articles.title: Le Starship sur la Lune fin 2027 : le calendrier détaillé que la NASA a fixé à SpaceX
articles.text:
À quoi faut-il s’attendre pour le programme spatial lunaire de la NASA et, plus particulièrement, pour tout ce qui est prévu du côté de SpaceX dans le cadre des missions Artémis ? L’agence spatiale américaine a fait un point à l’occasion du Congrès international d’astronautique (IAC), qui se tenait à Antalya, en Turquie, du 5 au 9 octobre 2026.
Un point d’autant plus nécessaire que les contours du programme Artémis ont évolué au cours des derniers mois. Steve Creech, qui dirige à la NASA le programme des atterrisseurs lunaires habités (HLS, pour Human Landing System), a présenté un calendrier actualisé pour le Starship, avec des jalons attendus trimestre par trimestre.
L’actuel planning découle du remaniement annoncé le 27 février 2026 par Jared Isaacman, administrateur de la NASA. Artémis III devait être le premier alunissage habité depuis Apollo 17, en 1972. Elle est devenue une mission d’essais en orbite autour de la Terre, avec quatre astronautes à bord, dont un Européen.
D’après la présentation, Artémis III doit décoller en 2027 (cela correspond aux plans présentés ce printemps) pour tester l’amarrage du vaisseau Orion avec les deux atterrisseurs en concurrence, celui de SpaceX et le Blue Moon de Blue Origin. Le premier alunissage passe à Artémis IV, début 2028, et le deuxième à Artémis V, fin 2028.
Les deux engins sont très différents. Le Starship lunaire est l’étage supérieur de la fusée lui-même : 52 mètres de haut, six moteurs Raptor au méthane, une cabine tout en haut et un ascenseur pour descendre les astronautes jusqu’au sol. Le Blue Moon, lui, mesure 16 mètres et ses passagers descendent par une échelle.
Ce calendrier laisse à Starship un peu plus d’un an pour réussir deux choses qu’il n’a jamais faites : faire le plein en orbite, puis se poser sur la Lune sans équipage, avant la fin de 2027. Le créneau est très serré, mais SpaceX a récemment progressé avec le Starship, notamment en matière de vol orbital.
Le plein en orbite début 2027, la Lune fin 2027
Voici les grandes étapes que le calendrier de la NASA fixe à SpaceX :
- fin 2026 : premier Starship rattrapé par la tour de lancement, premier vol depuis la Floride, première réutilisation d’un propulseur Super Heavy V3, et fin de la construction de « Cabin One », une cabine d’équipage grandeur nature testée au sol à Starbase, au Texas ;
- début 2027 : démonstration de transfert de carburant et deuxième pas de tir en Floride ;
- printemps 2027 : test des pieds d’atterrissage, essais du sas sur Cabin One et transport du vaisseau de test vers la Floride par barge ;
- été 2027 : mission Artémis III ;
- fin 2027 : premier vol d’un ravitailleur, lancement de l’atterrisseur de démonstration et alunissage sans équipage.
Pour la NASA, le transfert de carburant est l’un des plus gros défis techniques du programme.
Starship arrive en orbite les réservoirs quasi vides, car il a brûlé l’essentiel de son méthane et de son oxygène liquides pour quitter la Terre. Pour filer vers la Lune, il doit donc être rempli par d’autres Starship, qui servent de ravitailleurs. Ces liquides sont stockés sous les -160 °C, et personne n’a encore fait ce transfert d’un vaisseau à l’autre à cette échelle.
SpaceX n’a pas encore remporté la mise (le premier alunissage n’est pas attribué)
L’affaire n’est pas encore gagnée pour SpaceX. La NASA écrit noir sur blanc que l’atterrisseur d’Artémis IV n’est pas choisi à ce jour. Certes, SpaceX avait été retenu seul en 2021 pour ce premier alunissage. Depuis, il faut compter avec Blue Origin, qui prévoit son propre atterrissage sans équipage au cours du premier trimestre 2028. La concurrence est là.
SpaceX a d’ailleurs déjà pris du retard. Dans un rapport publié le 10 mars 2026, l’inspection générale de la NASA estime que le Starship lunaire a pris au moins deux ans de retard depuis la signature du contrat, en juillet 2021, et que d’autres décalages sont à prévoir. Les échéances posées par Elon Musk peinent ainsi à être respectées.
Au-delà de ce premier alunissage, la présentation esquisse la suite pour SpaceX, après 2028. Une version cargo de Starship, capable de déposer environ 15 tonnes sur la Lune, devrait y livrer un rover pressurisé développé par l’agence spatiale japonaise (JAXA). La NASA compte confier cette mission à SpaceX, mais pas avant son exercice budgétaire 2032, qui démarre en octobre 2031.
Jared Isaacman doit faire le point sur Artémis III et Artémis IV ce vendredi 23 octobre, à 20 heures (heure de Paris), lors d’une conférence de presse au centre spatial Kennedy, en Floride.

articles.title: "La première d'une longue série", Elon Musk va donner une action SpaceX à des millions d'enfants
articles.text:
Elon Musk s’est engagé, lundi soir sur son réseau social, à offrir une action SpaceX à chaque enfant américain en 2027. Le don est évalué à plus de 10 milliards de dollars, et ne serait qu'un début.
Il est toujours difficile de savoir si Elon Musk déborde d'ambition politique, ou s'il maîtrise toujours autant les actions disons « coup de tête ». Une action SpaceX pour chaque enfant américain, telle est la promesse lâchée lundi 19 octobre par le milliardaire sur X, avec en prime un « ce sera la première d'une longue série » qui laisse songeur. Le boss de Tesla venait d'expliquer à Anthropic comment, selon lui, l'entreprise devait distribuer ses actions. On est déjà curieux de voir comment il parviendra à glisser plus de 70 millions de titres dans autant de petites mains.
Actions SpaceX : un cadeau à 10 milliards d'Elon Musk, sans notice
Elon Musk veut donc donner une action SpaceX à chaque petit américain. Très bien. Faisons le calcul. Les États-Unis comptent un peu plus de 70 millions de mineurs. À raison d'une action chacun, soit un minuscule morceau de l'entreprise valant environ 146 dollars (130 euros), la facture dépasse les 10 milliards, près de 9 milliards d'euros. Vous avez dit vertigineux ? Pas pour Elon Musk, qui ne céderait qu'à peine plus de 1 % de ses actions SpaceX. Le titre, introduit en juin à 150 dollars, avait grimpé jusqu'à 225 dollars avant de reculer nettement. L'annonce lui a redonné un peu d'élan : environ +1,32 % au moment d'écrire ces lignes, à quasi 148 dollars.
Pour le reste, c'est flou comme un brouillard d'automne. Qui sera éligible, quand, et par quel canal ? Elon Musk n'a donné aucun détail. Une piste tient la corde, celle des « Trump Accounts ». Ces comptes d'investissement pour enfants, ouverts via le Trésor américain, peuvent recevoir des dons d'actions. Brad Gerstner, investisseur à l'origine du dispositif, a salué l'annonce et suggéré d'y verser les titres.
Il présente ces comptes comme offrant à chaque mineur « un compte d'investissement gratuit, à vie ». Dire qu'en juillet, Gwynne Shotwell, présidente de SpaceX, et son mari avaient promis une action à plus de deux millions d'enfants. On peut évidemment douter de la neutralité d'Elon Musk, lui qui a déjà dépensé environ 300 millions de dollars pour aider à faire élire son ancien-futur-ex-actuel (on sait plus) ami Donald Trump.
Quand Elon Musk répond à Anthropic par l'exemple
L'entreprise Anthropic n'est pas étrangère là-dedans. Dimanche, l'entreprise qui exploite le chatbot Claude a annoncé vouloir placer 5 % de ses actions dans un fonds d'intérêt public, sous réserve du feu vert de ses actionnaires. Après sa future introduction en bourse, ce fonds financerait des associations ou redistribuerait directement à certaines populations. Elon Musk a recommandé de donner plutôt « directement au public ». Quatre heures plus tard, il précisait : « C'est ce que je vais faire. » L'annonce sur SpaceX a suivi dans la nuit.
Le milliardaire, pourtant peu tendre avec la philanthropie, ira-t-il jusqu'au bout ? Ses dons passent jusqu'ici presque tous par la Musk Foundation, cinquième plus grande fondation caritative privée des États-Unis. Rendez-vous en 2027 pour juger sur pièces.

articles.title: How Operation Sindoor reshaped India's private defence tech industry
articles.text:
How Operation Sindoor reshaped India's private defence tech industry
From faster procurement to direct engagement with the armed forces, Operation Sindoor has opened new opportunities for private defence companies developing critical military technologies.
Following Operation Sindoor, India's private defence technology sector is seeing a shift in how the armed forces engage with domestic manufacturers. The transformation is marked by faster procurement, greater private-sector participation, and renewed emphasis on developing critical military technologies domestically, according to industry executives.
At TechSparks 2026, Ankit Kumar, Co-founder and Chief Business Officer of Tonbo Imaging; Priyanka Singhal, Founder and CEO of Ammunic Systems; and Radhika P, Co-founder of Pinaka Aerospace; discussed how Indian private companies contributed to recent military operations and what the country must prioritise to prepare for the battlefield of 2035.
In a panel discussion titled 'War Room 2035: What technologies must India build for the battlefield' moderated by Adith Charlie, Managing Editor of YourStory and The CapTable, the founders pointed to growing opportunities for indigenous companies in night-vision systems, electronic warfare, smart munitions, and autonomous defence platforms.
Operation Sindoor and the private sector's growing role
Priyanka Singhal, Founder and CEO of Ammunic Systems, a defence R&D firm specialising in electronic fuzes and munition technologies, described Operation Sindoor as a turning point for the industry. “The operation was an eye opener,” she said, adding that it had exposed the limitations of traditional defence procurement cycles.
Singhal said Ammunic supplied loitering munitions and gravity-drop bombs during Operation Sindoor, working with drone platform partners to integrate its weapons into systems used in the operation. According to her, the armed forces have begun moving away from an excessive focus on procedural compliance towards deploying equipment that meets immediate battlefield requirements. Initiatives such as iDEX and emergency procurement mechanisms have helped accelerate the process, she said.
Radhika P of Pinaka Aerospace echoed this assessment. Previously, private defence companies often worked through defence public sector undertakings (DPSUs), the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), and other established channels. Following Operation Sindoor, she said, the armed forces had increasingly engaged directly with private companies, particularly in electronic warfare, avionics, and sensor technologies.
Radhika said Pinaka had contributed to the indigenisation of missile systems that were deployed during the operation. She argued that the effectiveness of military equipment increasingly depends on its payloads, including sensors and electronic warfare systems, rather than the platform alone.
“If there is an electronic countermeasure system, it can neutralise a platform which is probably 10 times more expensive,” she said, underscoring the strategic importance of developing indigenous payload technologies.
Kumar of Tonbo Imaging, which specialises in electro-optical and infrared technologies, said the shift towards indigenous defence procurement had begun even before Operation Sindoor, particularly following developments along India's eastern border. That had encouraged the armed forces to reduce their dependence on technologies sourced from countries sharing land borders with India.
Tonbo, which has spent nearly two decades developing indigenous imaging systems, was positioned to benefit from that shift, Kumar said. Its night-vision technologies have been deployed across several Indian military operations, including Operation Sindoor, when air-defence systems used the company's capabilities, he added.
Kumar said close engagement with the armed forces, including product trials and feedback from users, had helped Tonbo develop its technologies. “We've learned things the hard way. We've learned things on the ground. We've learned things with the customers,” he said.
What India must build by 2035
Looking towards 2035, Kumar said defence systems would increasingly move towards autonomy, reducing the need for direct human involvement in certain operations. He pointed to the potential use of autonomous systems in air combat and on the ground, including the possibility of humanoid robots supporting border operations.
As military platforms become more autonomous, sensors and intelligence will become critical to their ability to detect threats, interpret their surroundings and respond without constant human intervention.
“For autonomy, sensors, intelligence, both are very critical, very important,” Kumar said.
He argued that India had strengths in both areas, particularly in developing intelligence capabilities that can operate directly on military platforms. Such technologies, he said, could improve operational efficiency and reduce dependence on human operators, but they needed to be developed as sovereign capabilities rather than sourced from overseas suppliers.
“Intelligence, connectivity, sensing, these will be the mainstay of how the wars will be fought tomorrow,” he said.
For Radhika, a key battlefield priority is control over the electromagnetic spectrum, which underpins radar, communications, electronic warfare, and several other military capabilities. She argued that future military advantage would increasingly depend on how effectively forces detect, interpret and disrupt electromagnetic signals.
That also makes ownership of the underlying technology critical. Developing or assembling defence platforms in India is not sufficient if the software, electronics architecture and intellectual property remain controlled by foreign suppliers.
“It is very important to have good control on the source code, the board design, and things like that,” Radhika said.
She also emphasised that technology transfer should strengthen India's ability to develop and integrate systems independently, rather than create continued dependence on overseas suppliers. Control over intellectual property and systems integration would be especially important in reducing the risks associated with foreign supply chains, she added.
Closing the gaps in research and deployment
Singhal, meanwhile, called for greater integration across the three armed services.
She argued that the Army, Navy and Air Force needed better-connected platforms and weapons systems to coordinate effectively during emergencies. She also highlighted materials research as an area requiring greater attention.
Advanced materials would play an increasingly important role in developing next-generation weapon systems, including those requiring greater effectiveness and stealth capabilities. India, she said, needed to place more emphasis on materials R&D alongside investments in autonomous systems and other defence technologies.
The founders also identified persistent challenges in bringing together the armed forces, government research institutions and private industry. Singhal said startups and smaller defence companies could move faster than government research programmes, which often face bureaucratic delays.
Radhika said the challenge stemmed partly from differing expectations. The armed forces want sophisticated systems delivered quickly, research organisations operate through lengthy validation cycles and private manufacturers need commercially viable development timelines.
One way forward, she suggested, was to involve private industry from the prototype stage, with the armed forces funding development projects, research organisations working alongside manufacturers and clearer pathways to production orders.
She pointed to the Development-cum-Production Partner model as a mechanism that could help bridge the gap between research, development and large-scale manufacturing if implemented effectively.
For India's private defence technology industry, the next challenge is not simply to manufacture more equipment domestically. It is to develop and control the technologies that make military platforms effective, while building a procurement and research ecosystem capable of moving those technologies from the laboratory to the battlefield.

articles.title: Google Traduction : la grande refonte de l'interface arrive enfin sur Android
articles.text:
Google Traduction s’offre un lifting important sur Android. Repérée sur plusieurs smartphones tournant sous la version 10.39.34.99 de l’application, la nouvelle interface évolue pour se rapprocher des standards graphiques Material 3 Expressive que l’on retrouve sur d’autres services de la marque.
Une nouvelle barre de navigation et plus de place pour saisir le texte
La barre de navigation en bas de l’interface adopte désormais un positionnement similaire à celui que l’on trouve déjà dans Google Photos ou Google Lens, par exemple. On remarque également que le champ de texte au centre est bien plus grand que sur la version précédente de l’interface.
L’ancien design à gauche, le premier redesign au milieu et le nouveau design à droite. – Source : Android Authority
Le bouton à trois points qui regroupait auparavant le sélecteur de modèle de traduction et l’option d’écriture manuscrite disparaît également. Cette dernière fonctionnalité bascule directement à l’intérieur de la boîte de texte, placée juste à côté d’une icône de microphone (légèrement modifiée elle aussi). Enfin, l’option pour coller le texte se trouve désormais sur la gauche.
Quelques compromis inévitables
En revanche, l’agrandissement important de la zone de saisie du texte laisse malheureusement trop peu de place pour afficher les raccourcis contextuels, comme celui de l’entraînement du jour ou de la reprise rapide d’une conversation. Les autres sections de l’application comme les onglets Traduction instantanée, Appareil photo et Entraînement, ne subissent pas de modifications majeures.
Source : Android Authority
À lire : Google Traduction veut faire le ménage dans nos hésitations orales
Côté graphique, on retrouve une cohérence des couleurs et des nouveaux éléments avec le style Material 3 Expressive de Google. Le déploiement de cette nouvelle version de Google Traduction se poursuit au compte-gouttes, ce qui signifie que vous devriez le voir arriver sur vos smartphones et tablettes Android dans les semaines à venir, si ce n’est pas déjà le cas.

articles.title: Hackers hijack AOMEI update servers to secretly spread malware
articles.text:
Hackers reportedly compromised AOMEI's servers to distribute malware through a built-in promotional feature in its backup software, briefly tampering with configuration files before restoring them to their original state to hide the attacks.
The supply chain attacks took place between April and July 2026 and targeted the update and notification systems used by AOMEI Backupper, a Windows application for backing up data, cloning disks, and restoring systems.
Researchers at ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), working with Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, uncovered the campaign and investigated the attacks.
In reports published by Google and ManageEngine, the activity is attributed to a threat actor tracked as UNC7017, who used the compromised infrastructure to distribute a previously unknown malware downloader called CROSSROAD and a backdoor named SHINYROAD.
The researchers identified affected organizations in multiple countries, including the United States, Australia, India, Singapore, Spain, and Switzerland, across sectors such as IT services, telecommunications, and higher education.
However, Google warned that the attacks were opportunistic and could have affected additional organizations that checked for software updates during the brief periods when malicious files were being distributed.
Software
The attacks were first detected on May 28, when ManageEngine said its endpoint security software spotted AOMEI Backupper suddenly installing the legitimate remote administration tool Radmin on computers at two unrelated companies in different countries.
The Radmin installation was suspicious because AOMEI's built-in promotion processes launched it, which normally handle downloading and displaying promotional content and notifications.
However, when researchers attempted to reproduce the behavior on their own test systems, they found nothing malicious. Instead, the software contacted AOMEI's servers and downloaded the legitimate configuration file.
Further testing showed that instead of permanently replacing files on AOMEI's servers, the attackers briefly modified two configuration files used by the promotion and notification systems:
https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini
https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini
The first file, down_html.ini, tells AOMEI Backupper where to download update packages. The second, Notifycfg.ini, controls notifications and can trigger content to run on the computer.
By modifying these files, the attackers redirected the software to download a malicious ZIP archive and then used the notification mechanism to execute the malware without requiring user interaction.
Researchers at Google later confirmed this execution flow in their own tests.
After failing to reproduce the original attack, ManageEngine began continuously monitoring AOMEI's servers.
On July 16, that monitoring finally captured the malicious modifications as they happened, confirming that AOMEI's systems were serving the malicious content.
The researchers also found that the attackers had modified the expected checksum in the update configuration, allowing the malicious archive to pass the software's file verification checks.
Google and ManageEngine say they identified three windows where the malicious configuration file was being sent by Aomei's servers:
- May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC)
- July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC)
- July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC)
The attackers restored the configuration files back to its original form within minutes, making the compromise difficult to detect.
During these windows, the malicious configuration file was used to install the CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD malware.
When launched, the CROSSROAD downloader checked the performed reconnasaince on the infected computer, downloaded additional components, and established persistence through a scheduled task.
SHINYROAD is a backdoor that used legitimate Radmin components to load malicious code and establish an outbound connection to an attacker-controlled command-and-control server.
This allowed the attackers to potentially execute additional commands and payloads on compromised computers.
During the July 20 attack, Google also observed a second technique that attempted to steal Windows authentication hashes by forcing the software's notification system to access an attacker-controlled WebDAV resource through an invisible popup.
This technique could expose NTLM hashes that can be collected by the attacker-controlled server and later cracked using various tools.
The researchers also identified several IP addresses and hostnames used during the attacks, including 8.210.84[.]56, serv.oss-cn-hongkong[.]aliyuncs.com, hostnames under storage-data[.]com, and storage.googleapis.com, a legitimate Google Cloud Storage endpoint.
AOMEI says CTO is investigating
ManageEngine told BleepingComputer that it first notified AOMEI about the suspicious activity on June 7, more than a month before researchers directly captured the malicious configuration files being served from its servers.
At the time, AOMEI initially suggested that the content may have been intercepted and modified while in transit, an explanation the researchers disagreed with.
"The evidence did not support AOMEI’s explanation of interception in transit," reads ManageEngine's report.
"Both endpoints had retrieved the content over HTTPS from AOMEI-owned hostnames, across different countries and unrelated network paths, and the executable had arrived through the application’s own extraction sequence rather than being written directly to disk by an external process. The content had been altered before it reached either endpoint, within the vendor-hosted delivery path."
When ManageEngine captured another attack on July 16, it immediately provided AOMEI with the original and modified file hashes, file differences, and altered files.
"AOMEI engaged, conducted its own review, and told us its initial examination had not found evidence of a breach," ManageEngine told BleepingComputer.
The researchers said AOMEI indicated that it planned to move the affected configuration files to new infrastructure with more detailed logging.
ManageEngine told BleepingComputer it advised AOMEI to preserve existing evidence before making those changes and to bring in incident-response specialists, connecting the company with Mandiant to assist with the investigation.
AOMEI later informed the researchers that its technical team had upgraded its servers, patched potential vulnerabilities, and verified that the files hosted on its infrastructure were correct.
Google also confirmed in its report that Mandiant notified AOMEI about the configuration file tampering on July 17 and that the company responded on July 29th, stating it took corrective action.
When contacted by BleepingComputer about the findings, AOMEI said it was treating the matter as a high priority and that its chief technology officer was leading an internal investigation.
"We have also internally detected this report and have classified it as a high-priority matter. Our CTO is currently leading a dedicated investigation to ensure accurate issue identification," AOMEI told BleepingComputer.
The company said its CTO would provide a more detailed response about the incident and the investigation's progress, and BleepingComputer will update this article if we receive new information.
AOMEI did not immediately confirm how attackers gained access to its update infrastructure or whether the reported compromise had been fully resolved.
While AOMEI says it has secured its servers, ManageEngine warns that these changes would not remove malware previously installed on customers' computers.
"A server-side fix stops new infections; it does not remove the backdoor from machines that received it during an earlier window," ManageEngine told BleepingComputer.
Organizations using AOMEI Backupper are advised to review the indicators of compromise published by Google and ManageEngine, including suspicious scheduled tasks, unexpected executable files in AOMEI installation directories, and connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Nine months after putting R13.9 billion ($855.5 million) on the table, Nedbank is finally at the end of its NCBA takeover. The South African lender’s offer to acquire 66% of NCBA Group, one of East Africa’s largest banking groups, is now unconditional after clearing the remaining regulatory approvals. Settlement begins this week, with the transfer of shares to Nedbank expected from early November. NCBA will become a Nedbank subsidiary, but keep its name, Nairobi headquarters, management, and Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) listing, according to its Monday filings . Catch up: Nedbank first announced the deal in January. In February, Kenya’s capital markets regulator allowed it to buy 66% without making an offer for the entire company. The tender opened in May, and by July, shareholders had offered 79.9% of NCBA’s shares, more than Nedbank wanted. Those offers had to be scaled back to 66%. Shareholders who sell will receive 80% of their payment in newly issued Nedbank shares and 20% in cash. The remaining 34% of NCBA will stay in public hands. Between the lines: Nedbank is buying more than a Kenyan bank. NCBA already operates across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda, with digital businesses in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire. Its digital business accounted for 32% of group profit in 2025, and it disbursed KES 1.4 trillion ($10.8 billion) in digital loans. The deal also shows how Nedbank’s Africa strategy has changed. In 2025, it sold its 21% stake in Ecobank and shifted towards markets where it can control the banking operation rather than remain a minority investor. NCBA gives it that control, plus customers, licences, and infrastructure across East Africa, without building them country by country. What to watch: Nedbank has previously talked about using NCBA as a springboard into Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Now it has the platform to try. Happy customer service week. Your success and ours are the same story. Happy Customer Service Week. This year’s theme is The Extra Mile, and it’s the only way we know how to do this. Visit: fincra.com . Fintech Why Onafriq shut down its Nigerian agent banking business Image Source: Baxi In hindsight, it is not hard to see the play Onafriq, the pan-African payments company, was making when it expanded into Nigeria by acquiring Baxi in 2021. Nigeria still relied heavily on cash, and Baxi already had more than 90,000 agents. Onafriq could enter with a ready-made distribution network instead of spending years building one. The timing looked good, too. OPay and Moniepoint had begun building large agent networks in 2019, while PalmPay entered agent banking later . In 2021, Baxi was already one of Nigeria’s biggest independent agent networks, giving Onafriq an early lead over some newer competitors. But the lead did not hold. By the end of 2024, PalmPay reportedly had more than 700,000 agents , while Moniepoint had over 800,000 point-of-sale (PoS) terminals. But as of 2025, Baxi had just over 460,000 agents , paling in comparison. In October, it finally decided to shut down the business, months after trying to sell Baxi . Between the lines: Agent banking became a scale game. Rivals poured money into terminals, agent recruitment, and incentives, making it easier to close the distribution gap. At the same time, agents could work with several providers, making a large network less defensible than it first appeared. The economics also changed. More terminals entered the market much faster than transaction volumes grew, so providers competed over the same payments. Meanwhile, account-to-account (A2A) transfers—direct bank payments—gave customers another way to move money without visiting an agent. Onafriq’s attempt to sell Baxi before shutting it down shows that the problem was bigger than one bad year. The company had already decided the agent business no longer fit where it wanted to put capital. Zoom out: Onafriq bought Baxi partly because physical distribution was scarce. Five years later, the market had plenty. Being early gave Baxi a head start, but it did not stop competitors from catching up and, eventually, passing it. Ten years of telling African tech stories. Class of 2016, stand up! Meet the storytellers behind a decade of storytelling for African tech. 230+ startups, VCs, and more. From first cheques to unicorns. Have a story to tell? Let’s make it count . #TheWimbarts Ecommerce South African union want Shein and Temu banned to protect local jobs Image Source: Temu Behind the low-cost tops you see on Shein and Temu is a dispute over how foreign shopping platforms compete with local businesses, and what that means for the people who make and sell clothes in South Africa. What happened? The Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), the country’s largest trade union federation, wants South Africa to ban Shein and Temu . It backed a proposal from the Southern African Clothing and Textile Workers’ Union (SACTWU), which says the platforms hurt local jobs by undercutting domestic retailers and manufacturers. Explain like I’m new here: Shein entered South Africa in 2020, while Temu followed in 2024. Both sell directly to consumers online, offering a wide range of clothing and other goods at prices that traditional retailers can find hard to match. A 2025 study by the Localisation Support Fund (LSF), a South African organisation focused on strengthening local production, estimated that Shein and Temu generated R7.3 billion ($444 million) in South African sales in 2024, equivalent to roughly 3.6% of the country’s retail market. Can South Africa ban them? South Africa has already taken steps to narrow the tax advantage to benefit some low-value imports. Previously, goods worth less than R500 ($30.41) were cheaper to bring into the country. In 2024, the South African Revenue Service (SARS), the country’s taxman, introduced value-added tax (VAT) on low-value imports and subsequently ended their special customs-duty treatment. However, COSATU’s proposal goes further than changing tax rules. If both platforms are banned, some consumers could pay more without automatically creating new jobs in local factories. South Africa still has to work out how to protect local jobs while allowing competition and preserving affordable choices for shoppers. Closing tax loopholes is one part of that effort; making local manufacturers more competitive is another. Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world! Image Source: Business in Cameroon Building a fibre-optic network requires a place to lay the fibre, permission to use the land, and a lot of money. But what if the poles that already carry electricity could also help carry the Internet? Cameroon is exploring that option. What happened? On October 16, Camtel, Cameroon’s state-owned telecoms operator, and Socadel, the country’s electricity provider, signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore sharing infrastructure for fibre deployment. How would it work? Camtel has the fibre network and telecoms expertise, and Socadel has electricity infrastructure, such as utility poles and rights-of-way. Instead of Camtel building entirely new infrastructure to carry fibre cables, it could attach overhead cables to suitable electricity poles and use existing routes to reach more locations. The two companies will now study whether they can combine those assets for faster Internet access. Cameroon has tried this before: In 2023, the government transferred about 812 kilometres (km) of overhead fibre that Eneo, Socadel’s predecessor, had installed on electricity poles along Cameroon’s southern interconnected grid to Camtel. That network served major cities including Douala and Yaoundé, its capital, and added to Camtel’s fibre infrastructure, which stood at about 12,000km. The latest agreement focuses on closer infrastructure sharing, including the possibility of incorporating fibre into future electricity infrastructure projects. What happens next? The companies have not yet announced a nationwide rollout or a specific number of new kilometres. Their immediate job is to determine where the arrangement makes sense and identify pilot sites. If the model works, Camtel could expand fibre routes without building every supporting telecom structure from scratch, reducing deployment costs. articles.title: OVHcloud promet son propre LLM open source « très en avance sur son temps », et Octave Klaba tacle Mistral — Frandroid
articles.text:
OVHcloud va sortir son propre LLM, un de ces grands modèles de langage qui font tourner les assistants comme ChatGPT. Octave Klaba, fondateur et PDG de l’hébergeur roubaisien, l’annonce pour fin novembre dans un entretien à La Tribune publié ce mardi 20 octobre.
Le modèle sera open source, donc téléchargeable et modifiable par tous, et Klaba le décrit comme « très en avance sur son temps » sur le plan de l’architecture. Pour une entreprise qui loue surtout des serveurs depuis 1999, le changement de métier est net.
Klaba a choisi le jour des résultats annuels pour en parler. Sur l’exercice clos le 31 août, OVHcloud affiche 1,145 milliard d’euros de chiffre d’affaires, en hausse de 7,2 % à périmètre constant. L’Ebitda ajusté (le résultat d’exploitation avant amortissements) atteint 480,5 millions d’euros. Il représente 42 % des ventes, contre 40,4 % un an plus tôt.
Surtout, le groupe garde enfin de l’argent en caisse une fois ses investissements et sa dette payés. Son flux de trésorerie positive passe à 24,7 millions d’euros, alors qu’il était négatif de 27 millions un an plus tôt. La fin d’exercice a aussi accéléré, avec +10,5 % au quatrième trimestre et plus de 100 millions d’euros de chiffre d’affaires par mois.
Ces comptes servent de bilan à Octave Klaba. Il a repris la direction en octobre 2025, après l’éviction de Benjamin Revcolevschi, qui avait lui-même succédé à Michel Paulin, avec la promesse d’un grand changement de cap.
Des puces jusqu’aux applications, OVHcloud veut tout faire
Dans La Tribune, Klaba détaille une stratégie IA en cinq couches, de la plus matérielle à la plus proche de l’utilisateur.
- Les GPU, ces puces graphiques qui entraînent et font tourner les IA, installés dans ses propres data centers, qui disposent de 250 mégawatts de puissance électrique.
- L’orchestration, c’est-à-dire le logiciel qui répartit le travail entre ces puces.
- Les tokens as a service : le client paie l’IA à l’usage, au nombre de tokens (des morceaux de mots) traités.
- Des outils pour héberger les applications d’IA des entreprises.
- Les usages, avec OVHai Workspace, une plateforme qui mêle e-mail, stockage, visio et agents IA, dans la lignée de la suite bureautique qu’OVHcloud prépare face à Microsoft 365.
Pour le modèle lui-même, OVHcloud a fait ses courses. Le 25 mars 2026, le groupe a annoncé le rachat de Dragon LLM, une start-up parisienne fondée en 2011 sous le nom de Lingua Custodia, d’abord spécialisée dans la traduction pour la finance.
Dragon a mis au point une architecture hybride Mamba-Transformer. Mamba est une autre famille de réseaux de neurones que le Transformer (la base de ChatGPT), et ce mélange traite des textes plus longs en consommant beaucoup moins d’énergie. OVHcloud n’a pas dit si le LLM de novembre reprendra cette architecture, et il n’a donné ni sa taille ni ses performances.
Les modèles suivants viseront trois domaines. La cybersécurité, défensive et offensive, passe en premier, devant la génération de code et l’IA agentique (des IA qui enchaînent seules des tâches) pour la finance, les RH ou le juridique. Fin septembre, devant les députés, Klaba justifiait le volet sécurité par l’histoire du groupe : « On vient de là, on doit être bon en sécurité. »
Le sujet est concret pour l’hébergeur, qui a récemment dû demander à ses clients de changer tous les secrets stockés sur leur PC.
Le budget d’entraînement n’est pas public non plus. En juin, Klaba estimait qu’un projet qui aurait coûté environ un milliard d’euros pourrait désormais se mener avec 150 à 200 millions d’euros. Même le bas de cette fourchette représente six fois le trésorerie dégagée cette année.
Mistral, une « ESN de l’IA » selon Klaba
Octave Klaba écarte aussi toute alliance avec Mistral AI, la start-up parisienne fondée en 2023. Il la compare à une « ESN de l’IA » qui ferait surtout de l’intégration. Une ESN, ou entreprise de services du numérique, installe et adapte des logiciels chez ses clients, à la manière de Capgemini.
Pour appuyer la comparaison, il met en avant 1,2 milliard d’euros de chiffre d’affaires et 1,6 million de clients. Le premier chiffre est arrondi, puisque les comptes publiés le même jour donnent 1,145 milliard.
En face, Mistral a annoncé en février un revenu annualisé (le rythme de ventes du moment, projeté sur douze mois) de plus de 400 millions de dollars, soit environ 340 millions d’euros. La start-up vise le milliard de dollars de revenus récurrents (environ 860 millions d’euros) d’ici la fin de l’année. Elle a aussi levé 3 milliards d’euros avec Samsung en septembre. Dans le même entretien, Klaba s’interroge sur ces montants : « Est-ce que cela vaut cet argent-là ? »
Sur le papier, la comparaison est bancale. OVHcloud encaisse depuis 27 ans les loyers de ses serveurs, alors que Mistral dépense pour entraîner des modèles, comme tout le secteur. Chez Anthropic, l’éditeur de Claude, on dépense près de trois dollars pour chaque dollar gagné.
Pourtant, les deux entreprises se rapprochent sur un point : Mistral publie lui aussi une partie de ses modèles en open source. Il a sorti Large 4 cette année, avec des résultats passés au crible par des benchmarks indépendants. Mistral a aussi perdu un client connu, Ecosia, parti vers des IA chinoises.
OVHcloud promet son modèle pour fin novembre. Le même mois, son Summit annuel doit lancer la bêta d’OVHai Workspace. La taille du LLM, son architecture exacte et ses scores face à Mistral n’ont pas encore été communiqués.

articles.title: The Future of Web Apps: Will AI Agents Generate UIs on the Fly?
articles.text:
Rachel Lee Nabors, former React core team member, dives into the architecture and philosophy behind local-first applications, exploring how small language models (SLMs) running directly on-device can deliver privacy-focused, low-latency, and cost-effective alternatives to cloud-hosted LLM wrappers. Rachel shares key insights on evaluating models with golden datasets and leveraging client-side AI for moderation and social content aggregation.
The discussion also looks ahead to the future of web and application architectures in an AI-driven ecosystem. From the potential rise of OS-level personal agents and dynamic UI rendering standards like A2UI, to the evolving skill set required of software engineers.
Key Takeaways
- Building apps local-first delivers fast, offline capability for users while keeping cloud infrastructure costs low for developers.
- Utilizing SLMs locally (like Llama 3.2B) avoids high API costs, reduces latency, and protects PII compared to large cloud LLMs.
- Systematic evaluation using golden datasets is essential for right-sizing models and picking the best option for specific tasks like summarization or moderation.
- OS-level personal agents and standardized UI schemas (like A2UI) may replace traditional web apps and native interfaces for consumption.
- Software engineering is moving beyond basic code generation towards computer science fundamentals, system design, and AI collaboration.
Subscribe on:
Transcript
Olimpiu Pop: Hello everybody. I'm Olimpiu Pop and I have in front of me Rachel Lee Nabors. They are quite a creative person. They did a bunch of comics, I think, right? And also, they were involved with React and React Native frameworks. And because I don't know how to put it in a better light, Rachel Lee, can you please introduce yourself?
Rachel Lee Nabors: Thank you so much for the introduction. Yes, you may remember me from my pandemic babies, the react.dev and reactnative.dev portals. I worked on the React team for the pandemic. I've worked for FAANG on browsers for many years and with the W3C on web standards. But before all of that, I used to make comic books for teenage girls. I was one of the first web cartoonists that had their own personal website and mailing list, et cetera. So, I take my inspiration from Japanese comics and anime to this day. You can still find me illustrating my own slides and creating mascots for the different open source projects I work on.
Olimpiu Pop: Nice. Thank you for the idea for what you put so far. So, probably my kids will read some of the comics. Today we're going to talk about another endeavor that you have and that's local, I don't know, aggregator. It would be probably the best interface for the social literature that we use.
Rachel Lee Nabors: Oh, yes. I used to be really big on developer advocacy. When I moved to London, I was a developer experience consultant for lots of startups and AI in the Bay Area, but I've always wanted to get back into engineering. And finally, I found a project that inspired me to return to building again. And it's Mima, that's M-I-M-A. You can find it at mima.social. It is the client I've always wanted for managing all of my social and news connections. I don't know about you, but you can't do business in tech without being on X and LinkedIn and probably also Bluesky and Mastodon, depending on where your friends are. If you've got friends and data, you probably need to be on Bluesky.
If you got friends in open source, you got to be on Mastodon. I don't have time to check all of those different apps every day. And every one of them is like, "Oh my God, you got to spend all your time here on X. What are you doing posting links to other websites? How dare you?" They are very protective of their little circles, their bubbles. Problem is you stay in one of those bubbles, you only hear from people in that bubble. If you only listen to X, you'd think that everyone's using coding agents, but there are so many grads coming out these days that they've never touched Claude for coding. So, there's a whole world that you don't experience.
I built this to make it possible for me to exist and to see things coming in from any social network I wanted to connect to. So, I can repost something from X to Bluesky. It forms a local graph of all of my social connections, everything I've been saying, and it uses native web APIs under the hood. So, there's nothing particularly magical happening there. It's the browser I always wanted because for me, all of the big leaps I've made forward in my life in terms of career, understanding, et cetera, they all came through these social networks. But over the years, social networks have become harder and harder to access from outside the bubbles.
So, I started building Mima to solve my own problem, which was I just wanted to see what everyone was saying in one place and be able to reply from one place. And it's turned into its own little local app. It's got little local models on it to make the experience better. It's all privacy first and local first, which was kind of on purpose, kind of by accident. The truth is I just don't want to have servers with your personal information on it. The last thing I want is to have various countries come in and be in like, "Hey, we need all the DMs from user X, Y, Z." And me being like, "What? Oh, no."
So, I have no interest in owning other people's information. So, that's how it ended up starting. And yes, I'm actually going to be in San Francisco doing a little pop-up soft launch for Mima next week. It's really exciting.
Olimpiu Pop: Okay. Good luck with that. We are just curious about the technical details because you mentioned that you are part of the React crew and did a bunch of stuff. So, I'm curious about what were the choices you've made while building it, because you did mention also models and rather than having an L in front of the large language model, you have an S. So, guide us through the decisions, the technical decision you've made.
Local-First Architecture and Small Language Models [05:36]
Rachel Lee Nabors: I have been following along with the evolution of LLMs since GPT-3. One of the things I've noticed, especially in hackathon scenes, because developer experience consulting is like my bread and butter. So, I go to a lot of hackathons, I see what people are building, and I noticed a lot of what people started to build as soon as LLMs became API accessible was a wrapper. It's an app that takes everything the user gives it, sends it over to someone else's server somewhere where they do God knows what with that information, probably train your competitors model, and then they send you back a response.
First, this is incredibly wasteful. I did a series of articles on web.dev with Google about right sizing the model and a lot of research on the cost, the energy cost of running inference. On a multimodal model, it's four times higher than necessary to do most of the work that you could do with it. So, it's energy intensive. That means that cost gets passed to you in terms of the API costs. Now you've got linear costs going up with every time you call that. And also it brings in all these wonderful privacy concerns. Is that PII? We've had so many instances of private personal information showing up in public because somebody sent a prompt to a model and it got passed onto a search engine.
So, there are reasons why you don't want to just round trip with a big inference. Luckily for us, the technology has moved forward so fast, so well that small language models now do pretty much all the same things that people were trying to send off to big inference back in the day. Small models are perfectly fine for summarizing things. We've got Jev, which is great for picking the right tool or offering a simple yes or no. Jev just completely blows the lid off of everything. So, there's a lot we can do with a little model that we don't need to round trip to Gemini or to Claude to get done.
And I think it's the first thing we reach for. The idea is can we prove that it can be done with a big model? That's fine, but you probably don't need to be shipping to production the round trip or the high API costs that you are.
Olimpiu Pop: Kim, thank you. So, you have multiple models in Mima or you have one that has multiple hats?
Rachel Lee Nabors: Well, that is a great question. What's the right model for the job? Mima does have multiple different little models inside her. The one that I got started with was Llama 3. 2B. I was using Claude Sonnet to summarize, for instance, conversation threads when I first started building her, but very quickly I started feeling uncomfortable with sending my private messages to Claude. So, I actually set up some evals and with post-processing, I was able to get Llama 3. 2B to perform as well as Claude Sonnet at summarizing locally the conversations that I was having. Evals are really your best friend here. They let you actually rate and judge the inputs and outputs.
If I had just listened to my friends, I would've chosen Gemma four because Gemma four was really hot right then, but it turns out Gemma four would've actually substantially increased the latency on these summarizations and it wouldn't have provided as good summarizations as Llama 3. 2B did. So, I used Phoenix, which is a little evals library that you can set up there to run tests amongst real information and used a large model as a judge to pick the best model that could do the job. It turned out, of course, it was Llama 3. 2B, which is one of Facebook's models that they've trained on user data. So, it makes sense that it would be good at summarizing conversations between humans.
However, that model might not be the best at doing things like identifying when people are being toxic or if images, for instance, contain alarming things in them. I'm a big believer that our clients should be able to moderate for us rather than relying on the platform to do that because platform owners, Facebook, LinkedIn, et cetera, they always don't really invest in moderation. It's a cost center for them, so they cheap out on it. And that means that it's our Lord of the Flies, the kids are running the schoolroom in there. So, it's better if your client can do things like, "Oh, this is an incoming message from somebody this person doesn't follow. I'm going to check to see if it's abusive content."
You post a picture one night, you wake up, there's 40 comments on it. How many of them are, "That's a great picture," versus how many of them are like, "Oh, how dare you take this picture of a dog?" And you never know. But the idea is that you can use models that are specifically trained to check for different kinds of things to help you write better or to check to see if incoming content is abusive or unfriendly. And Mima is mostly geared around moderation right now, making sure your trigger warnings aren't being tripped up, et cetera. And for that, summarization's not necessarily the best option. There are smaller, lighter models that can do a better job of that, and all of them are opt-in.
If a person turns on a feature that needs another little model, they have the option to turn that on, download an additional model. It's never installed by default. I think this is something that companies who should know better, who have a lot of experience building products for humans have missed from back in the day when 15 years ago we were all reinventing the wheel and learning how to build apps and progressively enhance the user experience. There is this idea that the user should be able to opt in to enhance their experience. But if it's going to cost extra, extra storage space, et cetera, you need to ask their permission.
And of course you could always offer them a cloud solution as well, but for the reasons I already stated, I'm not really providing one of those at this time. It's not like, "Well, would you like me to process all of your incoming tweets on my servers or would you like to download this model?" You could do that, but for me, it's just going to be, "Would you like to download the model?"
Olimpiu Pop: That sounds closer to home. And also, I like the fact that the information doesn't leave your machine. So, that's quite useful from my perspective and probably others as well. And the moderation, it's highly important.
Rachel Lee Nabors: It is. I think one of the things we're going to see happening with AI assistance and personal agents in the near future is we've been building them thinking about HubSpot integrations and how to do business with them so far. But once they hit the consumer market, they're missing something important, which is your personal context. Yes, you can connect them to your email, but how are you going to connect them to your LinkedIn to help you find your next job? How are you going to connect them to your Facebook to keep up with the kids? How are you going to connect them to all of these walled gardens out there, each one of which wants to keep your data in their databases?
And remember that the power of that data is only really unlocked when it's cross-contaminated, which is a huge security risk I know. But there's also so much to be said for if we could just have access to the graph, our own social graph across multiple different networks, our own posts across multiple different databases, our personal agents would become much more powerful for having that context, not even necessarily to post, but they would just know more about us and be better able to help us as individuals.
Olimpiu Pop: Well, I like that you're looking only at the positive part and I'm all in supporting that. You did mention evals and that tweaking your model for that particular use case, it gives you the option of having the same output as a large language model. Well, outcome, I think it's more appropriate. Maybe a couple of hints on that, especially given that you discussed about something that doesn't have a terministic form. You spoke about text summarization, right? That's a bit polymorphic. Probably a summary for you to be different than a summary for me. How did you attack that problem? What would be the tips that you can give me if I intend to do someUse Caseimilar?
Model Selection and Model Evaluation Strategies [14:36]
Rachel Lee Nabors: So, I am a big fan of Hamel Husain. I don't know if you're familiar with his work, but he is like the demigod of evals, evals, evals, evals. articles.title: Reseller says $470,000 worth of Nvidia RTX 5090s went missing at São Paulo airport
articles.text:
Connecting the dots: Thanks to the unprecedented boom in AI server and data center projects, Nvidia's most powerful GPUs have become extremely hard to come by. If a story out of Brazil is accurate, specialized thieves may now be targeting these components at specific points during shipment.
Oderço Distribuidora is a Brazilian hardware distributor that has been in business for more than 38 years, about 18 of them importing computer hardware. According to a recent message from company president Oderço Matos, the company has lost an undisclosed number of GeForce RTX 5090 cards after two pallets went "missing" at São Paulo/Guarulhos International Airport.
Matos said the company has never been through anything like this. Oderço was expecting to receive pallets full of Zotac GeForce RTX 5090 cards, worth R$2.5 million (around $470,000), but the goods never reached the company, and no one has offered an explanation so far.
The company now wants to understand what happened, and how a cargo of such valuable consumer electronics can disappear inside an international airport without leaving any trace. São Paulo/Guarulhos is the main airport serving the city of São Paulo, the largest in Brazil and, by most measures, in Latin America, and one of the 50 busiest in the world by passenger traffic.
He added that the company decided to go public after receiving no explanation from public authorities or the airport itself. There is also no video footage of the pallets being moved. Oderço is looking for "answers" about the disappearance, but also hopes whoever is responsible will eventually let the company get its GPUs back.
Airport officials are reportedly unwilling to cooperate, either with the press or with Oderço. Brazilian media have received no answer about the incident, while the Brazilian Federal Police and Federal Revenue Service have yet to issue an official statement.
Technically, no one has officially confirmed that the goods were stolen. Oderço, for its part, has not provided specific details or tracking information on the Zotac cards.
Although not designed to run in data centers or accelerate AI workloads, GeForce RTX 5090 cards are now among the most sought-after pieces of computer hardware ever. Individual GPUs are selling for thousands of dollars, and recent rumors claimed the model would soon disappear from the market. Nvidia has since said the RTX 5090 is still being manufactured, but the cards are now even more expensive than they were a few days ago. I guess thieves have taken note.
