articles.title: GTA 6: cuál es la versión más barata del juego y qué diferencia hay con la edición Ultimate
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI llegará el 19 de noviembre de 2026 a PlayStation 5 y Xbox Series X|S con dos versiones que generaron un fenómeno de preventa sin antecedentes en la industria de los videojuegos.
Rockstar Games confirmó la Edición Estándar y la Edición Ultimate, con una diferencia de apenas 20 dólares entre ambas, pero casi nueve de cada diez jugadores que ya reservaron el título eligieron pagar la versión más costosa.
La cifra la difundió la firma de análisis Sensor Tower: el 88,5% de las reservas en PlayStation y el 90% en Xbox corresponden a la versión premium. Karl Kontus, vicepresidente sénior de la compañía, calificó ese dato como inédito: “Nunca había visto una participación del 90% para una edición premium”, aunque anticipó que la proporción se acercará a un 50/50 más realista a medida que se sumen los compradores casuales.
Qué incluye la Edición Estándar de GTA 6: la más económica
La Edición Estándar tiene un precio de 79,99 dólares y es la opción más barata para acceder al juego. Incluye la experiencia completa de GTA VI, con la historia de Jason y Lucía a lo largo del estado de Leonida y Vice City.
Esta versión está disponible en formato digital o como código en caja, ya que las copias físicas no contienen un disco, sino un código de descarga canjeable. Es la alternativa adecuada para quienes solo buscan el juego base, sin contenido adicional.
Elegir la versión más económica no cierra la puerta al contenido premium. Rockstar permite a los propietarios de la Edición Estándar adquirir después, por separado, la actualización a la Edición Ultimate a través de PlayStation Store o Microsoft Store, una vez activado el juego.
Qué trae la Edición Ultimate y por qué cuesta más
La Edición Ultimate cuesta 99,99 dólares, solo existe en formato digital e incluye el juego base más 16 elementos y funciones exclusivos. Entre ellos figuran cinco locales propios: Rideout Customs, el salón unisex de Sara, la tienda de ropa Stock 305, el taller One-Eyed Willie’s y el estudio de tatuajes Electric Fang, con más de 50 diseños del colectivo FAILE.
También suma dos misiones secundarias adicionales: el asalto al complejo de la banda PTT Youngin$ y la Colección de Autos Clásicos, encargada por un intermediario llamado Wyman. A eso se agregan tres vehículos exclusivos (el ’95 Grotti Cheetah, la moto acuática Shitzu Squalo y el buggy ’67 Vapid Dominator) y armas y vestimenta especiales, como los revólveres Hawk & Little Morgan y los paquetes Vice City Styles y Goodtime Gear.
Rockstar precisó que este contenido no se desbloquea todo el primer día, sino que está distribuido a lo largo de la historia y aparece detrás de cada capítulo. Quien pague por la Ultimate Edition no tendrá acceso inmediato a todo su contenido apenas encienda la consola.
Qué pasa con la edición Edición Deluxe oficial
Pese a que términos como “clave de la Edición Deluxe de GTA 6” generan búsquedas masivas, esa versión no existe. Según la lista oficial de Rockstar Games, solo hay dos ediciones confirmadas: la Estándar y la Ultimate.
La confusión suele originarse en la actualización a la Edición Ultimate, un complemento independiente pensado exclusivamente para quienes ya poseen la Edición Estándar. No incluye el juego base y no funciona por sí sola, por lo que no debe confundirse con una tercera versión del título.
Fechas clave y bonificaciones de lanzamiento
Las reservas comenzaron oficialmente el 25 de junio de 2026. Todas las compras que cumplan los requisitos, realizadas antes del 20 de noviembre de 2026, reciben sin costo adicional el Vintage Vice City Pack, sin importar la edición elegida.
Ese paquete incluye un sedán Vapid Stanier del ’55 con garaje, atuendos y peinados, y un patrón de arma exclusivo. Las reservas digitales que cumplan los requisitos suman además un mes de suscripción a GTA+.
La precarga comienza el 12 de noviembre de 2026 a medianoche hora local, mismo día en que se espera que las copias en caja estén disponibles para envío o retiro en tienda. El lanzamiento oficial es el 19 de noviembre de 2026 para ambas plataformas.
¿Vale la pena pagar más por la Ultimate?
A diferencia de otros lanzamientos de la industria, la Ultimate Edition de GTA 6 no otorga acceso anticipado: todos los jugadores, sin importar la edición, entrarán al juego el mismo día. Rockstar aún no detalló los horarios de desbloqueo por zona horaria.
Tampoco hay urgencia para decidir antes del estreno, porque quien compre la Estándar puede actualizar a Ultimate después, pagando los mismos 20 dólares de diferencia.

articles.title: Microsoft Targets Rogue AI Agents With Dynamic Permissions, Risk Scoring
articles.text:
Microsoft on Monday announced new controls to monitor and restrict potentially rogue AI agents in enterprise environments, arguing that organizations should treat these agents as insiders rather than trusted software.
The capabilities extend Project Perception, the agentic security system Microsoft launched in July. Perception was initially pitched as a defense against AI-driven attacks from outside, but it is now being applied to the agents companies run internally.
Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, said companies tend to trust the agents they deploy by default. She warned that frontier models are trained to get results and aren’t built around organizational norms or judgment. “These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes,” Gallot wrote.
Nadim Abdo, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of identity and network access, clarified the insider label. “This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised,” he explained.
One of the new features, Dynamic Permissions, gives agents no permissions, or the bare minimum, at the outset. Access is then granted per task and expires or shrinks as the task changes or ends, while high-impact actions require human review.
Dynamic Agent Risk gives each agent a risk score that is continuously updated, drawing on the agent’s activity as well as identity, data, endpoint, cloud, network and runtime signals. The score factors in the agent’s security configuration, the resources within its reach, how much damage it could do if something goes wrong, and whether it is straying from what the user or organization intended.
Dynamic Conditional Access, which brings Entra Conditional Access to agents, acts on those risk changes. Rather than simply allowing or blocking an agent, it can scale back its permissions, let it read but not write, limit the data and network resources it can reach, or require a person to approve consequential actions. If the risk climbs high enough, the agent’s runtime can be isolated or its execution halted.
To make this work at scale, Microsoft is introducing Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. Humans establish the rules and approval limits, Playbooks specify what the security response should achieve, and Guardian Agents execute it, looking into why an agent’s risk shifted and suggesting or enforcing containment.
Microsoft is also expanding discovery to 35 more types of local agents, bringing the supported total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot.

articles.title: Anthropic quer barrar IAs apenas diante de riscos extremos • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Anthropic quer barrar IAs apenas diante de riscos extremos
Projeto prevê bloqueio de modelos que ameacem causar mais de 50 mortes ou ferimentos graves, ou prejuízos acima de US$ 1 bilhão.
A Anthropic, dona do Claude, propôs que o governo federal dos EUA só possa bloquear modelos avançados de IA diante de riscos catastróficos, incluindo ameaças de morte, ferimentos graves em mais de 50 pessoas ou prejuízos acima de US$ 1 billhão (R$ 5,08 bilhões).
O site Politico obteve o rascunho do projeto de lei. A iniciativa da Anthropic seria uma forma de estabelecer regras mais claras sobre o desenvolvimento e o uso de modelos avançados de inteligência artificial.
O texto prevê análises regulares dos laboratórios e de seus modelos por avaliadores independentes. Se identificassem um risco iminente previsto no documento, eles deveriam comunicar suas conclusões em até 72 horas ao Departamento de Comércio. Caberia ao órgão apresentar as evidências a um juiz federal, que decidiria sobre a suspensão.
Outros departamentos, agências ou autoridades federais também ficariam impedidos de suspender o desenvolvimento, a implantação ou o uso de um modelo. O texto transferiria esse poder apenas ao Departamento de Comércio e Justiça federal.
A discussão ocorre após episódios de segurança relatados pela própria Anthropic. Em uma revisão de mais de 141 mil execuções de testes, a companhia identificou incidentes envolvendo acesso não autorizado a sistemas de organizações reais. Segundo a empresa, uma falha de configuração permitiu que modelos alcançassem a internet durante avaliações que deveriam ocorrer em ambientes isolados.
Em setembro, a Anthropic também afirmou ter bloqueado consultas ao Claude que poderiam contribuir para a criação de armas biológicas. Em paralelo, o desenvolvedor Jacob Coxon deixou a companhia e criticou a corrida pela superinteligência, alertando sobre possíveis riscos à vida humana.

articles.title: OPINION: Europe needs more than just successful exits | EU-Startups
articles.text:
The acquisition of Berlin-based Talon.One by Dutch payments provider Adyen in July 2026 offers a useful perspective on European technology investing. A company founded in Germany developed technology valuable to a global payments business, and its next chapter is being written within Europe. This is a significant outcome for the founders and investors. However, it also raises a larger question: how can Europe turn individual successes into an ecosystem capable of producing them repeatedly?
The answer is not simply to encourage more European acquisitions. Successful startups need access to the best opportunities available, whether their future lies with a European buyer, an international technology group or the public markets. What matters is that these decisions reflect commercial potential rather than a lack of viable alternatives. For Europe, the challenge is to create the conditions in which successful companies can scale, attract investment and generate lasting economic value.
Exits are a measure of maturity, not the final destination
From a venture capital perspective, exits matter because they return capital to investors and founders, establish reference points for valuations, and help to finance the next generation of start-ups. Therefore, an acquisition is more than just the end of an investment cycle. The wider impact of an acquisition depends on whether experienced founders start again, whether employees launch new businesses, whether investors reinvest, and whether specialist knowledge remains accessible to the local ecosystem.
The Talon.One transaction is particularly interesting in this respect. Adyen paid €750 million for the loyalty and incentives platform, combining complementary European technologies together in a business with international reach. The company’s founders also reinvested some of their proceeds in Adyen shares. This is one possible model for maintaining continuity, although the long-term consequences for jobs, innovation and further investment will only become apparent over time.
Yet a European buyer does not automatically guarantee a better outcome. An acquisition by a US technology group can also give European innovation access to new markets, capital and expertise. The relevant questions concern what happens after the transaction: where future investment takes place, whether technological capabilities continue to develop and how much value flows back into the startup ecosystem. While the identity of the buyer is important, the industrial logic and long-term consequences also deserve equal attention.
Germany’s progress reveals the next challenge
Germany is a useful test case for Europe’s progress. According to the German Startup Monitor 2026, the country added ten unicorns in 2026, indicating that more companies are achieving significant valuations. Yet 62% of respondents considering a stock market listing favour the US. These figures measure different things, but together they capture a tension: Germany is producing ambitious technology companies while many founders still see stronger exit opportunities outside its domestic market.
This preference is not irrational. Founders and their investors have a responsibility to consider factors such as access to capital, market depth, suitable buyers, and prospects for future growth. US markets can offer genuine advantages. Rather than persuading companies to reject opportunities abroad, Europe needs to build more competitive options.
This is important long before a potential exit. Investors assess the availability of future funding and realistic exit routes when deciding whether to back a company. If these options appear limited, promising businesses may struggle to attract the necessary capital to reach their full potential. Therefore, a stronger exit environment can support investment across the entire startup lifecycle.
What a stronger European exit market would require
Three priorities stand out:
- Deeper growth capital: European startups need access to substantial later-stage funding and patient institutional investors, without having to reshape their strategy around capital availability elsewhere. This would also give founders greater flexibility over when and how they pursue an exit.
- More strategic buyers: Acquisitions can provide distribution, customers and resources for expansion. Talon.One and Adyen illustrate the potential of cross-border European combinations. A broader base of established technology companies willing to acquire and develop innovative businesses would create additional exit opportunities.
- Earlier exit planning: Founders should consider which investors could fund the next round, which buyers could offer strategic value, and the potential impact of a transaction on teams, research and future ventures. Investor nationality alone is no substitute for that assessment.
The objective is choice
Europe’s ambition should not be to keep every company, every shareholder or every exit within its borders. International capital and global customers are essential for building competitive businesses. In my experience, a European startup acquired by a US company can still create substantial value for its founders, employees and investors, and a European acquisition can likewise bolster a regional technology group.
The more meaningful test is whether European founders have real alternatives, such as sufficient capital to scale up, credible paths to public markets and a strong base of strategic acquirers and investors who can recycle returns into new ventures.
Successful exits show what European technology can achieve. A mature ecosystem makes those successes less exceptional. This requires a joint effort by founders, investors, established companies and policymakers alike.
Editor’s note: IRIS was an investor in Talon.One.

articles.title: Review: Lanterns is a truly unique twist on the superhero genre
articles.text:
The trailers for HBO’s DC Universe series Lanterns teased a show that eschewed the usual superhero hijinks in favor of a gritty realism more in the vein of True Detective or Slow Horses. Personally, I liked the change. My verdict: Ignore the review bombing; it’s wonderful. The season wrapped with an emotionally charged, almost elegiac finale that fully delivered on that initial promise. I’ve found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives. But Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre.
(Spoilers below, but no major reveals.)
There are two primary storylines. The first takes place in 2016 with a mass shooting at a local football game in Rushville, Nebraska. Current Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and his new trainee, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), get involved in the investigation, to the annoyance of Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald), who initially doesn’t think the case has any extraterrestrial connection. She is soon proved wrong when the suspect (an alien) self-detonates. Hal’s power ring controls the damage, but the mystery remains.
Hal and John soon discover that the suspect was one of a group of aliens who survived a genocide on their home planet committed by so-called Manhunters: a race of extraterrestrial beings created by the Guardians of the Universe as a forerunner to the Lantern Corps. The Manhunters rebelled against the Guardians, and most were killed; the sole survivor is hiding out in Rushville disguised as a human. The alien leader, Antaan (Paul Ben-Victor), gives Hal and John 48 hours to locate the Manhunter and hand them over, or they will destroy the town.
The second storyline takes place in 2026 and concerns the murder of none other than Hal Jordan, who returned to Rushville as a social pariah after the terrible events that transpired 10 years before. That mystery becomes the focus of the second half of the series, as Stewart teams up with the sheriff to solve Hal’s murder.
Green Lantern’s light
The entire cast brings their A game to their portrayals, and you couldn’t ask for better leads than Chandler and Pierre, both of whom have plenty of meaty, substantial material to work with. Showrunner Chris Mundy has said that one of the major themes of the show is deciding when it’s time for one person to step aside and let a replacement take over, embodied in the push and pull of Hal and John’s relationship. The two men are very different personalities: Hal is cocky, arrogant, and trusts his gut instincts; John is controlled, disciplined, logical, and methodical. Hal has no intention of giving up the power ring; John questions whether Hal really deserves it. Naturally they’re going to clash, and given the stakes, that conflict has severe consequences, both for them and the town.

articles.title: Creality Pika 3D scanner review: Good things come in small packages
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Creality Pika is a truly portable scanner with excellent software. We were impressed with its ability to work cordlessly when paired with an iPhone 15 or Android 10 (or newer).
Reasons to buy
- + Inexpensive
- + Small and lightweight
- + Doesn’t need marking dots with NIR mode
- + No problem with small, shiny, or black colored objects
- + Improved calibration routine
Reasons to avoid
- - Tracking using Near-Infrared (NIR) mode is challenging
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
A 3D scanner is an amazing tool to add to your 3D printing workflow, allowing you to scan real-life objects to import into sculpting or CAD software, then print out your own modified copies on a 3D printer. In the past, a good scanner cost thousands of dollars, but Creality has finally given us a device within reach of hobby-level consumers. The Creality Pika is easy to use, with the look, feel, and size of a point-and-shoot digital camera. It can wirelessly tether to a mobile phone running a Creality scanning app, which makes scanning on the go easier than ever before.
It can also be tethered to a laptop wirelessly or with a cable for more stable scanning, but marker-free laser scanning can only be performed while physically tethered to a computer. The scanner runs on AA-sized rechargeable batteries, which are provided.
It weighs just 260 grams (just slightly over a half-pound) with the batteries installed, reducing arm fatigue when operating without a tripod. A tabletop tripod and manual turntable are included for scanning small items. While not as precise as Creality’s Sermoon series, the Creality Pika, currently on pre-order for $699, is a fraction of the price. The best part is that both use the same software, Creality Scan, which is excellent.
The Creality Pika’s portability and price make this one of the best scanners we’ve reviewed in 2026.
Specifications: Creality Pika
| Scanning Mode | Blue laser | NIR structured light | 
| Light Type | 7 parallel lines | NIR (Near-Infrared) | 
| Single Frame Accuracy | .03mm | Up to .08mm/m | 
| 3D Resolution | 0.05-2mm | 0.1mm | 
| Working Distance | 160-400mm | 140-1000mm | 
| Min Scan Volume | 10 x 10 x 10 mm | 50 x 50 x 50 mm | 
| Scan Speed | Up to 90fps | Up to 90fps | 
| Alignment | Markers/global marker/marker free | Geometry/Texture | 
| Connectivity | Wired USB, Optional WiFi | Row 8 - Cell 2 | 
| Color Texture | Supported | Row 9 - Cell 2 | 
| Output Format | OBJ, STL, PLY | Row 10 - Cell 2 | 
| Operating System | Windows or Mac | Row 11 - Cell 2 | 
| MSRP | $699 | Row 12 - Cell 2 | 
| Release Date | July 22, 2026 | Row 13 - Cell 2 | 
Included in the Box: Creality Pika
The Creality Pika comes with a very nice tripod. Also included are the glass calibration board, a manual turntable, marking blocks, batteries (including a spare), a generous pack of marking dots, and a mostly useless quick start guide. The Quick Start guide is just a packing list in eleven different languages and QR codes to Creality’s website and Facebook community.
Design of the Creality Pika
The Creality Pika is a small handheld scanner that weighs only 260 g with its battery. It has a 3-inch touch screen on the back that shows the scan in progress while paired to a phone or PC on Wi-Fi, or allows exposure and zoom adjustments when scanning via cord. There are two buttons on the top of the scanner for power and start/stop, and a selector switch for USB or Wi-Fi.
The scanner has a play button to start and stop scans, as well as a button to adjust the lights and a toggle for zoom. The front of the scanner has an RGB camera, two 3D scanning cameras, a DOE projector, a parallel-line laser, four blue and white fill lights, and four infrared fill lights. There is an always-on cooling fan with grills on the top and bottom of the scanner. Two batteries are included, which can be charged in the camera or via a USB-C port located near the top of the battery.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The batteries, curiously, have both positive and negative terminals on top of the battery. Care should be taken when carrying these to avoid shorting them together with anything metal in a purse or pocket.
Getting Started and Calibrating the Creality Pika
The Creality Pika uses a glass calibration board to do an initial calibration of the scanner. The calibration process involves holding the scanner above the board at various heights and at various angles. The process takes about ten minutes.
Installing the Software for Creality Pika
Creality Scan app can be downloaded from Creality's website, with versions for PC, Mac, Android, and iPhone. A really good user guide with links to tutorials and troubleshooting help is located on the Creality Scan homepage. The discovery tab has links to items scanned by other Creality users.
The Pika must be tethered by cable or Wi-Fi. Though the Pika does have an onboard 8-core 2.0 GHz CPU, it passes along a big chunk of computer processing to whatever it’s connected to. My iPhone 15 has just enough oomph to power the scanner, so you may have an even better experience with a newer device. Either way, using a wireless connection is slower, and using it with hardware near the minimum requirements can be frustrating.
My old laptop, with only 8GB of RAM, did not work, despite being enough to run previous scanners. Thankfully, my admittedly low-end gaming laptop, with 16GB of RAM, was good enough to run the scanner quite well. The software installed on the computer is used for both scanning and processing.

| For Mac | · macOS 14 or above · M2 Apple CPU · 16GB RAM | · macOS 14 or above · M3/M4/M5 Apple CPU · 32GB RAM | 
| For iPhone | · iOS15+ with an A15 chip or above · 6GB RAM | · iOS15+ with an A17 chip or above · 8GB RAM | 
| For Android | · Android OS 10+ · Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen2 chip or better · 8GB RAM | · Android OS 10+ · Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen4 chip or better · 12GB RAM | 
Creality Scan can export scans as STL, PLY, OBJ, or ASC files. These files can be tidied up in other modeling software or uploaded directly to your 3D printer’s slicer.
Blue Laser Line 3D Scanning with the Creality Pika
The Creality Pika uses blue laser line scanning for detailed geometry capture, with seven parallel laser lines. The provided manual turntable works well when plastered with a bunch of the included marker dots. Unfortunately, it has a few millimeters of play in the center bearing, which can lead to a rough surface texture if not careful.
The photo above shows the raw scan of a copy of Michelangelo’s David. I did get much better scans later, but even this one is easily made usable in the software. The first step is fusing the model, which allows you to remove the marker dots and noise from the scan.
After fusing, the model is much smoother. There are still some unattached pieces and holes, and the bottom of the model is not flat. The lasso tool can select and remove the unattached pieces, and a clipping plane can be generated by choosing markers surrounding the scan. The plane can then be raised or lowered to give you the best base of the model.
The next step is mesh processing of the model. In this step, you can further smooth the model, simplify it, and fill small holes shown in yellow. Don’t select “make watertight” if you have a large hole (like the bottom of a model), as it will cover the holes by ballooning out a good bit. After running the mesh processing, you will have another opportunity to simplify, smooth, and fill holes.
Use Plane type hole filling for large flat surfaces.
The final model: filled, smoothed, simplified, and ready to export for printing.
This bust of David came with an early Creality scanner, so I’ve been using it as a test model for some time now. This may be the best scan I’ve gotten of it. The main reason is that the Creality Pika is small and lightweight, and tracks well enough to scan the underside of David’s hair and chin for the most part. The software’s hole filling and smoothing did the rest, with phenomenal results.
The above image on the right was printed on the Prusa Core One L with Inland Bone White PLA. The model looks nearly perfect.
Since the Pika did so well with David, I decided to try a smaller model. This little guy (below) came with my kid’s Fisher-Price castle. He’s only 62 mm tall and was just too small to paint for 3D printing. He was also printed in Inland bone white on the Prusa Core One L.
Both the print and scan are nicely detailed.
I swiped my husband’s vintage Saint Louis University Billiken bobblehead for more tests. I had to put some sticky tack on his head to keep it steady on the turntable. Creality Scan did a terrific job smoothing out the wrinkles, and the model is perfect. I used the clipping plane to remove the logo of an old wireless company that provided the game day freebie. I gave it a quick coloring job in PrusaSlicer, but skipped doing the face.
The model was printed on the Prusa XL using Anycubic turquoise and orange PLA, with Creality white and black PLA.
NIR 3D Scanning with the Creality Pika
I spent a ton of time putting random dots on the included turntable, which made Blue light scanning a breeze. NIR 3D scanning doesn’t use them. Scanning a person seems to work well until you get hair involved. Then it gets dodgy.
I ran two good scans using NIR. This time I borrowed my husband to operate the scanner, since scanning yourself is a bit more difficult than taking a selfie. I stitched together two scans of my foot, which I’ll use later to size some TPU shoes. I was able to further clean up the scan in Nomad Sculpt, since the scan wasn’t very flattering. It works quite well for sizing, however. The shoes will turn up in a future printer review.
After the less-than-stellar scan he took of my head for the Creality Sermoon S1, my husband graciously volunteered to have me scan his head for this review. Using any of the modes available, hair just seems to flummox the scanner. Fortunately, my husband has less hair than I do, so the scan did complete, and no, I’m not going to 3D print it. 3D scans are quite brutal, but if he ever wants a custom driver for his Death Racer, we’re covered.
Bottom Line
The Creality Pika is a small and light, yet totally capable scanner. It needs a good mobile phone or fairly decent laptop to drive it. The software backing up the hardware is easy to use and really does an excellent job cleaning up the rough areas of your scans. Currently, it is available at a comparatively bargain-basement pre-order price of $699.
If you want a scanner with a little more horsepower, check out the Creality Sermoon S1, which retails for $2,069. Creality also makes the Sermoon P1, which can run completely untethered and retails for $3,299.
Denise Bertacchi is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering 3D printing. Denise has been crafting with PCs since she discovered Print Shop had clip art on her Apple IIe. She loves reviewing 3D printers because she can mix all her passions: printing, photography, and writing.

articles.title: Replika’s founder built the AI assistant she pitched at Disrupt 12 years ago | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Twelve years ago today, Eugenia Kuyda stood up onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt and presented a conversational chatbot called IO that acted as a lifestyle concierge to help people book restaurants and vacations along with other tasks.
IO, the first product from her startup Luka, came before the deep learning breakthroughs that would eventually lead to today’s large language models. “It still worked,” Kuyda told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It was pretty magical … but, of course, it’s nowhere near what we have today.”
Luka ended up becoming Replika, the popular AI chatbot companion company. Last year, Kuyda left as CEO of Replika and founded Wabi.
The technology has finally caught up with her original vision for Luka, just in time for Wabi to take on a wave of new personal AI assistants such as Muse and Instinct, which promise to do everything from manage your inbox to find you the best flight deals.
On Monday, Kuyda officially launched Wabi for all users, a multiplayer personal AI assistant that functions as a messenger app, allowing users to maintain multiple agentic threads dedicated to different tasks and long-term goals. Within each thread, users can build and use custom apps, like a weight-loss tracker inside a health thread or an app showing nearby children’s events inside a family thread.
The launch is something of a pivot for Wabi, though Kuyda describes it as more of an evolution. When TechCrunch covered Wabi’s initial launch last year, along with its $20 million pre-seed round, it was described as more of a social platform where you could create mini apps with prompts that you could share with friends or across the app.
Over the past year, Kuyda said the team realized that while people love personal software rather than “one size fits all solutions in the App Store,” they “maybe don’t want to spend a lot of time, or any time, building it.”
With Wabi 2.0, the agent decides what apps to build. The moment you connect it to your email, it automatically spins up a number of threads and apps to start with, and users can add to that by requesting custom apps or starting new threads.
“It’s doing what Instinct and Muse do, but it also has all these apps, which helps users do more stuff,” Kuyda said.
App-building isn’t Wabi’s only differentiator. Kuyda is also betting on its multithreaded, multiplayer design.
“It’s not just everything in one single thread like with Instinct and Muse, where you get buried in the information that it sends you every day,” Kuyda said. “Single thread experiences, if you think about it, get worse over time because it’s just so much context in one endless conversation.”
The longer an AI chatbot conversation goes on, the more likely it is to hallucinate, lose track of context, or respond in ways that would otherwise be blocked by safety guardrails, according to interviews with AI researchers.
Threads can also be shared, functioning as group chats.
“Today, all the agentic apps are just [conversations] between you and the agent, and I feel like it should be a lot more about bringing people together in a group chat together,” Kuyda said. “Not you doing it separately with your AI, and I’m doing it separately with my AI … I don’t think anyone has yet cracked multiplayer.”
Kuyda walked TechCrunch through some of her own shared threads. In one with her boyfriend, a row of apps along the top helps the two of them connect and find things to do together, including a live music tracker, an app that asks a question every day about their relationship, a running list of restaurant suggestions, important events from their shared calendar, and a list of books they’re reading together with suggestions for what to read next.
In her more family-focused thread, there is an app tracking her daughter’s schedule, another for finding kid-friendly events nearby, and another that quizzes her daughter on Japanese.
Within any shared chat, users can share as much or as little as they want, from email and calendar information to bank account details.
“So my partner can ask Wabi in the chat, ‘Is Eugenia free next Thursday?’ or ‘Did she buy those tickets?’” Kuyda said. She noted that access is scoped to individual chats, and everyone in a chat can see when someone’s personal information is requested.
On privacy more broadly, Wabi is SOC 2 compliant, meaning its data security controls have been independently audited. Wabi runs entirely in the cloud, and most user data is stored in the U.S., Kuyda said.
“My previous company Replika worked on AI that will make people feel … less lonely,” Kuyda said. “To a degree, that is [in Wabi] as well. AI can bring people together, even when it comes to just helping you spend time better together in real life, whether it’s going out and seeing a concert together or finding the next book that you will read together.”
Wabi is free for now, and the company hasn’t settled on a business model yet. Kuyda said Wabi is in talks to raise more funds.

articles.title: Pulsar Gaming Announces eS Xlite Gaming Mouse
articles.text:
Monday, October 19th 2026
Pulsar Gaming Announces eS Xlite Gaming Mouse
Pulsar Gaming Gears (AplusX Inc.), a leading developer of high-performance esports peripherals, and VAXEE Corporation, a respected innovator in gaming hardware, today announced the official launch schedule of the new Pulsar eS Xlite. This highly-anticipated product line is the result of the strategic exclusive partnership and joint development work between the two companies, aimed at delivering unparalleled innovation and performance to the esports community.
The Pulsar eS series is a unified vision for the future of competitive gear. Crafted from the absolute finest materials with flawless finishing and extreme precision, the eS Xlite is in running production and is not a limited edition, confirming Pulsar's commitment to making this reference-standard equipment widely available.Evolved Ergonomics for the Biggest Stages 
Retaining the beloved ergonomic advantages of the original Xlite, the eS Xlite introduces refined geometry to maximize grip stability and comfort. The mouse features a slimmer width that allows for an agile, secure grip, while the raised rear and rearward-shifted center of gravity provide full, stable support for the palm. This advanced shape allows the wrist to rest in a more natural, lower position, significantly reducing strain during extended tournament sessions. Additionally, the sensor position has been moved forward to perfectly align with the user's index and middle fingers, delivering highly consistent and precise horizontal tracking. 
Uncompromising Hardware & Next-Generation Performance 
Under the hood, the eS Xlite is powered by the next-generation XS2 Sensor, boasting up to 42,000 DPI, 800 IPS, and 70G acceleration. This significant upgrade ensures flawless tracking without spinouts, even during the most aggressive flick shots. The mouse fully supports an 8000 Hz (8K) polling rate in both wired and wireless modes. To drive this extreme performance, Pulsar integrated a dual-core-class MCU alongside a high-capacity 500mAh battery—delivering 2.5 times the capacity of its predecessor (200mAh) and offering up to 119 hours of continuous use at 1KHz. 
Weighing a perfectly balanced 51 g, the eS Xlite is presented in the signature Pulsar eS blue color. To guarantee hardware longevity and prevent double-clicking issues at the source, it is fully equipped with Pulsar Optical Switches. 
The Link 8K Dongle Integration
The eS Xlite signals a major milestone in competitive peripheral design with its seamless integration of the Link 8K Dongle. Functioning as an active controller rather than a passive wireless receiver, the Link 8K allows players to instantly adjust critical settings—such as DPI, polling rate, and profiles—using its built-in buttons, eliminating the need to interrupt intense gameplay by flipping the mouse or accessing software. 
Pricing & Availability 
The Pulsar eS Xlite carries a suggested retail price of $179.95 USD. The Pulsar eS Xlite is available as of today.

articles.title: Spektakuläre „Weltraumqualle“: Das steckt wirklich hinter dem SpaceX-Phänomen
articles.text:
Abgase im Sonnenlicht: Wie SpaceX-Raketen das Phänomen der „Weltraumqualle“ erzeugen
Die Mission SpaceX CRS-35 ist am 13. Oktober um 6:33 Uhr Ortszeit von der Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida gestartet. An Bord der gestarteten Cargo-Dragon-Rakete befinden sich laut dem Kennedy Space Center der Nasa eine Reihe von wissenschaftlichen Geräten, Experimenten und Fracht, die als Nachschub zur Raumstation ISS geliefert werden sollen. Doch die Nachschubmission sorgt derzeit nicht mit ihrem Ziel, sondern mit ihrem Start für breite Aufmerksamkeit.
Wie entsteht der „Space Jellyfish“ am Himmel?
In den sozialen Medien werden unzählige Bilder und Videos gepostet, die einige Zeit nach dem Start aufgenommen wurden. Am Himmel ist dabei ein bläulicher Schimmer zu sehen, der die Form einer Qualle hat. Was zunächst wie ein KI-generierter Fake aussieht, ist ein echtes Phänomen, das unter bestimmten Umständen nach einem Raketenstart auftreten kann.
Der „Space Jellyfish“, der auch als „Jellyfish Ufo“ oder „Rocket Jellyfish“ bezeichnet wird, besteht aus den Abgasen der Rakete, die sich in den höheren Luftschichten sammeln und dort verharren. Das Phänomen wird allerdings nur sichtbar, wenn der Raketenstart in den frühen Morgen- oder späten Abendstunden stattfindet. Genau dann, wenn die Sonne nicht auf die Erde scheint, aber noch den Himmel beleuchtet.
Dadurch trifft das Sonnenlicht auf die Raketenabgase und erleuchtet sie. Da wir auf der Erde im Dunkeln stehen, werden sie für uns sichtbar. Die aktuelle Weltraumqualle von SpaceX ist dabei kein einzelnes Phänomen. Schon seit den 70ern gab es zahlreiche Raketenstarts, die einen „Space Jellyfish“ nach sich gezogen haben. Als das Phänomen noch nicht weitläufig bekannt war, wurden die Sichtungen oftmals als Ufos oder Anzeichen für nukleare Raketenschläge gehalten, wie die Washington Post schon 2017 berichtete.
Für SpaceX ist das Phänomen natürlich eine willkommene Werbung für den Flug zur ISS. Ob die Uhrzeit so gelegt war, dass die Möglichkeit eines „Space Jellyfishs“ erhöht ist, ist nicht bekannt. SpaceX musste den Flug schon zweimal verschieben. Er sollte ursprünglich im November 2026 stattfinden, wurde dann aber aufgrund von Schäden an einem russischen Launch-Pad auf August vorgezogen. So sollte sichergestellt werden, dass die Astronaut:innen auf der ISS ausreichend Nachschub für das kommende Jahr bekommen. Als das Launch-Pad schneller als erwartet repariert werden konnte, wurde der Start wieder nach hinten geschoben.

articles.title: Spotify’s new podcast memberships let you pay for extra perks
articles.text:
Spotify is enabling podcast creators to earn more money through the platform by providing their fans with a way to pay to access exclusive content. First announced in May, the new Memberships subscription feature is starting to roll out in 34 regions today, allowing podcasters to offer perks including additional content, early access, bonus episodes, and reduced ads behind a paywall.
Spotify’s new podcast memberships let you pay for extra perks
Creators can offer bonus content, early access, fewer ads, and more.
Users can find Memberships on a podcast’s Spotify page, with the ability to subscribe, pay, and access the exclusive benefits “in just a few taps,” according to Spotify. Podcast creators can set their pricing options and bundle benefits across multiple subscription tiers, and keep 90 percent of membership revenue. Spotify is providing podcasters with tools to analyze and build their Memberships audience, including targeted promotions and free trial offers, alongside community engagement features like member badges, welcome clips, and more.
That makes this more like a Patreon-style membership system in which fans can choose to give additional support to their favorite creators, and is distinct from the podcast subscription feature that Spotify introduced in 2021. Podcasters can utilize Memberships alongside other Spotify revenue streams, including ads and the Spotify Partner Program.
To qualify for Memberships, shows must be hosted on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, and have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and three published episodes. Spotify is also making it easy for podcasters who manage their subscriptions on other services to try Memberships, allowing them to bring their paywalled content to Spotify via its Open Access feature.

articles.title: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
articles.text:
How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
I helicoptered into the Alaskan wilderness with scientists on the frontlines of permafrost research.
Andrew Haverdink, a tall grad student in a rain bib and rubber boots, wrenched a double-handed drill from the frozen soil that underlies much of Alaska’s Denali National Park and then unclipped the hollow barrel from the end of the bit.
He knelt in front of a blue tarp, lined the barrel up with a plastic tray, and pushed a rod through the opposite end. A perfect solid, cylindrical core of ancient soil emerged—dark, rich permafrost at least a foot long.
On that late morning in early July, Haverdink was among a team of Northern Arizona University students and staff gathering samples and data from a research plot, divided by surveyor’s tape unspooled atop tussocks, alders, and fireweed.
In late June of 2013, a lightning strike sparked a fire in this stretch of mostly treeless tundra, in the northern backcountry of the park. Whipped by the Chinooks, intense downslope winds created as moist ocean air surmounts and then descends the Alaska Range, the fire ripped across nearly 35,000 acres. It burned through much of the vegetation and deep into the topsoil, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves the frozen permafrost, a massive storehouse of carbon that underlies 85% of Alaska.
During their first survey, in 2016, the researchers found that in places where the fire burned hottest and deepest, the thawed soil above the permafrost (known as the active layer) extended between a foot and nearly two feet deeper than in plots outside the burn scar—an indication of deep thawing.
Crucially, the fire also crossed two sets of survey grids that the National Park Service established in 2001, including the one where the researchers stood that morning. That pre-fire snapshot offered the Northern Arizona group a rare opportunity to study how the blaze has altered the vegetation, carbon, and permafrost across time, says Xanthe Walker, one of the principal investigators on the project, who was watching over Haverdink’s work that morning.
These direct observations from high-latitude fires are helping scientists to better understand the impacts of wildfire and permafrost loss on climate change, she says.
“There’s a lot of uncertainty,” Walker says. “These are huge biomes with massive fires that no one’s ever been to or ever looked at.”
They’re among a growing group of researchers striving to untangle what happens in the aftermath of fires in the Arctic-boreal region as they occur more often, burn hotter than before, and expose the landscape and frozen permafrost to a warming climate.
The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects: As warming temperatures fuel more frequent and severe fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires, and permafrost loss.
Understanding just how powerful these effects are, how they compound, and to what degree other transformations of the landscape may mitigate them is essential to gain a clearer picture of our climate future.
Notably, past modeling suggested that the carbon dioxide uptake from expanding trees and plants may largely offset the release of carbon from warming soils and melting permafrost, at least over long periods and under moderate levels of warming. But the improving observations and analyses have revealed worrisome signs about the impacts of rising Arctic-boreal emissions in the immediate decades ahead, as the world struggles to keep global warming within relatively safe boundaries.
The permafrost problem
Permafrost makes up 15% of the land surface of the Northern Hemisphere and holds about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, roughly twice the amount in the atmosphere. Most of it formed during the last ice age, but it’s been thawing at an accelerating rate during the last half-century, amid rising temperatures and worsening fires. As it melts, microbes begin to break down that organic matter, releasing it into the air in the form of carbon dioxide and methane. Both are powerful greenhouse gases that fuel climate change.
The impacts of permafrost loss, however, aren’t as straightforward as they may initially seem. Notably, there has been a long-running scientific debate over what would have the strongest effect on the exchange of greenhouse gases over the next few centuries: the loss of carbon in soil and permafrost or the carbon uptake from so-called “Arctic greening,” which describes the spread of carbon-absorbing plants across the landscape as temperatures rise.
Thawing permafrost itself can contribute to the latter phenomenon as the unfrozen soil layer deepens and makes more nitrogen, phosphorus, and other nutrients accessible to plants. Carbon-sucking trees and shrubs with deeper root systems can take hold and thrive in places where they wouldn’t have been able to in the past.
But as more Arctic-boreal fires ignite and more permafrost melts, researchers have been able to closely study what exactly happens in the aftermath, using on-site surveys like those conducted by the Northern Arizona University team, satellite observations, lidar flights, a widening network of greenhouse-gas-measuring towers, and other tools.
The findings have alarmed many researchers.
In particular, permafrost seems particularly prone to abrupt thawing rather than the gradual version that major climate models have simulated. A 2020 paper found that this could release far more carbon than previously understood, doubling the emissions from thawing permafrost and offsetting the carbon uptake from future plant growth.
In addition, even if carbon levels eventually net out through Arctic greening, the emissions from high-latitude fires and permafrost loss appear to be accelerating warming right now.
Susan Natali, an Arctic climate scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, and her colleagues have published several papers in recent years concluding that the combined emissions from these feedback effects will push the planet past 2 °C faster than currently predicted. She and other researchers also found that about 40% of the Arctic-boreal zone has already flipped from a carbon sink into a carbon source, when the emissions from permafrost melting, fires and other forces are taken into account.
“The more we learn about processes like abrupt thaw, deeper-burning fires, and cold-season emissions, and the more we see disturbances increasing, the more likely it is that the sink will weaken and source areas will expand,” Natali said in an email.
But there’s still considerable uncertainty about the differences between the ways fires and thawing permafrost might alter landscapes, under different circumstances in different biomes.
“This is just a challenge of the science, because it's really hard to measure such a huge area, which is not one system,” she says. “It’s many, many, many, many different types of ecosystems.”
Results may vary
The Northern Arizona University researchers have been at the forefront of efforts to study the aftermath of intensifying fires across different parts of Alaska. Over the last two decades, Michelle Mack, a professor of ecosystem ecology who was previously Walker’s postdoctoral advisor, has overseen repeat survey work on fire sites across forests and tundras, from the relatively warm southern interior to the frigid North Slope.
Her husband and frequent collaborator, Ted Schuur, is also a professor at the university and oversees several permafrost monitoring and experimental research sites at the Eight Mile Lake study area, just north of Denali National Park.
If there’s a single takeaway from the body of science that the Northern Arizona scientists have produced, it’s this: It’s complicated. The local climate and ecosystem, the severity of the fires that have occurred, the type of permafrost, and numerous other factors can substantially shift the uptake or loss of carbon, the amount of permafrost that’s thawed, the extent to which it may recover, and the future flammability of the landscape.
In one early study, the researchers and their collaborators surveyed dozens of stands dominated by black spruce trees in the aftermath of a series of large boreal fires in 2004, between the Brooks Range and the Alaska Range. One of the notable findings: Severe burns that left little behind of the decaying organic matter in the topsoil induced a shift toward faster-growing and less flammable deciduous trees. The sites where deciduous trees dominated stored about five times as much soil carbon as stands that returned to black spruce, Mack, Walker, and their coauthors noted in a 2021 Science paper.
That means the subsequent uptake of carbon on those stands “more than compensated” for the amount released in the initial fire, Walker says.
But the 2007 Anaktuvuk River tundra fire, which remains the largest fire on record in Alaska’s North Slope, offers a starkly different case study. In the initial analysis there, Mack, Schuur, and their coauthors found that the fire released more than 2 million tons of carbon to the atmosphere, basically negating the amount that tundra ecosystems around the world removed from the air that year.
Subsequent studies found that more than a third of the scorched landscape sank, slid, and crumpled as the ice wedges below collapsed, the telltale signs of abrupt permafrost melting. Nearly two decades later, much of that thawed, decaying organic matter continues to release carbon dioxide and methane in the most severely burned patches of the fire scar, says Adrian Rocha, an associate professor at the University of Notre Dame.
It will take decades to centuries to recover all the carbon lost there, if ever happens at all, according to Rocha, who continues to monitor the site using Eddy covariance flux towers, which measure the exchange of greenhouse gases between Earth and atmosphere.
Mack says these on-the-ground measurements are critical to understanding what sorts of ecosystems recover, which shift into new states, whether they release a lot of carbon or a little, and when and where plant growth can offset that.
That said, the stakes of thawing permafrost are clear.
“If we step back as ecosystem ecologists, we know that there’s a lot more carbon stored below ground in permafrost than there is above ground in vegetation,” she says. “If permafrost carbon is released, it could swamp all of these other interesting details.”
In the lab
The Northern Arizona University research team shipped a pallet of soil samples back from Denali. The material included plugs of moss and decaying plant matter known as “brownies,” as well as permafrost cores and samples of the unfrozen soil layer. In the months since, they’ve cut, dried, weighed, combusted and analyzed various samples and inputted their field and lab findings into databases.
Walker says they’re exploring a variety of research questions, including how much that top organic layer has recovered since the initial post-fire survey and how much carbon has been lost and recovered since the fire.
The analysis is still underway, but in the most severely burned sites, it appears that the thawed layer of soil above the permafrost remain deeper some 13 years.
“Thaw still reaches further into the soil each summer than it probably did before the fire, which exposes more soil to decomposition,” Walker explained in an email.
They’re now hoping to use lab analyses to determine how much of that carbon is being lost.
Stepping into the climate future
On my last afternoon in Healy, Alaska, I followed Schuur along a narrow walkway of wooden boards suspended above a tundra field just north of Denali, hoping to get a glimpse into our climate future.
In 2008, he and his research team devised a way to subject permafrost to the temperature levels expected two or three decades from now by setting up snow fences around dozens of designated research plots. That allowed extra snow to build up—which, counterintuitively, acts like a blanket, adding thermal insulation during the winter that kept the test plots warmer than the controls.
Over the course of the 13-year experiment, the soil carbon levels in those 10-by-10-meter plots declined by 23%, Schuur and his coauthors found. The land collapsed in many of the sites, forming craters several feet deep.
As I stepped heel-to-toe along the planks into the middle of one plot, I descended about four feet, experiencing subsidence in three dimensions. Looking up at the edge from the walkway, I felt as if I were diaphragm deep in an empty pool.
Schuur, though, had another thing to show me. As we crested a ridge between plots, he pointed down to a shallower—though no less obvious—pool on the other side. It was a control site that had melted and collapsed on its own, without any assistance from simulated warming or fires.
“Every plot is just going off in its own trajectory,” he said. “This stuff is happening because the whole place is warming … and all these changes just go faster if you first burn the surface.”
Schuur expects that the permafrost underlying the whole field will thaw deeply by the end of 2040.
“There won’t be any surface permafrost based on our current warming,” he says.
Unless the world radically cuts emissions and gets fires under control, this same phenomenon will creep up the state, decade by decade, until even the permafrost under Alaska’s North Slope sinks to similar depths and gives up the carbon it has held for millennia.

Possible new Cellebrite iPhone Radio Zero-Day
Justin.sh is reporting on a confidential Cellebrite document that has been leaked to him:
Cellebrite calls it Advanced Unlocks (AU from here on), not to be confused with the “advanced unlocking services” they’ve marketed for years. A press release from earlier this year confirms AU is a new product for 2026.
[…]

articles.title: El Galaxy A56 recibe One UI 9: todo lo nuevo que llega con la actualización de Android 17
articles.text:
Samsung ha comenzado el despliegue global de One UI 9 para el Galaxy A56. Uno de los móviles más populares de la gama media recibirá por fin la actualización a Android 17, que viene cargada de novedades y un diseño más refinado. Tras lanzarse en Corea del Sur, la actualización ya comenzó a llegar a más países, por lo que pronto podrás instalarla en tu móvil.
De acuerdo con SamMobile, la actualización a One UI 9 para el Galaxy A56 se identifica con el firmware A566BXXUEDZJ1 y pesa unos 2,3 GB. Samsung la ha catalogado como una de las actualizaciones más importantes para este móvil, ya que incorpora Android 17 y una larga lista de mejoras en productividad, personalización y seguridad.
Entre los cambios más importantes de One UI 9 se encuentran las opciones de personalización para el panel rápido, cambios en DeX y actualizaciones a casi todas las apps de Samsung. Esta versión cuenta con un rediseño en el que se mejoró la organización de algunos elementos del sistema y se añadieron más posibilidades de configuración para que cada usuario adapte el móvil a sus preferencias.
El Galaxy A56 recibe estas funciones con One UI 9
En el apartado de la IA, Samsung añadió tarjetas generativas y editables a Now Brief, que permiten personalizar la información que aparece en el resumen diario. En el caso de Now Nudge, el sistema ofrecerá sugerencias contextuales en tiempo real para mejorar la productividad. One UI 9 también incluye Creative Studio, que propone ideas visuales para cumpleaños o festividades, así como My FanCam, una función de la cámara que sigue automáticamente a una persona y ajusta la toma según su movimiento.
Pasando a la seguridad, One UI 9 añade alertas de privacidad más avanzadas, las cuales te avisarán sobre posibles comportamientos sospechosos. Si bajas una app y el sistema detecta permisos inusuales, tu Samsung lanzará una notificación para que no caigas en la trampa. La compañía también ha reforzado los mecanismos de protección para identificar software potencialmente peligroso, de modo que tu dispositivo se mantenga protegido siempre.
Otros ajustes incluyen una actualización a Samsung Notes, que recibe nuevas herramientas creativas y mejoras orientadas a la productividad. Las funciones de accesibilidad añaden opciones que facilitan la lectura y mejoran la interacción con personas con distintas necesidades. Por último, el panel rápido ofrece un mayor nivel de control, mientras que varias aplicaciones del ecosistema reciben pequeños retoques destinados a agilizar las tareas diarias.
¿Qué móviles de Samsung recibirán One UI 9?
El Galaxy A56 no es el único que ha recibido la actualización de One UI 9. Hace unos días, Samsung anunció el despliegue para el Galaxy S23 y otros modelos que tuvieron que esperar algunos meses para tener la versión estable. articles.title: Shopify CTO Mikhail Parakhin to depart after two years
articles.text:
Former Microsoft executive Mikhail Parakhin is departing as CTO of Ottawa-based retail technology giant Shopify after just over two years in the role, BetaKit has confirmed.
The news: An anonymous X post from Saturday was the first to indicate Parakhin’s departure. BetaKit has since confirmed with Shopify that Parakhin is leaving that position and transitioning to an advisor.
Shopify did not disclose when or why Parakhin is departing, or share any other details regarding this move. BetaKit has also reached out to Parakhin for comment, but he had not responded by publication time.
From the source: “Mikhail has left an indelible mark on the company and has helped us level up in engineering and machine learning [ML],” a Shopify spokesperson told BetaKit over email. “As he leaves, we’re grateful for his contributions and glad that he’ll continue as an advisor.”
The context: Parakhin previously served as CTO of Moscow-based tech firm Yandex, and held senior executive roles at American tech giant Microsoft, including CEO of advertising and web services. Shopify brought on the Russian-trained physicist-turned-ML engineer as CTO in late 2024 for his deep expertise in AI. In that role, he took over for Allan Leinwand, who stepped down in early 2023 for “personal reasons.”
Final thought: Under Parakhin’s leadership, Shopify has invested heavily in building AI for merchants and deploying the tech internally to improve its efficiency and expedite product development. Parakhin’s LinkedIn profile, which is not yet updated, lists his focus as “bringing AI into the shopping space.” Parakhin appeared in an ad for OpenAI’s Codex just last week, highlighting how he was using the agentic tool at Shopify. Time Magazine recently named him one of its tech executives of the year for his work rebuilding the commerce platform for the age of AI. It is not yet clear what Parakhin plans to do next or who, if anyone, will replace him in Shopify’s CTO chair.
Disclosure: BetaKit majority owner Good Future is the family office of two former Shopify leaders, Arati Sharma and Satish Kanwar.
Feature image courtesy Shopify.

articles.title: SA’s Injini launches EdTech for Employment incubation programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African ed-tech incubator Injini has launched a new two-year programme that will support 10 early-stage South African edtech startups building solutions that create or support employment pathways for young people.
Founded in 2017, Injini, which is a member of the UVU Africa Group, is a registered non-profit company that exists for the sole purpose of improving educational outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa. Its programmes and research via the Injini Think Tank contribute towards its mission to increase the quality, accessibility, and relevance of education in the region. It announced its latest cohort earlier this year.
The EdTech for Employment Incubation Programme, which is financed by Zurich-based Leopold Bachmann Foundation, will run from October 2026 to September 2028, and targets startups whose solutions serve youth aged between 15 and 30.
The programme comes against the backdrop of a South African youth unemployment rate that stood at 46.1 per cent in the first quarter of this year, according to Stats SA, which is among the highest in the world. Injini said the figure reflects a structural shortage of quality vocational and work-readiness pathways connecting young people to the economy.
A growing number of edtech startups are building solutions in this space, including teacher training platforms, tutoring and mentorship tools, and technologies that prepare young people for economic participation. However, Injini said these companies often lack the structured support, market access and proof-of-concept evidence they need to scale.
“South Africa’s youth aren’t short on ambition or ability. What they need are structured pathways into work,” said Krista Davidson, executive director at Injini. “We’ve spent years watching talented edtech founders build real solutions to this problem, without the support to test what works, prove it, and scale it. This programme is designed to close that gap.
The programme will run two cohorts of five startups each. Each cycle begins with a recruitment and selection process, followed by a six-month incubation period built around four pillars: product foundations, business sustainability, market access, and impact measurement.
Participating startups will receive hands-on support from Injini’s team, as well as access to a network of specialist consultants matched to their needs. Founders will also have opportunities to network and engage with the wider ecosystem and potential users.
Over its two-year run, the programme aims to reach 20,000 underserved youth, help up to 2,000 of them access work or income-generating opportunities, and create 20 direct jobs within the cohort companies.
“We’re looking for ed-tech companies that are already doing the hard work of connecting young people to skills and income,” Davidson said. “Over the next two years, we want to give ten of them the structural support, proof points and market access they need to grow.”
Both non-profit and for-profit edtech startups with a clear social impact mandate are eligible, with priority given to those working in work-readiness and digital skills, teacher training and professional development, and tutoring or peer-learning models that generate income and employment opportunities for young people.
Interested startups can apply here.

articles.title: Toyota Corolla électrique : le modèle le plus vendu passe enfin au 100 % électrique
articles.text:
Soixante ans après la première Corolla, Toyota prépare une version 100 % électrique de sa compacte vedette et la fera d’abord construire en Chine. Sa coentreprise FAW Toyota assemblera dès 2028 une treizième génération déclinée en plusieurs motorisations, sur une base technique commune.
Toyota a vendu plus de 57 millions de Corolla depuis 1966, nous apprend notre confrère Electrek et aucune n’a jamais roulé sans moteur thermique. Fin octobre 2025, au Japan Mobility Show de Tokyo, le constructeur avait dévoilé un concept très anguleux de la future génération, avec la promesse d’une déclinaison électrique à côté des versions hybrides. D’après Nikkei Asia, sa production démarrera en 2028 chez FAW Toyota, la coentreprise formée avec le groupe public chinois FAW. Toyota lancera donc sa première Corolla électrique sur un marché où ses ventes baissent mois après mois, à des milliers de kilomètres des usines qui fournissent les Corolla vendues en France.
Une plateforme multi-énergie pour reconquérir la Chine
En juillet, Toyota a vendu 114 747 véhicules en Chine, soit 24,3 % de moins qu’un an plus tôt, selon les chiffres mensuels du constructeur. Les automobilistes chinois boudent ses modèles à essence et hybrides depuis la hausse des prix du carburant, et Electrek rapporte un septième mois de baisse consécutif. Akio Toyoda, président du conseil d’administration, avait prévenu en juillet sur la chaîne publique NHK que le groupe devait s’adapter à la concurrence et aux technologies chinoises, faute de quoi « elle ne peut pas survivre ».
La future Corolla sera la première à utiliser la nouvelle plateforme multi-énergie de Toyota, compatible avec plusieurs types de motorisation et utilisée sur certains modèles Lexus. Avec cette base unique, FAW Toyota gagnera en souplesse dans un marché chinois au ralenti, explique Nikkei Asia. Concrètement, l’usine pourra produire plus d’électriques ou plus d’hybrides au gré des commandes, sans changer de modèle.
Toyota n’a encore rien publié sur la batterie de sa Corolla électrique. Il faudra donc se contenter de ce que dit Electrek, qui l’attend avec un ou deux moteurs et une autonomie d’au moins 250 miles, environ 400 km. Les ingénieurs de Toyota ont confié à Car and Driver que la version hybride associera un nouveau quatre-cylindres 1,5 litre à un moteur électrique, pour environ 134 chevaux et un rendement estimé de 10 à 20 % supérieur à celui de l’actuelle Corolla. Aux États-Unis, le magazine estime le prix de l’électrique autour de 30 000 dollars, contre 27 000 dollars environ pour l’hybride, et la présentation officielle de la nouvelle génération est attendue en 2027.
Les Corolla vendues en France sortent d’usines anglaise et turque
En Europe, Toyota assemble la Corolla à Burnaston, au Royaume-Uni, et à Sakarya, en Turquie. L’usine turque, la plus grosse du groupe sur le continent avec une capacité de 280 000 véhicules par an, expédie la majorité de sa production vers les pays européens, d’après l’association des constructeurs turcs. Nikkei Asia ne dit rien d’une exportation de la Corolla chinoise vers l’Europe.
« La Terre est vaste, et le monde est divers. Les routes diffèrent, tout comme les réalités énergétiques », avait lancé Koji Sato à Tokyo lors de la présentation du concept. Alors P.-D.G du groupe, il a été remplacé en avril par Kenta Kon. En Europe, Toyota défend cette stratégie jusque devant la Commission européenne. Le constructeur réclame une catégorie VEEF, réservée aux voitures thermiques qui roulent exclusivement aux carburants renouvelables, et teste depuis juillet en Espagne une vingtaine de voitures de série alimentées à l’essence 100 % renouvelable.
Toyota paierait d’ailleurs cher l’importation d’une Corolla fabriquée en Chine. Bruxelles et Pékin ont conclu ce mois-ci un accord pour plafonner à 350 000 véhicules par an les importations d’hybrides chinoises. Sur les électriques fabriquées en Chine, l’Union européenne applique depuis octobre 2024 une surtaxe de 35,3 % au maximum, en plus des 10 % de droits habituels. Pour l’heure, Toyota n’a programmé sa Corolla électrique que dans les usines de FAW Toyota, à partir de 2028.

articles.title: Bullhorn takes staffing platform offline to contain cyberattack
articles.text:
Staffing software company Bullhorn has disabled access to its platform to contain a cyberattack that caused a system-wide outage.
The company says it has isolated the issue and eradicated the immediate threat. Currently, its team is working to restore services following thorough security reviews conducted with help from CrowdStrike specialists.
Bullhorn is an American software company specializing in cloud-based staffing and recruitment solutions. Its platform helps staffing firms manage the recruitment lifecycle, including candidate tracking, onboarding, and payroll.
The company says it serves more than 10,000 customers worldwide.
According to a status page on the incident, customers started to experience issues with job posting in the Bullhorn application on Friday.
The next day, the company said it was "experiencing a system-wide outage affecting the Bullhorn platform," and later confirmed that the issues were caused by a cyberattack.
"We have detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. We have temporarily disabled access to our systems in order to contain the activity while we investigate further," the company said in an update.
In a FAQ page, Bullhorn says that a forensic investigation has been started and "not yet determined whether customer data was exfiltrated." Bullhorn promised to notify affected individuals directly if a data breach is confirmed.
According to the firm’s status page, most of the services are under maintainance or have degraded performance, except for Adapt, eEmpACT, and StaffSuite, which remain operational.
Major outages affect ATS/CRM, Automation, Back Office, Talent Platform, and sandbox environments.
At the time of writing, degraded performance was reported for Bullhorn for Salesforce and associated products, Onboarding365, and additional solutions including Amplify, Analytics, Messaging, SourceBreaker, VMS Sync, Data Hub, Erecruit, SalesDuel, and VMS Access.
Bullhorn has not provided any timelines for when those services will be restored. Customers should check the company’s service status page for the latest updates.
Also, the latest update mentions that all non-SSO users will be required to reset their passwords on their next login.
Also, as per the FAQ page, API passwords require rotation to protect integrations, while client-secret changes will follow later. For Bullhorn-hosted instances, this will take place automatically.
Customers can request data exports through the firm’s support to minimize business disruption.
Unposted time records will be reprocessed after restoration, and service credits will be reviewed against applicable SLAs once the incident is resolved.
BleepingComputer has contacted Bullhorn to request more information about the attack, and we will update this post with their response when received.

En cette fin d’année, Huawei a donné un second souffle à sa MatePad Pro 12″. La marque a sorti une nouvelle version avec un nouveau processeur : le HiSilicon Kirin T93. Avec lui, Huawei permet à sa tablette d’avoir de nombreuses cordes à son arc puisqu’elle peut assurer quelques tâches créatives. Pour vous faciliter la vie, un stylet est inclus avec la tablette. Actuellement, la MatePad Pro 12″ est disponible pour 100 euros de moins sur le site du constructeur chinois.
Pourquoi choisir la Huawei MatePad Pro 12″ ?
- Un écran 3K de 12 pouces
- Une batterie de 9 760 mAh avec la charge filaire
- Un stylet est offert
Sur le site de Huawei, la MatePad Pro 12″ passe de 1 099,99 euros à 999,99 euros.
Une tablette passe-partout
Avec sa MatePad Pro, Huawei a mis au point une tablette particulièrement discrète puisqu’elle ne fait que 4,7 mm d’épaisseur pour un poids contenu inférieur à 500 grammes.
Comme son nom l’indique, cette tablette se présente avec un écran 3K de 12 pouces. Cet écran arrive à faire oublier les fines bordures présentes puisque l’appareil affiche un ratio taille-écran de 93 %. Cette dalle est sublimée par la technologie OLED Flexible PaperMatte qui offre à la tablette un filtre antireflet et réduit les scintillements. Côté luminosité, il faut compter 1 600 nits, ce qui est suffisant pour une utilisation en extérieur.
Pour faire fonctionner sa tablette, Huawei a opté pour le processeur maison : le HiSilicon Kirin T93 et 12 Go de RAM. Ainsi, vous pourrez scroller sur les réseaux sociaux, aller sur les plateformes de streaming et même effectuer quelques tâches bureautiques. Pour cela, vous aurez besoin du clavier dédié à cette MatePad Pro, mais il n’est pas inclus dans l’offre.
Un stylet fourni pour le bonheur des créatifs
Si le clavier est absent, Huawei complète cette offre en incluant le M-Pencil Pro pour pouvoir travailler sur Canva ou Photoshop par exemple. Il s’agit d’un stylet avec de nombreuses fonctionnalités. Logiquement, vous pourrez réaliser des dessins ou des graphiques. L’accessoire est aussi muni d’un bouton qui permet de faire défiler les slides d’une présentation. Un bouton IA est aussi présent pour obtenir des réponses instantanées à une question.
Autre fonctionnalité intéressante de ce stylet, celle qui permet d’ouvrir un menu dédié à la création artistique. Ici, vous pourrez choisir des couleurs adaptées à votre image ou encore ajuster l’épaisseur du pinceau.
Vous l’aurez compris, la Huawei MatePad Pro 12″ est une tablette polyvalente. Par conséquent, il faut que la batterie soit à la hauteur pour profiter de toutes ces fonctionnalités le plus longtemps possible. Huawei annonce que son produit tient 13 heures et qu’il est compatible avec la charge filaire inversée de 40 W.
