articles.title: OpenCode hack exposes API keys amid AI distillation attacks
articles.text:
The open-source AI coding project OpenCode has notified some users that stored API keys they used with external providers were exposed in a security breach.
Multiple users reported that the incident led to unauthorized API charges and suspended projects in Google Cloud.
According to the project maintainer, the breach affected 1.4% of OpenCode Console users, with some reporting more than $1,700 in unauthorized charges overnight.
OpenCode is a model-agnostic AI coding agent that helps users understand code, write features, and fix bugs using natural-language instructions, through a terminal, desktop app, or code editor.
Users can connect AI models from multiple AI providers to the OpenCode console to streamline and automate the development process.
Distillation attack
On Saturday, OpenCode announced that it suffered a large distillation attack that impacted only developers who linked external providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google.
“We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the project maintainer said.
“We have notified them all this morning via email. If you did not get an email, you were not impacted, it was a subset of users who had external providers linked.”
Distillation is a legitimate machine-learning technique that trains smaller AI models using responses generated by more powerful models. The goal is to create cheaper, faster models that retain many of the capabilities of their larger counterparts.
However, the technique becomes an attack when it involves large-scale training through unauthorized queries.
OpenCode co-founder Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting the company's systems for at least 48 hours using AI agents.
He also said OpenCode's investigation of the attackers were blocked when the AI models it was using began refusing requests due to built-in security safeguards.
Raad said the situation stabilized after OpenCode began using OpenAI’s Daybreak AI cybersecurity model for defensive work, which it was approved to use on Saturday.
The email sent to impacted users notes that the earliest possible exposure of the users’ keys was on October 17, 2026, 00:30 UTC, and that no data appears to have been exposed.
OpenCode also said it was working with Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic to address the incident but could not share further details at this time.
User reports claim rogue charges following the private key leaks, ranging from several hundred USD to up to $1,700. OpenCode’s message to impacted users mentions the possibility of reimbursement for those impacted.
Some users reported that Google suspended their projects after detecting "abusive activity consistent with hijacked resources.”
BleepingComputer contacted OpenCode for more details, but we have not heard back as of publication.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Panne Revolut : Google Cloud et son centre de données de Londres pointés du doigt — Frandroid
articles.text:
Quand une carte est refusée à la caisse, on soupçonne d’abord son solde, puis le terminal, puis sa banque. Personne ne pense à une salle de serveurs. C’est pourtant la piste la plus solide pour expliquer la panne de Revolut de ce mardi 20 octobre, qui empêche une partie des clients de payer, de faire des virements et parfois même d’utiliser l’application.
    Pour aller plus loin
Cartes refusées, application bloquée : Revolut reconnaît une panne sans donner de cause
            
Revolut a réagi auprès de Frandroid avec cette déclaration : « Nous rencontrons actuellement une perturbation de nos services qui en affecte plusieurs. Nous pouvons confirmer que l’argent et les données de tous nos clients sont en sécurité. Nous travaillons à résoudre ce problème depuis qu’il a été identifié ce matin et nous présentons nos excuses aux personnes concernées, ainsi que pour tout désagrément occasionné. »
Rappelons que la page de statut de la néobanque a affiché ce matin ses 31 services en indisponible. La banque ne donne toujours ni cause ni horaire de rétablissement.
Google Cloud reconnaît un incident à Londres
Sur sa page d’état, Google signale depuis le début de la matinée un taux d’erreurs élevé et des pannes réseau intermittentes dans la région europe-west2.
Derrière ce nom se cachent les centres de données londoniens où des milliers d’entreprises louent serveurs et stockage.
L’incident a démarré à 8 h 08, heure de Paris, environ une heure avant le pic de signalements Revolut sur Downdetector. Une source proche du dossier citée par Reuters relie directement la panne de Revolut à celle de Google, dont la néobanque est cliente de longue date.
Revolut n’est pas seule dans ce cas. Sur la version britannique de Downdetector, Lloyds Bank, HSBC et Bank of Scotland grimpent aussi, aux côtés de Royal Mail, DPD ou Rightmove, comme l’a expliqué Clubic. L’application de gestion de budget Emma a confirmé que son indisponibilité venait de Google. Pour les banques traditionnelles, en revanche, aucun lien direct n’est établi à ce stade. En France, Numerama recensait dès le matin des clients incapables de payer par carte.
Une zone qui tombe, des millions de clients bloqués
Une région cloud est découpée en plusieurs zones indépendantes, justement pour qu’une défaillance locale ne fasse pas tomber un service entier. D’après The Register, l’incident serait parti d’europe-west2-b, l’une des trois zones de Londres.
Si la piste se confirme, Revolut devra expliquer pourquoi un problème chez un seul fournisseur suffit à bloquer des cartes jusqu’en France, où elle revendique plus de 8 millions de clients. Le scénario a un air de déjà-vu : le 20 octobre 2025, un an jour pour jour, une panne d’AWS avait coupé Lloyds, Halifax et des dizaines d’autres services.
La séquence tombe mal pour une banque déjà secouée le mois dernier, entre des passeports et selfies transmis à des escrocs et un chantage autour de 680 dossiers d’identité. En attendant le retour à la normale, une carte d’une autre banque ou un peu de liquide restent le plan B le plus fiable.
Revolut n’est peut-être pas à l’origine de la panne, mais c’est bien sa carte qui se fait refuser en caisse. Une banque qui vend toute sa relation client dans une seule application doit pouvoir survivre à la mauvaise matinée d’un fournisseur.

articles.title: Buildkite Adds Scoped Secrets and New Agentic CI Tools
articles.text:
Continuous integration provider Buildkite has introduced pipeline-scoped secrets and new Model Context Protocol tools for validating pipelines, diagnosing failed builds and repairing webhooks. The company has also added Linux arm64 support to its GitHub Actions compatibility layer and expanded OpenTelemetry data in Buildkite Agent v4.1.0.
The new secrets view is available under Pipeline settings. It lets engineers create cluster secrets whose access is restricted to the current pipeline, rather than managing every secret from the wider cluster interface. Teams can add conditions for a branch, queue, build source or build creator. Secret values remain hidden after creation.
Matt Mejia, writing in Buildkite's announcement, says the change "keeps pipeline-specific secrets together" while showing how many other secrets the cluster manages. Users need permission both to edit the pipeline and manage its cluster. GitHub Actions pipelines also display a prompt linking to secret configuration before their first workflow runs.
"Pipeline secrets are cluster secrets restricted to the current pipeline, and branch, queue, build source, or creator conditions narrow access further."
Matt Mejia
The Buildkite CLI now includes a command for migrating GitHub Actions secrets. Version 3.59.1 fixes handling of relative workflow paths during that migration. Agent v4.0.9 also redacts Buildkite tokens by prefix in job logs, while v4.0.8 redacts captured job errors using secrets registered for the job.
The work addresses several places where credentials can be exposed or configured incorrectly, although scoped storage does not remove the need to control their use inside steps. InfoQ reported in 2025 that HashiCorp was advocating prevention-first secret management throughout developer tools and CI/CD systems. Buildkite's own documentation advises teams to expose a secret only to the steps that require it.
The most extensive feature changes are in Buildkite's open-source MCP server. The new validate_pipeline tool checks pipeline YAML syntax and structure against Buildkite's official schema without uploading it or starting a build. It returns paths and error messages that an AI coding agent can use to correct invalid steps. The check does not cover environment variable interpolation, plugin configuration, dependency references or dynamically generated steps.
A second tool, compare_builds, compares a failed build with the most recent earlier successful build on the same branch, or with another selected build. It reports steps that have newly failed, recovered or remained broken, together with changes in runtime and retries. For up to three newly failing steps, it includes the end of the job log so an agent has some immediate diagnostic context.
"Log access alone does not debug a build."
Matt Mejia
The MCP release also adds Test Engine execution traces and slowest-execution queries. Another tool, create_pipeline_webhook, can add a missing GitHub webhook to an existing pipeline, avoiding the need to recreate it. Version 1.23.0 changed create_pipeline so that callers must specify create_webhook, which is a breaking change.
Buildkite reversed one earlier default after running evaluations, with failure summaries now again including jobs that never ran because making that behaviour optional led agents to issue extra tool calls. Remote MCP connections can now be pinned to one Buildkite organisation by adding it to the server URL. The option works with both toolset and read-only URLs.
Giving agents discrete validation, comparison and repair tools should reduce their reliance on parsing full logs and composing lower-level API calls. Permissions remain important because webhook repair and pipeline creation can modify CI configuration. InfoQ's coverage of GitHub agentic workflows describes a related security model based on isolated execution, restricted permissions and auditable actions.
Buildkite's GitHub Actions compatibility layer can now run its importer and generated jobs on Linux arm64 agents. Labels such as ubuntu-24.04-arm require an explicit queue mapping and do not fall back to x86-64 or emulation. The feature allows organisations with arm64 CI fleets to retain that architecture when bringing compatible Actions workflows to Buildkite.
Other compatibility fixes resolve environment values, named secrets, runtime variables and matrix values in service-container configuration. Buildkite has also exposed more strategy.* values to job and step expressions. The changed-file limit used by path filters has risen from 300 to 3,000, alongside a fix for push workflows where a branch moved after the original push.
Agent v4.1.0 adds cache save and restore durations and sizes to Buildkite telemetry. OpenTelemetry job spans now include the commit, pull request and build author. These fields add context for teams investigating slow jobs or retry patterns. Pinterest previously described using Honeycomb with Buildkite to separate agent waiting time from script execution and identify jobs behind build-time spikes.
The associated Elastic CI Stack v7 release brings Agent v4 to Linux and Windows instances on AWS. It removes Agent v3 support and retires or replaces some tracing and cancellation parameters. Buildkite advises users to review custom parameter files, deployment automation and values supplied through AgentEnvFileUrl before upgrading. Support for all Agent v3 releases ends on 3 September 2027.

articles.title: La generación Z no puede escapar de la IA. Tiene que aprender a dominarla
articles.text:
Casi ocho de cada diez estadounidenses pertenecientes a las generaciones Z y millennial afirman, según una encuesta de Operation HOPE y Beyond Finance que se ha hecho entre el 16 y el 18 de marzo de 2026 a 2.000 personas que nacieron entre 1981 y 2008, que suelen aplicar la estrategia de “gasto de supervivencia” (gasta ahora, ahorra más tarde) y que consideran que la creación de patrimonio es cada vez menos alcanzable (en concreto, un 71 %).
Conviene recordar que Beyond Finance es una empresa de consolidación de deudas. Sabiendo este dato, David Carroll Orr, un creador multidisciplinar con intereses en medios digitales, poesía, arquitectura y narrativa (así se define), argumenta que los jóvenes no actúan por apatía, sino que hacen una evaluación racional de un sistema que no les da dónde agarrarse, y que la inteligencia artificial está eliminando los puestos de entrada.
¿Se está cerrando el paso a la primera oferta de trabajo de forma definitiva?
Orr recurre a los datos del Burning Glass Institute sobre la contratación en puestos de nivel de entrada, que se ha ralentizado, y cita a responsables del sector de la inteligencia artificial que afirman que la mitad de los puestos de nivel júnior se automatizará.
No menciona nombres, pero la opinión más conocida al respecto es la de Dario Amodei, director ejecutivo de Anthropic, quien en una entrevista concedida ya avisó de que la IA podría eliminar la mitad de los empleos de oficina de nivel inicial en el plazo de entre uno y cinco años y de que el paro en Estados Unidos podría subir al 10-20 %.
El propio Burning Glass Institute había publicado en julio de 2025 el informe The Expertise Upheaval, donde identificó el impacto de la inteligencia artificial en la pérdida de los primeros peldaños de la escalera de la experiencia. Era aquel espacio en el que, según Orr, el becario redactaba memorandos, revisaba documentos o escribía código y aprendía equivocándose.
Para Orr, esos peldaños corresponden al Lore (en inglés, el ensayo y error de la experiencia humana), en contraposición al Ledger (libro mayor), el registro rígido de la administración. Los puestos de entrada son el Lore de una carrera profesional, mientras que la IA generativa sería una nueva evolución del Ledger.
“Lanzar proyectiles contra la fábrica automatizada no nos devolverá los puestos de trabajo en los peldaños más bajos”, escribe Orr. Basándose en sus investigaciones sobre los archivos de la frontera estadounidense del siglo XIX, propone una salida, la “persistencia forense”: aquellas comunidades aprendieron a moverse entre los registros de tierras y los juzgados para ganar margen dentro del sistema.
Así pues, tanto la educación universitaria como la formación en el trabajo tienen que dejar de preparar a los jóvenes para comportarse como “software humano” y enseñarles a dirigir y auditar las herramientas automatizadas. “Estamos utilizando tecnología del siglo XXI para imponer una perspectiva del siglo XIX sobre el valor humano”, remata.
Las nóminas revelan, con cifras reales, los efectos de los que habla la columna. El Stanford Digital Economy Lab trabaja con datos de nóminas que ADP pone a disposición de los investigadores. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar y Ruyu Chen publicaron el 12 de agosto de 2026 una actualización de su estudio que calcula que los trabajadores júnior (22-25 años) en los puestos más expuestos a la inteligencia artificial tienen un nivel de empleo un 19 % inferior al esperado frente a sus homólogos en áreas menos expuestas. Con datos de julio de 2025, esa brecha era del 15 %.
Según el estudio, el empleo de esos trabajadores jóvenes en los puestos más expuestos cayó casi un 11 % entre noviembre de 2022 (lanzamiento de ChatGPT) y junio de 2026, en contraste con un aumento de alrededor del 10 % en los empleos menos expuestos. En el caso de los trabajadores más experimentados, no se aprecia una brecha comparable. En el conjunto de datos, los cambios observados se deben principalmente a que se contrata a menos gente, y no a despidos.
Los autores no son catastrofistas: no ven un desplazamiento generalizado del empleo y advierten de que sus datos describen un patrón, pero no demuestran que la inteligencia artificial lo cause. Además, el nivel educativo desempeña un papel significativo, ya que la brecha se reduce al tenerlo en cuenta. Y hay un matiz que encaja con lo que defiende Orr: en los casos en los que la inteligencia artificial refuerza a los trabajadores en lugar de sustituirlos, el empleo se mantiene o crece.
En España, los datos sobre la reducción de oportunidades en puestos de entrada también son evidentes. Según el Barómetro de Talento Digital 2026 del Observatorio del Talento Digital de DIGITALENT Group, presentado el 24 de septiembre de 2026, el 51,7 % de las empresas prevé que se reduzcan las oportunidades para perfiles júnior debido a la inteligencia artificial.
El 39,6 % sitúa el pensamiento crítico y el criterio profesional como prioridad, y solo el 2,4 % señala la programación. Solo el 20,8 % de las organizaciones considera que su plantilla está bastante o muy preparada para trabajar con IA, y solo el 29,5 % cuenta con un marco formal y comunicado sobre el uso de la inteligencia artificial.
Estos datos revelan, en línea con lo que plantea Orr, una brecha significativa en la preparación de las empresas para trabajar con inteligencia artificial. Las personas sin experiencia, aquellas que entran en el mercado laboral para adquirir el Lore en la empresa, se encuentran en una situación de incertidumbre. Según datos de la patronal DigitalES de mayo de 2026, las ofertas de trabajo para programadores júnior se han reducido un 33 % en España en un año, en comparación con un aumento del 13 % en las de perfiles sénior.
La capacitación en inteligencia artificial en el trabajo ya está regulada
En Europa, existe un reglamento que establece que las empresas que utilicen sistemas de inteligencia artificial deben ocuparse de formar a sus trabajadores en el tema desde el 2 de febrero de 2025, fecha en la que empezó a aplicarse el artículo 4 del Reglamento de IA. Esta disposición ha sido modificada por el Reglamento (UE) 2026/1744 de 8 de julio de 2026, en vigor desde el 27 de julio de 2026. Ya no exige a las empresas que garanticen un nivel concreto de capacitación, sino simplemente que adopten medidas para apoyar la formación de su plantilla y de quienes usan los sistemas en su nombre.
Las empresas ya no están obligadas a garantizar el logro de objetivos de aprendizaje, pero la obligación de poner medios sigue existiendo. Si su empresa utiliza asistentes de inteligencia artificial en el trabajo, pregunte qué formación ofrece y solicítela. Ninguno de los estudios mencionados resuelve quién formará dentro de diez años a los perfiles sénior si se reduce el número de personas que aprenden el oficio en los puestos de nivel bajo.

articles.title: Estados Unidos destinó USD 4.400 millones a reabrir tres centrales nucleares para la IA
articles.text:
El Departamento de Energía de Estados Unidos otorgó préstamos por hasta USD 4.400 millones para reabrir tres centrales nucleares cerradas y usar esa energía en centros de datos de inteligencia artificial, según informó la agencia Associated Press.
Las plantas son Palisades, en Michigan; Crane Clean Energy Center, en el sitio de Three Mile Island, Pensilvania; y Duane Arnold, en Iowa. Juntas sumarán 2,25 gigavatios, suficiente para abastecer a unos 2 millones de hogares y comercios.
Ningún reactor comercial había vuelto a generar electricidad después de iniciar el proceso de desmantelamiento, aunque sí hubo reactores reactivados tras largas paradas sin llegar a esa etapa, según precisó Associated Press.
Microsoft y Google pagan la cuenta
Dos de las tres plantas ya tienen comprador. Constellation Energy, dueña de Crane, firmó un acuerdo a 20 años con Microsoft para venderle la energía una vez reactivado el reactor, con una inversión prevista de USD 1.600 millones y un préstamo del Departamento de Energía de USD 1.000 millones.
NextEra Energy, propietaria de Duane Arnold, selló un contrato a 25 años con Google para abastecer a sus centros de datos. El gobierno le otorgó a la compañía un préstamo de hasta USD 1.900 millones, según confirmó el Departamento de Energía en septiembre.
“Este es un ejemplo perfecto de que los centros de datos pagan su propia cuenta”, dijo John Ketchum, presidente y director ejecutivo de NextEra Energy, en referencia al contrato con Google. “Ninguno de los costos lo pagan los clientes residenciales de Iowa”, agregó.
El gobierno de Donald Trump impulsa la reactivación de plantas nucleares como parte de una estrategia para ampliar la oferta eléctrica frente a la demanda creciente de la inteligencia artificial y la industria manufacturera.
La reactivación de Duane Arnold generaría más de USD 9.000 millones en beneficios económicos para Iowa durante 25 años, según un estudio de la consultora Strategic Economic Research citado por NextEra Energy.
El proyecto crearía cerca de 1.500 empleos durante la construcción y mantendría más de 450 puestos permanentes una vez que el reactor vuelva a operar, de acuerdo con datos del Departamento de Energía.
Plantas que cerraron por costos, no por fallas
Palisades funcionó entre 1971 y 2022, cuando su entonces dueña, Entergy, decidió abandonar el mercado eléctrico mayorista. Holtec International compró la planta y empezó a desmantelarla antes de que el estado de Michigan impulsara su reapertura.
En agosto, Holtec comenzó a cargar combustible nuclear, uno de los últimos pasos antes de reactivar un reactor, pero pausó el proceso después de que un ensamblaje de combustible se inclinara de su posición vertical. La empresa debe determinar la causa antes de continuar.
Duane Arnold operó desde 1975 y cerró en agosto de 2020 tras sufrir daños por una tormenta, antes de lo previsto en su plan original de cierre. El reactor de Three Mile Island que ahora busca reactivar Constellation fue apagado en 2019 por pérdidas económicas.
Esa misma central fue escenario, en 1979, del peor accidente de la historia de la energía nuclear comercial en Estados Unidos, que destruyó uno de sus dos reactores. El otro, el que hoy se busca reactivar, siguió operando hasta su cierre por motivos de rentabilidad.
Apoyos y objeciones a los subsidios
Todd Allen, experto en ingeniería nuclear de la Universidad de Michigan, comparó el proceso con volver a poner en marcha un auto que estuvo parado varios años: hay que revisar que cada pieza funcione y que los permisos sigan vigentes. “Hay una demanda en el país de más energía”, dijo Allen. “Para cualquiera que quiera cero emisiones de carbono, la energía nuclear lo ofrece. Para el gobierno de Trump, que realmente quiere apostar por lo nuclear, esto también encaja con ese objetivo.”
Edwin Lyman, director de seguridad de energía nuclear de la organización Union of Concerned Scientists, cuestionó que el dinero público no se esté usando para reforzar la seguridad de plantas diseñadas entre 1970 y 1990, antes de que el cambio climático agravara los fenómenos extremos.
Jack Spencer, de la Fundación Heritage, dijo que no puede pensar en un peor uso del dinero de los contribuyentes, porque considera que estos proyectos tienen una demanda garantizada y no necesitan fondos federales. Jennifer Gordon, del Atlantic Council, defendió en cambio el financiamiento como una forma eficaz de conseguir energía necesaria.
La Asociación Mundial Nuclear señaló que la reactivación de reactores debería celebrarse, aunque consideró preferible evitar que las plantas cierren antes de tiempo. Países como Canadá, Armenia, Bélgica, Japón, India y Corea del Sur ya reactivaron o repotenciaron reactores tras paradas prolongadas.
Palisades podría convertirse en la primera planta del mundo en volver a generar energía después de haber iniciado formalmente su desmantelamiento, de acuerdo con la asociación. Sus contratos de compra de energía exigen que esté en servicio antes de marzo de 2027.
Las tres reactivaciones todavía dependen de aprobaciones de la Comisión Reguladora Nuclear de Estados Unidos, el organismo que autoriza el funcionamiento de los reactores. Ninguna de las plantas tiene, por ahora, una fecha de reinicio confirmada ante ese regulador.

articles.title: Super Mario 64's 30-year-old plaque mystery may finally be solved
articles.text:
The big picture: For more than 30 years, Super Mario 64 players have wondered what's written on a plaque on the fountain in the courtyard of Peach's castle. The text, which measures just 32 x 32 pixels, is far too small to decipher with the naked eye. Fans of the game came up with their own interpretations over the years but now, we might have a somewhat definitive answer as to what the text actually says.
The leading theory up to this point is that the text reads, "L is real 2401." This theory gained traction after it was published in an April Fool's Day feature in Nintendo Power magazine in 1998 and without a better answer, it stuck.
Nintendo originally planned to include Luigi in Super Mario 64 but he was cut from the game near the end of development. Fans held onto hope that he somehow might be a secret character and thus, the L is real 2401 legend stuck.
Armed with modern AI tools, enthusiast supermochi64 decided to take a deeper look at the plaque. Using Claude (Opus 5.5), he tackled the problem exactly like a texture artist would have made the plaque in the mid-90s. Then, a GPU was used to test millions of fonts, settings, and words and gave them a score.
The best guess using this technique is, "Eternal star / We hope so."
AI determined the text was written in Palatino Bold Italic, from Adobe's original 1990 version that shipped with Macs of the era. When "L is real" was plugged into the AI, it scored twice as badly as "Eternal star" in terms of being a likely match.
The truth is, we may never know for certain what was originally written on the plaque. The most definitive answer would be to track down the artist responsible for the graphic, but that could be like finding a needle in a haystack considering it was made over three decades ago. What's more, Nintendo often prefers to let little mysteries like these persist.

articles.title: Espoo's Coherence Quantum raises €2.78 million to build infrastructure for larger quantum computers | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Coherence Quantum, an Espoo-based quantum hardware company developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform for future quantum computers, has raised €2.78 million in Seed funding to develop a new approach to the cryogenic infrastructure surrounding solid-state quantum processors.
The round was led by Helsinki-based early-stage investor Lifeline Ventures, with participation from technology entrepreneur Mårten Mickos.
Petteri Koponen of Lifeline Ventures said, “The quantum industry has proved that increasingly capable processors can be built. The next challenge is building the infrastructure that allows them to scale. Coherence Quantum is going after a fundamental part of that problem.
“They have an exceptional technical team with a clear view of where the industry is heading and the ambition to build far more than a single component. If quantum computers are going to scale, the architecture around the qubits has to scale with them, and we’re backing them to become a key part of how larger quantum computers are built.”
Coherence Quantum was founded in 2026 by Aashish Sah (CEO), Suman Kundu (CTO), and Erkki Soininen (CPO), and originated from research at Aalto University’s Quantum Computing and Devices group. The company is also supported by founding advisor Mikko Möttönen, a professor of quantum technology at Aalto University.
Sah is a quantum physicist specialising in superconducting qubits and their interaction with the electromagnetic environment. Kundu is an experimental quantum physicist who played a key role in building and setting up Aalto University’s 20-qubit Q20 quantum computer. Soininen holds a PhD in Physics and previously held a product leadership role at the cryogenics company Bluefors.
Coherence Quantum is developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform for solid-state quantum computers, including superconducting and spin-qubit systems. 
According to the company, its goal is to help quantum systems scale, enabling more qubits while maintaining the low-noise, high-coherence environment needed for reliable operation.
But it says that scaling quantum computers by adding more qubits creates another scaling problem: everything needed to control them must scale as well. “As quantum processors grow, more control and readout signals need to reach the quantum processing unit (QPU). Conventional approaches require more wiring and signal-conditioning hardware inside a system with very limited space and cooling power. At the same time, the qubit environment has to remain protected from thermal noise and other disturbances that can affect performance,” the Finnish startup explained.
Coherence Quantum claims to be developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform to address this scaling challenge. It notes that its first technologies focus on cryogenic signal conditioning, helping protect the environment around the qubit. From there, the company is developing higher-density signal interfaces and working towards bringing more control functionality inside the cryostat and closer to the quantum processing unit.
Sah said, “Quantum computers won’t scale by adding qubits alone. The infrastructure around them has to scale too. We’re starting with signal conditioning and building towards higher-density interfaces and, ultimately, more integrated cryogenic control. Our aim is to give quantum-computer builders an architecture that can support larger systems without wiring, cooling requirements, and complexity growing at the same rate.”
The company is building dedicated R&D, testing and manufacturing capabilities in Espoo, Finland, close to Aalto University and Finland’s growing quantum technology ecosystem. It plans to use the fresh capital to establish its lab in Espoo, build its first product prototypes and manufacturing process, continue R&D, and grow the team.
Starting with cryogenic signal-conditioning technologies, Coherence Quantum is working towards higher-density interfaces and increasingly integrated control inside the fridge. Its long-term ambition is to help establish a standardised blueprint for the cryogenic signalling and control stack, bringing its own technologies together with complementary technologies from across the quantum ecosystem.

articles.title: Falha na Revolut afeta pagamentos, saques e transferências de clientes
articles.text:
Clientes da Revolut enfrentam dificuldades para acessar suas contas nesta terça-feira (20). A falha afeta pagamentos com cartão, transferências, saques e outros serviços do banco digital.
A empresa afirmou que o dinheiro e os dados dos usuários estão seguros. A interrupção coincidiu com problemas registrados pelo Google Cloud no Reino Unido, mas não há confirmação de que os dois incidentes estejam relacionados.
O que parou de funcionar no aplicativo
Ao tentar abrir o aplicativo, usuários receberam mensagens de erro e orientações para tentar novamente mais tarde. Sem conseguir entrar nas contas, alguns ficaram impedidos de movimentar o próprio dinheiro.
Pouco depois das 8h, no horário de verão britânico, o Downdetector já havia registrado mais de 1.500 relatos de problemas com os serviços da Revolut.
A empresa informou que parte de suas operações estava indisponível. A falha também atingiu funções que vão além das movimentações financeiras:
- Cadastro de novos clientes;
- Serviços relacionados a criptomoedas;
- Atendimento ao cliente.
Nas redes sociais, usuários reclamaram da dificuldade para realizar operações e buscar ajuda. Em comunicado, a Revolut confirmou a ocorrência e declarou: “Podemos confirmar que o dinheiro e os dados de todos os nossos clientes estão seguros”.
A empresa pediu desculpas pelos transtornos e afirmou que trabalhava para corrigir a falha desde que a identificou naquela manhã.
Problemas no Google Cloud levantam suspeitas
A Revolut não informou a causa da interrupção nem esclareceu se clientes de todo o mundo foram afetados, mas na página que mostra o status do sistema, clientes no Brasil também foram afetados.
Na mesma manhã, o Google Cloud relatou problemas em vários serviços na região europe-west2, no Reino Unido. Segundo a empresa, havia “um aumento de erros e falhas intermitentes de rede”.
A Revolut utiliza a infraestrutura do Google Cloud para operar seus serviços, por meio de uma parceria estratégica. Essa ligação levanta a possibilidade de uma relação entre os incidentes, mas não comprova que os problemas na nuvem tenham provocado a queda do aplicativo.
Outros bancos britânicos também apareceram nos relatos de dificuldades. Clientes do Lloyds Bank e do Bank of Scotland, ambos pertencentes ao Lloyds Banking Group, enfrentaram problemas com alguns serviços on-line.
Um porta-voz do Lloyds afirmou que o aplicativo do banco funcionava normalmente, embora alguns clientes tivessem dificuldades com determinados serviços digitais. A instituição disse estar ciente de problemas semelhantes em outras organizações e que monitorava a situação.
Revolut tem mais de 80 milhões de clientes
A Revolut informa em seu site que possui mais de 80 milhões de clientes em todo o mundo. A empresa oferece serviços financeiros principalmente por meio de seu aplicativo e concorre com bancos tradicionais.
Até o momento descrito nas informações divulgadas, a empresa não havia esclarecido a causa da falha nem delimitado seu alcance geográfico. Também não havia previsão confirmada para a normalização de todos os serviços.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: 970,000 Medi-Cal Members Affected by Paradigm Healthcare Data Breach
articles.text:
Paradigm Healthcare Services has told the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) that a data breach discovered last year affected more than 970,000 people.
San Francisco-based Paradigm processes billing for Medi-Cal, California’s Medicaid program, under a data use agreement with the California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS). It also maintains Medi-Cal member identification numbers on the department’s behalf.
The company says it became aware of unauthorized access to its local network on October 13, 2025. “On August 18, 2026, we determined that certain files containing select individuals’ protected health information may have been accessed by an unauthorized party between October 8, 2025, and October 15, 2025,” Paradigm said.
The compromised files contained names, dates of birth, gender, and Medi-Cal member identification numbers. Paradigm says its online service documentation and billing platform, Student Health Network (SHN), was not impacted.
Paradigm’s notification letters are dated September 14, 2026, roughly 11 months after the intrusion was detected. “We have no evidence that any of your information has been used to commit fraud or identity theft as a result of this incident,” the company said.
The notice doesn’t name the threat actor, explain how the attackers gained access, or say whether data was exfiltrated. Paradigm says it took certain systems offline, notified law enforcement, and brought in outside incident response experts.
No known cybercrime group appears to have taken credit for an attack on Paradigm.
Tarter Krinsky & Drogin and Ridgeway Pharmacy data breaches
The HHS healthcare data breach tracker has been updated to show that a significant number of individuals were affected by separate incidents disclosed recently by the law firm Tarter Krinsky & Drogin (TKD) and Ridgeway Pharmacy Ltd.
TKD, which serves healthcare providers, started notifying individuals in early September that it had detected suspicious activity on its network in September 2025.
The company completed its investigation one year later and determined that attackers accessed certain servers between July 9 and September 9, 2025.
TKD told the HHS that the incident affected more than 196,000 individuals.
Ridgeway Pharmacy, which started sending out data breach notices on September 21, discovered unauthorized access to personal information on August 21, 2026.
The company discovered that its website was hacked and the attacker may have gained access to information such as name, address, date of birth, health and insurance information, prescription information, and payment card information.
Ridgeway Pharmacy informed the HHS that more than 258,000 individuals are affected.
Related: Healthcare data breaches

articles.title: 'AI is no longer just supporting the business — it has become the business model': IBM VP tells us how your business can balance AI excitement with realism as governance becomes more important than ever
articles.text:
'AI is no longer just supporting the business — it has become the business model': IBM VP tells us how your business can balance AI excitement with realism as governance becomes more important than ever
A lot needs to be done to scale AI, IBM warns
As excitement around AI continues to build among businesses of all sizes, many leading voices are urging caution for those who might scale too quickly.
At its recent Think EMEA event in London, IBM revealed research which claimed efforts to stay aware of potential risks and challenges posed by AI deployment and scaling are falling somewhat short of expectations.
So what can companies do in order to balance the hype and excitement around what AI can offer, with the need for sensible and thorough governance.
AI as the enabler
"What we are seeing is that if you don't provide an answer to security, to accountability, to responsibility, it is going to be very hard to scale AI in the corporate environment - particularly when we're talking about highly regulated industries - so for us, it's more of an enabler, than something that is going to slow down the adoption,” Ana Paula Assis, Senior Vice President and Chair for IBM EMEA and APAC told us in response to that very question during a media Q&A at the event.
“The question here is really, how do you balance the speed of innovation with the implementation of governance?”
IBM recently released research on the current state of AI and governance, finding that 80% of the companies surveyed claimed that an AI incident had been escalated to board level. However only 40% of those had then been able to use the incident to secure new investment in governance, or cement a new policy.
“I think the reason for that is because it's very hard to balance that innovation with the application of tools, processes, methodologies, to ensure that you are deploying AI at scale in a safe way,” Assis continued.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
IBM is reportedly well placed to discuss such growth and progress with AI, with the company’s earlier keynote at Think EMEA claiming it had seen savings of around $5.5 billion in terms of improved productivity and efficiency utilizing AI to improve core processes - money that it was able to redirect to areas including R&D and innovation.
“But we are seeing this as an enabler, and as a key component of the architecture for agentic AI going forward, because these companies have tremendous responsibility - they need to ensure that they have trust from their clients, and they will only be able to do that if they have AI that they can observe and that they can govern.”
“AI is no longer just supporting the business,” Assis said. “It has become the business model. The organizations pulling ahead are not just adding AI, but rethinking how systems, decisions and processes work together with AI.”

He has worked as a B2B and B2C tech journalist for over a decade, including at one of the UK's leading national newspapers and fellow Future title ITProPortal. articles.title: Galaxy Buds 4 têm promoção histórica com queda de 50% de desconto • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy Buds 4 têm promoção histórica com queda de 50% de desconto
Galaxy Buds 4 têm ANC e áudio Hi-Fi de 24 bits; fones da Samsung saem pela metade do preço em oferta histórica no Pix com cupom do Mercado Livre, que vai acabar logo
Os Galaxy Buds 4 estão em promoção por R$ 804 no Pix com cupom OFFSOHJ no Mercado Livre. Os fones de ouvido sem fio da Samsung, com áudio Hi-Fi de 24 bits e ANC, alcançam o menor preço histórico com desconto de 50% sobre o original de R$ 1.599.
Mas seja rápido: este cupom é válido apenas nesta segunda-feira (19) e pode esgotar a qualquer momento.
Os Galaxy Buds 4 estão entre os melhores fones wireless da Samsung. Eles possuem suporte a áudio Hi-Fi (alta fidelidade) de 24 bits, que oferece experiência sonora com grande foco nos detalhes, e o cancelamento de ruído ativo (ANC) filtra quase todos os sons externos, mas não todos, por questões de segurança.
Assistentes de Inteligência Artificial (IA), como o Bixby da Samsung, Google Gemini e Perplexity, oferecem funções por comandos por voz para acionar menus e realizar pesquisas. O Galaxy AI conta com um tradutor automático de conversas, que só funciona quando os fones são pareados a gadgets da linha Galaxy.
Outros recursos incluem o Voice Pickup Unit, que trabalha para tornar as chamadas de voz mais nítidas, e o equalizador adaptativo, que ajusta as frequências sonoras com base no formato do canal auditivo do usuário, de modo a personalizar a experiência sonora.
Os Galaxy Buds 4 suportam Bluetooth 6.1, que oferece menor latência em jogos e/ou transmissões em tempo real, enquanto a função Auto Switch torna mais simples parear o wearable com mais de um dispositivo, ao permitir navegar entre gadgets conectados facilmente.
As baterias de 45 mAh dos fones resistem até 5 horas de reprodução com o ANC ligado e 6 horas com o recurso desativado. A bateria de 515 mAh do estojo de transporte garante ao kit uma autonomia total de até 30 horas de uso, segundo a fabricante.
Os Galaxy Buds 4 (R$ 804 no Pix com cupom OFFSOHJ) possuem certificação IP54, que adiciona aos fones wireless da Samsung resistência moderada contra poeira, suor e respingos d’água.

articles.title: Tenstorrent hits $6.2B valuation to scale open-weight AI chips | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation. The round comes five months after the 10-year-old Nvidia challenger reportedly received acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations of as much as $5 billion.
The fresh round, which more than doubled Tenstorrent’s valuation from the $2.6 billion it fetched in late 2024, was led by Trace Capital, a new firm launched by Quiet Capital co-founder Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X. Other backers included Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price.
Jim Keller, a prominent microprocessor engineer and Tenstorrent CEO, told Bloomberg that the company decided to remain independent and raise more capital after it showed that its Galaxy servers could run DeepSeek models. The new capital will go toward scaling chips tailored for serving open-weight AI models and video generation.
Tenstorrent is part of a wave of AI hardware startups trying to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance. Among them is Etched, an AI chip maker that was fielding investment offers at valuations of $40 billion or more, TechCrunch reported earlier this month.

articles.title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
articles.text:
Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift. For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced, and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro.
But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.
That’s right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.
An off-the-shelf VR pad keeps things semi-comfortable.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
An off-the-shelf VR pad keeps things semi-comfortable.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
The DIY VR landscape
I stumbled into this space about a year ago. I primarily use VR for sim racing to practice driving the world’s greatest cars on the world’s greatest tracks while at home in my pajamas. At that time, I was using an HP Reverb G2, a virtual reality headset built around the Windows Mixed Reality (WMR) standard.
As part of its own cooling on VR tech, Microsoft was nixing support for WMR, and I feared that I might need a new headset. (I need not have worried. Many talented folks have kept WMR headsets alive through third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam.)
That’s when I found YouTuber CNCDan’s video on building a VR headset for $150. The price was certainly compelling, and as someone with a particular set of electronics skills developed over years of disassembling and repairing pinball machines, I thought it sounded kind of fun.
That opened the door to a rich landscape of DIY VR development, complete with software tools and hardware advice on how to get started.
The best starting place is Relativty VR. This project, started in the late 2010s by Jonas Ceccon, Gabriel Combe, and Maxime Coutté, includes all the code, configurations, and guidance you’ll need to get started.
But there are others, like OpenVR Arduino HMD, Project North Star, and the full-body tracking SlimeVR. There are plenty of ways to piece together your headset. As my first attempt, I kept it simple, sticking with the Relativty software and relying on the 3D headset models provided by CNCDan as part of his build. First step: the hardware.
An Arduino, an IMU, and a set of tiny displays are all you really need.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
An Arduino, an IMU, and a set of tiny displays are all you really need.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Bill of materials
A DIY VR headset is a mixture of hardware and software, and while you can have the software ready to go in just a few clicks, chances are it’s going to take some time to get the hardware you need. That’s doubly true given the uncertainty in global shipping.
The biggest and potentially most important piece of hardware is a 3D printer. Although I’ve seen some compelling DIY VR headsets made out of repurposed VR phone holders—Google Cardboard among others—most projects fit in shells that come out of a 3D printer. If you don’t have access to one, services like Formlabs can handle it via mail order, but given the amount of tinkering here, it’s certainly advantageous to print at home.
Regardless, you need to buy quite a few things. Let’s start with the most expensive: displays. You might think a pair of panels small enough and good enough for a VR headset would be difficult to find and prohibitively expensive, and you can certainly spend a lot here, but the standard option is a set of 2.9-inch LCDs, which can be purchased with the necessary controller for about $125.
Each has a 1440×1440 resolution. They offer 150 nits of brightness and a contrast ratio of 600:1. Not exactly world-class specs, but plenty enough for this application, and though they’re pretty ugly to view from odd angles, since you’re literally going to be sticking them a few inches from your eyeballs, that’s not really an issue.
Cheap plastic lenses keep everything in focus.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Cheap plastic lenses keep everything in focus.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
The next missing piece is a sensor module containing an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. This device detects the headset’s position. You’ll want a GY-91, a sensor board that has an onboard accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and barometer. You can find one for around $5, but buyer beware for reasons I’ll explain shortly.
Next is the circuitry that ties it all together. Some DIY VR projects call upon custom PCBs riddled with components. The Relativty project just relies on an Arduino Pro Micro, which can be bought at any number of electronics retailers for $5 or less.
You’ll also need a pair of 34 mm-diameter lenses to focus those tiny displays, some miscellaneous hardware to connect the pieces, and a nylon strap to hold the thing to your head. Oh, and a pad from an HTC Vive, because nobody wants the sharp edges of layered plastic extruded from a 3D printer rubbing against their face.
My total spend for all that came to just under $180.
Breadboarding isn’t strictly necessary, but it helps with early testing.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Breadboarding isn’t strictly necessary, but it helps with early testing.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Breadboard time
Before you break out the soldering iron and fire up your 3D printer, I suggest you start with a breadboard and some patch wires. Wiring on this project is on the simple side, but trust me when I say it will be much easier to figure out why your firmware isn’t flashing with a few components on your workbench than when they’re all crammed inside a headset.
I won’t include all the wiring details here, as it’s best to follow the guide in the GitHub above, but in general, you need to connect your IMU to your Arduino to provide both power and data.
You can also optionally connect the display controller to the Arduino for power, as suggested in the video above. That’s what I did for my testing, but be advised, this isn’t necessarily a good idea given the power requirements of the displays vs. the capabilities of the Arduino. You’re better off running a separate USB cable to the display or a USB splitter inside the headset.
Once you’ve wired everything and powered it on successfully, you’re ready to start with the software.
A legit Arduino and a bogus IMU.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
A legit Arduino and a bogus IMU.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Firmware fun
Flashing the firmware to the Arduino should be the easy part, but this is when things started falling apart for me. In theory, you install the Arduino IDE on your desktop, download the FastIMU project, connect your Arduino via USB, and then click compile. Easy.
Mine just kept failing. I got a basic error message, e:-1, again and again. After a bit of research and tinkering, I finally figured it out, and the news wasn’t good.
Although I ordered and paid for a GY-91 with an onboard 9250 IMU, and that’s what it identified as, in actuality, it was a basic, cheaper 6500 IMU, one that lacks the magnetometer.
As I learned (the hard way), this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience. Many shady electronics companies are happy to sell you the wrong component for the wrong price. The two devices are compatible and operate much the same way, but without the magnetometer, tracking performance drops substantially.
Once I updated the code to reference the 6500 I had and not the 9250 I thought I had, everything flashed beautifully, and I was instantly up and running. I calibrated my IMU through the Arduino IDE, and I was ready for final assembly.
Be extremely careful in placing your displays.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Be extremely careful in placing your displays.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Putting it all together
You can find various shells online for custom VR headsets, many of which are designed to accommodate this specific set of boards used in Relativty. I decided to use CNCDan’s files, as it looked like a clean and clever design, even allowing for adjustment of the distance between displays, known as interpupillary distance, or IPD.
That makes for a complicated assembly process, requiring numerous printed parts, a handful of threaded receivers melted therein, plus rods and screws to hold it together. You’ll also need a pair of eye boxes, each one holding a lens on one side and the display on the other.
This was where I made a painful mistake. The design’s eye boxes contain small clips, and the instructions suggest you just pop the displays in there.
This is not what you should do. The exposed LCDs are extremely fragile, and by clipping them in, I managed to break both. The small amount of pressure required was enough to shatter them, and the damage was invisible until I turned them on.
Given that, I highly recommend modifying those boxes, either by printing them without the clips or by breaking them off after the print is complete. I used a few strips of thin painter’s tape to hold mine in place.
A little tape held things secure.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
A little tape held things secure.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Getting in the game
With all the wires jammed into place, I screwed the headset together, stuck on the face pad, threaded on the head strap, and proceeded to spend about five minutes trying to get a comfortable fit. I never quite succeeded.
I booted into SteamVR’s living lounge space and was immediately discombobulated. For one thing, I was staring straight at the floor. For another, turning my head just sent the view spinning in different directions in a way that quickly threatened nausea.
I had forgotten to recalibrate the headset after mounting all the components, and my cut-rate IMU was now oriented differently than it had been when it was on my workbench.
After recalibrating and a little more firmware fiddling, I got back into SteamVR’s setup room and could tell I still had a problem. Holding my head perfectly still, I could see the perspective slowly spinning.
Additionally, the IMU axes seemed slightly crossed, so the perspective change didn’t quite match my head movement. I verified the IMU was mounted correctly in the case and recalibrated a few times with no improvement.
You can print any manner of shells for your headset.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
You can print any manner of shells for your headset.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
I soldiered on, booting into iRacing, my favorite SteamVR-compatible racing sim. Before I was even out of the pits, my perspective was drifting. I mapped the recenter view command to a button on my steering wheel, and had to reach for it quite often.
Still, the image quality was not nearly as bad as I expected. Those cheap plastic lenses work surprisingly well, and though I could make out the pixels on the displays (the dreaded “screen door” effect of VR), it didn’t bother me. Brightness and contrast were more than adequate, and the refresh rate of 60 Hz was enough for casual practice.
But sensor drift and headset comfort were real issues. Without a proper cable-routing solution, the headset kept tugging to one side, and despite the padding, it was smashing my nose and cheeks.
I’ve done hourslong endurance races in multiple mass-market VR headsets. After 15 minutes in this one, I was ready to quit.
Projects like this are never really done.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Projects like this are never really done.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Final thoughts and future upgrades
My total outlay for this project was $239.93. But that includes the extra $62 I had to spend on a second set of displays. Avoid that expensive gaffe, and you’re looking at around $180 in components.
That makes it roughly half the cost of a Meta Quest 3S, one of the cheapest headsets on the market right now. That’s a substantial savings, but I’d certainly recommend that most people pay the extra. The tracking issues in my headset are maddening, the image quality is middling at best, and this is far and away the least comfortable headset I’ve ever worn.
All that can be fixed, though. Some projects use a MinIMU-9 IMU, which looks miles more accurate and is less likely to be faked, but it’s also substantially more expensive at $35. You can also step up to higher-quality LCDs or even tiny OLED panels that come with all the color and contrast you could ever want. There are options for onboard battery packs, wireless adapters, and of course you can spend as much time as you like designing an ultra-comfortable housing for it all.
But even if you ignore the time commitment, once you start adding those upgrades, you’re not far from the cost of that Quest, a far-from-perfect headset that still works effortlessly and comfortably out of the box.
As always with these projects, it depends on what you want. If you just want a cheap, easy, reliable headset for your next-gen immersive gaming fix, this probably isn’t it.
If, however, you want a fun project that will help you appreciate the industrial design required to make a good-looking and comfortable wearable device, this could be it. I learned a lot and, despite the frustrations, I’m glad I embarked on this journey.
That said, while I’ll keep tinkering and likely throw a few more upgrades at this thing, I can’t see it replacing my other headset for regular racing duties, deprecated though it may be.

articles.title: Arm says its AGI CPU delivers nearly 2X the performance per rack of AMD EPYC 9755 in new agentic AI CPU tests
articles.text:
Arm claims AGI CPU delivers double the performance per rack of AMD EPYC 9755 in independent analysis — new CPU evaluation methodology developed by Arm evaluates agentic AI performance across seven workloads
AGI CPU delivers a 20% average per-chip performance lead
Arm announced last week that its AGI CPU, the company's data center CPU for agentic AI workloads, delivers twice the performance per rack as AMD EPYC 9755, calculated from chip performance and server-power assumptions measured across seven workloads. The claim stems from modeled rack results from tests aligned with Arm’s new CPU evaluation methodology, developed with support from Fujitsu, Meta, and OpenAI.
The results — verified in an Arm-commissioned independent analysis by Signal65 — do not establish the AGI CPU as the overall leader for agentic AI, as they apply to the selected processors, workloads, and configuration. They also use the specific Arm-developed evaluation methodology that Arm says should be the new standard for assessing performance. However, other chipmakers like AMD and Intel make performance claims based on different benchmarks. So, how is Agentic AI evolving CPU performance benchmarks, what does Arm propose to measure, and how do the different approaches compare?
Arm’s new CPU evaluation methodology
Agentic AI is changing the role of CPUs in modern AI data centers, requiring them to handle complex, multi-step workflows. Beyond inference, which the accelerator handles, AI agents execute tools, retrieve data, and maintain state within isolated environments, acting like virtual users. The CPU handles these critical surrounding workloads, from running those tools and serving database or API requests to preparing data and coordinating work for accelerators.
As these workloads scale rapidly with agentic capabilities, it becomes increasingly important to gauge CPU performance not just by how many agents can run concurrently, but also by how much useful work gets done. Arm argues that CPU performance is increasingly defined by how much useful work a system can sustain while staying responsive. Supporting more agents simultaneously offers limited benefit if their executions throttle or accelerators have to sit idle waiting for the CPU. Power, cooling, and physical space also limit how much hardware operators can deploy, extending the performance question to the rack.
Arm’s proposed methodology for evaluating CPU performance, developed with support from Fujitsu, Meta, and OpenAI, centers on representative agent workloads, repeatable CPU measurements, and validation against end-to-end task outcomes. In practical terms, the methodology identifies the tools and services an agent uses, measures their CPU performance under controlled conditions, and checks whether improvements help the agent complete its task. For example, a database test can establish how quickly a system handles transactions. An end-to-end evaluation would then examine whether faster database access actually improves the workflow that depends on it.
Executing the second aspect of the methodology, making these comparisons repeatable, presents another challenge, as an agent might choose different commands or take a different route through a task each time it runs. Model inference and remote services also introduce delays. Arm proposes replaying recorded agent actions to separate CPU performance from this variability, allowing different systems to execute a consistent sequence of work. Its whitepaper sets out a framework for selecting and interpreting these measurements, leaving the industry to develop an agreed benchmark suite and scoring approach.
To evaluate the CPU work described in its framework, Arm ran seven workloads — spanning tooling, agentic workflows, and reasoning/planning, plus Sandbench, which measures sandbox-creation overhead for agent execution — on its AGI CPU and AMD’s EPYC 9755. The tests combine established server applications with benchmarks focused on agent workflows.
| Workloads and breakdowns |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Workload | What it represents | Metric | 
| MySQL | Transactional database behind agent tools | Transactions per second | 
| NGINX | Web and API request handling | Requests per second | 
| Milvus | Vector search for retrieval | Queries per second | 
| Terminal-Bench 2 | 72 agent task types in sandboxed containers, 128 copies at once | Task completion time | 
| SWE-bench replay | Software-engineering agent workflow, 259 tasks | Tasks per minute | 
| fastText | CPU word-representation training | Words per second | 
| vLLM CPU overhead | CPU serving overhead with model compute bypassed | Requests per second | 
The vLLM result measures the CPU work around model execution, not GPU inference throughput. Similarly, the report’s “reasoning/planning” category groups supporting CPU workloads and does not assess how intelligently a model reasons.
ARM AGI CPU vs AMD EPYC 9755
For the tests, Arm used two AGI CPU configurations because of hardware availability: a 128-core chip at 2.8 GHz with DDR5-7200 for Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-bench replay, and a 136-core chip at 3.2 GHz with DDR5-8000 for the other five workloads. The AMD comparison used one socket of the 128-core EPYC 9755 with DDR5-6400. Both platforms ran the same benchmark scripts but used different software environments. Arm used custom Linux 7.1.3 builds, with Ubuntu 24.04 for most tests and Ubuntu 26.04 for SWE-bench, while AMD’s main recorded configuration used Ubuntu 24.04 and Linux 6.8, with settings varying by test.
At the chip level, Arm’s AGI CPU won the majority of comparisons when compared to its AMD counterpart in five of the seven tests. With the EPYC 9755 as the baseline, Arm led by 9% on Terminal-Bench, 13% on SWE-bench, and 97% on fastText, but lagged by 12% and 5% in MySQL and Milvus throughput, respectively. On average, the AGI CPU led by 20% (1.20x) per-chip advantage, calculated across the seven normalized performance ratios.
| Results |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Workload | Measured per-chip performance vs EPYC 9755 | Modeled per-rack performance vs EPYC 9755 | 
| MySQL | 0.88x | 1.43x | 
| NGINX | 1.20x | 1.95x | 
| Terminal-Bench 2 | 1.09x | 1.93x | 
| SWE-bench replay | 1.13x | 2.00x | 
| Milvus | 0.95x | 1.54x | 
| vLLM CPU overhead | 1.16x | 1.88x | 
| fastText | 1.97x | 3.19x | 
| Arithmetic average | 1.20x | 1.99x | 
At the rack level, Arm’s modeled performance averages 1.99x AMD’s, with a lead in all seven workloads. The model uses rated server-power estimates of 950 W for the 128-core Arm configuration, 1,050 W for the 136-core version, and 1,700 W for AMD, including memory and other system components. After reserving about 8% of a 24 kW rack budget for networking and power distribution, this leaves room for 23 or 21 Arm servers versus 13 AMD servers.
For SWE-bench, the 2.00x per rack result was obtained by multiplying the roughly 1.13x chip result by 23/13. The larger gain comes from fitting more servers into the same power budget. Furthermore, these projections use modeled whole-server power, not throughput measurements from two fully populated racks.
Arm’s model also gives the AMD servers about twice as much RAM: roughly 2 TB against 1 TB for Arm. It allocates 4 GB per hardware thread, with each AMD core supporting two threads while each Arm core supports one. This puts the memory-power allowance at 336 W for AMD and 192 W for Arm. Signal65 also calculated what happens when memory is allocated per physical core. In this setup, AMD’s memory and power allowance falls, and Arm’s average modeled rack advantage drops from 1.99x to approximately 1.81x. The usefulness of the 2 TB AMD configuration depends on how much memory the workloads actually need, as SMT does not inherently require twice the memory.
To verify the findings, Signal65 remotely observed Arm’s test runs and examined the original logs, result files, scripts, and configuration records. A separate review team rebuilt the calculations with its own code and reproduced all seven results within 0.5%. However, Signal65 did not run a separate hardware rerun in its own lab. In addition, Signal65 could independently confirm BIOS and memory settings for only the EPYC 9965 system. These settings were unavailable for independent verification on the Arm and EPYC 9755 systems. Along with the software differences, these gaps slightly affect the certainty with which the results can be attributed to the processors themselves.
Arm’s approach vs AMD and Nvidia
While Arm believes its methodology should be the standard, it does not hold a monopoly on how the industry evaluates agentic CPU performance. For example, AMD promotes agents per watt, dollar, and rack. Footnotes on its EPYC 9006 page identify available CPU threads as a proxy for agent capacity, with actual throughput depending on the workload and system. Its separate workload analysis models a 100 kW rack and claims 2.37× performance for EPYC 9965 over Nvidia's Vera, using a geometric mean across six infrastructure workloads.
Nvidia, on the other hand, emphasizes Vera’s single-thread performance and memory bandwidth, and says a 256-CPU rack supports more than 22,500 concurrent CPU environments. These numbers describe different things and do not directly imply any specific advantage. Methodologies vary across manufacturers by workload, power assumptions, and aggregation methods, making direct CPU comparisons complex. The current comparison is against AMD's fifth-generation “Turin” processor with 128 cores. The company launched its latest sixth-generation EPYC 9006 “Venice” family this year, dedicated to agentic AI.
Etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in big tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

articles.title: Manitoba says tax on data centres, crypto miners will be used to lower utility rates |
articles.text:
Manitoba plans to use money from a levy on AI data centres and cryptocurrency mining to lower utility rates for residential customers.
The news: Last Thursday, provincial Finance Minister Adrien Sala said revenue from Manitoba’s tax on cryptocurrency mining and AI data centres would be used to lower Manitoba Hydro rates for residential ratepayers. The levy, passed into law last summer, includes 100 percent markups on electricity used by crypto operations and data centres over 5 megawatts. Sala said his government predicts the levy could draw as much as $20 million in revenue, offsetting rates by $50 per year for Manitoba households. The province will begin to lower Manitoba Hydro bills early next year.
From the source: “Our government is focused on making life more affordable for Manitobans, and that includes keeping hydro rates as low as possible for families,” said Sala in a statement. “Large cryptocurrency operations and AI data centres use significant amounts of electricity, and they should contribute fairly to the system we all rely on.”
The context: Manitoba’s levy came into effect last June, when Manitoba passed a law requiring its provincial utility, Manitoba Hydro, to create distinct customer classes for crypto and data centre customers and other large electricity consumers. Under those classifications, the utility effectively doubles the standard rates cryptocurrency and AI operators pay for the Manitoba Hydro electricity they use.
While the levy takes aim at large-scale AI data centres, Manitoba is not currently home to data centres big enough to pass the threshold for the tax to take effect. The province is home to only one proposed data centre operation that would qualify under the legislation: a 5.5 megawatt project in development near Rosser, Man. That means that presently, revenue will be almost entirely generated via the cryptocurrency industry, which argued earlier this year that the impacts of the legislation would effectively close down Manitoba’s crypto sector. 
RELATED: Manitoba premier says air force base expansion only possible thanks to data centre rejection
Final thought: While much of Canada’s prairie provinces have been actively courting the AI data centre boom, Manitoba has been an outlier. The province has been proactive in disincentivizing the development of large-scale projects within its jurisdiction through restrictive regulations and steep fees. Instead, Manitoba has focused on investing in public infrastructure, renewable energy, and cost-of-living issues. The decision to direct this revenue toward Manitobans’ pocketbooks continues that trend.
