articles.title: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
articles.text:
These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
Beef is a climate burden. Can “blended meat” finally succeed in getting us to cut back?
In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge set up a six-foot folding table in the cafeteria of Cane Bay High School in Summerville, South Carolina, to conduct a taste test. When the first rush of about 150 hungry students hit, he was waiting with slow cookers filled with steaming marinara sauce and meatballs.
Kids love a taste test, but they’re also discerning, and Dodge wasn’t sure what they would make of his product, a blend featuring both meat and mushrooms. As students swarmed the table and tapped out their opinions on an iPad or scanned a QR code to use their phones, Dodge asked those who lingered to guess what kind of vegetable might have been mixed into the meat. Few of them could—the meatballs had tasted like moist, flavorful beef.
The school enrolls a few thousand students, and Dodge estimates that the majority of them came by. In the end, the survey showed that 92% of those who tried the meatballs wanted them on the menu; they easily cleared the bar to be added for the 2026–2027 school year. Comments described their flavor as “bussin’.”
Through his consulting company, K–12 Food Solutions, Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The proprietary blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the most intractable challenges of the climate crisis, at least on the individual level: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef.
Livestock production accounts for somewhere between 10% and 20% of all greenhouse-gas emissions related to human activity, and nearly two-thirds of that comes from ruminants like cows raised for meat and dairy products. Beef herds create four times the emissions of dairy herds per kilo of food produced. And for US households, food makes up as much as 30% of emissions.
Unlike other polluting sectors, such as electricity and transportation, cattle farming has little potential for a big fix. Ruminants produce about 30% of the methane associated with human activity, and this gas has 28 times more global-warming potential than carbon dioxide. What’s more, it would be virtually impossible to raise them in a perfectly climate-neutral manner. “We don’t have a technical solution to change the stomach of a ruminant,” says Fredrik Hedenus, a professor in sustainability and systems analysis at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden. Technologies to dampen the impact of their burps have been in the works for a while but have yet to scale. They also fix only part of the problem with red meat: Cows need a lot of land for pasture and for feed, which has made livestock a top driver of deforestation in the Amazon and elsewhere around the world.
Even if the world stopped burning all fossil fuels tomorrow, emissions from agriculture would push the planet past 2 °C over preindustrial temperatures by 2070, Hedenus says. According to his research, more efficient livestock farming methods would still leave agriculture eating up over half of humanity’s carbon budget by that time. Only with the addition of dietary changes does his model show a winning scenario.
He’s far from alone in his conclusions: A 2024 survey of more than 200 climate scientists, conducted at Harvard, found that the vast majority believe reducing emissions from livestock is important to meeting climate goals. People have to eat less beef. “Essentially, you need a culture shift,” Hedenus says.
Yet the culture has proved intractable. Not only do people like the taste of meat, but across most of the world, meat-eating tends to be associated with status. As societies have grown wealthier, it has increased. A United Nations report showed that global meat production quadrupled between 1961 and 2022, while vegetarianism has held steady at about 4% of the population in the US since 1999.
What could move the needle is a carbon-light and delicious meat replacement. But from a food-tech standpoint, all we have to show is a menu of mostly failed solutions. Lab-grown meat has generated endless headlines since the 2000s but has yet to become commercially available (and affordable) at scale. And while breakthroughs in taste and texture inched plant-based meats from companies like Impossible Foods and Beyond Meat toward mass adoption, the hype—and the appetite—has somewhat fizzled.
So instead of asking people to change their preferences, startups like Joyn are trying a different tack. They’re creating what are broadly referred to as blended meat products, which combine plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat.
Paul Shapiro, cofounder of the startup BMC Ingredients, which markets a plant protein related to mushrooms, says the math is easy to understand: If we imagine that Impossible Whoppers at Burger King account for about 2% of sales, that’s only a 2% reduction in meat. But if a conventional Whopper were 20% plants, that would be a 20% cut right off the bat.
Those aren’t quite the numbers climate models are calling for, but some estimates say they could lead to outsized gains relative to the status quo: A 2022 study in Nature found that replacing 20% of beef globally could halve the annual rate of deforestation. And unlike the other solutions tried thus far, this particular Hail Mary is one a lot of omnivores seem open to giving a try.
The idea of blending meat and vegetables together is, of course, nothing new. Food cultures from around the world boast an array of dishes that combine small amounts of meat with plants. Today, home cooks still add veggies and legumes to dishes to stretch tight grocery budgets or to sneak extra greenery into their children’s supper.
But in the mid to late 2010s, however, the focus was largely on companies that appeared to have cracked the code for ditching meat entirely. When Impossible debuted its namesake burger in 2016, it impressed with an ingredient called heme, an iron-rich molecule in the protein soy leghemoglobin that allowed all-plant burgers to “bleed” like beef.
Impossible and its biggest competitor, Beyond, swaggered through the media and the markets. In 2019, Impossible’s founder told the New Yorker he intended to wipe out all animal agriculture by 2035. Beyond’s 2019 IPO was the most successful since the 2008 financial crisis. A flood of imitators followed.
But within a few years, tastes shifted. In 2023, Impossible employees’ stock values tumbled 89% from a 2021 high. That same year, Beyond laid off 20% of its staff, and a bruising Businessweek feature labeled the entire sector a fad. Sales have been slipping for years, with a 10% year-over-year drop in 2025, according to the Good Food Institute, a think tank focused on alternative proteins.
 Any quest to wipe out animal agriculture could now seem farcical. In 2025, Americans downed $45 billion worth of beef.
Several factors were likely at play. Megan Krogius, a spokesperson for Impossible Foods, says the dip is a “correction not a crisis” after “an outsized pop in demand” between 2020 and 2022. She also says that a flurry of plant-based products muddied the category’s reputation. Indeed, some disruptors (and their imitators) have struggled to compete on the sensory level. Nectar, an organization that conducts research on meat alternatives, has found that taste and texture are among the major factors that keep people from adopting plant-based meats. “Our consumers identify products as having bad aftertaste and off flavors five to six times more than in animal counterparts,” says Caroline Cotto, the group’s director.
At the same time, discourse around processed foods tarnished plant-based meat’s halo. In 2019, the Center for Consumer Freedom, a since-dissolved lobbying group backed by the meat industry, launched an ad campaign against plant-based alternatives, demonizing them as “ultra-processed imitations.”
While Impossible’s Krogius warns against conflating processed food with junk food (she points, for example, to a study in The Lancet finding mock meat to be nutritionally preferable to red meat), some of the bad press stuck. Now, the term “ultra-processed” has become something of a political cudgel—one wielded by the meat-loving MAHA movement and the US secretary of health and human services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In 2025, he flipped the food pyramid and stacked a steak on top.
Any quest to wipe out animal agriculture could now seem farcical. In 2025, Americans downed $45 billion worth of beef, and consumption rose by 4.3% over the previous year, according to an industry report. Rising prices could be slowing this down a bit, but cost can dampen only so much demand.
Blended meat, which has meat’s own juiciness and texture, rose alongside the plant-based superstars, but it did not get New Yorker profiles or headlining IPOs. At the height of mock-meat hype, companies like Tyson and Perdue launched blended products, and firms working on lab-grown meat explored cutting their products with plants.
The big advantage of blended meat is that large numbers of consumers—what some call “flexitarians”—are curious about it, and when they try it, they like it. A blind taste test co-funded by the USDA in 2022 showed that diners preferred blended burgers to fully plant-based ones. And a report from the major food processor ADM found that large proportions of every generation of Americans were interested in trying blended meats, including 75% of millennials. “This is a solution that we can do today, that consumers will accept today,” says Tim Dale, a director at Food Systems Innovations, the nonprofit group that oversees Nectar.
At this point, even Impossible has acknowledged the potential. In a wide-ranging interview with the Wall Street Journal in 2025, the company’s former CEO Peter McGuinness admitted the brand’s struggle to win over consumers, and suggested a hybrid burger could bridge the divide.
Plenty of newcomers are entering the fray. “Shiitake-infused beef burgers” from Australia-based Fable Foods are in restaurants and moving “incredibly well” at the high-end grocery store Central Market in Austin, Texas, says CEO Michael Fox. The Both Burger from Los Angeles–based 50/50 Foods is available in a smattering of California stores and eateries. And Spare Food in New York signed a deal with Premier, one of the nation’s biggest spenders in the health-care sector, for its blend of surplus produce and ground beef.
One major insight for all these upstarts is that consumers react best when marketing focuses on pleasure, not environmental virtues or health benefits. Though many companies actually create a burger or meatball with a better nutritional profile (fiber!) and fewer of meat’s downsides, like saturated fat, that doesn’t get people to buy it. They like that it tastes good. Beef and mushrooms, for example, contain complementary flavor compounds, including the glutamates that yield deep umami, which is why they’re so often paired in dishes like beef Wellington and stroganoff.
Food-production companies are a big target. BMC Ingredients, which collaborated with Perdue on a line of blended nuggets, markets a plant-based protein that can be mixed with meat to up its nutrition and flavor. BMC grows mycelium—the root-like structures of fungi. It underpins popular meat alternatives like Quorn and also features alongside mushrooms in Joyn’s 50/Cut. Shapiro likens his factory to a brewery, but instead of yeast fermenting barley, a fungus called Neurospora crassa digests starch to produce a protein with a dense network of fibers that makes for a meat-like chew. “We grow four hours before we get a harvest,” Shapiro says. “It’s among the most efficient ways to produce protein on Earth.”
Joyn also sees its path forward outside the grocery store. Food eaten away from home accounts for more than half of what US consumers spend on grub, according to the USDA. Padraic Doherty, who joined Joyn from the meat distributor D’Artagnan and holds the title of chief growth officer, says its main areas of focus are K–12 and college cafeterias and other major food service providers, like stadiums. These organizations, he says, often have sustainability goals and also are pressured to find both nutritious and affordable options. The 50/Cut Joyn sells to cafeterias is between 5% and 15% cheaper than beef.
But can cafeteria mushroom burgers prompt a larger cultural shift?
The folks touting the idea of going halfway see it as a bridge. BMC’s Shapiro thinks the movement toward meat-light eating reflects the reality of how these changes happen. Nectar’s Cotto compares blended meat to a hybrid car. “Moving people toward blended products [is] a way to drive demand for some of the fully plant-based ingredients that don’t scale right now to bring the price down,” she says. “So it’s both a short- and a long-term approach.”
Not everyone is so sure market forces will be enough, though. Nil Zacharias, a longtime entrepreneur in food sustainability who offers plant-based options to New York City delis through his company Plantega, isn’t sold on the notion. “Too many people in the space believe that as long as we create meat that is not from an animal but tastes like meat and costs the same, people will eat it,” he says. “I think the plant-based backlash to ultraprocessed foods shows you that’s not necessarily how things are going to go.” He believes blended meat’s main impact will be on institutional dining, in places like schools and health-care facilities.
 “People in this space believe that as long as we create meat that is not from an animal but tastes like meat, people will eat it.”
Nil Zacharias, founder and CEO, Plantega
Meat hybrids could, however, taste just familiar enough to open consumers’ minds to alternatives. Some research has found that thinking about mock meats prompts people to reconsider the whole system. In the 2010s, Clemens Driessen, a cultural geographer who teaches at Wageningen University & Research in the Netherlands, worked on a project that asked people in pubs, supermarkets, and other public spaces what they thought of lab-grown meat. “There’s a first response, which is ‘Oh, that sounds horrible,’” Driessen says. Then people tended to reflect that the meat they consume is also heavily industrialized. “A whole train of thought emerges out of proposing something very new,” he says.
If the category succeeds, climate advocates will need to make peace with imperfection. A life-cycle analysis Joyn commissioned on the 50/Cut burger confirms that the product has half the greenhouse-gas footprint of a beef patty, which—if you go by company claims—means it has about five times the impact of a burger from Impossible or Beyond. Hedenus, the climate scientist, says that even if blended products don’t reduce impact as much as plant-based ones, he’s all for trying any solution that works. “It is very difficult to change how we eat, so I think most good suggestions should be explored,” he says.
Meanwhile, the products are finding their way to more plates. They’re in cafeterias, high-end grocery stores, and small burger chains. They’re in the catalogues of major distributors like Sysco. The Both Burger has even been at Disneyland.
The 50/Cut meatball is on the menu this school year in seven states. At Cane Bay High it’ll take the form of a sub. The school is buying 200 cases at a time, with 150 meatballs in a case. Jason Ciaccia, the systems specialist for child nutrition in the school district, says he won’t be using the word “mushroom” to describe it. “If they hear ‘mushroom,’ they’re going to skip over it,” he says.
He is, however, considering his branding. He’s asked AI to help him come up with something fun. He thinks “Marvelous Meatball Sub” has a nice ring.
Meghan McCarron is a food and culture journalist based in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Gemini 4 logra lo imposible y termina 'Minecraft' sin ayuda humana
articles.text:
Google se ha apoyado en los videojuegos para demostrar lo que puede lograr su inteligencia artificial. Hace unos años, AlphaStar se convirtió en la primera IA en derrotar a un jugador profesional de StarCraft II, alcanzando el rango de Gran Maestro. Ahora toca el turno de Gemini 4, que consiguió vencer Minecraft sin intervención humana.
De acuerdo con una publicación científica de Google DeepMind, Gemini 4 Argon logró derrotar al Ender Dragon de Minecraft sin recibir ayuda durante una partida. Un equipo conformado por cuatro agentes de IA logró su objetivo y terminó el juego luego de casi 30 horas.
La prueba de DeepMind consistió en colocar a cuatro agentes de Gemini 4 Argon dentro de un mundo de supervivencia aleatorio en el que tenían el objetivo de acabar con el dragón. Los agentes no recibieron estrategias predefinidas ni herramientas especiales creadas para Minecraft. Cada uno controlaba a un jugador a través de Mineflayer y se coordinaba con los demás por el chat del juego y una memoria compartida.
El documento señala que los agentes se repartieron el trabajo desde el comienzo. En lugar de actuar como un sistema centralizado, la IA dividió el trabajo de forma espontánea, asignando tareas como recolectar recursos y alimentos, explorar el mapa o llevar a cabo tareas esenciales para avanzar. En el chat, los agentes se avisaban de amenazas, intercambiaban consejos de combate o se ayudaban mutuamente cuando uno perdía su equipo tras morir.
Gemini 4 venció Minecraft sin ayuda
Con el paso de las horas, cada agente terminó especializándose en determinadas actividades. Uno fabricó herramientas necesarias para la aventura, mientras que otro reunió comida y suministros y un tercero activó el portal para llegar al final. El cuarto agente construyó refugios para obtener recursos de los Endermen, además de asestar el golpe final contra el Ender Dragon.
Según DeepMind, la partida completa duró 27,23 horas, de las cuales la mitad se usó para alcanzar el End y el resto para derrotar al dragón. A lo largo de la aventura, los cuatro agentes intercambiaron 229 mensajes, ejecutaron 2.783 programas distintos y murieron 605 veces. Para llegar al final, Minecraft exige completar varios objetivos intermedios, como obtener materiales, fabricar herramientas avanzadas y conseguir las perlas de Ender, que son necesarias para fabricar los Ojos de Ender que nos ayudarán a encontrar y activar el portal.
Los investigadores revelaron que esta es la primera vez que un grupo de agentes de IA completa Minecraft de principio a fin usando herramientas estándar y sin instrucciones sobre cómo resolver el juego. Otro dato interesante del experimento es que la partida consumió unos 1.350 millones de tokens de entrada, lo que equivale a unos 1.620 dólares considerando la tarifa estándar.
Aunque completarse el juego suena a un hito para Google y Gemini 4, la hazaña más impresionante sigue en poder de los humanos. Un speedrunner consiguió terminarse Minecraft partiendo de las herramientas más básicas hasta vencer al Ender Dragon en apenas 6 minutos 36 segundos.

articles.title: "Pro and tell": Apple kündigt zweites Oktober-Event an – und könnte mit ganz neuen Macs überraschen
articles.text:
„Pro and tell“: Apple kündigt zweites Oktober-Event an – diese Produkte könnten überraschen
Nach dem iPhone Duo und dem Homeview-Display will Apple am 28. Oktober die nächsten Neuheiten präsentieren. Das kündigte Marketing-Chef Greg Joswiak erneut per X-Posting an. „Ich kann nicht erwarten, euch nächste Woche zu proen und zu erzählen“, lautet die ungefähre und ungelenke Übersetzung seiner Botschaft. Dabei handelt es sich um ein Wortspiel. „Show and tell“ ist ein Format an US-amerikanischen Schulen, bei dem Kinder Gegenstände von zu Hause mitbringen und sie vorstellen.
Die Anspielung „Pro“ macht dabei schon klar, dass es, wie üblich Ende Oktober, um neue Pro-Macbooks gehen dürfte. In der Regel stellt Apple dann das Einsteigermodell mit neuem Prozessor vor. In diesem Fall wäre das der M6, der bereits im neuen Mac Mini steckt. Doch wie Mark Gurman von Bloomberg berichtet, dürfte das nur die kleinste Neuerung sein.
Touchscreen-Macbook mit Dynamic Island
Das Hauptaugenmerk soll auf einem Macbook Pro liegen, das erstmals sowohl mit einem OLED-Display als auch mit einem Touchscreen ausgestattet sein soll. Wie auf dem iPhone soll zu dem die Dynamic Island im Display verbaut sein. Laut The Verge seien die neuen Geräte mit 14- und 16-Zoll-Bildschirm zu dem leichter als die bisherigen Modelle. Sie sollen mit den M5‑Pro- und -Max-Prozessoren ausgestattet sein, die auch in den Macbook-Pros stecken, die Apple im Frühjahr vorgestellt hatte.
Nachdem das iPad mit iPadOS 26 echte Multitasking-Optionen mit Fenstermanagement bekommen hatte, wären Touchscreen-Macs die nächste Verschmelzung von Macbook und iPad – trotz Apples jahrelangem Bestreben, genau dies nicht zu tun.
iPad Mini mit OLED und neuer iMac.
Neben den neuen Macbooks soll Apple einen aufgefrischten iMac mit M6-Prozessor und ein überarbeitetes iPad Mini vorstellen. Bei letzterem soll das Unternehmen ebenfalls ein OLED-Display verbauen. Zudem wandert die Kamera für Selfies und Video-Calls wohl in die Längsseite des Gehäuses.

articles.title: Baseus’ new security camera has a spotlight that tracks and follows moving targets
articles.text:
Baseus announced a new addition to its lineup of AI-assisted security cameras that’s more proactive about discouraging unwanted visitors instead of just recording and alerting you to their presence. The Baseus Security PrimeSentinel U2 Pro Outdoor 3K Dual Camera introduces a motorized spotlight that shines directly on a moving target, even as they’re running across your property, so they know they’ve been detected. The targeted light also improves the quality of video captured in the dark to increase the chances of a subject being identified, and it can assist your family with after-hours activities like taking the dog out.
Baseus’ new security camera has a spotlight that tracks and follows moving targets
The Baseus U2 Pro can deter intruders instead of just capturing them on camera.
The Baseus U2 Pro is now available through Amazon in the US for $269.99, while European availability starts on October 15th at €269.99. Alongside the spotlight feature, the U2 Pro pairs a 3K fixed camera designed to constantly monitor a specific area of your property with a second 3K camera that can zoom, tilt, and pan 360 degrees to monitor everywhere else. Full-color night vision capabilities make it easier to identify people, animals, or even the color of a suspicious vehicle.
Using “AI-powered analysis,” the U2 Pro will provide alerts when motion is detected with summaries and descriptions of what was seen that differentiate between people, pets, vehicles, and activities like delivered packages. It’s also smart enough to ignore movements that aren’t relevant, such as tree branches blowing in the wind, or activities that regularly occur so as not to overwhelm you with notifications. Footage is captured only when motion is detected and is stored locally on a 512GB encrypted memory card. It can be accessed remotely through Baseus’ mobile app, while live views from the cameras can also be monitored on Amazon Alexa or Google Home smart devices.
Baseus claims the U2 Pro can be installed in about two minutes using mounts that connect to walls or ceilings. The camera connects wirelessly to your home network and features a rechargeable battery good for up to 150 days of use, although that will potentially be reduced depending on how much activity there is on your property. An included 3W solar panel can be mounted atop the cameras or a short distance away to ensure it can see the sun. Just 40 minutes of sun exposure generates enough power for a full day’s use.

articles.title: EcoFlow's new Titan 5000 home battery systems get $50 reservation launch
articles.text:
EcoFlow's new Titan 5000 home battery range promises serious backup power, and $50 gets you an early discount and free solar panels
The three models are Titan 5000 Classic, Titan 5000, and Titan 5000 Plus
EcoFlow has unveiled a new range of home backup batteries designed to keep essential appliances running during power outages, with enough capacity to provide electricity for several days. The Titan 5000 series includes three models, with a $50 reservation securing a 5% discount and two free 220W solar panels.
• Best for: Homeowners who want a good amount of backup power, particularly those concerned about outages or looking to make better use of solar energy.
• Why it matters: These aren't ordinary portable power stations. They're expandable home energy systems designed to supply thousands of watts of electricity and integrate with selected household circuits.
• What you need to know: The offer ends on November 2, and EcoFlow hasn't revealed shipping dates yet.
Best EcoFlow Titan 5000 deals
This home battery system offers 5kWh expandable storage, 4000W output, 120V power, 3200W solar input, automatic backup switching, smart app control, and compatibility with EcoFlow's Smart Home Panel 10 system.
This home battery system features 5kWh expandable storage, 7200W output, 120V/240V support, 4000W solar input, automatic backup switching, smart energy management, and compatibility with EcoFlow's Smart Home Panel 10 system.
This advanced home battery system features 5kWh expandable storage, 7200W output, 8000W solar input, PV Boost technology, 120V/240V support, automatic backup switching, smart energy management, and home integration capabilities.
Why we recommend taking a closer look
The Titan series offers the ability to choose how much electricity you want to store separately from how much power you need to deliver. The 5kWh starting capacity is useful for shorter outages, while expansion batteries can increase the available runtime.
A 5kWh battery could theoretically power a continuous 500W load for around 10 hours, although the actual runtime will vary because of conversion losses and other factors.
Expanding to 30kWh provides six times the stored energy, but additional batteries increase the total cost.
The Titan systems also offer automatic backup switching within 20 milliseconds, while the compatible Smart Home Panel 10 can manage up to ten selected circuits. EcoFlow's OASIS 3.0 software adds monitoring and energy management, including the ability to schedule charging around electricity tariffs.
Three models, three different power requirements
The entry-level EcoFlow Titan 5000 Classic starts at $2,499 and provides 4,000W of output. It can power essential 120V appliances, including fridges, lighting, and more. It comes with approximately 5kWh of battery storage, expandable to 30kWh with additional batteries. Solar charging supports up to 3,200W of input.
The Classic only provides 120V output, so if you need more power consider the Titan 5000. Priced at $3,199, it gives you 7,200W of output and support for both 120V and 240V appliances. Solar input also increases to 4,000W, and the system works with EcoFlow's 240V Smart Home Panel 10 for automatic backup of selected household circuits.
The $3,699 Titan 5000 Plus shares the standard model's 7,200W battery output but doubles the maximum solar input to 8,000W, using two independent 4,000W MPPT controllers. Its PV Boost technology can increase available output to 10,000W when enough solar power is available.
Which EcoFlow Titan 5000 should you buy?
✅ Buy the Titan 5000 Classic if...
You mainly want to keep essential 120V equipment running during power outages and don't need backup for large 240V appliances.
✅ Buy the Titan 5000 if...
You want 120V/240V backup power and enough output to support more demanding household equipment.
✅ Buy the Titan 5000 Plus if...
You have substantial solar generation capacity or want the additional power options for demanding appliances. Its 8kW solar input and PV Boost capability are the main benefits.

articles.title: EU-Startups identifies 20 startups among 77 projects selected for €3.4 billion net-zero funding | EU-Startups
articles.text:
According to research by EU-Startups, 20 of the 77 European net-zero technology projects selected for €3.4 billion in EU Innovation Fund support involve startups, scaleups and younger technology ventures, highlighting the role of emerging companies in Europe’s industrial decarbonisation efforts.
Announced on 19 October 2026, the European Commission’s latest selection covers projects across 23 countries in the European Economic Area, spanning clean energy, industrial manufacturing, carbon removal, sustainable fuels and critical raw materials.
While established industrial groups account for much of the programme, EU-Startups’ analysis of the selected projects and their coordinating companies identifies 20 projects associated with younger technology businesses, representing approximately 26% of the total selection.
These 20 businesses span all five funding categories, from large industrial developments to smaller-scale demonstrations and manufacturing facilities.
Big industrial ambitions, startup origins
Among the 12 large-scale projects selected, two companies previously covered by EU-Startups stand out: Germany’s Vaeridion and France’s GravitHy.
Munich-based Vaeridion
- Founded in 2021, is developing the Microliner, a fully battery-electric regional aircraft designed to carry nine passengers. Its CAROLUS project aims to advance the aircraft towards certification, industrial production and commercial operation in Germany, with a targeted range of approximately 400 kilometres.
- In December 2024, EU-Startups reported on Vaeridion’s €14 million Series A funding round in order to support aircraft development and progress towards certification. Total funding sits at €17 million.
France’s GravitHy
- Founded in 2022, aims to decarbonise the steel industry by producing low-carbon iron using hydrogen instead of conventional coal-based processes. Its Fos-sur-Mer project plans to establish a facility capable of producing two million tonnes of hot briquetted iron annually, which steelmakers can use as an input for lower-emission steel production.
- In March 2025, EU-Startups covered GravitHy’s €60 million financing round. The capital was earmarked for engineering, permitting, recruitment and preparations for the company’s flagship industrial facility.
The remaining startup identified as large scale projects is Spain’s Greenertis.
From waste to circular chemistry
The medium-scale category includes five startup-associated projects, four of which involve companies previously covered by EU-Startups.
Netherlands-based ChainCraft
- Founded in 2010 as a spinout from Wageningen University, develops fermentation technology that transforms organic waste into valuable fatty acids. These chemicals can replace fossil-derived or palm oil-based ingredients used in products ranging from animal feed and lubricants to coatings and industrial chemicals.
- The company was previously included in EU-Startups’ overview of biotechnology companies in the Netherlands, which highlighted its proprietary fermentation processes and the range of applications for its medium-chain fatty acids. Total funding sits at €18.5 million.
Germany’s traceless materials
- Founded in Hamburg in 2020 by Dr Anne Lamp and Johanna Baare, develops natural polymer-based materials from agricultural residues as alternatives to conventional plastics. Total funding sits at €39 million.
- In September 2023, EU-Startups reported on the company’s €36.6 million financing round to support the construction of its first industrial production facility in Hamburg, which opened in 2026.
Spain’s H2SITE
- Founded in 2021 as a spinout from TECNALIA and Eindhoven University of Technology. The company develops membrane reactor technology that enables hydrogen to be separated from different gas streams and hydrogen carriers, including ammonia.
- EU-Startups previously covered H2SITE’s €36 million Series B round in January 2025. The company planned to use the investment to expand its hydrogen production and separation technologies into additional markets. Total funding sits at €57.9 million.
Sweden’s Cemvision
- Established in Stockholm in 2020, is pursuing a different industrial challenge: reducing the emissions associated with cement manufacturing.
- In March 2024, EU-Startups reported on Cemvision’s €10 million seed financing. The company was already working towards commercial adoption of its technology, having secured an initial customer contract.
The remaining startup in the medium-scale category is Sweden’s GreenIron.
Small projects, tangible applications
Among the 20 small-scale projects selected, EU-Startups identified four startups.
Dublin-based XFuel
- Develops technology for converting waste streams into lower-carbon fuels suitable for existing transport infrastructure. Its approach focuses on producing drop-in alternatives that can be used without requiring major modifications to engines or fuel distribution systems.
- In January 2026, EU-Startups included XFuel in its weekly funding roundup, following a €16.76 million financing announcement to support its development of sustainable fuels for road, marine and aviation applications. Total funding sits €30 million ($33.8 million).
The three other startup-associated small-scale projects are France’s Enosis, Lithuania’s Refinis and France’s Epyr.
Pilot projects put emerging technologies to work
Five of the 16 pilot projects selected involve startups identified by EU-Startups, including several companies that have previously attracted venture capital investment.
Brussels-based Sirona Technologies
- Founded in 2023 by Thoralf Gutierrez and Gauthier Limpens, develops modular direct-air-capture technology designed to remove carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere.
- Its Project Furu, located in Øygarden, Norway, has been selected for a grant of up to €9.1 million, subject to the finalisation of the funding agreement. In June 2024, EU-Startups reported on Sirona’s €6 million seed funding round to support the development and deployment of its direct-air-capture systems.
Germany’s Reverion
- Founded in 2022 as a spinout from the Technical University of Munich, is developing reversible power plants capable of converting gases such as biogas and hydrogen into electricity, while also enabling electricity to be stored through gas production.
- The company has featured several times in EU-Startups’ reporting, most recently in September 2026, when it announced a €154.2 million Series B financing round. The financing is intended to expand the company’s production capabilities and bring its reversible energy systems to additional industrial customers. Total funding sits at €228 million ($256 million).
Berlin-based C1 Green Chemicals
- Founded in 2022, is developing new chemical production processes using advanced catalysis. Its initial commercial focus is renewable methanol, which can replace fossil-derived methanol in industrial manufacturing and serve as an alternative fuel for shipping.
- In March 2025, EU-Startups covered C1 Green Chemicals’ €20 million financing package, comprising €15 million in investment and €5 million in approved research grants. The financing was intended to support the development of a demonstration plant and accelerate commercialisation. Total funding sits at €25 million.
Completing the startup-associated pilot projects is Germany’s ICODOS and France’s Flying Whales.
Manufacturing Europe’s CleanTech future
The CleanTech manufacturing category includes three startups – all companies previously featured by EU-Startups.
Sweden’s Orbital Systems
- Founded in Malmö in 2012 by Mehrdad Mahdjoubi following collaboration involving NASA and Lund University, initially gained attention for its water-recycling shower technology.
- Orbital Systems was featured by EU-Startups in March 2019 as one of ten European CleanTech startups developing solutions for a more sustainable future. Total funding sits at €61 million ($69 million).
France’s HoloSolis
- Established in 2022, is developing a large-scale solar photovoltaic manufacturing facility in Sarreguemines-Hambach, France.
- In November 2025, EU-Startups reported that HoloSolis had secured more than €220 million in public and private financing. The company expects the facility to support European solar manufacturing and create jobs in the region. Total funding sits €220 million.
Germany’s Additive Drives
- Founded in Dresden in 2020 by Philipp Arnold, Axel Helm and Dr Jakob Jung, develops high-efficiency electric motors using a combination of additive manufacturing and conventional production technologies.
- In February 2026, EU-Startups covered Additive Drives’ €25 million financing to accelerate industrial scaling and international expansion.
The Innovation Fund
The broader Innovation Fund selection reflects the European Commission’s efforts to support technologies at different stages of commercial readiness. The programme includes 12 large-scale, 17 medium-scale, 20 small-scale, 12 CleanTech manufacturing and 16 pilot projects.
According to the Commission, the 77 selected projects could collectively avoid approximately 290 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions during their first ten years of operation. The programme is financed through revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System, which reinvests carbon market proceeds into low-carbon technologies.
The December 2025 call attracted 358 applications requesting €17.5 billion in funding, considerably exceeding the initially available budget of €2.9 billion.
However, selection does not yet constitute a final grant award. The 77 project promoters have been invited to prepare grant agreements with the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA), with final funding amounts and contractual arrangements expected to be confirmed in the first quarter of 2027.
Although the precise share of the €3.4 billion that will ultimately support startup-associated projects remains unclear, our findings highlight the involvement of emerging technology companies in Europe’s industrial transition.

articles.title: Kyla Scanlon on why AI dominates the stock market | BetaKit
articles.text:
Recently on The BetaKit Podcast, managing editor Sarah Rieger joined me to identify the biggest and brightest red flags indicating an AI bubble.
We left that conversation with a strong familiarity with the behaviour driving the markets into an AI frenzy while lacking any clear understanding of why it was happening. So we called in the big guns.
“The United States economy definitely has a cold right now. And when the US sneezes, the whole world catches a cold.”
According to economic commentator and New York Times bestselling author Kyla Scanlon, the United States has caught the AI bug—one that might fuel a public-markets pandemic.
OK, maybe it’s not that bad. Scanlon notes on the podcast that the consensus is the AI bubble will likely deflate through a slow release of air, given the amount of money and participants tied up in it.
That’s not to say there won’t be pain involved. Scanlon also spoke to the concerning connection between debt and the AI data centre buildout (which could go bad depending on how much gets borrowed and from whom), and how President Donald Trump has given AI companies the green light to drive the US economy with impunity. As Gen Z’s favourite economist, she is also keenly aware of the negative impacts of AI adoption on the labour market, particularly for young people.
This type of market analysis, which deals with what’s happening right now, inevitably leads to a discussion of what happens next, and Scanlon points to a few options, including reframing AI back to being a human-led tool.

“The way that we’ve been talking about AI is this horrible Job-Killer 1000 bot, but in reality it could be just a complement to humans,” she notes.
Doing so might also require holding frontier AI companies accountable for their actions, and on this front, Scanlon is paying close attention to the tweets of Pope Leo XIV. What does the leader of the Catholic Church have to say about AI? Let’s dig in.

articles.title: Data is not a moat: What India’s CTOs say will define the next tech edge
articles.text:
Data is not a moat: What India’s CTOs say will define the next tech edge
At TechSparks 2026, technology leaders from ShareChat, Angel One, Amagi and Innovaccer said India’s next competitive edge will depend on deep industry expertise, customer insights, trust and the ability to turn AI into real-world solutions.
India’s technology industry has long relied on talent, cost efficiency and scale. But as artificial intelligence makes advanced tools more accessible, these advantages alone may no longer be enough to differentiate companies.
The next edge, according to technology leaders at TechSparks 2026, will come from how effectively companies use AI to solve specific problems, understand customers and build products that are difficult to replicate.
During a panel titled The New CTO Playbook: India’s Next Tech Advantage, Nitin Jain, CTO of ShareChat and Moj; Ajit Narayanan, CTO of Angel One; Srividhya Srinivasan, CTO of Amagi; and Ankit Maheshwari, founder and CTO of Innovaccer, discussed how Indian technology companies can remain competitive in an AI-driven market, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks.
India’s complexity is an advantage
For ShareChat and Moj, India’s linguistic and cultural diversity offers an opportunity to build products for varied audiences. Nitin Jain said companies must account for differences in languages, devices, network quality and user preferences.
ShareChat, which Jain said has around 200 million monthly active users, uses audience behaviour to improve content recommendations and identify emerging preferences.
He said the challenge is to deliver experiences comparable with global platforms while operating within India’s cost constraints. Building flexible technology that accommodates diverse users, he added, can help companies expand faster.
Data alone is not enough
In healthcare, Innovaccer’s Ankit Maheshwari said proprietary data is valuable but does not automatically create a competitive moat.
Healthcare information is often fragmented across medical records, billing systems and medication databases. Connecting these sources is only the first step; the real challenge is using the information to determine what action should follow.
“Data in itself, or having proprietary data, is not a moat,” Maheshwari said.
He argued that companies need a context and intelligence layer that understands industry workflows, exceptions and operational requirements. In healthcare, this means moving beyond general-purpose AI to solutions that can work reliably across hospitals, providers and complex processes.
Trust must be built into AI
For Angel One’s Ajit Narayanan, trust can be a differentiator in financial services, where technology failures can have direct financial consequences.
He cited the example of a trading order for which a customer receives no acknowledgement. Without knowing whether the order was processed, retrying could result in duplicate positions and potential losses.
Narayanan said trust must be embedded in system design through accurate information, safeguards and accountability, rather than treated merely as a brand promise.
He also outlined three considerations for AI automation: the cost of an incorrect decision, whether it can be reversed, and whether it can be audited. Human oversight, he argued, should focus on meaningful safeguards rather than simply assigning responsibility when systems fail.
Building in India, scaling globally
Amagi’s Srividhya Srinivasan said India’s complex media environment has helped the company develop products for global markets.
Multiple languages, subtitles, audience demographics and advertising formats expose technology providers to challenges that also arise in international media operations.
Srinivasan said Amagi developed solutions for India before taking some of them global. Emerging AI applications, including real-time dubbing, subtitling and short-form content creation, offer further opportunities.
However, she said expansion should depend on market readiness rather than a fixed India-first strategy. Companies must identify where customers are prepared to adopt a product and where it solves an immediate need.
The advantage lies in execution
Jain said AI is helping ShareChat accelerate content production and improve recommendations by analysing how users engage with videos and other formats.
The platform can use these signals to test content ideas, understand audience preferences and refine recommendations. The ability to feed user responses back into AI systems quickly creates a continuous improvement cycle.
The broader message from the panel was that access to AI alone will not guarantee a lasting advantage. Companies must combine technology with specialised knowledge, customer understanding, reliable systems and the ability to execute at scale.
For India’s technology industry, talent, cost and scale remain important foundations. But the next competitive edge will depend on how effectively companies turn those strengths into products that solve complex problems and deliver measurable value."

articles.title: Raz-de-marée ou coup de com' ? L'incroyable rupture de stock de l'iPhone Duo
articles.text:
Vous aviez soigneusement économisé pour glisser la toute dernière révolution technologique sous le sapin de Noël, à savoir l’iPhone Duo, le tout premier smartphone pliant d’Apple ? Il va peut-être falloir préparer une enveloppe avec un mot d’excuse, ou réfléchir activement à un plan de secours.
La semaine dernière, Apple a officiellement ouvert les précommandes de son petit bijou. Si l’on se doutait que les fans seraient au rendez-vous, l’engouement général a pris des proportions impressionnantes.
La firme de Cupertino n’a d’ailleurs pas caché son enthousiasme. Lors d’une déclaration accordée à la chaîne CNBC, Apple a qualifié cette ferveur initiale d’« absolument extraordinaire ».
Mais ce succès fulgurant a un prix, et ce sont les consommateurs qui vont en faire les frais. Aux États-Unis, les délais d’expédition s’allongent à vue d’œil pour quiconque passe commande aujourd’hui. Si vous espériez frimer avec votre téléphone pliant pendant les repas de fin d’année, c’est raté. Les dates de livraison pour les nouvelles précommandes ont d’ores et déjà glissé jusqu’en janvier 2027.
Un succès à nuancer tout de même
Il faut bien sûr toujours prendre avec un grain de sable ce genre de déclarations. Comme nous ne disposons d’aucun chiffre, ni les stocks qui étaient disponibles au départ, ni le niveau d’engagement que visait Apple, la marque peut très bien trouver que cela dépasse ses propres attentes, sans que ces attentes ne soient particulièrement impressionnantes dans l’absolu pour un observateur extérieur. De même, il n’est pas exclu que la communication en forme de bombage de torse puisse servir à calmer les fans déçus. Mieux vaut tourner une difficulté logistique en victoire plutôt qu’en échec.
Conscient de la frustration générée par ces délais à rallonge, Apple a assuré travailler d’arrache-pied pour expédier son nouveau produit vedette le plus rapidement possible et continue d’accepter les commandes en ligne.
On peut tout de même reconnaître que l’organisation est plutôt transparente. Les acheteurs de la première heure pourront récupérer leur commande en boutique dès le 23 octobre. Pour la vague suivante, les réceptions s’étaleront entre les mois de novembre et décembre, cela est déjà entendu.
Quant aux retardataires laissés sur le carreau ? Il reste un petit espoir. L’Apple Store en ligne suggère aux clients de revérifier les disponibilités pour un retrait en magasin à partir du 24 octobre. Attention toutefois : la firme de Cupertino n’a pas garanti que ses boutiques physiques disposeraient de stocks en libre-service.
Enfin, la solution viendra peut-être des distributeurs tiers. Des enseignes comme La Fnac, Boulanger ou Carrefour affichent encore la possibilité de précommander pour le 23 octobre. Une dernière fenêtre de tir qui risque, elle aussi, de se refermer très vite.

articles.title: 10 African startups named semi-finalists for $2m Milken-Motsepe Prize in Circular Economy - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ten African startups have been named semifinalists for the Milken-Motsepe Prize in Circular Economy, and will share US$500,000 in unrestricted funding as they compete for the US$1 million grand prize.
The Milken-Motsepe Prize is aimed at companies in Africa revolutionising using different technologies to revolutionise the circular economy on the continent. Run by the Milken Institute and the Motsepe Foundation, the prize will distribute a total of US$2 million in non-dilutive capital to companies using technology to scale circular economy solutions across Africa. Alongside funding, participants receive mentorship, investor connections and global exposure.
The 10 semi-finalists have now been announced, who will be whittled down to five finalists by judges assessing them on commercial viability, scalability, workforce and social impact, and environmental impact. The grand prize winner will be announced at the 2027 Milken Institute Global Conference in Los Angeles, with a US$250,000 runner-up prize also on offer.
Kenya leads the way with three semi-finalists. Bottle Logistics East Africa combines digital reverse logistics with industrial glass recovery to turn discarded glass into returnable packaging, cullet and other products; Sanergy converts urban sanitation and organic waste into organic fertiliser, biochar and other agricultural inputs; and Safi Organics turns rice husks and sugarcane bagasse into a carbon-negative organic fertiliser.
Ethiopia, Tanzania and Egypt each have two startups in the running. From Ethiopia, EKT Trade and Investment manufactures products from plastic waste, and Zafree makes tree-free pulp and paper for the packaging industry using banana farm waste. Tanzania’s Country Materials uses AI to identify, trace and recover scrap metal for the continent’s steel industry, while SafeSip recycles plastic waste into pressure-rated resin and drip irrigation equipment.
The Egyptian contingent comprises Papyrus Egypt, which converts banana plantation waste into biodegradable packaging and liquid fertiliser, and Triple M Electrical and Electronic Contracting, which extends the lifespan of power infrastructure by purifying transformer oil and refurbishing transformers, switchgear and panels.
Nigeria’s Cold Hubs, which builds and runs solar-powered cold rooms, refrigerated trucks and reusable crates for food markets and farm clusters, completes the list.
“Africa is uniquely positioned to lead in this transition,” said Emily Musil, managing director at the Milken Institute, who added that the prize backs entrepreneurs turning resource efficiency into competitive, job-creating businesses.

articles.title: .NET 11 Release Candidate 2: Go-Live License and Updates across Libraries, F#, MAUI, and WinForms
articles.text:
Microsoft has released .NET 11 Release Candidate 2 with a go-live license for production use, as stated in the announcement. The build is supported in Visual Studio 2026 Insiders and in Visual Studio Code with the C# Dev Kit. As reported, it brings changes across the libraries, runtime, SDK, NuGet, F#, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows Forms, with no new C# language features.
In the libraries, CborReader can now read a payload delivered in chunks, using isFinalBlock and SlideData, in Lax conformance mode only. Two experimental cryptography types arrive: CompositeMLKem combines post-quantum and classical key encapsulation, and Hpke provides Hybrid Public Key Encryption with classical DHKEM suites only.
Both require opting in through SYSLIB5009 and SYSLIB5006, as described in the release notes. ValidationAttribute.FormatMessage lets a host supply a message template for the attribute to fill in, and SocketsHttpHandler.InitialHttp2MaxConcurrentStreams caps streams on a new HTTP/2 connection until the server's SETTINGS frame arrives.
The runtime release focuses on reliability but carries one breaking change. CoreCLR now disables advisory file locking by default on iOS and tvOS, because, as stated, FileStream lock in RC 1 could cause the OS to terminate an app entering the background. FileShare restrictions are no longer enforced there, and setting DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING to 0 restores locking, according to the release.
ASP.NET Core has few new features but several changes for apps upgrading from RC 1. QuickGrid's AnchorMode and ItemComparer parameters are no longer experimental. IValidationMessageFormatter has been removed in favor of FormatMessage, the Blazor BasePath component moved to the Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components namespace, and the experimental device-bound sessions package was pulled from this build. As reported, the remaining AddRazorRuntimeCompilation overloads now warn with ASPDEPR003.
In the SDK, file-based programs accept quoted values in #:property directives, and the #:package, #:project, and #:ref directives take trailing Name=Value item metadata. MSBuild gains faster wildcard matching during project evaluation, which, as reported in Microsoft's Windows benchmarks, puts it at 10–13% faster with 16–34% fewer allocations.
NuGet adds --min-publish-age-hours to dotnet nuget add source and update source, and restore fails with NU1020 when a package cooldown leaves no eligible floating version.
F# ships several preview features. The compiler gains return and await intrinsics for building custom computation-expression builders on the runtime-async model, though FSharp.Core does not yet ship such a builder, as stated in the notes.
let calculation () =
    runtimeTask {
        let captured = 40
        let! delta = delayed 2
        return captured + delta
    }
The reraise() now works inside the with handler of async and task expressions. Outside preview, more List and Array functions inline their callbacks to cut allocations, Async.parallelLimit bounds concurrent work, and bitwise operators on non-integer enums now fail at compile time with FS0001.
The .NET MAUI maui template gains a --ui csharp option that generates the app, shell, and main page in C# rather than XAML, and the multi-project template adds an --avalonia option for an Avalonia desktop project.
MauiIcon accepts Apple Icon Composer .icon bundles, and UseiOSShellHandler opts into a handler-based Shell on Apple platforms. Android adds API 37.2 bindings and JDK 25 support, while Apple workloads now require Xcode 27.0 and apps built with its SDKs must adopt the UIKit scene lifecycle, as described in the breaking changes.
Windows Forms refines the .NET 11 visual styles. Application.SetDefaultVisualStylesMode selects the renderer version, but ToolStrip and DataGridView keep Classic rendering even under Net11 for now. Application.SystemVisualSettings exposes a snapshot of the Windows accent color, text scaling, and high-contrast state, and FormRevealMode defers a top-level form's first presentation to reduce background flashes.
New analyzers WFO3000 to WFO3002 flag code that cannot round-trip through the Designer, which the release notes say is particularly useful when AI tools generate or refactor forms.
Other changes in this release are MSBuild property expansion in launch-profile arguments, an F# RequireNamedArgumentsAttribute, a private-member R8 obfuscation default on Android, SuspendPainting and KioskModeManager for Windows Forms, EF Core SaveChanges and JSON projection fixes.
On Reddit, discussion focused less on the features than on upgrade cadence. Commenters asked how many teams still skip odd-numbered releases, and others replied that since .NET 9 a standard-term release shares its end-of-support date with the preceding LTS version, moving to .NET 11 costs no support time.
Other developers reported MAUI workloads breaking on every preview upgrade, questioned Blazor server-side rendering performance against Razor Pages and MVC, and welcomed the KioskModeManager component for Windows Forms.
For interested readers and developers, the full release notes for .NET 11 RC 2 are available on the dotnet/core repository on GitHub.

articles.title: Siemens Software Center Vulnerability Exploited in ClickFix Malware Attacks
articles.text:
Siemens revealed on Monday that threat actors have exploited a vulnerability in Siemens Software Center as part of a malware campaign.
Siemens Software Center handles the download, installation, activation and updating of software that customers have bought, and it can also be used to start free trials.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-110936, exists because the program doesn’t properly restrict the locations it searches for DLL files. An authenticated local attacker could plant a malicious DLL in one of those folders and have their code executed with the same privileges as Software Center.
Siemens disclosed the flaw on October 15 in an advisory that assigned it a CVSS v4 score of 8.4. Two days later, the company updated the advisory to tell customers that version 4.0.9.8 resolves the issue.
Users who already have the application installed will receive the fix automatically the next time they launch it.
The advisory didn’t mention in-the-wild exploitation until Monday, when Siemens added a link to a new blog post describing the attacks.
The attackers paired a legitimate copy of the Siemens program, which carried a valid digital signature, with malicious DLL files they supplied themselves. When the program started, it loaded the attacker-provided files from its own folder.
Siemens noted that version 3.5.8.7, the newest release at the time, did not validate these helper files before loading them.
The company said its software was not tampered with, and that the malicious package was not spread through Siemens’ distribution channels.
“No Siemens system, product or update channel was breached to our knowledge,” the company said.
Siemens is sharing threat intelligence with authorities and EDR providers. Its blog post lists indicators of compromise (IoCs), as well as signs that a computer may have been infected.
Because the Siemens file used in the attacks is legitimate, the company recommends that defenders focus on suspicious behavior and the folders associated with the malware instead of relying on file hashes.
Huntress researcher Jose Oregon has been credited with reporting the vulnerability to Siemens.
Siemens links the attacks to the Romulus ClickFix operation
Siemens has linked the attacks to Romulus, a multi-platform ClickFix campaign. ClickFix attacks rely on fake prompts, such as bogus CAPTCHA checks, that instruct users to paste and execute malicious commands on their own devices.
Last week, Forescout published research on Romulus, a ClickFix delivery platform that can serve several different malware payloads. The security firm found the platform running on several servers, including the one Siemens identified as the distribution server for the malicious bundle containing its software.
Forescout saw the platform deliver the LegionLoader malware, as well as a trojanized installer that leveraged a legitimate Stardock application for DLL side-loading.
The researchers could not determine who runs Romulus. They said it could be a private tool, a service sold to cybercriminals, an affiliate program, or software copied by different threat actors.
Huntress described the same Stardock-based package in a late-September report on a campaign that used rogue ChatGPT Custom GPTs to lure users to ClickFix pages. In those attacks, signed programs from Canon and later Stardock were abused to side-load malicious code that ultimately deployed a RAT.
Huntress responded to at least 40 incidents linked to the campaign, and said it believes signed programs from other vendors are probably being misused as well.
Siemens Software Center is not mentioned in the Huntress or Forescout reports. However, the overlapping infrastructure and the similar side-loading approach suggest the Siemens program may have been added to the same toolkit.
