articles.title: Drupal Warns of Fast Exploitation Risk for Critical Core RCE Flaw
articles.text:
Drupal has rolled out patches for five vulnerabilities, including two critical-severity bugs that could be exploited for remote code execution (RCE).
The first resides in the Entity List module, which allows users to create lists of entities without Views, and is tracked as CVE-2026-108099. It is not exploitable with the module alone, but exploit paths exist with other contributed modules.
“At least one known exploit path does not require authentication. Custom code may also expose the vulnerable functionality,” Drupal notes.
The second impacts the Field UI module in Drupal core and is tracked as CVE-2026-108097.
It is not exploitable with Drupal core alone, but contributed modules provide serious exploit paths, including at least one that does not require authentication. As a mitigation, users can uninstall the core Field UI module.
To address them, users are advised to update to Entity List version 3.0.10 and to Drupal versions 11.4.10, 11.3.19, or 10.6.19. Previous Drupal releases have reached end-of-life and no longer receive security updates.
The fresh Drupal updates also resolve cross-site scripting (XSS) holes in the Drupal core Link module (collectively tracked as CVE-2026-108515) and an XSS flaw in the Navigation module (CVE-2026-108514).
Additionally, Drupal announced patches for a security defect in the administration theme Gin that could lead to XSS attacks. Gin versions 5.0.16 and 4.1.4 contain fixes for the bug.
Drupal makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild. On October 12, however, it urged users to reserve time for core updates, warning that “exploits might be developed within hours or days.”
Additional information can be found on Drupal’s security advisories page.

Que retenir de l’Oppo A7 Pro 5G ?
- Une batterie de 7 400 mAh qui tiendra facilement une journée
- Une expérience boostée par l’intelligence artificielle

Proposé sur le site officiel au prix de 499,99 euros, l’Oppo A7 Pro chute à 399,99 euros sur le site de Carrefour.

La charge rapide de 80 W est aussi présente et le smartphone retrouvera toute son autonomie en seulement une heure. Sous le capot, Oppo a choisi le MediaTek Dimensity 6360 MAX et 6 Go de RAM extensible à 18 Go. Pour obtenir cette RAM supplémentaire, il faudra puiser dans les 256 Go de stockage de l’appareil. L’intelligence artificielle est aussi présente sur la partie photo pour améliorer les clichés en mode portrait ou ceux pris la nuit pour ajouter plus de détails dans les zones les moins éclairées.

articles.title: AI assistant startup Town nabs unicorn valuation 4 months after launch | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Town, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based startup developing AI assistants, nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B funding round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures. The company launched publicly just four months ago and said it reached millions of dollars in annual recurring revenue in a matter of weeks. It has raised at least $160 million to date, having previously announced a $55 million Series A round in June.
Town — founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze — is one of many AI assistants flooding the market right now. Town targets businesses, giving each employee an AI assistant called a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems. Employees’ Townies can talk to each other and share approved information; they can also now work with customers and others outside the company.
Alongside the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates employees’ Townies with new business information rather than requiring each worker to update their own Townie. Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures, and First Round Capital also participated in the round.
We’ve reached out to the company for comment.

articles.title: El Pentágono deja de utilizar las herramientas de IA de Anthropic tras incluir a la empresa en una lista negra, según pudo saber la BBC
articles.text:
El Departamento de Defensa de Estados Unidos ya no utiliza la herramienta de inteligencia artificial Claude, según declaró el pasado 5 de octubre un funcionario del Pentágono, que indicó que el departamento “ha dejado de utilizar los productos de Anthropic”.
El secretario de Defensa, Pete Hegseth, había fijado como límite finales de agosto, y nadie ha explicado por qué se tardó más de un mes en completar la retirada.
Hasta finales de septiembre, Claude se utilizaba para investigación, análisis y recopilación de inteligencia, así como para operaciones militares contra Irán, según exfuncionarios del Departamento de Defensa y contratistas que han trabajado con el Pentágono en proyectos de inteligencia artificial, la mayoría de ellos bajo anonimato porque no estaban autorizados a hablar con la prensa. Para estas fuentes, Claude era una herramienta fundamental para procesar grandes cantidades de información, y Anthropic no ha querido hacer declaraciones al respecto.
Las relaciones comerciales comenzaron en 2024, cuando en noviembre Anthropic, Palantir y Amazon Web Services anunciaron una alianza para llevar Claude a agencias de inteligencia y defensa en un entorno certificado para información clasificada, denominado nivel IL6. Palantir presumió entonces de ser el primer socio que llevaba los modelos de Claude a entornos clasificados. A principios de 2026, el Pentágono pidió que Anthropic eliminara las salvaguardas de Claude y diera a las fuerzas armadas acceso sin restricciones.
Sin embargo, la empresa se negó en dos puntos concretos y, en su comunicado del 27 de febrero, pidió excepciones tanto para la vigilancia masiva de ciudadanos estadounidenses como para las armas totalmente autónomas. Ese mismo día, Pete Hegseth anunció que la empresa sería designada “riesgo para la cadena de suministro” de la seguridad nacional (una etiqueta que suele reservarse para proveedores de países considerados hostiles), y Donald Trump ordenó a las agencias federales que dejaran de utilizar sus productos.
El plazo de seis meses empezó un día antes de que Estados Unidos e Israel atacaran Irán, y Anthropic, que ya había calificado la medida de “sin precedentes”, demandó al Gobierno el 9 de marzo.
El papel que desempeñaba Claude en Maven
Claude formaba parte de Maven Smart System, la plataforma que opera Palantir (fundada por Peter Thiel, multimillonario aliado de Trump) y que el Pentágono emplea como sistema principal para organizar inteligencia y otros datos.
Se dice que los analistas reunían en Maven imágenes de satélite y grabaciones de drones y luego las pasaban a Claude (y también por otros grandes modelos de lenguaje) para tareas como identificar posibles objetivos militares. Una persona a la que Palantir hizo una demostración a principios de año llegó a contar que se utilizaba con frecuencia para elaborar informes de una página que ascendían por la cadena de mando.
Algunos de los aliados de Estados Unidos también utilizan Maven para compartir inteligencia con Washington. Además, el papel del modelo tiene matices: un análisis sobre Claude en el CENTCOM (el Mando Central, que dirige las operaciones en Oriente Medio), publicado el 30 de marzo, lo describe más como una pieza que coordinaba los módulos y modelos del sistema que como el componente que propone objetivos.
Dicho análisis también enumera que la política del Departamento de Defensa exige que sean personas quienes seleccionen los objetivos, y que el 9 de marzo el subsecretario de Defensa Steve Feinberg ordenó que Maven pasara a la oficina central de datos e IA del Pentágono.
Esa integración explica exactamente la razón de no retirarse de inmediato. “El hecho de que el Pentágono haya tardado hasta ahora en eliminar todo uso de Claude en el sistema indica que estas cosas no son simplemente de ‘conectar y usar’”, afirmó Lauren Kahn, analista del Centro de Seguridad y Tecnología Emergente de la Universidad de Georgetown y antigua funcionaria de Defensa. Y añadió: “Una vez que se integran, puede ser complicado eliminarlas”.
Los empleados del Pentágono siguieron utilizando Claude, incluidos los modelos Mythos, “durante todo el período de la controversia”, según una de las fuentes. Y, cuando llegó la orden, “existía preocupación por pasar de Anthropic a OpenAI” y a otras herramientas, recuerda un exfuncionario de alto rango.
El detalle de Mythos tiene interés porque no era un modelo accesible para cualquiera. Anthropic presentó Claude Mythos Preview el 7 de abril dentro del proyecto Glasswing, reservado a un grupo cerrado de socios (Microsoft, Apple, Google, Cisco o CrowdStrike, entre otros) y a más de 40 organizaciones que mantienen software crítico, debido a la capacidad del modelo para encontrar y explotar vulnerabilidades. La propia empresa avisó de que no pensaba abrir esa versión al público general.
La relación con la Casa Blanca parece ser distinta, ya que entre finales de septiembre y principios de octubre el presidente Trump se reunió dos veces con Dario Amodei, consejero delegado de Anthropic. Amodei declaró a la prensa que le seguían preocupando los riesgos de la inteligencia artificial: “Aún se está discutiendo cómo abordar esos riesgos”. Sin embargo, “si trabajamos con el presidente, podemos ganar de manera segura”, añadió, y el propio Trump lo describió como “genial” y “fantástico”.
OpenAI estableció límites muy parecidos
El Pentágono ha cerrado contratos también con Google, xAI y OpenAI, y dos personas que conocen el uso de la inteligencia artificial en el Departamento de Defensa afirman que las herramientas de OpenAI se han extendido a algunos departamentos durante los últimos meses.
Esa misma noche del 27 de febrero, Sam Altman anunció el acuerdo con el Pentágono y aseguró que el Departamento aceptaba dos principios de la empresa: la prohibición de la vigilancia masiva doméstica y la responsabilidad humana en el uso de la fuerza, armas autónomas incluidas.
Sobre el papel, estos límites son muy parecidos a los que llevaron a Anthropic a la lista negra. Sin embargo, Altman afirmó que la diferencia estaba en que ya figuraban en la ley y la política del Departamento de Defensa, y en que OpenAI los había incorporado al acuerdo con salvaguardas técnicas. El propio Altman reconoció que la vigilancia masiva doméstica ya es ilegal.
Dos tribunales, dos respuestas
Las dos designaciones se basan en normas diferentes. La primera se apoya en el artículo 3252 del título 10 del código federal estadounidense, y la jueza federal Rita Lin, en California, la declaró ilegal el 27 de agosto: la consideró una represalia que vulneraba la libertad de expresión, una decisión arbitraria y sin el debido proceso, y escribió que invocar la seguridad nacional no es “un cheque en blanco” para castigar a los críticos del Gobierno. Ese fallo sigue vigente.
Un mes después, el 25 de septiembre, el Tribunal de Apelaciones del Distrito de Columbia avaló la otra designación por dos votos a uno, la que se apoya en la ley de seguridad de la cadena de suministro en las compras federales (FASCSA). La mayoría consideró que las restricciones de Claude y el hecho de que el contrato siguiera sin cerrarse podían hacerlo poco fiable para operaciones militares, mientras que la jueza Karen LeCraft Henderson votó en contra. Anthropic ha recordado que otro tribunal ya había anulado la designación paralela y está estudiando pedir una nueva revisión.
¿Y si usas Claude?
Si alguien utiliza Claude en casa o en su oficina, nada cambia: Anthropic dejó clara su postura el 27 de febrero y explicó que el acceso de particulares y empresas no se ve afectado por el conflicto.
Para las empresas que trabajan con el Pentágono, en cambio, la situación es más confusa. Según un análisis del fallo de septiembre, el Departamento ha pedido a algunos contratistas que retiren los productos de Anthropic de ciertos sistemas y entregables, e incluso ha sugerido vetarlos en sistemas que no forman parte del contrato, lo cual podría ir más allá de lo que permite la FASCSA. Tampoco ha publicado aún la orden formal de exclusión en el registro federal de contratación (SAM).
Dado que la designación de la FASCSA continúa en vigor, Claude sigue fuera de Maven y Anthropic no ha concretado qué revisión pedirá.

articles.title: The fossil fuel comeback is here
articles.text:
The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows.
The fossil fuel comeback is here
Data centers are demanding more energy, and the Trump administration is making sure fossil fuels meet the moment.
Electricity demand is also climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid. Despite those growing demands, the Trump administration has sought to hobble the wind and solar industries in favor of fossil fuels.
America’s energy landscape is already shifting as a result, according to the report published last week by the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund and research firm Atlas Public Policy. If all the gas projects in the development pipeline complete construction, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades, the authors warn.
“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point”
“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says.
While the US still generates 60 percent of its electricity from fossil fuels, renewables have quickly gained ground. Wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal for the first time in 2024. Solar was the fastest-growing source of new electricity generation that year, accounting for 81 percent of added capacity. Globally, solar has become the cheapest power source in most of the world.
Then Donald Trump stepped into his second term as president with a plan to “drill, baby, drill” for fossil fuels, his preferred power source for energy-hungry data centers. His administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects by issuing stop work orders, blocking permits, and removing tax incentives. We’re still seeing a rush of new solar and wind farms driven by relatively low costs, although many of them make up the last wave of projects that benefited from Biden-era incentives.
The winds are shifting in favor of gas-fired power plants. Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 percent of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 percent by the second quarter of 2026, according to the new report, which analyzes data from the US Energy Information Administration. If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 percent of the development pipeline by the end of the decade. Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 gigawatts by 2030, reflecting a 45 percent jump from construction plans just six months ago.
Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown. But for now, renewable energy projects are being canceled at a faster clip than fossil fuels, at 4.9 percent compared to 2.9 percent of projects, respectively.
New utility-scale solar and wind farms still beat gas when it comes to cost, coming in at $68 to $69 per megawatt-hour on average compared to $90 per megawatt-hour for new combined-cycle natural gas plants, the report finds. Fossil fuels are also subject to increasing price volatility, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran. Gas and coal power plants also emit air pollutants and the greenhouse gases causing climate change, leading to more health costs. Electricity bills have risen across the nation as utilities upgrade power grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.

articles.title: Anthropic signs lease for $10-billion Nova Scotia data centre
articles.text:
San Francisco-based Anthropic has been revealed as a long-term leaseholder for a large Nova Scotia data centre project—the AI giant’s first data centre in Canada.
The news: Halifax-based EverWind Fuels announced plans for a $10-billion data centre project at its existing campus in Point Tupper, NS, on Friday. The investment includes more than $8 billion to develop the campus, alongside $2 billion for its onshore wind energy portfolio.
The campus is planned to begin with a 95-megawatt (MW) phase in late 2027, followed by a 325 MW expansion slated for 2028. At full development, the campus would hold 420 MW in compute capacity.
While EverWind didn’t initially reveal the project’s inaugural long-term leaseholder, Anthropic told media that the data centre will power Claude models and serve growing demand from its Canadian and global customers.
From the source: “Canadians are using Claude in growing numbers, and we want our infrastructure to be closer to the people who rely on it,” Anthropic Canada Public Policy head Jacob Glick said in a statement, according to Global News. “Canada has set a high bar for responsible data centre development, as has the Premier of Nova Scotia, and we are committing to meeting it.”
The context: Anthropic and EverWind have both signed onto Canada’s Responsible Data Centre Development Principles, a voluntary, non-enforceable framework that guides hyperscalers and regulators on how data centre projects should consider factors like electricity and water use. So far, in line with the framework, EverWind has committed to fully funding all electricity system network upgrade costs associated with the project and to use a closed-loop cooling system.
Anthropic’s involvement in the project comes shortly after the company opened job postings for a Canadian data centre community engagement manager and compute lead, the latter of which would be responsible for bringing “gigawatts of compute online in Canada.”
Final thought: Despite public pushback, data centre projects continue to facilitate record-breaking investment for provinces. EverWind said its project represents the largest privately funded investment in Nova Scotia’s history, shortly after Bell’s $50-billion data centre buildout in Saskatchewan broke that province’s investment record as well.
Feature image courtesy Tim Houston via X.

articles.title: Anthropic creó un fondo de interés público para ayudar a la sociedad mientras crece Claude: destinará el 5% de sus acciones
articles.text:
Anthropic anunció que destinará el 5% de sus acciones a un nuevo fondo de beneficio público, sujeto a la aprobación de sus accionistas. La empresa detrás del asistente conversacional Claude informó que su directorio podrá sumar un 2% adicional de capital por cada aumento del 50% en la valoración de la compañía.
Anthropic es la compañía responsable de Claude, uno de los principales chatbots de inteligencia artificial, que compite de cerca con ChatGPT, de OpenAI, y con Gemini, de Google.
El nuevo vehículo se llama Fondo de Beneficio Público de Anthropic y funcionará como una sociedad de responsabilidad limitada de propiedad exclusiva de la empresa, no como una organización sin fines de lucro tradicional.
Según el comunicado oficial de la compañía, ese formato le da mayor flexibilidad para decidir cómo repartir el dinero, desde donaciones grandes a organizaciones sociales hasta transferencias directas a poblaciones específicas.
Anthropic precisó que ninguna porción del capital asignado al fondo se usará para actividades de cabildeo ni para contribuciones políticas, ni en Estados Unidos ni en otros países. La compañía adelantó que en los próximos meses dará a conocer más detalles sobre la estructura y el gobierno del fondo, incluidos los umbrales de valoración que podrían ampliar la participación.
El esquema está diseñado de manera que, cuanto más crezca el valor de Anthropic, mayor sea la porción de la empresa dedicada de forma expresa al bien público, según el texto difundido por la compañía.
El dinero y el impacto en el empleo
Entre los usos posibles que mencionó la empresa figura el impacto de la inteligencia artificial en los puestos de trabajo. “La inteligencia artificial podría generar un enorme valor económico, pero también provocar inestabilidad en muchos trabajadores”, advirtió Anthropic en su anuncio.
La compañía ya había destinado USD 200 millones a estudiar y atender ese problema, pero sostuvo que, dado el ritmo del progreso de la IA, podrían hacer falta enfoques más audaces para enfrentarlo. No precisó montos ni plazos para esas eventuales iniciativas adicionales.
Cuando se fundó la empresa, sus cofundadores se habían comprometido a donar el 80% de sus propias tenencias accionarias. Desde entonces, Anthropic también mantiene un programa de igualación de donaciones de capital en el que participa aproximadamente la mitad de su plantilla.
Sumado a este nuevo compromiso, cerca del 20% de las acciones de Anthropic quedará destinado al bien público, sin contar el porcentaje adicional que podría agregarse si la empresa alcanza determinados hitos de valoración, señaló la compañía.
Qué queda dentro de la empresa y qué pasa al fondo
Como sociedad de beneficio público, Anthropic explicó que gran parte de su trabajo en favor de su misión ya ocurre dentro de la propia empresa: investigación en seguridad e interpretabilidad de la inteligencia artificial, estudios biomédicos aplicados y descuentos en el acceso a Claude para organizaciones sin fines de lucro e instituciones científicas.
Esas actividades, según la compañía, combinan un componente de beneficio público con valor comercial, por lo que permanecen dentro de la estructura corporativa.
El nuevo fondo, en cambio, tendrá más escala para iniciativas que no encajan en ese esquema, como donaciones a terceros o transferencias directas de dinero a poblaciones puntuales.
Anthropic comparó la decisión con una práctica habitual en la industria tecnológica: ofrecer compensaciones accionarias crecientes a los ejecutivos a medida que sube el valor de una empresa. “En cambio, estamos dirigiendo ese capital al beneficio público”, señaló la compañía en su comunicado.
La industria de la IA bajo la lupa
El anuncio llega en medio de un clima de desconfianza pública hacia la industria de la inteligencia artificial. El director ejecutivo de Anthropic, Dario Amodei, describió ese escenario como “fundamentalmente una crisis de confianza”, según declaraciones recogidas por TechCrunch.
Anthropic opera como una sociedad de beneficio público, una figura legal que obliga a sus directivos a sopesar objetivos sociales además de las ganancias para los inversores. La compañía prepara una salida a bolsa que podría convertirse en una de las mayores de la historia bajo esa estructura, según informó la agencia Reuters.
La empresa, que se presenta como una firma centrada en la seguridad de sus sistemas, ya había expuesto los riesgos de sus propios modelos en el prospecto de esa oferta pública, donde mencionó que la IA podría exhibir comportamientos de “autoconservación”, de acuerdo con una exclusiva previa de la misma agencia.
Anthropic adelantó que en las próximas semanas publicará un informe de beneficio público con el detalle de los avances logrados hasta ahora respecto de su misión declarada, junto con la información pendiente sobre la gobernanza del nuevo fondo.

articles.title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
articles.text:
“We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating.
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.
Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal.
After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built.
That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X: “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.”
Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.”
I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.”
“I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.”
Knotted networks
It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge.
Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. (MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025.)
Back in 2020, Cammarata and his colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1. When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats.
The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Looking at other models appeared to back this up. The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot.
Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot. But despite a few breakthroughs, progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to understand an LLM in fine-grained detail.
Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says. But then he took the trouble to really look.
Nothing but neurons
At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks. He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don't know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says.
What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don't want to give up too quickly.”
Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith. Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias. When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’”
But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.”
Back to cars and cats
Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says. But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around. Take the car-and-cat neuron. Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common.
It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says. “But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently. It probably took me five seconds.”
It turns out that the image-recognition model was packing cars and cats into the same place because pictures of both those things often feature a prominent shape that looks like a V: the face of a cat; the front of a car seen from the side.
Cammarata ran a few experiments to check what other things the neuron responded to and found they included the corner of a pool table, the pointed nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water into the air from its deck. He also checked what turned the neuron off and found that it included images with a round O shape, a kind of anti-V.
The model had stored cats and cars in the same place because at some level they look the same, says Cammarata. “And I was like, ‘Whoa, okay, I think I might just be misunderstanding neural networks in general.’”
Cammarata is not saying that he yet fully gets how LLMs (or any models) work. Not even close. He is saying that he thinks full understanding is at least possible. “I previously thought there would be some really hard problems to solve,” he says.
“I now feel like if I had 100,000 years to go look through a frontier language model just one circuit at a time, there’s, like, a pretty good shot I would come up with a good understanding.”
He adds: “And if that's true, things are really good, because you’re about to get insanely smart agents at a ridiculous scale. And what would have taken me, you know, 100,000 years, we will be able to do much faster. Automated scientists are getting really good.”
Boundless optimism
Built by Google in 2014, Inception v1 is a far simpler model than anything at the cutting edge today. Cammarata and his colleagues have started looking at modern LLMs and plan to publish the technical results of that work soon. A lot of researchers are looking forward to seeing those details. “I appreciate that he looked at thousands of examples, but even a large number here is not a substitute for rigorous evaluation,” says Stanford University’s Potts.
In the meantime, some are pushing back hard on the hype. Jacob Hilton at the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit research lab based in Berkeley, who has collaborated with Cammarata in the past, doesn’t think his claims are as important as people are making out.
In a series of posts on X, Hilton notes that researchers understand less than 0.01% of the inner workings of top-tier LLMs. “I always appreciate Nick [Cammarata]’s boundless optimism when we hang out, but unfortunately this is giving the public an unrealistic picture of the state of the field,” he wrote. “For a full understanding, we need to go beyond neurons, and explain how they connect together to form circuits. How is this going? If we are aiming for a full understanding, things are not looking good!”
Neel Nanda at Google DeepMind, who helped pioneer mechanistic interpretability alongside Cammarata, is also skeptical. “This is interesting work, but I don’t think it’s a significant update to the big picture of interpretability,” he wrote on X.
Nanda agrees that understanding what individual neurons do could help researchers figure out why specific models misbehave. But like Hilton, he notes that neurons are just one piece of a far larger puzzle. “I do not agree with some people’s grander inferences like that this is substantial progress towards ambitious reverse engineering [or] solving interpretability,” he wrote.
Cammarata admits that a lot of people have taken what he said too far: “It’s not infinitely good news; it’s not everything solved,” he says. “There’s a bunch of open questions around, like how much the combinations of neurons matter versus just one at a time.”
Cammarata says his blog post landed at a time when people are looking for hope. In particular, he thinks the AI safety community—the researchers and policymakers most worried that powerful models will bring huge risks—needs a lifeline right now. They think that things are looking bad and that even if things do turn out okay, it will be because we got lucky, not because we fixed anything, he says: “I don’t really hear a lot of optimism.”
That’s why Cammarata thinks what he has to say matters. The job of figuring out how this technology works, and thus how to control it, has barely begun. But at least it’s not a nonstarter. “I think our job is to sort of try to think like the neural network,” he says. “My guess is that things will turn out pretty well, because it was in some sense designed to be read.”

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.
In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

articles.title: Estaba cansado de tener varios cargadores por casa; ahora unifico todo en una única base de carga y me ha cambiado la vida
articles.text:
En mi casa cada noche, justo antes de dormir, cuando ponemos a cargar el teléfono, siempre hay un poco de desorden. Somos dos personas, los dos con teléfono, reloj inteligente y auriculares y cada dispositivo con su propio cargador. Algo tan sencillo como poner a cargarlos era un poco jaleo porque o bien tienes todos los cargadores en los enchufes conectados las 24 horas del día, con todos los cables por ahí sueltos, o bien no encuentras el que necesitas en ese momento: como la base de carga para el reloj inteligente.
Por eso, hace unas semanas decidimos poner fin a eso. Al mismo tiempo que ponemos un poco de orden en cuanto a cables, hacemos que sea mucho más sencillo cargar todos los dispositivos. En concreto, hemos comprado la base de carga UGREEN MagFlow Pro 3 en 1, para teléfono, auriculares y reloj; y la base UGREEN MagFlow 2 en 1, para teléfono y auriculares.
Dos estaciones de carga simplemente perfectas
En mi caso uso un iPhone 18 Pro, un Apple Watch Series 10 y unos AirPods. En el caso de mi pareja, un iPhone 17 y unos AirPods. Los teléfonos los cargamos cada noche, mi reloj lo cargo cada dos días aproximadamente y en el caso de los auriculares, yo los cargo cada semana pero mi pareja un par de veces a la semana. Con esta actividad de carga, era necesario una estación de carga que pueda unificar en un único lugar todos los dispositivos.
A la hora de elegir la estación de carga perfecta para nosotros teníamos una serie de requisitos. La primera es la velocidad de carga. Acostumbrado a la potencia que nos da un cargador de pared, no queríamos procesos lentos de carga. En segundo lugar, queríamos una base de carga que fuese bonita. Si va a estar expuesta todo el día, tiene que ser bonita y cómoda, donde podamos dejar cada noche el dispositivo de una forma sencilla y segura.
Para reducir aún más el proceso de búsqueda, decidimos ir a una marca con prestigio, que más y mejores valoraciones positivas acumule. Y en este sentido, UGREEN es la número uno. Ya tenemos algún cable y algún cargador de ellos y cuando vimos que tenía estaciones de carga, lo tuvimos bastante claro.
UGREEN MagFlow Pro 3 en 1: el complemento perfecto para usuarios exigentes
En mi caso opté por la nueva serie MagFlow, que ha sufrido cambios considerables con respecto a la versión anterior. La estación de carga UGREEN MagFlow Pro 3 en 1 me entró por la vista desde el minuto uno, pero desde que la uso, estoy sencillamente encantado.
Uno de los aspectos más importantes y diferenciales es su sistema de refrigeración que mantiene en todo momento los dispositivos alejados de temperaturas altas. UGREEN llama a este sistema CryoPulse™ TEC Active Cooling System y lo que consigue es que el teléfono, mientras recibe potencias alta de carga, no se sobrecaliente, lo que podría afectar tanto al rendimiento como a su vida útil y salud de la propia batería.
Estamos hablando de potencias de carga de 25W usando la carga magnética, compatible con el estándar Qi2.2 . Sólo hay que acercar el teléfono por la parte del MagSafe y el teléfono empieza a cargar. En mi caso, he podido recargar la mitad de la batería de mi iPhone en menos de media hora. En el caso del Watch, recarga la batería de 0 al 80% en 30 minutos, perfecto mientras me ducho o desayuno por las mañanas. Y al mismo tiempo, también se cargan los AirPods. Es sin duda lo más cómodo que he visto en mucho tiempo: poder cargar los tres dispositivos, al mismo tiempo, y con potencias de carga muy buenas. 
Tanto el proceso de carga como la temperatura se puede controlar desde la pantalla que incorpora la base de carga. Puedes ver el estado de la carga de cada dispositivo de manera diferenciada.
Seguramente haya todavía personas que desconfían de otras marcas de cargadores diferentes al fabricante de su teléfono, pero en el caso de UGREEN no hay ningún motivo para preocuparse puesto que en todo momento, el proceso de carga es seguro, rápido y con la temperatura controlada.
UGREEN MagFlow 2 en 1: carga tu reloj y auriculares
Mi pareja, al no usar reloj inteligente, no necesita una base de carga tan completa como la mía. Además no tendría sentido comprar dos iguales. Sin embargo, al ver el modelo UGREEN MagFlow 2 en 1, lo tuvimos claro: compraríamos los dos modelos.
Es una estación de carga dos en uno, para teléfono y auriculares, pero sorprende mucho su tamaño compacto, plegable y que se puede guardar y llevar a cualquier lado. De hecho cuando hemos tenido que viajar, lo hemos llevado guardado en su bolso.
Aunque sea pequeño, anda sobrado de especificaciones. Primero en potencia, donde llega a los 25W con la carga inalámbrica, también usando el estándar Qi2.2 . En segundo lugar, la potencia de su imán magnético que se adhiere al teléfono con total seguridad y firmeza gracias al uso de hasta 16 imanes.
Su diseño también hace que no sólo funcione como una base de carga, sino también como trípode. Podemos colocarlo de tal manera que podemos seguir viendo nuestra serie favorita o hacer la videollamada que teníamos pendiente, sin que la falta de batería cambie nuestros planes.
Es una estación de carga sencilla, pero muy versátil y con un precio visiblemente inferior a la anterior. Aunque la base 3 en 1 es perfecta para mí, este modelo 2 en 1 es perfecto para el 99 por ciento de la población. Para personas que buscan simplificar los cables en su casa para tener estancias mucho más limpias.
Las dos bases de carga MagFlow se pueden comprar tanto en Amazon como en la propia tienda de UGREEN. Además te recomendamos que estés pendiente porque suelen estar sujetos a bastantes ofertas, lo cual hace que sea una compra todavía más recomendable.

articles.title: From Macro to Micro, and Back - EE Times
articles.text:
Looking at this year’s Nobel prizes, I was struck by how many of them explain the behavior of a large system through its smallest parts.
Four different Nobel prizes, one common theme
The medicine prize went to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel for optogenetics. Hegemann and Nagel found that a protein from green algae could make cells respond to light, and Deisseroth put its gene into neurons, so researchers can switch specific brain cells on and off with a flash of light. For the first time, neuroscientists could test what an individual neuron does and how groups of neurons produce memories, feelings, and behavior.
The chemistry prize went to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for their work on chirality, the property of molecules that come in two mirror-image forms, like our left and right hands. Living organisms use only one form of each, and the long-standing puzzle was how that happened. Soai found a reaction in which a minuscule imbalance between the two forms amplifies itself, which the Nobel Committee described as the first time anyone had created chirality from non-chiral molecules since the dawn of life. It is a striking example of micro shaping macro, since a tiny imbalance between individual molecules, amplified by feedback, ended up determining a property of all life on Earth.
The physics prize went to Francis Halzen for his decisive contributions to IceCube, a detector spanning a cubic kilometer of ice at the South Pole. Neutrinos barely interact with matter, so they cross the universe unimpeded and are extremely hard to catch. IceCube’s light sensors wait for the rare flash of a single neutrino interaction, and from those individual events physicists learn about cosmic sources too distant to observe by any other means.
Finally, the economics prize went to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, with a citation that says it outright: “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” After the Keynesian models seemed to fail in the oil crises of the 1970s, they helped rebuild models of the whole economy from the decisions of individual, forward-looking households and firms. Those models are now used by central banks and governments around the world.
How does this map to chip design?
All four prizes move from micro to macro, explaining a system through its parts. That is also how we have traditionally designed chips, bottom-up: from transistors to logic, from logic to blocks, and from blocks to a full system-on-chip.
In fact, chip design depends on abstraction. We characterize the smallest devices, package them into building blocks with well-defined behavior, and then stop thinking about what is inside. The next level uses those blocks the same way, all the way up to the system. Each level hides the details of the one below, and that hiding is what lets relatively small teams of engineers deliver a chip with billions of transistors.
Our design flow also runs top-down, of course. We start from a specification and work our way down to the physical implementation. But we descend the same ladder we climbed, one rung at a time, accepting the abstractions at each rung as given. A goal at the system level, such as performance per watt, never really sees the low-level choices that might serve it best, because the layers in between filter them out. To cope with the scale and complexity, we pay a margin of lost optimality that is hard to even measure. So it seems natural to ask what our field can take from these prizes, and in particular whether AI might help us cross these layers in both directions.
A glimpse from 2024
In hindsight, the 2024 chemistry prize previewed what AI can do here. It was shared between Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, for predicting a protein’s structure from its sequence, and David Baker, for designing new proteins starting from the shape and function he wanted. The first is micro to macro and the second macro to micro, and AI made both practical.
It is worth noting who led the first. Hassabis co-founded DeepMind, which Google acquired in 2014, and he is now chair of Google DeepMind and chief scientist of Alphabet. Since this was a chemistry prize, some eyebrows were raised that half of it went to computer scientists, and that same year the physics prize went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for their work on neural networks. This says something about how hard such methods will be pushed into other fields, ours included.
Reaching through the layers
AI is already automating individual steps of the chip design flow, and that is useful. The bigger change, IMHO, could come from being able to move between levels in both directions, testing a system-level objective directly against low-level choices without passing through every intermediate abstraction.
Micro to macro would let us predict, quickly and with reasonable accuracy, how a small change near the bottom of the stack ripples up to the power, performance, and area of the whole chip. Conversely, macro to micro would let us ask which low-level changes would best achieve a system-level target, and get useful candidates back. Together, they would turn abstraction layers from walls into something closer to windows.
It is worth being precise about where we are. Today, AI models can learn the behavior of one level well enough to serve as fast stand-ins for slow simulations, and they can propose designs across one or two levels in fairly bounded problems. Research is pushing toward models that link several levels at once, so a change at the bottom can be traced to its effect at the top. Reasoning freely across many levels of a full chip, in both directions, remains speculative.
The price of skipping layers
There are good reasons for caution. The first is that the downward direction is much harder than the upward one. Many different low-level configurations can produce the same system behavior, and some of them produce it only under the conditions you happened to test.
The second will be familiar to anyone in our industry. Abstraction is also a contract, and a layer with a clean, well-defined interface is a layer you can verify. Verification already consumes a large share of the effort on any chip, and if AI optimizes across those boundaries, we may lose the very structure we rely on to prove that a design works. IMHO, verification, more than generation, will decide how far this can go.
The third brings us back to the economics prize. Hall and Woodford’s work was needed because earlier models, built on statistical relationships between aggregate numbers, broke down when conditions changed. This is a word of warning about the limitations of AI models, which are themselves based on a limited set of training data, and statistical in nature. They can be excellent within the range they were trained on and badly wrong outside it. Moving across scales with learned models will require some caution.
A different role for abstraction
If this works, even partially, the role of abstraction in chip design changes. We would still need layers, because engineers need them to think, to divide work across teams and to verify results. But they might become a view we choose for a given question rather than a limit on what the design can reach. Designers could then spend less time on the hand-offs between levels and more on objectives and the tradeoffs that matter. Most importantly, we might reach levels of optimization that are out of reach today.
When Francis Halzen was asked what IceCube might reveal, he answered, as quoted by The Economist, “The real excitement is that I cannot answer that question yet.” I feel similarly here, so I will end with a question rather than a prediction. What happens when we no longer have to choose between thinking about the system and thinking about its smallest components?

articles.title: London-based “Surgical Intelligence” company XRlabs raises €7.48 million to bring AI into the operating room | EU-Startups
articles.text:
XRlabs, the London-based Surgical Intelligence company built by surgeons for surgeons, has raised €7.48 million ($8.4 million) in Seed funding.
The round was led by Playground Global, the DeepTech-focused venture firm based in Palo Alto, with participation from London-based HealthTech investor Eka Ventures. Alongside the fundraise, XRlabs also announced that Omar Ishrak, who led Medtronic as Chairman and CEO from 2011 to 2020 and previously served as chairman of Intel’s board, has joined as Chair of its Board of Directors.
“The best physical AI companies come from people who’ve experienced a problem in their field firsthand and have the deep expertise to know how to fix it,” said Bruce Leak, General Partner at Playground Global.
Founded by practising neurosurgeon Dr. Ali Haddad in 2024, XRlabs is headquartered in London at the London Institute for Healthcare Engineering, with a second office in Palo Alto, California. The company develops modular, device-agnostic software that sits as an external AI layer across the surgical systems hospitals already own.
Its platform uses computer vision and deep learning to transform live video from surgical scopes, navigation telemetry, and pre-operative CT and MRI imaging into a single real-time, anatomy-aware view of each procedure. XRlabs says its platform has been deployed across more than 100 surgical cases on three continents.
The company offers two core products: XRlabs SIM and SurgicalOS. The XRlabs SIM is a patient-specific planning and rehearsal tool that transforms standard CT and MRI scans into interactive 3D reality models or digital twins, while SurgicalOS is an intraoperative intelligence layer that brings the digital twin created in SIM into the live operative view.
The XRlabs SIM and SurgicalOS together form what the company describes as “Pyramid of Surgical Intelligence,” a layered approach to building AI surgical understanding that mirrors how surgeons are trained, starting from anatomy and building toward real-time operative skill.
“Our conviction is that the operating room is the next frontier for physical AI. Surgery generates extraordinary data, yet almost none of it becomes intelligence in the moments that matter most. This financing lets us change that at scale, moving Surgical Intelligence from landmark first cases to foundational infrastructure in every operating room,” said Dr. Haddad, founder and CEO of XRlabs.
The funding comes on the back of major clinical achievements, including first-in-human use of physical AI in cranial neurosurgery, integrated with an ORBEYE 4K 3D exoscope under research conditions and a world-first in AI-designed patient-specific implants, used in the successful separation of craniopagus twins.
XRlabs says it will use the Seed funding to support the buildout of its engineering and clinical teams, advance its products through regulatory pathways in the UK, Europe, and the US, while extending the clinical evidence base at partner institutions globally. The company has also been awarded a compute allocation on the UK AI Research Resource (AIRR), the UK’s national AI compute infrastructure, which supports the development and scaling of its AI capabilities.

articles.title: Investitionsgipfel: Warum Milliardenversprechen der Bundesregierung nicht reichen
articles.text:
Investitionsgipfel: An diesen Stellschrauben muss die Bundesregierung drehen
Deutschland braucht dringend mehr Investitionen. Die Bundesregierung will deshalb am Montag und Dienstag beim Investitionsgipfel in Berlin internationale Wirtschaftsentscheider:innen davon überzeugen, hierzulande zu investieren. Mit Nvidia-Chef Jensen Huang ist sogar einer der derzeit gefragtesten Manager der Technologiebranche in Berlin dabei. Doch prominente Gäste und große Investitionsversprechen allein werden die deutsche Wirtschaft nicht wieder in Schwung bringen. Dass der Nvidia-Chef hier auftritt, ist kein Zufall. Die Bundesregierung sieht in künstlicher Intelligenz – wenig überraschend – eine der wichtigsten Schlüsseltechnologien für die nächsten Jahre. Nvidia könnte sich laut Medienberichten zum Standort Deutschland bekennen und industrielle KI, Robotik und leistungsfähige KI-Modelle damit voranbringen.
Doch damit es Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz zusammen mit Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche (beide CDU) und Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) gelingt, Milliardenbeträge und neue Technologiestandorte einzuwerben, braucht es mehr als warme Worte. Die Anlageinvestitionen in Deutschland sind zwischen 2019 und 2025 um 6,4 Prozent gesunken, während die im restlichen Euroraum im selben Zeitraum um 6,7 Prozent anstiegen, in den USA sogar um 20,2 Prozent zulegten.
Dass diese Bilanz so ausfällt, hat weniger mit fehlendem Vertrauen und fehlendem Kapital zu tun, sondern eher mit den Rahmenbedingungen, unter denen sich Investitionen zuverlässig planen und wirtschaftlich umsetzen lassen. Deutschland muss hier konkret werden – und an jenen Stellschrauben drehen, die in der Vergangenheit zu wirtschaftlichem Wachstum und Wohlstand beigetragen haben.
Da ist zunächst einmal die Bürokratie: Wenn wir ehrlich sind, kommt die im Koalitionsvertrag versprochene Bürokratieentlastung bislang weder bei den Unternehmen noch bei jedem einzelnen von uns an. In einer Ifo-Umfrage vom September 2026 nannte jedes zweite der befragten Unternehmen Bürokratie und Regulierung als größtes Standortproblem. Das beginnt bei Dokumentationspflichten und beim Ausfüllen von branchenspezifischen Formularen, hat aber vor allem auch mit der Komplexität und zeitlichen Unberechenbarkeit von Genehmigungen zu tun. Gerade für investierende Unternehmen bedeutet das, nicht verlässlich kalkulieren zu können, wann sich eine Maßnahme rechnen wird.
Natürlich kann das nicht heißen, dass sämtliche Vorschriften abgeschafft werden, denn Genehmigungsverfahren erfüllen wichtige Funktionen beim Umwelt-, Sicherheits- und Verbraucherschutz. Dennoch ließe sich manches vereinfachen, ohne die gewohnten Standards aufzugeben. Ziel muss es daher sein, verbindliche Bearbeitungsfristen und parallele Prüfungen vorzugeben – und einen digitalen Zugang für alle Beteiligten zu schaffen. So könnten Unternehmen zentral alle Genehmigungen beantragen, die beteiligten Behörden hätten Zugriff auf sämtliche Erkenntnisse der anderen Beteiligten und Daten, die einer Behörde bereits vorliegen, müssten nicht erneut eingefordert werden.
Klingt vielleicht utopisch, ist aber in skandinavischen und baltischen Ländern schon üblich. Und auch die Initiative „Gemeinsam Schneller Gründen“ des Bundesdigitalministeriums zeigt, dass das mit der zentralen Anlaufstelle auch in Deutschland in vielen Fällen gut funktioniert. Ziel sollte es daher sein, die Zeit zwischen Investitionsentscheidung und Projektbeginn deutlich zu straffen und entsprechende Kennzahlen als aussagekräftiges Signal an die Wirtschaft zu schicken.
KI-Infrastruktur und –Anwendung müssen gemeinsam gedacht werden
Dass Deutschland mit seiner vielfältigen Industrie, seinen Forschungseinrichtungen und seiner großen Zahl an Hidden Champions über gute Voraussetzungen verfügt, KI-Technologien in konkrete Anwendungen zu überführen, daran besteht kein Zweifel. Doch nachhaltiges Wachstum ist mehr als der Bau großer Rechenzentren. Es funktioniert nur, wenn die Unternehmen die KI produktiv einsetzen und daraus neue Produkte und Dienstleistungen oder effizientere Prozesse entstehen.
Es geht daher nicht nur um die großen Leuchtturmprojekte, die medienwirksam angekündigt werden (und in der Vergangenheit dann nicht in allen Fällen Realität wurden), sondern vielmehr auch um den Nachholbedarf im Mittelstand.
Laut dem KfW-Digitalisierungsbericht 2025 haben zuletzt nur noch 30 Prozent der Mittelständler Digitalisierungsprojekte durchgeführt – weniger als vor der Pandemie. Auch die Digitalisierungsausgaben sind gesunken. Wenn also über industriellen KI-Einsatz gesprochen wird, kann es nicht nur um prominente Großprojekte gehen, sondern vor allem auch um die gesamte Wirtschaft.
Standort für Startups und Scaleups attraktiver machen
Neben dem Mittelstand könnte aber vor allem aus der Startup- und Scaleup-Welt nachhaltige Innovation kommen. Hier hat sich in den letzten Jahren das Bild verändert: Investorenkapital fließt vor allem in einige wenige Unternehmen, wohingegen viele andere weiterhin Schwierigkeiten haben, ihre nächste Wachstumsphase zu finanzieren.
Auch wenn die USA über viele Jahre als bevorzugter Platz für Gründer:innen mit besten politischen und wirtschaftlichen Rahmenbedingungen galten, sind zuletzt gerade einige KI- und Deep-Tech-Unternehmen wie Codesphere, Langdock und Focused Energy nach Deutschland zurückgekehrt. Sie berichten durchaus davon, dass Kunden diesen Reverse Flip im Hinblick auf digitale Souveränität und Planbarkeit schätzen.
Doch damit Deutschland in der Startup-Welt relevant bleibt, braucht es neben dem entsprechenden Investitionsklima auch verlässliche Vorgaben, mit denen die Unternehmen arbeiten können. Das gilt insbesondere für die steuerlichen Rahmenbedingungen sowie für Rechtssicherheit im Kontext mit KI‑Entwicklungen. In diesem Bereich hat Deutschland in den letzten Jahren schon an vielen Stellen EU-Recht mitgestaltet.
Zwischen Grundstimmung und harten Fakten
Letzten Endes wird aber auch ein weiterer Faktor relevant sein, wenn es darum geht, dass das „starke Willkommenssignal“, das die Bundesregierung senden will, bei den Entscheider:innen auch verfängt: die Grundstimmung im Land. Deutschland steht nämlich in einigen Feldern deutlich besser da, als es in den öffentlichen Debatten über den Standort rüberkommt: Da sind zum einen solide Staatsfinanzen mit einem Triple-A-Rating (als einziger G7-Staat), zum anderen immer noch hervorragende Forschungseinrichtungen und Universitäten mit gut ausgebildeten Fachkräften (insbesondere in Bereichen wie Biotechnologie und künstlicher Intelligenz).
All das könnte für eine nach wie vor hohe Innovationskraft stehen. Auch bei den Patentanmeldungen am Europäischen Patentamt liegt Deutschland weit vorne. Hinzu kommen die zentrale geografische Lage, die Größe und Bedeutung des Marktes und nicht zuletzt der Zugang zum europäischen Binnenmarkt. Dass diese Faktoren international schon wahrgenommen werden, belegt eine aktuelle Befragung der Deutschen Bank unter 1.200 Führungskräften aus außereuropäischen Ländern. Demnach ist Deutschland das attraktivste Investitionsziel innerhalb Europas. Der Blick von außen fällt damit positiver aus, als es die wirtschaftspolitische Debatte hierzulande vermuten lässt.
Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz warb erst vor wenigen Tagen beim Deutschen Arbeitgebertag für mehr Zuversicht – und verhedderte sich in der Frage, ob das Glas nun halb voll oder halb leer sei. Tatsächlich spricht einiges dafür, Deutschlands wirtschaftliche Perspektiven nicht ausschließlich durch die Brille der aktuellen Probleme zu betrachten.
Und doch lässt sich Zuversicht nicht einfach verordnen, sie entsteht dann, wenn Reformen greifen und sich wieder wirtschaftliche Erfolge einstellen. Vielleicht ist also gerade das die zentrale Aufgabe, die auf die Bundesregierung nach dem Investitionsgipfel zukommt: dafür zu sorgen, dass das Glas mit schnellen Sozialreformen tatsächlich voller wird – statt nur darüber zu diskutieren, wie voll es bereits ist.
