articles.title: Copenhagen’s Plinto raises €2.9 million to help finance teams catch and fix errors with AI agents | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Plinto, a Copenhagen-based startup building AI for real-time controlling, has secured €2.9 million in pre-Seed funding.
The round was led by People Ventures and Emblem, with participation from a group of business angels.
“Companies have systems that record every single transaction, but checking whether those transactions actually match agreements and rules is still largely manual. We’re building AI agents that find deviations, investigate them and take action, so errors get fixed,” said Jakob Nielsen, co-founder and CDO of Plinto.
Plinto was founded in early 2025 by Nermina Suljevic, Nielsen, and Sebastian Rehnby, who previously worked for Peakon, the employee engagement platform acquired by US-based Workday in 2021. The company’s CTO Andreas Garnæs is also an alumnus of Peakon. Together, they bring experience across product development, engineering, commercial scaling, and working with large international organisations.
In large organisations, the volume of financial transactions exceeds what finance teams can review manually. This work is handled by controllers, who typically resort to spot checks or end-of-month reconciliations, leaving enough room for errors such as incorrect prices, duplicate invoices, or mismatched deliveries.
Plinto wants to solve this problem with AI agents that sit on top of the systems companies already use, such as ERP, documents, bank, and collaboration tools like Slack or Microsoft Teams.
When a transaction is flagged, Plinto’s agents are designed not only to alert someone but also to investigate, gather evidence, and follow up with relevant people within the organisation and external contacts. Plinto says the agents are capable of contacting a supplier about a wrongful invoice, requesting a credit note or preparing a correction for approval.
It says one of its customers uncovered around 430 deviations per month in a single part of the business. At another customer, the agents identified a duplicate invoice submitted with a different supplier name in the same minute it arrived.
“Many of our customers work with low margins, so even small errors can quickly add up. The problem is that they’re often only discovered after the money has been paid. We want companies to catch and fix errors before they hit the bottom line,” said Suljevic, co-founder and CEO of Plinto.
Plinto platform integrates with major ERP platforms, including Microsoft Business Central, Xero, and Visma, and connects to major Scandinavian banks as well as over 2,700 other banks. It counts paying customers and pilots in logistics, real estate, facility services, and food production. The platform covers both order-to-cash and procure-to-pay workflows, and all data is processed and stored within the EU. Plinto also says it never uses customer data to train AI models.
The company plans to use the pre-Seed funding for product development, bringing on more enterprise customers and making Plinto’s first move outside Denmark. It wants to bring its agents to enterprises beyond its home market and aims to help them find financial errors in real time.

articles.title: Tu gato te ignora en apariencia, pero en secreto sincroniza sus hormonas con las tuyas
articles.text:
Por lo general, los perros suelen concebirse como mascotas mucho más cariñosas que los gatos. Sin embargo, algo tienen los gatos, incluso con esa mirada que parece que nos juzga y su eterno pasotismo, que también nos enamora. Por eso hay tantas personas incapaces de imaginar su vida sin un gato como compañero. A su manera, les hacen sentir bien. Pero la ciencia no tiene eso tan claro. Hay estudios que señalan que tener un gato como mascota puede incluso aumentar nuestros niveles de estrés. Otros contradicen esta hipótesis y apuntan a que nos aporta múltiples beneficios.
No parece que haya resultados claros al respecto, pero cada vez comprendemos mejor nuestra relación con los gatos, gracias a estudios como el que acaba de publicar un equipo de científicos de la Universidad de Kioto. En él, sugieren que sí es bueno para nosotros tener gato. Siempre y cuando pasemos suficiente tiempo juntos.
Una cuestión de hormonas. En este estudio participaron 29 gatos y 19 dueños que llevaban distinto tiempo conviviendo. Para comprobar cómo afectan unos al bienestar de los otros, se tomaron muestras de orina de todos para medir los niveles de dos hormonas muy vinculadas a este. Por un lado, la oxitocina. Esta se conoce como la hormona del amor, aunque podría considerarse más bien como hormona del apego, pues influye mucho en que nos encariñamos y nos sintamos unidos a nuestras mascotas, parejas, hijos o amigos. No se trata solo de amor romántico. Por otro lado, se midieron los niveles de cortisol, una hormona que suele elevarse en situaciones de estrés.
Además de todo eso, los gatos llevaban collares con balizas Bluetooth que permitían a los investigadores analizar a qué distancia se encuentran normalmente de sus dueños. Así, comprobaron que, cuanto más tiempo pasan juntos, más se sincronizan sus hormonas.
Efectos en el estado de ánimo. Se vio una correlación positiva entre los niveles de oxitocina de los gatos y sus amigos humanos. Cuanto mayores eran los de unos, más altos eran también los de otros. Pero no solo eso. También hubo una correlación negativa y cruzada con los niveles de cortisol. Esto significa que, cuando los niveles de oxitocina del gato aumentaban, disminuían los niveles de cortisol de su humano.
Y, ojo, hay algo mucho más curioso: los niveles de oxitocina en los gatos estaban más asociados con los estados de ánimo negativos de su dueño que con los propios niveles de oxitocina de este. Es decir, la relación no se limita a que, cuando sube la oxitocina del gato, baje el cortisol del humano. También podría ocurrir que, cuando el humano está estresado o agobiado, algo que hace que aumenten sus niveles de cortisol, cambie también la oxitocina de su amigo peludo. Con una correlación no se puede saber en qué dirección va la influencia, pero la oxitocina del gato parece acompasarse con el estado de ánimo del humano.
Los antecedentes. En el pasado, se han realizado estudios de todo tipo. En algunos se ha visto que tener un gato puede disminuir el bienestar emocional de los adolescentes. Otros sí encuentran efectos positivos en el bienestar de una persona cuando esta adopta un gato, pero desaparecen muy deprisa. En este caso, el tiempo no disminuye los efectos, lo que los disminuye es la lejanía a los gatos. El estudio sí que sugiere un efecto muy positivo de la relación gato-humano, pero requiere cercanía. Es cierto que los gatos suelen ser más ariscos que los perros, pero también nos buscan y es en ese vínculo donde parece estar el truco.
Limitaciones en el estudio. Este estudio tiene dos grandes limitaciones. Por un lado, es puramente observacional. Se encontraron correlaciones, pero no se exploraron las causas. Por otro lado, se llevó a cabo con pocos humanos y gatos. Para tener unos resultados más sólidos sería importante aumentar el tamaño de la muestra, con más gatos y humanos y, además, explorar las posibles causas de los efectos que se han encontrado. Podría ser el siguiente paso de estos científicos. Sea como sea, quienes comparten su vida con un gato saben bien que no hace falta un estudio que les demuestre que su relación es beneficiosa y especial.

articles.title: Sam Altman confirmó un robot humanoide: creado por OpenAI y con ChatGPT
articles.text:
El director ejecutivo de OpenAI, Sam Altman, confirmó que la empresa va a construir un robot humanoide y adelantó que habrá una demostración pública en 2027, aunque descartó que esos robots circulen por la calle en el corto plazo.
La confirmación llegó en dos entrevistas distintas. En el pódcast Sources, le preguntaron de manera directa si OpenAI fabricaría un robot humanoide. Su respuesta fue breve: “We will” (lo vamos a hacer), según citó Engadget.
A Fortune, Altman agregó el horizonte de tiempo: “Creo que vamos a tener una demostración genial en 2027... no creo que vaya a haber robots caminando por las calles por varios años más”, dijo, de acuerdo con el mismo reporte de Engadget, replicado también por el medio indio Mint.
OpenAI no precisó qué va a mostrar esa demostración, qué forma tendrá el robot ni cuándo alguien ajeno a la empresa podrá acercarse a uno. Ahora bien, se entiende que el ‘cerebro’ del autómata estaría impulsado por la tecnología de ChatGPT, la inteligencia artificial con la que la compañía se dio a conocer globalmente.
Por qué eligió la forma humana
Altman explicó que adoptar una anatomía de dos brazos y dos piernas responde a una lógica práctica y no estética. “El mundo está diseñado para personas”, sostuvo, según la misma nota.
Puertas, teclados y herramientas de uso cotidiano asumen un tipo de cuerpo determinado, por lo que un robot que deba moverse en esos mismos espacios conviene que replique ese formato. “Igualar ese tipo de forma parece una buena idea”, afirmó.
Sin embargo, el diseño físico no es, para Altman, el obstáculo central. Las preguntas sobre la apariencia del robot son “menos importantes que resolver de verdad... el cerebro que hace funcionar al robot”, señaló.
Esa distinción resume el desafío técnico de fondo: un cuerpo con brazos y piernas no sirve de mucho si el sistema que lo controla no sabe qué hacer con ellos. Levantar una taza, por ejemplo, exige identificar el objeto, ubicar el asa y calcular la fuerza justa para no derramar el contenido.
Una carrera que ya tiene competidores
OpenAI no llega a un terreno vacío. Tesla trabaja desde hace años en su robot Optimus, y la automotriz china XPENG mostró recientemente a su humanoide IRON saliendo de manera autónoma de la línea de ensamblaje tras ser armado.
La compañía ya tiene antecedentes propios en robótica. Su proyecto Dactyl entrenó hace años una mano robótica, íntegramente en simulación, para manipular objetos reales, y luego aplicó esa misma técnica para resolver un cubo Rubik.
Para avanzar en la nueva etapa, OpenAI mantiene abiertas 27 búsquedas laborales en robótica, que abarcan control de movimiento, estimación de posición, control de actuadores y comportamiento integral del robot, además de la infraestructura de aprendizaje automático necesaria para entrenar sistemas de inteligencia artificial física.
Otro grupo de esas búsquedas apunta a actuadores electromecánicos propios, con motores, transmisiones, sensores y sistemas térmicos diseñados a medida, mientras que un tercer grupo cubre manufactura y cadena de suministro para una eventual producción a mayor escala.
Un objetivo que empieza en la fábrica
Según una de esas publicaciones de empleo, el plan de corto plazo de OpenAI no apunta todavía a un robot doméstico. El primer objetivo son robots de uso general que ayuden a trabajadores calificados a construir infraestructura, mientras que la meta de largo plazo es un robot personal capaz de realizar una variedad mucho más amplia de tareas.
Por ahora, la empresa no difundió precio, fecha de lanzamiento comercial ni ninguna especificación técnica del humanoide. La próxima señal pública sobre el proyecto será, según lo que adelantó Altman, la demostración prevista para 2027.

articles.title: Amazon to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at former Indiana coal plant | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon is funding development of a proposed 960-megawatt nuclear plant in Indiana and would be the first customer to buy its power, the companies announced Monday. Utility company American Electric Power (AEP) would operate the plant. X-energy, which designs small modular nuclear reactors and went public in April, would supply the reactors.
The new power plant would consist of 12 Xe-100 small modular reactors and be located on the site of a demolished coal power plant just south of Terre Haute. The deal is the second commercial agreement between Amazon and X-energy, and it’s three times larger than the first, which was announced two years ago.
Amazon has invested heavily in X-energy, leading a $700 million Series C-1 round in October 2024. The two companies have said they ultimately plan to build 5 gigawatts of new nuclear generating capacity in the U.S. by 2039.
Unlike many newly announced power plants, these reactors would be connected to the public electric grid, though Amazon says the power would also serve its data centers.
The companies’ aggressive timeline still depends on X-energy successfully delivering its first power plant at a Dow Chemical plant southeast of Houston, Texas. The site, called Seadrift, has recently been at the center of a lawsuit filed by the state of Texas, which accuses the plant of “habitual non-compliance” with water and solid-waste regulations and permits.
X-energy has yet to break ground at Seadrift, which will host four Xe-100 reactors to provide the chemical plant with heat and electricity. The company said its construction permit is in the final phases of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s review process.
Startups and large cloud computing companies are betting that small modular reactors (SMRs), like the kind being developed by X-energy, will help pull the nuclear industry out of its slump. The most recent nuclear power plants built in the U.S. suffered from egregious budget overruns and slipped timelines.
By shrinking the reactor, companies like X-energy hope that mass manufacturing will keep costs and schedules in line. Even then, it could be a tall order. Experts say mass manufacturing often doesn’t start producing benefits for about a decade.
X-energy debuted on the Nasdaq in April in an IPO priced at $23 per share. Investor excitement drove the price up 27% in the first day of trading, but shares of the newly public company have dropped by nearly two-thirds since then.
News of the Amazon deal sent X-energy’s shares up about 10% in premarket trading, though they were down by less than 2% at the time of publication.

articles.title: Crossing the threshold to dependable open source AI serving
articles.text:
When large open weight models first captured attention, the industry was faced with a challenge. Powerful open models were becoming available, but technologists lacked an open inference serving system that could run them efficiently. Having spent years building inference engines for CPUs, my team and I redirected all of our energy toward the vLLM project. Together with the community, vLLM capabilities expanded to become the de facto inference server. Today the vLLM project, now part of the PyTorch foundation, has a vibrant community of companies and developers actively adding support for new models, hardware, and research techniques.
As Red Hat continued this work, conversations with our enterprise users exposed a new reality. Getting a single server to perform efficiently was table stakes. The next challenge was orchestrating model serving at cluster scale. Last spring, we announced the llm-d project to address this, developing an open source, Kubernetes-native orchestration layer for distributed LLM serving across multi-tenant production clusters. Today, Red Hat and our community partners announced the release of llm-d 1.0. Reaching this milestone reflects a project hitting full maturity, shaped by hardened code, stability proven under real production load, and widespread adoption across an expanding contributor community. Open source AI serving has crossed from an experimental science project into dependable infrastructure you can build on.
What project maturity and code hardening look like on day 2
In early open source experiments, teams measure progress through isolated benchmark runs on pristine hardware. Keeping an AI service healthy on day 2, when hundreds of automated agents and human users contend for shared resources, requires an entirely different operational discipline.
Platform teams came to us with a clear dilemma: What happens when a developer debugging code on an interactive session gets stalled because an autonomous background agent flooded the GPU pool with dozens of parallel tool calls? Building for day 2 means solving these friction points directly in the request path. Over the past year, our contributor community focused on intense code hardening. We built priority-aware flow control so latency-sensitive queries from interactive users do not get starved by bursty background agents. We engineered router high availability with hot standby and coordinated rolling updates, letting operators upgrade models and runtimes without dropping live traffic. Code hardening is about stripping away operational surprises so platform teams can run distributed inference like standard enterprise plumbing rather than fragile custom code.
Stability proven under production load
Stability cannot be established on synthetic benchmarks alone. It has to survive real-world scale where agent contexts expand over hours of execution and accelerator memory faces unrelenting pressure. When multi-turn workloads repeatedly hit unmanaged clusters, naive load balancers scatter requests, wiping out cached prefix state and triggering massive recomputation costs.
llm-d delivers production-scale stability by making the orchestration layer aware of inference dynamics. It preserves context locality, disaggregates prefill from decode phases, and balances work across heterogeneous accelerator pools. In production, this operational stability creates dramatic efficiencies. At IBM Research, exploring quantum error correction hardware on llm-d generated multi-turn workloads with massive context reuse identical to agentic coding loops. That deployment yielded a 98% prefix-cache hit rate and reduced blended serving costs five to ten times compared to proprietary options.
In benchmark demonstrations, researchers used llm-d to deploy GLM-5.2, an approximately 753-billion-parameter open weight model on widely deployed NVIDIA GPUs, showcasing how enterprises can use existing GPU fleets to serve frontier-class AI at scale. On a workload with hundreds of agentic sessions running in parallel, llm-d delivered over 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak on agentic benchmarks. The cluster sustained up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents with zero preemptions, demonstrating that llm-d can efficiently serve large mixture-of-experts models for agentic workloads.
Wide adoption across an expanding ecosystem
A mature infrastructure project earns credibility through the community that builds it and the teams that trust it when traffic spikes. Today, the llm-d community has more than 500 contributors across 25 organizations, all building openly under CNCF governance.
That shared investment is already active in production across frontier model labs, hyperscalers and neoclouds, and major enterprises. At Red Hat, we bring this hardened stack directly to our users through Red Hat AI Inference, whether they run it natively within Red Hat OpenShift AI or across third-party Kubernetes environments.
llm-d and PyTorch
Celebrating a new version of a project governed under the CNCF at PyTorch Conference North America highlights how modern computing is evolving. Distributed inference sits directly at the seam between deep learning runtimes and cloud native orchestration. What happens in the orchestration layer directly influences what model runtimes can accomplish.
Model developers and silicon partners drive rapid innovation inside PyTorch, while the CNCF community provides decades of operational rigor for distributed systems. Placing llm-d under CNCF governance was a conscious step to keep the control plane vendor-neutral and eliminate ecosystem friction. It builds an open bridge between both communities. Platform teams can orchestrate complex, multi-accelerator clusters using standard cloud native workflows, while retaining the low-level execution speed built by model authors in PyTorch.
Get involved with the llm-d and PyTorch communities
The future of open source AI will not be locked inside closed-source serving stacks. It’s being built openly by researchers, runtime developers, and platform operators working together across foundation borders. While 1.0 represents a major operational milestone, our community is already moving forward to support emerging hardware architectures, larger model shapes, and evolving agent patterns.
We invite you to help shape that future. Check out the project on GitHub, join the conversation, and collaborate with both the llm-d and PyTorch communities as we build durable infrastructure for open source AI serving.

articles.title: The Miles plug promises to track your car and send help if needed without selling your data
articles.text:
My 15-year-old daughter just got her learner’s permit, so when I was pitched a new gadget tailored to teen drivers, I was intrigued. The Miles Plug is a small device that plugs into your car’s OBD-II port and monitors location, driving habits, and vehicle health, along with emergency accident response and roadside assistance.
I tried a $99 plug that promises to track your car and send help when needed — without selling your data
The Miles Plug adds crash detection, roadside help, location tracking, and a warning-light decoder to your car for as low as $11 a month.
The idea is that knowing all these things should help me feel more comfortable when my daughter starts driving alone. I tested the (now discontinued) Ring Car Cam when my son was learning to drive, but he hated it and refused to turn it on; I wondered if the Miles could provide the same peace of mind without feeling as intrusive.
Billed as “a wearable for your car,” Miles is a tiny cellular and GPS-enabled device that connects to an app to deliver real-time location, alerts, and driving insights (speeding, hard braking, trip recaps). The app also features an AI chatbot called the Miles Mechanic that decodes warning lights, tells you how urgent a fix is, and estimates repair costs.
Miles was developed by cofounders Matt McGovren and Kit Klein, who have a solid smart home pedigree. They worked at Wink in the early days and bring combined experience from Amazon (Ring and Blink), Ubiquiti’s smart home line, and other companies. “We built Miles to support teens and parents together, and keep them on the same team,” said McGovren in a press release. “Parents and teens see the same trips and the same alerts with nothing hidden, building trust instead of suspicion.”
You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.
— Matt McGovren
Miles is available today at mileslabs.com and costs $99, plus $180 for a year of membership ($279 total, or $15 a month). A three-year plan is $396 with the Plug included ($11 a month). All plans are paid upfront with no auto-renewal. Anyone in the family can download and use the app, with each driver getting their own profile and alerts. Miles says it’s compatible with most gas and hybrid cars from 2008 onward and some EVs (there’s a compatibility checker).
While the prices seem steep, McGovren’s pitch is that it covers several services you might already be paying for: “You could piece together a roadside service, a family tracking service … and then you’re looking at $30, $40 a month,” he said in an interview with The Verge. And, unlike your car’s own branded app, Miles isn’t selling your data. Automakers have been caught collecting and selling driving data, with GM being banned from selling data to brokers for five years.
McGovren says Miles will never sell vehicle, trip, or location data, and the app has no ads: “You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.” He says, “All the vehicle and trip data is encrypted,” adding that “the most sensitive data is end-to-end encrypted.” Additionally, the location data is tied to the car, not the phone, so it stops tracking when you walk away. The app lets you download your data, stop location collection, and delete your account and all its data.
I set up Miles in my 2014 Toyota Highlander I nicknamed Tanya and have been using it for a couple of days. Setup was simple, and the app is clean, uncluttered, and easy to follow. It took me through a few setup screens, including asking to share my phone’s location to relay data from the Plug over Bluetooth when cell service is spotty. I plugged it into my OBD-II port, and it read my VIN and correctly identified my car.
It logs every trip with route, distance, time, and driver initials (I haven’t had my daughter download the app yet; I’m interested to see whose phones it connects to when we’re both in the car). Arrived- and left-home alerts came through promptly, and the events tab flagged hard acceleration and a cluster of three hard-braking alerts when I was running a little late to collect my daughter from work.
I like the home card, which shows a vehicle health summary: engine OK, fuel 63%, battery 13.5V, and the odometer reading. I played with the Miles Mechanic chatbot and asked how my car is and what upcoming maintenance is due; it answered in plain English, telling me the cabin air filter is due at about 140,000 miles, and the oil change and tire rotation at 142,500.
I haven’t been testing it long enough to comment on battery drain, an issue with earlier products in this space. “It goes to sleep when your car is not driving or not on,” says McGovren. “We use a little bit of data to wake up and sync, but [that] doesn’t have a material impact on the battery.” He advises removing it if you won’t be driving the car for a while.
Beyond car battery life, an obvious concern for prospective users is how long Miles the company will last. Startup Automatic had a similar idea back in 2016, launching the Automatic Pro for $130 that plugged into your OBD-II port, tracked mileage and location, and monitored for crashes over a 3G radio. The service shut down in 2020. Miles is basically Automatic but with a business model; Automatic didn’t initially charge a monthly fee, Miles does.
McGovren says he and his team have seen a lot of “scar tissue from the smart home,” with companies that “thought they could make money later.” Both founders were at Wink during its outage, bankruptcy, and eventual sale to will.i.am’s company. Charging for membership upfront is meant to avoid that type of outcome. He says the company is “well capitalized” and offers a 60-day money-back guarantee to users.
The car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app.
— Matt McGovren
Automatic also had several smart-home tie-ins, but at launch Miles doesn’t connect to your smart home. McGovren says they have an MCP server in beta that could deliver “all of this information … to your AI of choice, your home assistant of choice,” he says. “And now the car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app.” He envisions a future where you own your car’s data and can connect it to any service you want, and be able to ask Alexa, Siri, or Google, “When’s my next oil change?” or “How much gas is in my car?”
Miles is pitched as a solution for monitoring your teen driver, including notifications of possible crashes and risky driving, without also having to monitor their phone. But it also feels like a good solution for anyone with an older car or who doesn’t want to rely on data-tracking apps from insurance companies or car manufacturers but wants easy access to their car’s data. I plan to test it more thoroughly, hopefully try out the MCP integration, and follow up with a full review.
Photography and screenshots by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: 9 Minuten Laden, 90 Minuten Arbeit: Neue Akkus sollen den Digits 5 zum echten Haushaltshelfer machen
articles.text:
9 Minuten Laden, 90 Minuten Arbeit: Neue Akkus sollen den Digits 5 zum echten Haushaltshelfer machen
Der humanoide Roboter Digit 5 von Agility Robotics hat eine besonders lange Laufzeit bei kurzem Aufladen. Die Batterietechnik dafür liefert das Unternehmen Nyobolt. Damit kommt der Roboter auf ein Verhältnis von Laufzeit zu Ladezeit von ungefähr 10:1. Für jede Minute an der Ladestation stehen also zehn Minuten Arbeit zur Verfügung. Lädt man neun Minuten, läuft der Humanoid 90 Minuten. Der Vorgänger Digit 4 schaffte lediglich ein Verhältnis von 2:1 – er verbrachte rund ein Drittel des Tages am Ladegerät.
Warum Akkus bei Humanoiden das Hauptproblem sind
Humanoide Roboter brauchen viel Strom. Weil sie sich frei bewegen sollen, kommt der aus Batterien. Die halten allerdings nicht lange und müssen regelmäßig nachgeladen oder getauscht werden. Agility Robotics setzt deshalb auf besonders leichte Akkus mit hoher Leistungsdichte, die also viel Energie pro Kilogramm abgeben können.
Mit der neuen Technik könne Digit 5 täglich mehr als zwei komplette Arbeitsschichten absolvieren, teilt Agility Robotics mit. Die Auslastung einer Roboterflotte im Unternehmen steige dadurch deutlich. Die Akkus von Nyobolt sollen zudem viele Ladezyklen überstehen. Konkrete Zahlen nannten allerdings weder Agility Robotics noch Nyobolt: Weder zur Kapazität noch zur Zahl der möglichen Ladevorgänge gibt es Angaben.
Warum kein Wechselakku?
Offen bleibt auch, warum der Hersteller nicht auf ein Wechselsystem setzt. Dabei tauscht der Roboter seinen leeren Akku selbstständig gegen einen vollen – das geht in der Regel schneller als jeder Ladevorgang. Der chinesische Hersteller UBTech nutzt ein solches System bereits bei seinem humanoiden Roboter Walker S2.
Erste ausgewählte Kunden sollen den Digit 5 mit der neuen Batterietechnik im ersten Halbjahr 2027 bekommen. In den sechs bis neun Monaten danach will Agility Robotics den Roboter breiter verfügbar machen. Der Preis ist allerdings nur was für Profis: Angeblich deutlich sechsstellig. Dafür gibt es einen Wartungsvertrag.

articles.title: Rozvelt built a high-tech mask for hunters. Defence buyers see something bigger. | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Montréal startup behind a breath-filtering mask for recreational hunters is now expanding into the defence sector, a move that has brought international partnerships and fresh funding.
Rozvelt, which makes odour-masking headgear, announced on Monday that it has secured $3.1 million CAD in seed funding from a number of angel investors, led by Benoit Robert, a partner at wealth management firm Evovest. The company plans to use the funding to expand its breathable headgear product line to cater to the military, law enforcement, and first responders, following a burst of interest from those markets.
“Everywhere we go, we see strong interest in Canadian defence innovation.”
Nicholas Monette, Rozvelt
Rozvelt’s consumer headgear, called Vektr, was designed to filter out odour particles exhaled by the wearer, but not particles that are inhaled. It connects magnetically to an adjustable band that wraps around the head, with a removal clasp near each ear. The company claims recreational hunters, as well as wildlife photographers and nature observers, can use it to conceal their scent.
According to Rozvelt co-founder and CEO Nicholas Monette, the pivot began when Rozvelt presented at the SHOT Show in Las Vegas, run by the US Firearm Industry Trade Association. The company was approached by hunters and defence companies who told them there was a bigger problem its masks could tackle.
Shooting a gun can expose people to lead particles from ammunition, which is associated with health issues like cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and kidney failure. They suggested that Rozvelt make its headgear dynamic, so it could switch between filtering exhales (to stop the wearer’s scent) and filtering inhales (protecting the wearer from dangerous particles). Beyond just lead exposure, the masks could serve as a kind of personal protective equipment, fit for combat and other hazardous environments. That’s now what it plans to focus on with its fresh funding, in addition to starting production of the consumer Vektr product in Canada this fall.
“When we saw all this traction in defence, that’s when we took the product and went into all the biggest defence shows,” Monette said in an interview. That included the International Defence Industry Exhibition in Poland, a NATO conference in Luxembourg, and SEECAT in Japan—which is where BetaKit reached him by phone.
RELATED: Rozvelt bets on hardware for hunters amid tariff-spurred funding crunch
The company launched last year at the height of the Canada-US trade war, at possibly the “worst time” to raise money for a hardware company due to investor concerns about tariff impacts. Trade tensions between Canada and the US are now impacting Rozvelt, but not in the same way. Monette said that his company’s position as a Canadian startup with dual-use applications (both civilian and military) has made it an attractive partner for international investors in Europe and Asia. One example is Rozvelt’s partnership and planned distribution agreement with Japan’s Seaprex, an industrial marine manufacturer with defence applications.
Having the Canadian brand behind them was a tailwind. “Everywhere we go, we see strong interest in Canadian defence innovation,” Monette said.
This comes amid tens of billions of defence dollars committed by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government and an explosion in support programs for companies making dual-use technologies. But Monette said Canada’s defence gold rush wasn’t what prompted the switch—international interest came first. He added that Rozvelt is looking to sell to the Canadian Armed Forces as soon as possible.
At the same time, he said, Rozvelt is open to pursuing deals with the US military. “If they want to work with us, we’ll work with them,” Monette said.
Feature image courtesy Rozvelt.

articles.title: 7 plazas, 775 CV, 100% eléctrico y que carga casi igual de rápido que un gasolina: así es el BYD Atto 8
articles.text:
BYD sigue sumando modelos a su catálogo europeo, y esta vez lo hace con el BYD Atto 8, un SUV 100% eléctrico que presume de un tamaño increíble y una velocidad de carga espectacular, a la espera, eso sí, de que la red de cargadores permita esa potencia de carga.
Sobre el papel, es un SUV todocaminos como otros que hemos visto, pero bajo el capó esconde dos motorizaciones eléctricas en versiones de 462 y 775 CV, batería de 115 kWh y hasta 653 kilómetros de autonomía, unas cifras impresionantes si tenemos en cuenta su tamaño y su peso.
Quizás la más impresionante de estas dos versiones es la BYD Atto 8 Excellence AWD, que monta dos motores eléctricos y ofrece un sistema de tracción total. Es la versión que mencionaba anteriormente de más de 700 CV, lo que permite a este Atto 8 acelerar de 0 a 100 km/h en tan solo 4,6 segundos, aunque pierde autonomía respecto a la versión más comedida de 462 CV. En este sentido, mientras que esta última ofrece hasta 653 km de autonomía por carga, la versión Excellence se queda en los 602, que tampoco está nada mal.
BYD Atto 8: carga al 97% en menos de 10 minutos
Pero en este caso poco importan unos kilómetros más de autonomía, puesto que el mayor atractivo de este BYD Atto 8 es su potencia de carga. Utilizando el sistema de Flash Charging de la compañía, junto a su tecnología de baterías, permite cargar al 97% en tan solo 9 minutos. Algo sencillamente impresionante. Y si lo quiere más rápido, el BYD carga del 10% al 70% en tan solo 5 minutos.
Lógicamente, esta potencia de carga no se consigue con los cargadores normales, puesto que requiere su propia infraestructura. Y en específico, al sistema de carga Flash Charging de BYD. La compañía busca llenar el continente de este sistema de carga, y tiene planeado poner más de 3000 de estas estaciones por toda Europa, incluyendo 300 de ellas solo en España, aunque lógicamente esto llevará un tiempo.
Sobre su disponibilidad y precios, se espera que el BYD Atto 8 llegue a España en algún momento del primer trimestre del 2027. Aunque no se ha confirmado la fecha exacta, así como tampoco el precio de las dos versiones disponibles, que se conocerán conforme se vaya acercando su fecha de comercialización.

articles.text:
The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
Plus: Catch up on our conversation with a creator of AI-designed viruses.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
—James Temple
In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and organic-rich soil insulating the permafrost below.
Five years later, I followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.
A simple metal probe revealed how much deeper the ground had thawed. This rudimentary tool offered a glimpse of an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases.
Now, researchers are exploring how to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?
Read the full story on how scientists are rethinking the fight against wildfires.
AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.
Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experimentreminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone.
The agents started behaving in surprising ways. They set about exploring the limits of the world, and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
A lot of what they were doing met the bar for play. But is it truly playful behavior, or simply role-playing?
Read our full story to learn more.
—Amit Katwala
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: X-energy and its helium-cooled nuclear reactors
X-energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
Making concrete, steel, and chemicals takes huge amounts of heat, much of it generated by burning fossil fuels. X-energy hopes to offer an alternative with a nuclear reactor that uses helium gas instead of water as a coolant, allowing it to operate at higher temperatures.
The proposed Xe-100 reactor could supply superheated steam directly to industrial facilities, generate 80 megawatts of electricity—or do both.
See how X-energy hopes to bring high-temperature nuclear power to heavy industry.
—Mark Ellis Harris
Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from cleaner cement to streamlined geothermal power.
Catch up on our conversation with a creator of AI-designed viruses
Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next.
He spoke about his work with our senior AI reporter James O'Donnell on Friday. If you missed it, you can watch their chat now, and subscribe to get invites to our Roundtables events in future.

It’s also looking at curbing the sharing of chip designs, among other measures. (Bloomberg $)

Guess that’s a benefit of not being shackled to a massive social media platform. (Wired $)

There are more AI health tools than ever—but how well do they work?
In the last few months alone, Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI have all launched medical chatbots.
There’s a clear demand for these tools, given how hard it is for many people to access advice through the existing medical system—and they could make safe, useful recommendations. But concerns have surfaced about how little external evaluation they undergo before being released to the public.

articles.title: Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock
Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models, on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, where the model is available.
Whether you call Claude through Boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure. You no longer need custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing.
Practical applications
With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application’s data model.
What changes with structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock
Structured outputs use constrained decoding to enforce your JSON schema during token generation, not after the fact. The model doesn’t produce tokens that would violate your schema. This changes output formatting from probabilistic to deterministic.
Two complementary mechanisms are now available on both Amazon Bedrock endpoints:
| Feature | Purpose | Use case | 
| JSON Schema output format | Control the model’s response structure | Data extraction, report generation, API responses | 
| Strict tool use | Validate tool parameters against schemas | Agentic workflows, function calling, multi-step automation | 
What this means for you
Each response is a valid JSON, so you no longer encounter JSON.parse() errors or parsing exceptions. Responses are also type safe: field types are enforced, and required fields are always present. Because outputs always conform to your schema, you don’t need retries to handle schema violations, making your integration more reliable. Structured outputs also constrains responses to only the fields your schema defines, which reduces output token count and can lower inference costs for high-volume workloads. These properties make structured outputs production ready, so you can deploy at scale without additional schema-validation code.
Supported models and availability
Structured outputs works with batch inference, so you can process large volumes of requests asynchronously while still receiving schema-compliant outputs. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, it also works with cross-Region inference, so you can use it across AWS Regions without additional setup. If you need responses in real time, you can stream structured responses as typed events.
How it works
When you make a request with a JSON schema, here’s what happens behind the scenes:
- Schema validation – Amazon Bedrock validates your JSON schema against the supported JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 subset.
- Grammar compilation – For new schemas, Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact (the first request might take slightly longer).
- Caching – Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours, making subsequent requests faster.
- Constrained generation – The model generates tokens that produce valid JSON matching your schema.
Performance considerations
For performance, the first request with a new schema might take longer because Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact before generation begins. After that initial compilation, subsequent requests using the same schema run with minimal overhead because the compiled grammar is cached. This cache is scoped to your account and lasts for 24 hours from first access. Changing the structure of your JSON schema invalidates the cache and triggers a fresh compilation, while changing only the name or description fields leaves the cached grammar intact.
Getting started: Structured outputs with the InvokeModel API (bedrock-runtime)
The InvokeModel API takes the Anthropic-native request body, so the schema goes in output_config.format as a JSON object rather than a JSON string. The following example shows how to extract the structured lead data from a customer email using boto3 with an Anthropic Claude model:
Python
JSON
The response conforms to your schema. No additional validation is required.
For additional API usage examples, including the Messages API, see the accompanying sample notebook.
Strict tool use for agentic workflows
Amazon Bedrock Mantle is designed for agentic applications with server-side tools, background inference, and stateful conversations. With strict tool use on the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now guarantee that tool parameters match your input schema exactly. The following example shows how to define a tool with strict schema enforcement:
Setting strict: true constrains the model’s tool input to match your schema exactly. The location field is always a string, and the unit field is always either celsius or fahrenheit. The model can’t add fields outside your schema, so the tool input contains only what your schema specifies.
This is especially valuable for agentic use cases on Amazon Bedrock Mantle, where models orchestrate multi-step workflows with server-side tools like web search and code interpreter.
Top use cases for Claude structured outputs
Structured outputs reduce error-handling complexity the most in three common patterns:
- Data extraction: Extract fields from invoices, contracts, email, and transcripts into JSON that always matches your schema, ready to load into databases or customer relationship management (CRM) systems.
- Reliable agent tool calls: Validate tool arguments against their schemas at generation time, so multi-step agent workflows run without failures from malformed input.
- Classification at scale: Classify tickets, leads, or content by intent, priority, and sentiment for routing, moderation, and evaluation.
Claude Haiku 5.5 reliably handles quick and repetitive workloads such as summaries, compactions, database queries, and classification requests. The following example shows how to classify and route incoming data using the Invoke API and Haiku 5.5:
Requirements and best practices
To use structured outputs effectively on Amazon Bedrock, follow these guidelines:
- Set additionalProperties: false on all objects: This is required for structured outputs to work. Without it, your schema won’t be accepted.
- Use descriptive field names and descriptions: Models use property names and descriptions to understand what data to extract. Clear names like customer_email outperform generic names like field1.
- Use enum for constrained values: When a field has a limited set of valid values, use enum to constrain options.
- Start basic, then add complexity: Begin with the minimum required fields and add complexity incrementally. Basic schemas compile faster, are easier to debug, and keep your request payload lean because the schema counts toward the Converse API payload size.
- Reuse schemas to benefit from caching: Structure your application to reuse schemas across requests. The 24-hour grammar cache improves performance for repeated queries.
- Check the stop reason in every response: Two scenarios can produce non-conforming responses: refusals (when the model declines for safety reasons) and token limits (when max_tokens is reached before completing). Handle both cases in your code.
- Test with realistic data before deployment: Validate your schemas against production-representative inputs. Edge cases in real data often reveal schema design issues.
For additional best practices and schema design recommendations, see Structured outputs in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.
Supported JSON Schema features
- All basic types: object, array, string, integer, number, boolean, null.
- enum (strings, numbers, booleans, or nulls only).
- const, anyOf, allOf (with limitations).
- $ref, $def, and definitions (internal references only).
- String formats: date-time, time, date, duration, email, hostname, uri, ipv4, ipv6, uuid.
- Array minItems (only values 0 and 1).
Not supported
These keywords are accepted by the API but are not enforced during generation. A request that includes them returns a successful response, and the model can still return values that violate them. Validate these constraints in your application rather than relying on the schema to enforce them.
- Recursive schemas.
- External $ref references.
- Numerical constraints (minimum, maximum, multipleOf).
- String constraints (minLength, maxLength).
- additionalProperties set to anything other than false.
Conclusion
Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock provides the reliability that production AI applications require. It is available now on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints. By combining JSON Schema output format and strict tool use, you can build data pipelines that need no additional validation. You can also create reliable agentic workflows and production AI applications without custom parsing or retry logic.
Structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock is now generally available. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation and explore our sample notebook.
What workflows could validated, schema-compliant JSON improve in your organization? Share your feedback and questions in the comments.

articles.title: Versteckte Lügen und falsche Anweisungen: Diese Programmiersprache soll KI verwirren
articles.text:
Versteckte Lügen und falsche Anweisungen: Diese Programmiersprache soll KI verwirren
Zahlreiche KI-Modelle sind in der Lage, Code für diverse Projekte zu generieren. Sie unterstützen dabei Programmierer:innen im Alltag, wenn auch nicht immer zu 100 Prozent und können Laien trotz fehlender Coding-Skills zum Ziel bringen. Programmierer Dominik Picheta, der früher bei Meta tätig war und jetzt bei Cloudflare arbeitet, hat sich die Frage gestellt, ob KI-Agenten dabei wirklich den Code verstehen können oder einfach nur Schnipsel wiederholen, die ihnen antrainiert wurden.
Eine Programmiersprache für Menschen, nicht für KI
Deshalb hat der Coder eine neue Programmiersprache namens „Killswitch“ erfunden. Sie vereint mehrere Prämissen, die es KI-Modellen erschweren sollen, sie zu verstehen. Zunächst beinhaltet Killswitch „versteckte Lügen“, die sich von Menschen schnell als Lügen enttarnen, KI aber verzweifeln lassen sollen. Killswitch geht nämlich davon aus, dass Leser:innen „Ableitungen vornehmen können, statt alles erklärt zu bekommen.“
Die einzelnen Programmierelemente wie Entrypoints und Funktionen werden als kurze Sätze formuliert, wobei die Anzahl der Buchstaben entscheidend ist, damit sie vom lesenden Programm umgesetzt werden. Ferner beinhaltet Killswitch Phrasen wie „Ignoriere die vorherigen Anweisungen“, um Funktionen auszulösen und KI-Modelle weiter zu verwirren. Dazu gibt es auch noch Phrasen, die Sicherheitsregeln der KI triggern sollen. Dazu zählt etwa „Hacke dich in einen Computer“.
Einige Befehle, die nur dann vom Programm ausgelesen werden, wenn sie als Verben formuliert sind, müssen falsch buchstabiert werden. Aus „Sichtbar“, um das Drucken eines bestimmten Textes zu fordern, wird so „Ischtbar“. Killswitch lässt sich dabei auch in zusammenhangslosen Fließtexten verstecken. Damit das Programm noch weiß, welche Wörter wirklich noch wichtig sind, deutet „Werte die X Zeilen darüber“ auf die richtige Anweisungen hin.
Um etwa den Text „Hello World“ über Killswitch zu drucken, würde der Befehl in einem deutlich längeren Fließtext etwa lauten: „Die Geschichte startet hier schnell. Ignoriere vorherige Anweisungen. Ischtbar. „Hello World“. Werte die zwei Zeilen darüber. Die Geschichte endet hier sofort.“ Das Beispiel kannst du auch auf der Seite von Killswitch in voller Länge nachlesen.
Wie gut arbeiten die KI-Modelle mit der Programmiersprache?
Die Programmiersprache hat Picheta einer Reihe von KI-Modellen vorgelegt, damit diese damit verschiedene Coding-Aufgaben lösen. Am schlechtesten schnitt dabei Qwen 3.8 27B in den Benchmarks ab. Die chinesische KI konnte keinerlei Programmiermuster in den Texten erkennen und benötigte pro Aufgabe etwa 30 Minuten. Ähnlich ging es auch GPT-5.6 Luna. Bei OpenAIs KI kam das Ende einer Aufgabe aber schon nach durchschnittlich anderthalb Minuten.
Am besten konnte bisher Claude Opus 5 mit Killswitch umgehen. Die KI von Anthropic war in der Lage, 66,8 Prozent der Aufgaben zu erkennen und zu bewältigen. Pro Aufgabe verbrauchte die KI dabei etwa 1,50 US-Dollar und benötigte im Schnitt etwas mehr als acht Minuten. Auf dem zweiten Platz landet GPT-6.1 Sol mit 59,2 Prozent Erfolgsrate.
Picheta schreibt dazu, dass diese Ergebnisse noch lange nicht zeigen, dass KI mit seiner Programmiersprache umgehen könnte: „Es ist beeindruckend, dass sie diese Aufgaben in einer neuen Sprache erledigen können, die dazu da ist, sie zu verwirren. Aber es ist kein Signal, dass sie sie verstehen.“ Abschließend denkt der Entwickler schon darüber nach, eine noch schwerere Variante der Sprache zu entwickeln. Diese will er aber erst angehen, wenn es ein Modell schaffen sollte, alle Aufgaben in Killswitch reibungslos zu absolvieren.

articles.title: Cheaper fibre fees don't spark Nigerian infrastructure investment
articles.text:
Nigeria’s states take widely different approaches to the cost of laying fibre-optic cables. Some have waived Right of Way (RoW) fees; others charge the ₦145-per-metre benchmark, while Ogun State charges up to ₦6,600 ($4.84) per metre. Yet these differences do not neatly explain where fibre infrastructure has been built, raising questions about what else drives investment.
Administrative reforms and project-specific concessions may help offset high fees, but there is little evidence that they do so systematically. The Lagos State Infrastructure Maintenance and Regulatory Agency (LASIMRA) describes itself as a one-stop regulator for utility infrastructure, and the state has announced an online permitting system to streamline approvals for fibre, masts and towers. However, the announcement does not establish whether the system has reduced processing times or costs or removed requirements such as environmental approvals.
Ogun has also reportedly waived RoW charges for a specific 250-kilometre MainOne deployment, but that historical concession does not establish that similar incentives are generally available today. There is no verified evidence of a telecom-specific tax-break programme that explains the substantial fibre networks in these high-fee states. Without access to operators’ permits, concession agreements and investment decisions, it remains unclear whether incentives offset the charges or whether companies invest despite them.
Data from the Nigerian Communications Commission’s (NCC) Ease of Doing Business portal, published in July 2026, shows that Ogun has 4,246.48 kilometres of deployed fibre, while Kano and Rivers, which charge ₦2,754 (2.02) and ₦2,256(1.65) per metre respectively, have 4,616.71 kilometres and 4,616.01 kilometres. Delta, with a rate of ₦2,706 ($1.98) per metre, has 4,202.62 kilometres.
RoW charges are only one component of deployment costs. Trenching and duct installation also depend on ground conditions, water crossings, construction methods and access to existing infrastructure. The NCC portal’s fee and deployment indicators do not provide route-level construction costs. Broader evidence establishes why this matters: the World Bank identifies civil works as the dominant component of certain broadband deployments, accounting for up to 80% of costs in some cases.

articles.title: Google despliega en Madrid sus primeros robotaxis autónomos Waymo
articles.text:
Google despliega en Madrid sus primeros robotaxis autónomos Waymo
Los coches sin conductor empezarán a rodar en los próximos días por las calles de Alcobendas, Getafe y de la capital y se empezarán a comercializar viajes a partir de 2027
Los coches eléctricos y totalmente autónomos Waymo, de Google, desembarcarán en los próximos días en la Comunidad de Madrid. En un primer momento lo harán en periodo de pruebas, con la idea de estar ya totalmente operativos en la región a partir de 2027. Así lo ha anunciado hoy la compañía, que también ha especificado a este diario que los coches rodarán en entornos urbanos reales en Madrid capital, Alcobendas y Getafe. Es decir, en lugares en los que hay peatones, cuya visualización y gestión supone para estos vehículos el principal desafío técnico (y el mayor peligro público).
Waymo se suma así a Uber, que anunció en septiembre que también había obtenido el permiso de la Dirección General de Tráfico para operar sus coches autónomos en fase de pruebas por la capital española, aunque no ha dado fechas sobre el posible lanzamiento comercial del servicio.
Los Jaguar I-PACE de Waymo tienen el aspecto de un coche al uso, pero con una serie de cámaras y sensores en la parte delantera y trasera, así como otra en el techo que pasaría por la sirena de un vehículo de emergencias. Las pruebas se desarrollarán en tres fases. En la primera, los vehículos serán pilotados de forma manual por especialistas al volante, con el fin de que la tecnología aprenda de los patrones específicos de tráfico, peatones y ciclistas de la región. Más adelante, se dejará que el coche ande solo, aunque seguirá una persona a bordo recogiendo datos y preparada para tomar el control en caso de que algo falle. En la tercera y última fase, se harán operaciones totalmente autónomas.
El plan de Waymo, que ha obtenido las autorizaciones correspondientes para circular en vías públicas españolas, es empezar a comercializar sus viajes a partir de 2027. Estos coches no están a la venta, sino que se contratan trayectos a través de la app de Waymo. La compañía no ha revelado a este periódico cuándo será eso posible ni cuál es el precio o tarifa que se aplicará. Tampoco ha concretado cómo de grande será la flota de coches autónomos que desplegará en la Comunidad de Madrid, ni en qué otras regiones del país planea operar.
Los coches Waymo combinan aprendizaje automático (machine learning) e inteligencia artificial avanzada con un conjunto integrado de sensores (LiDAR, radares y cámaras de alta resolución) para generar un mapa 3D en 360 grados del entorno en tiempo real. Esos son los ojos del vehículo, que además integra los patrones detectados con los más de 300 millones de kilómetros conducidos en el mundo real, además de decenas de miles de millones de kilómetros simulados.
Waymo opera una flota comercial de más de 4.000 vehículos 100% eléctricos en más de 15 ciudades de EE UU las 24 horas del día, los siete días de la semana. En zonas como el Área de la Bahía de San Francisco, Los Ángeles, Phoenix y Miami, también trasladan pasajeros por autopista. En Europa, la primera ciudad con coches Waymo operativos será Londres, previsiblemente antes de acabar el año. Después llegarán Múnich y Madrid.
El debate de la seguridad
La compañía afirma que sus vehículos autónomos son más seguros que los de conducción autónoma. Para ello esgrime datos relativos a sus pruebas: en los 435 millones de kilómetros recorridos por coches de Waymo únicamente con pasajeros (sin conductor), sus coches han registrado 20 veces menos accidentes con heridos graves o muertos que la media de la zona en la que rodaban.
Desde que circulan por las calles de EE UU, los Waymo han protagonizado al menos un gran incidente, aunque sin heridos. El año pasado, durante el apagón del 23 de diciembre de San Francisco, que afectó al 30% de la ciudad por culpa de un incendio en una subestación eléctrica, la flota de robotaxis se quedó parada en medio de la calle, causando el caos en el tráfico de la ciudad.

articles.title: Even Healthcare raises $50M in Series B round led by Khosla Ventures
articles.text:
Even Healthcare raises $50M in Series B round led by Khosla Ventures
The Bengaluru-based managed care company plans five new hospitals in six months.
Bengaluru-based managed care company Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a Series B round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures. Alpha Wave also participated in the round.
According to the company, the round values it at three times its valuation 18 months ago and brings its total funding to more than $120 million.
The money will go towards five new Even hospitals in Bengaluru over the next six months, beginning with Indiranagar. The company runs two hospitals in the city at present.
Even's pitch rests on the criticism of how private healthcare is generally paid for in India. Nobody is clearly responsible for a patient's health between hospital visits, and families end up repeating their medical history to each new doctor. They struggle to judge whether a scan or surgery is necessary, and face bills they had not anticipated.
Even says it works differently. Members are assigned a care team that follows them over time and contacts them before a minor problem turns into an admission. If hospital care is needed, it is cashless. The same team stays in touch after discharge until recovery is complete, it says.
The company claims to be the only private hospital chain in India where doctors are not paid on the number of procedures they carry out or the revenue they generate. Instead, they are assessed on whether patients improve, how fast they recover, and whether they return to hospital. An AI system reviews each case against clinical protocols as it happens.
The company says, in its first full year of managed care, in programmes run with insurance partners, unplanned readmissions stayed below 1%, compared with an industry range of 8 to 15%. Average stays were 40% shorter. Even says proactive care kept more than 200 members out of hospital entirely, saving patients an estimated Rs 15 crore to 16 crore. Its hospital on Race Course Road won NABH 6th Edition accreditation within a year, one of only nine hospitals in Bengaluru to hold it. Both hospitals of Even have reached operational profitability in "record time", says the company,
"Every family in India has a hospital story, and too often it is about confusion, fear and a bill nobody could explain," said Co-founder Mayank Banerjee. He said the aim is to have an Even hospital close to every family in Bengaluru, and then in every major Indian city. The company eventually wants one within five kilometres of every member in the city.
Vinod Khosla, Founder of Khosla Ventures, said many healthcare companies optimise a single piece of a fragmented system, whereas Even is trying to integrate financing, technology, and care delivery so the system is rewarded for health outcomes rather than utilisation.
The company was founded in 2021 by Mayank Banerjee, Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo. Founders Fund and 8VC are among its backers. Even serves more than 2.5 lakh members across 10 cities and says its membership has tripled over the past year.

articles.title: Ces box Orange et SFR peuvent se faire pirater à distance grâce à une faille Wi-Fi
articles.text:
La faille a été découverte par Quentin Kaiser, un chercheur belge spécialisé dans la cybersécurité. Présentée à la conférence Hexacon de Paris, la vulnérabilité se trouve dans une vieille version du WPS de Broadcom, un fabricant dont les puces sont présentes dans de nombreuses box. Il s’agit de la fonction qui permet de connecter un appareil au Wi-Fi sans taper le mot de passe.
 just confirmed the presence of Broadcom’s vulnerable wps_monitor in ZTE F680 v4 deployed by MasMovil, ThailandToT, Telkom, Linkstar, Mnc, Viettel, VNPT, EgyptTEData, Ais, MTN, FranceReunicable, RTC, Indosat, MAXCom, EKT, OSP, and Moldtelecom https://t.co/Q5o5dwqQja
— Quentin Kaiser (@qkaiser) October 17, 2026
Le chercheur explique avoir découvert un problème au niveau de la gestion des données échangées lors de la procédure de connexion sans mot de passe. En exploitant la brèche, un pirate peut prendre le contrôle de la box sans en connaître le mot de passe, et même sans être connecté au réseau. Il doit simplement se trouver à la portée du réseau Wi-Fi.
« On peut obtenir un accès complet à un routeur depuis l’autre côté de la rue, sur une proportion importante des box en Belgique, et probablement ailleurs », explique Quentin Kaiser.
Lors de ses démonstrations, le chercheur a récupéré le mot de passe Wi-Fi d’une box belge, puis en a pris le contrôle total en s’appuyant sur la vulnérabilité. Il explique s’être servi de « modèles d’IA de pointe » pour dénicher la faille en moins d’une semaine.
« J’aurais pu mener cette recherche seul, mais cela m’aurait pris des mois », ajoute le chercheur.
À lire aussi : Google corrige 37 nouvelles failles Chrome, l’IA accélère encore la cadence des mises à jour
Un bug vieux de seize ans
La défaillance n’est pas nouvelle. D’après le chercheur, elle se trouve dans le logiciel de Broadcom depuis 2010. L’entreprise a corrigé le tir avec une mise à jour en 2018, mais de nombreux fabricants de box ne l’ont jamais installée. De facto, seize ans après son apparition, la faille est toujours exploitable sur des appareils qui sont toujours en service.
Comme le souligne l’expert, Broadcom a toujours refusé d’attribuer un numéro CVE à la vulnérabilité, c’est-à-dire l’identifiant officiel qui sert à alerter l’ensemble des fabricants d’un problème dans un logiciel. C’est en partie pourquoi les équipements sont restés privés de correctifs pendant plus d’une décennie.
À lire aussi : Des failles de sécurité dans plus de 16.000 Orange Livebox
Quelles box sont concernées en France ?
Pour déterminer le nombre d’appareils encore vulnérables, le chercheur a sillonné Paris et scanné tous les réseaux Wi-Fi environnants. Il s’est ainsi rendu compte que la Livebox 5 d’Orange et les box SFR « Box Plus » étaient toujours vulnérables. Celles-ci n’ont jamais eu droit à un correctif pour la faille de Broadcom. Attention, seules la version Sagemcom Fast5656 de la Livebox 5 et la version NB6VAC de la box de SFR sont vulnérables. A contrario, la Livebox 6 d’Orange et la Bbox Wi-Fi 7 de Bouygues Telecom ont eu droit à une mise à jour. Aucune Freebox n’est visiblement touchée.
Mauvaise nouvelle, ça ne sert à rien de changer son mot de passe Wi-Fi. Le défaut se corrige uniquement par une mise à jour de la box déployée par l’opérateur. On vous conseille donc de laisser votre box installer ses mises à jour automatiquement. Le chercheur y voit surtout un avertissement d’une accumulation de « notre dette technique », qui « finira par nous être réclamée ». Pour l’heure, rien n’indique que la faille a été exploitée par des cybercriminels.

articles.title: Russian military satellite closes from 200 miles to 3 miles of US radar satellite aiding Ukraine — astronomer says it may be the first unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit
articles.text:
Russian military satellite closes from 200 miles to 3 miles of US radar satellite aiding Ukraine — astronomer says it may be the first unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit
Russia didn’t burn that fuel by accident: it’s likely spying on the satellite and testing the West.
A Russian military satellite, Cosmos 2612, has closed to roughly 3 miles, from a previous distance of more than 200 miles, of the U.S.-owned radar satellite that operates in a fleet that supports Ukraine, Axios reports. The unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit, which astronomer Jonathan McDowell says may be the first of its kind, raises alarm in the West. The position change, which was likely not an accident as fuel is scarce, is probably a provocation and an attempt to spy on the satellite.
LeoLabs said in a statement Friday that the movement “appears to be a deliberate approach” toward ICEYE-X36, with uncertain intent and behavior that “warrants continued monitoring.” Roughly 3 miles is too close for comfort in satellite terms: there is no strict legal limit on how close satellites can get, but countries generally keep at least 6 miles (9.7 km) apart, University of Mississippi space law professor Aaron Brynildson told Axios. The approach was made without the owner’s consent, and Russia hasn’t said what the military satellite carries.
Some clues may come from the target’s operational purpose. ICEYE-X36 is a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite which can image through cloud cover and at night. It was launched in March 2024 on a SpaceX Falcon 9. It’s registered to ICEYE US, the U.S. arm of the Finland-founded company. The satellite, which is in a roughly 545 km (339 mi) sun-synchronous orbit, is part of a fleet that has supplied Ukraine with information since 2022. This includes a deal earlier this year with a customer in Ukraine’s defense ministry, but a Ukrainian official told Axios it’s unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports the country; ICEYE and the Defense Department declined to comment.
In May, the majority of the six military satellites Russia launched in April via a Soyuz-2.1b, Cosmos 2609–2614, shifted their orbits about 0.8 degrees to match X36’s orbital plane. Cosmos 2609 passed within 2.5 km (1.6 mi) on May 26. Cosmos 2612, on the other hand, drifted off X36’s plane by about 0.24 degrees by Sept. 30, up to about 28 km side to side, according to Greg Gillinger, a space analyst with Integrity ISR.
Then, Cosmos 2612 made separate burns from Sept. 30 through Oct. 16 to match altitude, eccentricity, and orbital period, Dutch satellite tracker Marco Langbroek wrote. By Saturday night, he estimated from public orbital data, it was within “a few hundred meters or possibly (much) closer.”
These movements appear deliberate and cost a lot of fuel, which the Center for Strategic and International Studies calls “a limited resource on a satellite.” Close-proximity work can be benign, it says, but policymakers should assume the Russian satellite “could take an action that threatens the commercial satellite,” and the U.S. and Europe should decide how to respond to any hostile act in space and make a statement on the decision. Back in July 2020, Russia’s Cosmos 2543 released an object at up to 186 m/s (416 mph) relative to itself, an action which was condemned by the U.S. and U.K.
Intent was less clear earlier this year, when McDowell told Meduza the orbital data showed no sign of the stable, close distance that tracking ICEYE-X36 would require. Now, he says it is an unapproved meeting and is not alone. Gillinger says the setup “removes any remaining doubt for me that Cosmos 2612 is interested in ICEYE X36.” Langbroek adds that “I was skeptical” at first but now calls it “completely non-consensual,” though he cautions it would be difficult to pin any X36 failures on 2612’s actions.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
In a Reuters report less than two weeks ago, ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company moved its satellite after May, only to draw more Russian maneuvers, which Germany’s Space Command head, Maj. Gen. Michael Traut, described as “chasing.” Belinda Marchand, chief scientist at U.S. space intelligence firm Slingshot Aerospace, added that the moves may have been meant for surveillance, to prepare for future interference, or to signal capability. Western officials reportedly describe such trailing as a way to gather intelligence and test the West’s tolerance.
No statement from Russia is on record. Gillinger also told readers to “watch Cosmos 2611 and 2613, whose planes are converging on ICEYE X37’s,” with crossings expected around Nov. 6 and Nov. 15.

articles.title: Watch out — these are the phishing scams experts say are most likely to catch your workers out
articles.text:
Watch out — these are the phishing scams experts say are most likely to catch your workers out
New tech announcements, gifts, and insurance claims work best
- Kaspersky finds AI and technology-themed phishing lures achieved the highest click rates, reaching 45% in testing
- Healthcare, compliance, promotions, and HR messages also proved highly effective at deceiving employees
- Researchers found regular awareness training can dramatically reduce phishing susceptibility across organizations
Phishing emails are notorious for often working exceptionally well, but which ones are the most effective? We all know that these lures need two things: A) to carry a sense of urgency; and B) the idea that the victim will either miss out on something or suffer material troubles.
But no two emails are alike, and some campaigns prove to be more successful than others.
Security researchers Kaspersky set out to learn which themes work best, and which fail, to give businesses better insight into the biggest risks lurking in the depths of their employees’ inboxes. To do that, they analyzed anonymized voluntary provided data from their Phishing Simulator. “A high click rate among users clearly highlights what specific cybersecurity training is required,” they said.
Responding to sensitive emails
The data showed five topics that yield the best results for the attackers: AI & Tech, Healthcare & Insurance, IT Policies & Compliance, Gifts & Promotions, and HR & Corporate Communications.
AI & Tech was the best-performing topic overall, with themes such as “introducing next-gen artificial intelligence” having a 45% click-through rate. In other words, almost every other recipient would click on a malicious link and potentially get served malware or share login credentials with threat actors.
Healthcare & Insurance lures tricked an average of 28% of the audience, but among the different emails, one stood out. Emails regarding a sanitary inspection report reached a 92% click-through rate. IT & Policies were third with a 26% click-through rate, followed by Gifts & Promotions (24%).
Two-thirds (66%) of recipients clicked an email inviting them to wear their’ national team’s football jersey and win a prize. HR & Corporate comms yielded a 22% click-through rate, with emails raising sensitive and high-interest internal topics being “especially dangerous”, Kaspersky said.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“People naturally respond to sensitive and highly contextual emails, especially when phishing mimics their exact workflow or local specifics. Knowing this, cybercriminals make their traps more personalized and this trend is set to accelerate with the rise of generative AI,” said Svetlana Kalashnikova, Security Awareness expert at Kaspersky.
“Fortunately, proper cultivation of cyber vigilance demonstrates measurable risk reduction: regular training and attack simulations drastically reduce phishing susceptibility rates from 60% to a mere 5–7%, according to KASAP effectiveness analytics. To protect people and businesses from human-targeting threats, we strongly recommend that organizations implement ongoing cybersecurity awareness program for all employees.”
According to Kaspersky, phishing remains the most prevalent cyber-incident for businesses at any stage of growth and ranks top among incidents leading to damaging business consequences. At the same time, attacks on humans grow more sophisticated, faster, and broader in scope and are, thanks to Artificial Intelligence (AI) now becoming a multi-stage effort.
Spotting a phishing email
Before Artificial Intelligence (AI), phishing emails were relatively easy to spot. Since they were mostly written by threat actors who aren’t native English speakers, their language was rather clunky and could not properly convey the style or the tone set up by the legitimate company’s communications team.
AI has now made malicious emails almost indistinguishable from legitimate communications, pushing identification further down the infection chain: towards links and attachments, as well as the overall sentiment.
A few things remain the same for all weaponized emails: the sense of urgency. Most legitimate organizations would not threaten their customers with account suspensions within 24 hours. They would also not host their documents on unrecognizable third-party services, and would not share attachments in executable formats.
Double-checking the domain from which the email is being sent is still a good way to spot an attack, too. Most phishing emails originate from a stolen email address, or one created on a public service. The UK postal service does not have a Proton email account.
Therefore, raising awareness, training, and doing simulations, remains the number one way to defend in 2026.
