articles.title: NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026
articles.text:
At OCP 2026, we saw the new NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for Context Memory (CMX). Partners had been asking for this, and NVIDIA delivered. Onboard, we have a lower-cost design than the dual-Vera setup we saw previously. Let us take a look at the new board.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026
For context, this is the previously shown BlueField-4 DPU. That one, pictured below, is a dual Vera CPU setup, each with SOCAMM memory, plus four ConnectX-9 SuperNICs. NVIDIA calls this a DPU, but it is clearly more costly than a BlueField-1 or BlueField-3, which are much smaller and lower-power devices. For partners looking at building storage platforms, the below is more akin to a dual CPU server than a traditional DPU.
At OCP 2026, multiple partners showed off the BlueField-4 STX server for context memory (CMX). Here is the much smaller card, which still uses high-density connectors for PCIe and system connectivity.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs encompass both NVIDIA Grace and Vera CPU cores, but this one looks like a Vera package. That is a very substantial CPU. To be clear, this is not like the embedded-class CPUs that we typically have seen in DPUs previously. This is more like having a high-end single-socket server platform.
Another interesting feature is that the boards at OCP 2026 are using SOCAMM memory, so these should be relatively easy to put either a heatsink or a liquid cooling block on top of it.
Onboard, there is an M.2 slot. Usually these are for OS drives, but if you saw our recent Inside the Secretive AWS Networking Lab, the M.2 SSDs there are being used for log devices.
This may seem like a small feature, but it means NVIDIA designed this less like a traditional motherboard replacement and more like something that is easy to assemble automatically.
Something that may not immediately hit you if you are looking at photos is just the size of this board. A soldered CPU and LPDDR5X here, over traditional DDR5 DIMM slots, give NVIDIA a platform where the “motherboard” is roughly the size of an Intel DMR 16-channel socket or a 16-channel AMD EPYC Venice platform.
Final Words
This is just a neat platform. It almost feels like NVIDIA needs some brand between the Vera server line and the traditional BlueField DPU line. Something notable that we did not see on the boards shown at OCP 2026, or at least in our photos of them from various booths, is an NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNIC. We expected that, but did not see it on this board. For context memory platforms, a single Vera versus a dual Vera makes this a lower-cost platform, and that will likely help the STX/ CMX systems come to market as the price of NAND has been rising meaningfully over the past year.

articles.title: Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience
Today, we’re excited to announce that new Amazon SageMaker AI customers can now land inside a fully configured Amazon SageMaker Studio environment in only a few steps after signing up for AWS. You can use a sign-in method that you already have, such as Amazon, Apple, GitHub, Google, or an email address. You don’t need to set up an advanced AWS account, enter a credit card (for most customers), or configure an environment manually. New customers also receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including model customization, training jobs, Studio notebooks, and endpoint deployments.
This post follows on from our previous post, From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in One Click, which introduced deep links from Hugging Face model pages directly into SageMaker Studio workflows. Earlier this year, we also sped up Studio environment creation time from 2 minutes to about 20 seconds and pre-configured model customization permissions in every new Studio domain. Together, these changes removed much of the friction after a developer reached Studio. One major hurdle remained before they got there: creating an AWS account. New customers had to verify an email address, enter contact information, verify a phone number, provide payment details, and select a support plan before they could start building. For individual developers and small startup teams used to signing in and building within a few minutes, that was still a significant barrier.
What’s new
With this launch, SageMaker Studio is now integrated with the updated AWS sign-in and sign-up experience, which introduces new options for creating and managing AWS accounts along with simplified collaboration. New customers can create an account using an identity that they already have and start building in SageMaker Studio right away.
New sign-in experience
New customers can now sign up using their Google, GitHub, Apple, or Amazon account, or with an email address, in 2–3 steps. You don’t need to complete the advanced AWS account sign-up, verify a phone number, or enter a credit card (for most customers):
After you sign up, SageMaker AI automatically creates your Studio environment in about 20 seconds. You then land on the page that matches where you started. For example, you might discover and select a model from Hugging Face for deployment through Deploy on SageMaker AI. Studio then opens the Deployment page with the model pre-configured for endpoint creation:
Up to $200 in Free Tier credits, no credit card required for most customers
New customers receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including endpoint deployments, model customization, Studio notebooks, and model training. You also have the chance to earn an additional $100 worth of credits. Credits are applied automatically to your usage, and you receive an email notification as you approach your limit. The Free Tier period ends after 6 months or when you’ve used all your credits, whichever comes first. At that point, resource usage stops automatically, so you won’t be surprised by unexpected charges. You can upgrade to a paid plan at any time by adding payment details.
Built on the foundations of previous launches
New environments created through the new sign-in experience include the improvements from earlier launches. Permissions for model customization, training, evaluation, and deployment are pre-configured, so you don’t need to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Eligible accounts get default access to G5, G6, and G4dn GPU instances for endpoints, training jobs, and Studio notebooks. Additionally, the instance selection menu in Studio shows quota availability, so you can quickly see which instance types are available for use.
Getting started
You can try the new sign-in experience today:
- Browse models on Hugging Face, choose Deploy, select Amazon SageMaker AI and then choose Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported model. Alternatively, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page and choose Get started with Amazon SageMaker AI.
- On the AWS sign-in page, choose Google, GitHub, Apple, or Amazon, or enter your email address, and follow the prompts to create your account in a few steps.
- Land in your fully configured SageMaker Studio environment and start building with your Free Tier credits.
The new sign-in experience is available for new AWS accounts. If you already have an AWS account, there’s no change to how you sign in.
Conclusion
The new sign-in experience removes the last major hurdle between discovering and building with Amazon SageMaker AI. Combined with faster environment creation, pre-configured permissions, deep links from Hugging Face, and default GPU access, individual developers can get started quickly. Startup teams can now go from finding a model to customizing or deploying it in minutes, using an identity they already have.
To get started, visit aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/studio or explore models on Hugging Face.

articles.title: F5 releases out-of-band patches for critical NGINX vulnerabilities
articles.text:
F5 has released out-of-band security patches to address multiple NGINX web server flaws, including three critical-severity vulnerabilities that can let attackers execute code on vulnerable systems.
The three critical vulnerabilities were found in the ngx_http_v3_module (CVE-2026-15176 and CVE-2026-97205) and the NGINX map directive (CVE-2026-93479).
Remote attackers without privileges can exploit them to launch denial-of-service (DoS) attacks or gain code execution on NGINX systems with non-default configurations.
Successful exploitation causes a heap-based buffer overflow or use-after-free in the NGINX worker process, leading to crashes or a restart. However, attackers may also be able to "execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR."
F5 released security patches for multiple NGINX software products affected by these two vulnerabilities, including NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source, NGINX Ingress Controller, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Instance Manager.
Security teams and admins who can't immediately install these security patches can mitigate CVE-2026-15176 by not using the 'alias' directive in a location block or the $request_filename variable, and CVE-2026-97205 by disabling asynchronous file I/O (AIO) or Server Side Includes (SSI).
CVE-2026-93479 can also be mitigated by using named captures instead of unnamed captures and limiting their use to the block with the regex match.
While F5 has not yet flagged these security issues as exploited in the wild, cybercrime and nation-state threat groups have often exploited vulnerabilities in F5 products in recent years.
For instance, attackers have targeted F5 security flaws to breach corporate networks, map internal servers, hijack devices, deploy data-wiping malware, and steal sensitive documents from victims worldwide.
Since November 2021, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged eight F5 vulnerabilities as actively exploited, four of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.
One year ago, in October 2025, F5 also disclosed that state-sponsored threat actors breached its systems in August 2025 and stole source code and information on undisclosed BIG-IP security vulnerabilities.
F5 is a Fortune 500 tech company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to over 23,000 customers, including 80% of the Fortune Global 500 and 48 Fortune 50 companies.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

articles.title: La UCO arresta a un adolescente de 16 años como presunto líder de KillSec, responsable de mil ciberataques
articles.text:
Los investigadores del Departamento de Cibercrimen de la Unidad Central Operativa (UCO) de la Guardia Civil han identificado a un chico rumano de 16 años, que vive en la provincia de Alicante, como presunto administrador del grupo de ransomware KillSec tras analizar una imagen de perfil.
Según los investigadores, sus miembros habrían llevado a cabo más de 1.000 ataques cibernéticos en todo el mundo, de los cuales unos 500 habrían tenido éxito, contra más de 280 víctimas.
Algunas de ellas habrían pagado rescates de alrededor de 500.000 euros en criptomonedas. Durante los registros en una vivienda y en la oficina de un hotel de la provincia, los agentes intervinieron ordenadores, teléfonos móviles y carteras de criptoactivos, y una mujer quedó como investigada por su presunta relación con los hechos.
¿Cómo se llegó hasta un chaval de 16 años?
La Operación Rotoma se inició en 2025 a partir de la colaboración con la oficina del FBI en San Juan de Puerto Rico, que buscaba a personas relacionadas con KillSec que pudieran residir en España.
Por otro lado, los Mossos d’Esquadra habían abierto una investigación por un ataque contra la entidad pública catalana Infraestructures.cat a principios de 2025: los delincuentes accedieron a sus sistemas, sustrajeron información sensible e intentaron extorsionarla, con daños estimados en cerca de un millón de euros. La entidad asegura que no pagó ningún rescate.
El equipo conjunto de los dos cuerpos permitió localizar al sospechoso y relacionarlo con el ataque en Cataluña. Los investigadores le atribuyen cuatro papeles: administrador, desarrollador, negociador y afiliado.
La detención forma parte de la operación internacional KillSwitch, en la que Europol y Eurojust han coordinado a las autoridades de nueve países: Bélgica, Finlandia, Alemania, Grecia, Rumanía, España, Suiza, Reino Unido y Estados Unidos.
El 30 de septiembre, día de la acción conjunta, hubo ocho registros y tres detenciones en España, Grecia, Reino Unido y Rumanía. Las autoridades tomaron el control de la web de filtraciones del grupo, de cinco servidores centrales y de varios dominios, los cuales han pasado a mostrar un aviso policial, y se hicieron con al menos 110 terabytes de datos robados.
Los otros dos detenidos son dos hombres de veintitantos años, uno en Reino Unido y otro en Rumanía, y Puerto Rico ha pedido la extradición del arrestado en Reino Unido. El desarrollador que acaba de cumplir la mayoría de edad ha sido identificado, aunque no ha sido detenido.
KillSec: un ransomware de alquiler por 250 dólares
Aunque la edad del presunto líder es realmente llamativa, el negocio que montó el grupo también lo es. Según la empresa de ciberseguridad Group-IB, que colaboró en la investigación, KillSec alquilaba su ransomware a terceros: cualquier afiliado podía hacerse con la versión para Windows con un pago de entrada de 250 dólares (unos 221 euros al cambio del 1 de octubre de 2026) y cediendo al grupo el 12 % de cada rescate, una comisión que en enero de 2025 ya había subido al 20 %. Eso sí, ningún afiliado podía generar su propia versión del malware sin el permiso de los administradores.
Su primer mensaje en Telegram es de octubre de 2023, cuando buscaba perfiles de intrusión y de creación de malware, y fue en junio de 2024 cuando lanzó el programa de afiliados, con un panel de control accesible a través de Tor.
Los productos que ofrecía fueron creciendo poco a poco. En noviembre de 2024 llegó una versión para servidores VMware ESXi capaz de apagar las máquinas virtuales y eliminar sus instantáneas. Además, el grupo vendía directamente los datos robados, con precios de entre 5.000 y 500.000 dólares. Group-IB contó 274 organizaciones expuestas en su web de filtraciones, sobre todo de Estados Unidos (un 35 %) e India (un 17 %), con el sector financiero y el sanitario como los más castigados. Europa significaba un 14 %.
Para entrar, los atacantes aprovechaban vulnerabilidades de software y accesos mal protegidos, especialmente en servicios de almacenamiento en la nube. Copiaban la información interna a sus servidores y publicaban a la víctima en una web de la dark web, con la amenaza de que, si no pagaba el rescate, los datos quedarían disponibles para su descarga gratuita.
“Los servidores se pueden reemplazar en semanas; las personas que construyen la plataforma y aprueban cada ataque, no”, señaló el consejero delegado de Group-IB, Dmitry Volkov.
¿Qué consecuencias puede tener para un menor de 16 años?
Por su edad, el caso se rige por la Ley Orgánica 5/2000 de responsabilidad penal del menor, que se aplica a personas de entre 14 y 18 años. Para quien tenía 16 o 17 años cuando cometió los hechos, la medida puede durar como máximo seis años. Si el juez califica los hechos de extrema gravedad, debe imponer un internamiento en régimen cerrado de uno a seis años, seguido de hasta cinco años de libertad vigilada.
En marzo de 2022, la policía de Londres detuvo a siete jóvenes de entre 16 y 21 años relacionados con Lapsus$, el grupo que había atacado a Microsoft, Nvidia y Samsung. Aquella vez quedaron en libertad sin cargos, pero el caso no terminó ahí: en diciembre de 2023, un tribunal de Londres ordenó internar indefinidamente en un hospital a Arion Kurtaj, de 18 años, y a otro miembro de 17 años le impuso una medida de rehabilitación juvenil de 17 meses.
Precauciones para las empresas que guardan datos en la nube
Bitdefender, otra de las empresas que participó en la operación, ha dado algunas recomendaciones. La primera, parchear antes que nada el software expuesto a internet, porque es lo que escanean los atacantes. La segunda, revisar quién tiene acceso a los servicios de almacenamiento en la nube.
Sobre todo, los espacios que ya no gestiona nadie: los que quedaron tras terminar un proyecto, los heredados de una compra de otra empresa o las pruebas que se dejaron abiertas.
Y si el ataque ya se ha producido, el Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE) aconseja no pagar el rescate y contactar con el 017, su línea gratuita de ayuda en ciberseguridad, también disponible por WhatsApp en el 900 116 117.
Para los archivos cifrados existe el portal No More Ransom, puesto en marcha en 2016 por Europol y la policía neerlandesa, con una herramienta llamada Crypto Sheriff que identifica el tipo de ransomware a partir de dos archivos cifrados y la nota de rescate, y busca si hay un descifrador gratuito.
La Guardia Civil continúa analizando los dispositivos y los datos intervenidos, así como rastreando las criptomonedas del grupo. Los investigadores no descartan nuevas actuaciones.

articles.title: Intel Core Ultra 4000 : quels noms pour les futurs processeurs mobiles ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une nomenclature à quatre chiffres pour Nova Lake. Ce n’est pas la première fois que l’on en entend parler. Depuis quelques semaines déjà, il se murmure qu’Intel utilisera la dénomination Core Ultra 4000 pour sa prochaine génération de processeurs de bureau, attendue en début d’année prochaine.
On apprend toutefois du leaker Jaykihn que cette nomenclature serait au bout du compte étendue à toutes les puces Nova Lake… qu’il s’agisse des références de bureau, des variantes mobiles hautes performances ou de celles, plus modestes, consacrées aux ultraportables et aux PC portables un peu plus abordables. Dans tous les cas, Intel miserait ainsi sur une gamme cohérente et unifiée portant le seul « badge » Core Ultra 4000.
Intel va mettre le bazar dans sa nomenclature mobile…
Ce qu’il faut préciser, c’est que Jaykihn avait au départ diffusé une information incorrecte, estimant que la nomenclature à quatre chiffres serait réservée aux références de bureau et aux processeurs mobiles « HX » à hautes performances (ceux consacrés aux PC portables gaming et créatifs). L’informateur avait ainsi suggéré que les références mobiles « H » et sans suffixe seraient quant à elles limitées à une nomenclature à trois chiffres de type Core Ultra 400.
Par souci de cohérence, Intel adopterait bien, finalement, une dénomination à quatre chiffres pour l’ensemble de sa gamme Nova Lake. Les Core Ultra 4000 constitueraient ainsi une seule et même grande famille de processeurs, unifiée autour d’une nomenclature commune.
Intel reviendrait donc à sa stratégie précédente en la matière. Rappelez-vous, avant les générations Arrow Lake (Core Ultra 200) / Panther Lake (Core Ultra 300), la firme misait sur une seule et même dénomination pour ses processeurs de bureau et ses processeurs mobiles, avec des suffixes différenciant les deux.
À noter toutefois que si le nom exact de certaines références Nova Lake-S (de bureau) a déjà fuité (on pense notamment aux Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC, Core Ultra 9 4950K ou au Core Ultra 7 4870K BFC), aucune information n’est pour l’instant disponible quant à la nomenclature exacte des références Nova Lake-HX / Nova Lake-H (mobiles). Intel n’a d’ailleurs pas encore confirmé quoi que ce soit en termes de « naming » dans l’immédiat. Cela dit, ces dernières informations semblent crédibles.

articles.title: L'informatique quantique va-t-elle rendre obsolète toute la cryptographie actuelle des PME ?
articles.text:
Des pirates informatiques stockent des données chiffrées dans plusieurs secteurs, en attendant qu'un ordinateur quantique suffisamment puissant puisse les déchiffrer. Si les PME françaises ne sont pas concernées par cette menace avant plusieurs années, l'ANSSI impose aux fournisseurs de logiciels et de matériel des échéances précises pour engager la transition. Voici ce qui est en jeu, sans dramatisation inutile.
Vos sauvegardes, votre messagerie professionnelle et vos connexions VPN sont chiffrées par RSA ou par les courbes elliptiques. Depuis la fin des années 1970, RSA est utilisé pour la sécurité de la plupart des connexions internet. Les courbes elliptiques constituent une famille d'algorithmes plus récente. Dans les deux cas, la sécurité dépend d'un calcul mathématique différent.
Un ordinateur classique ne résout pas ces calculs en un temps raisonnable, alors qu'un ordinateur quantique suffisamment puissant peut les résoudre en quelques heures grâce à l'algorithme de Shor. Aucune machine ne peut aujourd'hui exécuter cet algorithme sur des clés de la taille utilisée en production, mais des attaquants conservent des échanges chiffrés dans l'espoir de les déchiffrer une fois cette machine disponible.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Le mécanisme qui menace RSA et les courbes elliptiques
En 1994, bien avant l'apparition des premiers ordinateurs quantiques expérimentaux, le mathématicien américain Peter Shor a découvert cet algorithme. Le calcul de RSA consiste à factoriser de grands nombres premiers, tandis que celui des courbes elliptiques consiste à résoudre un logarithme discret. D'ici à 2029, IBM compte avoir lancé Starling, son premier calculateur conçu pour corriger ses erreurs de calcul à grande échelle.
Aux États-Unis, il a fallu huit ans à l'organisme fédéral de normalisation NIST pour évaluer 82 algorithmes soumis par 25 pays et finaliser, en août 2024, deux normes post-quantiques. Les échanges de clés sont chiffrés par ML-KEM, tandis que les signatures numériques sont protégées par ML-DSA. Microsoft a intégré ces deux algorithmes à Windows dès sa conférence Build de 2025, avant de les proposer sous Linux via SymCrypt-OpenSSL.
Les spécialistes de la cybersécurité appellent cette pratique « harvest now, decrypt later », littéralement « récolter maintenant, déchiffrer plus tard ». Un contrat commercial, un brevet ou un dossier médical chiffré aujourd'hui garde souvent sa valeur pendant dix à quinze ans, soit plus longtemps que l'horizon 2029 visé par IBM.
Les exigences de l'ANSSI et du G7
Dans sa feuille de route présentée aux Assises de la cybersécurité, à Monaco, le 8 octobre 2025, l'ANSSI impose qu'en 2027, les produits candidats à une certification officielle intègrent un algorithme post-quantique pour l'obtenir. Et comme vous pourrez le lire dans l'encadré ci-dessous, en 2030, elle prévient qu'acheter des produits sans cryptographie post-quantique après cette date « ne sera pas raisonnable ».
Dans l'intervalle, l'agence recommande une hybridation. Elle propose de faire fonctionner un algorithme post-quantique aux côtés de RSA ou des courbes elliptiques, plutôt que de remplacer l'un par l'autre d'un seul coup. En octobre 2025, l'agence a par ailleurs délivré ses deux premiers visas de sécurité post-quantique, une fois que le CEA-Leti a évalué une carte à puce de Thales et un composant de Samsung. Les deux produits utilisent une cryptographie à réseaux de points. En 2024, l'ANSSI a identifié, auprès d'une cinquantaine de ministères et d'entreprises stratégiques et d'une trentaine de prestataires informatiques, des freins techniques et organisationnels à cette migration.
Depuis l'an dernier, le Canada préside le groupe de cybersécurité du G7 et engage les travaux qui ont abouti cet été, à la déclaration du G7 sur la préparation d'une migration vers la cryptographie post-quantique. Cette déclaration recommande aux organisations une gouvernance dédiée à la migration, un inventaire de leurs usages cryptographiques, une gestion du risque quantique et des systèmes cryptographiquement agiles, avant que la France n'en fasse une priorité de sa présidence du G7.
Début septembre dernier, l'ANSSI a présidé le groupe de cybersécurité du G7, aux côtés du Canada, de l'Allemagne, de l'Italie, du Japon, du Royaume-Uni et des États-Unis, avec la Commission européenne et l'ENISA en observatrices. Le G7 a publié à cette occasion un rapport sous le titre « Preparing for the Post-Quantum Era: A Call to Action ». Dans ce rapport, le G7 met en garde contre la compromission de secrets industriels et le contournement des mécanismes d'authentification. Il alerte aussi sur la falsification de données et sur la compromission d'équipements dans des chaînes d'approvisionnement interconnectées.
Par ailleurs, le G7 recommande cinq actions prioritaires, dont la constitution d'un inventaire des usages cryptographiques et l'intégration de critères post-quantiques dans les marchés publics.
Les premières mesures à engager dans votre TPE/PME
Commencez par repérer où vos données les plus sensibles sont protégées par RSA ou par les courbes elliptiques, en particulier vos sauvegardes, vos échanges avec votre expert-comptable et votre VPN d'accès à distance. Vous n'avez pas besoin d'un inventaire exhaustif pour commencer, et l'ANSSI recommande de prioriser d'abord les données dont la durée de vie dépasse dix à quinze ans. Les secrets industriels, les données de santé et les informations classifiées ont typiquement cette durée de vie longue, si bien que les PME sous-traitantes de la défense, les cabinets médicaux et les entreprises titulaires de brevets ont plus à perdre qu'un commerce de proximité. Les données de ce dernier perdent leur valeur en quelques mois. Un simple tableau mis à jour une fois par trimestre suffit pour commencer ce suivi.
Interrogez ensuite vos éditeurs de logiciels et vos prestataires informatiques sur leur feuille de route post-quantique, et exigez d'eux la crypto-agilité. Grâce à cette capacité, vous pouvez changer d'algorithme cryptographique sans réécrire l'application entière. Concrètement, vos prestataires isolent alors les fonctions cryptographiques du reste du code, dans un module séparé et remplaçable. Certains appels d'offres publics français exigent cette capacité de leurs fournisseurs. Les TPE sans service informatique dédié peuvent aussi consulter les outils gratuits de Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr pour évaluer leur exposition numérique globale avant de traiter spécifiquement la question du chiffrement.
Ne migrez rien dans l'urgence. Aucune norme française n'impose de délai avant 2027, et cette première échéance concerne les produits candidats à une certification, pas les PME elles-mêmes. Gardez plutôt cette feuille de route sous la main pour vos prochains renouvellements de matériel et de contrats logiciels, et posez la question de la crypto-agilité à chaque nouveau fournisseur.
« Nous encourageons les administrateurs systèmes à commencer l'intégration dès maintenant, car l'intégration complète prendra du temps », a déclaré Dustin Moody, mathématicien au NIST, en août 2024.

articles.title: Le satellite russe Kosmos 2612 s'éloigne d'ICEYE-X36 après être passé à quelques centaines de mètres de sa cible
articles.text:
Après le rapprochement spectaculaire entre un satellite militaire russe et sa cible finno-américaine, à 27 000 km/h en orbite autour de la Terre, est-ce déjà le moment de la séparation entre les deux engins ? En tout cas, Kosmos 2612 a de nouveau manœuvré le dimanche 18 octobre, creusant un écart de plus en plus important avec ICEYE-X36.
Dans une mise à jour publiée le 19 octobre sur son blog SatTrackCam Leiden, Marco Langbroek, enseignant en surveillance de l’espace à la faculté d’ingénierie aérospatiale de l’université technique de Delft, aux Pays-Bas, a repéré une nouvelle manœuvre de Kosmos 2612, vers 12 h 26 UTC le 18 octobre. Quelques heures plus tôt, vers 1 h 35 UTC, il estimait que les deux satellites étaient passés à quelques centaines de mètres l’un de l’autre, voire beaucoup plus près.
Le spécialiste néerlandais ne tranche pas sur le but de cette manœuvre. « Il pourrait s’agir soit d’éloigner davantage le satellite de sa cible, soit de la première d’une série de manœuvres de mise en phase en vue d’une future nouvelle approche », a-t-il avancé.
ICEYE-X36 est un satellite radar de la société finlandaise ICEYE, qui a été mis en orbite en 2024. Il peut produire des images du sol de jour comme de nuit, même à travers les nuages. ICEYE fournit des images radar au renseignement ukrainien, même si l’entreprise n’a pas dit si ICEYE-X36 en fait partie. D’où les suspicions autour du satellite russe qui s’est rapproché de lui depuis la mi-octobre.
Pour l’instant, Kosmos 2612 s’éloigne
Adam Cohen, ingénieur de l’US Space Force et fondateur d’Orbital Engineering Lab, un projet personnel d’analyse orbitale, a modélisé la trajectoire de Kosmos 2612 à partir des données orbitales publiques, c’est-à-dire les paramètres qui décrivent l’orbite de chaque satellite. D’après ses calculs, la poussée a placé le satellite russe sur une orbite plus large, qui l’éloignera d’ICEYE-X36 sans autre manœuvre.
« Kosmos 2612 semble avoir encore élevé son orbite. Cela le fera dériver davantage de ICEYE-X36. […] Leur séparation était d’environ 292 km », écrivait-il dans l’après-midi du 19 octobre. La société américaine LeoLabs, qui suit aussi ces objets, a confirmé à CNN que Kosmos 2612 s’éloigne. Depuis, l’écart entre les deux satellites a grandi.
L’astrophysicien Jonathan McDowell, qui suit lui aussi l’affaire sur X, y voyait dès le 17 octobre le premier rendez-vous en orbite basse entre deux satellites actifs sans l’accord de l’un des propriétaires. Il a également noté un éloignement entre les deux engins, en se basant sur les données de suivi de l’US Space Force.

articles.title: Esta nave de LEGO de 'Star Wars' mide tres metros y pesa más de 120 kilos. Su creador ha tardado dos años en construirla
articles.text:
Al principio de 'Una nueva esperanza', el destructor imperial persigue y captura a la pequeña nave rebelde Tantive IV. Ahora, un aficionado de LEGO le ha dado la vuelta a la tortilla y ha hecho de esa pequeña nave un auténtico monstruo. Tras dos años de construcción ha creado una reproducción de la Tantive IV a escala de minifigura (aproximadamente a escala 1:40) que deja en absoluto ridículo a los sets oficiales de LEGO.
Más de 3 metros de largo. El creador de esta monstruosidad es el youtuber Dubbzi Bricks, que ya era conocido por sus proyectos de grandes dimensiones, aunque se especializaba en escenarios y dioramas. En un vídeo en su canal de YouTube cuenta que se le fue un poco de las manos porque había planeado que midiera unos 2 metros de largo pero al final se le fue a 3 metros. Para ponerlo en contexto, el Destructor Estelar Imperial oficial de LEGO mide 109 centímetros. Hablamos de que la creación de este aficionado casi triplica la longitud de uno de los buques insignia más grandes del catálogo de la marca.
No sabe exactamente el número de piezas que utilizó pero calcula que superó las 150.000. Lo que sí tiene claro es lo que se gastó en construirlo: 13.600 euros.
25 kg solo en propulsores. Si la longitud ya es brutal, el peso no se queda atrás. Cuando empezó a construir ni se planteó que iba a necesitar soportes, lo que le obligó a rehacer muchas partes. La sección trasera fue la que más dolores de cabeza le dio de todo el montaje porque sólo los motores de la nave ya pesan 25 kg. Al final, optó por usar unos soportes con piezas Technic.
Aún con soportes, durante su primera exposición pública en Dublín se llevó un buen susto porque la mesa estaba un poco inclinada y casi acaba en catástrofe. Tuvo que reforzar los soportes para que pudieran aguantar semejante peso en voladizo. En total, la nave pesa más de 120 kg.
Un interior cargado de escenas. La nave no es una simple carcasa vacía. El autor añadió paneles desmontables para acceder a varias estancias interiores, con detalles como el pasillo en el que Darth Vader estrangula al capitán Antilles, la entrega de los planos a R2-D2 o la sala de conferencias de 'La venganza de los Sith'. Además, cuatro cápsulas de escape pueden eyectarse del fuselaje.
También hay espacio para detalles cómicos y guiños a la producción cinematográfica original. Una de las salas oculta un jacuzzi inspirado en los videojuegos de 'LEGO Star Wars', mientras que la cabina de mando esconde una miniatura de una revista para adultos. No es una ocurrencia al azar: homenajea una broma idéntica que el equipo técnico escondió en la maqueta original de 1977.
Luces LED y componentes móviles. Por si fuera poco, la nave también tiene un sistema de iluminación que según el autor ha mejorado la construcción "hasta el infinito". Cuenta con un efecto de parpadeo en los once motores traseros y también ha iluminado todas las escenas interiores para que se vean mucho mejor. Las luces fueron aportadas por la empresa especializada Game of Bricks y, aunque no dice cuánto costó, sí que apunta a que fueron varios cientos de euros.
Una peculiar y destructiva tradición. Como decíamos al principio, este youtuber ha llevado a cabo otros proyectos de gran envergadura y al acabar suele hacer una cosa: los destruye y aprovecha para grabar un vídeo en time lapse al revés. No es lo que va a pasar con la Tantive IV, pero no porque le haya cogido cariño, sino porque el museo Redmond's Forge se la ha comprado para tenerla en su exposición permanente.

articles.title: Turbine Capital closes €54 million DeepTech fund to connect Nordic startups with industrial leaders | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Turbine Capital, a Swedish VC fund focused on early-stage DeepTech companies in the Nordics, announced the final close of its first fund at €54 million (SEK 608 million) and a new industrial investor.
Mycronic joins the fund alongside Saab, Scania, Volvo Cars and Stena, as well as a number of industrial family offices and private investors. Institutional investors in the fund include Saminvest and the European Investment Fund (EIF).
“Closing our first fund at more than SEK 600 million, with an investor base ranging from leading Nordic industry to European institutions, confirms that our model meets a real need. During our first year, we have shown that multi-corporate venture capital works in practice, not just in theory,” says Anders Ösund, Founding & General Partner, Turbine Capital.
Turbine Capital’s final close comes amid several specialised European VC fund announcements in 2026.
In Sweden, Norrsken Evolve reached a €62 million final close, also backed by Saminvest and the European Investment Fund (EIF). Elsewhere in the Nordics, Copenhagen-based The Footprint Firm closed its €76 million climate and DeepTech fund, PSV Tech finalised a €56 million early-stage fund, and Climentum Capital secured a €60 million first close for climate HardTech investments.
France’s 360 Capital also announced an €85 million closing for its research-driven DeepTech fund Poli360 2.
Together with Turbine Capital, these announcements represent approximately €393 million in reported fund capital.
Source EU-Startups”Mycronic brings cutting-edge expertise in semiconductors and advanced manufacturing that strengthens our entire industrial network. Together with Saab, Scania, Volvo Cars and Stena, we have a base of industrial partners spanning defence, transport, electrification and now also semiconductor technology – exactly the kind of cross-sector platform Europe’s DeepTech companies need to scale,” adds Pär Hedberg, founder of Sting, who also is initiator and co-founder of Turbine Capital.
Since its first close in April 2025, Turbine Capital says they have built a unique Nordic model for cross-sector collaboration in venture capital: close cooperation with seven university-affiliated incubators – ABI, Uminova, UIC, Sting, LEAD, GU Ventures and IDEON – combined with a broad base of industrial investors.
The model gives investors access to early-stage innovation, while portfolio companies gain access to capital, industrial expertise and customers.
As a new investor in Turbine Capital, Mycronic complements the fund’s existing industrial base. Mycronic is a high-tech company engaged in the development, manufacture and marketing of production equipment with high precision and flexibility requirements for the electronics industry.
The company is in a strong growth phase driven by AI-related infrastructure investments, and has at the same time strengthened its presence in defence-related electronics manufacturing. Mycronic brings deep expertise in semiconductor technology, photonics and advanced manufacturing – key areas within Turbine Capital’s investment thesis.

articles.title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
articles.text:
Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.
In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.
The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.
A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail.
In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route. About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors.
Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies 15% of the land around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.
A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface. But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground.
“That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.”
This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north. As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost. This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost.
Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada released more carbon than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023. As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats. Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon.
Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically. They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control. They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon.
“We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire," says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference."
Woodwell, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the nonprofit Alaska Venture Fund are now partnering on a multimillion-dollar initiative known as North Fire to study and raise public awareness about the potential benefits of these interventions, MIT Technology Review can report.
The idea is complicated and controversial for a number of reasons. Wildfire is a natural and necessary component of healthy forest ecosystems. Preventing or suppressing fires across huge stretches of largely unmanaged Arctic-boreal forests and tundra would take vast resources. And it’s not yet clear how much of a difference such interventions would make in emissions.
Ultimately, the mere fact that researchers are considering such extreme interventions into natural systems is a grim reflection of the dangers we’ve placed ourselves in by continuing to generate more and more greenhouse-gas emissions each year. Those threats are forcing us to grapple with increasingly difficult questions that involve ever steeper trade-offs: What’s the best way to spend our finite resources and dwindling time to avoid the worst dangers of climate change? And when, if ever, is it okay to put people in possible danger to reduce broader risks to the world?
‘A massive blind spot’
Emissions from forest fires have risen 60% around the world since 2001—but they’ve nearly tripled across the boreal forests in the far north.
This stretch of the globe is warming as much as four times faster than the rest of the planet, drying out the landscape. In addition, lightning strikes that set off fires have ticked up sharply as warmer air increases the convective energy in the atmosphere, driving the updrafts that trigger thunderstorms.
In that sense, humans have already interceded in these otherwise natural ecosystems by producing the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, subjecting forests to fire patterns well outside healthy historic norms.
“To me, that outweighs the existential dread of ‘Should we or should we not intervene?” says Kate Hayes, an assistant professor at Western Washington University, who is working with Woodwell to study the emissions benefits of fire interventions. “We’ve already intervened, arguably. And so from here, it’s a little bit of a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.”
The permafrost that encircles the northern latitudes, underlying large stretches of Canada, Greenland, Siberia, Scandinavia, and other Arctic nations, stores around 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, much of which froze in place millennia ago. The steady global rise in temperature, however, has already shrunk the footprint of Arctic permafrost by about 12 % since 1850, with that loss rapidly accelerating during the last 50 years.
By 2100, fire-driven thawing of permafrost could release about the equivalent of nearly 80 billion tons of carbon dioxide, under high warming scenarios. That’s more than half the emissions that fires will release from the direct combustion of vegetation, according to a January study. And it would be on top of more than 400 billion additional tons that could be released through thawing from general warming over that period.
Despite its growing contributions to climate change, only a minority of the models that have informed the UN’s major climate reports to date include the gradual loss of permafrost through warming temperatures, and none incorporate the abrupt collapse and accelerated thaw that can often occur after fires and heat waves. In light of those phenomena and other powerful and undercounted climate feedback effects, we’re almost certainly underestimating how rapidly the planet will warm up, as scientists warned in a paper earlier this year.
These warming-driven emissions are a “massive blind spot,” says Brian Buma, a senior climate scientist at the Environmental Defense Fund and a coauthor of the paper, who is working to develop tools that could help fire agencies decide which fires to prioritize.
As escalating fire and permafrost emissions become significant additional contributors to climate change, some researchers have begun to explore what it might cost to take on the responsibility of preventing them, in much the way we’ve sought to cut the pollution from power plants, vehicles, and factories.
A 2022 paper in Science Advances, led by researchers at Woodwell and the Union of Concerned Scientists, found that making greater efforts to put out boreal fires could be a cost-effective climate solution—comparable to, or even cheaper than, addressing emissions by building wind turbines, solar farms, or carbon-sucking factories.
The Yukon Flats pilot
Those economic findings were instrumental in getting more researchers to take the idea of tackling fire emissions seriously, says Peter Frumhoff, a coauthor of the 2022 paper and now a senior science policy advisor at Woodwell.
For several years now, Woodwell researchers have been in discussions with forest managers, fire agencies, Indigenous communities, and other groups across Alaska to communicate the potential of this approach.
It hasn’t been an easy sell, given the constrained resources and tightly defined mission of the federal and state agencies responsible for combating fires in Alaska. The general policy there is to allow fires in remote territories to burn unless they present a direct danger to communities.
“Those agencies are tasked with protecting life and property now, and to a lesser extent natural resources,” says Randi Jandt, a fire ecologist at the Alaska Fire Science Consortium. “But they’re not tasked to save the world.”
There was one notable early success, however.
The Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge is an 11-million-acre patchwork of wetlands, forests, and bogs. The foothills sit above a particular type of frozen soil known as yedoma. It’s an especially deep, ice-rich, and carbon-dense form of permafrost, composed of massive wedges of silty, wind-blown sediments frozen during the late Pleistocene, which ended about 11,700 years ago. (It also presented ideal conditions for preserving mummified remains of woolly mammoths.)
“It took kind of the last ice age to accumulate,” Hayes says. “So there’s no rapid way to re-accumulate it. We can’t really put it back.”
In 2019, the region suffered a series of devastating fires that burned some 750,000 acres. After an Alaska Fire Science Consortium meeting at which Woodwell scientists highlighted the possible climate benefits of more aggressive fire suppression, the refuge's then manager, Jimmy Fox, began exploring the possibility of putting out blazes when they threatened that permafrost, whether or not they threatened human habitations.
The early reaction was not encouraging.
“You’re going to have people jumping out of airplanes with parachutes to save frozen woolly mammoths—and maybe dying from that?” he recalls being asked.
But eventually, he persuaded managers at the US Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Fire Service to carry out a pilot project on a 1.6-million-acre section of the Yukon Flats. They agreed to try to put out fires there if they had the resources available and believed they could contain a blaze within 72 hours.
Woodwell and its partners agreed to study how that change affected permafrost loss and fire emissions, in the hope of making the case for similar programs elsewhere.
It wasn’t clear the pilot program would survive after Donald Trump was reelected, particularly once the DOGE initiative retroactively cut the public funding for that research collaboration.
But in February, the federal government formally preserved the program and broadened its rationale to include goals like protecting habitat diversity, water quality, and air quality.
Mapping and modeling
One of Woodwell’s main tasks now is determining when and where fire agencies should step in. Crucially, excessive efforts to stamp out fires in the past have allowed the buildup of dry plant material that fuels more severe fires later.
“We’re not going after all fires all the time,” says Rogers over lunch in a sunny courtyard on the Stanford University campus, where Woodwell and EDF hosted a workshop on potential fire interventions in January. “We can’t do that. We don’t want to do that. We shouldn’t do that. So how do we prioritize our resources?”
Woodwell and its collaborators are working to answer that question by developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across interior Alaska. The plan is to eventually expand it across much of Canada as well.
These maps will highlight the locations of rich reserves of yedoma and other forms of permafrost, forecast where fires are most likely to break out in the next 10 to 15 years, and predict how they’re likely to behave and spread.
“Our ultimate goal is to get a layer that can tell us, if a fire were to occur, what areas are most vulnerable to high carbon emissions, permafrost thaw, permafrost degradation,” Rogers says.
In response to a question about potentially putting firefighters at risk, Rogers stressed in an email that it’s “a very serious issue that needs careful consideration.”
He added that early fire detection technologies, preventative fire stewardship practices, improved fire suppression planning and other measures can all help to reduce dangers to firefighters as well as communities.
‘Mild fire’
Once areas of particular risk are identified, the first option is to take measures to prevent fires there, or at least to reduce the odds that they’ll become major ones. That generally entails using heavy equipment or intentional, controlled fires to clear away vegetation that could fuel new fires, or to create fire breaks that might check their spread.
Indigenous tribes carried out what’s known as cultural burning for thousands of years to reduce fire dangers, clear land for crops, and more. The practice was widely outlawed across North America beginning in the 1800s, though those rules have loosened in recent years.
Both cultural and prescribed fires, however, remain controversial because they can burn out of control. And even if they remain contained, the fires can still produce smoke that wafts into towns.
But rushing around to put out blazes after they’ve started will never get Alaska ahead of its surging wildfire problem, says Edward Alexander, cochair of the Gwich’in Council International, which represents the Indigenous Gwich’in peoples of the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, and Alaska.
“There’s not enough money in the world for this to be a chainsaw-and-ax problem,” he says. “This country is too big up here.”
Alexander, who also serves as senior Arctic lead at Woodwell, argues that Alaska should encourage much greater use of cultural burning to reduce the risk of conflagrations and the emissions that come with them.
“We need mild fire, not wildfire,” he says.
New pilot projects
The North Fire initiative will include several additional pilot research projects, including an effort to study the potential for cultural burning to reduce climate and fire dangers near Fort Yukon, Alaska.
The plan is for a wildland firefighting crew operated by the Council of Athabascan Tribal Governments, a consortium in the Yukon Flats region, to carry out cultural burns there next spring, Rogers says.
Researchers at Woodwell and the University of Alaska, Fairbanks, will then collect and analyze data flammability, carbon levels, and permafrost over several years, in the hopes of learning more about what such interventions do.
Similarly, the Polis researchers at the University of Victoria plan to study how adding fuel breaks, by logging or switching to less flammable trees, alters fire risks in British Columbia.
The broad aim of the North Fire initiative is to accelerate research and expand community involvement “in a way that helps us scale this as a meaningful global natural climate solution on a rapid timeline,” says Erin Harrington, a partner at the Alaska Venture Fund, a philanthropy focused on environmental, economic development, and Indigenous issues.
Detecting fires from space
Other observers, including Jandt, believe the bigger opportunity to reduce fire emissions and preserve permafrost may lie in the “initial attack.” That means marshalling planes, tankers, and firefighters to stamp fires out at the first sign of them, before they’ve had the chance to turn into conflagrations.
Once fires reach a certain size, it takes much more time to contain them—and the job becomes far more dangerous.
Accelerating response times is one of the chief promises of the FireSat satellite constellation, which is expected to begin delivering fire data at least twice daily from around the world to Woodwell, a handful of fire agencies, and other early adopters by the end of this year. The system will eventually include more than 50 satellites circling the globe, equipped with high-resolution cameras and thermal sensors that can detect smaller, lower-temperature fires than existing satellite systems, down to as little as five by five meters (16 by 16 feet).
Currently, it can take days to spot fires. But once the full constellation is in place, likely in the early 2030s, FireSat should be capable of detecting and providing updated images of fires anywhere in the world every 20 minutes or less.
The first prototype satellite launched in 2025, and three operational ones went into orbit in July. The Earth Fire Alliance, the nonprofit that manages the constellation, expects to launch four more by the end of next year.
A number of similar systems are also coming online. German-based OroraTech has launched 18 of its fire-detecting satellites in the last year and a half. Similarly, Canadian agencies are planning to launch their own satellite constellation, dubbed WildFireSat, beginning in 2029.
But as these systems produce more and more detections across the globe, it’ll become increasingly essential to build tools that can filter through that information.
EDF is supporting and collaborating on several projects that could potentially help with that, and it ultimately intends to develop an AI-powered triage tool that could help fire agencies prioritize responses as FireSat and other fire-spotting tools come online.
"All of this is kind of like building the data ecosystem around FireSat, so that when they start popping out “fire start here, there, fire start here, fire start there,” we won’t be like, ‘Oh shit, there’s fires everywhere,’” Buma says. “We’ll have a framework. It won’t be perfect, obviously. We’ll have to improve it, but we’ll have the machinery to incorporate those data.”
Rapid response
But faster detections and decisions do only so much. Regions would still need to get firefighting personnel and resources to those fires fast enough to prevent them from burning out of control.
“Say we have the full FireSat constellation up and running, and it spots a fire that just broke out in one of these sort of high-priority, highly vulnerable areas,” I said to Rogers and Frumhoff during our conversation in that Stanford courtyard. “How might we deploy firefighting resources to a remote area fast enough for it to matter in that scenario?”
“I think the answer, unfortunately, is that it depends,” Rogers responded.
Ideally, he said, we would have fire management policies in place that allow for putting out fires with a high risk of producing climate-warming emissions. In addition, regions could install more firefighting personnel and resources across more operational centers, strategically placed in locations that allow them to get to those blazes fast.
Frumhoff stresses that Woodwell isn’t promoting any particular companies but says there are additional technologies “in the mix of conversations” that might help to prevent or rapidly put out fires as well.
Those possible approaches include seeding clouds to suppress lightning strikes and pre-positioning autonomous firefighting helicopters to respond rapidly to high-emissions-risk fires.
Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, is developing and testing autonomous versions of the Black Hawk helicopter, equipped with thermal sensors and water tanks. It is collaborating with Rain Industries, a startup based in Alameda, California, that has developed software to track shifting conditions and steer unpiloted aircraft through the process of putting out wildfires.
The company says it has talked to fire agencies and the “broader Alaska fire community” about the potential use of its technology but declined to name any specific entities it has interacted with.
“The twin climate tipping points of the yedoma permafrost and the boreal forest, and the fact that it’s completely underresourced at the moment, from my perspective does make it an ideal use case for autonomous aircraft,” says Max Brodie, chief executive officer of Rain.
Defending carbon
Advancing technologies can only do so much if governments’ fire prevention and suppression policies don’t prioritize preserving carbon.
And that will remain a hard sell given the costs of managing extensive areas of land that nations have historically left largely alone.
The 2022 Science Advances paper estimated that additional fire suppression efforts would cost about $12.63 per metric ton of prevented carbon dioxide emissions—a number that drops when the carbon in permafrost is taken into account, according to upcoming research.
But that would still add up to about $7 billion in additional spending this decade to keep Alaska’s fire emissions at their historical levels, and another $7 billion to $50 billion over the subsequent 30 years as fire severity continues to rise.
Frumoff stresses that those figures just reflect what the researchers found it would cost to preserve the status quo, which is not necessarily what the policy goal would be.
But widening the scope of where we put out fires will inevitably create a big added cost for fire agencies that are already notoriously underfunded in the US. While Alaska produces about half the nation’s wildfire emissions, it receives around 4% of federal firefighting funds.
The US Wildland Fire Service provided a prepared statement in response to an MIT Technology Review inquiry asking whether preserving carbon could or should become a priority in certain fire management decisions. The roundabout reply suggests that this isn’t the agency’s prime concern: “Firefighter and public safety are the top priorities for the U.S. Wildland Fire Service.”
Frumhoff says it’s possible that landowners or government agencies could eventually use carbon markets to defray some of the additional costs. Woodwell has also had multiple conversations with Alaska’s federal legislators about the value of preventing catastrophic wildfires and the need to increase the “total pot” of public funding, he says.
Kicking the fire can
A few days after walking through the fire scar in Fairbanks, I drove slowly along a crumpled stretch of Stampede Road, just north of Denali National Park, where the underlying permafrost had melted without the aid of fire.
I arrived at a cramped wooden cabin to meet with Michelle Mack, a regents professor of ecosystem ecology at Northern Arizona University.
Mack studies how fire is altering ecosystems in the high northern latitudes as the region grows warmer and drier, and she sometimes collaborates with Rogers and other scientists working on the push to protect permafrost in other areas of research. But she’s unsure how much these interventions will accomplish as climate change continues.
“I’m an empiricist, and at this point, it’s not clear to me that the empirical evidence suggests that we can actually have any impact on these fires,” she says.
She expects there will be clear cases where we could and should act fast to put out fires and “keep carbon in the ground.” She points to the example of the 2007 Anaktuvuk River Fire, a massive tundra fire on Alaska’s North Slope that might have been extinguished with relative ease in its early days but was instead allowed to burn until the winter snows put it out nearly three months later. Over that time, it ripped across 400 square miles and, Mack’s research showed, released more than 2 million tons of carbon into the air.
“I feel like that’s the low-hanging fruit, something that doesn’t cost much—and that’s where the technology for detection I think is really important,” she says.
But she adds that fires in boreal forests can rapidly spread in unpredictable ways, frustrating efforts to quickly extinguish them even when they are spotted right away.
In addition, rapidly putting out a fire one season doesn’t necessarily reduce the fire risk for a given forest, so suppression may simply kick the “fire can” down the road—delaying but not preventing an inevitable loss of carbon, Mack says.
Her thinking more recently shifted “a little” after she came across an earlier modeling paper that showed some encouraging findings on the potential of early suppression to reduce the footprint of boreal fires. But she says that prevention through forest thinning, prescribed burns, and the introduction of less flammable deciduous trees to create “living fire breaks” is probably a more promising path than technology-augmented suppression.
“If we could solve this with a techno fix, that’d be great,” she says. “But what if we solved it with nature?”
‘A real difference’
Rogers, in an emailed response to Mack’s concern, said that the interventions they’re exploring, which do include both prevention and suppression, “can make a real difference.”
“I certainly agree that some fires are much easier to suppress via initial attack than others,” he wrote. “That said, until I see data showing me otherwise, I believe there is strong potential to bend the curve with management.”
EDF’s Buma acknowledges there are a number of unknowns, including how quickly agencies could act on faster detections from satellites—and how big the political obstacles will be to making necessary changes to fire management policies.
“We can’t overpromise what’s possible. We don’t know what’s possible,” he says. “It’s all new. But we’re in a new climate and have to consider trying new things.”
