articles.title: Claude für alte Fernseher: So macht die KI Android-TVs wieder flott
articles.text:
Claude für alte Fernseher: So macht die KI Android-TVs wieder flott
Wer schon mehrere Jahre einen smarten Fernseher mit Android benutzt, wird das Problem sicherlich kennen. Nach dieser langen Zeit fühlt sich das Betriebssystem nicht mehr so flott wie am Anfang an. Der Android-TV startet langsam und manche Apps brauchen eine gefühlte Ewigkeit, um ihre Inhalte anzuzeigen. Doch das könnte dank eines KI-Workarounds bald ein Ende haben.
So räumt Claude bei Android-Fernsehern auf
Das Projekt stammt vom Entwickler Ansub Khan, der es kostenlos auf GitHub zur Verfügung stellt. Zunächst handelt es sich um eine Anleitung, wie du deinen alten Android-TV mit Claude Code in Verbindung bringst und die KI anweist, auf dem Fernseher aufzuräumen. Um die beiden miteinander zu verbinden, müssen Nutzer:innen erst den Entwicklermodus auf ihrem Smart-TV aktivieren, indem sie in den Geräteeinstellungen unter „Über das Gerät“ siebenmal mit der Fernbedienung die Build-Version auswählen.
Im Anschluss muss noch der USB-Debugging-Mode in den Entwickleroptionen aktiviert werden. Sobald du Claude Code oder Codex dann auf einem Laptop oder PC betreibst, der im selben Netzwerk wie der Fernseher angemeldet ist, kann die KI auf den Android-TV zugreifen. Für die Aufräumarbeiten gibt Khan einen sechsteiligen Prompt, den Claude Schritt für Schritt abarbeiten kann.
Braucht es eine KI für einen schnelleren TV?
Die KI soll zunächst eine Verbindung mit dem TV herstellen und dann alle installierten Apps auflisten. Dabei soll die KI schon Empfehlungen geben, welche Anwendungen ohne Probleme deaktiviert werden können, um mehr Speicher freizugeben. Dann kommt das entwickelte Tool zum Einsatz, das Khan auf GitHub bereitstellt. Es handelt sich um einen neuen Homescreen für Android TV, der deutlich aufgeräumter ist, Werbung blockiert und Animationen auf ein Minimum beschränkt. So soll die Performance optimiert werden.
Claude fragt bei jedem Schritt nach, ob User:innen die Änderungen wirklich vollziehen wollen. Möglich ist das laut Khan auf Fernsehern mit Android TV 9 oder höher sowie Google TV 14. Andere Systeme wie Samsungs Tizen-Betriebssystem oder webOS von LG können von dem Tool nicht beeinflusst werden. Bei Amazons Fire TVs funktioniert immerhin noch die Aufräumarbeit, aber der neue Homescreen wird blockiert.
Bevor du zur Tat schreitest, solltest du beachten, dass Claude natürlich Fehler bei der Umsetzung machen kann. Wenn du die Anleitung befolgst, handelst du also auf eine eigene Gefahr.
Tatsächlich kannst du diese Aktionen aber auch bei den meisten TVs selbst händisch vornehmen. Navigiere dazu in den Einstellungen zum App-Bereich und wähle bei den Anwendungen, die du vorerst nicht mehr benötigst, „deinstallieren“ oder „deaktivieren“ aus. Selbst der neue Homescreen lässt sich mit ein paar Handgriffen ohne KI installieren. Dafür benötigst du einen Mac oder Windows-PC mit der Android Debug Bridge. Eine genaue Anleitung dazu findest du auf der GitHub-Seite des Projekts in den FAQ unter „Can I install the home screen without AI?“.

articles.title: IEEE Report Highlights How Members Are Engineering for Public Good
articles.text:
Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered.
Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles:
- Shaping trustworthy digital experiences for children online. An IEEE collaboration with Indonesian policymakers led to a new regulation to protect children, a first of its kind in the region. The advanced frameworks used for the design of Internet platforms and systems are based on the IEEE 2089-2021 and 2089.1-2024 standards. The IEEE 2089-2021 Standard for an Age-Appropriate Digital Services Framework Based on the 5Rights Principles for Children provides practical steps to qualify online products and services. The follow-up, the IEEE 2089.1-2024 Standard for Online Age Verification, provides a framework for designing, specifying, evaluating, and deploying age-verification systems. You can learn more about the two standards in “IEEE Makes Strides to Improve Online Safety for Kids.”
- Catalyzing humanitarian outreach. Last year IEEE launched its Mobile Outreach Vehicle (MOVE) program in India. The vehicle brings educational resources to communities and can provide communication and technology support to relief workers and survivors during emergencies. In 2024, for example, MOVE helped survivors of Hurricanes Helene and Milton in the Southeastern United States. When the vehicles are not deployed, IEEE MOVE remains engaged in outreach efforts, participating in 25 STEM educational events such as one in San Diego in 2023.
- Preserving Tech History. The IEEE Global Museum, developed by the IEEE History Center, presents traveling exhibits to educate the public about the history of technology and its impact on society. In “IEEE’s Global Museum Brings Engineering History to You,” you can learn about current exhibits “Unseen Signals: E. Howard Armstrong’s Radio Revolution” and “Microchips That Shook the World.”
- EPICS in IEEE. This program provides nonprofit organizations with technology solutions while broadening undergraduate students’ hands-on experiences. Last year US $290,000 was awarded to a record-breaking number of service projects around the world. Among the 48 projects was one in which a student team in Macedonia created IoT-driven sensing and display devices to help measure and promote awareness of pollution and air-quality issues in the capital city of Skopje.
- IEEE TryEngineering. This initiative inspires preuniversity students to pursue technology and engineering careers. It awarded US $70,379 in grants to 58 programs around the world. One is its TryEngineering Summer Institute, a nine-day summer sleepaway camp for students ages 13 to 17. More than 310 students participated last year, learning about aerospace and artificial intelligence.
- IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu. IEEE-HKN has more than 260 collegiate chapters worldwide and more than 200,000 members. The honor society encourages and recognizes excellence in education, professional practice, and meritorious work within IEEE’s designated fields of interest. IEEE-HKN members last year contributed 110,442 volunteer hours to universities and communities, and they held 827 service and outreach events and 137 STEM outreach activities. Last year IEEE and HKN celebrated the 15th anniversary of their merger.
- IEEE Connecting the Unconnected Challenge. This annual global competition solicits innovative solutions from startups, grassroots organizations, universities, and others working to bridge the digital divide. The Institute wrote about last year’s winners. They included a solar-powered community broadband network in Tanzania, a low-cost method for accessing the Internet that uses FM radio and a short message service, and a strategy for utilizing India’s rural broadband infrastructure to deliver medical services to people living in isolated, tribal, and other underserved regions.
- Supporting Sustainable Climate Efforts. IEEE helps foster the exchange of technical knowledge and information to develop technologies for a sustainable climate. “IEEE Plays a Pivotal Role in Climate Mitigation Talks” reported how the organization enhanced its standing as a trusted, neutral authority on the role of technology in climate change mitigation and adaptation. Leaders, including 2023 IEEE President Saifur Rahman, showcased tech solutions at COP30 and the International Symposium on Achieving a Sustainable Climate. Also, “IEEE Young Professionals Talked Sustainability Tech at Climate Week NYC” reported on the group’s activities during the 2024 Climate Week NY, the largest annual climate event, featuring more than 600 activities throughout New York City.
Engineering: A force for good
“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”
Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.
“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.
“IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”
- Reclaiming Social Engineering for Good ›
- IEEE President’s Note: Technology for Social Good ›
- What “Social Good” Means to Engineers ›
Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

articles.title: The Next Wave: Are layoffs good for AI’s business?
articles.text:
First published on October 18, 2026
Microsoft ADC offices at Dunhill Towers in Nairobi, Kenya. Image: TechCabal
Microsoft has shut its Africa Development Centre (ADC) in Nairobi, Kenya, leaving more than 400 engineers without jobs, following the closure of its Lagos engineering operation in May 2024. It has also closed sales offices in Windhoek, Abidjan, Dakar, Accra and Port-Louis. Microsoft says it “remains committed to Kenya”, but its retreat from the places where it once promised to build African engineering talent tells a different story. As the company and its peers pour billions into artificial intelligence (AI), these closures also reinforce a message that benefits the industry selling it. AI is coming for your job, and the companies building it are worth investing in.
The Nairobi decision is difficult to explain through performance alone. Employees familiar with the centre say it had no quality or performance problems, and some received strong appraisal ratings before learning their jobs were at risk. Microsoft has not publicly said poor performance prompted the decision. People close to the matter say about five employees across customer and partner solutions, recruitment, and sales will remain in the affected operation.
Announced in 2019, the centre was part of Microsoft’s $100 million commitment to build engineering capacity in Africa. The company planned to hire 500 engineers across Nairobi and Lagos, Nigeria, giving it access to local talent while offering African engineers the chance to work on products used worldwide. The Lagos hub closed in 2024, and Nairobi is now following suit, exiting Microsoft’s engineering business on the continent.
Microsoft may continue to serve African customers through its sales teams, cloud services, and other operations. But the closure of both engineering centres raises questions about the company’s long-term commitment to developing local technical talent. The people losing their jobs are not the only ones affected. Governments and universities that treated Microsoft’s investment as evidence of Africa’s place in the global technology industry must now reckon with its withdrawal.
The cuts also feed a narrative that AI will soon become central to how businesses operate. AI companies have raised enormous sums on the promise that their technology will change work, and layoffs attributed to AI give investors another reason to believe that promise.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Layoffs are becoming part of the AI sales pitch
Microsoft is not alone in using AI to explain workforce reductions. Amazon eliminated 14,000 corporate jobs in October 2025 and another 16,000 in January 2026, while Salesforce has linked its AI agents to a reduced need for customer support staff after cutting about 4,000 roles. In February 2026, Salesforce also laid off fewer than 1,000 employees across several functions. Across software, customer service, and other knowledge-based industries, AI has prompted companies to reconsider how many people they employ.
Some of these changes are real, given that AI tools can write code, summarise documents, answer customer queries, and handle repetitive administrative tasks. Companies have good reason to test whether these tools can reduce their costs, and some jobs will disappear as businesses automate work. It would be wrong to dismiss every AI-related redundancy as a publicity exercise.
The problem is that companies rarely separate the work AI can already perform from the work they expect it to perform in the future. A business might cut jobs because demand has weakened, teams overlap, or management wants to improve margins. AI may contribute to the decision, but it can also provide a convenient explanation for restructuring that would have happened anyway.
Cutting staff can improve a company’s financial results immediately, while the productivity gains promised by AI may take years to materialise. A company can reduce its payroll and report better margins before proving that its AI investments will generate enough money to cover its costs. The promise of future productivity can therefore help justify decisions whose immediate financial benefits come from employing fewer people.
There is also a commercial benefit to making AI appear unavoidable. When Microsoft, Amazon, or Salesforce announces cuts linked to AI, other executives face pressure to show they are preparing for the same future. Businesses fear falling behind, workers worry about their jobs, and investors look for companies positioned to profit. The announcements help sell AI as a necessity rather than a technology whose value must be judged against its cost.
There is no evidence that companies are coordinating layoffs to drive up demand for AI stocks. But the language surrounding the cuts can still benefit an industry whose valuations depend on investors believing that AI will become indispensable. That is worth examining, especially as two of its biggest players prepare to approach public markets.
The IPO is where the story gets expensive
OpenAI announced a funding round involving $122 billion in committed capital in March 2026, valuing the company at $852 billion after the investment. Microsoft has committed $13 billion to OpenAI through their partnership since 2019, of which $11.9 billion had been funded by June 2026, according to Microsoft’s annual filing. These figures cover different parts of OpenAI’s financing and should not be treated as separate investments.
Anthropic has attracted similarly large sums, raising $65 billion in May 2026 at a post-money valuation of $965 billion. That same month, the company reported an annualised revenue run rate above $47 billion.
A public listing would give the companies access to a broader pool of investors and allow some existing shareholders to sell their stakes. Investors who backed them privately could realise substantial returns if the market values them at levels above their previous funding rounds. The story they sell to public investors will need to justify those valuations.
OpenAI has reported rapid revenue growth, but it has yet to establish sustained profitability. Its spending on computing infrastructure and model development remains high, and projections suggest it may not generate positive cash flow until 2030. Revenue growth alone does not indicate whether the company can earn enough to cover the costs of developing and operating its systems.
Anthropic reported $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue in October 2026 and adjusted profitability for a second consecutive quarter, although its growth has slowed from earlier in the year. Adjusted profitability does not tell investors everything about the company’s long-term costs or whether it can sustain its margins.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have found strong demand for their products, and AI already has practical uses in software development, research, and customer support. They still need to prove they can turn that demand into profits and justify what investors are paying for them.
The blockchain boom of the 2010s offers a useful comparison, as investors were told the technology would change finance, agriculture, and supply chains, yet many promised applications never reached mainstream use. Blockchain had practical uses, but that did not make every company built around it a sound investment. AI could have a far greater commercial impact, but its potential does not guarantee that every company selling it will succeed.
Microsoft’s African closures do not prove a plan to inflate AI valuations, but they show how the company can abandon a long-term investment in local engineering while the industry it belongs to asks investors to believe AI will define the future of business. More than 400 engineers are losing their jobs, while investors are being offered a chance to profit from the technology being presented as the future of work.
The market should judge AI companies by the money they make, not just the money they raise or the jobs their customers cut. By the time OpenAI and Anthropic reach public markets, investors will have heard plenty about AI’s ability to replace workers. They will need to ask a harder question about whether the businesses promising that future can make enough money to justify their valuations.
Kenn Abuya
Senior Reporter, TechCabal

articles.title: Cómo proteger el número de teléfono y qué datos no compartir ante fraudes digitales en Centroamérica
articles.text:
Un número de teléfono puede parecer un dato menor, pero suele estar vinculado a cuentas bancarias, correos electrónicos, redes sociales y aplicaciones de mensajería. En Centroamérica, conocer los riesgos asociados a su exposición permite a los usuarios detectar maniobras de fraude antes de que los delincuentes obtengan información, dinero o acceso a servicios digitales.
La firma de ciberseguridad ESET Latinoamérica advirtió recientemente que un número telefónico puede convertirse en el punto de partida para fraudes, robos de cuentas y suplantaciones de identidad. El dato, por sí solo, no permite ingresar de forma directa a un celular, leer conversaciones de WhatsApp ni acceder a una cuenta bancaria. El riesgo aparece cuando los atacantes lo combinan con información disponible en internet o con engaños dirigidos a la víctima.
Para los usuarios de países centroamericanos, donde los teléfonos son una herramienta habitual para recibir transferencias, coordinar entregas, comunicarse con familiares en el exterior y validar operaciones digitales, la advertencia plantea medidas concretas de prevención.
El número puede ayudar a construir un engaño personalizado
Un ciberdelincuente puede vincular un teléfono con perfiles de redes sociales, publicaciones, nombres, direcciones de correo electrónico o datos que hayan quedado expuestos tras una filtración. Con esa información, tiene más elementos para hacerse pasar por un banco, una empresa de mensajería, un servicio de entrega o incluso un conocido de la víctima.
El propósito suele ser obtener contraseñas, códigos de verificación, datos personales o información financiera. También puede consistir en inducir a la persona a abrir un enlace malicioso que imita una página oficial.
La regla central es no entregar códigos de acceso ni datos personales ante llamadas o mensajes no solicitados. Si una entidad bancaria o una compañía pide información por WhatsApp, SMS o teléfono, el usuario debe cortar la comunicación y verificar el pedido mediante los canales oficiales de esa institución.
David González, investigador de seguridad informática de ESET, explicó que conocer un número no habilita por sí mismo el acceso al dispositivo. Sin embargo, puede servir para iniciar intentos de fraude que aprovechan la relación de ese dato con el resto de la vida digital de una persona.
Los códigos de WhatsApp no se comparten
Uno de los métodos más frecuentes apunta a tomar el control de cuentas de mensajería. La víctima puede recibir un código de WhatsApp que no solicitó y, poco después, un desconocido afirma que el mensaje llegó “por error” y le pide que se lo reenvíe.
Ese código puede ser la llave para registrar la cuenta en otro dispositivo. Si la persona lo comparte, el atacante podría apropiarse de su perfil y usarlo para pedir dinero a familiares, amigos o contactos laborales bajo una identidad conocida.
La recomendación también se aplica a códigos enviados por correo electrónico, plataformas de pago, redes sociales o aplicaciones bancarias. Son claves personales y temporales, por lo que ninguna empresa legítima debería solicitarlas por mensaje, llamada o chat.
El cambio fraudulento de SIM puede cortar el control del usuario
Otro riesgo es el SIM swapping, una modalidad en la que el delincuente intenta convencer a la empresa telefónica de que es el titular de la línea. Si logra transferir el número a otra tarjeta SIM, puede recibir llamadas y mensajes de texto que antes llegaban a la víctima.
Esto resulta relevante porque muchos servicios aún envían códigos de recuperación y validación por SMS. Una pérdida repentina de señal, llamadas que dejan de entrar o mensajes que no llegan pueden ser señales de alerta. Frente a esa situación, el usuario debe contactar de inmediato a su operador telefónico y revisar las cuentas asociadas a ese número.
Autenticación en dos factores y revisión de datos expuestos
Proteger las aplicaciones con autenticación de dos factores, revisar la información personal expuesta en redes y desconfiar de pedidos urgentes reduce la posibilidad de que un número telefónico habilite un fraude digital.

articles.title: ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Services in Response to Cyberattack
articles.text:
ConnectWise is scrambling to restore its Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management services after hackers abused a compromised credential to access customers’ M365 tenants.
The company suspended the Cloud Backup service (formerly known as SkyKick) on October 17, roughly 12 hours after it started investigating the suspicious activity.
“We recently identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment. As a protective measure for our Cloud Backup partners and their clients, we are shutting off Cloud Backup application access,” the company said.
The next day, it decided to shut down SaaS Security and Cloud Management as well, to implement mitigations, noting that customers’ backups remain encrypted and protected and that it has no evidence of unauthorized access to them.
The containment measure continues to impact scheduled backups, archive access, and restores, as well as SaaS Security monitoring and alerting, and Cloud Management user and license management, and ConnectWise has not provided an estimated restoration timeline.
However, it has shared information on the IP addresses used in the intrusion and has published guidance for reviewing MSPs’ Microsoft 365 environments.
According to cybersecurity firm Huntress, the compromised Cloud Backup credential was used to access Microsoft 365 tenants on October 15.
Cloud Backup’s identity was seen signing in to 162 Microsoft 365 tenants between October 15 and October 16.
“The authentication itself is certain: It comes from Microsoft’s own sign-in logs in each tenant. The credential type was a client assertion, which means the credential lives in the vendor’s own tenant. Nothing a customer did in their environment could have produced it,” Huntress says.
The activity originated from the same IP address that was used between October 13 and October 14 in password spraying attacks against four law firm tenants and in scripted sign-in attempts.
In one customer tenant, Huntress observed the ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams adding itself to the Global Administrator role on October 15, then running a Python script that added new client secrets to an MSP management application and to Huntress’s own application.
This happened roughly two and a half hours before the first sign-ins from the attacker’s IP address, and the access came from Microsoft’s internal cloud network rather than that IP. Huntress says it has not tied the two phases to the same operator.
“The app’s credential is in hostile hands. It was used to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenants in sorted GUID order, a few seconds apart, which points to a script working from a target list,” Huntress notes.
By October 17, the cybersecurity firm had identified sign-in activity from the attacker’s IP address in nearly 1,000 Entra tenants, with over 300 of the sign-ins being successful. However, a successful sign-in did not always mean access: in tenants lacking the relevant ConnectWise service principal, the attackers could not get in.
Huntress says it is highly confident the threat actor also abused the ConnectWise Cloud Management Exchange Online, MS Teams, and SharePoint Online applications as part of the intrusions. All three have been shut down by ConnectWise.
“ConnectWise has stopped the attack. But businesses unfortunately have the responsibility and difficult task to ensure that the threat actor didn’t change any Microsoft 365 configuration or establish any persistence within their tenant. More than a third of IT leaders wrongly believe that Microsoft automatically backs up their configuration, making recovery from such an attack all the more tricky,” CoreView VP of security strategy Kasper Lindgaard said.

articles.title: Anthropic wants AI models blocked only if they threaten over $1 billion in damage or more than 50 deaths or serious injuries
articles.text:
Winners & losers: Anthropic is pitching a draft AI safety bill to lawmakers. That might sound like a good thing, but there are some eyebrow-raising sections. One of them is that the government should be able to block the release of a new AI model, but only if it has the potential to cause at least $1 billion worth of damage or kill or seriously injure more than 50 people. It seems causing $999 million worth of damage and killing 49 people isn't really a problem.
Politico obtained the confidential draft of the proposal, which a company spokesperson said included "sensible policies we believe Congress should act on."
The headline provision would allow the government to block only models that could cause at least $1 billion worth of damage or kill or injure 50 or more people.
Moreover, the risk posed by the model must stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer's controls, or a cyberattack. Politico notes that the language mirrors California's AI laws, including SB 5, which was signed last year.
The bill proposes that independent evaluators, registered with the Commerce Department, periodically evaluate the lab and its frontier models. It's also noted that the lab may pay the evaluators, but only if their independence remains unaffected.
If an evaluator discovers these alarming-sounding potential risks in an AI model, they are required to report their findings to Commerce within 72 hours of completing their assessment.
The Commerce Department would then have to present the evidence before a federal judge in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, who would decide whether the model's release should be stopped. The proposal also states that no other US department, agency, or office could suspend the model's development, deployment or internal use.
"This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic's Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June," the Anthropic spokesperson added.
There have been plenty of concerns over the runaway pace of AI development recently. Following the numerous incidents of AI agents going rogue and hacking other companies, an Anthropic researcher resigned with a warning that AI could end the human race. The company even highlighted these risks in its preliminary IPO prospectus.
Lawmakers have been proposing AI safety rules in the wake of these incidents. Bernie Sanders wants to ban superintelligence and sentence developers who ignore the rules to 20 years in prison. There was also President Trump's Joint Commitment On Frontier Responsibilities, though that "morally binding" agreement relies largely on tech companies policing themselves.

articles.title: Sony pode gastar R$ 3,4 mil só com as memórias de cada PS6 • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Sony pode gastar R$ 3,4 mil só com as memórias de cada PS6
RAM e armazenamento NAND podem custar mais de US$ 680 por unidade. Alta nos preços dos chips deve pressionar o custo da próxima geração do console.
A memória RAM e os chips de armazenamento do PlayStation 6 podem custar à Sony mais de US$ 680, ou cerca de R$ 3.400 em conversão direta. A declaração veio de um informante conhecido como KeplerL2, que publica informações antecipadas sobre hardware da AMD.
Segundo a publicação no fórum NeoGAF, “apenas a memória RAM e o armazenamento NAND” devem custar esse valor. O rumor não traz informações sobre outros componentes necessários ao funcionamento do console, como o processador.
A postagem também não apresenta capacidades, fornecedores ou contratos. Por isso, o número permanece uma alegação sem confirmação da Sony. A empresa desenvolve a próxima geração do PlayStation, mas ainda não anunciou nada sobre preço ou data de lançamento. Os rumores sugerem um possível anúncio em 2028, mas até lá os valores dos componentes podem mudar.
Dados de mercado ajudam a ilustrar a situação. Em relatório recente, a consultoria de negócios TrendForce projetou novas altas de até 15% nos preços contratuais de chips DRAM no quarto trimestre de 2026, em comparação com o trimestre anterior. Para NAND flash, a previsão é de aumento entre 15% e 20%.
Segundo a consultoria, fabricantes continuam priorizando capacidade de produção para servidores, diante da forte demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. Esse cenário pressiona a oferta para outros segmentos, incluindo os consoles.
A possibilidade de um PS6 mais caro, na faixa dos US$ 1.000 (acima dos R$ 5 mil), também envolve a política comercial da própria Sony. Em reunião com investidores em junho, a empresa afirmou que não considera absorver os aumentos dos componentes e que não pretende vender hardware com prejuízos significativos.
Se o PS6 fosse lançado nos EUA por esse preço, o console poderia chegar ao Brasil superando os R$ 8 mil, considerando o efeito combinado de impostos, taxas e a relação entre os preços sugeridos atuais da linha PS5 nos dois países.
Como comparação, após o reajuste aplicado ao PS5 no Brasil em abril, os preços sugeridos passaram a R$ 4.599,90 para a Edição Digital, R$ 5.099,90 para o modelo com leitor e R$ 7.499,90 para o PS5 Pro.
Ainda assim, analistas citados pelo site VGC divergem sobre a possibilidade de a próxima geração do console ultrapassar os US$ 1.000. Esse patamar permanece uma projeção, sem confirmação oficial da Sony.

articles.title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
articles.text:
The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC)’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries.
Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal.
NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources.
An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch.
Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day:
Qatium’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the NVIDIA cuGraph library, the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework and NVIDIA Nemotron open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day.
OneCareAI, a research spin-off from BSC, used NVIDIA NIM microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs.
Avatia built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 open model family and the open source NVIDIA NeMo Curator library.
Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI, Elna Health, Lokutor, Montevive AI, Oppy, Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging.
The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more.
