articles.title: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for “vibe-coding” your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more.
One such solution, called “dumbtv,” describes its mission on its GitHub page thus: “Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for.”
Another, “cleanyourtv,” promises to strip the bloatware from any Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi, to replace the launcher with one that resembles Apple TV.
While hacking consumer electronics devices to gain more control over their systems is hardly a new idea, the latest advances in AI technology have made such efforts much more accessible to anyone. With smart TVs in particular, the hacks come at a time when people have grown frustrated with being forced to watch ads and put up with their devices surveilling their viewing habits.
Modern smart TVs ship with a technology called automatic content recognition (ACR), which identifies what’s playing on the screen using screenshots, audio clips, or other forms of digital fingerprinting.
If these “dumb TV” hacks become more popular among everyday consumers, they have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which profits from selling viewing data to advertisers or using it to display personalized ads on their own interfaces.
As the creator of cleanyourtv, Gathin T., puts it, the idea to clean up the smart TV interface started one afternoon when he got tired of seeing the ads on his parents’ TV set.
“I had Claude Code clean it up over Wi-Fi and build a simple home screen with just their apps on it. I put the prompt on GitHub, tweeted the before and after, and a few thousand people did the same to their own TVs over the next two days. Xiaomi, TCL, Sony, Fire TV, LG, a projector or two,” the developer wrote on a website for donations, linked from the project’s homepage.
The solution doesn’t require gaining root access to the TV, nor does it make it impossible to return to the factory default state, if desired.
Meanwhile, the dumbtv solution has been tested end-to-end on a Fire TV Edition television set and Android/Google TV platforms on TVs from Sony, TCL, Philips, Hisense, Xiaomi, and Shield. To use this hack, the developer, Muzzammil Yasin Sabuwala, suggests pointing your preferred AI agent at the dumbtv repository on GitHub.
Sabuwala said he was motivated to work on dumbtv because he was tired of the ads and not being able to delve directly into the content he wanted to watch. His solution was coded using a combination of Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, he told TechCrunch, and he plans to maintain the GitHub, adding support for more models over time.
Fair warning: All these solutions are works in progress, and various users are now testing them across different TV platforms and suggesting updates and fixes.
However, individuals don’t need to borrow someone else’s work from GitHub to get the job done.
In one newly viral X post, Ryan Doyle explains that he simply sent Claude Code the listing for his TV and asked “Can you hack this?” The agent then talked him through the process, allowing him to remove the ads and bloatware from the TV set, speed up the lagging user interface, and customize his screensaver, he claims.
Doyle then goes on to demonstrate in a video how fast and responsive the new interface is after the AI made the requested changes.
Seeing posts about people “vibe-coding their TVs,” inspired one X user, Mihir Gupta, to try it himself.
“One afternoon with Claude Code: 25 bloat apps disabled, the 192 MB stock launcher replaced with a custom 83 MB one, plus rotating wallpapers,” he wrote.
The end result of these hacks may be mixed, however. Some people have found that Claude wouldn’t respond to their simple suggestions to “hack my TV,” necessitating more complex prompts. Others warned that AI agents could make mistakes, possibly disabling important packages or breaking things in the process. One person even said they bricked their Android TV using Claude, and another got stuck halfway through hacking their Fire TV.
For those wary of using AI to fully hack their TVs, there are existing solutions for customizing Android-based smart TVs, such as home screen replacement apps ATV Launcher, Projectivy Launcher, and FLauncher.

articles.title: Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
articles.text:
For a very limited time, Sony’s latest high-end noise-canceling earbuds are actually cheaper than their last-gen counterpart, the WF-1000XM5. B&H Photo is selling Sony’s latest WF-1000XM6 in black for an all-time low of $238 ($92 off) at checkout. Other retailers aren’t currently offering a discount on the XM6.
Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
The flagship earbuds now cost about as much as their predecessor.
The XM6 are a solid upgrade over their predecessor and easily amongst the best noise-canceling wireless earbuds on the market. In his review, John Higgins noted that they do a better job of tuning out other people’s conversations than any other earbuds he’s tested. Sony has also improved the bone-conduction sensor and added AI-powered microphones that help keep your voice clear during calls, even in noisy environments.
The XM6 earbuds also deliver clean, balanced sound with impressive bass, raising the bar of what we expect with Sony’s WF-1000XM series. If you prefer to customize your listening experience, Sony’s Sound Connect app offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to adjust how much surrounding noise you hear without removing the earbuds. You can also personalize the touch controls.
The XM6 earbuds support Sony’s LDAC codec, which delivers higher-quality audio from compatible Android devices, too. New in the latest set is a listening mode that makes music sound more like background audio playing in a cafe, allowing you to listen to your favorite music without getting too distracted from whatever you’re doing.

articles.title: ResolvMD expands medical billing tech into Ontario | BetaKit
articles.text:
ResolvMD, an Alberta startup streamlining medical billing for doctors, has expanded its services into Ontario.
ResolvMD uses AI-integrated software to automate, manage, and optimize billing claims for Canadian doctors. Founded in 2019 by Calgary-based physicians Dr. Marshall Ross and Dr. Ryan Allen, as well as former investment banker Patrick Onyekweli, the startup uses a proprietary “physician insight portal” to check medical claims for errors or missing billing codes, and then submit those claims to provincial health authorities. Combining both AI-driven tools and human billing specialists, the “full service” platform also assists with claim preparation, rejections, and collects and provides data to medical practices on their billing trends.
“Over the course of an entire career … missed codes add up to a significant amount of income that physicians earned but never collected.”
Lauren Hauswirth, ResolvMD
Under Canada’s universal healthcare system, doctors and medical clinics bill provincial and territorial health authorities for the services they provide using a complex system of billing codes that are used to represent everything from a routine assessment to the time of day a patient was seen.
Lauren Hauswirth, the head of growth for ResolvMD, said codes and billing systems differ across jurisdictions, but that a single patient visit can often include several different billing codes.
“A single visit can have five or more codes, and each represents a monetary value,” Hauswirth said, adding that the breadth and complexity of coding guidelines and processing systems can often result in physicians leaving money they’re entitled to on the table.
“Over the course of an entire career, those missed codes add up to a significant amount of income that physicians earned but never collected,” Hauswirth added.
Moving east
Since its founding, ResolvMD has grown its client base to around 1,700 of Alberta’s roughly 14,000 registered physicians, leveraging financing from firms like PaceZero Capital Partners for product development across the province. Now, the startup has moved into Ontario, Canada’s largest medical billing market.
ResolvMD soft-launched in Ontario this past August, with an official launch taking place in early October at Ontario’s Digital Health Conference. Since then, Hauswirth said the company has added around 150 more clients onto the ResolvMD platform, which takes 1.95 percent of all of the paid claims it processes under individual user plans.
“It’s been growing quickly,” Hauswirth said. “We’re getting in front of a lot of physicians through our national partners.”
Ontario is home to more than 31,000 practicing physicians, according to the Ontario Medical Association.
New markets, new systems
Setting up shop in Ontario meant transitioning ResolvMD’s tech from AHS’s billing system to OHIP’s. To do that, the startup built a new operating system, which it says passed Ontario’s conformance testing—a mandatory technical review process required by provincial health authorities—earlier this year. It also hired a team of Ontario-based billing experts, which help review and address claims processed through the platform.
While ResolvMD is focusing on building its brand recognition in Ontario, where it faces competition from a handful of already established billing companies, the company told BetaKit in an interview that its experience building for Ontario could lend itself to expansions elsewhere, too.
“British Columbia is definitely the next place there could be an opportunity,” Hauswirth said. “That’s what we’re evaluating right now.”
Hauswirth added that ResolvMD is also considering international expansion opportunities alongside the potential for further Canadian expansion.
If there were to be a second Canadian expansion into British Columbia, Hauswirth said it would likely occur in 2027.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) hub within Amazon SageMaker AI that provides access to a curated catalog of AI models, solution templates, and example notebooks. It reduces the time it takes to go from model selection to deployment. You can use it to evaluate open source large language models (LLMs), deploy a vision model for document understanding, or fine-tune a compact model on your own data.
SageMaker JumpStart serves three primary use cases:
- Model discovery and evaluation — Browse hundreds of foundation models (FMs) from providers like Alibaba (Qwen), NVIDIA, Google, Mistral, Cohere, IBM, and more. Each model card includes architecture details, benchmarks, licensing information, and sample notebooks.
- One-click deployment — Deploy your choice of model to a SageMaker real-time inference endpoint with pre-configured settings optimized for your workload (low cost, low latency, throughput, or balanced). No manual container or instance configuration required.
- Model customization — Fine-tune models directly from the console or SDK using techniques like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Serverless customization options reduce infrastructure management.
You can access SageMaker JumpStart through the SageMaker Studio console (Models → JumpStart models), programmatically through the SageMaker Python SDK, or directly from Hugging Face using the recently launched deep link integration.
2026 onboarding at a glance
From January through September 2026, SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models across 30 distinct providers. This represents a significant expansion of the catalog, driven by the accelerating pace of open source model releases and growing customer demand for choice across model architectures, sizes, and capabilities.
Here’s a breakdown of the leading contributors and a link to our SageMaker JumpStart page:
- Alibaba (Qwen): 29 models spanning reasoning (Qwen 3.8-27B), large-scale mixture-of-experts (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B), agentic workflows (Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B), code generation (Qwen3-Coder-Next, Qwen 3 Coder 30B), speech recognition (Qwen3-ASR-1.7B), text-to-speech (Qwen3-TTS), embeddings (Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B), and reranking (Qwen3-Reranker-4B).
- NVIDIA: 17 models including the Cosmos3 world foundation model family (Super, Edge, Nano), Cosmos Reason 7B, MSA-Search, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Nemotron-3-Super-120B (FP8 and BF16), Nemotron3 Ultra, Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni (multimodal), and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for vision-language.
- Mistral: 7 models including the Ministral-3 family (3B, 8B, 14B in standard and BF16) and Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime for speech.
- Google: 6 Gemma 4 variants, including gemma-4-31B-it, E2B-it, E4B-it, 26B-A4B-it, assistant, and NVFP4 quantized.
- IBM: 4 models including Granite 4.0 h-micro/small/tiny and granite-speech-4.1-2b for multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) across 6 languages.
- Cohere: 4 models including Command A (A100) and Rerank v3.5, v4.0 Fast, and v4.0 Pro for retrieval augmentation.
- Others: 33 models from MiniMax, Zhipu AI (GLM), DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Allen AI, Microsoft, Meta (Muse Spark), Reflection (Beam), Black Forest Labs, JetBrains, OpenBMB, BharatGenAI, Kakao, OpenFold, and more.
Model onboarding highlights
The models onboarded in 2026 reflect several focused priorities in how we expand the SageMaker JumpStart catalog. These aren’t only industry trends. They represent the areas where we see strong customer demand and significant opportunity to help customers build production AI applications on SageMaker.
Expanding the NVIDIA open-model portfolio
NVIDIA is one of our significant model providers, and in 2026 their contribution extended well beyond language models. The Cosmos3 world foundation models, available in Super, Edge, and Nano tiers, bring video generation, physics simulation, and action planning into a single architecture for physical AI applications such as robotics, autonomous systems, and digital twins. Combined with Nemotron models spanning from efficient edge inference (Nano-12B) to large-scale reasoning (Super-120B), SageMaker JumpStart now offers a broad portfolio of NVIDIA open models. If you build on NVIDIA hardware, you can deploy these models on SageMaker with optimized containers and pre-configured endpoints.
Closing the multimodal gap
Customer workloads increasingly require models that process more than text. In 2026, we prioritized onboarding models that handle vision, speech, and document understanding natively. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni processes text, vision, and speech in a single model. Google Gemma 4 adds vision-language capabilities across multiple sizes. IBM granite-speech-4.1-2b handles speech recognition and translation across six languages. Mistral Voxtral-Mini supports real-time speech understanding. These additions mean customers can avoid chaining separate preprocessing models for multimodal workloads.
Making creative AI accessible
Image and video generation moved from niche to mainstream in 2026. We onboarded FLUX.2 Small Decoder and FLUX.2-klein-base-4B from Black Forest Labs for fast text-to-image generation, Meta Muse-Glimmer-30B for multimodal agentic workflows, and NVIDIA Cosmos3 for video generation. With these models, you can access creative AI capabilities with the same one-click deployment experience you use for language models.
Prioritizing efficient and quantized models
Not every workload requires a frontier-scale model, and many customers are focused on optimizing inference costs as they move to production. We onboarded multiple quantized and compact models: Zhipu AI GLM-5.2 FP8 delivers strong performance with a reduced memory footprint. JetBrains Mellum2-12B uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with only 2.5B active parameters for code generation. OpenBMB MiniCPM5-1B packs multimodal capabilities into 1 billion parameters. Microsoft Phi-4-mini-instruct and IBM Granite 4.0 h-tiny demonstrate that compact models serve production workloads on instance types like ml.g5.xlarge. These models can optimize latency and total cost of ownership (TCO) for targeted use cases.
Onboarding purpose-built models for targeted tasks
General-purpose LLMs are versatile, but purpose-built models are optimized for specific tasks. In 2026, we onboarded Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B for autonomous AI workflows with native tool-calling. GLM-OCR, LightOnOCR, and DeepSeek-OCR handle document text extraction. Qwen3-Reranker-4B and Cohere Rerank v4.0 improve retrieval precision in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. langcache-embed-v3-small provides lightweight embedding for semantic search. Qwen3-ASR and Qwen3-TTS bring speech recognition and synthesis. OpenFold3 supports protein structure prediction for scientific computing. With these models, you can build pipelines where each stage uses the specialized tool for the job, rather than forcing a single model to do everything.
Broadening provider diversity
Reducing concentration risk in model selection is important for enterprise customers. In 2026, we expanded the catalog to include 30 providers, up from a more concentrated set in prior years. Alibaba Qwen is the single largest contributor with 29 models spanning reasoning, coding, speech, and retrieval. Zhipu AI and DeepSeek add competitive LLMs and specialized OCR. MiniMax and Moonshot AI contribute emerging architectures. Cohere brings reliable reranking. BharatGenAI and Kakao expand regional model coverage. This breadth gives customers more options for performance, cost, licensing, and language support.
SageMaker JumpStart enhancements in 2026
Beyond model onboarding, SageMaker JumpStart also shipped significant improvements in 2026 that reduce friction across the model lifecycle, from discovery to deployment.
Simplified Model Hub on the SageMaker AI console
Previously, discovering SageMaker JumpStart models required navigating into SageMaker Studio and finding the SageMaker JumpStart section in the left navigation. The new Model Hub experience surfaces the full SageMaker JumpStart catalog directly on the SageMaker AI console landing page. You can browse models by category and filter by input/output modality, publisher, model size, license, and framework. You can also view sample notebooks and open models inside Studio with a single click. This avoids the multi-step navigation that slowed initial exploration.
Pre-configured endpoint deployment options
Choosing the right instance type, serving container, and optimization settings for a model deployment typically required manual benchmarking across dozens of combinations. SageMaker JumpStart now offers named deployment configurations, with optimization options for:
- Balanced — An even tradeoff between cost, latency, and throughput for general-purpose workloads.
- Throughput optimized — Maximum tokens per second using techniques like Speculative Decoding, ideal for high-volume batch processing.
- Latency optimized — Lowest Time to First Token (TTFT), prioritizing speed for interactive applications.
- Cost optimized — Lowest infrastructure cost per request, suitable for workloads that can accept higher latency.
These configurations include Neuron-optimized setups for AWS Inferentia and AWS Trainium instances, reducing deployment complexity and infrastructure costs. You can deploy a model with a single click and the right optimization profile, rather than spending weeks benchmarking configurations manually.
Hugging Face deep link integration
A new integration with Hugging Face connects model discovery directly to SageMaker Studio, for onboarded models. When browsing models on Hugging Face, you can choose Deploy on SageMaker AI or Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI. You land directly in a configured Studio environment with the model pre-loaded, permissions pre-configured, and GPU quota visibility built in. This avoids the need to set up AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, create a domain, or configure permissions before experimenting.
Getting started
There are three ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart:
- SageMaker Studio console — Open SageMaker Studio, navigate to Models → JumpStart models, and browse the catalog. Choose a model to view its details, then choose Deploy or Customize.
- SageMaker Python SDK — Deploy models programmatically using the SageMaker Python SDK. Visit the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog for SDK examples and deployment guides.
- Hugging Face deep link — Browse the HuggingFace Model Hub and choose Deploy on SageMaker AI to land directly in Studio for SageMaker JumpStart onboarded models.
Each model on SageMaker JumpStart includes deployment configurations, sample notebooks, and documentation. For a hands-on walkthrough, see our related blog post on “Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart”.
Conclusion
The first three quarters of 2026 have been a period of significant progress for Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. With over 100 new models onboarded from 30 providers, the catalog now spans a wide range of capabilities. These include frontier reasoning models, multimodal vision-language models, creative AI for image and video generation, speech recognition and synthesis, optical character recognition (OCR) and document understanding, embedding and retrieval models for RAG, agentic workflow models, and specialized scientific computing models.
These onboarding priorities reflect where we see the strongest customer demand and the greatest opportunity to accelerate AI adoption on AWS. They include expanding the portfolio, closing the multimodal gap, making creative AI accessible, prioritizing efficiency and quantization, onboarding purpose-built models, and broadening provider diversity.
Combined with the enhancements like simplified Model Hub, pre-configured deployment options, and the Hugging Face deep link integration, SageMaker JumpStart continues to lower the barrier between model discovery and production deployment. Visit the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog to explore the full lineup.
Next steps
There are many ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart. Try one of these out for yourself!
- Evaluate models and choose the right one for you
- Learn how to Deploy from HuggingFace to SageMaker Studio
- Use pretrained models in case-based deployments
- Design a Physical AI model factory on SageMaker HyperPod

articles.title: He comprobado todo lo que Google sabe de mi vida y esto es lo que guarda
articles.text:
He comprobado todo lo que Google sabe de mi vida y esto es lo que guarda
En los apartados de privacidad de la cuenta puedes consultar y borrar los datos sobre búsquedas, ubicaciones y actividad, y configurar qué sigue almacenando
Todos hemos escuchado alguna vez eso de que Google lo sabe todo de nosotros. Pero realmente no fui consciente de cuánto de verdad tiene esa afirmación hasta que decidí hacer una prueba: entrar en mi cuenta y revisar, uno por uno, los lugares que he visitado, las búsquedas que he hecho, los vídeos que he visto, los dispositivos desde los que he iniciado sesión y la información asociada a mis fotos.
¡Y ojalá toda esta información estuviera en un único espacio para consultarla fácilmente! Pero Google reparte esta información entre ‘Mi Actividad’, ‘Google Maps’, ‘Google Fotos’, ‘YouTube’, la sección de dispositivos y otros ajustes de la cuenta. Y, aunque muchas de estas opciones permiten eliminar los datos, borrar una cosa no significa necesariamente que desaparezcan todos los datos relacionados.
¿Por dónde empezar?
Lo mejor para saber qué información tiene asociada Google a nuestra cuenta es consultar primero el apartado de ‘Mi Actividad’. Aquí aparece una lista cronológica con buena parte de la actividad realizada cuando hemos iniciado sesión: búsquedas, páginas visitadas, vídeos de YouTube y otras interacciones con servicios de Google. Además, cada registro puede mostrar detalles como fecha, hora, aplicación utilizada, dispositivo e incluso información de la ubicación en la que estabas al realizar esa actividad.
La herramienta permite buscar por palabras y filtrar por fecha o producto. También es posible eliminar elementos concretos, un periodo concreto o toda la actividad. Y hay una opción especialmente interesante para quien no quiera estar pendiente de hacerlo manualmente: la eliminación automática, que puede configurarse para borrar determinados datos antiguos después de tres, 18 o 36 meses, según el tipo de actividad.
Pese a que las búsquedas no parezcan en principio un dato especialmente importante, decenas o cientos de ellas pueden dibujar con bastante claridad nuestros intereses, necesidades o preocupaciones. Además, estos historiales no están ahí únicamente para que podamos consultarlos. Google y YouTube explican que hay actividades que se utilizan para personalizar servicios y recomendaciones. Cuando eliminamos una actividad, deja de utilizarse para algunas funciones de personalización.
Lo que guarda Google Maps
Mi siguiente paso fue abrir Google Maps y entrar en ‘Tu cronología’. Es probablemente uno de los apartados que más impresiona cuando se revisa por primera vez. Si la cronología está activada, el navegador GPS puede mostrar los lugares visitados, las rutas y los trayectos realizados.
Desde la propia aplicación de Maps también es posible consultar un día concreto, editar información que sea incorrecta y eliminar visitas, días completos, periodos determinados o toda la cronología. Incluso ofrece la opción de establecer una eliminación automática de los datos que tengan más de tres, 18 o 36 meses.
Eso sí, hay que tener en cuenta que Google advierte de que, si tenemos activados otros controles como ‘Actividad en la Web’ y en ‘Aplicaciones’, pueden seguir almacenándose determinados datos de ubicación derivados del uso de otros servicios. Entre ellos puede encontrarse información relacionada con la zona general o la dirección IP.
¿Qué hay en ‘Google Fotos’?
Otro apartado que merece una revisión es Google Fotos, ya que la cámara del teléfono puede guardar la ubicación o estimarla a partir de elementos como puntos de referencia y de la información disponible en otras imágenes. En este sentido, conviene saber que Google permite modificar o eliminar determinadas ubicaciones estimadas, pero si fue incorporada automáticamente por la cámara, no siempre es posible modificarla o borrarla desde aquí.
Cuando se comparten álbumes, enlaces o conversaciones, también conviene saber que la aplicación permite decidir si se incluyen o no los datos de ubicación. La ubicación de las imágenes es privada de forma predeterminada en algunas formas de uso compartido, aunque existen excepciones, como la función ‘Compartir con colaborador’.
¿Qué dispositivos tienen acceso a mi cuenta?
La revisión no estaría completa sin entrar en ‘Seguridad’ > ‘Tus dispositivos’.
Aquí Google muestra los ordenadores, teléfonos y otros dispositivos en los que tenemos la sesión iniciada o en los que hemos iniciado sesión recientemente. Al entrar en cada uno de ellos, podemos consultar información de esa sesión y cerrarla si ya no utilizamos el dispositivo o no lo reconocemos.
Es un apartado que conviene revisar con cierta periodicidad, especialmente si hemos cambiado de móvil, utilizado un ordenador compartido o iniciado sesión en dispositivos que ya no utilizamos.
Por último, he revisado las conexiones entre mi cuenta de Google y aplicaciones y servicios de terceros. Aquí aparecen aplicaciones a las que hemos dado permiso para acceder a determinados datos o servicios en los que utilizamos ‘Iniciar sesión con Google’. Podemos revisar qué permisos tiene cada uno y retirar el acceso cuando ya no lo necesitemos.
Hay una diferencia importante: retirar el permiso impide que la aplicación siga accediendo a los datos de nuestra cuenta, pero no significa necesariamente que el tercero haya borrado la información que ya tenía. Para eso es posible que se necesite solicitar la eliminación directamente a ese servicio.

articles.title: Resumo do OD: Lula acusa Meta, Japão lança sonda a Marte, novo financiamento da OpenAI e mais
articles.text:
Este é um trecho da newsletter Primeiro Olhar, disponível para assinantes do Clube Olhar Digital.
Bom dia!
A campanha do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) vai pedir ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) a cassação da chapa de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) à Presidência da República. A iniciativa acusa a Meta, dona do Instagram, Facebook, Threads e WhatsApp, de favorecer o candidato adversário por meio de algoritmos de recomendação e ferramentas de inteligência artificial (IA).
O pedido será apresentado em Ação de Investigação Judicial Eleitoral (Aije). A campanha sustenta que os sistemas das plataformas teriam ampliado a distribuição de conteúdos favoráveis a Flávio e seus aliados, ao mesmo tempo que restringiram o alcance de publicações ligadas a Lula.
Japão lança sonda que tentará trazer pedaços de uma lua de Marte
O Japão lançou, nesta segunda-feira (19), às 16h41 (horário de Brasília), uma missão espacial que pretende trazer à Terra amostras de uma das luas de Marte. A sonda MMX (Exploração das Luas de Marte, na sigla em inglês) decolou a bordo de um foguete H3 do Centro Espacial de Tanegashima, no Japão, e iniciou jornada de aproximadamente cinco anos para investigar Fobos e Deimos, os dois satélites naturais do planeta vermelho.
OpenAI corre para levantar R$ 163,5 bilhões antes de IPO da Anthropic
A OpenAI está correndo para garantir compromissos de investidores antes da estreia da concorrente Anthropic na bolsa, prevista para meados de novembro. A nova rodada de financiamento pode avaliar a dona do ChatGPT em mais de US$ 1,4 trilhão (cerca de R$ 7,63 trilhões), segundo pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto ouvidas pela Reuters.
Samsung usará tecnologia da rival TSMC em chips de memória da Nvidia, diz jornal
A Samsung usará o processo de fabricação de 3 nanômetros da TSMC para produzir componentes das próximas memórias HBM personalizadas da Nvidia, segundo o jornal sul-coreano Seoul Economic Daily.
Noruega quer restringir TikTok, Snapchat e Roblox para menores de 16 anos
O governo da Noruega quer ampliar a proposta de restrição ao uso de redes sociais por menores de 16 anos para incluir plataformas de jogos e serviços de mensagens considerados nocivos. A iniciativa poderá atingir serviços, como TikTok, Snapchat e Roblox, segundo anúncio feito nesta segunda-feira (19).
Menores conseguem baixar apps que criam nudes com IA, aponta investigação
Adolescentes conseguem acessar aplicativos de inteligência artificial que criam imagens íntimas falsas sem consentimento, mesmo com os controles parentais da Apple e do Google ativados. A conclusão é de uma investigação do Tech Transparency Project, divulgada pelo The Guardian.
EUA mandam banir inteligência artificial DeepSeek de redes federais
O Departamento de Segurança Interna dos Estados Unidos (DHS) determinou que órgãos civis federais removam tecnologias de inteligência artificial da chinesa DeepSeek de seus sistemas de TI. A ordem também proíbe novas aquisições de produtos e serviços da empresa.
Físicos encontram evidências de fenômeno quântico previsto há quase 100 anos
Físicos encontraram novas evidências de um fenômeno quântico previsto em 1931 pelo físico Hans Bethe: a formação de agrupamentos de átomos que se comportam como uma única unidade, conhecidos como cordas de Bethe.
Apple prepara evento com possíveis novos MacBooks e iPad mini
A Apple convidou jornalistas para uma experiência presencial em Los Angeles, nos Estados Unidos, em 28 de outubro de 2026. A publicação do executivo Greg Joswiak com a frase “Pro and Tell” alimentou rumores sobre novos computadores e tablets.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock
On Oct 9, 2026 we announced the availability of TwelveLabs’ Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock. Pegasus 1.5 is a video language model that turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata. You describe the moments that matter to your workflow, and the model returns every matching segment as JSON.
Video represents a significant and complex category of unstructured data, yet most of it remains unsearchable and underutilized. Extracting structured, actionable insights from that content has historically required labor-intensive manual review or fragmented toolchains.
With earlier versions of Pegasus, you can point the model at a clip, ask a question, and get an answer. Now, Pegasus 1.5 analyzes the entire video, finds every segment that matches user-defined criteria, and returns structured, timestamped metadata. It also introduces video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing.
With Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock, you can analyze videos directly from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) URI or a base64 string with no pre-indexing required, and your data remains within the AWS data boundary.
In this post, we cover what’s new in Pegasus 1.5, how the model is packaged on Amazon Bedrock, and how to send your first request. We then walk through video segmentation, structured JSON output, and multimodal prompting.
What’s new in Pegasus 1.5
Pegasus 1.5 has the following changes compared to previous versions:
- Time-based metadata generation. You define the segments, events, or domain-specific cues that matter to your workflow, such as editorial segments, sports plays, speaker changes, or brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns every matching segment as JSON, with start and end times and the requested fields populated.
- Multimodal prompting. A segment definition can combine a text description with a visual reference. This makes it possible to locate a specific product, logo, or person, along with what they are doing on screen.
- On-the-fly processing. No ingestion pipeline or pre-indexing step is required. Videos are sent directly from Amazon S3 and results are returned in the response.
- Extended processing capacity. Pegasus 1.5 analyzes videos up to two hours long in a single request, up from one hour in Pegasus 1.2.
Pegasus 1.5 retains and enhances the core capabilities that made Pegasus 1.2 a powerful tool for video understanding, including:
- Video-to-text generation: Creates detailed textual descriptions based on video content.
- Granular visual comprehension: Analyzes objects, on-screen text, and numerical content within video frames.
- Temporal grounding: Accurately identifies timestamps of specific events within videos.
- Multimodal understanding: Combines visual, audio, and textual information for comprehensive analysis.
- Multilingual support: Full support for English, with partial support for Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, and Vietnamese.
How Pegasus 1.5 works on Amazon Bedrock
Pegasus 1.5 takes a video and either a text prompt or a set of segment definitions, and returns text or JSON. You call it on the bedrock-runtime endpoint with the InvokeModel API, or with InvokeModelWithResponseStream when you want the response streamed as it’s generated.
| Setting | Value | 
| Model ID | twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0 | 
| AWS Region | US West (Oregon), us-west-2 | 
| Inference | On-demand | 
| APIs | InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream | 
Each request runs in one of two analysis modes, chosen with the analysisMode field:
| Analysis mode | analysisMode | You send | You get back | 
| General | general (default) | A text prompt in inputPrompt | A text answer in message, or JSON when you supply a schema | 
| Time-based metadata | time_based_metadata | Segment definitions in responseFormat | A segments list with start and end times and the fields you asked for | 
You can point the model at video in two ways. An S3 location (s3Location) takes the object’s uri and the bucketOwner account ID, and suits long-form video. A base64 string (base64String) embeds the video in the request body, up to 25 MB, and suits short clips.
To track cost by application, create an application inference profile from the Pegasus 1.5 model, tag it, and call it by its Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in place of the model ID.
Getting started with Pegasus 1.5
The following section outlines how to get started with Pegasus 1.5.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, make sure you have:
- An active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access.
- Python 3.10 or later, with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) installed.
- AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream.
- Model access enabled for TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in the Amazon Bedrock console.
- Videos stored in an Amazon S3 bucket, or short clips you can send inline.
The following policy grants both invoke actions on Pegasus 1.5.
Boto3 signs requests with your usual AWS credentials. You can also authenticate with an Amazon Bedrock API key by setting it in the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK environment variable. For production, prefer a short-term key generated from your IAM credentials with the aws-bedrock-token-generator package, because it expires automatically. Bearer-token authentication also requires the bedrock:CallWithBearerToken permission.
Send your first request
Install Boto3:
The following example analyzes a video stored in Amazon S3 in general mode. This example uses the global Cross Region Inference (CRIS) endpoint. To target the US geographic endpoint instead, replace “global.” with “us.” in the endpoint URL.
The response carries the answer in message, the token counts in input_tokens and output_tokens, and the reason generation ended in stopReason. A stopReason of length means the answer reached maxOutputTokens before it finished, so check it before you rely on the output:
Request fields for general mode:
| Field | Required | Description | 
| inputPrompt | Yes | The question or instruction about the video | 
| mediaSource.s3Location.uri | One video source is required | S3 URI of the video | 
| mediaSource.s3Location.bucketOwner | With uri | AWS account ID that owns the bucket | 
| mediaSource.base64String | One video source is required | Base64-encoded video, up to 25 MB | 
| temperature | No | Randomness of the output, from 0 to 1. Default 0.2 | 
| maxOutputTokens | No | Maximum tokens to generate, from 512 to 98,304 | 
| responseFormat | No | A JSON Schema the answer must follow | 
| analysisMode | No | general (default) or time_based_metadata | 
For a short clip, you can send the video inline instead of from S3:
Note that the preceding example uses the optional includeMetering attribute. includeMetering: True makes Pegasus 1.5 add two billing-usage fields to the non-streaming response: outputTokenCount and inputVideoSecond (the analyzed video’s duration in seconds).
Stream the response
For interactive applications, InvokeModelWithResponseStream returns the answer in chunks as it’s generated. Each chunk carries the next piece of text in message:
Return structured JSON
In general mode, you can constrain the answer to a JSON Schema so downstream code can parse it directly. Set responseFormat.type to json_schema and put the schema under jsonSchema. The answer arrives in message as a JSON string:
Video segmentation: Turning video into structured data
Time-based metadata generation is where Pegasus 1.5 differs most from earlier versions. Instead of a prompt, you send one or more segment definitions, and the model returns every segment of the video that matches each one.
Set analysisMode to time_based_metadata and responseFormat.type to segment_definitions. The definitions take the place of inputPrompt, so leave that field out. Each definition has:
- id: a name for the definition, returned on every segment it matches.
- description: what a matching segment looks like.
- fields: the values to extract for each segment, each with a name, a type (string, boolean, number, integer, array, or timestamp), and a description.
The following example identifies each editorial section in a news broadcast and returns a title, summary, and key topics for each one:
The previous sample code when tested against a sports clip may produce an output like the following sample.
Each segment carries start_sec, end_sec, and the fields you defined. segmentTimeFormat controls how the times are written: seconds returns numbers you can do arithmetic on, while hh:mm:ss and hh:mm:ss.fff return readable timestamps as strings. The response also includes a definition_errors list, which is empty when every definition was processed.
A single request can include multiple segment definitions, for example one for editorial sections and another for on-screen brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns the matches for all of them in one segments list, and tags each segment with _definition_id so you can tell them apart. The following example adds a second definition to the previous request and groups the results:
Because the schema is defined once, the same definitions can be applied across an entire video library, producing consistent metadata for every asset.
Multimodal prompting: Adding visual context to your queries
Pegasus 1.5 introduces multimodal prompting, so you can include reference images alongside your text prompts. This is useful when you want to ask the model about specific objects, people, or scenes that are easier to show than describe.
For example, you can provide a product image and ask the model to identify every moment where that product appears in a video. Or you can provide a reference image of a specific logo and ask the model to detect brand appearances and their timestamps. This capability enhances the precision of video analysis, and opens up use cases such as visual brand monitoring, product placement analysis, and image-guided content search.
Reference images attach differently depending on the mode. In general mode, put them in promptV2.mediaSources, alongside the question in promptV2.inputText. In segmentation mode (analysisMode: time_based_metadata), attach them to the mediaSources of each segment definition inside responseFormat.segmentDefinitions. A definition can then match a visual reference as well as a text description. Each image needs a name, a media_type of image, and exactly one source: either an inline base64String or an s3Location with uri and bucketOwner. A single request can carry up to 30 reference images.
A general-mode request asks the model about an object shown in a reference image. The following sample payload and response provide an example in general mode.
In segmentation mode, the reference image lives inside the definition, so Pegasus returns only the segments where that product appears. The following sample payload and response provide an example in segmentation mode.
Monitoring usage
Pegasus 1.5 publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace under its model ID, including Invocations, OutputTokenCount, InvocationLatency, and InvocationClientErrors. Use them to track volume and latency. Pair them with application inference profiles when you need usage broken down by application.
Use cases
Pegasus 1.5 is designed for organizations that manage large volumes of long-form video:
- News and broadcast archives: Teams can define editorial segments, topics, and speaker changes once, then catalog years of footage that was previously searchable only by transcript keywords.
- Sports broadcasters and leagues: Detect plays, scoring events, and other key moments across full-length game footage, speeding up highlight production.
- Streaming applications: Scene-level metadata supports moment-based recommendations, contextual ad placement, and segment-level brand safety review.
In each case, people remain part of the workflow. Their work shifts from finding and tagging every moment by hand to reviewing and refining the metadata generated by the model.
Input requirements
Pegasus 1.5 supports the following video specifications:
- Duration: Up to 2 hours.
- File size: Up to 2 GB from Amazon S3, or up to 25 MB as a base64 string.
- Resolution: 360×360 to 5184×2160.
- Aspect ratio: Between 1:1 and 2.4:1, or their inverses.
- Formats: FFmpeg-supported formats.
Now available
TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 is available today on Amazon Bedrock in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Check the full Region list for future updates, and visit the Amazon Bedrock pricing page for pricing information. Pegasus 1.5 is billed through AWS Marketplace, so its charges appear on your AWS bill and in AWS Cost Explorer under TwelveLabs rather than Amazon Bedrock.
To get started:
- Visit the TwelveLabs models page on Amazon Bedrock to learn more about the model family.
- Review the Pegasus 1.5 model card for feature support, Region availability, and sample code.
- Send us feedback at AWS re:Post for Amazon Bedrock or through your usual AWS Support contacts.
We’re excited to see what you build with TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in Amazon Bedrock.

articles.title: The Pant Project bags Rs 109 Cr to accelerate retail expansion
articles.text:
The Pant Project bags Rs 109 Cr to accelerate retail expansion
The Pant Project is targeting a larger role in premium menswear after raising Rs 109 crore to expand retail outlets and develop new product categories.
The Pant Project, a premium menswear label specialising in trousers and other bottomwear, has raised Rs 109 crore in a Series B funding round led by Mirae Asset Venture Investments.
Existing investor Sorin Investments also participated, alongside family offices and angel investors including Anisha Saraf, B&K Securities, MGA Ventures and B2V Ventures. The company has also secured venture debt from Alteria Capital, with IndigoEdge advising on the equity transaction.
Founded by brothers Dhruv and Udit Toshniwal, The Pant Project began as a digital-first business focused on fit, fabric performance and comfort for Indian men. Its products include Malai Pants and Inklock No Fade Black Jeans, and it sells through its website, Myntra, Amazon and physical stores.
Sorin partner Mandar Dandekar said revenue had grown “more than 5x” since its Series A, alongside what he described as “industry-leading repeat rates.”
The new capital will help the company expand from 25 exclusive stores to more than 150 over the next two to three years. It also plans to widen its range to jeans, athleisure, meaning clothing suited to exercise and everyday use, and casualwear, while investing in retail technology to connect online and in-store shopping.
Chief executive officer Dhruv Toshniwal said its digital beginnings had provided “the data, the product knowledge and the brand equity to now go deep offline.”
The expansion highlights a wider shift among direct-to-consumer (D2C) brands, which sell directly to customers through their own channels. A recent report by WPP Media, Google and Elevation Capital, in partnership with Kantar, said brands need broader distribution to grow from around Rs 100 crore to Rs 500 crore in revenue.
A CMAI-1Lattice estimate projects India’s apparel market to grow from $96 billion in 2025 to $146 billion by 2029.
The Pant Project is entering a competitive funding market. Menswear brand Snitch raised $40 million in a Series B round led by 360 ONE Asset in June 2025. Meanwhile, House of Chikankari raised Rs 25 crore from Cap Alpha Ventures in April 2026 to expand its product range and physical presence.
On the manufacturing side, the government revised its textile production-linked incentive scheme in October 2025, widening eligible man-made-fibre apparel and fabric categories and easing investment requirements. The application window was subsequently extended through March 2026.

articles.title: Batteries tout-solide : “pour répondre aux besoins de demain”, le français Saft inaugure leur fabrication à Bordeaux
articles.text:
Batteries tout-solide : “pour répondre aux besoins de demain”, le français Saft inaugure leur fabrication à Bordeaux
Filiale de TotalEnergies, la société Saft inaugure ce 19 octobre 2026 de nouvelles lignes de production de batteries à électrolyte solide sur son site de Bordeaux. Cette première en France doit aboutir à un large spectre d'applications avec des batteries nouvelle génération.
Alors que les batteries silicium-carbone révolutionnent l'autonomie des smartphones grâce à la Chine, dans d'autres domaines de la tech ce sont les batteries tout-solide (ou Solid-State) qui sont à l’honneur. Ce 19 octobre 2026, Saft, une filiale de TotalEnergies, a annoncé l'inauguration à Bordeaux de nouvelles lignes de production de batteries à électrolyte solide.
Batteries tout-solide Saft : sécurité, légèreté et fabrication française
Saft se vante ainsi d'être “le premier fabricant français à disposer de capacités de développement et de production de batteries à électrolyte solide combinant les technologies sulfures et polymères à température ambiante”. Pour le moment, cette ligne de production devrait atteindre une densité énergétique proche de 400 Wh/kg, avec pour objectif de dépasser 500 Wh/kg dans quelques années.
	
Les batteries “tout-solide” figurent parmi les innovations les plus prometteuses pour répondre aux besoins de demain en matière d'électrification. Avec cette nouvelle ligne, Saft franchit une étape majeure en transformant plusieurs années de recherche en capacités industrielles concrètes.
Cette technologie remplace donc l’électrolyte liquide traditionnel par un électrolyte solide. Le gain obtenu est un niveau de sécurité accru en éliminant les composants inflammables, un poids inférieur, ainsi que des densités d’énergie jusqu’à 50 % supérieures à celles des batteries lithium-ion conventionnelles.
De plus, le procédé de fabrication serait plus écoresponsable en réduisant jusqu'à 40 % les émissions de CO₂, notamment lors de la production d’électrodes par voie sèche. L’absence de solvants les rendrait également plus propres.
Aéronautique et spatial : les cibles prioritaires de la technologie Solid-State
Ces batteries tout-solide ont pour vocation d'accompagner l’électrification et la décarbonation de deux secteurs en particulier, où sécurité et performances sont centrales, à savoir l'aéronautique et le spatial. Dans son communiqué, Saft indique avoir “déjà franchi une première étape avec la livraison de cellules semi-solides pour évaluer les futures architectures d'avions électriques et hybrides”.
Pour rattraper la Chine dans ce domaine, où elle est en avance, Cédric Duclos, directeur général de Saft déclare que “pour rester dans la course, le soutien des pouvoirs publics est essentiel, car cette filière a besoin de beaucoup d’investissements. L’Europe devra aussi faire ses choix, soutenir ses filiales souveraines pour ne pas aggraver sa dépendance aux importations étrangères.

articles.title: Germany Wants to Lead the World in Industrial AI: How NVIDIA Will Help
articles.text:
In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI.
Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing.
The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies.
Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA.
The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI.
Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.”
Germany’s Ambition to Integrate AI With Industry
Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition.
“We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.”
Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience.
“The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”
Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it.
“That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.”
Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included.
“If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.”
Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution.
“This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.”
Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI.
“I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.”
NVIDIA’s Investments in Germany
Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe.
NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs.
Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace.
Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare.
Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care.
Mirelo, a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen.
Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years.
Siemens and NVIDIA Advance Autonomous Manufacturing; Record-Breaking Quantum Simulation
Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory, advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%.
NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER, Europe’s largest supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a record-breaking simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The 104-qubit simulation is the largest and most detailed of its kind to date.

articles.title: Mecka AI recruits growth hackers behind “IRL sidequest” app Thirdspace
articles.text:
Toronto- and New York City-based Mecka AI, which aims to supply the training data necessary to deploy robots in the real world, has completed its second acquisition to date.
The buzzy AI startup announced today that it bought Ottawa’s Thirdspace, a popular social mobile app that Mecka described as a mix between BeReal, Instagram, and Snapchat. Thirdspace bills itself as a venue for “[in real life] side quests with friends.” The news comes shortly after Mecka revealed it had closed $60 million USD ($86 million CAD) in Series B funding from Sequoia Capital, Nvidia, Microsoft, Qualcomm, and Samsung, among others.
“They’ve captured this lightning in the bottle of what it takes to get viral.”
Launched last year by former Carleton University students Cedric Osagie and Eshan Betrabet, Thirdspace allows users to take and post photos of themselves doing fun things and invites friends to join. The images are only briefly viewable—once others have accepted the invite, they’ll get a location to join in and capture a pic together.
In an exclusive interview with BetaKit, Osagie said the goal was to build a fun, spontaneous way to encourage lonely university students to connect more in person. The idea has taken off: in less than two years, Thirdspace has amassed upwards of 20,000 downloads, 60 million views, and has been tripling its monthly active users on the back of $100,000 CAD in angel funding.
In an interview with BetaKit, Mecka special projects lead Mark Grinev said Thirdspace’s “small but mighty team” was “the most important piece,” noting that Mecka was drawn to the playbook that Osagie and Betrabet deployed to grow Thirdspace.
Both firms declined to disclose the acquisition price. The cash-and-stock deal, which closed a few weeks ago around the same time as Mecka’s recent $60-million USD Series B round, is effectively an acquihire, similar in nature to Mecka’s purchase of Vancouver-based Docula earlier this year.
While Thirdspace will remain operational going forward, Osagie and Betrabet have ceased working on it and have joined Mecka as heads of mobile capture and to expand the reach of its home capture app and lead its efforts “across all things mobile.”
“They’re exceptional growth hackers and thinkers, and they’ve captured this lightning in the bottle of what it takes to get viral,” Grinev said. “That is crucial because scaling the mobile app is imperative to hit these big goals of ours.”
RELATED: Mecka AI reveals $60-million USD Series B round backed by Sequoia, Nvidia
Mecka is betting that egocentric, or first-person video will help robots learn faster and scale more efficiently. Demand for this type of data—which, unlike the text, images, and video required to train large language models, cannot be scraped from the internet—is booming. The approximately 80-person startup has built hardware with sensors to capture video and the computer vision and multimodal models to turn it into usable robot training fodder for multiple frontier robotics labs and Big Tech firms.
While Mecka has already collected millions of hours worth of egocentric video from hundreds of thousands of individuals, that is still far from enough to train real-world robots, Grinev said. Given this, Mecka has set an ambitious video target for the end of 2027: 100 million hours of footage. Getting there will require millions of people to download its app, strap their phones to their heads, and collect and submit footage of themselves completing various tasks, he said.
Mecka is betting that Osagie and Betrabet can deploy some of the same strategies they used at Thirdspace to help the company get there, including their ability to leverage user-generated content and find and run with the right viral formats to fuel organic growth.
“This is actually the first team I’ve seen in the robotics realm that is growth-hacking their app like a traditional consumer product, which I think gives incredible advantages,” Osagie said.
RELATED: Mecka AI acquires Docula as it builds the data layer for robotics
While TechCrunch first reported last month that Mecka was raising a new round at a valuation of about $500 million, Grinev declined to share how Mecka’s all-equity, all-primary capital Series B financing valued the two-year-old startup, which has now raised $120 million USD.
Grinev said that Mecka, which claimed to have surpassed a $100-million USD run-rate in June and expects to hit $300 million by the end of this year, raised so much in close succession because it sees a big opportunity and requires a lot of capital to sustain its pace.
Mecka intends to use its Series B capital to grow its teams across Toronto and New York and expand to San Francisco. It also plans to use the funds to finance its compute and storage costs, fund payouts for the folks capturing data, and support its tech development plans.
Grinev acknowledged that the AI talent wars have become “quite intense.” While Mecka does not have any other acquihires planned at the moment, he said he would not be surprised to see the company pursue more such deals in the future.
Feature image courtesy Mecka AI.

articles.title: Microsoft fixes classic Outlook bug that hid Copilot buttons
articles.text:
Microsoft has fixed a known issue that removed the Copilot Chat and Copilot buttons in the classic Outlook desktop mail client for some Windows users.
As explained in an updated support document, affected users with the Copilot Chat (Basic) license or a Microsoft 365 Copilot (Premium) account no longer saw Copilot buttons in the side navigation and above the ribbon.
Those impacted by this experienced one or more of the following issues:
- The Copilot button missing from the top-right area above the ribbon.
- The Copilot icon missing from the left app bar or More Apps area in classic Outlook.
- In Add Apps, Copilot may appear as an available app, but selecting Open does nothing.
- Adding Copilot through ribbon customization may show the command as unavailable or grayed out.
- Copilot remains available from other entry points, such as Outlook on the web or the Microsoft Copilot standalone app or web experience.
Microsoft first announced in June that it had fixed the bug with a service change, but last month it said it had started investigating again after recent updates caused it to resurface.
Now, Microsoft says it has finally resolved this classic Outlook issue, blaming it on a bug that prevented Outlook from retrieving some account information from the user's Outlook profile.
"We fixed an issue in classic Outlook that could cause the Copilot entry point to be missing from the navigation pane when required account information could not be retrieved from the user’s Outlook profile. The Copilot button might be missing for several different reasons, including licensing, Microsoft 365 app configuration, update channel, privacy settings, or other environmental factors," an update to the original support document reads.
"Because the missing button is a symptom that can have multiple underlying causes, we recommend following the guidance in Copilot troubleshooters and How to find and enable missing Copilot button in Microsoft 365 apps to identify and resolve the issue."
Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround for those still affected by this known issue, which requires enabling the "Show Apps in Outlook" option in classic Outlook settings by selecting the File tab, then going to Options > Advanced and checking the "Show Apps in Outlook" box under "Outlook panes."
Affected users can also use the new Outlook email client or Outlook Web Access (OWA), which are not affected by this bug, or create a new Outlook profile.
Since the start of the year, Microsoft has also resolved known issues that prevented some classic Outlook users from sending emails via Outlook.com and rendered the classic Outlook client unusable when enabling the Microsoft Teams Meeting Add-in.

articles.title: La ley y los expertos coinciden: puedes instalar un cepo en tu plaza de garaje para que tus vecinos no la ocupen
articles.text:
Buscaste una plaza de garaje porque en tu barrio es horrible aparcar. Llegas a las tantas de la noche de un día entre semana de tus cortas pero merecidas vacaciones. Dejas las cosas a la puerta de casa y mientras tu pareja las sube, tú vas llevando el coche a tu plaza de garaje. Pero cuando llegas, hay otro coche en tu plaza. No es broma. Son las once de la noche, al día siguiente madrugas y te encuentras dando vueltas por un barrio saturado de coches aparcados en la calle.
¿Cómo evitarlo la próxima vez?
No es broma. Aunque yo creía que sí. Prometo que no es una licencia literaria lo que voy a contar. Un día, tomando algo con un amigo me cuenta que el otro día llegó a casa y alguien había aparcado en su plaza de garaje. "Me quedé a cuadros porque no tenía sitio dónde aparcar fuera, en la calle", me dijo.
Después de conseguir aparcar y tras un par de horas enganchados al teléfono conectando llamadas consiguieron enterarse de que la persona que había aparcado era el hermano de una vecina. Se había equivocado de plaza de garaje porque había anotado mal el número de la misma y se había ido de viaje. Aprovechando que su hermana estaba también de vacaciones, tenía un garaje gratis en Madrid.
"Y tanto", me dijo mi amigo que recalcó entre risas un "como que lo estaba pagando yo". Por suerte, quedaba libre la plaza de la vecina y pudo aparcar sin problemas hasta que ésta volvió e hicieron el intercambio.
¿Y si no es una equivocación? Eso nos hizo preguntarnos en la redacción de Xataka qué pasaba si llegas a tu plaza de garaje, está ocupada y no consigues dar con el dueño del coche. Y es que la cuestión es que en este caso fue una equivocación pero no siempre es así.
Hace unos meses contamos que existen los "okupas de garaje". Personas que utilizan las plazas de otros sin su consentimiento y bloquean su uso todos los días. Mi compañero Carlos Prego recogía casos y testimonios de Murcia, Galicia y de la cuenta de X "Líos de Vecinos", donde se recogen problemas de convivencia de todo tipo.
En estos casos, no queda otra que intentar contactar con el dueño del vehículo para demostrar que se ha intentado llegar a una solución diplomática. Si no queda otra, hay que hacer fotos y vídeos y denunciar el caso. Porque sí, se ha llegado al juzgado por este motivo.
O lo evito. Una solución habitual en este caso es instalar un cepo. Directamente. Es algo que está completamente permitido mientras la plaza es tuya. Primero porque es algo que puede llegar a contemplarse con la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal en la mano. Y es que en su artículo 7.1 se lee lo siguiente:
El propietario de cada piso o local podrá modificar los elementos arquitectónicos, instalaciones o servicios de aquél cuando no menoscabe o altere la seguridad del edificio, su estructura general, su configuración o estado exteriores, o perjudique los derechos de otro propietario, debiendo dar cuenta de tales obras previamente a quien represente a la comunidad
Es decir, según esta redacción, podemos poner un cepo que funcione con nuestra llave. Éste estará anclado al suelo para que, en el momento que saquemos el coche, lo levantemos y lo bloqueemos con la llave. Una vez llegamos, desbloqueamos la cerradura y se pliega para poder aparcar encima. De esta manera, nadie más puede aparar.
Aclarado. Preguntados sobre la posible instalación de este tipo de objetos en una plaza de garaje, el Colegio de Administradores de Fincas de Madrid (CAF Madrid) nos confirmaban que, efectivamente, no hay problema siempre y cuando se cumplan unas normas básicas:
"Mientras sea propietario de esa plaza, no habrá ningún problema siempre que no incurra en algún problema técnico al instalarlo. Llegado el caso, si la plaza se vende, el nuevo propietario será el que pueda decidir si quiere retirarlo antes de la compra o él mismo porque le dificulte el aparcamiento".
Por lo tanto, igual que sucede con el caso de quien puso una barandilla para que no le rayaran el coche, no hay problema en poner un cepo en la plaza de garaje siempre que, como decimos, no se incurra en ningún inconveniente para el resto de vecinos. Problema que en este caso, no debería producirse.

articles.title: Jailbreak PS5 : une faille trouvée sur le firmware 14.10 avant la sortie de GTA 6 — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est le jeu du chat et de la souris entre Sony et les développeurs de homebrews. Alors que le géant nippon déployait, la semaine dernière encore, une contrainte supplémentaire pour éviter que la version 14.10 du firmware de sa PlayStation 5 ne soit utilisée par des pirates, un développeur a semble-t-il réussi à trouver une faille dans le dispositif du constructeur.
Comme le rapporte aujourd’hui le site spécialisé NotebookCheck, le développeur homebrew « Gezine » a publié une vidéo expliquant comment accéder aux paramètres de débogage de la console… relançant par conséquent la course vers une éventuelle diffusion pirate de GTA 6 sur PS5.
L’enjeu ? Empêcher l’utilisation d’une version piratée de GTA 6 sur PlayStation 5…
Gezine affirme en effet avoir contourné les mesures de sécurité déployées par Sony début octobre, mais son exploit a ses limites… et elles sont pour l’instant importantes. En tout premier lieu, le contournement de l’hyperviseur, qui est pourtant essentiel pour créer et lancer des versions piratées de jeux, ne fonctionne pas. On apprend par ailleurs que le jailbreak vanté par Gezine n’a pas été diffusé à proprement parler.
On ignore si le développeur choisira de publier les fichiers nécessaires à sa reproduction par des tiers (en prenant ainsi le risque que Sony ne comble la faille exploitée au travers d’une nouvelle version de firmware), ou s’il choisira au contraire de garder le secret de sa « recette » jusqu’au lancement de GTA 6, dans l’espoir qu’elle puisse encore être utilisée. Une seconde option qu’une partie de ses followers lui demande d’ailleurs de considérer.
Ce jailbreak du firmware 14.10 de la PlayStation 5, s’il se confirme, sonne quoi qu’il en soit comme une très mauvaise nouvelle pour Sony qui semble avoir un léger temps de retard sur les pirates ces derniers mois.
Depuis juillet et l’exploitation du firmware 13.60 par les amateurs de homebrews (une avancée marquante, en leur faveur, puisqu’il fallait jusqu’alors passer par de vieilles versions de firmware pour hacker une PS5), Sony fait face à une succession d’exploits ayant déjà exposé à plusieurs reprises la PlayStation 5 aux jailbreaks.
Une situation peu confortable pour le constructeur japonais qui doit s’assurer que sa console phare est « sûre » dans la perspective du lancement, désormais très proche, de GTA 6.
Attendu le 19 novembre 2026, le titre nécessiterait justement la version 14.10 du firmware de la PS5… de quoi expliquer pourquoi l’annonce de Gezine trouve d’ores et déjà, en dépit de ses limites, un important écho dans la communauté pirate.
