articles.title: 250€ de moins sur la barre de son Samsung HW-S810D chez Boulanger aujourd'hui
articles.text:
Boulanger affiche la Samsung HW-S810D à 399 €, 250 € sous son prix de référence, et Darty comme Cdiscount suivent. Cette barre 3.1.2 très fine, livrée avec son caisson sans fil, vise les salons sans place pour des enceintes arrière, au prix d’une connectique minimale.
Lancée en 2024 dans la gamme S de Samsung, la HW-S810D associe une barre de 1,16 m pour seulement 3,8 cm de haut à un caisson de basses sans fil. Sa configuration 3.1.2 répartit dix haut-parleurs, dont une voie centrale pour les dialogues et deux haut-parleurs tournés vers le plafond pour la hauteur du Dolby Atmos. Boulanger la propose à 399 € au lieu de 649 €, son prix de référence, c’est-à-dire le plus bas pratiqué par l’enseigne sur les 30 derniers jours.
La Samsung HW-S810D, barre de son Dolby Atmos 3.1.2 avec caisson sans fil, passe à 399 € chez Boulanger, contre 649 € de prix de référence sur 30 jours.
Pourquoi choisir la Samsung HW-S810D ?
- Un gabarit qui se fait oublier : Avec 3,8 cm de haut et moins de 4 cm de profondeur, la barre se glisse devant la plupart des téléviseurs posés sans masquer le bas de l’image. Le caisson, sans fil, se place là où une prise de courant le permet.
- Une voie centrale pour les voix : Le haut-parleur central dédié aux dialogues est épaulé par l’Active Voice Amplifier, qui vise à garder les voix intelligibles quand le bruit de la pièce augmente. De quoi suivre un film sans monter le volume général.
- Le streaming sans boîtier : Wi-Fi, AirPlay, Chromecast intégré et Spotify Connect permettent de lancer la musique depuis un smartphone, iPhone comme Android. Le Bluetooth 5.2 dépanne pour les autres appareils.
Films en Atmos, musique en Wi-Fi : ce qu’elle change au salon
Devant un film, les deux haut-parleurs orientés vers le plafond ajoutent une dimension verticale aux pistes Dolby Atmos, que le caisson sans fil complète dans le grave. La calibration SpaceFit Sound adapte le rendu à l’acoustique du salon, le mode Nuit est pensé pour les écoutes tardives et un mode Game Pro figure parmi les préréglages pour la console. Avec un téléviseur Samsung compatible, Q-Symphony fait jouer ensemble les haut-parleurs de l’écran et ceux de la barre, et le Dolby Atmos peut même transiter sans fil.
Le profil idéal possède déjà un téléviseur Samsung récent et ne peut pas, ou ne veut pas, installer d’enceintes derrière le canapé. La barre convient aussi à qui écoute beaucoup de musique en streaming, grâce à AirPlay et Chromecast. Elle devient en revanche moins pertinente avec un ancien téléviseur sans prise HDMI ARC, car elle n’a ni entrée optique ni entrée HDMI pour brancher une console ou un lecteur en direct. Nous n’avons pas testé ce modèle : ces éléments reposent sur les fiches techniques de Samsung et de Boulanger.
Face aux barres Atmos avec enceintes arrière
À ce prix, la HW-S810D croise des ensembles plus complets. Dans notre comparatif des meilleures barres de son, la Hisense AX5140Q, retenue pour l’Atmos sans se ruiner, propose un système 5.1.4 avec satellites arrière, une entrée HDMI 2.1 et une prise optique, pour un prix affiché sous les 400 € lors de notre relevé. La Samsung répond par une barre très fine et l’intégration avec les téléviseurs de la marque, mais ses voies arrière passent par le kit optionnel SWA-9500S, vendu à part. Si de vraies voies arrière comptent plus que la discrétion, l’Hisense mérite d’être comparée avant d’acheter.
✅ Les points forts
- Barre de 3,8 cm de haut, facile à loger devant l’écran
- Configuration 3.1.2 avec caisson sans fil inclus
- Wi-Fi, AirPlay, Chromecast intégré et Spotify Connect
- Q-Symphony et Dolby Atmos sans fil avec un téléviseur Samsung compatible
- Même prix chez Boulanger, Darty et Cdiscount
❌ Les limites
- Une seule prise HDMI eARC, sans entrée HDMI ni entrée optique
- Q-Symphony et Atmos sans fil réservés aux téléviseurs Samsung compatibles
- Pas de voies arrière sans le kit SWA-9500S, vendu séparément
Vendue et expédiée par Boulanger, la Samsung HW-S810D s’affiche à 399 €, 250 € sous son prix de référence des 30 derniers jours.
À 399 €, la Samsung HW-S810D devient une option sérieuse pour qui cherche du Dolby Atmos sans transformer son salon. Sa finesse, son caisson sans fil et sa voie centrale répondent au besoin le plus courant : mieux entendre films et séries sans enceintes à placer derrière le canapé. Avec un téléviseur Samsung récent, Q-Symphony et l’Atmos sans fil ajoutent un confort d’usage appréciable.
Passez votre chemin si votre téléviseur n’a pas de prise HDMI ARC, ou si vous comptez brancher une console directement sur la barre. Si vous voulez un son qui vous enveloppe aussi par l’arrière, la Hisense AX5140Q de notre comparatif offre un ensemble plus complet pour un budget comparable. Dans les autres cas, regardez d’abord la prise HDMI de votre téléviseur : si elle porte la mention eARC ou ARC, la HW-S810D s’y raccordera avec un seul câble HDMI.

articles.title: Apple répare à distance des milliers de HomePod : iOS 27.2 corrige le bug du « fantôme »
articles.text:
Les propriétaires de HomePod la réclamaient depuis des années, Apple l’a enfin fait le 19 octobre 2026 avec la release candidate (RC) d’iOS 27.2 et de la version 27.2 du logiciel des HomePod (la mise à jour finale est attendue fin octobre).
Dans l’app Maison, les réglages de chaque enceinte gagnent un nouvel interrupteur appelé « Verrouiller les commandes ». Une fois activé, il désactive le toucher, le toucher prolongé (qui appelle Siri) et le réglage du volume sur le dessus de l’enceinte. Le HomePod perd ainsi son écran tactile… et se débarrasse du fameux toucher fantôme qui hante les nuits de certains utilisateurs depuis trop longtemps. Dans certains cas, le HomePod déclenchait de la musique tout seul à cause d’un défaut de son capteur qui simulait un toucher.
Officiellement, Apple ne dit pas qu’il s’agit d’un correctif au fameux bug : l’inverse consisterait à reconnaître un défaut matériel. La fonction vise les parents d’enfants en bas âge ou les propriétaires de chats et permet toujours de désactiver les minuteurs et les alarmes. Mais au vu de l’ampleur du phénomène, il semble évident que l’option vise à rendre les HomePod cassés de nouveau fonctionnels.
Ghost touch : jusqu’ici, il fallait démonter son HomePod (ou le remplacer)
Le « ghost touch » (toucher fantôme) concerne principalement les HomePod mini et les HomePod 2. La surface tactile enregistre des pressions qui n’existent pas : la musique démarre en pleine nuit, Siri s’active seul, le volume grimpe d’un coup. Dans les cas les plus graves, l’enceinte croit qu’on appuie en permanence sur son dessus et tombe dans une boucle de réinitialisation, avec un voyant rouge impossible à éteindre. Le produit devient ainsi inutilisable, voire peut faire peur la nuit.
Face à ce problème, Apple n’a jamais réagi officiellement. Le seul moyen de réduire le ghost touch et de jouer avec les options d’accessibilité : la « durée de maintien » permet d’ignorer les pressions courtes et d’exiger, par exemple, 3 secondes d’appui au minimum. Une solution très provisoire : le bug s’aggrave avec le temps et, au bout de quelques mois, provoque des touchers fantômes de plusieurs secondes qui passent outre le réglage d’accessibilité.
Les propriétaires des HomePod concernés finissent généralement par remplacer leurs enceintes (la réparation chez Apple coûte trop cher) ou à les mettre dans un placard. D’autres ont trouvé leur propre solution : ouvrir le HomePod et débrancher la nappe du panneau tactile. Il y a plein de tutoriels sur YouTube : il faut décoller la base fixée par un adhésif, faire glisser le tissu comme une chaussette, retirer de minuscules vis Torx, puis libérer le connecteur. L’enceinte fonctionne ensuite normalement, à la voix ou en AirPlay, mais sans aucune commande tactile. Le plus dur est de tout remettre en place.
Pour beaucoup, l’opération est trop risquée pour être tentée. Une nappe déchirée ou un tissu arraché condamnent l’enceinte à la poubelle : de nombreuses personnes abandonnent Des réparateurs se sont spécialisés dans l’opération et reçoivent tous les mois de centaines d’enceintes défectueuses.
Avec iOS 27.2, un HomePod victime de ghost touch redevient une enceinte utilisable avec un seul réglage. Le capteur reste défectueux mais ne se déclenchera plus sans raison. De quoi ressortir des enceintes du placard pour compléter son home cinéma ! Pour rappel, Apple sortira le HomePod mini 2 le 30 octobre.

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.text:
AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.
Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone. The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.
Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.
Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.
AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.
“There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed.
The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.
Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.”
As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.)
Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.”
Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.
“It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.”
Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.
Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”
“It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.”
As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.
“There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.”
“Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.

articles.title: MonoRace: Wie eine KI mit billiger Hardware die besten Drohnenpiloten der Welt abhängt
articles.text:
MonoRace: Wie eine KI mit billiger Hardware die besten Drohnenpiloten der Welt abhängt
Bei der Abu Dabi Autonomous Drone Racing Competition treffen jährlich die besten Renndrohnen und ihre Pilotinnen und Piloten in den Emiraten aufeinander. Mit bis zu 100 Kilometern pro Stunde fliegen die kleinen Drohnen durch die abgesteckten Tore des anspruchsvollen Parcours. Für Zuschauer sind sie oft nur als leuchtende Umrisse und am kreischenden Geräusch ihrer Rotoren erkennbar. Es ist ein Wettbewerb, in dem es auf Technik, Reaktionsgeschwindigkeit und Fingerspitzengefühl ankommt.
Im vergangenen Jahr musste sich der Weltmeister Yuki Hashimoto im großen Finale gegen Team MAVLab aus den Niederlanden geschlagen geben. Doch es war ein ungleiches Duell: Denn während Hashimoto seine Drohne selbst steuerte, schickte MAVLab eine Künstliche Intelligenz ins Rennen.
MonoRace heißt das System, das nun, rund anderthalb Jahre nach dem Rennen, von unabhängigen Expertinnen und Experten geprüft in der Fachzeitschrift Science Robotics vorgestellt wurde. Es zeigt nicht nur, dass KI-Systeme menschlichen Drohnenpiloten inzwischen überlegen sind. Das waren sie auch schon in früheren Vergleichen. Sondern vor allem, wie sich mit vergleichsweise eingeschränkter Hardware erstaunliche Ergebnisse erzeugen lassen. MonoRace hat nämlich nur eine einzige kleine Kamera in Kombination mit einer inertialen Messeinheit (IMU) benutzt, um durch den Parcours zu navigieren. Kein GPS, keine externen Tracking-Systeme.
Drohnenrennen mit begrenzten Ressourcen
„Das Fliegen mit sehr hoher Geschwindigkeit und nur einer Kamera ist eine Herausforderung, da die Bilder unscharf und verzerrt sind und das KI-System nur sehr wenig Zeit hat, um die Position der Drohne präzise zu bestimmen“, sagt Stavrow Bahnam von der TU Delft und Hauptautor der Studie.
Die Forscher haben das von den Veranstaltern bereitgestellte Drohnen-Modell mit einer Acht-Megapixel-Kamera, die es für knapp 30 Euro zu kaufen gibt, einem für KI-Anwendungen optimierten Jetson-Orin-Kleincomputer von Nvidia, sowie mit einem Flugcontroller ausgestattet.
Der Ansatz von MonoRace besteht darin, dass die Drohne nicht vorab den richtigen Pfad durch einen vorgegebenen Parcours mit mehreren Toren lernt, sondern in Echtzeit auf den Parcours reagieren kann. Um das zu gewährleisten, muss sich das System auf das Wichtigste beschränken, was in diesem Fall bedeutet: Es muss durch die Tore fliegen, ohne sie zu touchieren. „Anstatt die Drohne mit immer leistungsfähigeren Sensoren und Computern auszustatten, wollten wir herausfinden, wie viel Intelligenz wir aus sehr begrenzten Ressourcen herausholen können“, sagt der Forscher Christophe De Wagter.
Das Kameramodul gibt die Bildinformationen an den Begleitcomputer weiter. Um Rechenleistung zu sparen, verarbeitet die KI nicht das komplette Bild, sondern konzentriert sich auf einen bloß 384 mal 384 Pixel großen Ausschnitt. Zudem berechnet das System anhand der aktuellen Position vorab, wo die nächsten zwei Tore im Bild liegen müssten.
Bis zu 500 Steuerbefehle pro Sekunde
Die angepassten Bilder werden in ein neuronales Netzwerk eingespeist. Das verwandelt die Bilder in Masken, die die Pixel des Torrahmens vom Hintergrund trennen, sodass quasi nur noch weiße Objekte auf schwarzem Hintergrund zu sehen sind. Im nächsten Schritt werden diese Masken algorithmisch auf ihre Linien hin analysiert und die Schnittpunkte identifiziert – wodurch das System genau die Ecken des nächsten Tores berechnet.
Im letzten Schritt werden diese Informationen an den Flugcontroller weitergegeben, und zwar mit bis zu 500 Befehlen pro Sekunde. Die Steuerung wurde vorab mithilfe von verstärkendem Lernen in einer Simulation trainiert. Dadurch hat MonoRace unter anderem die physikalischen Eigenschaften und das aerodynamischen Verhalten der Drohne gelernt. Auch wurde es mit realistischen Störungseffekten konfrontiert, etwa mit Bildrauschen oder mit Bewegungsunschärfe (Motion Blur). Anders gesagt: Es hat gelernt, wie man die Drohne steuert und wie weit man an ihr Maximum gehen kann, bevor sie abstürzt.
Das System war so effektiv, dass es 2025 in Abu Dhabi nicht nur die besten menschlichen Drohnenpiloten (die natürlich auch noch in eigenen Rennen unter sich angetreten sind), sondern auch andere autonome Systeme geschlagen hat. Für das Team, der TU Delft sind Drohnenrennen eine gute Gelegenheit, um Roboter an ihre Grenzen zu bringen. Die Erkenntnisse könnten für andere autonome Systeme adaptiert werden. Die vorliegende Studie zeige, dass die neuronalen Netze das Potenzial haben, „selbst bei den kleinsten und kostengünstigsten Robotern eine optimale Steuerung zu ermöglichen“, heißt es in der Studie.

articles.title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
articles.text:
The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed
Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.
Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.
From ATRIAS to Digit
My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.
We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.
With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?
Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.
Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.
ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics
Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.
Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.
Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins
As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.
After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.
In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.
Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.
I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.
Turning Digit Into a Product
I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.
Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility
We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.
While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok
I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.
Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.
Digit 5
Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.
Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok
Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.
Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.
Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.
Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.
The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics
Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.
All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.
The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.
When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics
Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.
With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.
What Comes After Digit 5
I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.
Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 EVT [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok
But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.
We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.
I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.
With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

articles.title: The gap between financial inclusion and access to credit in Nigeria
articles.text:
This is Follow the Money, our weekly series that unpacks the earnings, business, and scaling strategies of African fintechs, financial institutions, companies, and governments. A new edition drops every Monday.
Nigeria has made progress in bringing more people into the formal financial system, but having a bank account does not necessarily mean being able to obtain a loan. While more Nigerians can now access financial services, borrowing costs, limited credit histories, and irregular incomes still shape who can obtain formal credit and on what terms.
According to the 2026 Access to Financial Services in Nigeria (A2F) survey by Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA), formal financial inclusion rose to 73%, up from 64% in 2023. The proportion of adults excluded from the financial system fell from 26% to 21%. EFInA estimates that 87.2 million Nigerian adults are now formally included, yet only about 12 million (10%) access formal credit.
These figures show that financial inclusion is not the same as access to credit. Financial inclusion encompasses access to and use of services such as payments, savings, insurance and borrowing. A person may have a bank account, receive payments digitally and save through a formal institution without qualifying for a loan.
For lenders, they must determine whether a borrower earns enough to repay, whether that income can be verified, what other financial obligations the borrower has, and how likely they are to meet the repayment schedule. As a result, people can participate in the formal financial system and still struggle to obtain affordable credit.
According to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), outstanding consumer credit fell from ₦4.72 trillion ($3.5 billion) in 2024 to ₦3.78 trillion ($2.8 billion) in 2025, a decline of 19.92%. For borrowers who struggle to obtain affordable loans from formal lenders, informal sources are offering an alternative, often with fewer procedural barriers. Stears estimates that potential demand for credit among informal borrowers transitioning to formal lending is worth $621 million.
The problem for borrowers
For borrowers, the problem is not just access to credit, but its cost. EFInA found that 16% of adults borrow through informal sources, and 10% from family and friends.
“Alternative finance often wins on lower friction—speed, simplicity, proximity and flexibility,” EFiNA said.
In 2025, Nigeria’s monetary policy rate stood between 27% and 27.5%. The policy rate is not the interest rate consumers pay, but it reflects the wider monetary environment in which lenders operate. When funding is expensive, lenders face pressure to charge more to cover their costs and the risk of non-repayment. Those higher rates, in turn, can make loans harder for borrowers to service.
For illustration, a ₦100 ($0.075) loan charged at a simple annual interest rate of 27% would accrue ₦27 ($0.02) in interest over one year, bringing repayment to ₦127 ($0.095) before fees.
Without lower interest rates, affordable consumer credit will be difficult to scale. But rate cuts alone will not solve the problem. Inflation must also ease sustainably. High inflation erodes borrowers’ purchasing power and leaves less income available for repayments, while making it harder for lenders to offer cheaper loans without taking on more risk. As inflation eases, the CBN can have more room to reduce its policy rate, potentially lowering funding costs and abating pressure on lending rates.
The challenge is to bring down both the cost of credit and the financial pressure on borrowers. Until inflation and interest rates ease, lenders will face pressure to charge more for risk, while the people who need credit most will continue to struggle with its cost, and formal credit access will continue to be a dream.
The problem for lenders
Digital lenders have expanded access to borrowing through mobile applications, automated lending decisions, and alternative data about potential customers. Where banks have retreated, digital lenders have filled the gap.
Commercial banks’ loan-to-deposit ratio stood at 48.07% in 2025, below the reported 80% benchmark.
Digital lenders use transaction histories and repayment records to evaluate people who have limited conventional credit histories. But faster lending decisions do not eliminate the underlying financial risk.
A lender that approves a loan must still fund the money, service the account, and collect repayment. If the borrower defaults, the lender may recover only part of the principal and interest it expected to receive.
This creates a basic economic constraint: lending revenue must cover expected credit losses and all other relevant costs before a lender can make a sustainable profit.
The CBN reported a non-performing loan ratio of 8.03% in January 2026, meaning roughly ₦8 ($0.006) of every ₦100 ($0.075) in bank loans was classified as non-performing loans (NPLs), which borrowers have failed to make scheduled repayments, typically for 90 days or more.
Fintech giant OPay’s reported lending figures offer a more direct illustration of the financial pressures that credit providers must manage.
The company reported $938.3 million in loan originations, $260.25 million in loan-financing revenue, and $121.29 million in provisions for expected credit losses in 2025.
Loan-financing revenue was about 27.7% of originations. Expected credit-loss provisions amounted to about 46.6% of loan-financing revenue.
While these figures do not establish OPay’s profit per loan, they illustrate why lenders plan a substantial portion of their lending revenue on the anticipated cost of loans that will not be fully repaid.
An analysis of 300,000 active borrowers by digital lender, Credit Direct, puts the average loan amount at approximately ₦430,962 ($323.18) for men and ₦478,117 ($358.55) for women. At a hypothetical simple annual interest rate of 28%, these loans would generate ₦120,669 ($90.49) and ₦133,873 ($100.39) in interest, respectively, over one year, before fees. However, this revenue would not represent profit. Lenders must still cover funding costs, operating expenses, and losses from loans that are not fully repaid.
For borrowers, the challenge is whether they can afford to take on and repay such debt. EFInA found that 59% of respondents would struggle to raise ₦156,000 ($116.99) within seven days, suggesting that many Nigerians have limited financial buffers to absorb unexpected expenses or repay loans when due.
What will unlock the market?
In Brazil, account ownership stood at 86.4%, while 45.9% of adults reported formal borrowing. China recorded account ownership of 89.4% and formal borrowing of 40.7%. Kenya recorded 90.1% of adults with a financial account, and only 12.6% reported formal borrowing. South Africa similarly recorded account ownership of 81.1%, compared with a formal borrowing rate of 12.4%.
In these countries, financial inclusion and borrowing are trending upward, driven by improving lending conditions, credit information, household incomes, and the availability of suitable loan products.
For Nigeria, the challenge is not simply to increase the amount of credit available. It is to make more lending both repayable for borrowers and financially sustainable for lenders.
Lower inflation and funding costs could help ease pressure on loan pricing. Better credit information could help lenders distinguish between borrowers with different repayment capacities. Loan sizes and repayment schedules that reflect borrowers’ cash flows could also reduce the risk of repayments overwhelming household budgets.
As Nigeria’s financial inclusion continues to grow, the quality of inclusion is becoming an increasingly important concern. Without access to credit, formal financial inclusion may not translate into meaningful opportunities for individuals to manage financial shocks, invest in their livelihoods, or meet major expenses.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Los despidos sin indemnizar ni justificar se disparan tras la reforma laboral y ya suman casi 3,2 millones
articles.text:
Los contratos indefinidos también pueden durar semanas; durante el periodo de prueba la empresa puede, con carácter general, acabar con la relación laboral sin tener que indemnizar y sin acreditar una causa. Su uso ha ido en aumento desde la reforma laboral de 2022; las bajas que se acumulan están en torno a los 3,2 millones, según Colpisa.
La información puede recogerse en la tabla de la Seguridad Social: en el periodo comprendido entre enero de 2022 y agosto de 2026 se registran 3.188.254 bajas por no superar la prueba con contratos indefinidos; los datos de 2026 son provisionales.
Hay que tener en cuenta lo antecedente: en 2025 se registraron 723.763, frente a los 75.004 de 2021, lo que son casi diez veces más. Si lo comparamos con 2019 (justo antes de la pandemia), las cifras fueron de 132.534, y el último año completo multiplica esa cifra por 5,46.
Nosotros ya hablamos del repunte de estos ceses. La dificultad que esto plantea se encuentra en que un contrato indefinido no tiene fecha de finalización; sin embargo, es algo que no impide que pueda terminar durante la prueba. Para quien ha cambiado de trabajo, tal posibilidad puede afectar a la estabilidad prevista por el contrato y a la protección por desempleo.
Una empresa puede prescindir de un trabajador porque no se ha adaptado al puesto, pero también (y aquí entra la picaresca) puede utilizar la prueba para una necesidad temporal. Las estadísticas que conocemos no permiten calcular cuántas de estas bajas son fraudulentas, ni adjudicarlas todas ellas a una causa única.
El Real Decreto 723/2026, publicado en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) y en vigor desde el 5 de octubre, refuerza la obligación de las empresas de facilitar información escrita sobre el periodo de prueba. Su régimen general sobre relaciones laborales de más de cuatro semanas exige comunicar por escrito la duración concreta de la prueba y las obligaciones para realizarla, aunque mantiene la posibilidad de terminar el contrato durante ella sin una indemnización automática.
También debe indicarse la función que se desempeña, diferenciando entre salario base y complementos, y exponer con claridad el cálculo de las cantidades variables de la remuneración, así como la jornada, los turnos de trabajo y las vacaciones. Si se utilizan algoritmos para tomar decisiones sobre las condiciones laborales, se informará de su existencia y sus reglas de funcionamiento. En el caso de contratos anteriores al 5 de octubre, la información pendiente puede solicitarse y deberá remitirse en treinta días hábiles.
Para nuevas contrataciones, la comunicación de estas condiciones se realizará antes del inicio del trabajo; puede incorporarse al contrato o a un documento adicional en papel o formato electrónico. La información ya facilitada al trabajador, si está completa y la tiene en su poder, no tiene que repetirse.
La prueba tiene sus límites
Es necesario saber que existe una precisión a la hora de aceptar seis meses de prueba. El artículo 14 del Estatuto remite en primer lugar a las disposiciones del convenio colectivo; si este no establece otra duración, se impone, para los técnicos titulados, un plazo máximo de seis meses y, para el resto de los trabajadores, de dos meses. En las empresas con menos de 25 trabajadores, el máximo es de tres meses para quienes no son técnicos titulados.
El Estatuto también establece que, cuando se han desempeñado las mismas funciones anteriormente en la misma empresa, el pacto de prueba es nulo, cualquiera que haya sido la modalidad de contratación anterior.
Asimismo, el Estatuto garantiza el derecho a la protección frente a la extinción por embarazo o maternidad, salvo que concurran motivos no relacionados con el embarazo o la maternidad. Y cuando el trabajador esté en prueba, tendrá los derechos y obligaciones correspondientes al puesto de trabajo, salvo los relativos a la resolución del contrato; la ausencia de obligación de indemnizar no exime a la empresa de la obligación de abonar el salario por el trabajo realizado.
La concreción de la duración de esta prueba no es una obligación descubierta en octubre de 2026, y la sentencia 551/2025 del Tribunal Supremo, de 5 de junio de 2025, publicada en el BOE, recuerda su doctrina. La remisión a un convenio colectivo que no fija una duración concreta, sino únicamente un límite superior, no basta. Si el convenio estipula una duración exacta, la remisión puede ser válida.
Esa sentencia recuerda además que el objetivo de la prueba es comprobar la idoneidad del trabajador para el puesto de trabajo, dejando claro que la libertad para decidir no ampara decisiones discriminatorias ni vulneraciones de derechos fundamentales.
Si el periodo de prueba resulta inválido o el cese es discriminatorio, el trabajador podrá impugnar la extinción. El artículo 103 de la Ley reguladora de la jurisdicción social establece un plazo de veinte días hábiles para presentar la demanda por despido; las normas de este capítulo se aplican también a la impugnación de otras decisiones empresariales de extinción, con las especialidades necesarias. Se trata, por tanto, de un plazo de caducidad; merece la pena revisar el contrato y la notificación de la baja para evitar que se pierdan los días.
El riesgo al cambiar de trabajo
La prestación por desempleo merece una aclaración independiente. El Servicio Público de Empleo Estatal incluye entre las situaciones legales de desempleo el cese por no superar la prueba a iniciativa del empresario y establece condiciones sobre cómo terminó el empleo anterior. Que la empresa acabe con la relación laboral con un trabajador en periodo de prueba no significa que este se vea privado automáticamente de todos los derechos a la prestación por desempleo.
Debe reunir los requisitos correspondientes a la prestación que solicite. Existe, no obstante, una excepción notable en el caso de aquellos que abandonan un trabajo para incorporarse a otro. El SEPE explica en la pregunta frecuente sobre la baja voluntaria que, si la segunda empresa acaba con la relación laboral por no superar la prueba antes de que haya transcurrido un plazo de tres meses desde esa salida voluntaria del empleo anterior, no se podrá optar por la prestación por desempleo. La causa y la fecha en que se produjo el cese del primer trabajo pueden ser decisivas.
La tendencia continúa, desgraciadamente. Las bajas de trabajadores con contratos indefinidos por no superar la prueba, registradas entre enero y agosto de 2026, ascendieron a 505.065, frente a las 478.268 de los mismos meses de 2025: un aumento del 5,6 %. Eso sí, se trata de datos provisionales y anteriores a la fecha de entrada en vigor del decreto.

articles.title: Permis de conduire valable 15 ans : la France va dire adieu au permis à vie
articles.text:
Plus que quelques mois. La France, comme une grande partie des États membres de l’Union européenne, n’a plus que quelques mois pour mettre en place la réforme votée le 21 octobre 2025. Celle-ci instaure une nécessité de renouveler son permis de conduire tous les 15 ans. Adoptée à 339 voix pour et 240 voix contre, la directive (UE) 2025/2205 datée du 22 octobre 2025 signe la fin du permis à vie dans les États qui le proposent, France en tête.
Le délai légal pour la mise en place de cette directive est fixé à trois ans après la signature. Concrètement, cela revient à dire que la mesure doit être appliquée en France avant le 21 octobre 2028. Il reste moins de deux ans au gouvernement pour engager ce changement. La France n’est d’ailleurs pas la seule à prendre son temps : ils ne seraient que cinq États, sur les vingt-deux à avoir officiellement franchi le pas (Italie, Danemark, Pays-Bas, Finlande et Portugal).
Que prévoit le texte ?
Le texte européen voté l’an dernier prévoit qu’un contrôle médical doit être effectué tous les quinze ans afin de renouveler la validité du permis de conduire pour une nouvelle période de quinze ans. C’est un cadre légal minimum, c’est-à-dire que chaque État membre est libre de durcir les règles.
Le seul durcissement évoqué par la directive européenne concerne les conducteurs de plus de 65 ans. Le Parlement européen précise que les pays de l’UE peuvent réduire la durée de validité du permis pour les conducteurs âgés de 65 ans ou plus, afin de les soumettre à des contrôles médicaux plus fréquents ou à des cours de remise à niveau. Un rapport de l’Assemblée nationale sur cette directive évoque dans le même sens une « visite médicale obligatoire tous les 15 ans puis tous les 5 ans après 65 ans ».
En ce qui concerne les chauffeurs de bus et de poids lourds, la règle reste inchangée. Elle prévoit, comme aujourd’hui, un renouvellement sous contrôle tous les cinq ans.
Examen médical ou auto-évaluation ?
Si la directive européenne prévoit bien une date butoir pour la mise en œuvre, la méthode de contrôle et de renouvellement reste à l’appréciation des États. Ainsi, contrairement à ce qui a pu être dit par ailleurs, l’examen médical obligatoire tous les 15 ans n’est pas la seule option sur la table.
Le texte européen prévoit une autre solution, moins contraignante : l’auto-évaluation. C’est l’alinéa 3 de l’article 11 du texte. Il s’agirait, pour l’heure, d’un système basé sur une déclaration sur l’honneur confirmant son aptitude à prendre le volant (après une éventuelle série de tests à faire chez soi). Ce second cas de figure est d’ailleurs celui qui est préconisé par les eurodéputés français dans une résolution déposée cette année.

articles.title: One pilot, two aircraft: F-22 Raptor directs autonomous combat drone in glimpse of future air warfare
articles.text:
What just happened? The US Air Force has announced the military's latest move toward an autonomous future. This time, an F-22 Raptor pilot directed a drone during simulated combat. The pilot issued high-level tactical directives to the YFQ-44A while flying, essentially turning it into an unpiloted wingman.
The demonstration took place earlier this month, when the Raptor and Anduril's YFQ-44A Fury took off from Edwards Air Force Base in California.
Once airborne, the pilot sent an updated mission plan over a tactical data link. The drone's onboard software interpreted those instructions and carried out the maneuvers and simulated combat tasks.
While it might sound like it, this wasn't a case of someone flying two aircraft at once. The pilot decided what the Fury should do, while the autonomous system handled the flight controls.
The test was part of the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. The initiative's aim is to field low-cost, semi-autonomous uncrewed aerial vehicles that fly alongside crewed fifth- and sixth-generation fighter jets.
The test involved just one Raptor and one Fury, but the longer-term ambition is for a single pilot to direct several autonomous wingmen. Those aircraft could bring extra weapons, sensors, and electronic warfare equipment to a mission.
There are still some unanswered questions about the test. The Air Force and Anduril haven't disclosed the full cockpit setup used during the demonstration – we don't know exactly how the pilot sent instructions to the drone. It also remains to be seen how well pilots can manage several other aircraft while flying their own jet in a frantic combat mission.
Fury is one of two designs selected for the program's first increment, alongside General Atomics' YFQ-42A. The Air Force wants 500 combat-ready semi-autonomous aircraft by 2032, with an eventual fleet of at least 1,000.
The military has been working toward this sort of automation for years. Back in March 2023, the Air Force detailed tests in which AI flew a modified F-16 through tactical drills and simulated combat. In April 2024, DARPA revealed that the X-62A VISTA had faced a human-piloted F-16 in a real-world dogfight exercise. Safety pilots were aboard the AI-controlled aircraft, but they never needed to take over during those engagements.
The next step is testing how these drones fit into larger formations. Fury and General Atomics' Vengeance are scheduled to participate in December's Emerald Flag exercise, their first large-force employment event.
Beyond autonomous drones and planes, the military has recently been experimenting with humanoid robots and AI, moving us ever closer to the Terminator-like future the movies warned us about.

articles.title: Salários em tecnologia se aproximam dos R$ 40 mil; veja principais cargos • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Salários em tecnologia se aproximam dos R$ 40 mil; veja principais cargos
Guia Salarial 2027 da Michael Page mostra que IA é diferencial no mercado de tecnologia, mas não significa maior salário.
O Guia Salarial 2027 da Michael Page aponta um forte crescimento da inteligência artificial no mercado de tecnologia, com 33% das empresas destacando o domínio de ferramentas do tipo como um diferencial no próximo ano. Mas em termos salariais, a área não tem profissionais de IA no topo: enquanto especialistas na ferramenta têm ganhos de R$ 14 a 20 mil, gerentes recebem até R$ 37 mil em grandes empresas.
As maiores remunerações seguem com profissionais em engenharia de dados, que podem chegar a R$ 42 mil mensais. Outras áreas mais tradicionais, como ciência de dados, engenharia de software e segurança da informação, já batem os R$ 40 mil. Isso mostra que, apesar do maior espaço para IA na indústria, as áreas mais valorizadas do setor seguem sendo aquelas mais especializadas.
Além disso, a pesquisa também aponta a flexibilidade como predominante no setor, com 51% apostando no trabalho híbrido. O Tecnoblog teve acesso exclusivo ao recorte de tecnologia do levantamento, que foi realizado em 1.955 empresas, considerando 15 setores diferentes e mais de 400 cargos. Ao todo, 5.762 profissionais foram entrevistados.
O principal destaque do Guia Salarial da Michael Page é o avanço da IA no mercado de tecnologia. Aparecendo entre áreas tradicionais como ciência de dados e engenharia de software, por exemplo, especialistas e gerentes de IA ganham relevância em 2027.
De acordo com a pesquisa, 36% das empresas de tecnologia destacam a importância de conhecimentos em inteligência artificial nos próximos 12 meses como diferencial na hora de contratar. Por aqui, 40% do mercado também oferece acesso amplo a modelos de IA, enquanto quase metade (49%) afirma ter a tecnologia como uma das prioridades.
Veja a seguir a relação de cargos levados em conta no levantamento da Michael Page para o mercado de tecnologia em 2027:
| Cargo | Menor salário | Maior salário | 
|---|---|---|
| Gerente de engenharia de dados | R$ 28 mil | R$ 42 mil | 
| Gerente de ciência de dados | R$ 28 mil | R$ 42 mil | 
| Gerente de segurança da informação | R$ 28 mil | R$ 40 mil | 
| Gerente de TI/Business Partner de TI | R$ 30 mil | R$ 40 mil | 
| Gerente de engenharia de software | R$ 25 mil | R$ 40 mil | 
| Gerente de infraestrutura | R$ 23 mil | R$ 38 mil | 
| Gerente de IA | R$ 22 mil | R$ 37 mil | 
| Especialista de TI/Business Partner de TI | R$ 20 mil | R$ 35 mil | 
| Especialista de cloud | R$ 22 mil | R$ 30 mil | 
| Especialista em ciência de dados | R$ 18 mil | R$ 28 mil | 
| Especialista em IA | R$ 14 mil | R$ 20 mil | 
A pesquisa é categórica: apesar do aumento do espaço no setor, profissionais de IA não têm necessariamente os maiores salários. Segundo Lucas Oggiam, diretor executivo da Michael Page Brasil, “ter uma habilidade muito procurada e consequentemente mais valorizada ajuda”, mas o cenário muda ao “ampliar seu escopo” e “responder pelo resultado daquela área”.
Frente a profissionais de engenharia de dados e de software, por exemplo, profissionais de IA seguem atrás em termos de salário, mesmo para cargos de liderança: gerentes das respectivas áreas ganham até R$ 42 e R$ 40 mil, enquanto o teto para quem trabalha diretamente com inteligência artificial é de R$ 37 mil.
Outro dado que reforça a relevância de áreas tradicionais frente ao crescimento da IA é a valorização salarial. A Michael Page enviou ao Tecnoblog um comparativo dos levantamentos feitos em 2025 e 2026 com os números projetados para 2027, destacando o aumento nos ganhos do setor por cargo.
Veja as áreas que mais tiveram valorização salarial no mercado de tecnologia nos últimos dois anos:
| Cargo | 2025 | 2026 | 2027 | Variação | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gerente de qualidade de software | R$ 20 a 25 mil | R$ 22 a 34 mil | R$ 23 a 36 mil | +31% | 
| Gerente de engenharia de software | R$ 24 a 30 mil | R$ 24 a 38 mil | R$ 25 a 40 mil | +21% | 
| Gerente de infraestrutura | R$ 23 a 28 mil | R$ 22 a 36 mil | R$ 23 a 38 mil | +19% | 
| Gerente de ciência de dados | R$ 27 a 38 mil | R$ 27 a 40 mil | R$ 28 a 42 mil | +8% | 
Gerentes de qualidade de software passaram a ganhar 31% a mais em relação a 2025, a maior valorização do mercado de tecnologia, enquanto lideranças de engenharia de software vêm logo atrás, com 21% de valorização. Completam o quadro os gestores de infraestrutura e ciência de dados, com 19% e 8%, respectivamente.
A flexibilização do presencial também foi levada em conta. No mercado de tecnologia, somente 17% das empresas apostam na presença física de seus funcionários, enquanto 28% têm um formato totalmente home office. Ir ao escritório algumas vezes na semana é o mais comum: 51% do mercado opera de forma híbrida. Para os profissionais da área, também pesam fatores como desafio técnico e autonomia.
Se o acesso às novas tecnologias é um diferencial, o tipo de gestão também importa: 63% dos funcionários entrevistados vêem uma liderança “desmotivadora” como motivo para abandonar projetos. Para o diretor executivo Lucas Oggian, a “retenção continua sendo muito humana”. Ainda assim, chama atenção que apenas 3% das empresas do setor veem impacto da liderança na manutenção dos seus funcionários.

articles.title: Bloquear robots que hacen domicilios puede llevarte a la cárcel: el caso de Uber Eats
articles.text:
La policía de Filadelfia arrestó a Carolyn Marvin, una profesora jubilada de 78 años, por impedir durante varios minutos que un robot de reparto de Uber Eats completara su recorrido por una calle céntrica de la ciudad.
Marvin, profesora emerita de la Universidad de Pensilvania, fue acusada de conducta desordenada después de negarse a moverse pese a las órdenes reiteradas de los oficiales que respondieron al llamado.
La policía informó que recibió un reporte de “travesura criminal con un robot” en la cuadra 1200 de la calle Filbert, cerca del mercado Reading Terminal, alrededor de la 1:16 de la tarde.
Según el parte policial, Marvin bloqueó reiteradas veces el paso del robot e ignoró varias órdenes de los agentes para despejar el camino, lo que terminó en su arresto.
Una protesta que venía de antes
Los robots de reparto operados por la empresa Avride para Uber Eats comenzaron a circular por las calles de Filadelfia en marzo. Marvin dijo que desde entonces los enfrenta cada vez que se cruza con uno.
“Sé que le están quitando el trabajo a los repartidores humanos, así que los vengo protestando cada vez que los veo, parándome frente a ellos para impedir que avancen”, declaró Marvin al canal local WPVI.
La exprofesora, que dictó una materia sobre libertad de expresión en Pensilvania, dijo que sus protestas previas ya habían circulado en redes sociales, pero que esta fue la primera vez que intervino la policía.
Una vecina del barrio, Ashley Baldwin, contó que presenció uno de esos episodios anteriores. “Pensé que el robot la había chocado”, relató Baldwin, y agregó que Marvin le explicó que tenía que “detener esto” porque, según la propia Marvin, los robots “se están apoderando del mundo”.
El derecho a protestar, en disputa
Marvin sostuvo que actuó amparada por la primera enmienda de la Constitución de Estados Unidos. “Creo que es mi derecho constitucional manifestarme públicamente en una vereda para protestar contra los robots de reparto”, afirmó.
La exprofesora aclaró que nunca bloquea el paso de peatones y que, pese al arresto, piensa seguir parándose frente a los robots. “Me permite hablar con la gente sobre lo que está pasando”, explicó sobre las conversaciones que surgen durante sus protestas.
Un vocero de Uber a cargo de reparto autónomo celebró, en un comunicado citado por The Washington Times, el lanzamiento del servicio en la ciudad junto a Avride y dijo que la empresa espera “seguir llevando esta tecnología a más clientes de Uber Eats en colaboración con la comunidad de Filadelfia”.
Bajo las normas estatales de Pensilvania para dispositivos de reparto personal, los robots están obligados a ceder el paso a los peatones, según el Departamento de Transporte del estado. Las infracciones de los operadores pueden implicar multas de entre 25 y 1.000 dólares, de acuerdo con el diario The Philadelphia Inquirer.
Otros residentes ya los enfrentaron antes
El caso de Marvin no es aislado. Otros vecinos de Filadelfia patearon, voltearon o bloquearon unidades del mismo tipo de robot desde su llegada a la ciudad, según reportó el Inquirer.
La policía advirtió que quienes dañen los dispositivos podrían enfrentar cargos por daño criminal o infracciones al código municipal, dependiendo de las circunstancias de cada caso. Uber Eats permite a sus clientes optar por no recibir pedidos a través de los robots cuando el servicio está disponible en su zona.
Marvin dijo esperar que la atención generada por su arresto abra una discusión más amplia sobre los robots de reparto, la inteligencia artificial y su creciente presencia en la vida cotidiana.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- S. Saner, O. Băzăvan, D. J. Webb, G. Araneda, C. J. Ballance, R. Srinivas, D. M. Lucas, A. Bermúdez. Aharonov–Bohm interference in a $${\\pmb{\\mathbb{Z}}}_{\\bf{2}}$$ lattice gauge theory on a hybrid qubit–oscillator quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03400-6
- Anton T. Than, Saurabh V. Kadam, Vinay Vikramaditya, Nhung H. Nguyen, Xingxin Liu, Zohreh Davoudi, Alaina M. Green, Norbert M. Linke. Quantum field theory dynamics on a spin–phonon quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03402-4
