articles.title: Plex2Shell Exploit Chain Weaponized Against Plex Servers Hours After Disclosure
articles.text:
Threat actors began targeting Plex2Shell, a chain of four Plex Media Server vulnerabilities, one day after technical details and a working exploit went public.
The researcher who found the Plex2Shell bugs released a write-up and proof-of-concept (PoC) code on October 16. Tracked as CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656, the flaws can be combined to run arbitrary code on an exposed server without valid credentials. The code runs with the same privileges as the Plex service.
The issues were reported to Plex on July 27, and the company confirmed them and awarded a bug bounty on August 4. On September 1, Plex announced it had already shipped fixes and asked server owners to upgrade.
A different researcher caught the attacks by setting up an internet-facing Plex honeypot running a vulnerable release. Before October 17, the decoy had drawn largely reconnaissance scans and generic attack attempts.
“As of this morning (Oct 17th), I finally saw in the wild exploitation,” the researcher wrote. The attackers used the publicly released exploit, the researcher said, though they may have tweaked the code.
The attackers were observed dropping a cryptocurrency miner built on XMRig. Later that day, a second program called myawesomeproxy also appeared on the honeypot. The researcher identified it as proxy software, and it shows a notice saying that anyone running it agrees to the potential use of their internet traffic.
“Plex may be hosted on residential IP and I think threat actors would love to have residential IP proxy to access corporate VPNs and emails,” the researcher wrote.
The researcher cautioned that the published indicators of compromise cover only activity seen on the honeypot.
In its September advisory, Plex recommended that all server owners install the newest release without delay.

articles.title: Nvidia launches new open models to run agents in the enterprise and on PCs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing.
The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise. While it uses fewer parameters than the Nemotron 3 Ultra model, Nvidia says it can deliver similar accuracy in instruction-following and tool-use tasks.
At the other end of the spectrum, the company also launched two lightweight Bolt models. These are intended to run locally on the new AI PCs (running the Nvidia RTX Spark chip) and workstations running the DGX Spark. Such PCs, aimed at consumers, programmers, and enterprise knowledge workers, are being released right now into the market through partners like Microsoft and Dell.
“Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models.
Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks. These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience.
While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL. These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity, and Salesforce.
Of course, these aren’t the first open-weight models that Nvidia has released that compete with the proprietary frontier labs — companies that are both its customers and its investments. The GPU giant has an entire family of Nemotron models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation.
However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips.
So Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers. “Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and own what they build,” Briski wrote.
But with the announcement or the smaller, local PC models, it is also trying to push forward the nascent trend of consumer AI assistants. While it seems a new AI assistant is introduced every day by startups and Big Tech alike, privacy-weary consumers may not want to invite such agents so deeply into their lives giving them access to info about their families, health, finances, and so on.
So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote.
Of the two Bolt models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74-billion parameter model designed for local agentic tasks. It is intended to balance speed with reasoning to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing. The smallest Bolt E4B is aimed at conversational agents.
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

articles.title: Will developing nations be able to handle millions of AI agents?
articles.text:
Big Tech’s newest personal agents — Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots — promise to book tables at restaurants, buy groceries, and carry out other types of digital grunt work for users.
Consumers are opting in. Muse has been downloaded 9 million times in the U.S. and Canada since its launch on September 8, market intelligence company AppMagic, told Rest of World. As many as 1.8 million people use the app daily.
Meta aspires to a global launch. “[We] are quite excited to bring personal agents to billions of people around the world,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, told the Financial Times.
Some startups are already building agents in markets that Big Tech hopes to reach. For instance, South African startup ManyHands offers Manny, a personal assistant designed to order groceries, book appointments and make payments through WhatsApp. But adapting agents to local conditions has its challenges. Anton Moulder, ManyHands’ founder, told Rest of World that getting the AI assistant to converse in all of South Africa’s 11 official spoken languages has been difficult.
Rest of World spoke to AI researchers and other experts to understand how these personal agents would perform outside Western nations.
Would AI agents understand the local language and culture?
English speakers could benefit more from AI agents, which run on top of large language models that underperform in many non-English languages.
“Linguistic inclusion is ultimately about power,” Payal Arora, professor of inclusive AI cultures at Utrecht University and the founder of Inclusive AI Lab, told Rest of World.
Meta has said that expanding Muse internationally would require support for local languages and integration with local services.
AI agents would also need to understand the local culture, including the unique ways people communicate and bargain. “In many parts of the Global South, meaning is deeply contextual, shaped by family, community, religion, local institutions, and informal social networks,” Arora said.
Without that understanding, agents might impose Western assumptions on their users, Usha Raman, an independent researcher on AI policy and digital culture, told Rest of World. “The danger then is that existing forms of cultural and economic hegemony continue and the rest of the world is forced to adapt,” she said.
What happens when millions of agents go online?
Agents searching and completing transactions for millions of people could stress networks and websites. “Internet connectivity may be poor [in developing nations], affecting not only the user’s interaction with AI, but what agents can do online,” Kentaro Toyama, professor of community information at the University of Michigan, told Rest of World.
A single task given to an agent can trigger repeated exchanges between the agent, its AI model, and different websites. Cisco describes agents as “network power users,” generating up to 450% more traffic per task than a human in its testing. Agent traffic is growing online: Daily requests from AI agents on Cloudflare’s network increased by more than 1,700% over the past year.
Rising traffic wouldn’t immediately affect regions that have spare network capacity, such as East Africa, Kyle Spencer, executive director of the African IXP Association, told Rest of World. But other places with poor networks, such as Niger, Burkina Faso, or eastern Congo, could face problems, he said.
The bigger challenge would be keeping connections reliable. Road construction often damages fiber cables, Spencer said. The network could also get disrupted if undersea cables bringing internet into a nation get damaged.
Though Muse and Dots could continue working as they are cloud-based, they may be unable to reach necessary services. They also wouldn’t be able to reach users who lose connectivity for instructions or approvals to complete a task.
Could personal agents widen Africa’s digital divide?
Only 36% of Africans used the internet in 2025, compared to 92% of Europeans and 88% of North and South Americans, according to the International Telecommunication Union. City dwellers in Africa were 2.6 times more likely to use the internet than people who live in the countryside.
“If agents were to work in Africa, they might unfortunately deepen inequality,” Jane Munga, a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Rest of World.
The cost of accessing agents could also limit who benefits, Munga said. Though Muse can be accessed for free, many other agents are paid. Dots is available for a minimum of $100 a month. “These are costs that most Global South users may not be in a position to absorb,” she said.
How would local businesses need to rewire for AI agents?
Local businesses would have to make their websites understandable, readable, and usable by bots. If they do not, they risk losing out on digital economic opportunities.
This would be challenging for small, offline businesses, such as a vendor at a vegetable market. They would have to go online, maintain an inventory, know how much stock they own, and create ways for bots to pay, Munga said. This requires money and skills.
Businesses may also have to invest more in customer support. “Agents might purchase more, and request more returns — when human users decide agents erred — putting stress on businesses,” said Toyama.
Could regulators hold agents accountable?
Agents perform better the more they know the user, Mercy King’ori, policy manager for Africa at the Future of Privacy Forum, told Rest of World. A user’s favorite restaurants, shops, and regularly visited places could help an agent build a picture of their tastes, habits, and daily life.
“An agent may draw conclusions about a person or a group, such as their likely income, health, creditworthiness, or behaviour from the data it handles,” King’ori said.
In cases where agents are developed and hosted outside the country, regulators may be unable to supervise the systems, said King’ori.

articles.title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI.
For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription.
The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability.
In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription.
Optimizing Nova-3 to Trainium2 with native PyTorch
Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and torch.compile. We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with torch.compile. The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected.
We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using torch.compile. Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target.
From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution.
We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size.
Kernel-level tuning with Neuron Explorer and NAD
Enabling kernels is only the first step of an optimization flywheel: enable an NKI kernel (custom or from NKILib), profile the workload, then either tune the existing kernel or replace it with a new one based on the profiling insights. This cycle repeats until the performance target is met. At each step, a different part of the Neuron stack accelerates the work: NKILib provides drop-in replacement kernels, Neuron Explorer is the go-to tool for profiling Neuron workloads, and the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) toolkit speeds up profiling analysis and kernel tuning through its profiling and kernel-writing skills.
In our case, the NKILib kernels got us most of the way, and profiling showed where a hand-written kernel would do better. Each time, the NAD profiling skills took us from a Neuron Explorer profile to a root cause, and the NAD kernel-writing skills helped produce the replacement kernels.
| Layer | What we found and changed | Gain | 
| FFN | The reference kernel’s tiling schedule reloaded the full set of projection weights from off-chip memory for every token tile, so memory bandwidth limited throughput as the token count grew. Our hand-tuned kernel loads each weight tile once, reuses it across multiple token tiles, and pipelines weight reads with on-chip compute. | 2.0x lower latency compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96 | 
| Depthwise conv1d | The experimental NKILib kernel framed the operation as an implicit general matrix multiply (GEMM), which left Tensor Engine utilization low. We rewrote it as a broadcast multiply-accumulate loop on the Vector Engine, reaching full engine utilization, enough to more than offset the Vector Engine’s lower peak throughput. | 1.5x speedup compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96 | 
| Conv2d | The model’s conv2d layers hit a compilation bottleneck: beyond batch size 32, these layers prevented the model from compiling as a single graph. Since NKILib had no conv2d kernel, we wrote one from scratch in NKI. The kernel went through several profiler-informed iterations following the flywheel described earlier, unlocking batch sizes above 32. | Up to 50x on the convolution module at batch sizes ≤32 | 
Data-parallel runtime in Rust
Each Trainium2 device features eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores (LNC2). Because each Nova-3 model instance fits comfortably on a single physical core, we reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one (LNC1). This configuration lets us host eight model replicas (DP8) per Trainium2 device. Inputs are processed concurrently while maximizing per-device throughput. The data-parallel runtime is driven by a work-stealing queue with one thread per replica.
Deepgram’s production serving stack is written in Rust, so porting Nova-3 to Trainium2 required more than compiling the model: it also had to run without Python or PyTorch in the serving path. We therefore built a lightweight runtime in which Rust coordinates model replicas through a shared work-stealing queue. A C layer loads and executes ahead-of-time-compiled Neuron Executable File Format (NEFFs) directly through the Neuron Runtime API (libnrt). The runtime integrates directly with Deepgram’s serving architecture and reproduced the reference token sequences exactly at every tested batch size.
We benchmarked it against multithreaded (MT) and multiprocessing (MP) Python data-parallel runtimes. Compared with the MP baseline, the Rust runtime removes the overhead of the Python interpreter entirely. Compared with the MT baseline, it further alleviates global interpreter lock (GIL) serialization, so dispatch calls from concurrent worker threads are no longer contended within a single process. These gains matter because Nova-3 performs a sequence of small decoder calls for each audio chunk, making host-side dispatch the bottleneck at low batch sizes. The throughput improvement is therefore largest there, and remains meaningful even at the throughput-maximizing batch size. There, the Rust runtime delivered a 7.5% throughput gain over the multiprocessing Python baseline.
Cost saving impact
We measured price-performance as audio processed per dollar. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, the single-device Trainium2 setup (trn2.3xlarge) processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running.
Conclusion
In this post, we demonstrated how Deepgram and the AWS FDE ported the Nova-3 speech-to-text PyTorch model to Trainium hardware using TorchNeuron, which provides native PyTorch framework integration for AWS Trainium. We improved performance by replacing layers directly with pre-built kernels from NKILib. We then assessed performance using Neuron Explorer and used the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) profiling skills to query profiling data and accelerate performance troubleshooting. Building on these insights, we adapted kernel source code using the NAD kernel-writing skills. Finally, we built a lightweight Rust data-parallel runtime for AWS Trainium, calling the Neuron Runtime API from Rust. Our setup demonstrated cost savings in offline, throughput-oriented scenarios, validating AWS Trainium as a viable and efficient option for Deepgram’s inference workloads.
To try this approach on your own models, start with the AWS Neuron documentation, which covers the compiler, the runtime, and the supported frameworks. The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) guide explains how to write the kernels described in this post, and the NKI samples repository holds the reference kernels we started from. The Neuron developer tools documentation covers the profiling and agentic tooling we used here, including Neuron Explorer and Neuron Agentic Development. For instance sizes and pricing, see Amazon EC2 Trn2 Instances. For help scoping a similar port, contact the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering.

articles.title: "Grampo" na OpenAI: juiz vê risco de fuga e nega liberdade a ex-engenheiro da empresa
articles.text:
Um juiz federal dos Estados Unidos determinou que Abdulrahman Alfozan, ex-engenheiro da OpenAI, permaneça preso sem direito a fiança enquanto aguarda o andamento do processo criminal em que é acusado de instalar um dispositivo de gravação clandestino em um escritório da empresa em São Francisco, na Califórnia (EUA).
A decisão foi tomada nesta segunda-feira (19), após o magistrado Alex Tse considerar que há risco significativo de o acusado não comparecer à Justiça. Durante a audiência, o juiz também questionou a proposta do consulado saudita de assumir integralmente o pagamento de uma eventual fiança, classificando a oferta como problemática.
Alfozan, de 35 anos, foi preso em 9 de outubro. Ele é acusado de interceptar comunicações orais por meio de dispositivo eletrônico e pode enfrentar até cinco anos de prisão se for condenado.
Promotores apontam contatos com a família real saudita
- Em documentos judiciais, os promotores afirmaram que Alfozan mantinha contato frequente com um integrante não identificado da família real da Arábia Saudita. Segundo a acusação, essa pessoa teria tentado recrutá-lo em diversas ocasiões para participar de uma iniciativa de inteligência artificial (IA) no país;
- Uma das mensagens trocadas pelo WhatsApp, reproduzida no processo, trazia a frase: “A Arábia Saudita precisa mais de você do que os Estados Unidos”. De acordo com os promotores, Alfozan respondeu com “100”, expressão usada para indicar concordância;
- Os procuradores também apontaram que o engenheiro havia comprado uma passagem aérea só de ida para Riade, capital saudita, com embarque previsto para 12 de outubro. Para a acusação, a compra reforça o risco de fuga;
- O advogado de defesa, William Pernik, contestou essa interpretação. Ele afirmou que Alfozan tinha uma entrevista para obter a cidadania estadunidense marcada para 6 de novembro;
- A esposa do engenheiro e o bebê do casal deixaram os Estados Unidos em 10 de outubro, um dia após a prisão. Segundo os promotores, as passagens foram pagas por um oficial militar saudita.
Leia mais:
- 8 estados dos EUA processam OpenAI e acusam ChatGPT de colocar jovens em risco
- OpenAI alerta Polícia Federal sobre ameaças contra Lula feitas no ChatGPT
- Deepfakes podem dificultar análise de provas, alertam OpenAI e Meta
Dispositivo foi encontrado em sala de reuniões
Alfozan trabalhava na OpenAI desde 2025. A empresa descobriu um dispositivo de gravação escondido atrás de uma televisão em uma sala de reuniões executiva, em setembro. O equipamento estava envolto em papel higiênico e conectado a uma porta USB.
De acordo com a acusação, as reuniões realizadas no local frequentemente envolviam informações confidenciais sobre pesquisas, produtos, estratégias comerciais e decisões da companhia.
Embora o caso tenha levantado preocupações sobre segurança nacional entre autoridades estadunidenses, Alfozan não foi formalmente acusado de espionagem. Os promotores afirmam que a investigação continua e que ela pode resultar em acusações adicionais.
A próxima audiência está prevista para 6 de novembro.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code
articles.text:
Ready to try it? Download the GitHub Copilot app, start a session, and open it in VS Code when you are ready to continue coding.
How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code
Learn how to move an agent session from the GitHub Copilot app into VS Code without losing the conversation, code changes, or working context.
The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it.
But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app… and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code?
You don’t. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing.
In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to:
- Open a Copilot app session in VS Code.
- Review the agent’s changes line by line.
- Continue the same conversation from your editor.
- Modify and test the code locally.
- Push your updates to the pull request associated with the session.
1. Start with a session in the Copilot app
Open the session you want to continue. Before handing it off, take a moment to review the task and the work Copilot completed.
A session contains more than a collection of modified files. It also records the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes. That context is important when you want to understand why Copilot chose a particular implementation or ask it to revise part of the work.
You do not need to summarize that history or copy it into a new chat before moving to VS Code.
2. Open the session in VS Code
From the session, select Open in VS Code. If the app presents more than one supported editor or VS Code installation, choose the one you want to use.
VS Code opens the project using the worktree associated with the session. It also displays the existing session in the Copilot sidebar.
That gives you three connected pieces of the original work:
- The session context: The task, plan, and conversation remain available.
- The diff: The files and lines changed by the agent are ready for review.
- The worktree: VS Code opens the same isolated working tree the session used.
You are continuing the existing session, not reconstructing it in a new editor window.
3. Review the agent’s changes
Before editing, inspect the diff in VS Code. Open the Source Control view to see the changed files, then select a file to review its changes line by line.
Review the implementation as you would any other proposed change. In particular, check that:
- The code solves the requested problem.
- The implementation follows the repository’s conventions.
- Error states and edge cases are handled appropriately.
- Tests cover the behavior that changed.
- No unrelated files or behaviors were modified.
The preserved conversation can help explain how Copilot arrived at the implementation. If something is unclear, continue prompting Copilot in the sidebar. For example:
Explain why you changed this function instead of adding a new helper. Identify any behavior this could affect.
You can also ask Copilot to make another change. Because the session and worktree remain connected, you do not have to describe the task from the beginning.
4. Make a hands-on edit
Once you understand the proposed changes, edit any file directly in VS Code.
This is useful for adjustments that are faster or easier to make by hand, such as:
- Refining a label or error message.
- Renaming a variable for clarity.
- Adjusting layout or styling.
- Adding a missing test case.
- Applying a repository-specific convention.
You are editing the session’s existing worktree, so your manual changes build directly on the agent’s work. You do not need to copy files between directories or manually re-create the branch.
5. Run and verify the project locally
Use the VS Code integrated terminal to run the project’s normal validation workflow. The exact commands depend on the repository, but some web app examples may include:
- npm install
- npm test
- npm run lint
- npm run dev
Treat agent-generated changes the same way you would treat code written by a person: run the relevant tests, inspect failures, and verify the behavior yourself.
If the development server prints a localhost URL, open it to test the change in a browser. When supported by your VS Code setup, you can open the URL in VS Code’s integrated browser and inspect the result without leaving the editor.
For a user-interface change, verify both the requested behavior and nearby states. For example, check the modified component at different viewport sizes and confirm that loading, empty, and error states still work.
6. Continue with Copilot or keep editing yourself
At any point, you can choose the interaction that best fits the next step:
- Prompt Copilot when the change requires repository-wide analysis or repetitive edits.
- Edit directly when you know the exact change you want.
- Use both approaches iteratively as you test and refine the implementation.
For example, after making a manual UI adjustment, you might ask Copilot:
Add a test for the updated label and run the relevant test file. Do not modify unrelated components.
Because you are still in the original session, Copilot retains the context needed to interpret “the updated label.”
7. Commit and push the finished changes
When the implementation is ready, review the final diff one more time. Then commit and push the changes using the Source Control view or the integrated terminal:
- git status
- git add
- git commit -m "Refine session changes"
- git push
Use your repository’s normal branch, commit, review, and approval practices. Because VS Code opened the worktree and branch associated with the session, pushing the branch updates the pull request already tracking that work.
There is no need to copy the finished files into another checkout or reconnect the work to the pull request manually.
A continuous workflow from agent to editor
Opening a Copilot app session in VS Code gives you a clean division of labor without splitting the work itself. Copilot can take on a larger or repetitive implementation, while you can move into the editor for detailed review, targeted changes, local testing, and final polish.
The session, diff, and worktree move with you. Start by directing the work in the Copilot app, switch to VS Code whenever you want hands-on control, and push the finished result through the same pull request workflow.

Written by

articles.title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT).
One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector, which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (AWS EFA, the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types, AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based: After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline.
This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates.
In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration.
We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.
Push-based KV transfer
This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path.
Architecture overview
Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons:
- It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token.
- It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance. That setup runs on the prefill side and on a background thread. It prepares the NIXL descriptors and submits the transfer, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase.
The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance.
The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together.
Implementation details
The protocol has three logical steps.
1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill.
2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests.
3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode.
Threading model
The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution.
The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request.
Timing comparison of pull and push
The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner.
The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready.
Performance data
For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B model on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To isolate P→D transfer performance, we configured the benchmark to disable prefix caching with --no-enable-prefix-caching. This configuration makes the decode node retrieve the full KV cache from the prefill node for every request. Otherwise, overlapping prompts could reuse the decode node’s local cache and bypass the transfer, which would produce misleading comparison results.
The following chart compares TTFT for push and pull KV transfer. We sweep input lengths 1k–16k and request rates of 1–8 queries per second (QPS). At low load and short prompts, the two modes perform almost identically. As QPS and input length grow, pull mode degrades sharply, reaching about 1,744 ms at 8 QPS and 16k. Push mode stays far lower at roughly 540 ms, around 3x reduction. The gap opens because pull mode posts NIXL descriptors inline on the decode worker, synchronously within its engine loop, so that work stalls token generation. Push mode moves it to a background thread, off the critical path.
This chart shows TPOT under the same conditions. The pattern mirrors TTFT. At light load, push and pull are close, around 5.6–5.8 ms. As load and input length rise, pull climbs to about 10.4 ms at 4–8 QPS and 16k, while push holds near 7 ms. The reason is that push offloads descriptor preparation and transfer submission from the decode worker. Token generation is not starved, so per-token latency stays flat even at high concurrency and long contexts.
How to run benchmark
To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, refer to the detailed instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how the push-based KV connector overlaps prefill computation with decode-side block allocation and registration, removing the post-prefill router round trip and decode-side transfer setup from the critical path. This reduces TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our Qwen3-32B benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode provided up to a 3x improvement in TTFT and 30 percent improvement in TPOT compared with pull mode. Results vary by workload and configuration. To use push mode, configure both the prefill and decode servers to use NixlPushConnector instead of NixlConnector.
Choose the push-based connector when early decode node selection is acceptable and lower TTFT is the priority. The pull-based connector remains the better fit for workloads that require bidirectional KV transfer or defer decode-instance selection until after prefill for load-aware routing. vLLM supports both push- and pull-based KV connectors, so you can select the approach that best fits your deployment.
As a future improvement, we are exploring bringing the background NIXL threading model to the pull-mode connector, moving NIXL setup off the critical path so that pull-mode workloads could benefit from the same optimizations. We have opened a pull request to explore this.
Related resources
Acknowledgments
We thank the vLLM community for their support in maintaining this feature.

articles.title: Accelerating Mamba-2 with High-Performance Forward Pass Kernels in NVIDIA CUDA Tile | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores.
As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. This post walks you through the three custom kernels powering the Mamba-2 forward pass and the cuTile optimizations behind them.
Overview and prerequisites
To use cuTile, ensure your environment meets the requirements outlined in the cuTile Python Quickstart guide. Import the package as cuda.tile and expose it as ct throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post.
Sequence modeling computational trade-off
Sequence modeling architectures face a computational trade-off: traditional softmax attention trains rapidly using matrix multiplication accelerated by Tensor Cores, but at inference, compute and memory requirements increase linearly with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length.
Mamba-2 architecture
The Mamba-2 architecture comes from a family of models aiming for the best of both worlds. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores.
The core recurrence of Mamba-2 is:
\(h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t\)
Where:
- \(x_t\), \(dt_t\), \(B_t\), and \(c_t\) are the inputs to the Mamba-2 layer (obtained by projecting the inputs to the block, like queries, keys and values in an attention layer) at token \(t\)
- \(y_t\) is the output at token \(t\)
- \(h_t\) is the fixed-size hidden state carried across tokens. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity)
- \(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters
Intuitively:
- \(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\)
- \(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention
- \(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention
- \(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention
The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size S,H (\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). To make computation easier to write, use \(a_t = Adt_t\) and call \(b_t\) the product \(dt_t B_t\). The equation is then simply:
\(h_t = \exp(a_t)h_{t-1} + b_t x_t^{\mathsf{T}}, y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t-1} + Dx_t\)
This recurrent formulation is ideal for sequential inference. However, training and prefill require something faster than a for-loop. While the linear state update allows for a parallel scan algorithm, this approach requires materializing an enormous hidden state tensor making it primarily memory-bound and unable to utilize Tensor Cores.
An alternative approach leverages Tensor Cores by computing any future hidden state directly through matrix multiplication. Ignoring the \(\exp(a_t)\) term for simplification, going from \(h_t\) to \(h_{t+T}\) is just:
\(h_{t+T} = h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + b_{t+2}x_{t+2}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+T}x_{t+T}^{\mathsf{T}}\)
If building a matrix \(B\) of shape (T, S) by stacking all of the \(b_{t+i}\) and a matrix \(X\) of shape (T, H) by stacking all of the \(x_{t+i}\) then this is just \(h_{t+T} = h_t + BX^T\):
With this jump formula, you can efficiently compute the hidden state at various chunk “checkpoints” in the sequence. The next step is to find a way to compute outputs \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\), \(y_4\) given only \(h_0\). This would be easy if computing \(h_1\), \(h_2\), \(h_3\), \(h_4\), … but doing so would defeat the point of the jump formula.
Still removing the decay term \(\exp(a_t)\) for now, the goal is to compute:
\(y_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t+i} + Dx_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+i}x_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) + Dx_{t+i}\)
Where the previous formula is used to expand the hidden state. The skip connection term \(Dx_{t+i}\) is easy to reason about. For the others, it looks like this:
Again, grouping a chunk of \(x_t\), \(b_t\), \(c_t\) and \(y_t\) in matrices enables re-expressing this with Tensor Core-friendly matrix products (Figure 3) where the triangle in the \(\mathit{C}\) by \(\mathit{B}\) product is a causal mask (like in causal softmax attention).
When computing the output \(y_{t+i}\) you have some product of \(c_{t+i}\) by all of the \(b_j\) for \(j \leq t + i\) so when computing the full matrix product, you need to mask out the ones in the future (above the diagonal). In math this becomes (adding back the skip connection):
\(Y = Ch_t + \left((CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\)
With \(M\) the traditional causal mask.
Note that this looks very similar to attention (without the softmax) because when the decay term is removed, Mamba-2 is just linear attention (with some renaming). Adding back the decay makes things a little bit trickier. The expansion of the recurrence will look like:
\(h_(t+T)=exp(a_(t+1)+a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) h_t+exp(a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+1) x_(t+1)+exp(a_(t+3)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+2) x_(t+2)+⋯+b_(t+T) x_(t+T)\)
Reformulating in log-space allows for replacing sequential multiplications with cumulative sums. This remains a matmul if the rows of \(B\) (or \(X\)) are pre-multiplied by the exponentials. Keeping track of the cumulative sum of \(a_t\) in a tensor \(G\), this results in the following new equation:
\(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\)
Plugging the new hidden state jump into the output computation results in the following:
\(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\)
where the matrix \(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\) contains at \((i, j)\) the term \(\exp(g_i – g_j)\). Note that all of the terms where \(i < j\) will be masked by the causal mask, so only keep terms where \(g_t\) is the sum of more of the \(a_t\) than \(g_j\). By construction, all \(a_t\) values are negative, which makes \(g_i – g_j\) negative. Any exponentials of positive numbers are never kept, guaranteeing numerical stability.
This will translate into three kernels:
- chunk_cumsum: Compute the cumulative sums of the \(a_t\) inside each chunk.
- fwd_pass_state: Compute the hidden state at the beginning of each chunk using the jump formula above.
- compute_out: Compute the outputs for each chunk using the initial hidden state for the chunk computed in the previous step.
Kernel 1: Computing cumulative sums
The cumulative sums of the \(a_t = Adt_t\) (the \(G\) in the previous math) are needed in both Steps 2 and 3. To avoid recomputing several times, this first kernel will compute \(a_t\) once and store it. Note that this is not a global cumulative sum, just the cumulative sum within each chunk.
The inputs to this kernel are a per-head scalar decay a and a per-token timestep dt. The effective decay at token t for head h is a[h] * dt[t, h], and the kernel accumulates that product along the chunk dimension. These cumulative sums are all in log-space and the exponential of them is always taken (or some linear combination of them). Since it’s much cheaper to compute exp2 instead of exp, the result is scaled by log2(e).
This kernel introduces the cuTile primitives that all three kernels use: ct.bid, ct.load / ct.store, and ct.cumsum.
The full kernel is short:
@ct.kernel
def chunk_cumsum_kernel(
    a: torch.Tensor,        # [num_heads]
    dt: torch.Tensor,       # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads]
    output: torch.Tensor,   # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads]
    chunk_size: ct.Constant[int],
    BLOCK_H: ct.Constant[int],
) -> None:
    chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2)
    dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx),
                          shape=(1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H),
                          padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32)
    a_tile = ct.load(a, index=(head_tile_idx,),
                        shape=(BLOCK_H,),
                        padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32)
    d_tile = ct.cumsum(a_tile * dt_tile, axis=1) * LOG2E
    ct.store(output, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), tile=d_tile.astype(output.dtype))
The kernel is launched with a grid of (num_chunks, num_head_tiles, batch_size), the first line determines where you are in the grid using ct.bid. The broadcast product of a_tile (shape [BLOCK_H]) and dt_tile (shape [1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H]) gives the effective per-token, per-head decay over the tile. ct.cumsum(..., axis=1) then scans along the intra-chunk token dimension, and the result is stored in the layout expected by fwd_pass_state and compute_out.
Kernel 2: fwd_pass_state
fwd_pass_state computes the initial hidden state of each chunk and the final hidden state after the last chunk. It does not directly compute the output. Instead, it prepares the carried state that compute_out will later project into outputs. At its core, the kernel is a sequential loop over chunks as described earlier. Each kernel launch loads one (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slice of the hidden state, as shown below. Within that slice, hid_tile has a shape [BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE] and will contain a tile of the initial hidden state for each chunk.
head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2)
batch = batch_head // x.shape[2]
head = batch_head % x.shape[2]
group = head // num_heads_per_group
hid_tile = ct.load(
    init_state,
    index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx),
    shape=(1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE),
).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE))
In each iteration of the loop, first store the hidden state:
num_chunks = ct.cdiv(b.shape[1], chunk_size)
for chunk_idx in range(num_chunks):
    ct.store(
        hiddens,
        index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx),
        tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)).astype(hiddens.dtype),
    )
The rest of the loop loads one chunk of x, b, dt, and decay_cumsum to compute the next chunk’s initial hidden state. As shown previously, the math is:
\(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\)
ct.extract enables taking the last token from the decay tile loaded (to compute \(G_last\)). Use exp2 instead of exp for performance reasons, as shown previously. ct.mma is the API that will execute the matrix-multiply add while leveraging the Tensor Cores.
 x_tile = ct.load(
        x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx),
        shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD),
        padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO,
    ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD))
    b_tile = ct.load(
        b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx),
        shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE),
        padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO,
    ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE))
    dt_tile = ct.load(
        dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head),
        shape=(1, chunk_size, 1),
        padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO,
    ).reshape((chunk_size,))
    d_tile = ct.load(
        decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head),
        shape=(1, chunk_size, 1),
        padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO,
    ).reshape((chunk_size,))
    d_last = ct.extract(d_tile, index=(chunk_size - 1,), shape=(1,))
    b_dt_d = b_tile * (dt_tile * ct.exp2(d_last - d_tile))[:, None]
    hid_tile = ct.exp2(d_last) * hid_tile
    hid_tile = ct.mma(x_tile.transpose(), b_dt_d.astype(b.dtype), hid_tile)
After the final chunk, hid_tile contains the final hidden state, which is stored. During inference this value can be fed back as the next call’s init_state; during training it is usually discarded.
ct.store(
    final_state,
    index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx),
    tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)),
)
The sequential dependence stays inside a single grid point (program instance), while the independent (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slices run in parallel across the grid.
Kernel 3: compute_out
compute_out is the final kernel in the forward pass. It takes the per-chunk initial hidden states produced by fwd_pass_state and computes the token outputs, implementing the output equation derived earlier:
\(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\)
A direct PyTorch implementation would compute these three terms separately, materializing the full [B, n_chunks, chunk_size, chunk_size] interaction matrix C @ B.T in global memory. compute_out fuses them into one tiled kernel and keeps that matrix in registers.
Each kernel launch owns one (batch, chunk, head, head_tile) output tile and works in two phases. Phase 1 loops over state tiles, using ct.mma to build the interaction matrix cb_tile = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state term C @ H.T at the same time.
chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2)
batch = batch_head // x.shape[2]
head  = batch_head %  x.shape[2]
group = head // num_heads_per_group
cb_tile  = ct.full((chunk_size, chunk_size), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32)
out_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD),  0.0, dtype=ct.float32)
# Phase 1: build CB = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state output
for state_tile_idx in range(state_size // BLOCK_STATE):
    b_tile = ct.load(
        b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx),
        shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO,
    ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE))
    c_tile = ct.load(
        c, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx),
        shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO,
    ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE))
    h_tile = ct.load(
        hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx),
        shape=(1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE),
    ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE))
    cb_tile  = ct.mma(c_tile, b_tile.transpose(), cb_tile)
    out_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, h_tile.transpose().astype(c_tile.dtype), out_tile)
Phase 2 applies the decay and causal mask to cb_tile (ct.arange and ct.where build the lower-triangular mask M, so no mask tensor is ever materialized) and then adds all of the terms to get the final output tile. Both accumulators start as ct.full register tiles, and the final ct.mma casts to ct.tfloat32 to run through the Tensor Cores at near-FP32 accuracy.
# Phase 2: decay + causal mask then final computation
d_tile  = ct.load(decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head),
                  shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,))
dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head),
                  shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,))
x_tile  = ct.load(x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx),
                  shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD))
d_val   = ct.load(d, index=(head,), shape=(1,))
cb_tile  = cb_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :])  # pairwise decay
idx      = ct.arange(chunk_size, dtype=ct.int32)
cb_tile  = ct.where(idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :], cb_tile, 0.0)  # causal mask
out_tile = out_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None])                   # decay carried state
dt_x     = dt_tile[:, None] * x_tile
out_tile = ct.mma(cb_tile.astype(ct.tfloat32), dt_x.astype(ct.tfloat32), out_tile)
out_tile = out_tile + d_val * x_tile                            # D * x skip
ct.store(out, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx),
         tile=out_tile.reshape((1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD)).astype(out.dtype))
As mentioned, while some numerical unstable exponentials are computed in the ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) line (some of those are positive numbers), immediately mask them out so potential overflows don’t end up poisoning the computation.
Mamba-2 performance optimization
With the Mamba-2 workload defined in the cuTile-Python DSL, several key performance optimizations are introduced:
- Latency hint: cuTile allows you to annotate ct.load and ct.store operations with latency hints to model DRAM traffic. The compiler leverages these hints to optimize instruction scheduling and pipeline buffer depth.
- Swap A/B: On the NVIDIA Blackwell fifth-generation Tensor Core, MMA operands are asymmetric: operand A can live in Tensor Memory, but operand B must live in Shared Memory. For an input-fusion pattern like the SIMT-op + Dot-op in fwd_pass_state, the identity \(B^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}} = (AB)^{\mathsf{T}}\) is used to route the fused operand (b_dt_d) to operand A, relieving shared-memory contention.
- GMEM layout: The default strided memory access for decay_cumsum and dt lowers to cache-unfriendly LDG instructions. Transposing to a [batch, head, token] layout ensures contiguous access, enabling the use of TMA.
- cuTile-Python autotuner: Since performance bottlenecks shift with input shape, no single optimization strategy fits every model configuration. These optimizations are integrated alongside cuTile parameters (block_size, occupancy) into a unified search space, leveraging cuTile exhaustive_search to automatically find the optimal setup for each input shape.
Mamba-2 forward pass performance benchmarks
This implementation of the Mamba-2 forward pass kernel is available through TileGym. A complete example is shown below.
import torch
import tilegym
from tests import common
from tests.ops.test_mamba2 import Mamba2ProblemSpec
tilegym.set_backend("cutile")
num_tokens, state_size = 16384, 128
torch.manual_seed(0)
spec = Mamba2ProblemSpec(batch_size=4, num_tokens=num_tokens, num_groups=1, 
num_heads=8, state_size=state_size, head_size=64, 
chunk_size=128, dtype=torch.bfloat16, state_dtype=torch.float32)
fwd_inputs = spec.get_sample_inputs(with_reference=False, with_backward=False)
fwd = common.benchmark(
    lambda: tilegym.ops.mamba2_chunk_forward(**fwd_inputs),
    use_cupti=True,
)
print(f"Forward: {fwd['forward']['median'] * 1000:.2f} us")
The performance of the implemented Mamba-2 forward pass was evaluated against an open source implementation of the Mamba-2 kernel written in Triton, under the following software and hardware configurations:
Software
- mamba_ssm 2.3.2.post1 (NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton reference), Triton 3.7.1
- cuTile: cuda-tile 1.5.0
- TileIR assembler (tileiras) 13.4
- PyTorch 2.13.0, CUDA 13.3 (Driver and Runtime API, NVCC V13.3.33), Driver 595.58.03
- cuda-python / cuda-bindings 13.3.1
- Python 3.12.3, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.8.0-107
Hardware
- Single NVIDIA B300 SXM6, compute capability 10.3 (NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra)
- 1920 MHz max SM clock, 1100 W power limit, 268 GiB HBM
The results show that the optimized cuTile forward-pass kernels are 1.14x to 1.82x faster, with speedups growing as sequence lengths and state size increases. Note that these are kernel-level speedups only and end-to-end training results will also depend on the backward pass implementations.
Get started with cuTile
cuTile enables you to write clear, readable, and highly performant kernels in Python. Stay tuned for a follow-up post describing how the backward pass is implemented in cuTile.
Get started with cuTile and explore the documentation, GitHub repos, and sample code.

articles.title: Peak XV’s big bets on Indian startups; How Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
articles.text:
Peak XV’s big bets on Indian startups; How Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
Indian startup founders are increasingly aspiring to build companies worth $50 billion or even $100 billion, a shift that is prompting venture capital firms such as Peak XV Partners to take bigger risks, according to its Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar.
Dear Reader,
Rising input costs are squeezing the profitability of FMCG firms. Should you be worried about price hikes?
Not for the moment at least, as companies have absorbed a part of the inflation costs to not hurt consumer demand during the festive season. However, as firms continue to face margin pressures, decisions on price hikes could be taken post-Diwali, from December onwards, say stakeholders.
In other news, US Vice President J D Vance has admitted that his rhetoric has been “imperfect” when he referred to foreign professionals holding H-1 B visas as “indentured servants”. He clarified that his criticism was of the visa system, which gives employers too much power over foreign employees, and not targeted at H-1B visa holders.
India had condemned the terminology used to describe foreign professionals, calling it “deeply offensive” and carrying painful historical and colonial legacy connotations.
Meanwhile, the Delhi government has approved the setting up of Go-Delhi Foundation with a corpus of Rs 50 crore to empower young innovators and startups. The foundation aims to promote startups, innovation and entrepreneurship in the capital and support young people, researchers and entrepreneurs in turning their ideas into practical products and successful enterprises.
ICYMI: In their new book The Lift-Off Nation, Peak XV’s Rajan Anandan and Saurabh Srivastava make the case for India’s startup golden age. Anandan calls for greater corporate investment in R&D and startups and discusses the government’s Rs 1 lakh crore RDI scheme.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Peak XV’s big bets on Indian startups
- How Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
Here’s your trivia for today: Which company’s famous plaid pattern is called ‘novacheck’?
Venture capital
Peak XV is taking bigger bets on Indian startups
Indian startup founders are increasingly aspiring to build companies worth $50 billion or even $100 billion, a shift that is prompting venture capital firms such as Peak XV Partners to take bigger risks, according to its Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar.
During a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, at TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, Bhatnagar said the success of companies such as Zomato and the growing acceptance of startups in India’s public markets have fundamentally changed what founders and investors believe is possible.
Key takeaways
- Bhatnagar was gung-ho about the ambition and aspiration of Indian founders which has grown multifold over the years. “The startup ecosystem is in a much better place today than it was 20 years back. The biggest difference is in ambition,” he said.
- He believes AI can be a big advantage for a country like India, and startups should be rooted in India but build for the global market.
- “I really hope we now see a 10x unleashing of entrepreneurial energy because it's become so much easier to launch a product, to try it in the marketplace, than ever before. You don’t need as much capital.”
ICYMI
How Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
Tally Solutions’ journey began much before the SaaS, UPI, GST, and startup boom. Founded in 1986, the accounting software company has outlasted several technology cycles and built a customer network of close to three million.
At TechSparks 2026, Tally’s Managing Director Tejas Goenka and Executive Director Nupur Goenka explained how Tally, a homegrown product company, has stayed relevant over four decades.
Key takeaways
- Nupur Goenka attributed Tally's success to its focus on ownership. Tally handcrafted its stack from the start, she said, with its own database, its own memory manager, and a programming language invented in-house.
- Tejas Goenka stressed on the company’s founding principle. “The cost post-purchase should be near zero,” he said, recalling the days when releases were shipped with a support team of one.
- Going forward, Tally is betting on new geographies, particularly the Middle East and Africa. “We have an incredible two, three decades in front of us... It would be a shame if we let that opportunity slip to create an impactful technology company out of this country,” said Tejas.
News & updates
- AI advancements: Rapidly improving AI capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said, with one of the company's internal models  forecasting that, under certain conditions, it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
- Export curbs: China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used to make solar equipment, citing national security concerns, as part of a broader revision that also covers AI and biotechnology.
What you should watch out for
Jio Platforms’ IPO will open for subscription from October 21 to October 23. This is expected to be the largest public issue in Indian stock market history.
Which company’s famous plaid pattern is called ‘novacheck’?
Answer: Burberry
We would love to hear from you! To let us know what you liked and disliked about our newsletter, please mail [email protected].
If you don’t already get this newsletter in your inbox, sign up here. For past editions of the YourStory Buzz, you can check our Daily Capsule page here.

articles.title: NVIDIA Advances Agentic Security for Media, From European Public Service Broadcasting to Global Content Production
articles.text:
At a creative industry event that took place today in Berlin — hosted in collaboration with Adobe, Bertelsmann, NVIDIA and UFA — the latest advancements in intelligent media were on display.
Key to the news: the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is collaborating with NVIDIA to expand its sovereign framework with cloud, open models and integration partners, while Adobe Frame.io is accelerating video agent search capabilities with NVIDIA GPUs, helping German TV and film producer UFA find the right moments faster.
Read more about both announcements below.
Sovereign Clouds and Open Models Built for European Broadcasters
The EBU and NVIDIA are expanding the sovereign standards they introduced last year for European public service media. The initiative now brings in sovereign cloud providers, open model developers and systems integrators to define how broadcasters can deploy agents while keeping control of their data, infrastructure, models and security.
The EBU is the world’s leading alliance of public service media, with over 115 member organizations in more than 55 countries reaching over 1 billion people. As agents move into newsrooms, production and audience services, those broadcasters need a foundation that protects editorial independence, data sovereignty and national resilience.
The expanded initiative is turning those principles into deployable services. It’ll define requirements and reference architectures for where workloads run, how data is governed, which models power services and how systems stay secure throughout their lifecycle.
“These standards give EBU members a shared foundation to strengthen resilience, retain control and deliver accountable advanced services that sustain audience trust,” said Annsofi Eriksson, chief technology officer at the EBU.
Cloud providers will map the standards to sovereign deployment options:
- Microsoft will bring expertise from Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, including Azure Local and Foundry Local, so broadcasters can process sensitive editorial material locally and keep critical services running when external connectivity is down.
- Nebius offers a platform for broadcasters to train, fine-tune and run their own models on European infrastructure.
Open models give broadcasters the visibility to inspect, evaluate and adapt AI for local languages, archives and editorial policies. NVIDIA Nemotron open models provide a foundation broadcasters can customize for domain-specific applications and public-service requirements.
“Sovereign cloud infrastructure and open models can help Europe’s public service media innovate while protecting data, editorial independence and cultural diversity,” said Delphine Ernotte, CEO of France Télévisions and president of the EBU.
Media-specific consulting and systems integration provided from Qvest and other system integrators to ensure that reference architectures are practical, interoperable and deployable in real world broadcast environments.
Adobe Frame.io Speeds Video Search With NVIDIA Accelerated Computing
Also at the event, Adobe is highlighting its latest enhancements that help creatives search through video data faster.
Adobe is using NVIDIA accelerated computing to help creative teams find and work with video content faster. Its GPU-accelerated search pipeline uses NVIDIA NVDEC for video decoding, TensorRT for optimized AI inference and the CUDA platform for preprocessing and embedding generation.
Adobe is also advancing GPU-accelerated media ingest using NVIDIA NVENC and NVDEC to accelerate video encoding and decoding, helping production teams process growing media libraries more efficiently.
The results: about 5x faster embedding generation, up to 4x higher throughput and up to 5x lower latency for search processing. A new two-frame-per-second proxy, about 80% smaller than the 360p version it replaces, cuts storage and transfer while keeping the visual detail search needs.
That speed matters for UFA, one of Germany’s leading film and TV producers. It delivers more than 3,500 hours of programming a year, including the daily drama “Gute Zeiten, schlechte Zeiten.” When editors build a recap or flashback, they may need a specific reaction or unresolved exchange from as far back as 15 years — something file names and folders can’t surface.
Frame.io semantic search finds moments inside videos by concept, action or setting, and hybrid search adds notes, transcripts and approval status. An editor can search for “a character looking concerned,” narrow by character name and filter to approved footage, then move straight into review.
The work is part of a broader Adobe and NVIDIA collaboration that also spans Adobe Substance 3D, Firefly Foundry and 3D digital twin workflows for enterprises.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Starlink cutoff is a blinking red light for Canada
articles.text:
Last Wednesday, as Russian missiles pummeled Kyiv, the Ukrainian military’s satellite communications were suddenly cut off. Ukrainian officials say the call to cut access to Starshield, Elon Musk’s military-grade Starlink product, came from the White House (allegations the US has denied). Almost simultaneously, across the Atlantic, US President Donald Trump revived his threats of Canadian annexation at a midterms rally in Arizona.
Calling Ukraine’s experience parallel to Canada’s would be disingenuous; our military does not rely on Starshield, and we are not currently at war. Our country and military do, however, rely heavily on US technology—an issue BetaKit has written about extensively. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has spent much of the past year pledging to change that. Carney has also promised to “diversify away from” Starlink, and has awarded a military contract to Telesat for secure Arctic satellite communications. The Department of National Defence is reportedly bringing together a suite of Canadian AI tech to build a “MAIple stack” for use in defence.
Despite a recognized need for change, the transition has been slow and uneven. Reporting from The Maple found that the DND has paid nearly $68 million to Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and their Canadian subsidiaries so far this year. Meanwhile, the European Parliament has switched its default search engine from Google to Qwant, the Netherlands built a domestic code repository to replace GitHub, and France is already three years into its plan to transition its public service toward Linux.
That retreat from US tech hegemony is evidence of growing global concern over where the US state ends, and its corporate giants begin. Starshield’s rug pull in Ukraine should be a blinking red light on the dangers of dependency back home.
Jesse Cole,
Prairies Reporter

articles.title: Microsoft: October Windows Server updates break Exchange sign-in, mail flow
articles.text:
Microsoft has confirmed that this month's Windows Server security updates are causing OWA sign-in and mail delivery issues on some Exchange Server systems.
In a new Windows release health dashboard update over the weekend, Microsoft said users may have trouble accessing email or signing in to Outlook after installing the latest updates on systems running Windows Server 2019 and later.
In some cases, affected customers are also reportedly seeing Exchange Server OWA failing with a "MapiExceptionMdbOffline: Unable to make connection to the server. (hr=0x80004005, ec=1142)" error and Event ID 1006 in the application log.
"After installing the October 2026 Windows security update [..], some on-premises Exchange servers might experience issues accessing or sending email. Users might be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web (OWA), or email messages sent from Outlook might remain in the Outbox and not be delivered. Additionally, Exchange might experience issues accessing mailboxes during mailbox replication," it said.
"The October 2026 update introduced a default limit on the amount of memory used by Endpoint Mapper when handling Endpoint Lookup calls. For workloads such as Exchange Server, the default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls might not be sufficient under heavy load. Administrators can use this registry setting to increase the maximum number of simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls, which increases the amount of memory that Endpoint Mapper can use."
However, Microsoft says these known issues aren't linked to the October 2026 Exchange server security updates and urges customers not to uninstall them.
"Issues reported are not related to installation of October 2026 security updates for Exchange Server. This is not a 'known issue' related to October 2026 Exchange update. Any version of Exchange that runs on impacted versions of Windows could be impacted," Microsoft added in a separate blog describing the issues.
"Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem."
While it works on a fix, Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround that should resolve these issues by modifying a registry key on affected Exchange Server systems.
To do that, you have to run the following command from an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange Server and then reboot the device:
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f
After the system restarts, customers should monitor the Exchange environment and raise the Endpoint Mapper memory limit if it reoccurs.
In July. Microsoft also announced that it will stop shipping extended security updates for Exchange 2016 and 2019 this month after a 6-month extension announced in April 2026 to the original Extended Security Update (ESU) program.
