articles.title: La Switch 2 a enfin droit à son patch pour The Witcher 3 Remastered
articles.text:
Geralt poursuit sa route vers une version toujours plus aboutie de The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered. Disponible depuis le 29 septembre 2026, cette édition remastérisée du RPG de CD Projekt RED a déjà reçu plusieurs mises à jour destinées à corriger ses problèmes techniques. Après un lancement qui a notamment mis en évidence des défauts d’éclairage et des soucis de performances, le studio continue d’écouter les retours des joueuses et des joueurs, et d’affiner son jeu sur les différentes plateformes.
Ce lundi 19 octobre, la Switch 2 a reçu à son tour le patch 5.01. Disponible depuis le 8 octobre sur PC, PlayStation 5 et Xbox Series X|S, cette mise à jour apporte son lot de correctifs, avec plusieurs ajustements spécifiquement pensés pour la console de Nintendo. Parmi les correctifs attendus, CD Projekt RED annonce sur la page dédiée plusieurs ajustements touchant au bloom, au tone mapping et à l’éclairage des personnages. Sur Switch 2 uniquement, le studio a aussi retouché la netteté de l’image et la résolution pour gagner en clarté.
La retouche de la netteté sur Switch 2 vise le principal reproche fait à cette version, une image trop floue et une résolution trop basse en mode portable. CD Projekt RED ne publie en revanche aucun chiffre, ni sur la résolution visée ni sur la fréquence d’images après ce correctif.
CD Projekt RED continue d’améliorer The Witcher 3 Remastered
Le patch 5.01 corrige également plusieurs bugs de gameplay, dont les esquives, la gestion de l’endurance, les collisions et le fonctionnement de certaines compétences. Il corrige aussi plusieurs défauts d’interface, des voix devenues moins audibles après un passage par le menu pause, ainsi qu’un problème de sauvegarde, avec un outil pour réparer les sauvegardes déjà touchées.
Sur Nintendo Switch 2, cette mise à jour corrige aussi un plantage rare lors des changements de région, optimise la gestion du cache pour les mods multiplateformes et corrige les vibrations HD Rumble, qui ne se faisaient sentir que dans le Joy-Con 2 gauche quand Geralt utilisait une échelle. Enfin, les marqueurs ne peuvent plus être placés sur les bandes noires entourant la carte. Dans les correctifs communs à toutes les versions, la végétation réagit de nouveau aux collisions.
CD Projekt RED poursuit donc, à un bon rythme de croisière, le travail d’optimisation engagé depuis la sortie du jeu. Le patch 5.01 est disponible depuis ce lundi 19 octobre sur Nintendo Switch 2. Il suffit de mettre à jour le jeu pour profiter des correctifs et des améliorations annoncés par CD Projekt RED.

articles.title: « On utilise l'IA » : un cadre de Xbox brise le secret avant de supprimer son compte — Frandroid
articles.text:
Chez Xbox, un cadre a dit tout haut ce que l’industrie du jeu vidéo évite de dire. Entre le dimanche 18 et ce lundi 19 octobre, Brandon Stirrup, responsable senior de la stratégie commerciale de la division, a publié sur X une série de messages qui se résument en une phrase : « on utilise l’IA ». Il se disait prêt à « encaisser » si cela permettait à « des centaines » de collègues d’arrêter de faire semblant. Lundi soir, ses messages avaient été supprimés et son compte X avait disparu.
Tout est parti d’un projet du week-end. Brandon Stirrup raconte avoir « vibe-codé » un jeu « mauvais mais améliorable » en deux jours, dont environ trois heures de travail actif. Le vibe coding consiste à décrire en langage courant ce qu’on veut à une IA, qui écrit le code à sa place. Sa conclusion : « n’importe qui peut créer un jeu ».
Puis le ton est monté. « Si je suis viré demain, ce sera parce que je vous ai dit la vérité que personne ne veut que vous sachiez », a-t-il écrit. Il assure qu’un simple prompt (la consigne écrite qu’on donne à l’IA) suffit déjà pour obtenir des jeux sur mesure, « pour le meilleur ou pour le pire ».
Le jeu vidéo, « seule industrie » à freiner selon lui
Pour Brandon Stirrup, le jeu vidéo est la seule industrie qui traîne des pieds, parce que les joueurs voient l’IA d’un mauvais œil. « Les utilisateurs veulent la vérité. On utilise l’IA », a-t-il insisté, en ajoutant que toutes les entreprises le font en 2026. Il est allé plus loin en estimant qu’un concepteur qui ne voit aucune place pour l’IA dans son avenir n’a rien à faire dans le monde des affaires.
Pour le joueur, cette IA utilisée en coulisses reste de toute façon invisible. Depuis la mise à jour de ses règles en janvier 2026, Steam n’oblige plus les studios à signaler les assistants de code et autres outils de productivité. Seuls les contenus générés que le joueur voit ou entend (images, voix, textes, musique) doivent être déclarés sur la fiche du jeu.
La parole de Brandon Stirrup n’engage toutefois que lui. Il travaille sur la stratégie commerciale, n’avait jamais développé de jeu avant ce week-end et ne s’exprimait pas au nom de Microsoft. Les « centaines » d’employés qui utiliseraient l’IA sans le dire ne reposent que sur ses messages.
Xbox n’a jamais caché son intérêt pour l’IA
Pourtant, Microsoft ne fait pas mystère de ses essais. En février 2025, Xbox a présenté Muse, un modèle d’IA capable de générer des visuels et du gameplay. Deux mois plus tard, pour les 50 ans de l’entreprise, Microsoft a montré une démo de jeu générée par IA, au résultat catastrophique.
Surtout, Asha Sharma, CEO d’Xbox et ancienne cadre de l’IA chez Microsoft, a lancé Xbox Labs le 13 octobre. Cette petite équipe doit explorer de nouvelles façons de porter, remixer et créer des jeux, après plusieurs semaines de mods faits avec l’IA, dont un Call of Duty qui tournait dans un navigateur web. Dans son annonce, elle ne parlait pourtant pas directement d’IA.
Sa ligne officielle date de sa nomination, en février : Xbox ne cherchera pas « l’efficacité à court terme » et n’inondera pas son écosystème de « bouillie IA sans âme ». Elle disait aussi n’avoir « aucune tolérance pour la mauvaise IA », tout en rappelant que l’IA fait partie du jeu vidéo depuis longtemps.
Les autres éditeurs avancent eux aussi avec prudence. En juin, Capcom a promis de ne pas mettre d’IA générative dans ses jeux, tout en reconnaissant s’en servir pendant le développement.
En septembre 2025, Phil Rogers, CEO du groupe suédois Embracer, reconnaissait déjà que l’IA risquait de produire des quêtes annexes « sans âme ».
L’IA bouscule aussi les projets d’amateurs. En juillet, Meta a lancé Pocket, une application qui crée des mini-jeux à partir d’une simple phrase, toujours indisponible en France. Le 15 octobre, le développeur Luke Street a fermé l’index public de decomp.dev face aux projets « finis » avec l’IA. Depuis 2024, ce site suivait la décompilation de jeux rétro, qui consiste à reconstruire leur code source à partir du programme final.
Brandon Stirrup, lui, n’a pas attendu que la polémique enfle. Une source chez Xbox a expliqué à PC Gamer qu’il avait lui-même désactivé son compte X, à cause du nombre de réponses reçues. Aucune sanction n’a été rendue publique pour l’instant.

articles.title: Alienware AW3226Q Tandem WOLED 32-Inch Review
articles.text:
The Dell Alienware AW3226Q is the cheapest 4K OLED gaming monitor yet to offer an RGB stripe subpixel layout. This display uses the latest generation of Tandem WOLED technology, including the much sought-after RGB stripe configuration, but costs just $700. That makes it one of the cheapest 4K OLEDs overall, and by far the most affordable way to get this type of WOLED panel.
The AW3226Q uses a variant of the 32-inch 4K panel we recently reviewed in the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM. That Asus model features the flagship version of this 2026 panel, with a 240Hz refresh rate and a 1080p 480Hz dual mode. The Alienware variant reduces the refresh rate to 165Hz at 4K and omits dual mode entirely, but otherwise retains the same core panel technology, including the glossy screen coating.
Now, while the Asus model is being sold at a whopping $1,400, Dell's model costs just half as much at $700. Yes, the refresh rate is reduced, but the overall package is substantially cheaper. In fact, despite offering newer panel technology, the AW3226Q launches at the same price as discounted, previous-generation 165Hz QD-OLED and WOLED monitors, making for an interesting comparison.
Other specs of interest include a DisplayHDR True Black 400 certification, Dolby Vision support, and the usual adaptive sync and variable refresh rate capabilities, in this case branded as both FreeSync Premium Pro and G-Sync Compatible.
RGB Stripe: Subpixel Layout and Text Clarity
Before getting into the results, here's a quick recap of what this panel offers and why the RGB stripe layout matters.
In 2026, LG Display offers two main variants of Tandem WOLED technology. One retains the white subpixel, which has been the standard configuration for LG panels for years, resulting in an RGWB subpixel layout. The other uses a pure RGB stripe, a new configuration for 2026 that matches the traditional subpixel arrangement used by LCD panels, delivering similarly excellent text clarity.
Despite omitting the white subpixel in the RGB version, both are still WOLED panels, as the W in WOLED refers to the underlying white-light emission technology, not the presence of a white subpixel.
The main benefits of RGB stripe include full compatibility with subpixel font rendering, resulting in the best text clarity you can currently get from an OLED display, and much higher color brightness than RGWB panels. There's also significantly reduced gray banding, leading to better overall screen uniformity.
However, as with most things, there are trade-offs. Removing the white subpixel leads to lower peak white brightness than RGWB panels in both SDR and HDR content, as we'll explore later in this review. It also results in worse efficiency in certain situations. Which option is better ultimately depends on your priorities, and that's why LG Display offers both variants.
One of the biggest selling points of RGB stripe is text quality, and text certainly looks excellent on the AW3226Q. That's thanks to a combination of the RGB stripe layout and glossy screen coating. The latter eliminates the slight haze associated with matte surfaces, improving the perceived sharpness of fine details like text. Compared to a typical IPS LCD, most of which use matte coatings, the AW3226Q actually looks better when displaying text.
However, we're talking about a relatively high pixel density here at 140 PPI. While RGB stripe is the best subpixel layout for text clarity, it doesn't have a huge advantage over other OLED layouts, such as triangular RGB on QD-OLEDs or RGWB on conventional WOLEDs.
The high pixel density tends to mask the artifacts associated with these other layouts, so unless you're particularly sensitive to issues like color fringing, there's a good chance you won't notice much difference between an RGB stripe WOLED and a QD-OLED.
Screen Coating: It's Glossy
The AW3226Q uses the same type of glossy screen coating we've seen on other glossy WOLED monitors. Dell doesn't have a specific brand name for this coating, unlike Asus with its "TrueBlack Glossy" branding, but the results are essentially the same.
The screen maintains excellent black levels across a variety of environments, including brighter rooms, without the purple tint or raised blacks associated with QD-OLED panels. This is a key advantage of glossy WOLED over glossy QD-OLED: WOLED panels like this maintain meaningfully deeper blacks under moderate ambient lighting.
The trade-off is reflectivity. Glossy WOLED has a more pronounced mirror-like finish and is more likely to reflect your surroundings than QD-OLED. Which option works best depends heavily on your setup. If lights or sunlight from a window hit the display directly, those reflections will be more noticeable on WOLED, so avoiding direct light sources is particularly important.
HDR Performance and Configurations
As with other RGB stripe WOLEDs we've tested, HDR performance is one of the more interesting aspects of this display. All the fundamentals are here: perfect black levels, per-pixel lighting control, and effectively infinite contrast. OLED can display bright pixels directly alongside dark ones without blooming or zone bleed, making it an excellent technology for HDR.
However, unlike previous WOLEDs with a white subpixel, the new RGB stripe models perform quite similarly to QD-OLEDs in HDR, for better and sometimes for worse. This extends to the HDR configurations, with the AW3226Q offering three main modes similar to those found on QD-OLED monitors. Dell provides several additional options, but we'll focus on the best configurations.
The first is DisplayHDR True Black, which offers broadly accurate EOTF tracking in both bright and dark content. In other words, the screen generally delivers the brightness levels requested by HDR content. However, peak brightness is limited to just 400 nits, a significant trade-off. We also observed some panel dimming in bright scenes, though it wasn't huge.
The second option is HDR Peak 1000, which behaves similarly to the peak brightness modes found on QD-OLED monitors. It unlocks the panel's full brightness potential, reaching up to 1,000 nits for small highlights while maintaining good accuracy in dark scenes.
The downside is panel dimming in bright scenes. When the display encounters content with a high average brightness level, it can reduce the brightness of every pixel by roughly half. This makes bright scenes look noticeably dimmer than intended, reducing the impact HDR should deliver in these situations.
The third option is HDR Peak 1000 Bright, which attempts to correct this behavior by boosting brightness in brighter scenes for more accurate EOTF tracking. Unfortunately, it also raises the brightness of dark content, making those scenes considerably brighter and less accurate than they should be. Like the regular Peak 1000 mode, it retains access to 1,000 nits of peak brightness.
There are positives and negatives to Dell's approach. Having all three configurations gives users plenty of choice over how HDR content looks, but there's no single mode that delivers accurate performance in both bright and dark scenes. Bright content generally looks best in True Black or Peak 1000 Bright, while darker scenes are better served by the regular Peak 1000 mode. This isn't entirely Dell's fault. Panel limitations force manufacturers to make these compromises, and we've seen similar behavior across many QD-OLED and RGB stripe WOLED monitors.
There are a few other details worth mentioning. By default, Dell uses display-side tone mapping to provide a gradual brightness roll-off when HDR content exceeds the panel's capabilities. The roll-off varies depending on the peak brightness metadata sent to the display and generally does a decent job of preventing highlight clipping. However, it can also limit brightness in certain situations.
Compared to other HDR monitors, both Peak 1000 and True Black deliver decent accuracy in dark scenes. The AW3226Q performs better than the PG32UCWM, which only offers a boosted brightness configuration, and ends up similar to QD-OLEDs like the MSI 321UPX.
In bright scenes, True Black is somewhat underwhelming compared to the equivalent HDR mode on the Gigabyte MO32U24. Meanwhile, Peak 1000 suffers from significant inaccuracies caused by panel dimming, though its behavior is comparable to other OLED monitors with similar limitations.
Color accuracy is decent without being exceptional. Performance is comparable to the AW3926QW, while color space coverage reaches a respectable 78% of Rec. 2020. That's slightly higher than the PG32UCWM and in the same ballpark as 32-inch 4K QD-OLED monitors. Color volume is also higher than on the Asus model and comes very close to QD-OLED, though it still trails slightly. This is one area where RGB stripe WOLED has a significant advantage over previous-generation WOLED panels.
HDR Brightness
Starting with synthetic HDR brightness tests, the AW3226Q reaches 260 nits at full screen, matching first-generation QD-OLED panels and previous-generation WOLEDs.
That's 13% brighter than the PG32UCWM, although it falls short of the AW3926QW, which currently delivers the highest full-screen brightness we've measured from an RGB stripe WOLED. There's also a gap to the latest 2026 QD-OLED panels, such as the Gigabyte MO32U24 and Asus PG32UCDM3, which reach 300 nits or more, around 15% brighter than the Alienware.
Brightness at a 10% window was disappointing on our unit, reaching just 430 nits. That's 16% below the PG32UCWM when comparing peak modes, and also behind previous-generation QD-OLEDs.
Performance recovers with a 2% window, where the AW3226Q manages to exceed 1,000 nits, similar to current QD-OLED offerings. However, WOLEDs with a white subpixel, such as the XG32UCWMG, can achieve higher brightness in this test. Dell's 39-inch AW3926QW ultrawide also gets brighter despite using largely similar technology.
Moving to real-scene brightness, the AW3226Q struggles in its True Black configuration. We recorded an average of just 291 nits, which is 23% behind the 2024-generation QD-OLED panel used in the MSI 322URX in its True Black mode. It's also more than 30% behind the newer 2026 panel found in the MO32U24 using its HDR mode. It's difficult to recommend True Black on the Alienware because it simply isn't very bright, rarely reaching 400 nits in our tests.
Peak 1000 is better, but still somewhat underwhelming. Compared directly with the RGB stripe WOLED panel in the PG32UCWM, the Asus was 8% brighter on average. However, the Asus uses a boosted brightness configuration that avoids panel dimming at the expense of accuracy in dark scenes. The AW3226Q performs much better in that regard.
A typical 32-inch 4K QD-OLED from 2024, such as the MSI 321UPX, is also 13% brighter on average when comparing peak modes. Both panels exhibit similar brightness behavior across individual tests, but the QD-OLED generally comes out ahead.
The reality is that this RGB stripe WOLED panel isn't especially bright in HDR and suffers from many of the same weaknesses as QD-OLED. It's certainly not unusable, reaching over 850 nits in real-world scenes and up to 1,000 nits in smaller highlights, but peak brightness is clearly not one of its strengths.
Dolby Vision
The AW3226Q also supports Dolby Vision, which is enabled by default but can be disabled through the OSD. There are no additional configuration options, and brightness is limited to around 450 nits, similar to the True Black HDR mode. When connected to a Windows PC, the monitor generally operates in Dolby Vision mode, switching to HDR10 when compatible content is detected. This involves a brief black screen as the display changes modes.
For the most part, this works reasonably well. The monitor correctly switches to HDR10 in many games, allowing users to take advantage of brighter configurations such as Peak 1000. However, HDR10 detection isn't always reliable, and the display sometimes remains in Dolby Vision mode. We encountered this behavior when watching HDR YouTube videos in Chrome, for example.
For Windows users, we'd generally recommend leaving Dolby Vision disabled. Very few PC games support it, and none have been released recently. Some streaming services may use Dolby Vision, but for gaming, sticking with HDR10 avoids unnecessary mode switching.
Dolby Vision becomes more useful when connecting other devices. Many media players support Dolby Vision playback through streaming apps, while the Xbox Series X also supports Dolby Vision gaming. Even then, the limited brightness of Dell's Dolby Vision implementation means HDR10 may sometimes be the better option.
Motion Performance
Motion performance is one of the key differences between this 165Hz OLED and most competing models, which offer 240Hz refresh rates. An important consideration when buying an OLED, especially one with a lower refresh rate, is that motion clarity is directly tied to refresh rate.
At the same refresh rate, two OLED monitors will look virtually identical in motion clarity, so the refresh rate you'll actually use matters more than the monitor's maximum capability. For example, a 240Hz OLED and a 165Hz OLED running a game at 120 FPS with a 120Hz refresh rate will deliver essentially the same experience.
Higher refresh rate OLEDs become beneficial when you can take advantage of their additional headroom. Running at 240Hz produces a clearer image than at 165Hz, with better smoothness and responsiveness. However, if you play most games below 165 FPS, the benefits of a 240Hz model will be relatively small.
This raises the question of how much you're sacrificing by choosing a cheaper 165Hz model. In our opinion, higher refresh rate variants are best suited to multiplayer gaming. If you play a lot of fast-paced competitive titles where motion clarity and low input latency are priorities, 240Hz is the better choice. For story-driven games, 165Hz is often more than sufficient for an excellent experience.
However, 165Hz monitors have less headroom for future GPU upgrades and frame generation. With frame generation enabled, you generally want to stay within the monitor's refresh rate ceiling to avoid tearing. On a 165Hz display using 2x frame generation, the maximum base rendering rate before exceeding that ceiling is approximately 82 FPS. In other words, even with frame generation, you're limited to the input latency characteristics of a game running at around 80 FPS, plus any additional frame generation overhead.
On a 240Hz display, that base rendering rate increases to 120 FPS, which provides a more responsive experience. This is a potential limitation of 165Hz displays, even for single-player gaming.
Input lag is as expected, with a processing delay below 1ms. Our latency measurements combine processing delay and refresh lag to provide a useful indication of overall responsiveness.
The fastest 240Hz OLEDs lead the charts, while 144Hz and 165Hz models generally sit further down due to their lower refresh rates. That's ultimately the main difference between the AW3226Q and faster OLED alternatives: the lower refresh rate results in somewhat higher latency.
SDR Performance
The AW3226Q performs quite well out of the box in SDR grayscale testing. An average Delta E of around 5 is better than usual, with very good color temperature and reasonable gamma tracking. However, like many wide-gamut monitors, it doesn't enable sRGB emulation by default, so colors appear oversaturated out of the box.
Default Color Performance
There are two ways to achieve more accurate SDR colors: the dedicated sRGB mode in the OSD or Windows Auto Color Management (ACM). The latter produces reasonably accurate results, but Dell's built-in sRGB mode is even better, although it locks several settings and offers limited customization.
Default ACM Color Performance
Despite those restrictions, the sRGB mode is outstanding. Grayscale calibration is nearly perfect across the board, while saturation performance is excellent, with fantastic adherence to the Rec. 709 color space.
sRGB Mode Color Performance
A ColorChecker Delta E ITP average of just 1.53 is the sort of performance we typically see after a full manual calibration, making additional calibration unnecessary for most users.
Compared to other monitors we've tested, the AW3226Q ranks among the very best for sRGB accuracy. A handful of models deliver similarly impressive results, but that ColorChecker score is particularly exceptional. Across 202 sRGB modes we've tested over the years, the AW3226Q ranks third overall, with Dell monitors occupying all three top spots.
SDR brightness is largely as expected given the full-screen HDR results. The AW3226Q reaches 254 nits with a full-screen white image, putting it on par with 2024-generation QD-OLED panels. Most OLEDs fall within this range, with only the latest models, such as 2026 QD-OLEDs, pushing into the 300-nit territory. We still consider 250 nits sufficient for most users. Minimum brightness is also very good, and Dell uses a uniform brightness configuration in SDR mode.
Uniformity
Uniformity is an interesting aspect of the AW3226Q. Thanks to the new RGB stripe Tandem WOLED design, gray uniformity has improved significantly compared to previous WOLED panels, something further helped by the lower 165Hz refresh rate.
There's minimal dirty screen effect when viewing dark grays and virtually no dark gray banding. This makes the AW3226Q a better option for productivity work, particularly in applications with gray backgrounds, than previous WOLED displays.
However, the panel isn't without uniformity issues. In its settled state, the edges are dimmer than the center, creating a mild vignette effect that we don't typically see on QD-OLEDs or even other WOLED panels. This is reflected in the higher Delta E measurements around the edges. The PG32UCWM exhibited similar behavior to some degree, although it's more noticeable on our Alienware unit. By comparison, QD-OLED panels typically deliver better edge-to-edge uniformity.
This issue is further exacerbated by dynamic edge dimming through a system called CPC, or Convex Power Control. CPC dims the edges of the screen during dynamic content, including gaming, making the vignette effect more pronounced than our static uniformity measurements suggest. The effect can be difficult to spot while gaming, as the constantly changing imagery tends to hide uniformity problems. We also didn't notice any saturation issues around the edges of this display.
CPC is an OLED care feature designed to reduce the risk of burn-in, but unfortunately, Dell provides no option to disable it. In fact, the AW3226Q offers no user control over its OLED care settings. On several competing monitors from brands like Asus and MSI, users can adjust these features, including disabling edge dimming to restore better panel uniformity. With the Alienware, you're stuck with Dell's default configuration.
Finally, full-screen white power consumption came in at 94 watts, similar to QD-OLED alternatives and 6 watts lower than the PG32UCWM. However, removing the white subpixel makes the AW3226Q less efficient than the previous-generation RGWB WOLED panel used in the XG32UCWG. Gaming power consumption is considerably lower, averaging a very manageable 42 watts in our test.
Ports, Features and Design
The AW3226Q comes with a standard selection of ports, including one DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC, two HDMI 2.1 ports supporting the full 48 Gbps bandwidth with DSC, and a three-port USB 5 Gbps hub.
The USB hub is quite convenient, with one Type-A port on the back, another Type-A on the bottom edge, and a USB-C port alongside it. The USB-C connection supports data and 15W power delivery, but not DisplayPort Alt Mode.
All display inputs support the full 4K 165Hz at 10-bit through DSC. One of the HDMI ports also supports eARC, which could be useful in certain setups. There's a 3.5mm audio jack, but no built-in speakers.
Dell has included several features in the OSD, controlled through a directional toggle on the rear of the display. These include multiple picture presets and color controls, a dark stabilizer, picture-in-picture mode, and RGB lighting controls. Most gaming-specific features are grouped under AlienVision, which allows you to display crosshairs and apply color filters to selected areas of the screen.
Unfortunately, Dell offers virtually no control over its OLED care features. Dell has implemented the usual protections, including pixel shifting and automatic dimming in certain situations, but these features are always enabled and cannot be adjusted or disabled. On the positive side, Dell continues to offer a three-year warranty covering burn-in.
As for the design, the AW3226Q follows Alienware's recent aesthetic, although this model has a darker, almost black finish rather than the dark blue used on earlier versions. It's a relatively minimalist design that isn't overly "gamery," and I think it looks great. Build quality and surface finishes are also good, despite most of the exterior being plastic.
The Alienware logo on the rear features some RGB lighting, although it's fairly subtle on this model. Ergonomics are good, with height, tilt, and swivel adjustments, along with a compact, squarish base that doesn't occupy much desk space and still allows you to place items on top of it.
The front looks excellent, with uniform bezels and that attractive glossy finish. I also love that Dell has abandoned the curve here. The AW3226Q uses a standard flat panel, unlike the original 32-inch QD-OLED AW3225QF, which featured a curved display.
A Great OLED Faces Tough Competition
Overall, the Dell Alienware AW3226Q is a bit of a mixed bag. There are certainly aspects of this monitor that I really like, but whether we'd recommend buying it depends on a few factors. The 32-inch 4K OLED market is extremely competitive, especially on pricing, making it difficult for the AW3226Q to stand out even at its $700 MSRP.
Let's start with the good stuff. This monitor gives you a brand-new RGB stripe WOLED panel with an excellent glossy finish for half the price of the Asus PG32UCWM we recently reviewed. The main sacrifice is refresh rate, dropping from 240Hz to 165Hz, along with the removal of dual mode support. Otherwise, performance is very similar, making Dell's offering a much more affordable way to access this panel technology.
And there are good reasons to go for an RGB stripe WOLED. Performance is quite similar to QD-OLED, including excellent color brightness and good gray uniformity, but it also addresses some of QD-OLED's weaknesses.
While color fringing isn't a major issue on 32-inch 4K QD-OLEDs, the RGB stripe layout eliminates it thanks to a subpixel arrangement better suited to text rendering. The glossy coating is another significant advantage, delivering deeper blacks across more lighting conditions without the reddish-purple tint associated with QD-OLED.
Dell has also done an excellent job in a few areas. The sRGB mode is outstanding, with near-perfect SDR calibration. We also appreciate having all three main HDR configurations available. Dolby Vision and HDMI eARC are welcome additions that aren't available on every competitor.
As for downsides, HDR brightness in particular is somewhat disappointing. Panel dimming in bright HDR scenes used to be something you could avoid by choosing WOLED over QD-OLED, but the new RGB stripe WOLED panels exhibit similar behavior.
Between panel dimming and the limitations of this new RGB stripe design, the AW3226Q is actually less bright in HDR scenes than first-generation 32-inch 4K QD-OLED panels released more than two years ago.
So, should you buy the AW3226Q?
The first comparison worth making is against similarly priced 165Hz QD-OLED monitors using the original 2024 panel design. Models like the Asus XG32UCDS can typically be found for around $700, exactly the same price as the Alienware. So at price parity, the Alienware AW3226Q is the better buy. Panel performance is similar except for slightly lower HDR brightness. However, the Tandem WOLED panel has superior screen coating, which avoids the raised black issue, and its RGB stripe layout, which is better suited to text rendering.
What holds us back from giving the AW3226Q a broader recommendation is that 4K 240Hz OLED monitors aren't much more expensive, and sometimes cost exactly the same. In recent weeks, 32-inch 4K 240Hz QD-OLEDs have regularly been available for around $750, with recent sales bringing models like the MSI 321UPX down to $700.
That puts the AW3226Q in a more difficult position. For the same $700, or perhaps a $50 premium, you can get a 240Hz QD-OLED with broadly similar panel performance. Instead of comparing two OLED technologies at the same price and refresh rate, you're now weighing the advantages of RGB stripe WOLED against a substantially higher refresh rate. Do you prioritize the better motion clarity, responsiveness, and headroom of a 240Hz monitor, or the superior screen coating and text clarity of the AW3226Q?
It's a tough choice. If you really dislike the raised blacks and reddish-purple tint of QD-OLED, this Tandem WOLED is a better fit. But for most gamers, we would pick the 240Hz option.
Of course, pricing varies by region and it's also worth noting that we're comparing discounted prices for QD-OLED monitors that have been on the market for months against the launch MSRP of a brand-new product. Dell could easily make the AW3226Q a more compelling option with a price adjustment. At $700, it's a good monitor facing some very strong competition. At a lower price, it could become a much easier recommendation.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Light Mkhumbuza, Pedro Ornelas, Angela Dudley, Isaac Nape, Kayn A. Forbes. Topological control of chirality and spin with structured light. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02278-6
Cite This Page:

articles.title: One Compromised Login Exposed Millions of California Students’ Records
articles.text:
Personal information on current and former California public school students was copied from a file transfer system belonging to Educational Testing Service (ETS), according to the California Department of Education (CDE).
ETS is a nonprofit that handles state and federally mandated testing under a contract with the state. The organization supports California’s CAASPP and ELPAC assessment programs and relied on a secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) site to share testing data with CDE.
The organization spotted unauthorized activity on the site on September 25, but the earliest access dates back to late May.
“The investigation determined that an unauthorized party used a compromised login credential at various times during the period from May 22, 2026 to September 18, 2026 to access the SFTP site to copy files containing California student information,” according to the CDE’s breach notice.
No victim count has been provided, but the notice says, “Information about California students, including but not limited to all students enrolled in the three previous school years, was accessed and copied.”
CDE’s own enrollment figures put that in perspective: more than 5.7 million students were enrolled in California public schools in 2025-2026. The department’s incident FAQ notes that the impacted population also extends to students who left a California school as far back as 2006 and whose transfer to another school was not confirmed with CDE.
Compromised records can include information such as student name, birth date, home address, school, district and grade, state and local ID numbers, gender, race or ethnicity, primary language, country of origin and English learner status.
Some entries go further, revealing disability and Section 504 status, the primary disability type, testing accommodations, English proficiency data, and test registration and results. They may also indicate whether a student qualifies for Title I, McKinney-Vento or military-connected student designations.
The notice says the files did not contain Social Security numbers, passwords, or financial account or payment card details. Information on parents and guardians was not involved either.
ETS shut down the account the intruder used and pulled the SFTP site offline. Its response also includes building a replacement site with stronger safeguards.
The official disclosures do not explain how the login credential was compromised, and they do not identify the attacker.
“After working with law enforcement as well as with cybersecurity experts, ETS has taken steps to reduce the potential risk of the data being made publicly accessible,” the notice states. ETS did not elaborate, but said its web monitoring has so far found no evidence that the data has been published.
CDE informed county and district superintendents and charter school administrators of the incident in a letter dated October 2, two weeks before family notifications started. According to that letter, ETS stopped its regular processing of enrollment data and suspended some testing work while its systems’ security was evaluated.
Student notifications started going out on October 16, and CDE expects them to continue into early November. Affected current and former students can sign up for two years of free identity protection services.
Related: Deal Reached With Hackers to Delete Data Stolen From the Canvas Educational Platform
Related: Mount Royal University Confirms Data Stolen in Ransomware Attack

articles.title: Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
articles.text:
Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to provide up to 960 megawatts of carbon-free energy for both the regional power grid and Amazon’s data centers.
Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
The proposed nuclear plant would provide 960 megawatts to power the grid — and Amazon’s data centers.
No timeline for construction or operation has been announced for the facility, which Amazon says “could” create 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent roles. The facility in Indiana is targeting to build 12 Xe-100 SMR’s, an advanced (but unproven) reactor that’s still undergoing development and licensing. These reactors can be cooled using either air, water, or a hybrid solution of both, which Amazon says should allow them to be deployed in water-constrained regions without impacting water demand in local communities.
Indiana also happens to be home to a famously expensive and uncompleted energy project called the Marble Hill Nuclear Power Plant. It was abandoned half-finished in 1983 after $2.5 billion had already been sunk into it, and has been under continued demolition since 2008. Terms for Amazon’s agreement in Fairbanks haven’t been disclosed, so we can’t compare the cost between the facilities.
This marks the second nuclear energy project that Amazon and X-energy are collaborating on, with the collective goal of working with regional utilities to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity in the US by 2039. In October last year, Amazon shared an early preview of its first planned nuclear plant, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington. That project is similarly set to build 12 advanced reactors and create local jobs, but construction isn’t expected to start until the end of this decade.
Amazon is one of several tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, and Google, that are exploring their own nuclear energy projects to power AI data centers. Investing in energy grid infrastructure was also one of the commitments that Amazon outlined in a lengthy blog post earlier this month that aimed to sway some of the growing negativity around data center projects, though it’ll be many years before anyone — including Amazon — can reap the benefits of these new facilities.

articles.title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation, each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response.
Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT).
When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow.
In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (AWS EFA), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types, AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes.
We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.
Bi-directional KV transfer
Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router.
NIXL KV connector enhancements for bi-directional transfer
We extended the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) KV connector to let prefill nodes consume remote KV blocks, similar to how decode nodes already consume KV blocks that the prefill node provides. This is not a trivial change, because the two node types are architecturally different: prefill nodes compute KV representations for new prompt tokens and can provide complete prompt KV blocks. Decode nodes lack the capability (or efficiency) to generate complete KV representations and can only serve previously cached KV blocks. As a result, prefill and decode nodes still carry their own roles and logic for computing the metadata of remote and local KV blocks. The actual KV transfer mechanism (a NIXL READ), however, is common to both the P->D and D->P directions.
The following diagram first shows the existing flow in blue. The router sends the request to prefill node, prefill node computes the prompt KV and returns its block metadata, and the router forwards the request and metadata to decode node for the standard P→D NIXL READ. The numbered red path illustrates the bi-directional KV transfer additions: (1) decode node retains eligible KV blocks after generation, (2) returns their metadata in the streaming response, and (3) the router caches that metadata for the next prefill request. Prefill node then (4) checks the remotely reusable KV after it applies local cache matches, (5) queues an asynchronous receive when the reusable token count meets the threshold, and (6) performs a D→P NIXL READ before computing the remaining suffix.
KV-cache-aware router
vLLM includes connector-side support for bi-directional KV transfer, while coordinating KV reuse across conversation turns requires a KV-cache-aware router. vLLM GitHub provides an example proxy that implements the flow used in this post which can be adapted for your environment.
The KV-cache-aware router is a lightweight, stateful control-plane component between the client, prefill, and decode nodes. It maintains an in-memory mapping from the client-provided conversation_id to decode’s kv_transfer_params. The router stores only block-location metadata, not KV tensors, and obtains that metadata from the response stream rather than separately querying decode node.
The following diagram shows how the router manages KV metadata across conversation turns. On the first turn, the cache lookup misses and the request follows the standard P→D flow. The router then saves decode’s metadata from the response stream. On later turns, the router retrieves that metadata using the conversation_id so prefill can reuse KV from decode. It then refreshes the metadata after generation for the next turn.
Block retention TTL
Normally a decode instance frees a request’s blocks as soon as generation finishes. Under bi-directional KV transfer mode, it holds them for a configurable lifetime (decoder_kv_blocks_ttl, default 480 seconds) and publishes their location and expiry. The conversation’s KV, both prompt prefix and generated response, then stays available for the next turn. For a turn that arrives before the time to live (TTL) expires, prefill node reuses the KV. One that arrives later falls back to normal prefill. Because this TTL is fixed and not renewed, tune it to the expected time between turns to balance KV reuse against accelerator-memory usage. A natural next improvement is to extend the heartbeat-renewed lease to the decode side. A decode instance could then reclaim blocks as soon as a conversation goes idle rather than at the end of a fixed timer.
KV recompute threshold
KV reuse isn’t always faster than local recomputation. For a short reusable prefix, interconnect and coordination overhead can exceed the time needed to recompute the tokens. The kv_recompute_threshold setting, which defaults to 64 tokens, controls this decision. Prefill node recomputes when the token count to compute is below the threshold and pulls KV from decode node when it is at or above the threshold. Deployments can tune this value based on model computation time, KV size, and interconnect performance.
Performance data
For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B and GLM-5-FP8 models on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To emulate scenarios in which the prefill node has evicted its local cache or the router selects a different prefill node that does not have the conversation’s KV blocks, we disabled prefix caching on prefill node with --no-enable-prefix-caching.
Across both the models, turning on bi-directional KV transfer reduces prefill computation on multi-turn conversations, and the benefit typically grows with prompt length. With the feature OFF, the prefill instance recomputes the entire grown context each turn, so TTFT rises steeply. Qwen3-32B climbs from 158 ms at 2k to 778 ms at 24k, and GLM-5-FP8 from 500 ms at 2k to 2,334 ms at 20k. With it ON, the decode instance’s retained KV is reused instead of recomputed, keeping TTFT far flatter. Qwen3-32B rises only from 122 ms to 460 ms over the same range (about a 1.6x reduction at the longest prompt), while GLM-5-FP8 rises from 358 ms to 702 ms and runs up to 3.3x below the recompute path at long prompts. The prefill-duration breakdown explains why.
Bi-directional transfer adds a small KV-transfer time (about 30 ms to 130 ms for Qwen3-32B; about 29 ms to 110 ms for GLM-5-FP8), but the prefill compute it removes far outweighs that KV-transfer time. As a result, the total prefill duration with transfer ON (Qwen3-32B: 128 ms to 414 ms; GLM-5-FP8: 316 ms to 541 ms) stays well below the recompute-only path (Qwen3-32B: 153 ms to 744 ms; GLM-5-FP8: 500 ms to 2,331 ms). The larger GLM-5-FP8 model shows a bigger absolute and relative gap, since its higher per-token recompute time makes KV reuse pay off even more as models and contexts scale.
Qwen3-32B
The following chart plots TTFT against prompt length for Qwen3-32B, comparing bi-directional KV transfer ON versus OFF.
The next chart breaks the prefill duration for the same runs into its recompute and KV-transfer components.
Together the charts show TTFT staying nearly flat with the feature ON while the OFF path climbs steeply as context grows, because the small KV-transfer time is far outweighed by the recompute it removes.
zai-org/GLM-5-FP8
The same two views follow for GLM-5-FP8. The first plots TTFT against prompt length with the feature ON versus OFF.
The second breaks the prefill duration into its recompute and KV-transfer components.
GLM-5-FP8 shows a much larger gap than Qwen3-32B, up to about 3.3x lower TTFT at long prompts, because its higher per-token recompute time makes KV reuse pay off even more as context length grows.
How to run benchmark
To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA, follow the step-by-step instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how bi-directional KV cache transfer can reduce TTFT as an agent’s conversation history grows. In P-D disaggregated deployments, the feature lets prefill node reuse KV blocks retained by decode node across turns, reducing repeated computation. Configurable block-retention and recompute thresholds determine when reuse occurs. On a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, at the longest prompt lengths tested, we observed TTFT reductions of 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8. Results depend on the workload and deployment configuration. To implement this in your environment, use vLLM v0.21.0 or later with NixlConnector, enable bidirectional_kv_xfer on both prefill and decode servers, use a kv-cache-aware router, and follow the GitHub reproduction guide.

articles.title: Mozilla asks UK CMA to consult on browser choice screens now | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
Why is the CMA asking us to choose the furniture before the house? The UK’s search choice screens need browser choice screens alongside them
Mobile browsers are a key gateway to the internet for 56 million people in the UK. Smartphone users spend around half an hour a day in these apps, and opening a browser is the most common way they look up information online.
Yet most people are using a smartphone browser that was preinstalled and set as the default for them, without ever being asked which browser they would actually prefer.
Mozilla believes people deserve an active choice in the tools they depend on every day, which is why the latest proposals from the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) matter. We welcome the CMA’s plans to give people a choice of search service and are asking it to consult on browser choice now, so both screens can launch together.
On September 23rd, the CMA published updated plans that would require Google to show people in the UK a choice of search service on new Android devices, covering the default search app and home-screen search widget as well as Chrome. Search choice screens would also appear in Chrome on other platforms, including through a major update for existing users. Some AI assistants would also be eligible to appear alongside search engines.
The proposals are well designed, but solve only half the problem
The CMA’s mobile browser investigation found that preinstallation, prominent placement and default settings restrict browser competition. Mozilla’s innovative 2023 experiment showed that properly designed browser choice screens can help people choose a browser they expect to keep using, and can be an effective tool for giving people agency over their online life. It also showed that an overwhelming majority of people (98%!) want to see them.
The EU Digital Markets Act has since demonstrated their impact in practice. We welcome the CMA’s work on search choice, but people in the UK deserve browser choice too. Asking people to pick a search service inside a browser that most of them never actively chose in the first place leaves some of the biggest issues identified in the CMA’s own mobile browser investigation unaddressed.
The CMA commissioned user research on search choice screens to refine and improve the proposals it first consulted on in January. Providers’ positions on the choice screen would be fully randomised. Users would have to scroll to the bottom before confirming, and could “test drive” a search provider for at least a week.
The CMA has also recognized that search is changing. Its research found that many people were already using AI assistants to search alongside traditional search services. Under the revised, more technology-neutral eligibility criteria, an AI assistant could also qualify to appear on the search choice screen if it meets the requirements, including being able to search the web and attribute its sources. But browser choice should not be left behind.
Why the two choices belong together
- Less confusion. The CMA’s new research found that participants often confused browsers with search services and were unsure what their search choice would change. Mozilla’s research has revealed similar confusion. These findings support designing and testing the two screens together, with clear explanations of each decision.
- Less duplication. The CMA’s work on search choice can also inform browser choice. Developing the two together would allow the design, order and timing to be tested as one journey, helping to avoid separate rounds of changes and interruptions for users.
- Order matters. Nobody chooses the furniture before the house. Browsers have their own search defaults, which is why we recommend showing the browser choice screen first, followed by the search screen, with wording that makes clear these are two separate decisions.
The EU and Japan already show both screens
The EU’s Digital Markets Act introduced browser choice screens on iOS for the first time and brought browser and search choice together during Android set-up.
Browser first, then search, so the relationship between the two makes sense. In Japan, search and browser choice screens are presented on both Android and iOS.
And people are making use of the browser screen to select alternatives. In May, we reported Firefox is selected through a DMA choice screen once every ten seconds, with retention five times higher than for organic downloads. Other independent browsers have also reported substantial growth.
Choice matters more as AI moves into the browser
The CMA’s proposals recognize that AI is changing how people search. AI is also changing what browsers offer, adding to the ways they compete on features, privacy and user control. Firefox already lets people on desktop pick which AI assistant sits in the sidebar, and our Smart Window beta extends that choice to the model behind the browser’s own assistant. There are meaningful differences between browsers. AI is the latest example of why giving people an active choice matters.
When people aren’t offered an active browser choice, they may be choosing search and AI services within a browser someone else picked. One decision taken at the factory can end up shaping the ones that follow. A search choice screen gives people a say over their search provider; offering browser choice alongside it would give them a say over that first decision too.
Our ask of the CMA
We’re asking the CMA to consult now on browser choice screens for Apple’s and Google’s mobile platforms, so they can launch alongside the search screens. Apple and Google already offer browser choice screens in the EU and Japan. The CMA can draw on that experience and its own research to give people in the UK an active choice of both browser and search service.
Mozilla’s response to the consultation is available here.
